I was actually nervous to start this game. So many said it is worse than Human Revolution and having loved it, I wanted a sequel that could live up to it.
And imo, it did.
TL;DR at the end.
Let's get a few things straight, the microtransactions are practically nonexistent. You can easily play through the game without knowing they are an option. Now the cosmetic and one-time consumable DLC is pretty bad, but they are completely unneeded to enjoy the game in full.
Another large complaint I see is that the world in-game changed too much from its predecessor. After the Incident from HR, the world changing like it has is a very logical next step. We go from a technology renaissance to a world tearing itself apart and attempting to force an entire demographic into isolated areas. Everything becomes more negative, there is a lot more suffering, the world looks bleak, etc. Not to mention the game takes place in a completely different part of the world, I found it all very fitting.
The next complaint I hear is the fact that there is only two cities, while in HR you hopped from multiple cities around. Now, even though Prague is not the prettiest site to look at, is is overflowing with activity. Everywhere you go it feels real. Everything around you aids to the setting and nearly everything has a backstory. Everything that is there has a purpose for being there that makes sense. The detail given to the side quests and points of interest brings everything to life. I actually cared about a lot of the NPCs and their outcomes. And Golem City, while small (even smaller than Prague), still had a good bit going on that'll leave you shocked.
Yes HR had multiple cities, but they lacked this level of detail and depth. I spent hours just sightseeing and exploring in Prague every time I came back from a mission to see what changed and what the NPCs were up to now.
The gameplay is a grand improvement from HR. Everything feels cleaner, the new additions are more than welcome (in depth gun customization and experimental augs), and it feels good to play. There are countless ways to get things done befitting to your playstyle and unlike HR, that tended to make it hard to find resources to charge your batteries, we have biocells (a throwback to the original Deus Ex's bioelectric cell) that you can not only find and buy, but craft. You can still run out of them if you aren't smart with them, but they are a welcome addition. A major difference is that in this installment, most of the boss fights, save the last one, are mainly focused on negotiating and dialogue. If you want the best possible outcome, you gotta choose the right dialogue (very much like the end of HR). I personally enjoy these as it brings out more to the characters you are going against. It makes them more than an ememy. You can still fail the dialogue and kill them if you want, but it is far more satisfying to win a battle of wits imo.
Graphics are stunning and demanding on your rig. The upgraded models make HR look very dated and add to the submersion. I would recommend that you have plenty of RAM, 16 GBs did me fine and helps things run so much better than just 8GB.
Now to get to the story, we are continuing 2 years after HR with the world now questioning augs and if augmented people are safe. It has caused a massive divide with some events that feel eerily real, like they could really happen should we ever reach this technology to this level. At times, it is hard to take in seeing the fear and brutality from both sides of the coin. The world is most definitely in chaos.
Most of the story is in the details. I highly recommend taking time to read emails, books, and pocket secretaries. Stop and listen to the NPCs talking about current events or watch the news to really get a sense of what is going on (or what is being spun). Don't rush through the game or you are going to miss a core part of it. Do the side quests, go to points of interest, explore everything. The devs took the time to fill this changed world with tons of backstory, stop and enjoy it. It adds so much to the main quest.
There are a couple key points that will change things for your end game. Deciding to save one person over another has consequences. How fast you do certain things can change an outcome. Going to one place instead of another can affect you later. Even small sidequests and how you went about doing them, or not, affects how the worlds ends up in the end. Not every choice is this heavy, but I feel the right amount is. Every choice just about feels like it matters in some way.
Overall the story pacing feels pretty good. I do wish it wasn't as predictable as it is, but it still caught me off guard at some points. The final could have been more intense, but I wasn't too let down. Things are set up very well for the next installment.
Yes the game can be buggy at times, but no where near as bad as launch and the ramaining bugs can be worked around.
TL;DR Give the game a shot. It isn't as bad as people make it out to be and is pretty solid (still has a few bugs, but they are easily worked around). Just make sure to explore the world and really get into reading emails and such for all that backstory otherwise you are missing out.

Mankind Divided comes off as Human Revolution's lesser brother- that younger sibling that looks like his older sibling but can't do anything as well.  Since this is a direct sequel to Human Revolutions, there will be comparisons galore.
Pros:
-Expansion of augements over what you had in HR given pretty early in the game.  While these are these are neat to play with, but none are mandatory.
-Visuals are still good.  Environments seem a bit more drab in color.  This may or may not have been a deliberate choice to reflect the more run down mood of the locations.
-You still have the option to silently sneak past enemies to get to objectives or kill them all.  If it matters to you, all boss encounters may be ended non-lethally as well.
Cons:
-Much buggier than HR.  Crash to desktop every 3-4 hours, menu auto-opening after a certain conversation- continuously so you can't do anything, etc.  In comparison, I've done multiple playthroughs of HR without a hitch.
-Story seems a bit more stilted and lacking coherence.
-The game is shorter.  Exploring everywhere, reloading a lot to try different approaches to situations, etc, took about 30 hours.  At the end, you beat a boss, tie up a loose end, and then the game ends.  It really feels unfinished.  Like if you just finished the Picus segment of HR and the game just ended.  Um, hello?  I would like to carry on with derailing the plans of the Illuminati.  Not capture a pawn on a chess board and have the game declare victory.
Overall, a disappointment.  Skip it while its at $60.  Pick it up at $30 or $20.

I don't like ragging on games too much, but I believe this is an extremely poor game. It's way too late to write a review to warn people against buying it, but I can at least make the case for those who will look at it in the future. The gameplay is bad, because of a number of design choices:
The use of large areas that inflate the game time by forcing you to walk back and forth through them, that become increasingly empty and devioid of meaningful interactions the further you go into the game (said large areas are also often bland and anonymous, the art isn't much better than what you could expect from the standard RPGMaker tilesets, althogh the palette fits the mood and the urban environment are reasonably portrayed);
Game mechanics that are more suited for point and click adventures. perhaps visual novels or time-management games, that weren't correctly translated into a game using the RPG Maker engine. Often, you waste insane amounts of time conferming your actions/choices over and over again, the dialogue that is the meat of this game is served in minimal tidbits, the choices suffer similar restrictions, the "fatigue" mechanic is poorly implemented, since you just need to have some of it right before you go to bed, opening it to being exploited, the money-making is easily exploitable too, especially if one wants to save-scum (there really isn't a need for it, for the most part, although you might be screwed if you go to a new area without some starting money or at least food and you don't want to exploit the game);
A huge amount of choices you make seem to matter very little, you briefly encounter people and then you don't interact with them ever again, or just get a few lines near the ending. Considering most of the gameplay is bad mini-games, poor resource management mechanics AND choices, you'd expect at least this one to be explored in-depth, but you'd be wrong.
The writing is also bad, which is particularly jarring in such a narrative-focused game. The plot is set on having you go at your ex's wedding at all costs (that's the entire push behind the entire plot, that sees you struggle with your financial situation to try and get together enough money to get there and survive), but at the same time the story lets you re-affirm everytime that you are over him/her. The ending you get if you are consistent with this behavior makes no sense, though, as you are seemingly destroyed by the fact that things go just as planned.
The ending is the least of the game's problems, though, and in fact it at least embraces the theme that permeates the game about circumstances dictating a lot of what our choices actually are, the problem is that the writing is bad through the entire experience, and the ending couldn't possibly escape from that. The plot is a string of contrivances usually solved by deus-ex-machina or similar, obvious narrative devices. For a game that goes for a serious approach, and could be classified as a drama, having such unbeliavable/stupid plot points severely undermines the struggles of the protagonist, making the whole even less believable. I found the comedy in the game to be frankly terrible, but I am going to concede this might be subjective, I do think that regardless of that, it further clashes with the themes, taking the believability of the drama further down, as it pops-up whenever it damn well pleases it. The presence of the game's authors in the game itself is just icing on the cake, beating you over the head with commentary on the themes in the story (which you could argue are flatly stated early on anyway). I can say, without kidding, that I have played porn games made in RPGMaker and similar engines, that have more nuanced and interesting writing than this. I believe you need incredibly low standards to be okay with it, especially since you can't rely on the gameplay to entertain you.
The music didn't have particularly catchy or emotional tunes, I don't think it's terrible, but it's extremely forgettable.
I will conclude by saying that I can only assume this game wasn't created to tell a story that also had a message, but instead it was written because they wanted to express a message, and reverse-engineered a story to suit said message. The characters are there to serve one function and little else, and I honestly regret spending my life playing this game. I checked 3-4 endings, although there might be slight variations to each and even some I didn't see, but the staggering amount of repeated dialogues even in these put me off from trying another playthrough, so after seeing the ones I could easily get by reloading a previous save file, I am more than done with this.

This can be a very good game, depending on how you play it, as it is a very choice based game, and it's not just the ending that is affected by your choices, your gameplay is as well. This game has very varying gameplay, very great character choices, but it can be quite confronting.
Sometimes when you play the game you will be faced with a difficult choice, and what you choose will not only affect the storyline of the game, but also the gameplay. So for example, if you choose to work in a tofu factory instead of a meat factory for temp work. If you work in the meat factory you will get more money, which will help massively in the rest of the game, but the gameplay will be a lot more boring, as you cannot leave until work is finished. But in the tofu factory you can leave anytime you want, so if you get bored of the gameplay, you can leave, but you get less money overall, which may affect your game. Also making a choice may also affect your morality. If you make a 'good' decision, as opposed to an 'evil' decision, things will turn out very differently. If you deicde to do something, it might mean you cannot do another thing. You might end up missing out on oppitunities and experiences. So experiences require you to do boring tasks, while other require you to do exciting and interesting things. It's really up to you.
The character choices are quite good. You are allowed to play as a homosexual couple, an interracial couple or a heterosexual couple. Obviously you will experience different things depending on what you pick. The game will even let you be transgender! This is very important if you want to have your character as close to yourself as possible, or if you want to try and understand the situtation that others are in. It will not make you completely understand the complexity of another person's mind and experiences, but it will at least give you a chance to empathise. Having a character that it like yourself will (in my case at least) make you feel closer to the character and become more involved in the story.
Despite all this great stuff, the game is quite confronting in many places. This can be seen as a good or a bad thing. It can be seen as a good thing to make an impact and to get you more emotional about the story/game, but it can also make you feel very uncomfortable to play. If it does make you feel uncomfortable, it is just a game, that you can turn off, and leave for as long as you want, before you can continue playing again (if you wanted to continue playing). The game has some slurrs mixed in to the dialogue, and some harsh statements as well, they don't come up extremely often, but often enough to make a bit of an impact. I have probably not experienced all the harsh statments myself, as I have not done that many playthroughs, but be warned that if you pick a gay couple, a woman, or a person of colour, you might run into some slurrs and/or harsh words, so to avoid confrontation I guess you could play as a straight, white couple and a man, but don't feel obliged to. Outside of the character choices, you will still hear some words, but not as often.
This is a pretty good game, not just in the basics of the characters, the dialogue and the choices, but it is quite beautiful, even with the style. It also has some pretty good music. The storyline is the classic 'must get my lover back', but you can also choose to just ignore them and focus on yourself. The only big problem with it is how tedious it is to start a new game, as you need to click through a lot of text boxes at the start, but it can also be quite fun to replay, as there are so many ways to play the game.

Summary: "Always Sometimes Monsters" is a story-only RPG. There's no combat, no skill systems, no hidden item search, and the puzzles are for the most part optional. The story is about a young, penniless writer. It begins with the main character being evicted from their apartment, and on the same day receiving a wedding invitation to their ex-boy/girlfriend's wedding in one month's time. They set out to bus and hitchhike across the country to the wedding within 30 days.
For me it was kind of a mixed bag. I tentatively recommend it, mainly because I just love this genre of game. Most of the gameplay consists of exploring the three towns the main character visits, getting involved in characters and conflicts, and making choices to help or hurt them. The game contains a pretty large set of things to discover and choices to make, and I loved that.
Also, you can choose your avatar and their boy/girlfriend from a range of men and women of different races. You can play as a man or a woman, gay or straight. That didn't matter much to me, but I'm sure it's a selling point for some folks out there.
The main downside to this mixed bag, is that the game drags. You move at a walking pace around the map, with no option to run (none that I found anyway). You can't skip cutscenes, only individual lines of dialog. And you pretty much have to spend a decent amount of time on boring temp jobs to earn the bus money needed to get to the end of the game. This wouldn't be a huge problem if you were set on treating this like real life and just playing through it one time, accepting the unforeseen outcome of every choice and mistake. But with so many choices and mutually exclusive paths through the game, it implicitly invites you to play it again to see what would have happened if you'd chosen differently, or even just to back up to a save point if it turns out that a line of dialogue you picked means something different than you thought it did.
Even before I got into the game proper, I had to rewind through two excruciatingly slow scenes. The game is told as a flashback, so it opens with a scene from the frame story, and partway through that you have the choice to make the POV character shoot the character who's going to have the flashback. If you choose that (and of course I did to see what would happen), you get an early "Game Over" and have to restart from the beginning of this non-skippable cut scene. This is immediately followed by a scene at a party where the POV character chooses who to have a drink with, which turns out to be how you pick your avatar. If you don't realize this before you make the choice (as I didn't) you later get a chance to return to the start of the scene, which I did, forcing me through another annoying repetition.
Another minor annoyance is the game's level of preachiness. It's like one of those moralistic anime series where the main characters are warm-hearted and human but most people in society are completely depraved selfish monsters. This wasn't a deal-breaker for me; I just kind of took it with a grain of salt, as part of the fictional world the game is set in. But it would have been nice if some of the moral choices you were making were more two-sided, instead of clearly always having a "good" side and a "bad" side. Indeed, to get the happiest ending at the end of the game you have to, at one point, say that you are unqualifiedly sorry for every single thing you did that transgressed the normal rules of society, even if you were doing it to save someone's life. It's like Kant's categorical imperative up in here.
And then there's that ungrammatical title. I guess it's supposed to mean "All people can sometimes be monstrous". But the awkward self-contradiction of "Always Sometimes" just irks me a little every time I see it. At least the game itself pokes some fun at this, with a character in-game seeing it as the title of a book and puzzling over what the heck it means.
Lol, so now I've written a lot of details about what was bad about the game, but I'm still going to recommend it. If you like RPGs based on exploration and character interaction rather than combat, you'll probably enjoy this game. At least, the first time through. If you're patient.

This game is a perfect example of a love/hate relationship. I have had a lot of great times in this game. Over 1,150 hours on PS3/PS4 and I repurchased it on Steam as it was on sale.
I’ll be covering the GTA Online portion of the game since that's been the main topic for a lot of reviews for this game.
I’ll get right to the point. GTA Online is an absolute mess. On one side, you have a very fun game to play with randoms or with your mates. You can have plenty of fun blowing people up, doing missions and anything of the sort. I have only played around 70 hours on Steam as I’m typing this and I can assure you, as a low rank with little to no money, not a lot of friends on Social Club as of right now and not a whole lot of weapons, cars or facilities and bunkers to help me make money, it is still a load of fun to play.
And then there’s the other side. Obvious corporate greed.
Rockstar and Take-Two have made some rather sketchy decisions in the past and it has left a bad taste in my mouth in regards to how much respect those two companies have for consumers. Don’t get me wrong, companies need to make money. It’s how they get by. Unfortunately, Rockstar has been forcing their shark cards down their player’s throats a lot more recently, and as more DLC and patches come to reality, it becomes a whole lot more obvious.
As a long-term player, I don’t care too much in regards to their overly-somewhat expensive DLC, but people have been complaining about it, and for good reason too.
“You want those super cool cars? Do you want those really awesome bunkers and facilities that can help you make a lot more money? Do you want clothes? Do you want those really nice houses? Do you want a firework launcher? Want anything that looks even remotely cool in this game? Well, how about you buy our shark cards! They’re definitely worth the money you’ll be throwing at us, and we’ll even chuck in a bit more GTA $$$ money into your purchase, just for you! Or… you can play those really grindy missions. Those painful, overly-long unfun missions! You don’t want to play those for hours on end, do you? Nah. Give us money.”  -Rockstar.
That’s how a lot of people see this company as of late, and I can understand why.
I love grinding. Warframe is a perfect example of grinding done right. It’s fun, and it’s the core aspect of the game. GTA Online strives to do this in certain areas, but it’s noticeable Rockstar have been a lot more aggressive when making this aspect more obvious.
In Warframe, you don’t have to pay a single goddamn cent unless you want to. In GTA’s case, the grinding can get so bad for other players that it feels like one of the very few things they can do is purchase shark cards. Of course, you don’t have to buy them, but it’s like Rockstar is dangling a fishing rod in front of your face with a shark card as the bait, just waiting for you to bite it so they can reel you in.
But… you don’t have to buy any shark cards like I said. What if you just want to play the game without spending any money on microtransactions? What if you just want to have fun, grinding and working towards getting better at the game?
Well… welcome to my mindset. You can do that easily if you ignore all those expensive and gimmicky cars. If you generally do not care about the pressure Rockstar puts on you to buy shark cards one bit, you can have a load of fun. As a matter of fact, in my personal experience, grinding isn’t even that hard.
Yes, there will be times where your cargo will be blown up. Yes, there will be times when a modder will mess with the session you are in (although this has rarely happened to me). Yes, you will team up with incompetent people when working towards completing a certain goal. Yes, all of these things will happen to you one way or another, and it will happen to you a lot as you continue to play GTA Online, but that is apart of the fun that I have had with this game. You will have no idea what will happen in a dynamic online environment like this, and that is why I love it. It's silly, fun and chaotic.
What I am not a big fan of is Rockstar's anti-cheat system, but I'm not going to write about that as I don't have a lot to say about it, other than the fact that it is rather disappointing.
TD:DR/My conclusion? Read other reviews such as this one, watch videos, read discussion boards, help gather a better image for yourself before you decide on whether or not to buy this game to play GTA Online. Personally, I'd grab it on a sale, since it does get discounted regularly and the fact that it's a bit ridiculous to pay full price for a game like this. It's a fun game, just a tad bit flawed with a negative public image as of late.

By far the very best free game I've ever played.
The devs are very attentive to the freedback and needs of the players. If there are any issues with the game, they immediately (and I do mean
) investigate the issue. If an issue is found, they respond swiftly to resolve it. They're always happy to help players out with problems they're having, or even if they're having a little trouble understanding something about the game. (I know I've misunderstood a few things and felt like a complete idiot, but they never treated me as such.)
The devs have another game here on Steam that I believe they give equal attention to. It doesn't seem like they favor Time Rifters (their paid game) over Time Clickers, but I don't know for sure because I've yet to save up enough to buy Time Rifters.
This game doesn't even have a cash shop! There is absolutely no way to advance by paying real money! Now, if you play the mobile app (which you can link to your Steam copy via cloud saves) you can opt in to watch ads for bonus gold, time cubes, and weapon cubes (when the rainbow ball shows up) but it is
Don't want to watch a really short ad? No problem! Just opt out of the ad experience in the options menu, and you'll just get gold whenever a rainbow ball appears (which is all you get on the PC version).
This game is aesthetically interesting but also pleasing. However, it's not for all, and some machines might not like the beautifully animated fireworks and such. Well, you don't have to worry about that! You can simply adjust the options to better suit you and your PC without making the overall graphics quality go way down.
This is definitely one of those increment games where you'll have to start over a whole lot, but gain something by doing so. (One thing to note is that in this game, even the time cubes you spend will continue granting a bonus, so you don't have to save up a bunch and not spend them to get a nice big boost.) While I do tend to overall enjoy the genre, I often find the starting over rather annoying. Time Clickers does a fantastic job with making it a lot less annoying. Just remember to put points into starting out with more gold as you keep playing, and things'll be fine. (If you don't, it'll slowly become a miserably slow grind every single time.)
Better yet, you can completely reset your stats without being forced to pay real money to be able to and without having to completely wipe out or edit your save file!
The devs even give us small holiday events!
Time Clickers is
the best free game on Steam, and easily one of my all-time favorite games, free or paid for.
The devs have been doing a fantastic job and I very much look forward to seeing what they come out with in the future. I also very much look forward to the day when I get my hands on Time Rifters!

Dragon Age: Origins may be from 2009, and the graphics have evolved and improved a lot since then, but damn, this game is amazing in every way.
First off, since it's an RPG game, you can build your "hero" just the way you want him/her to be. From race, gender, background story, classes, and more.

You'll want to try out being evil or good, generous or selfish, kind or rude, it's all up to you. The choices you make impact certain events of the game, and the choices you make can have dire consequences as well. So choose wisely who to side with, and consider your options.
The negative aspect of the game, though, is that it can be pretty linear, and some areas are reused. The graphics are a little outdated, but it shouldn't matter. It still looks great with certain mods that can easily be implemented.
Overall I highly recommend this game if you love RPG and are looking for an epic story and fun gameplay.

The way that the characters react to you, depends on your race, class, and party accompanying you, and that makes you experience something different everytime. - The plot itself. (Uniting the Dwarves, Elves, Werewolves, Templars, Mages and humans to defeat the archdemon and end the Blight.)
- All of the side-quests.
- The  wide range of equipment, armor and weapons.
- The whole of Ferelden that you can explore.
- 6 Origins to choose from.(Which depends on the race you choose.)
And a few things that could have been better.

- The fighting mechanics and fighting animations.

After complaints of FFXIII's too linear gameplay, FFXIII-2 seems to be the answer to everyone's cries. In the beginning, you still get some of the "run to the yellow pointer" moments, but you can also take on various side-quests from NPCs to either find something or kill a monster. And once the game gets going, depending on what gates you open, you can have your choice of next destination. And you can take a break on minigame quizzes, chocobo racing, or slot machines if you feel inclined to do so.
The one complaint I personally have is compared to FFXIII's story (personally I loved it), FFXIII-2 falls a bit short. The time travel trope makes it feel a bit cliché, and I found Noel to be quite boring in terms of personality and back story. Personal opinion, but even if the story isn't your thing, the game is a lot of fun.
In combat, the ATB gauge and paradigm shifts are back so that will feel familiar. But with only two protagonists, the third slot is filled by monsters you tame. With all the tameable monsters out there, you can really customize your party to your needs, and you have to level your monsters up as well. I was a bit annoyed that neither Serah or Noel learned Faith/Bravery/Haste as Synergists so you have to rely completely on monsters to buff you on that front.
As for the PC port, the keyboard can be a little awkward with the more complicated constellation puzzles, when the camera gets a little wonky, but it's still possible, if not, frustrating. I've also had the game just close on me once or twice (guessing my laptop was overworked when playing this game for an extended amount of time). Other than that, I have no issues. (Note the DLC doesn't unlock until you beat the story once.)
Basically, the game is a load of fun even if the story fell short of expectations. The story isn't bad per se, but it wasn't great either. That said, the gameplay makes up for it. Still working on those final fragments.

Warning. This is a personal review. Everyone has their own opinions and Mine are just shown throughout this review.
If you did not play the first game do not worry you are not missing out too much.
HOWEVER
This game is much more open compared to the significantly linear FF13. I believe that is one reason why people hated the first game.
This game will use various tactics to keep you from progressing at a later point in the game which really will annoy anyone who plays this game. The puzzle challenges for example are by far the most annoying additions to this game.
COULD BE LIKE ANY OTHER FF GAME WITH A BOSS BUT NO. PUZZLE CHALLENGES ARE ALL THE RAGE.
Seriously, that crap made me stop playing. And sure I could go and watch someone do them, but I'd rather do it myself, especially seeing as my network connection isnt that great especially with video content.
ANYWAY other than the annoyances
For the good things so far
-RESOLUTIONS:
CAN CHANGE TO SOMETHING OTHER THAN 720p
-A lot of elements from the first game reappear, giving you some idea just how the first game went.
-A LOT of crap people hated in the first game is fixed
(Like, if the leader dies, it used to be game over, yeah no, thats gone now)
-If you have played Tales of Symphonia 2 THIS GAME FEELS SLIGHTLY LIKE IT
Well in battle that is. You will only have two playable characters, and other characters like Snow joining in, but not in the party as they are not of the same timeline.
-You will also be able to collect monsters to help in battle which is cool.
Oh they also troll you a bit by making the game look like an older FF tittle, (like with an actual level system) But its not.
-You get all DLC from the ps3 version included too!
TL:DR the game is vastly more simplified than the original, My guess is the creators saw how annoying the first game was and aimed to change it up somewhat.
The bad
-THERE IS NO LINUX PORT. STEAM TROLLS YOU.
-Character selection and world/timeline selection can be a pain to deal with at first and for some reason to me if feels like I'm playing kingdom hearts in a way due to Noels looks, however like all games you play for hours, you will get used to it.
-The AI has a mind of its own, screwing up story lines, in more than one way.
--Becareful how you talk to people, the camera may be in an odd position
-Grinding does help lots here, ESPECIALLY WHEN THE GAME TROLLS YOU TO TAKE ON BOSSES WAY HIGHER LEVEL INSTEAD OF GOING THROUGH THE WHOLE MISSON TO MAKE IT EASIER.
-Graphics options are available although limited. SE seemed to have borrowed the settings changer that was created for the first game, however I will say one thing..

>>There is no option to change the texture quality, so you WILL NEED A HIGH END PC FOR THIS GAME<<
-Even though its a PS3 Port, the game has a significant performance hit even on low settings. So if you played the first game, thinking you can play the second one easily, think again.
-The AUTOSAVE FEATURE WILL KILL YOU: By being stressed out, as for some reason steam needs to be not only online and active, but if steam gets disconnected, the game will LOCK UP DURING AUTOSAVE MOMENTS. Just keep that in mind if you have a faulty internet connection or you are playing during times where steam goes down for repairs.

Despite the horrible FPS issues, this game was worth every hour, minute and second of gameplay!
+ DLC included in purchase
+ More open than its predecessor
+ Moderate difficulty
+ The main protaganist Serah developes more than her sister Lightning did (protaganist of XIII)
- FPS drops are really horrible sometimes
- Serendipity is not that fun

=Story 7.5/10=
One of the weaker points of the game was the story. Everyone can agree on this and I'm no exception to that. The whole “let's save Lightning” angle felt forced from the start. I would have taken a game where we play as Lightning the whole way thr- Oh, right, that's what Lightning Returns is about. Anyway, a lot of plot points and major story elements felt forced or like they didn't belong. This didn't hold it back all the time, but it could have done far better.
=Art 9/10=
On the PC, this game is absolutely stunning. When you throw all the settings up to max and optimise your graphics settings, you end up with a game that is so beautiful you sometimes forget you're playing a game. Admittedly a lot of people have complained about FPS issues, but I felt that the way it was solved in FFXIII (Editing general graphics settings through my Nvidia Control Panel) solved the issue for me before it even became one. The game played in 60 fps steadily throughout the entire playthrough. If you're having problems, Google around and try to fix it before complaining. It's worth it.
=Sound 10/10=
Music and Final Fantasy are synonymous terms for me. Whenever I play any of the FF games, the soundtrack is the first thing I listen out for. What sort of instruments are we leaning towards? What sort of feel does this game want to give me? Every boss fight is unique, every average fight is energetic and every area has a theme that suits it perfectly. I've listened to the FFXIII-2 soundtrack more than enough times as I do other things to know how much I love it.
=Characters 7/10=
Admittedly the weakest point of this entire game is its character lineup. Why Serah? Why Noel? Why do I care about them? A lot of the twists towards the end felt both forced and pointless. The Goddess Etro wasn't even introduced in FFXIII and now I'm supposed to believe she's a big thing that's a big part of everyone's lives? No one else seems to know who she is, so it feels a little stupid. Whatever, it's no big deal. I would have rather focused on Hope and thrown a boomerang around, to be completely honest.
=Gameplay 9/10=
I don't like the way prior FF games handled combat. Sue me. FFVII was absolutely trash with the Materia system. FFVIII's Draw system was only marginally better. FFXIII's system made it so that some characters were only viable because they had skills others didn't. FFXIII-2's Crystarium does the same thing as FFXIII, but makes good on a few faults from its predecessor. Haste and Slow aren't casual abilities to throw around now, which were absolutely broken prior. Your bonuses from stacking multiple Roles into a Paradigm is better, meaning that swapping to 3 SEN's is now a really smart move whenever you see a charge up attack. This game involves more thinking than most people care to admit. For that, I salute you, FFXIII-2. For the record, playing with Keyboard and Mouse is so easy that it's criminal.

I've never seen a game where you watch the devs descend into madness (read: awesomeness) as the game progresses.
I played this for a few hours, wasn't too enthusiastic, and forgot about it until a few months later.
Big mistake. I'd stopped at precisely the moment the developers stopped caring about what a game was "supposed" to be like, and what they actually WANTED to.
One minute I'm shooting space cops in a clunker spaceship. Next thing you know, I'm going back to the drawing board and building spaceships that should be IMPOSSIBLE so I can blow up a galaxy's Parent-Teacher Association and bill them for Dvorak keyboards.
And it just KEEPS GOING. Forget "characters you care about"--most of the games you hear people say that about don't HAVE characters. You know what's a REAL character? A REAL character says "this mission has been boring, let's pretend the mission objective was to get in the arena anyway" because THAT'S WHAT YOU WOULD DO IF YOU HAD LASERS.
The game opens up the hangar and you get bogged down in minutiae because you don't know what all those numbers mean--at first. A few hours later, you're saying stuff like "okay, I'll make this ship out of paper but it'll be REALLY FAST, and by going fast it recharges shields to cover the duct tape armor, but I'LL NEED TO ALWAYS BE FIRING so my generators don't overload because then the enemy could tap me and make me EXPLODE."
Since the ships at the beginning suck, they're not much fun to pilot under the game's Newtonian physics. It's like if all you knew about Gran Turismo was driving a 1970s Volkswagon. But after a certain point? Hotrods with lasers, baby. Hotrods with DRILLS and SPACE MACES YOU SWING AROUND. You want turrets? How does 19 TURRETS, 1 SPACESHIP sound?
I'd say something trite like "the game goes NUTS after a certain point and I love it forever, forgive the weak start" but you know what? No. NOPE. Even at the game's worst, before the plot and ship customization gets great, it's still only as 'bad' as pretty much any game out there. I want you to sit down and ask yourself: is this other game I'm going to play gonna give me a SPACE MACE?
No, no it's not. Ain't happenin'.
Toss that 'other game' out the airlock. Now.

I first heard about Ronin when the developer of Gunpoint showcased it and described how he was happy someone was finally using his ideas:
Ronin is definitely not as polished as Gunpoint (it's easy to compare the two but they are quite different games). Ronin doesn't have clever and funny writing - but the writing is concise, subtle, and conveys a revenge story with hints of the protagonist's backstory. Ronin doesn't have Gunpoint's clever save system, but the checkpointing is pretty good and generally not frustrating. The load times off my SSD feel a bit long but are tolerable.
The interface is pretty terrible. The menus are fine - you often have nothing selected and have to move down to select the first item (whatever). The bigger frustration is the upgrade screen where you cannot tell what you have selected and you have to move diagonally to get between adjacent rows. Maybe it's fine with a mouse, but it's a mess with a gamepad. At most, you upgrade every two missions so it's not a big deal. The biggest problem is the controls.
The controls are wonky and sometimes you can't slip into turn-based when you want (swinging through glass especially when an ! is caused) or it leaves turn-based when you don't want (last enemy lost sight of you and now you're sailing through the air and missed your ninja rope. The button prompts for abilities are positional which should make it easier to anticipate, but instead makes it harder to use muscle memory (I did as sequence on the last level 20 times and I think the button prompts changed depending on my vertical position). This mix of uncertainty about turn-based means a lot of dying because you're trying to be quick with your inputs but you don't actually know what button to hit (lots of hitting A to kill a guy, but instead you retract your ninja rope).
Despite it's flaws, Ronin is a fun and innovative action game. You feel like a badass when you clear a big room of bad dudes. The tutorial does a good job teaching you how the game works and a lot of the level design hints at ways to approach problems (obvious single dude who can be taken out with stealth kill or swing through glass).
I've read that some people think the sword throw/recall skill is a required first purchase, but that tree was my last choice, so I guess the upgrade tree gives you meaningful choises about how you play the game.
Some of the levels were tough and the last level felt like a third of my playtime (I retried so many times), but finishing my revenge story was very satisfying. Definitely worth playing.

FF13-2 tries to fix what FF13 did wrong, and mostly succeeds.
Now you can freely travel between all unlocked locations, interact with NPCs, choose what to say (through this wont have any significant effect on the story). Combat got some nice tweaks: you can change leader in a middle of a fight and add almost any monster in your party. But the best part - developers stopped to threat players like idiots and you'll get access to most features almost from the start.
Ofcourse there are some bad things. Enemies appear randomly, just like in classic FF games. And some side quests (for example gathering data on all existing monsters) are practically unfinishable without reading guides (another trademark of classic FF games).
Story starts exactly where 13 ends so playing prequel before 13-2 is a must (there is a "beginners primer" in the main menu, but its hardly enough). So, the story... one of the game's features is time travelling, and its even more confusing (at first) and even more epic than before. There are only 2 main characters this time (instead of 6 in FF13) so developers could develop them better and make player more attached to them. Also Caius is easily the best FF antagonist so far.
Conclusion. There are 3 games in "lightning saga", 13, 13-2 and lightning returns (13-3). 13-2 is by far the best chapter in this trilogy.

Most of the negative comments I read here are on the controls, inconsistent jumps and stuff like that. My only suggestion to new players is: hang in there! There's a really fun game waiting for you (my 15+hourse of gameplay for a game that takes ~5/6 to finish prove this).
I had the same negative feeling at the beginning. I went on with the game, even though I couldn't get all challenges in all levels. As a result, I rarely got skill points, and this made later levels pretty much impossible to beat, hence my frustration. Then, the revelation: why not start the game from scratch, with all the experience I had gathered with mastering the controls? As soon as I did that, I found a much more rewarding game. What seemed impossible at first became a nice challenge, I knew how most enemies would behave, what really happens when you hit enemies while jumping and hooking (despite what the arc seems to suggest) and I did manage to get all the skill points I needed, especially some I had neglected on my first ru and that are instead of paramount importance (e.g., hanging unsuspecting enemies and the decoy). Skill points are REALLY important, so anytime you know you break one (e.g., the alarm went on) just load the last checkpoint and try again. At the end, I found myself really hooked, and played the last level several times until I got it perfectly right (there are two different endings).
If I have to complain about something, it's the story, or lack of. I mean, it's not bad, and you get the feel of it: a group picture clearly makes you understand you're on a revenge path. Anyway, you never get to know what triggered the revenge in the first place, and even the two different endings are actually very much alike.
That said, although I'd say wait for a sale (it's probably not worth 20 bucks), I do suggest the game if you're into a challenge, especially if you liked Gunpoint, with which it does have some similarities (but less than you'd expect).

Despite the fact I had tons of fun playing this game, it will be the only Prince of Persia I don't recommend, and I don't recommend it for two reasons:
First off, it's not a Prince of Persia game. I get that they were trying to go new character, new kind of story, but really for all the differences between it and the feel of the games in the Sands of Time series, (which this is supposed to resemble), it really just has success by loose association. The platforming looks similar, but feels completely different. Plus, there is absolutely NO way to die. You have a partner with magic powers who will use them to catch you if you fall, push enemies off you before they can deliver deathblows, and pull you out of slime. This turns mistakes into minor inconveniences, instead of a need to restart. In the Sands of Time series, you could stop yourself from dying, but every time you use the Sands means that there's one less mistake you can make somewhere else. In this, Elika has seemingly unlimited power. This means you get unlimited restarts. You go back to the last place with solid ground. The enemy gets back the last round of damage you dealt to it. I think every element of this game is great and that they were all mixed together well. However, at the same time, it didn't feel like a challenge in the slightest. Even the Warrior, who you had to button mash to defeat and if you didn't send him over the edge he'd send you through the floor, never once stood a chance because you could survive ANYTHING thanks to Elika.
On the topic of the Warrior, let's talk about the battle system. You had five main enemies to face, and some smaller soldiers along the way. The battle system was rebuilt around the fact you couldn't die. It was a fun battle system, but again it wasn't the free-form battle system I had come to expect from Prince of Persia. Yes, there were combos, but you really couldn't choose your own battle style. There were only two combos that did large amounts of damage: 4 sword strikes, or elika, elika, grapple, jump, elika, sword. Everything else was either there to push enemies into things, or the combos were just too short for damage to add up. Ubisoft could make a killing on a game based around this concept, but I wouldn't call it a Prince of Persia game and the system needs major refinement.
Now, for the second thing I didn't like about the game: Story. Until the final sequence at the Temple, I thought it was fine. The intro was a bit weak, but hey, not every game deserves a cinematic. However, this is Prince of Persia. Ubisoft has made the whole series around a theatrical experience, and then they suddenly killed it in this one. Again, I get they were trying to go new hero, new kind of experience, but, as much as I like to bash Call of Duty for not innovating, They at least know that people like to play games with the same title for the same sort of experience. They changed this one a bit too much from the Sands of Time formula. Anyway, back to my problems with the plot. Other than the intro and the ending, it was actually fine. You had four different areas to explore and you could do them in whatever order you wanted. The plotline was built in such a way that it didn't matter which one you went to first. That was nice. However, I had to restart the game at one point because of a thoughtless error on Ubisoft's part. It didn't matter which power you unlocked first. However, the one that you choose second pretty much has to be the one that lets you progress further into the same area you were just in. Which means that you have to face down one boss at a time, four, maybe five times in a row. They make him "harder" every time, but it doesn't make a difference because you can't die. I had to restart the game because I chose the wrong second power. The Hunter in my opinion was the easiest to defeat, so I wanted to save him for last. However, becaue I chose to fight him after gaining my first power, it meant I couldn't possibly get enough pickups from the areas I had access to to unlock the third power. This forced me to COMPLETELY RESTART THE GAME!!!
Now, I'm gonna try and talk about the ending without any spoilers. The whole game (when I played through the way Ubisoft wanted me to) had a pretty nice flow. You couldn't really get lost unless you found a way to skip cutscenes. So here's pretty much how it goes: weak beginning, good flow, good flow, good flow, good flow, mostly stable climax, panicked platforming sequence, then WTF? As far as I can tell I didn't accidentally choose an alternate ending. Your unnamed character undoes everything you worked so hard for the whole game, and it's not even like one of those "rewind" endings. If it was, I might not be so upset. This was an ending where he saves the world, changes his mind, and then ends it. Thanks a lot, Ubisoft! I thought this was supposed to be a reboot. How are you supposed to return to a world that NO LONGER EXISTS????

Great atmosphere, with the Joker giving constant commentary on what you're doing, he's always one step ahead of you so you're constantly playing catch-up. The arkham island consists of 5 buildings (medical, botanical, mansion, treatment, and penitentiary), as well as the sewer system. Most action take place in one of these buildings, so you usually don't have much open space. The rooms and corridors are beautifully detailed, thought.
The combat system is simple to learn, but difficult to perfect. While the combat looks really cool, it lacks a bit of variety. The predator, aka stealth, sections of the game, where you take on multiple enemies armed with guns, are perhaps the most entertaining part of the game. Too bad there's few of them. They also become easy once you realize the power of the unconcious enemy + explosive gel/triple batarang combo. The enemies feel too unaware, even on hard mode. They are never a real threat unless you get recklessly aggressive. But still, it's good fun picking them off one by one and have them running around in total distress.
I do wish the boss enemies were more interesting, they all just involve dodging attacks and throwing a batarang at the right moment.

First, no game in this series will be better than the first Deus Ex. That said, this game combines has the best world building of the series along with the refined gameplay from Human Revolution. The story isn't as outrageous as the previous entries. This is more of a Law & Order: Deus Ex. There's a toned down threat with a satisfying noir ending. The game play is the same sneaky/shooty as the series is famous for. If there's a goal, you can be sure that there is more than 2 ways to get there. If I had to nit pick this game, I would say that I was a little underwhelmed with the gunplay. But then again I went lethal stealth so I didn't really use guns that much in the first place. But you can spec your augs to fit any style of gameplay.
The world building to me is one of the best parts of the game. Cyberpunk has always been, to me at least, the plight of small individuals against giant faceless corporations or entities. Every detail of this game reinforces that Augmented people are not welcome and are feared/hated. There's cutscenes nearly everytime you get off the subway where a cop stops you to ask you for your papers. The message is clear: you are not welcome. Thy dynamics between the greater society and the marginalized augmented class are very prescient. Good sci-fi can will take a mirror to the harsh reality of modern life and reflect back all the♥♥♥♥♥♥we ignore or don't want to see. The world in all of its bleakness sucked me in and I enjoyed walking around the city and exploring the ins and outs of the different buildings.
**Minor story ending spoilers below**
The best part of the story is how toned down it is. Unlike the first few games the big threat isn't world changing. It's like classic Gibson. You are placed in this world and tasked not with making large sweeping changes but to simply figure out the conspiracy. As with typical noir, the world isn't really better off in the end. The story threat is gone, but life will still remain to be ♥♥♥♥♥♥. And that makes this game highly recommended by me.

I'll never forget when this game originally came out. Initially, there wasn't a HUGE amount of fuss surrounding the build-up to it. Gaming publications and sites were quietly wary about it due to it being another licenced game, but then the game came out and we all know what happened then.
I first played it right as it came out so weren't 100% sure what I was getting into. Within about 10 minutes, I knew there was something special going on here as the presentation was just fantastic. Following Joker as he gets wheeled into Arkham Asylum felt very different to what I was experiencing with a lot of action games recently, which had lost a lot of steam.
About an hour into the game, I then realised this wasn't just your bog-standard action game. Suddenly I was dealing with puzzles, hidden collectables, a gripping story which really drew me in and the now popular free-roaming gameplay which the Arkham series became loved for. There's loads of Batman villains in the game, including such classics as Riddler, Killer Croc, Clayface, Poison Ivy, plus loads of references to further villains. The Riddler challenges are one of the best parts of the game. He'll have you hunting for wind-up teeth, hidden Riddler question marks, and the best part is hunting for actual riddles which reference Batman characters from over the years.
The combat is simple enough in-game and you often find yourself taking on 5 - 10 goons at a time with ease due to the great range of moves on offer for the Bat. A combo system ensures you feel like a proper bad♥♥♥♥♥ and you#ll only ever die because you lose your flow and can#t get back into the rhythm of the battle. Basically, it'll have been your fault!
Graphically, the game is still gorgeous even now after 8 years. The locations never feel empty with all the clutter and props on view, the characters all look very unique, and the whole thing comes across very sharp. I'm not one for getting into the intricacies of graphical properties, and polygons, shaders, AA, frame rates etc. I simply boil it down to it looks great and carries out the function it's intended to.
Voice acting is carried out here with expert aplomb, with Mark Hamill especially standing out as always playing The Joker. With the exception of Harley Quinn, all characters sound fantastic and their voices truly fit the menace needed by them. Harley unfortunately is a squeaky annoyance who wouldn't go amiss in 'Singin' in the Rain'. Outside of the voice-work, the mood is set well with audio cues hitting at the right times and the ambience provided by a very fitting set of sound effects which always keep reminding you of where you are. Music is great, sounds like bintage Batman movie soundtracks.
The game provides a long first time experience for the average gamer, and can easily get a good few extra hours on top if you want to 100% it. Enjoy this enough and you'll definitely want to go on and try out the sequels with Arkham City being the pinnacle, and Origins unfortunately feeling a little stripped back.

Never Always Sometimes Monsters: A Review
A friend and I played this together and we honestly have no idea where to begin in describing this. The prologue was interesting, but the segue into a flashback (which coincidentally takes up almost the entirety of the game) was jarring and awkward - a theme that the game would be sure to carry through to its bitter end. Selecting and naming both our character and our love interest was nice, but everything was downhill from there. From polarizing, bioware-esque decisions to repetitive, repetitive, REPETITIVE gameplay, ASM really had us gritting our teeth and desparately scraping humor from anything we could.
There were some genuinely funny moments and interesting concepts, of course, but they were very, very small parts of a game that would rather put its own developers in it and then punish you for robbing their smug, stupid faces. As other people have pointed out, ultimately none of your choices matter, nor do your resources, which robs the game of any sense of accomplishment for completing its purposely monotonous tasks. Every minigame in this game is about as fun as polio and we are definitely worse people for having played them.
Even if all of that could be set aside (which it can't, to be absolutely clear), there are so many minor ♥♥♥♥-ups that really show how little effort anyone involved in this game really put in. Have pizza pockets? Hope you microwaved them at the very beginning of the game, jerk, because you will have no other opportunity to eat your perma-frozen cheeseblock over the next month. Someone gave you work gloves as a reward for a job well done? May as well shove them up your nose for all the good they'll do you. Make it to San Verdano with time to spare? Don't worry - the bachelorette party will just take ELEVEN DAYS to get things back on track. I'm not kidding when I say that we've seen better games come out of 24 hour game challenges than this tripe. As for the typos - the occasional typo is understandable (hell, I'm sure there are a few in here, but I'm not making a game I expect people to pay money for), but many of the typos in this game could have been caught with a simple automated spell check, for ♥♥♥♥'s sake. Get your act together.
Many people have said that this is a game about narrative, and I don't blame them - the narrative, no matter how absolutely threadbare and bland, is a much better thing to cling to than the gameplay itself. That being said, the narrative has been banned from being translated into any other language for fear of violating the Geneva Conventions by initiating a memetic attack on a foreign nation. Most of the narrative is defined by you, but only though questions that are asked by other people, leaving you to wonder if your character is lying out of their♥♥♥♥♥or if this is actually how everything went down. Sometimes a dream sequence will follow one of these decisions to confirm that it is true, but often you're just left wondering what the significance of your response was. Nothing. It was nothing, to save you the trouble of wondering. It could be argued that this is intentional - our narrator could be unreliable, after all - but that would take talent and there is clearly none to be had here. More often than not, the most important decisions of the game are made for you. Did we want to steal our best friend's girlfriend? Absolutely not. We saw where things were heading and tried to avoid it, but we ultimately had no choice in the matter. For a game leaning so heavily on its narrative for substance, it was lacking.
I cannot in good conscience recommend this game to anyone. To quote the game itself, "I've heard some long and pointless stories in my life but this one takes the cake!"

There's a lot to be said about the Final Fantasy XIII series of games and a lot to debate about. Some love it. Some hate it. If you dig your RPGs to be a little more action-oriented and faster paced, XIII-2 will be right up your alley (after you play through XIII first as this is a direct continuation of that story line.)
For a game from 2012 built for hardware from 2006 it's a pretty game. Sadly, concerning the graphics/performance of this title is my big, and only, gripe: the PC version is not well optimized and has some pretty wacky stuff going on.
You'll notice that the features of the game specify that the title sports a 60fps framerate and that's technically true, but misleading in how one would expect. First of all, you're going to need a decently beefy rig to play this game smoothly at 30fps due to the pitiful optimation for PC. Second of all, yes, you might hit 60 fps here or there, but the internal engine applies restrictive frame limiters at multiple points so don't expect that frame rate to stick.
Any cutscene shot that focuses on Noel runs nice and smooth at 60. Shift to Serah or any other character? Hard drop to 30. Running around the map at a nice 60 before it loads a new area and you've got another drop. Battle start? Drop to 30 until the victory animation, then snap back to 60. My system is not being taxed, mind you, it's just how the game operates, which is disappointing. XIII did not have this problem on my end (save for some cutscenes that were hard-limited to 30 fps here and there).
The soundtrack is amazing - wide variety of styles and genres. There's plenty of tracks that hit the right emotional beats to go with the story and lots of great blood-pumping battle tunes to get you into the fight, ready to take on the world.
The story is great, not entirely needed as a follow up to XIII as it feels pretty shoe-horned in to make some more money, but it's serviceable and enjoyable. It's nice to play as the damsel in distress from the first game and Noel is a good companion and a welcome addition to the cast.
Fun RPG, great experience, and while far from being the PC port it could have been, it is the superior version to the console editions.

I have played this game a lot across three seperate platforms. PS3, Xbox 360, PS4, and now PC.
So, up top, I do not recommend you buy this game if you're just playing multiplayer. I played the multiplayer a lot on console, and I can't say it's worth it. I've also read plenty of stories about Rockstar's awful Anti-Cheat system that takes money from innocent players, so no, I don't believe you should get this game for the multiplayer.
The singleplayer is a different story. Everything from the writing to gameplay is nearly perfect. The main three characters are funny psychopaths that you somehow end up liking, and the gameplay between the three really does feel different. Each one has different skills, different houses and different vehicles, and they're all great.
The story is a lot of fun, and can be pretty emotional at times. Most of the famous Heists are really amazing, definitely some of the best heists in video game history.
I played this game with a Duelshock 4 controller, but I did play about an hour with my keyboard, and in my opinion, the keyboard controls suck. I would recommend playing with a controller.
That's all you need to know. Didn't talk about the flaws because there really aren't many of them, but even though the game is amazing, the price is very steep. Wait for a sale if you don't think it's worth the $75 USD.

And it ruined me as a person.
Many interactive story-driven adventure games draw emotions out of me, and in those games it feels like each decision I make affects the story.
In Always Sometimes Monsters, the story constantly forces its way into the darkest parts of my consciousness, tears it to shreds, picks out the parts it wants, then obliterates what's left as it makes me question life itself.
I've never come across a game that pushes one's morals
beyond their breaking point, a game whose story is so decision-based on what
- the player - believes in, a story so immersive is an absolute must-have.

TLDR: Do not get fooled by a price. You could easily find more enjoyable games and with more content via the Internet in a form of flash games.
Details:
0 - 2 minutes of playtime - Wow, this may be good!
2 - 5 minutes of playtime - Dying and destroying, dying and destroying...
6 minutes of playtime - Oh, this is getting boring. Shooting over and over again...
7 minutes of playtime - No, I can not stand playing this any longer
+ Graphics looks are unique and somehow nice.
+ Concept seems to be good, it did not work here though.
- No tutorial or any tips or explanation of what the game is about - simple "click here to play" and nothing else.
- No setting options other than a single thing: "Press "F" to toggle Full screen". This actually gave me a lot of laugh - I think it was supposed to be a joke or something.
- However graphics look nice, as for a person with bad eyesight, it was really difficult to see anything. All these shooting, crashing boxes, tanks and other things were floating around making everything a big mess. Everything was hard to be seen.
- Only one basic vehicle/tank available to play, NO starting options or customization.
- Gameplay is extremely boring already after few minutes of playing - it is just holding left mouse button and using keys to move from time to time to pick up some upgrade. I was aware of bombs which could be used with RMB but I have used them twice only - nothing special.
Summing up - eventhough TeraBlaster is cheap (especially while on sale), it is completely not worth buying. Go find some free flash game on the Internet and have much more fun!

The Way Of Life is a free to play, first person, indie game currently in early access as I'm writing this review. It is an instanced adventure game where you play as 3 characters: a child, a business man and an elderly gentleman. Today I decided to give the game a shot in its current state and I have to say, even with the small amount of playable content available, I feel it has a really interesting story to tell.
The first thing to remember is that this game is completely free. The developers aren't forcing potential players to pay any money for the game although they do mention a few times that if you're interested in helping to crowdfund the final product, you can do so here:
From the moment I laid eyes on this game I have been in love with the art style. The minimalistic theme works especially well with the type of feeling the developers are trying to deliver with their gameplay and it genuinely makes spending time in this game's world very relaxing and atmospheric. It should also be mentioned that the designers of this game were able to pull off this art style for a number of different moods. For example when you're playing as the old gentleman, the game becomes greyscale and gameplay becomes more lethargic, the camera less easily controlled, whereas when you are the child you'll find yourself in colourful environments, able to look and move far more responsively. Small touches like this help to create a far more immersive experience for players.
The Way Of Life's actual gameplay content is lacking. There are only a few scenarios and some  of these areas feel kind of stunted and unpolished. I also feel that the way you transport between levels, whilst seemingly clever at first with the use of non-euclideon looking spaces, is kind of blunt. One moment you're immersed in a wonderful world, finding out all about the character you are currently playing as, the next you are standing in a white room, surrounded by a volley of doors. Jarring to say the least. Another noticible issue that the game's text feels inconsistently written, as if the text was briefly translated from another language into English. On a more positive note, the way the developers expressed the credits to the game was quite unique, dedicating an entire room to a modelled version of each member of the team. When each member is interacted with, their team roles are displayed.
But what is this game trying to do? What is the purpose of this game? According to the developers, this game started as a project for a 48 hour Game Jam where the developers had 2 days to throw together any type of game they could based around the topic, "We don't see things as they are, but we see them as we are." This says a lot about the game and the topic really shows throughout a playthrough. As well as learning about your character and how he feels, you are also learning about yourself as a person. The game often allows you to decide what to do in certain situations and no matter what you decide the game always tries to justify your position on the situation so you never feel like you made the "wrong" choice.
Audio wise, this game neither great nor awful, you will find nothing particularly groundbreaking here. The music is very relaxing to listen to but in some situations it felt somewhat like psuedo music that didn't really fit the situation. Without spoiling any story plot I will say I found it rather concerning that there was cheerful music playing during a serious case of domestic abuse. Thankfully this only happened in a couple of instances, for the most part the audio felt very natural and added to the game's minimalistic and relaxing atmosphere. As a whole, I feel that the music does remain true to the rest of the game's minimalistic identity.
This game performed perfectly on my GTX780 never once dropping below 60 frames per second which is quite impressive for an early access game created in Unity Engine. I should also note that I played the game on the maximum possible graphics settings with a resolution of 1920x1080. Although there is no in-game options menu the game comes with Unity's standard video settings menu before the game launches.
Overall, I feel that this game predominantly succeeds in what it has set out to do. Obviously it isn't anywhere near finished yet but assuming the developers continue along their current path I must say I have very high hopes for this game. The game has already succeeded in creating its own identity and is absoultely captivating to look at. The minimalistic style of the game and non-intrusive yet conspicuous UI features fit together fluently and create a wonderful atmosphere that will provide you with the desire to explore. Whilst the audio in The Way Of Life isn't winning any awards, it isn't debilitating the rest of the game either and fits the game's atmosphere. The hour of content that the developers have released was genuinely enjoyable and I really hope that this game is able to fulfil its potential. It is definitely something I will be keeping an eye on and I do highly recommmend that everyone follows this game's progress so that they may play the complete experience when finished.

Played through it once using a wireless Xbox 360 pad, this PC
on Normal difficulty and collected everything in the story mode.
The game is a fantastic execution on making you explore the island of Arkham Asylum in the DC comic book world of Batman, specifically the 1992 animated series by WB Animation and a lot of the voice cast reprises the roll in. But I will only call the game good since it does have a few flaws.
First flaw is the character redesign of a few villains namely Harley Quinn and Poison Ivy. The skimpy, titillating outfits are blatantly there to pander and it does mean they distract from the experience. Also the characters would fit in better with the artwork used in the character sheets, must have been someone in Eidos Interactive that pushed to pander to teenagers. Just a small, personal gripe.
Secondly the controls. I hear they improved them in Arkham City, while also lowering the quality of the story and going open world with the game is a bit weird for the good execution of a 3rd person 3D Metroidvania with Beat ‘Em Up combat in an Action Stealth game, more on that later. First of all, too many commands are on the A button on the gamepad including running and double pressing for a roll dodge, climbing, jumping, descending while hanging; you see my point. Why running couldn’t be done on by default rather than a perpetual press is an odd and unwieldly choice, and makes less sense than the RB+A for sprinting in Assassin’s Creed 1. Otherwise the movement does well, except the off time the game becomes a comedy and Batman stands on some slight bit of geometry protruding from the wall, like he has solid ground under him. Stealth is done well, even if the line of sight basis means it can’t get more complicated than not getting spotted.
Thirdly the combat. This was improved in the later sequels no doubt. My main gripe being it largely devolves into a first try through of Simon without the full prompts shown; or in other words it’s basic. Not helping are the hordes of goons you have to take care of. More so when guns, electric rods and knife wielding maniacs get involved and becomes a chore.
Fourth are the boss fights. Mainly going back to the combat they involve contextual use of a battarang and dodging nearly after so the Venom filled behemoths deck themselves on a wall and you beat them down until they recover from the confusion. With the hordes of goods it becomes tedious. Few boss battles are different, a good example is Poison Ivy’s one, but even then becomes repetitive soon after halfway through. Killer Croc is an area boss fight with failed potential. Victor Zsasz is largely a tutorial and is left forgotten soon after the 2nd time you tackle him. Scarecrow has a unique premise and is the one executed the best with well-planned interludes between them. The Riddler is an interesting take on an optional boss in the background you have little way of interacting with. The Joker is done well, even if the final battle deflated it majorly. Also can I please ask for mid boss fight checkpoints?
Fifth. It became obvious to me the game was a tech demo for PhysX and the then Ageia PPU showcase, even if mid development they got bought out by nVidia. Even if turned off, the game still has to run basic PhysX on the CPU and in a certain section where you need to detonate 2 walls the framerate dropped to 20fps. Otherwise it was a mostly 62fps, the game’s cap. Being a DX9 game it doesn’t use all the resources well so unless you have an nVidia card it will not look or run as well. Yes on Radeons it doesn’t look all that well with textures not being the right colours or the game stuttering because of CPU overhead issues, no thanks to PhysX. The games engine also has texture pop-in issues.
Also I forgot to mention the walking talking segment in this game might have started the trend with them. Just to be fully honest: I do not like them. Give me full control and not waste my time.
As a whole package the game is still something I recommend with at least one playthrough just for the experience. I’d score it a 15/20. Has a lot of issues, but still has enough to engross you.

This game is something else. Now, I prefer Arkham City over this one just a little bit, but seeing as how this game started it all, it makes sense to review this one first.
Arkham Asylum is the superhero game that all superhero games wanted to be but none succeeded at. Diverse gameplay? Check. Smooth gameplay? Check. Both of those at the same time? Check. Appeal to classic fans? Check. Appeal to a wider audience? Check. Tons of hidden content, easter eggs, and references througout the entire game? Check.
I mean, I just can't praise this game enough. Before this game was released, superhero games were targeted at niches, mostly children and hardcore collectors. They didn't have to be good, you just had to get the player excited that they were going to be playing as their favorite superhero. Arkham Asylum changed that. It appealed to a much wider audience, ranging from the comic enthusiasts to children to fighting game lovers to fans of Batman Begins and The Dark Knight. It has dark tones taken from the Dark Knight trilogy (at the time just the first 2 movies), and I know that the Dark Knight took those tones from several comic series, but that doesn't really matter that much to cinema lovers.
Anyways, it also has a great combat system that is super easy to learn, but hard to master. Fights feel great, and it's really awesome that you can use your gadgets during them. Stealth sequences are by far the best I've seen from any video game series. You have multiple strategies you can use, and for most of these levels, none of them are wrong. You can bash your way through, or be patient and isolate individual targets, or use your gadgets to throw off the enemies and take them out that way. It's just really cool how you can always try out a different strategy in the next room, and the game still feels the same. I personally would rate the stealth gameplay in this one slightly higher than Arkham City, because to me in City it feels like you hit someone, and then run away and wait. But in Asylum, it feels like you're expected to "hide" more, almost feeling forced to stay within arms reach of danger. Now, for indoors this is probably because I had the experience in Asylum to know how to play better in City, but as for outdoors you literally just go hide on a billboard until the enemies stop caring that their buddy just passed out.
Story is great, and in my opinion it's simply because in my opinion it feels like a comic book. All of the other games in the series have this effect too, but Asylum executes this the best out of all of them. It has a consistant feel and style in the visuals, the story feels like it was taken right out of a comic. It's just a really enjoyable experience.
Overall, I would recommend this game to anyone. I'm mainly a fps and rpg player, but I was raised on Zelda, so 3rd person action felt great to return to. Play it for the story, play it for the gameplay, play it because it's just fun and feels good. The experience is good on both controller and keyboard, but I personally prefer the keyboard for a lot of reasons. If it's on sale, don't hesitate to pick it up. This is one of the few games I've run into where regardless of how skeptical you might possibly feel at first, everyone I know who's played it has been sucked in right away, myself definately included.

A few weeks ago I stumbled upon the clicker/idle/incremental genre. AdVenture Capitalist hit me, and it hit me good. Now I found an even better one by the name of Time Clickers.
In similar games you will likely run into many, many brick walls - which will have you either buy real-money upgrades or quit that game for good. Time Clickers also has its brick walls. But you gain power aka damage fast enough to overcome them after the next few resets. In fact, it has no real-money shop - or I just haven't found it yet. Another difference is that offline-idling will not really get you anywhere in Time Clickers. You need to actually PLAY this game. And after 89 hours I'm nowhere near "completing" it.
The final proof of how great this game is: It made me write my first review ever!
