The comparisons to Gunpoint and Shadow of the Ninja are inevitable, but that's more grounded in how Ronin presents itself. In gameplay terms, Ronin is less an action platformer and more a puzzle game built around iteration and execution -- think like a turn-based, sidescrolling Hotline Miami.
Crash through windows, take down enemies and plan openings to chop them to bits while dodging gunfire. Get shot down, return to the problem and try to take it from another angle or with another plan of attack. Repeat until you start getting it right. And if you want the tools you'll need to fight through the last challenges, you'll need to get through it with full kills, all civilians spared and unalerted, and no alarms triggered.
Ronin is a fun brain-tickler but not without its problems. Controls can be finnicky, espeically if you want to make an arc jump off a platform to a lower surface, maneuver around a ledge during turn-based sequences, or get a quick input during a grappling hook swing. The game plots the arc of your jump but doesn't adjust for loss of momentum if you collide with an enemy in midair. Shadow Strike (a teleport and stun ability) is also nearly mandatory in the late game but utterly trivializes a lot of early game content if you make a beeline for that in the skill tree. But overall it's not enough to take away the fun of Ronin. Pick it up on a sale.

Out of all the Prince of Persia games I've played this version is still my favorite. I love the art style in this game. Its not your everyday, traditional realistic 3D graphics nor the cartoonish 2D graphics you see. This has more of an artistic, comic book, 3D style to it.
There isn't a lot of battle like in the other POP games but I believe the story, characters, and artwork make up for that. This game has lots of parkour in it. But don't be afraid to fail. There is no true death in this game. If you mistime your job, fall of a ledge, or you run out of health, no need to worry. Your partner, Elika, will save you from falling and heal you.
Try not to get too attached to the storyline because while this was supposed to be a trilogy, Ubisoft cancelled it (can't remember the reason why). There is dlc available for the game but it only available on the PS3 or Xbox 360. The dlc is also known as the epilogue. This epilogue picks up right after the game finishes and sets the storyline for the second game. You can find the gameplay and cutscenes on YouTube.
This game is fully compatible with a contoller. I would reccommend using the Xbox 360 controller because that is what the game commands are shown as.
I played this game before I bought my Xbox 360 computer controller and I have to say that I was not disapointed with the keyboard controls. Unlike other games that have loads of commands to use this game is simple enough to play with the keyboard and mouse (I do not reccommend using the track pad to play this game). Once you know (and remember) which keys controls what command it gets easier.
I never ran into any glitches/bugs or any compatibility issues. I was running this game on Windows 8 with 1.3 GHz. Which surprised me now because when I went back to look the min requirements for this game is 2.6 GHz. Course whenever I play computer games I like to but the graphic settings on low. So even when the graphic settings where on low I still got beautiful graphics. I had lag/decreased frame rate every know and then but nothing that ruined my gaming experince (remember I was running this with 1.3 GHz when it was supposed to be 2.6 GHz)
Overall I give this game an 8/10. Give it a shot and try it out! It's a fun game!

- No limit Omaha is a nice addition, as you don't see that in nearly as many games.
- New, fresh characters.
- Win percentage is now added.
- The new bounty system.
- More TF2/BL2 items if you are into that.
- Unlike Poker Night 1, you only have to win the tournament now instead of knock a player out to get an item. This makes it more fair.
Cons:
-  Dialogue. The banter is funny but unlike Poker Night 1, there are so few lines. This means the lines get repetitive almost immediately.
- No Skip Buttom (bar some certain cases). This makes the repetitive dialogue even worse and slows the game down.
- The game puts you down too much, always saying how your move was stupid, which often turns out to be wrong or hypocritical.
- The AI is basic. Any semi experienced poker player will easily beat it. It has no pattern recognition and will go all in often for no reason.  It might actually be easier than Poker Night 1 (which also had a difficulty setting, which this game lacks).
- Like Poker Night 1, the game still runs slow. It is buggy; it crashes. The menus are still clunky and slow. This really feels like a rushed job; at least Poker Night 1 felt like it has some thought put into it.
- The little things - like when a oppoents hand is dead on the river, they acknowledge it, then the drum rolls and they look nervous for the turn. Your hand is dead, there is meant to be no suspense. I could name 10 more examples. These little mistakes makes the game development feel rushed.
- The "Win a showdown with only high card" bounty is pretty rough; too rough in my opinion.
- The "tell" and drink system is ok but I feel like it could have been expanded upon.
Summary:
- This game could have built on the Poker Night 1 formula and been a really fun poker game. Instead it feels like a useless cash-in that will have you bored in under 2 hours. Only buy it if it is on sale.

In the dawn of time, there was platforming. The demands and rules of the genre fit perfectly with the limits and possibilities of early gaming hardware, be it consoles or personal computers. It is a genre I have not spent any significant time in since NES and SNES so seeing the Prince of Persia in action at a time when his entire franchise is in limbo was an exotic experience in more ways than one.
The 1989 original has a reputation of a sadistic masterpiece of gaming design but in 2008 the Prince was an entirely different beast altogether. For one, the visual design greeting the player is eye-catching to say the least. Considering the age of the technology the essentials have not aged to any significant degree. The cel-shaded artistics immediately sets a mood of Arabian Nights - storybook fantasy that carries through the entire game. Character animations are as detailed as their appearances and the same applies to the milieus. All this is complimented by an equally lush orchestral soundtrack, so detailed in its themes that a 12-hour game has three hours of musical accompaniment.
That detailed wonder does not follow through to the story. An ancient evil stirs in its sleep so hero and heroine put him back to bed. The simplicity is understandable given the fairytale whole but it does not leave permanent impresssion either. It is the writing department that is also responsible for the games main weakness: the nameless Prince leading the whole show. He is snarky, cynical, whiny and arrogant without any wit or insight into anything and accordingly comes off as total male genital. Given how few people talk in the game it is all but insufferable to have to listen to him the most. Fortunately the female lead Elika shows more human warmth and expressiviness in the course of the story. She does not complain about her fate and shows concern for others and is accordingly the human counterbalance for all the ornamental fantasy around her. And finally she adds to the gameplay in several crucial ways so she is not an ornament herself.
Inside the aesthetics are the gaming mechanics and they complete the silky smooth whole. Level designers have clearly embraced the possibilities of the setting. Platforming in corrupted citadels and ancient gardens looks and plays flawlessly and it is easy to forget that all these places are designed levels. The Prince jumps, wall-runs, swings and more with well-designed controls that the series is famous for. Camera movements are equally controlled and only shows problems during some combat sequences. Yes, the Prince draws his sword when platforming fails but the melees are more of a condiment than anything. You lock into your foe and a combos-and-QTEs system takes over. It is not particularly challenging or innovative but all the visual pyrotechnics involved do make it worthwhile fun. This is complimented by the interesting system of enemies and their domains.
There are four domains altogether with one Evil Lieutenant ruling over each. You face each six times in total which means there is actual history between you and the badguys so the climactic duels are all the more rewarding for that. Another very natural and rewarding idea involves healing the lands after driving off the aforementioned undead thugs. The black and grey surroundings literally filled with corruption regain their color and life which in fact felt better in this context than any loot and XP system would have. There is also important business to do then, namely collecting light orbs which unlock new means of moving deeper into the corrupted realms. Using these powers of motion adds yet more flair into the platforming so there is sufficient motivation to pursue them.
About the technical aspects there are a few things worth mentioning. Firstly the game does not support the Steam overlay and there is nothing to be done about that. You also have to play with VSync on or remain stuck in the loading screen but the game worked with no hiccups otherwise. There is also no need to use UPlay which balances the scales a bit regarding the overlay issue. One thing that has drawn criticism from series veterans is the extremely forgiving attitude towards the player. Should you miss a jump or fall in battle Elika will save you and you only lose a moments progress. This essentially means you cannot lose. On the other hand losing this system would mean quicksave-quickload which never really works and concerning my platforming skills I was quite relieved by these saves. Suffice to say those looking to challenge themselves should look to other titles instead.
Sometimes you come across a game that breezes on by, never wears out its welcome and ultimately leaves you feeling refreshed and relaxed. And sometimes that is all a game needs to be. Those looking for a few nights or stimulating escapism will be rewarded by the world the Prince of Persia inhabits.

Batman: Arkham Asylum is a 2009 action-adventure video game based on the DC Comics superhero Batman, developed and published by Rockteady Studios. Arkham Asylum is the first game in Rocksteady's Arkham Trilogy. The plot of this game is great in the most part, sometimes a bit clicheic. Batman sends The Joker back in Arkham Asylum after The Joker surrounded very easily. When they arrive, Joker and Harley Quinn makes an ambush, freeing most of the Asylum's patients and prisoners also blocking Batman in Arkham Island. Batman must stop The Joker and secure the Island once again and that's the main plot. The gameplay is maybe the best part of the game. This game makes you feel like Batman! You have a large gallery of gadgets to use in the fight against the crime. And they managed to make exploring fun as Batman even without the Batmobile. The combo is one of the most iconic things about Arkham Asylum. You might see many, many games trying to mimic the satisfaction, mechanics and the fun of AA's combos *looks at The Amazing Spider-Man*. The game is powered by Unreal Engine 3. Great graphics as always, but sometimes it kinda looks ugly and a bit dated, even on high settings. This game's succes is so simnificant for Batman, this game started the best superhero games ever, it started a new Batman world and made Batman one of the best and iconic gaming character, besides beeing one of the cinematography, comics and pop culture. I can describe this game with one word: Fun. The gameplay is fun, the combat is fun, boss fights are fun, everything in this game is fun. We shouldn't forget about the voice acting. Oh my god...the voice acting is fantastic! Kevin Conroy and Mark Hamill are returning as the characters that they gave them voice for over 20 years! It's a pleasure as always to hear Hamill's voice as The Joker. Overall, this is the begining of a great game series and I highly recommend this game for any comic book fan and even to a non one, as an introduction to Batman and his many characters and villians.
PERSONAL RATE: 9/10

I'm a person who has started playing video games as a kid in 1994.
Because of this, I have been in a situation where I felt very sorry for all those very fun and very well made games which have unfortunately not survived the test of time, and no matter how good they used to be, playing them today just doesn't have its original spark.
Batman: Arkham Asylum is the first game that made me have that feeling of enjoying it IMMENSLY while completing it years ago, then picking it back up after so much time in 2016, and enjoying it just as much as I used to when I first played it!
It gives me hope that the experiences video games provide us will no longer be diminished by their age, at least not on a scale that matters that much.
As for the game itself - I am AMAZED with Rocksteady as a developer! There's so many obvious and also minute things that just scream QUALITY and EFFORT about their Batman series. On all levels! (gameplay, story, voice acting, riddles, puzzles, design, artwork, graphics etc..)
I'm recommending this game as someone who never even read comics or was a big fan of superheroes.
Their three Arkham games (Asylum, City and Knight) are simply put BRILLIANT, in my oppinion.
I really didn't enjoy Origins, and believe the absence of Rocksteady in its making is more than obvious.
All in all - one of my favorite games of all time. Thank you Rocksteady!

Linux Gamer - Ubuntu Mate 16.04.3 - I got this game 2x. 1st time was during the Early Access phase. Did not like it due to some bugs. Got refunded. Saw it on sale when it went into official release. Picked it up again to give it another shot. The graphics were and still are great. The music and sound effect are also excellent. Maps are well made. I want to like this game and really recommend it to others but I can not.
Here the main issues, I have.
- In your HUD or team score view you will be unable to see your ping, it is hidden to the players. The game does a decent job of putting you on a OK server most of the time but when it doesn't it's gonna be a few kills before you figure out you're on a bad server very far away.
- Team based matches must be even, otherwise it's going to be heinous for those will fewer players. Team stay uneven for a LONG TIME. Many matches that I've been in have had 7 players on one team and 3 on another - WITH NO FORCING others to switch. I've had to switch a few times manually because the game is so lopsided. There is just no excuse for this even older games like Doom (1993) and UT99 had auto-team balancing. I don't get why that is not in here.
- On team based matches, you team starts in a safe area. The map designs for these safe rooms are interwoven into your game. It's not like other games where you start off in a safe area but drop off into a map. When a match is close in points during team-death match you will find the winning team either staying in their safe room til time runs out and or coming in and out of safe room area taking pop-shots. Unless, someone comes all the way out and feeds the other team points (I've seen a few ppl do this because they are upset @ their team for staying in the safe room) you just gonna wait in-game til the match is over and then wait again during the vote and tally portion at the end of the round results. I highly suggest the devs to make it so that once you leave the safe room you can not go back in and/or if you are in the safe room after a certain amount of time - you get choke damage til you are killed and give those points to the other team.

Story and Universe:
I played this game for an hour or two yesterday, and Im already looking forwards to playing through the entire game. You start off the game by waking up with an artificial intelligence implanted into your mind (Nero) and that machine has the greatest sense of sardonic and sarcastic humor that I've ever seen. It has a  (So far) Captivating story set in a well built and fully fleshed out Sci-Fi fantasy universe, so if you're looking for a game with character and soul, this is a great pick. 10/10
Visuals:
I run a toaster of a laptop, but even so, I was able to run this game on standard graphics, and let me tell you, this game is beautiful. Whether you're fleeing explosions, exploring a sprawling junkyard, or assauling a space station, I sometimes need to stop and just gaze at the beauty. Yes, it's a 2D map, but it's rendered with 3D objects in a way that makes it look fully 3D without obscuring the gameplay. 10/10
Gameplay/Controls:
The only places I see negative reviews on this game are concerning the gameplay; Movement is controlled by turning in directions and having a unidirectional thruster and a directionless brake. Steering is difficult, but realistic... I personally found it refreshing, creative, and unique, but some people think it is hard to control and painful to use. I do recomend you try the demo to see if its a style that you like, but I love the unusual movement controls.
The actual combat itself gets rather hectic. Amidst the sea of torpedo's, tractor beams, bombs, plasma trails, lasers, and waht appears to be an inexhaustible supply of different weapons and utilities, it can sometimes be easy to lose track of what's going on in the chaos. Despite that, the combat itself is unique, varied, and captivating... provided that you like the movement system. I like the movement system and learned early on how to set myself in an orbit by hammering down the thrust in a constant turn to dodge and point towards the enemy at the same time, but again, this has a VERY non-standard movement system that dictates the way combat works. It takes some practice to learn the ropes, but the early campaign levels are easy enough that you have time to experiment and learn the ropes. Try the demo before you buy the game.
In addition, this game was made to be played with a game pad. Yes, you could probably do it with a keyboard and mouse, but I took one look at the controls and grabbed my pad, because this game was designed around a controller. I would STRONGLY reccomend that you try using a gamepad for this game, and if you don't have one, then MAKE SURE YOU PLAY THE DEMO before you buy it. 8/10
Price:
I paid 2$ for this gameon a steam sale. The normal price is 10$. I'd have ben happy paying 15$. People tell me that the game has an extensive single player campaign, the median play time for reviewers hovers around 30 hours of playtime. In dollers per hour of entertainment, that's excellent! 10/10
Summary:
Try the demo. If you can wrap your head around the semi-realistic inertia based movement system, then you'll love the way the combat flows around that. If you like a good story with well written characters, you'll love Nero's quirky addiction to PBC's. If you want a game that challenges you, or just a cinematic experience, the game has 7 different difficulty modes for all styles of play. (I picked the third easist; Sage (Looking for a challenge) And that's been a favorable ammount of challenge so far.) I haven't even touched the ship building and customization aspects yet because I've been having so much fun with the campaign and using the pre-made ships.
9/10
Post-Note: If you have problems launching or playig the game, check the troubleshooting part of the forums. I had a problem that prevented me from starting any levels that was fixed in three seconds by clicking something in the options.

--AI is awful and I mean ....awful : They get stuck on every corner (and since most of the game is made of "block like" tiles like Neverwinter Nights, it means they get stuck everywhere). Your companions keep shooting at enemies even when their shots are "blocked". The game becomes a micromanagement hell, even more so since you cannot have it pause every turn by itself (Like lets say BG2), you cannot chain command your companions and even if you do manage to pause every 2 seconds and give them orders, you have to check them one by one to make sure they actually are able to do what you told them to do because 1/3 times, they will get stuck or will just stand there.
--Combat is pathetic : Your party consists of only 4 members. That would be passable. even more so because of the bad AI, but you are always ...-always- pitted against 3-4 times that number. You may have your tank with its taunts, he simply cannot keep aggro of so many mobs by himself and survive no matter what you do. "Heal him then" would you say ....okay, that means out of my 4 members, 1 tanks (and doesnt do much damage), one heals the tank (so doesnt do damage). That leaves 2 members to be able to do damage. One will be busy trying to clear the mobs your tank aggroed. The other is at your discretion but lets not forget that while half the mobs are on your tank, the other "ranged" half is busy DPSing you from way out there. Unless you exploit the game's badly designed skills/magic or if you try to make "your own" char, and by that I mean a char you -think- will be great but isnt part of the game's almost forced mold, youll will have a hard time in every possible fights.
--Magic is OP : If you read any forums or posts about the best class or best party, you will only see "make a mage" or "mages are the♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;. Why?, because they are. Forget about the level 1 weakling of BG1 with 6 HP and 1 magic missiles. People solo Dragon Age on Nightmare with mages. There is basically no casting time (except with a few selected spells), an unending supply or Lyrium potions (which are basically your typical Mana potion) and by the first half of the game, youll have the most powerful spells that can clear about every fight in 2 minutes. Lets not forget that that can be said for the enemy as well. So often, my "normal" party ran into a room with a mage simply waiting for me at the far back of it, simply to throw an instant fireball right in the middle of my group (since there no way to create some sort of formation), knocking them all down, burning them with DoT, making them lose half of their HP ...and that is without the "fighting tune" even starting. I then chug healing potions long enough for the same mage to throw a chain lightning right after ....and finishing with yet another fireball after a mere 10 secs later because ♥♥♥♥ you.
--Lack of info on a lot of things : I equip supposedly an armor set (all chainmail I guess) I get an icon that says "Set item bonus" ....cool ....what is it?! ...theres nothing that explains to me what that bonus is. I have to google it...I alt-tab to do so, come back to the game...it crashes ...ah ok, its alt-tab incompatible.
My weapon says "Weakens nearby Darkspawns"....cool...how do I know that it works? I see no visual effect, I see no status on any mobs at all. Does it work, I have no idea...Again, I google it but this time, I make sure I already quit the game (because its 2010 and they cant make games alt-tab compatible yet, its too high tech) and from what I read, they havent implemented the effect on game release.
I have 3 activated (with upkeep) skill for my sword and board protagonist. Each one says about the same thing, being "Gives bonus against missile attacks" ...why do I have 3 of those, how great (or bad) is that bonus?! I dont see any numbers nowhere yet this is an RPG.
--Skill tree is badly designed : I want a fireball spell ...why do I have to go through the whole damn line just to learn it? What do I care about Flaming Weapons or the "cone of fire" thing? ITs Fireball I want and I have to waste 3 skill points for it?! I want lethality for my rogue yet I need below the belt and Dirt Throwing before I can get it ...but I do -not- need those. Even worse, I cannot respec (Unless I have the DLC or use a mod). So what I think might be great early on becomes useless later on so Im stuck with those choices. I once made a build using Morrigan that was based on Sleep/Horror kind of spells. It worked very well early where the Darkspawn are weaker but I noticed at about mid-game that the combo I was doing wasnt working anymore because the Darkspawn became more and more powerful and thus resisted my attempts to put them to sleep making my mage simply useless with no way to change that.
--Minor but still find it annoying : When even in BG2, you could make your mage awesome looking with its Robe of the Archmage and Staff of Power, I find it hard to believe that in a game from Bioware, with 3D visuals, Overpowered mages, they couldnt come up with better looking gear for mages. They simply look like giant♥♥♥♥♥♥♥with their robes and hats, their staffs looking like twigs picked up from a cow's behind.
--Camera is too limiting : I remember reading that you could play the game as a "3rd person" kind of game or go back to the original "overview" type especially in battle to facilitate giving orders and seeing the battlefield. I didn't play this game until late 2015 (so a bit late to the party) and not until after playing Batman: Arkham Origins so my perspective is naturally compared against my experience with the later title. Since then I've played all of the Arkham titles and am a big fan.
Arkham Asylum, being the first entry into the francise for Rocksteady, is the simplest of the bunch. The gameplay is far more linear and the graphics are noticeably simpler (mainly the cape). However, despite the minor drawbacks, if you've played any of the other entries in the series and enjoyed them, you will not be disappointed here. The gameplay itself is very similar and the story is great.
If you've never played a Batman Arkham game before, I highly recommend that you do and you might as well start here because it is the beginning of the story (well, in a way Origins is). I had been away from gaming for several years (far too long) and it was Arkham Orgins that pulled me back in. The prospect of playing as Batman in an open-world 3rd person environment was the initial grab. The game mechanics and the story kept me hooked. The fighting mechanics are so much fun but take a bit of practice to really master. I'm not an expert on the Batman comics but I understand that the story here pulls from some of the most acclaimed comic material. And execution was made wonderfully with some notable voice acting talent from 'Batman The Animated Series.'
It's the game Valve deserves, but not the one it needs right now.

This game is good, however I don't think it's the great superhero game to settle them all, but I feel it necessary to post, as a prelude to my Arkham City review.  I have owned this game twice, (got it on sale to re-play because I decided to give Arkham City/Origins the chance they deserve).  I don't know what about the game keeps me from "feeling it", but some reason, both times I finished, I just didn't feel like I had fullfilled the idea that I was Batman.  The voice acting is pretty good, the plot is decent, but more or less your run of the mill Superhero genre storyline.   There are a good variety of characters from the universe, and the fabled combat system makes you feel like you are kicking ***, ....once you are able to get used to it (which was admittedly a struggle for me for a little while, until you 'catch on', which might be part of the reason I was turned off of this game at first).  I think the main reason I can't get into this game as much, is just because the Asylum (to me) feels somewhat small, it feels a little claustrophobic and stacked on top of itself at times, with a moderate amount of backtracking, that can become repetitive, especially, when trying to finish all the riddles/trophies.  The color palette is for the most part, dark, metallic or rocky, I guess I was just bored with the scenery by the end.  However those shortcomings don't break the experience, and it is most definitely worth a playthrough at least once, but if you need to choose one or the other, definitely take Arkham City, hands down.

This is a great, unique little game. Your character is the ultimate glass cannon: she can kill enemies by the dozen but dies in 1 hit. This works perfectly as a turn based action game, since you can take your time and carefully plan your approach and feel genuinely badass when you pull it off... Since you know 1 hit is all it takes to kill you.
Yes, it's difficult. You'll need to 100% the missions to get skill points from them, which is an odd choice (though it does force you to learn new mechanics). The game could also use some polish, there's some bugs and awkward physics here and there as well as a couple of encounters that seem plain unfair at first. I can see why these issues might turn people off.
Despite all that it's a very innovative, fun and well designed game and I can't recommend it enough. I know it has mixed reviews, but if you have any interest in turn based action you should give it a shot.

I'm a huge stealth fan and I heard people championing Mark of the Ninja as an amazing stealth experience from pretty much release day onward. I played the crap out of it originally on the Xbox 360 before I fully converted to a PC gamer, after which I purchased it on Steam and have played through it a few times here. I just bought Invisible, Inc. tonight, which is made by the same developer, Klei, and it made me realize I should get off my butt and write this gushing review about what an awesome ♥♥♥♥ing game Mark of the Ninja is. I should have written this review years ago, but hey, I'm lazy. So here it is now.
The put it simply: Mark of the Ninja is one of the best pure stealth games ever made. Yes, ever. It's up there with the classics of the genre like Thief, Splinter Cell Chaos Theory, Tenchu, etc. It's that good. If you enjoy the stealth genre and you for some reason have yet to play this game, buy it this instant. It's easily worth full price. Don't even read the rest of my review, just thumb it up for knocking some sense into you, buy Mark of the Ninja, install it, and play it all night until you're surely ♥♥♥♥ed for class/work/whatever you have to wake up for tomorrow morning. You can thank me later.
If you need some more convincing, then feel free to read on.
Immediately noticeable is the beautiful, comic book-esque visuals and the amazing work from the animation team. The environments are vibrant, colorful, and full of atmosphere. There's not a bad one in the game. And the character models are what Klei has come to be known for: Cartoony, charming, but with a gritty edge to them. The art design in general is utterly fantastic. Seriously, I'd hang a print of some of the backgrounds in this game on my living room wall as art. And the cutscenes are beautifully animated as well. They wouldn't be out of place in any feature animated film of years past. Simply put: It's a gorgeous game. It does a lot without using many resources; it should run very well on most machines.
Another thing worth mentioning is the gameplay role that lighting takes. The art design blends into gameplay on harder difficulties when a background blur and varying directional light shift with where your player character is looking. It functions very well as a gameplay features but also looks really cool. Win-win.
The sound design of this game is another thing that stands out. Ambient sounds are engrossing and carefully crafted, the effects themselves are also phenomenal. Footsteps from running are crisp and sound like the real thing, they're also louder than you'd expect and serve to remind you that you're being a bit too noisy. Everything sounds remarkably crisp and has a solid echo and weight to it. It seems as though the volume levels of your actions have all specifically been altered to sound more jarring than they normally would have, which fits great with a stealth game since it constantly makes you feel like you're making too much noise even when you aren't. It serves to craft your mood as you're playing the game. It's brilliant.
The core stealth gameplay itself is actually remarkably simple. There are few bells and whistles here, which is good considering that the core gameplay is more than robust enough to carry the rest of the game. Level design is superb, enemies are interesting and challenging. You're given enough tools to make you feel superbly bad♥♥♥♥♥when you pull of something cool, but still vulnerable enough to require quite a bit of skill to get through unscathed.
The replay value of this game is a huge plus. The various challenges and collectibles in each level in addition to the heightened difficulties (which are the best way to play the game in my personal opinion) left me with a feeling similar to what platforming fans must feel when they're repeating the same level of Mario in order to get the perfect score. There are also a number of different costumes you can wear that alter your abilities, there are a number of different tools you can equip to augment your favorite way of getting past guards, etc. There's a lot of modularity (is that a word?) here, and quite a few different ways to play through the levels. There are also some neat developer commentary tracks that are worth a listen as well.
I've never been a platforming fan, but this game is definitely influenced by them. There's
8 hours of gameplay here if you're taking your time, but you can easily triple that with replays. I still jump back into this game from time to time and it not only does it offer significant replay value, but it also stands the test of time very well. The gameplay is so no frills that there's nothing that'll really grow old, and the animated visuals will never go out of date. Hell, Chrono Trigger still looks good, and that game released in, what, 1995? 1996? Sprites, man, how do they work?
Anyway, this is the point when I'd typically bring up some of the drawbacks of a title, but Mark of the Ninja is a game I honestly can't find anything wrong with. It's just that good. I suppose I can see how non-stealth fans might find it slow, maybe? But not really, because there's also some combat involved if you get caught, and it's totally viable to play this game in a more run-and-gun style. It is kind of short, I guess? But the price reflects that.
I don't gush very often and I tend to be a harsh reviewer in general, but this one is a masterpiece in every sense of the word and you're missing out as a stealth fan until you experience it. Buy it gladly and thank Klei on Twitter for making such an awesome video game.

At a glance, this seems like an action game, with the usual script flipped and you're playing as a bad guy. Though the premise stays true to that, it is decidedly NOT an action game. This is 100% a puzzle platformer, and a pretty unique one at that.
You traverse through a series of dungeons in an MMO. Your goal is to chase down some pay to win jerk who killed your father. Along the way you encounter many locked doors, platforms, and traps. This leads to many hidden paths and goodies for those who don't want to just stick to the basic path. The big selling point of the journey is that you can kill other heroes along the way. Being a puzzle game, most of this will be via traps; opening trap doors into spike pits, dropping boulders on their heads, and so on. But there's room for creativity, such as making them chase you into a bit, occasionally getting grenades to throw at them, and even making the idiots kill one another. It's satisfying every time you pull it off.
However, there's one really frustrating aspect of the game that seems to turn it off to many people: the physics. While the controls are pretty tight, sometimes things can get screwy, like being crushed by boxes you push, the hit box not registering on wall or chain grabs, or just the enemy AI going insane and ruining your traps. It's not game breaking by any stretch, but these frustrations DO hold back the fun sometimes.
If you like puzzle platformers, and are looking for one with a bit more of an action undertone, this is the one for you. Just be aware the game physics WILL♥♥♥♥♥♥you off sometimes. But at least the devs pretty consistently update it.

The game is a plaformer first and puzzler second with puzzles rarely going beyond moving an object from A to B or pulling a lever to open a new area. That in itself isn't a bad thing and the developer has gone a long way to mix things up as you progress through the levels, including transmutating the player into a goblin chicken, is that a Chicklen? Gobken? This all pretty much follows the humour of the game with NPCs having conversations about MMOs and bickering as you'd see in game chat of multiplayer games. It's light hearted and can take away the sting of rage and failure on some of the more tricky levels. That said seeing the same joke 20+ times may force you to smash your keyboard too.
Graphically the pixel art style works well, animations are nice, bonus points for having the character wobble on the edge of the platforms! Woo! There is nice modern lighting effects and objects have physics which play into combat, puzzles and numerous deaths. Which is worth a mention, as you'll probably die a lot and the respawn system in the game (statue checkpoints) are sometimes infinite and sometimes just number in the lower digits. This means a particularly tricky section can result in you spawning further and further back.
There is a level editor build into the game along with sharing functionality that lets you rate the user created maps and see a Complete/Rage Quit indicator similar to Mario Maker. This provides some extended longevity to the core game alonside the additional maps provided by the developer, although it should be noted there aren't a huge number of them. It's a nice addition to the game and mean if you end up being totally smitten with it there is no reason you can't make some tricky maps for yourself in the years to come.
On the whole I'd say this is well worth a look if you enjoy platformers with some tricky precision jumping required. The physics can get in the way sometimes but it's not the end of the world. For those dedicated to the genre a full price purchase might be in order but I'd say the courious and casual amonst you would fare better picking it up on sale or inclusive of a bundle.

While this game is technically sound and interesting visually it just feels... empty. You're trying to help a princess recover her city from an evil force that's been released upon it but the entire city is deserted, even when you cleanse an area it's still devoid of people. After a while it made me a little disinterested in actually finishing because it seemed pointless to save an empty city. Even the enemies wait to spawn in until you're close. Done right this isolation can work for a game but in Prince of Persia they don't play to that or address it in any way.
Similarly the mechanics are feel hollow as well. Mostly this is due to a yawn inducing combat system. For each of the four bosses (which you fight multiple times each) there is an OP combo that you repeat over and over until the fight is over and really the only move that changes is the first one between bosses. All the combos are available at the beginning of the game and you can look them up in the menu. Once again the emptiness rears it's head as you only ever fight one enemy at a time. The "free" running is actually entertaining at times but by the end of the game the lack of variety will begin to erode it. The non free running puzzles aren't bad but also don't break any new ground.
The visual style of Prince of Persia is, while not exactly beautiful, interesting and different. The cel shading/illustration style works for the game but doesn't look as good in-game as the screen shots and doesn't appear to be aging as well as you'd expect from the style. Probably the biggest disappointment in the visual aspect is the lack of those stunningly deep environments and landscapes from some of the previous games. There are a few but the visual style let them down a little.
One thing that has swung back and forth in the previous PoP games is the writing, especially for the companion, and it's one of the aspects that this game actually does well with. The dialog between the two is believable and has that good snarky humor from the early games. The princess is capable (actually at some points I wondered why I was needed at all. In fact the Prince needs more help from her than she does from him, in general) and has a real personality. But talking of writing leads to the games biggest flaw: the endgame. There was huge potential for this game to have a real, deep impact on the player. A chance to elevate itself as one of those games that sticks with you long after you've set the controller down. Instead you're left wondering why you spent so many hours doing the tasks you did. You could honestly cut from when the prince and princess meet to the final cut scene and have the same feeling of accomplishment. Here, once again, the worlds emptiness hamstrings everything else because a living, populated world would have at least left the ending the devs went with salvageable.
In the end I didn't actually dislike the game, a more appropriate word would be disappointed. Greatness was within it's reach but it seemingly didn't even try to grab on. Simply trying is all I'm looking for. If you're a diehard PoP fan or enjoy puzzle platforming then this is a solid entry but for the average player I can only recommend it on deep discount, and if you decide to pass you're not missing anything.

Oh! Lookout! I better dodge the enemies attack! But...wait...why should I? I take no damage from enemy attacks, and after a "killing blow", Elika, the companion to the prince, leaps to my aid (even when bound by corruption) and saves my life without any interaction from myself.
Wow, climbing this tower looks fun, and challenging! On second thought, no it's really not. I pressed Y on my controller 5 times and now I'm at the top, fighting the mini-boss, which I will now subsequently have to fight 4 more times, all the while being spammed by mindless quick time events, which are meaningless since I take no damage and cannot die even if i fail them miserably, or completely take my hands off of the controller during the fight.
The bottom line is, if you want to create a game for a mindless zombie that requires no skill and has no depth, then you create this game.
If you enjoy difficult gameplay with tense platforming sections, and a combat system that you can subtly master throughout play to pull off that extremely rewarding combo, please, go purchase Warrior Within. You will no enjoyment here.

One of the best games I've ever played, probably the best game I've played since the last instalment in 2011. Everything that Human Revolution did well Mankind Divided improves upon.
I very highly recommend making your first run of this game a ghost one, with as much of a completionist mindset as you can muster. Whilst it can be played in whatever fashion you choose, the game is designed more so to be explored rather than stomped through. I wouldn't pay as much heed to reviews written with less than 25 hrs played because in my opinion they haven't played it the way Deus Ex games are truly meant to be played, and as a result missed out on a fair amount of the stellar work that has gone into this game.
DX:MD is less of a global adventure than its predecessors, mainly taking place in one region. But I found this choice to be entirely beneficial as part of the narrative is seeing how society reacts and changes as events unfold. Prague and the other locations you visit are among the most richly designed and beautifully realised environments in any game. This can be attributed to the artist and designers at Eidos making full use of the resource hungry tech they built DX:MD on (make sure your system can actually run this game before you invest btw).
A lot of reviews complain about the ending but I found it to be perfectly fine. DX:MD was from the outset clearly a middle chapter in a much larger story arc; its own internal arc is resolved well here and sets up for an intriguing third act that should be made down the road according to Square Enix. In this case being left wanting more is definitely a good thing.

Compared to the other games in this series, this is probably the shortest game but nonetheless awesome and exciting to play. I had some issue during installation though (Direct X 9 not installed and stuff but I got around that by installing some third party program). The game really puts you into the Dark Knight's shoes, going around investigating some stuff and beating up some baddies. Reasons to buy this game:
1.) If you love Batman, get it.
-You finally get to be the Bat and do the stuff he does best, solving crime and serving justice (YAY!)
2.) The combat mechanics of the game are simple but challenging.
-The combat mechanincs of the are really simple but challenging enough to have you thinking your next attack. Plus the combat is so fluid, you'll enjoy playing as much as watching the fight play out.
3.) The riddles are challenging and really satisfying to do.
-I finished all the riddles and yeah, I feel pretty proud of myself for finishing all the riddles and yes, you do feel like the Bat when solving the riddles. Think like your enemy and you would know how to react ;)
4.) PC compatibility.
-I played this game on a notebook with Intel Celeron (N2840 2.16 GHz) and 2GB ram. The game had some lag to it but I was still able to play it. So my notebook specs are pretty bad and I'm still able to run this game so yeah, as far being able to play this on low spec computers, the game wouuld still run okay.
5.) Challenge modes pack quite a challenge.
-Even after you've finished the story mode, there are still some challange modes you could complete (like extra missions). So the game does not stop in the campaign and you could still relive those butt-kicking scenes over and over again.
So in the end is it worth it? Yes, and it is amazing. This game just set the standards of superhero games. In the Arkham series, this may be my favorite one (I have yet to play Arkha Knight but meh, I don't really expect much). I just hoped the campaign did not end so fast. So yes, I love this game as much as I love Batman. So yeah, buy it! *Now, to the Batcave!*

Overall, though, it's an enjoyable experience when the game is working as you'd expect.

Ino was a game I was quite excited about at first. I voted for it on greenlight the day it was added there, and I waited for it to be finished. I even shared it with a few friends saying this looked like a pretty quality game for an rpg horror game and recommended that they vote for it. Some of them said it looked like it was not actually going to be quality and that it was probably actually poorly made and generic. And it makes me sad to say this, but they were right.
Starting with the goods, Ino actually has some neat graphics and mapping. The soundtrack isn't particularly great (I'm pretty sure most of the music is pre-bought, which is fine) but it isn't horrible. The art is pretty great and stylish, even though some bad coding gets in the way (more on that later). The story seems interesting
but ultimately turns out to be disappointing (again, more on that later).
The gameplay itself is sort of generic. You collect keys and items that unlock doors that lead to more keys and items. There are a few chase scenes, ''find the password'' and block pushing puzzles thrown in but those aren't anything new either. There is one puzzle which I liked, though I forgot what it was now. I just remember it had something to do with colors and numbers.
Anyway, one aspect that really drags the game down is the coding (or eventing would be more accurate since this is made in rpg maker). The game is
with bugs through and through. For example, you can break the game in the last scene with the bloody knife if you try to leave the room. There's also a corpse which changes graphics when you interact with it (a result of the event not being set to ''direction fix'' in the editor) and there's objects that you can interact with even when you're not facing them, especially near the beginning. The character portraits are below the light effects layer making them look sort of weird and sometimes even get cut off by tiles. Speaking of light effects, if you press F12 and then try to load the game, it will crash. The light effects script being used is to blame for this.
Another really bad aspect of the game is the story. Like I said earlier, it starts off interesting and mysterious. There's some sort of project going on in a hospital. There's multiple characters and as you play you keep wondering how they all tie together. Spoiler, they don't. The story leads absolutely nowhere. It is FILLED with plot holes and doesn't explain ANYTHING. It delivers a generic twist which is really out of nowhere, and again, makes absolutely no sense. Not to mention there's loads of grammar issues in the dialogue (I'm ok with grammar errors in games but this game is asking for money for ♥♥♥♥s sake, get a proofreader.)
The characters are all boring and no one is really likeable. They're all just sort of... there. Especially that red haired dude you play as in the prologue and third chapter. Seriously dude, who the ♥♥♥♥ are you exactly?
I mean, I didn't bother getting the true ending or bad ending and just left after the good ending, so maybe it gets explained, but I doubt it.
I've said ''generic'' quite a few times in this review, and that's because it describes Ino well. The story and gameplay is generic, the characters are generic, even the bugs are generic as they're found in a lot of other rpg maker games too. While it's not exactly expensive I still wouldn't really recommend buying Ino.

First of all, I rather enjoyed this game. It has some glaring flaws, such as how the story doesn't neatly wrap up in the end, and some basic grammar issues (wrong words, sentence structure, or words spelled wrong, for example) BUT it was still worth the price of admission. The story itself, plot holes aside, was interesting and engaging. Also, the 'Run' sequences didn't feel annoying or poorly done; you had enough time to react instead of dieing the first time and trying again. Far too many RPGMaker games utilizing this do it POORLY. This is an example of it being done right.
+Great Price Point
+Interesting Story
+Custom Sprites
+Great use of Music, sound effects and atmosphere
=Some grammar needs work. Thought instead of though, poorly worded sentences, etc...but they are the exception not the norm.
=The custom art, while not the best, DID fit the game and didn't feel disjointed from it.
-Very short. Can be beaten in about an hour and half that time if you speed run it. I'd say about 1-1.5 hours for all achievements.
-The plot has some glaring holes in it, and doesn't explain or neatly tie things up by the end. Even after getting two of the three endings I'm left scratching my head as to what is really going on.
TLDR: Not your standard RPGMaker game, and avoids most pitfalls the genre tends to fall into. Good use of atmosphere to produce suspense and intrigue, even if the story falls apart towards the end.

This is prety much the videogame equivalent of watching an indie movie, and yet another proof that games can work as interactive artistic experiences.
The storyline may not be about some life-altering magical quest (you're basically just a normal person trying to make ends meet and going through a roadtrip) but the day-to-day freedom and agency you're given as a player, as well as the emotional connection you develop for your own character, make for a very compelling narrative.
In the end playing this game becomes a very personal journey, one that invites self-reflection and leaves a lasting impression. Definitely worth playing if you like story focused games.

I felt like writing a review because of all the negativity I found towards the game online. (Sorry, it turned out kind of long)
Though it has some rough edges, I think this is fundamentally a good game and that it's worth playing, even if a lot of people will hate the outcome.
I have to admit, I did not enjoy the ending I got myself, but that doesn't make it bad, that's the way it was meant to be.
I enjoyed the story and narrative of the game overall, I enjoyed the process of playing the game and the pursuit of the goal.
I played the game I'd like to think I would react if I really found myself in these situation, or as near as I could since sometimes I didn't like any of the options or didn't see how to choose the alternative I'd go with if it were me.
That made the game more and more personal as I played, I identified more with my character, I identified other characters with people in my life and some of the events with real experiences I've had. The end result was that some of the choices towards the end were actually very difficult for me, I knew what I'd choose but I also knew I didn't want to because if this were really me, it'd be unbearably hard and/or painful.
At the very end, though I knew what I'd choose I probably spent a solid 5 minutes choosing 'breath in', 'breathe out' on a loop to prolong the moment, not wanting to make the final decision, though I always knew what I was going to choose.
I came to identify so much with the characters and story that I felt truly devastated and sincerely affected by the ending, not least because this was the outcome of making the choices I would really make, and I knew it wasn't going to lead to a happy ending.
In short, I do recommend this game, in spite of the tedious parts, in spite of some choices I didn't like, in spite of the fact that the end was unpleasant. This game made a connection with me, brought me on a journey and emotionally affected me quite deeply, whether you like the end or not, I believe this is
.
I look forward to more emotional narrative and difficult choices from Vagabond Dog even if I do have to breathe in and breathe out for 5 minutes and lose sleep all over again. Any story that can get inside your heart and twist it up is a successful story whether you really enjoy the experience or not. Not all stories were meant to be happy. I applaud the brave decision to tell such a story.

You and your friends spent twenty minutes rounding up the cars necessary to initiate a segment of the latest heist, only for a griefer to dampen his existential ennui by destroying your crew with the new Orbital Cannon. Why would a troll invest so much money to cause you pain, when each shot costs $500,000? Because it's not real money! And remember: griefers do not grind through repetitive supply missions to earn money. They can simply make more money through widely-available hacking tools.

It's just a game.
After a heavy sigh, you explain that your time after work (a job that pays real money) allows for only a couple hours (if that) to game, and you'd like to spend that time building up enough in-game cash to purchase that DeLorean or Stealth Attack Helicopter. Twenty minutes in, you find yourself trying to hide or evade a player hell-bent on your destruction for reasons that will erode your faith in humanity. Remember: It's just a game.
Rockstar encourages players to destroy others' supply missions, or to steal vehicles you've sourced for initiating heists. So why blame a player who takes an exorbitant amount of time and pleasure in doing this?
And why bemoan the fact that trolls and griefers have tools to evade the one law of Los Santos (physics)? Griefers can teleport--directly into your co-pilots seat. You may find yourself racing against time to get supplies back to your bunker, only to have a metal cage materialize around you. Nice. You're stuck watching the timer run out. Another twenty minutes gone. But isn't that funny? Isn't it all in good-natured fun? Toying with virtual players? C'mon!
It's just a game.

Batman: Arkham Asylum pioneered its own kind of "Simon Says" reaction-based brawling system that is still used in AAA action games today such as Mad Max, Shadow of Mordor, and the other Arkham games. The game is fine for what it is. It looks great, and it plays fine. If I sound unenthusiastic about it, it's because I was kind of sick of its unchanging formula by the time it was over. You go from point A to point B in effortless Batman style: running, sneaking, or grappling-hooking your way stylishly around the environment. Sometimes you'll unlock new areas of the map with new abilities a la Metroid games. If you feel like it, you can find optional hidden things along the way. Occasionally, you'll run into a bunch of bad guys, and you'll dispatch them with the same collection of dial-a-reaction moves every time--even up until the final battle. Occasionally, the game will try to mix up this formula with a special boss encounter, and the results are mixed depending on the encounter.
I think everyone should try Arkham Asylum, both because it's quite cheap by now and because if you like the formula, there are 3-4 other games in the series that do basically the same thing, so you'll know right away if this genre is your thing. After it was over, I felt no particularly strong motivation to play the next game in the series. There are plenty of people who love it, though.

As an avid fan of Lovecraft and Lovecraft-inspired games, I was immediately attracted to the idea of an old-school RPG set in a Lovecraftian environment.  We've had adventure games, "shooters" (or at least, first-person games) and strategy games based on the works of the gentleman from Providence, but no straight-up RPGs that I can recall.  The Dark Stone from Mebara therefore seemed to fill some void in the gaming world.
I've not played a great deal of it yet, but here are my impressions so far:
Graphics:
Yes, they are 2D.  But they are really rather good for 2D - certainly, the games looks better at fullscreen than, say, Gemini Rue.  The graphics most resembled Arcanum's, to my eye, and although 3D graphics have evolved to the point where we now have good levels of detail, there will always be something artistic and interesting about 2D graphics done well.  Not a 5 because there are some oddities - a secretary standing inside of her chair instead of being seated, etc.
Sound:
I like the music quite a bit.  Sounds good, very atmospheric and does a good job setting the mood.  It is perhaps not particularly original in concept, but well-executed all the same.
Story/Writing:
Haven't gotten that far yet, but the story so far seems a bit different from other HPL-inspired games, so points for originality and for tapping into the "unknown from beyond" theme of Lovecraft's that was so central to his work, instead of simply focusing on the horrible monsters (though those are in plentiful supply as well).  The dialogue and descriptive text is functional but well-written.
Gameplay:
I died 5 times in the first fight before finally winning on a lucky critical hit.  Going to hope that the recent changes to difficulty plus gaining some levels will help here.  The first monster one-hit killed anyone that wasn't guarding, and confusion would usually cause one of my own party to kill the other remaining member.  Probably the first monster should either hit less hard, or not use confusion.  Smelling salts didn't seem to work when I used them.  On the positive side, movement is easy, interface is simple, and I'm used to the old-school notion of interacting with everything to see if anything is there.
Overall:
I would recommend this to those with a fondness for Lovecraft or for old-school RPGs.  Very little in the way of hand-holding, so if you've only experienced games that highlight all your interactable objects and tell you everywhere to go, you're going to need to put your big boy/girl pants on for this one.  The only area with which I have any qualms is the difficulty, and it's possible those concerns will be alleviated as I move onward in the game.  As far as 2D, old-school games go, as well as in filling the need for Lovecraftian RPGs, I'm definitely encouraged by the Dark Stone from Mebara.

Do you like ninjas? Real ninjas?
Buy this game.
Please join me as I explain why this game deserves TONS of praise and credit.
There are many ninjas in video games. Being a gamer, youve probably heard of a few of them.
Ryu Hayabusa from ninja gaiden. Strider from his self titled games, Scorpion and sub zero from mortal kombat, Grey Fox from metal gear, etc, etc.
But you havent heard of the main character of Mark of the Ninja. because nobody has. And why havent they? BECAUSE HES ACTUALLY A NINJA.
In popular culture, ninjas have turned into something that they historically never were to pander to the masses. They are portrayed (in games, movies, cartoons, and all popular media) as super invincible Rambos who come in and lethally destroy hundreds of people who should on all accounts kill them immediately. theyre given super human strength, agility, reflexes, to the point of being rediculous, because people like to watch that. It makes them appeal to the audiences who want to watch them do exactly that. The problem is that is NOT what ninjas did. In fact, you couldnt make them do anything that was MORE against the souce material.
The biggest point to this that makes it kind of insulting is that they are making these changes to ninjas to make them more badass, when ninjas were already badass to begin with, and didnt need any help.
The art of the ninja was the art of nonexistence. They were shadows. Whispers. They were sent on missions that noone else could be sent on. They would sneak through places undetected to gather information, or yes, sometimes to assassinate people. They were very skilled at killing people, but did so ONLY at the absolute last resort, to prevent themselves from being discovered. They kept their identities secret. They covered their faces. They tried their hardest to NOT EXIST.
The fact that everyone knows ryu hayabusa and strider (even in their oen worlds) and that characters like them run around in the open massacreing hundreds of people and not caring who knows means that they are NOT ninjas. not even that they are bad ninjas. they arent ninjas at all.
This game lets you play as a REAL ninja, and is one of the only examples of a game Ie seen that actually lets you do that. You cant fight the gaurds, or at least its VERY difficult to beat them in combat, even one on one. Why? I thoght you were a ninja? You are, but they have GUNS. Just because youre a ninja doesnt give you the ability to easily defeat a trained soldier with a loaded gun in fair combat. But you can very easily defeat them if you sneak up on them. thats what a ninja would do if he had to kill. the game also gives you extra points for hiding bodies, which is again, what a ninja would do. The game gives you MORE points if you can go through the level without killing people or being detected. The goals a ninja would have.
The game is very fun. and it points out that you can have  REAL ninja, as opposed to a hollywood ninja, and still be badass. arguably even more badass.
Give the game a try.

I'll just make a quick rundown of what my initial thoughts on the game is and then explain a little more.
- Game seems to be a mix of Tibia and Runescape
- Game is clearly and vividly inspired by Runescape... A little too much. So much you might as well go play Runescape
- Extremely unstable servers, lacks consistency in terms of balancing connection issues [As of writing this review]
- Dialogues and interacting with NPCs and other things are inefficiently done and abysmal in technical and visual design
- Many people have pointed out the unbalanced PvP, where ranger, is insanely superior to any other class
- Art style is acceptable but the world design is lacking
- Huge freeze-spike whenever you enter a new map. Very frustrating
So where do we begin... The game has a Tibia-style of gameplay set in a systematically-designed Runescape world. It's so similar to Runescape that the starting area is just a poor Lumbridge where going south has you coming down to cows within the fence along with the sheeps further down, which in Runescape would just be northeast of Lumbridge and north for the Sheep. The Tibia aspect comes in play where you walk with WASD/Arrow keys and use hotkeys for certain functions and abilities, as well as the top-down camera look.
One thing that drove me insane with the crafting and NPCs is; Instead of simply clicking on an anvil, you have to open your inventory which happens to not be on the ''I'' hotkey for whatever reason, and then DRAG the item on to the anvil. Why on earth would you make it that way? You could make this whole process much simpler and easier. Once you do this, it copies the whole ''Make 1, 5, X'' from Runescape as well, except you create it all instantly in your inventory instead of taking your time in doing it. The dialogue boxes are the absolute worst. Sometims you can't even tell what the NPC is trying to tell you because the font along with a relatively bad design, along with overlapping certain objects, terrain etc, makes it nigh impossible to read. Ridiculous.
One reason to never even touch the Warrior class in this game is for one simple reason that can be easily fixed. Warrior has to walk to the enemy, turn to look at it, and THEN attack. Why have the target mechanic if your character does not automatically turn around and 'target' to attack? However, if you are a ranger or mage, it does in fact turn to your selected target and shoots at it. Hence, Warrior is extremely frustrating, especially when you play it with the back your head always thinking that your are undermined and inferior in comparison to the other classes. Really doesn't even make you feel like playing it at all, as if a waste of time.
Tibia is simply a superior version in terms of gameplay for this game, and Runescape is better in every aspect this game takes ''inspiration'' from, such as equipping a bow just makes you a ranger, unlike Tibia where you dedicate yourself to one role, like Paladin. They clash, and not in a way that turned out well. Both Tibia and Runescape are vastly superior games in every aspect that this game has.
However, this game still is both of Tibia and Runescape, and neither Tibia or Runescape has much in common with each other if you were to play one or the other. That's one thing you could possibly give Orake some credit for. It is still a combination of both if you would want to play such a thing. It's not the end for Orake. It is possible this game can become something interesting if the Developer/s take a considerable amount of time to really work on environment, general texture quality, interface design, and the system that is working behind the scenes for all of the game to work.
However, as of writing this review, i have to say this game is just straight up trash for what it currently is. The full 0.6 hours i've played in this game was spent trash talking and laughing at it with my friend on Discord, without a single minute going by in silence. It's not even bad in a fun way, it's just so bad it's sad.
Can't recommend it at all, but i genuinely hope within a year or so that if dedicated work and nurturing of this game is continued, it could become a stable and interesting game.

Another clicker game! Why are these so appealing?
With a busy schedule between my work and home life, I don't get a lot of time to just sit and play for hours on end. Many games require a 1 hour minimum of play time just to get in a good session. The clicker games are good for people who only have a few minutes to play, and may have to leave at any time.
Time Clickers is an off-shoot of Time Rifters. Pretty straight forward for this type of game. You shoot blocks. You buy upgrades. You hire a squad. You upgrade your squad. Ever once in a while you get "Time Cubes" that allows you to go back in time (i.e. reset the game) with higher DPS and the ability to spend Time Cubes on upgrades. There are also steam achievements.
When you are short on time, it's a good way to kill some time by killing some pixels.

The only thing I really didn't like was the boss fights, which were below average but still not horrible and this does not outweight the good parts of the game.

If you're looking for a game that you can get 100% in, this will also be the right choice, as getting all the achievements takes around 30-35 hours if you're not horrible at combat like me. The game is also not hard to run, so if you're like me and you're stuck with a PC that mosly runs 2D games, get ready for some 3D fun.

The only microtransactions you can make are from the Community Market to buy weapon skins or loot chests for weapon skins, and the only DLC is skins for the characters which I personally think they did really well with.
The price is extremely good for such a high quality game in my opinion, it's very addictive, progess feels good with getting new weapons/equipment every time you level a character, the balance is actually pretty good even though some of the other reviews are biased because those reviewers likely only play one or two classes, and like Overwatch every class counters other classes, AND is countered by other ones. I really love everything about this game. The story is fun and interesting, and it actually requires skill, timing, and strategy to complete the stealth missions. The challenges keep me entertained even after I have finished the story, and the infinite challenges could be their own game in and of themselves. I have almost all those dang Riddler Trophies, some of which are really hard to find, and take some real patience to seek out. I have only completed the game in Easy mode, so I hope to play through it a couple more times in Normal and Hard mode.
PROS:
-GREAT story and plot!
-Voice acting is superb! I really love Mark Hamil's Joker, and it really makes this feel like a Batman game!
-Music is AMAZING! It really adds tension and helps the situations feel more real. This is most apparent, to me, during the killer croc fight.
-The SOUNDS in ths game are great!  I can feel it in my gut every time I dislocate someone's elbow or snap their leg, and all the gadgets have great sound effects as well!
-Great combat OVERALL. There are a few minor issues, but I can work around them. Combat really does take skill in this game. You have to have good timing and tactics.
-Stealth mechanics are fun. I love being able to clear out a room of baddies without a single one seeing me, and there's always more than one way to complete a stealth mission.
-Gadgets are fun to play around with. Batman has everything from remote control batarangs to explosive gel. The gadgets are all fun in their own way, and are really essential to completing stealth missions.
-Movement is pretty good. I love the feel of gliding, and for some reason it's fun just running around and jumping over stuff.
-I can easily plug in a controller and start playing without havingto adjust any settings (but I prefer keyboard controls). With a keyboard combat is much faster, and I can look around alot faster.
CONS:
-BIGGEST PROBLEM WITH THE GAME: Once you complete the story, there are no more goons to fight in the asylum. It makes sense in context with the story, but I would really like to be able to explore the Asylum AND fight some baddies. After the story is over, it becomes really boring to wander around looking for trophies.
-While I may enjoy the combat overall, there are a few frustrations. Sometimes my counters seem to lag, or if the game goes into slow motion, sometimes I can never counter at all. Other than that combat is great!
-Movement is fine, however there is very little precision. This is really obvious when you are trying to line up riddler trophy spray paint, which you have to look at from a specific place and at a specific angle. It is also apparent when you are trying to sneak around. Often it's hard for me to be sneaky when I keep bumbling around. I can work around this, however, so it's a minor complaint.
-I have an XBox controller I plug in to let people who are not accostumed to keyboard control play. However, whenever I try playing with a controller, I find the controls clunky and very slow. It is much easier to play with a keyboard and mouse. This is another very minor complaint because I never use the controller if I can help it.
Overall I give this a 9/10. There are a few minor issues, but the good things far outweigh the bad!

I really love everything about this game. The story is fun and interesting, and it actually requires skill, timing, and strategy to complete the stealth missions. The challenges keep me entertained even after I have finished the story, and the infinite challenges could be their own game in and of themselves. I have almost all those dang Riddler Trophies, some of which are really hard to find, and take some real patience to seek out. I have only completed the game in Easy mode, so I hope to play through it a couple more times in Normal and Hard mode.
PROS:
-GREAT story and plot!
-Voice acting is superb! I really love Mark Hamil's Joker, and it really makes this feel like a Batman game!
-Music is AMAZING! It really adds tension and helps the situations feel more real. This is most apparent, to me, during the killer croc fight.
-The SOUNDS in ths game are great!  I can feel it in my gut every time I dislocate someone's elbow or snap their leg, and all the gadgets have great sound effects as well!
-Great combat OVERALL. There are a few minor issues, but I can work around them. Combat really does take skill in this game. You have to have good timing and tactics.
-Stealth mechanics are fun. I love being able to clear out a room of baddies without a single one seeing me, and there's always more than one way to complete a stealth mission.
-Gadgets are fun to play around with. Batman has everything from remote control batarangs to explosive gel. The gadgets are all fun in their own way, and are really essential to completing stealth missions.
-Movement is pretty good. I love the feel of gliding, and for some reason it's fun just running around and jumping over stuff.
-I can easily plug in a controller and start playing without havingto adjust any settings (but I prefer keyboard controls). With a keyboard combat is much faster, and I can look around alot faster.
CONS:
-BIGGEST PROBLEM WITH THE GAME: Once you complete the story, there are no more goons to fight in the asylum. It makes sense in context with the story, but I would really like to be able to explore the Asylum AND fight some baddies. After the story is over, it becomes really boring to wander around looking for trophies.
-While I may enjoy the combat overall, there are a few frustrations. Sometimes my counters seem to lag, or if the game goes into slow motion, sometimes I can never counter at all. Other than that combat is great!
-Movement is fine, however there is very little precision. This is really obvious when you are trying to line up riddler trophy spray paint, which you have to look at from a specific place and at a specific angle. It is also apparent when you are trying to sneak around. Often it's hard for me to be sneaky when I keep bumbling around. I can work around this, however, so it's a minor complaint.
-I have an XBox controller I plug in to let people who are not accostumed to keyboard control play. However, whenever I try playing with a controller, I find the controls clunky and very slow. It is much easier to play with a keyboard and mouse. This is another very minor complaint because I never use the controller if I can help it.
Overall I give this a 9/10. There are a few minor issues, but the good things far outweigh the bad!
