Jesus christ. The game is ridiculously, overwhelmingly awesome.
Combat:
Gratitious Space Battles combat was dull. SPAZ combat was fun. Reassembly combat is great. Ring Runner's combat is just outstanding. It's super dynamic, fast-paced but not chaotic: you control the pace of fight. It's like an action-RPG with a very deep skill system, where every skill is indeed unique. Most abilities have very low cooldowns, so you'll have to blink, dodge, slow time, push, pull, manage your heat, shield and energy and destroy your enemies in any way you can imagine. 10/10.
Customization:
No, you can not build your ship from scratch like you can in reassembly. But hell, this game's customization system is just way more advanced and balanced! Every hull has a set number of mounting points for different types of devices. Every mounting point has a capacity: the more capacity it has, the more comlex gear you may equip to it grating you passive bonuses or active abilities. You may equip multiple devices into a single mounting point if you have the capacity. It's so way better than in any other seemengly similar game like Gratitious Space Battles or SPAZ.
10/10.
Abilities:
Basically everything including evasion and weapon autofiring is an ability in this game. And wow, varied they are. Abilities are designed to be very synergetic and they often let you turn your downsides into an advantage. For example you can grab a super-powerful engine that generates a ton of heat. Overheating is generally not the thing you want. But you can attach a freaking molten laser that dissipates all your heat in one shot if you're overheated! Or you can equip an engine with high top speed but low acceleration and get an ability that instantly accelerates you to maximum speed in any direction.
Basically there are only 2 games I know that have as synergetic abilities as this: Tales of Maj'Eyal 4 and Baldur's Gate 2(wizard). Please tell me if you know another!
10/10 here, no doubt
Graphics:
The game is developed by one family. Graphics are 3d while game mechanics are 2d. They pretty advanced, run smoothly but I personally am not a huge fan of this game's graphical content. SPAZ or Gratitious Space Battles look better if you ask me. But it's nowhere close to being game-breaking or unlikable.
7/10
Story:
I have not completed the story yet. So far(10 hours of story) it is pretty fun and well-written. It's not a Planescape: Torment in space but there's a decent sci-fi story that utilizes some very well-though physical concepts. Like Mass Effect is based on physical phenomon called Mass Effect(some materials may change their density when electrical current is applied to them) this game has numerous concepts that I found even more interesting(physics is my major).
8/10(?)
Music:
Game's music is atmospheric enough and fits it well though it it sometimes a little repititive. You're unlikely to listen to game's OST when you're not playing like you listen to Silent HIll's or Final Fantasy's but it is a great soundtrack and you won't end up listening to your own music instead of built-in soundtrack.
7/10
Controls:
As I said before, most abilities have low cooldowns and you may end up equipping a lot of them. Ability management, movement, evasion and heat/energy/ammo may will be as challenging as you want them to. If you can't handle too much active abilities, equip passives instead. But I love controlling as much as my brain can handle and the game certainly gives me opportunity to equip enough active skills. My gamepad acts funny with this game(analog joystick sticks to 8 discrete directions)  but controlling with mouse + keyboard is great anyway and controlling multiple skills is more convinient with keyboard.
General impression:
The game is Loved by its developers. You can feel it in every aspect in every small detail. It's like the opposite to stuff you see in android market or most early access garbage that are developed to get as much money and as soon is possible. This game is so detailed, so well-though, so *lived* by it's developers I just can't help but admire it. It's very strange and disappointing to see how unknown it is and it's 75/100 metascore rating is just frustrating. Do not let AAA-crap reviwers fool you, this is a true indie game gem.

Essentially a reboot of the series after the much adored Sands of Time games (which Ubisoft ended up revisiting after this game with the interquel, Prince of Persia: The Lost Sands), this title streamlines some of the game mechanics from the previous titles. This is not necessarily a bad thing.
In this game the Sands of Time ability is replaced with a plucky female companion, a princess with magical powers who can assist the Prince in combat against mystical adversaries. For better or for worse, her powers also prevent the Prince from falling to his death, thus serving a purpose similar to the "rewind time" ability from the Sands of Time series of games, but taking away control of said ability from the player.
Overall, really fun. Don't overlook this one just because of the "no death" feature or the fact that it's a reboot. Sands of Time itself was a reboot of the original side-scrolling POP games, after all.

I've been following Prince of persia for a long, long time now - my fondness for it dates back to throwing my NES controller through a screen when I was a kid*. Sands of Time is probably one of my 10 most-played games and one I can always go back to. Finally, after waiting forever to have a worthy comp, I got to play this version of it...
And darn it, is this a mixed bag or what? Visually, this game is absolutely gorgeous. The environments are well-rendered, the cell-shading not overly distracting, and painted, distant sky is one of those small, fairytale-esque touches that you don't get often enough with franchises such as these. On top of that, the story is basic, but it all unfolds in a pretty logical manner in that the characters always remain true to themselves. The questionable existence of free will is front and center here, and while it doesn't break any ground, it at least gives you a reason to keep pressing forward.
What did not keep me pressing forward, though, was the gameplay. I mean, what happened? The Sands trilogy (well, game 1 and 3 anyways) managed to create platforming puzzles that required a keen sense of where to go next. Here, you are literally shoved in the right direction and simply have to time your button pressing correctly. There's no real challenge to be had. The combat is just plain redundant - block, block, wait, strike BUTTOM COMBINATION.
The fact that you literally cannot fail at this game, though, shows you that the creators clearly cared for their environments and story than actually gameplay value. It's a frustrating result and one that I can't, sadly, endorse with any real enthusiasm. In a word, this game is satisfactory. Nothing more, nothing less. Waiting for a sale is the right move.

It's a physics-based puzzle platformer. While the images/videos might hint towards a slightly more open-worldish type affair, the levels themselves are fairly straightforward with the exception of side areas you can muck around with for the sake of increasing your score... Which is just a score, there doesn't appear to be anything interesting associated with the number other than that deeply satisfying feeling of watching something get bigger because of you.
...*ahem*.
Now, from my handle and profile picture, you might presume I have a certain appreciation of all things goblinoid. This is true. I suppose I just feel a natural sense of connection with small, green, warty little beasts that are regularly and often deservedly reviled...  So seeing a game where you play as a goblin, surrounded by other goblins, beating up entitled tin-can heroes using deviously improvised traps and pitfalls felt like Steam had finally answered my prayers and delivered an indie title that wasn't completely terrible. The charming art style only added to that impression.
The problem is... The art style is pretty much the one good thing here. The player controls are manageable once you get used to them, certainly, but there's always the occasional hiccup associated with being something that tries to obey the fickle laws of video game physics.  The main problem arises from the fact that you don't have quite as much, if any, control over everything else in the game that is also having issues trying desperately to not exist in the same physical space as something else.
Dragging a massive boulder will of course be slow going, until the boulder suddenly and inexplicably flips into the air and sails over your head if you're lucky, or onto it if you're unlucky. Crates and barrels will sometimes be perfectly obedient, other times they will bounce just high enough to count as being lethally dangerous when they touch you again.
Unpredictable, bizarre and frequent deaths are really just part of the fun with doing anything in a game with a physics engine though, and the game is kind enough to have a mercifully short turnover time in regards to respawning.
However, you can't just run around willy-nilly and smash your bristled little green head against the puzzles until you find the right solution, despite several of them only being solveable by doing just that.
The reason you can't use trial-and-error is that, first of all, respawn checkpoints are limited. I mean this in the sense that you can only respawn at a specific checkpoint a certain number of times, after which you get sent back to the last checkpoint before that one, and so on until you're respawning at the very start of the level again.
This doesn't make the game more difficult or challenging, it just makes it more tedious. The only thing you have to do is just run and jump a bit more through old territory to get back to where you were, only to die to the same puzzle again and have to make the trek one more time. Or, if your luck's particularly foul, you get sent to a checkpoint that was before a point-of-no-return, so you actually CAN'T get back to where you were and need to restart the whole level from scratch.
Second, even if you don't have a particularly fatal puzzle at hand, it is entirely possible in far too many circumstances that you end up accidentally pushing something too much or not pushing it enough, in which case the thing you needed for the other thing gets irretrievably jammed into some spikes somewhere, and you have to start the level over since no amount of blood sacrifice will make the spike-gods relinquish their prize of a small throwable pebble.
Now, again, there's a chance for redemption here. Games with puzzles that can lock down like that will generally have fairly short levels and a quick way of resetting the puzzles so you can give it another try... Not so in Goblins and Grottos. The game shows off its really quite wonderful art style by having these large, sprawling maps for you to explore and maneuver around... Which is great in and of itself, and was really what I was looking for. The problem is when you combine that with tricky puzzles that can permanently stick themselves to the point where you need to do all the exploration all over again. This is particularly irritating when the only reason things got borked was because the physics engine♥♥♥♥♥♥itself while doing a routine calculation, and sent something inexplicably flying (which, let's face it, is one of the biggest reasons we love physics engines in games).
The game basically needs to decide what it is... Is it a casual, quick little puzzle platformer with difficult trial-and-error puzzles? Or is it a slightly more open exploration game for fiddling around? Trying to combine the two just results in a puzzle platformer that takes too long to get anywhere and that you're too scared to explore for fear of accidentally jamming the system again.  Considering the game has already been released and doesn't even bear the cautionary label of "Early Access", I think it's fair to assume that Goblins and Grottos isn't going to be making any particularly big changes to its fundamental gameplay anymore.
I really, really wanted to like this... I really did. Again, the art style is fantastic, and the humor wasn't nearly as irritating as it potentially could have been... But it's all just a bunch of polish on a game that isn't there.
You can't make a game that requires tight controls and exact reactions, then throw in a chaotic physics engine to make things interesting. You can't make a puzzle that demands trial and error, and then punish the player for not getting it right the first time.
On the plus side, the game does have a map editor... So I guess you could just make your own maps that have nothing to do with how the rest of the game runs, and then just marvel at how pretty it is.

So I promised to update my review, and here it is.  I haven't played this game in 3-4 weeks.  Why is that? Well here is why I feel I haven't been back to Lawbreakers, and at the current point in time, I don't feel like going back right now.
So lets get the obvious out of the way.  Nobody is playing it!!!  But theres got to be a reason why.  Here is why I really truly feel people play it, say they like it, and stop comming back:
1)  The look of it doesn't stand out among other FPS shooters.  It looks just like the futuristic COD games.
a)The asthetic of the game almost totally matches COD BLOPS3. Even one of the
levels, can't remember the name, looks extremely similar to Nuketown in BLOPS3.
b)The characters have no personality other than "IM A MEAN GUY/GAL".  They are
super generic. Ok, Summer is the one exception. She is really happy and cheery, and
stands out the most to me.  And then there is Bomchelle and Kitsune.  Bomchelle
takes a lot of inspiration from Zarya from Overwatch.  Hard to imagine her existing if
Zarya didn't come first.  Kitsune is a total ripoff of Sombra.  If you don't immediately
see Sombra when you look at Kitsune, I don't know.  Almost the same hair without the
side being shaved, and the outfit is almost identical in looks and color.  Its pretty crazy.
2)  The gameplay doesn't stand out enough.  Its really solid. Don't get me wrong.  It feels good.  Feels like your shots are hitting the mark.  There are no jitters or stutters on my system.  And it feels like a cross between Quake and COD.  It moves more like Quake, while the game modes and team play feels more like COD.  Those are both great games series, depending on who you ask, but combining them doesn't make Lawbreakers feel too original.
3)This is kind of a tricky one.  The class system.  So, I don't hate it.  But... maybe it needs some changes.  I feel like the healers need to go.  I sort of feel like the healer Tokki also has one of the more stand out personalities, so maybe the characters themselves could stay, but make
them not be healers anymore.  Nobody wants to be a healer.  Its not fun in this game.
Its fun in Overwatch to be a healer.  Here, all you want to do is shoot people in the face.      Healers are no fun to play.  Maybe put more health packs into the maps so people can
heal themselves rather than auto-regen health.  They are all very mobile characters, so
running to health packs I feel is the best way to heal, as long as there are enough, but not too many.  Also, maybe if you are getting rid of healers, maybe just implementing the progression, unlock weapons system Cliffy B was talking about in an interview before release should be reimplemented.  If that happens, do not make weapon/ablitiy unlocks come out of lootboxes.  That needs to be a progression system.

As for what is great about the game and does set it apart:
1) Shooting behind your head.  Have I been able to use it in combat very effectively? No, but its super cool. Plus it pushes you forward in the anti gravity, and I think thats cool too.
2) The anti gravity.  Its anti gravity done right.  You feel pretty in control and its fun to be in.  Its kind of hard to explain.  Anti gravity in other games can feel not all that satisfying, but It feels good here.
3) The boot!  Ok, so in all reality, its just a melee attack.  That in itself doesn't set itself apart from any other online FPS that has one.  It does a little damage, but could be enought to finish an opponent.  But, the way it is executed in this game is one of the only things in this game that I feel give this game any personality.  If you get killed by a boot, WHAP!  You get a big foot print on your screen.  You can choose which foot print you want the other person to see when they get killed by you.  I thought that was really cool, but about the only time I felt this game truly had its own personality.

I don't know, in the end, I guess all I can say is if this game wants to be successful, it needs some big changes.  I hate to change my review to a negative one, but especially after writing this update, I really can't honestly recommend it to anyone.  It sounds like in interviews before launch, nobody really knew what they wanted it to be.  Maybe thats why it turned out to be so generic.  They played it too safe, and ended up with something that can't really make a claim to innovating anything.

In my humble opinion this is the greatest of all the Batman games. I'm not such a big fan of third person 3D games, although I have played many of them, but this game plays so well that it drew me in almost instantly. The fighting is fantastic, albeit even better in the sequel, and the story telling is first rate. However, I think it's actually the smaller game world that I like most about this first Arkham game. It's more compact and it feels like nothing is wasted. As technically impressive as Arkham Knight is, at least on the PS4 it is, it's scale of this original game that I much prefer. No out of place "Bat-Tank" driving sections here.
If you've never played an Arkham game, if you're not into third person games, and even if you don't think much of Batman, I'd still recommend this game. It's certainly worth the full asking price (£14.99 at tie of writing) but, if you have some reservations, wait around a couple of months as it's regularly discounted by 75%.

I had been wanting to get to Ronin for a while though, I was pretty excited about it. After beating Gunpoint and I saw this one, it’s a slightly turn based version of Gunpoint, very similar anyway, except even in the hints in the game itself it says “this is not Gunpoint” haha. But the similarities are Very high. Graphics are very similar, level design is extremely similar, gameplay is quite similar. I don’t remember Gunpoints soundtrack, but the Ronin soundtrack is pretty good.
First, the bad, the really really bad, stupid idiotically bad. You can’t play this game in anything other than 1920x1080 resolution. [I don’t know if smaller works or not, I’d wager it does not]. My screen is 2560x1440. The options only allows a checkmark for full screen or not full screen. Obviously I play full screen, but when I got to a point where I had to kill a guard, a little red sword button pops up. Except I couldn’t click it. Somehow I did it accidentally. I pressed every key on the kb and nothing worked. I couldn’t progress. I looked for a manual or guide as to what button to push. I almost quit the game outright, never to be played again. Then I found a steam forum post about the resolution issue. Unchecked fullscreen, which puts it to 1920x1080 and it has worked flawlessly ever since.
So, once I was able to actually play, you jump around like gunpoint, you hack terminals by pressing up like gunpoint, you avoid and attack guards like gunpoint, you hide in shadows like gunpoint. It’s so ridiculously similar to gunpoint, EXCEPT, it’s semi-turn based, in a weird kinda way. Every second of time equates a movement, or something. It’s hard to explain. The game is real time until action starts and It auto-pauses. You can choose to jump (and choose your arc, which apparently is occasionally a lie) and sometimes your jump would last longer than a full turn, so you would land on the second turn (or do something else), you can attack, you can use grappling line, or another special unlocked ability. If you choose to attack while in a red line of death (enemy gun aim or whatever) then you would do your attack and then be shot. Unless your attack moves you, which it seems to do randomly – this is bad because it’s not always entirely predictable, though it usually is. So, you do a whole lot of jumping around until you get a clear attack of opportunity.
Which brings me to the next point, the difficulty spike is pretty intense. This game is HARD. There are, idk 7 bosses I think, and each one has a couple preliminary missions where you hack terminals. There really doesn’t seem to be much of a story. Gunpoint at least had an ok story mixed with some humor. But I haven’t even gotten to boss #2 yet. I have died SO MANY times. I enjoyed playing but I eventually got fatigued and went on to play some [semi]brainless OW. It’s almost like a puzzle game or a test of patience. So, if you can’t do that, then I don’t recommend it. Taylor, since you liked Dark Souls so much, you might like it, especially since you liked Gunpoint. Gunpoint is a piece of cake in comparison.
Combat tends to be in a room with 3-4 enemies. There are basic guards, who stay in one spot and shoot at your last location. Samurai that do a slash-n-dash in a straight trajectory, soldiers that seem to basically be the same as guards but have machine guns (I really don’t know the difference yet – apparently guards shoot second, soldiers shoot first), and some guys that are more prone to call for lockdown. [more on this in a minute] I think later on there are a couple more types. Guards, soldiers, and whatever the other guy is called can be knocked down and it takes two turns for them to get back up. You can kill them after knocking them down. Samurai are the most troublesome. You can’t jump at them, they take two hits to kill and you can only hit them in certain circumstances it seems. One hit stuns them, next hit kills. And of course they are dashing all over the room. Occasionally you can knock someone off a high ledge to kill them, but it doesn’t happen often.
The lockdown – locks certain doors impeding travel, calls more guards (I think), and more importantly fails one of your objectives. There are three objectives (usually) to each mission. If you complete them all, you get a skill point. If you don’t you can move on, but no point. Skill points give you things like the ability to throw a sword, throw shurikens to stun, have a body double, silently hang people from the ceiling, etc etc.
So, ultimately, it’s a really neat, cool game with some problems, but I really enjoyed it so far. I’ll definitely be playing again when I can devote the brain power.

As everyone pointed out, the game has a cool style and the turn based action seems cool originally, but then you realize it's actually not very good at all. First off, its stupid how gaining skills is tied to arbitrary extra objectives in the game, meaning if you make a mistake, set off any alarm, or don't skill every single guy in levl (which should be your decision) you have to continually restart checkpoints over and over until everything happens perfectly. Then there's the combat. You die from any single 1 hit. Its fine when there are few guys and when you can play parts how you want, using stealth to whittle down numbers. But when forced into fights against multiple people the game runs out of fun and becomes frustrating. Many times you can't tell if an attack will hit you, or know all the information for the enemies next turn. Trying to plan your jumps is annoying also. To get to someone close to you and knock them down you have to jump either way too high up so youre out of range of hitting them, or too low that youll come back down to the ground and get killed by another enemies attack. Also the jump ability is terrible with the mouse, and doesn't work half the time. The fighting system can be super dumb. You will jump and knock someone down, but then everyone is on you, meaning you can't kill them, you have to jump up again, then you need to jump down. But with attacking takking a turn and with enemies being able to kill you that turn, its useless. I would constantly knock someone down and have to jus jump away, and go around a room knocking people down but never able to kill them because there would be 3 other enemies always attacking me. I could never end next to someone where I could fall and kill them on same turn. Then other times land by someone will just net you getting auto killed. It's also annoyhing there's no way to stun civilians in early stages. Meaning if you get detected you just must restart. Juging from other people's reviews the forced combat get's even worse at later stages. Some people say jus mash space bar, but you move too quickly that you can't time it to be right where you want. Better control or dual actions, landing where you want, more option for avoiding fights, taking out forced stupid objectives, and better mouse support this game could be fun. In current state can't recommend.

First off, I want to say that this game got me to invest enough time into it to complete it 100%. Yes that includes the NEW GAME PLUS mode and all Steam Achievements despite barely having over 12 hours put into it.
You start off as a young woman on a mission of revenge. Exposition of the world and her backstory are given mainly through short intros and dialogue between missions. There isn't much story besides that.
The gameplay itself is something refreshing, mixing together 'beat em up' aspects with stealth and careful planning. However, this is not purely a stealth game as the branding on this may seem. You will have to engage in open combat many times in order to properly play this game. You will also die, many
times. Enemy patterns and behaviors are learned through experience. You'll die to them and learn from it. These patterns can be exploited later to your advantage and are usually reliable enough to do so consistently. However, as a result of this, interactions with enemies can seem really repetitive, especially if you're stuck on a level and don't change your tactics or try coming in from a different angle.
of your time playing won't be on new levels, but rathe on the same ones trying new things out. On a similiar note, the soundtrack suffers from this repetition. While not bad, it can get dull after hearing it for the 30th time.
Bugs popped into gameplay during my personal experience. A handful of times I phased through a wall and out of the map after grappling to it, and other times enemies would spot me despite being compltely out of sight. A majority of the game, however, was perfectly fine. Yet it does seem that a large amount of other players are reporting more bugs than what I witnessed.
This game brings something new to the table in the form of its turnbased stealth combat system, yet the game itself is pretty short. Great concept with adequate gameplay to back it up that requires patience, timing, and skill. Bugs are present and probably will not be fixed as the last update was a year ago. Can be repetitive at times.

Sadly, Steam does not allow for a "neutral" rating, so I have to give this one a negative.
But first of all, what is good about Ronin? The art style, the setting, the music, the animation quality, the level design and obviously the game mechanics (in theory).
Now to the reasons why I CANNOT recommend it...
There is really only 1 reason and that is above mentioned game mechanics (and partially the controls).
I'll talk about the controls first. You can play the game with Mouse and Keyboard or with a Gamepad. The controls with the mouse are horrible...simply horrible. However, the gamepad controls are even worse. And this is mainly a problem because of the game mechanics:
In Ronin you move around in real time, you can go left and right only really, or crawl up or down walls. Everything else is done via "jumping". Now the jumping mechanic stops time completely. And it's really finicky. With the controller you can aim better (right stick), but there is no easy way to abort your move. With the mouse you have this weird half-inverted or not "aiming", meaning if you want to jump to the left, you hold the left mouse button and drag your mouse either to the left or right until you have the correct angle for your jump. Like I said...I can't even explain it properly. It might have been a better idea to at least have a confirmation command, as misjumping is pretty easy. You can also use a grapple mid air, which is necessary to advance the game. Too bad I only found out now that grappling with the mouse is WAY easier than with a controller, since you can manually stop time by pressing and holding space bar, which is not the case with a controller, where you simply press "start" to stop time, but which is, again, a lot more difficult to pull off in time.
On to the combat. This is the most exhilarating part of the game and I really digged it...at first, until all the flaws became apparent. Combat in this game is turn based and more of a puzzle than anything else. Enemies will aim at your last known position, usually, until you are out of line of sight, knock them down (or kill them of course), they decide to call for reinforcements, or they have to reload. It is important to learn the different enemies' move sets (there aren't that many...standard pistol guy, MP gunner and samurais...haven't encountered anyone else). You do this by jumping around and avoiding shots until you can safely kill an enemy, which can take quite a while. At the same time you want to watch out for enemies sounding off the alarm, since that means you don't "100% the level", and that's quite necessary, unfortunately. In this mode you can also "plan" your moves more carefully, since one jump can take several turns (red indicator). If you're good this looks really skillful. However, there are some extreme flaws with the combat and controls in conjunction. Some examples:
Inconsistent results: Killing a guy the same way over and over again may result in different outcomes. I once killed a guard and did not trigger an alert (barely avoiding line of sight), only to find out that a few deaths later it was almost impossible to do that again, since I was spotted immediately (static enemies) without a way to respond. Same with another try later on where I more or less "abused" the pause feature to kill about 5 guards before triggering actual combat. Try as I might, the same strategy (you see on YouTube) didn't work anymore. I was instantly spotted and had to deal with like 8 enemies at once.
Unclear visuals: The game tells you which move is possibly and which one is not...in theory. In praxis this means that the game clearly displays your jumping arc, but your character doesn't move...one...bit. Why? Because there's a ledge in the way. If the jump can't be made, then why show it as a possible move? All other impossible moves are greyed out as well. Similar issues with the grappling hook. Mid air, tried to latch on (black dots, instead of white ones) and well, I jumped to my death, because the character decided not to do it.
Unclear threats: I've encountered 3 enemy types so far: The basic gun man is pretty straight forward. He shoots where you were, you move out of the way, you kill him, as they only shoot AFTER you move. You can use all moves on him. Easy. The MP gunner fires three consecutive bursts without changing aim as far as I can recall, but he fires BEFORE and in between your move...so you're ♥♥♥♥ed if you can't avoid that shot...and the hitbox of your dude is weird. These are a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥and for some reason you can't dash towards them, as they instantly kill you. The final one are the samurai who will just endlessly charge after you and take 2 consecutive hits to die. They will also just kill you if you move through them, or if they happen to land near you in an awkward way, etc. The problem is, that it's not always clear who can hit you and who can't...or why they killed you.
Controller issues: In some fights you have too many options for the controller to handle, which means some options will just not have a button prompt assigned to them...can you believe that? How can you develop a game with controller support and then fail at this critical part? You can still use the mouse, but it's often not displayed clearly if you've been using the controller.
Last bit. Each mission is pretty much the same: Hack into computers and run away until you fight one of the "big bads" and move on to the next chapter (5 in total). You have three side objectives: Don't kill any civilians, kill all enemies and don't trigger the alarm. Civilians are a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ since they WILL trigger the alarm once they've so much as cought a glimpse of you or any structural damage you've caused (and of course finding bodies you leave behind). Killing all enemies is imho just part of finishing the mission. Not raising the alarm is annoying, since it's possible that enemies suddenly decide they no longer want to fight you when you're dealing with their 6 buddies. That means you need to engage them in active combat again. Sometimes it's enough to get in their line of sight, sometimes you need to knock them over. It's highly disruptive of the game play imho.

Of course you don't HAVE to do any of that, but if you don't "perfect" a level you don't get a skill point, and you need those skill points to get vital skills like throwing your sword, teleporting, decoys and stringing people up on the ceiling without raising an alarm, which causes another gripe for me...I mean it's extremely restricting. If you can't perfect all levels you're just going to have a much harder time with any future levels...it's counter productive. I want to be awarded for playing well, but it should not be a mandatory skill system. I mean, it's possible to beat the game without any skills I guess, but it's damn hard and pointless. Not to mention that some skill points are just wasted, because you need to invest them in order to get to a better skill down the line, but they don't do anything for you...extremely annoying.
The game could also do with a better tutorial...(did it even have one? Can't remember) and a better narrative, because there's not really any story, apart frome some 3 lines per boss character from your character's memories...which don't explain anything.
Summary: This game was a nice conceptual idea. It's not even terribly implemented, but it's got too many flaws to really recommend it in my opinion. Kinda sad, really. There just isn't enough variety, too many things are mandatory and you can only be sneaky when the game wants you to. Mark of the Ninja might be a comparison here, apart from the combat. I think most people will prefer that one.

I've played several of the idle/clicker games on Steam now; Adventure Capitalist, Clicker Heroes, Sakura Clicker, and this one, Time Clickers. And by far, this one is my favorite.
Rather then fighting monsters, instead you are shooting at large masses of blocks, each one with different colors and HP levels, and of course they drop gold. You shoot a pistol which you have to actually aim, as opposed to just clicking anywhere on the screen. As you go you get allies as usual, in this case represented by several different guns. As you go you earn abilities and upgrades that give you more and more damage.
What I like about this game, as opposed to say something like Clicker Heroes, is that when you reach wave 100, and buy all the upgrades on your clicking weapon, you earn what are called Time Cubes; they give you bonus DPS for each one and you can spend them on upgrades (in Clicker Heroes, you have to give up the DPS when you spend the equivelant)
The soundtrack, sound effects, and visual effects are all great and very appeasing to the eye, and again, the fact that you can aim your gun and shoot as opposed to just clicking randomly makes all the different in a game like this.
So what are you waiting for? It's free, go download the damned thing!

It's time!
I can't say I expected much after the dissapointment that was Final Fantasy XIII.
But I ended up enjoying this game a lot more than the original.
If you want to read my review for the original XIII :
Time for pros and cons:
+The game is no longer a long corridor, the areas are open with things to be discovered and time travel gives a good excuse to see many diverse and interesting locations. There is a nice amount of different locations and some areas are the same location but in a different time period.
+Good music overall and some tracks are superb. Like these:


+The narrative is very focused compared to the muddled mess in the original. This is mostly thanks to there only being a handful of main characters.
+The villian is great, you completely understand why he is doing the things he does.
+The combat is a lot better this time around while still feeling like the same system:
+When you changed your partys roles in the orignal game there was a animation that took you out of the battle for about 2         seconds, this might not seem like a big deal but removing this animation and just letting the battle flow like it was before does a lot to improve the pacing of fights in this game.
+If the character you are controlling dies you just take control of the other person in your party. This was lacking in the  original game and it is very nice to see them address this problem.
+You can also change what character you are controlling mid battle, a very welcome addition.
+The leveling system is actually very open to customization compared to the linear mess in the original. If you want to you could go through the entire game without ever getting the ability to heal. Not that I would reccomend it but it's awesome that you can do that.
+You have 2 characters that are stuck in your party and a third slot open for a monster that you have tamed. You can tame most of the monsters in the game and every monster has its own abilites and base stats. I say base stats because you could have 2 "Behemoth" monsters but level them up completely differently. You can also find a lot of cosmetic items for the monsters, including hats. Each monster also has a unique limit break ability.
+There is loads of optional content. Through the story you will be collecting "Fragments" to unlock new locations and time periods. You get these items by doing side quests and just finding them in chests. When I finished the game I only had 36 out of 160. So if you want to, you could spend a lot of time with this game.
+This time around they included some actual graphics options. Including resolution, MSAA up to 16x and shadow resolution.
+The game CAN run at 60 fps but...
+There is dual audio, I played it in english and everyone was fine except for Lightning. She has less peronality than Microsoft Sam. Good thing Lightning only has about 10 minutes of screentime in the entire game.
+Weapon system is better than in the original. In the original you could upgrade your weapons meaning that if you just kept upgrading your original weapon you had no reason to ever buy a new one. And because of the effort and gil needed to upgrade a single weapon you literally had no reason to ever get a new weapon. In this one you get access to new weapons in the shop the further you progress in the game, some are just a straight up upgrade, stat wise anyway. But other weapons have special abilites stuck to them but these require some additional items aswell as gil to be bought. All in all it's a straightforward system but at least it works, unlike the original.
+Game leads nicely into XIII-3.
-Time travel elements are very "It's magic I ain't got to explain♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;, but then the characters waste a lot of time in cutscenes talking about how it works and it just ends up wasting time.
-The combat is still very much a case of just switching your classes to match the situation and pressing the "Auto" button. There was only one time in the game where I actually selected commands and that was because I was against an enemy that had health regen but my character refused to cast poison with auto.
-You can't control your characters in battles. This can be really annoying in a lot of different sittuations, like when you have somebody as a tank with the ability to divert enemy attention to themselves and the party just stands around really close to each other, as a result everyone gets hit regardless. This defeats the entire purpose of a system that works in a 3D space.
-Story was okay at best but a lot of time was wasted on nonsensical time travel ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and in the end it just came down to "X thing is a paradox, we must kill/fix it!". X often being just a random boss enemy in the area. The story was more interesting when it focused on the stories of Ciaus, Yuel, Serah and Noel.
-The game has very unstable framerate. I never dropped under 30 though, nonetheless it can be very annoying to watch as the framerate jumps all over the place.
- The game crashed at least once every 2 hours. The biggest time lost as a result was 1 hour. Regardless, this was very annoying and by doing a short google search I can see that I am not the only one with this issue.
-This time around there are minigames, something lacking from the original but all of them are luck based and some are even locked behind DLC.
I must admit I wasn't excpecting much out of this game but all the non-linearity and freedom came as a big surprise.
With loads of optional content, much improved combat system and non-linearity in almost every aspect, this game is actually worth playing unlike the original. As long as you are fine with a combat system that is very simplistic and a story that makes little to no sense.
I will likely edit this review soon if I forgot to talk about something.

you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

Gameplay is fast, brutal and fun.
The maps play around with gravity, which means that there are certain zones which have a lot less gravity. Navigating through them may take skill but it's fun.
Characters may seem boring or generic at first., but let me assure you: they're not, they're likable with lots of personality...
The Law and the Breakers are the two factions. They both have the same classes which are the same gameplay wise.
You can play as a crazy robot who's LED face plays pong and who has some nice voice lines like "R-R-R you not entertained?!" or "Keep the change, your filthy animal!"
His name is "Nash" and he's the Juggernaut of the Breakers.
The Law's Juggernaut is named A.E.G.I.S., he's a robot too.. and he strongly reminds me of Robocop, since his voice lines have the same amount of "coolness". For example: You kill someone with the kick and he goes: "Bullets are precious. Breakers are not!"
The characters swear and make fun of the enemies etc... even the announcer says things like "Point B is a fnckin' warzone!" or "Double motherfnckin' kill!"
Everyone has abilities and an ultimate. Everyone is useful and everyone should be able to win a 1v1, of course some classes have it a little harder, but it's no "Mercy vs. Roadhog".
Precision, movement etc matter.
No pay to win. You can get cosmetics through stash drops, which are lootboxes. If you get doubles, you get in game money. You can not purchase in game money, but you can get more stash drops with real money.
With Patch 1.4 you get 50coins per day, if you log in.
The skins look very neat. There are weapon skins, character skins, stickers that you can slap on your weapons (unlimited use) and kick decals.
Kick decals are like sprays: You kick a wall and your decal is being sprayed onto the wall.
If you kill an enemy player with a kick, he will see your kick decal over his screen throughout his whole respawn time.
Blindfire: You can shoot behind you without looking. Helps you fly around in zero gravity.
The soundtrack is great.
9/10

Summary: Great game, well worth full price, would be an absolute steal on sale!
The premise and play of LawBreakers seems like one done on several different occasions and upon watching gameplay seems to be nothing extraordinary. However, it is a fun game and one which genuinely requires skill, but can still be played by non-hard-core gamers with the same level of enjoyment.
It has a few drawbacks, the most mentioned being the player base which is somewhat lacking unfortunately. This isn't a major issue and certainly not as prevalent as has been made out by some comments. The only time it became an actual issue for me was early morning (5am-8am) where the number of players on both the EU and American servers were prohibitively low.
Another "drawback" is more a suggestion that there aren't a lot of maps, which I thought would be a major issue for replayability, but trying to master the 8 heroes makes a majority of the gameplay fun regardless of the same-y repetition of the maps.
On the whole though, LawBreakers is totally worth it for a fun, easy to play hard to master fps. A very good revamp of the quake-style arena shooter!

You played FFXIII and want to know if this one is worth playing?  That depends on what you did and didn't like about XIII
I'll compare the two games some to give you an idea of how the sequel changed up the formula.
Linearity:
XIII-2 is much more open than the first game.  Each area can be explored and has hidden objects to discover, there are also occasionally different enemy types for different parts the zones.  There are less unique locations than the first game, but I think the openness of the areas makes up for it.
Party members:  There are 2.  The first game had 6 characters to choose from and while many parts forced you into specific configurations of party members, there were times that you had a choice of how to compose your party.  XIII-2 only has two human party members and the third slot is for monster party members that you capture and level up sort of like pokemon.  There is quite a bit of depth to this mechanic, but I still would have liked some extra speaking party members.
Combat:  Largely unchanged.  Big improvements are the ability to continue fighting a battle when your party leader dies, and the ability to change leader mid-battle.  Some of the SAB and SYN abilities appear to be missing, making those roles a bit more simplified(Those skills may be present in monster party members that I haven't used yet)
Monsters are not sitting out of the world in this game, at least for the most part.  They act more like the random encounters of older JRPGs, with the exception that you can still occasionally avoid them after they have spawned by running away.  I feel like this is a better system because it mostly prevents you from farming a single enemy over and over like the optimal CP grind in the first game which ultimately led to me giving up on its endgame.
Crafting:  I disliked the crafting system in the previous game, largely because it wouldn't tell you which items were required to improve weapons, and it had no indicator to show when a piece of equipment was at it's max level or could be upgrading another rank.  XIII-2 has solved these problems but also has a much simpler system which lost some of the depth that could have been.  A vendor sells you new weapons in exchange for crafting materials and occasionally an old weapon too.
Story:
I found FFXIII's story to be enjoyable but also easily forgettable.  I didn't think any of the characters were well written or very likable(except for maybe Saszh) and only a few months later I barely remember any of the major plotpoints.  XIII-2 is much the same case, There are parts of the story that I liked, but the character dialogue was mostly bland and often grating.  In particular I found one of the main characters very unlikable, and with no option to remove him from my party I had to play the entire game with him.
Endgame:  I find that I am enjoying XIII-2's end game much more than that of the previous game.  The path to max level is almost over and I have just been going around doing quests for fragments with barely any true grinding. There is a lot to do with the monster party members that I have not done yet; that appears like it could get grindy later on.  I haven't fought any of the hardest bosses in either game yet, but for XIII-2 I do think I will end up doing that, while I don't know if I can stand the grind in XIII long enough to get there.
New Things:
Puzzles:  There are some puzzles that are required to be completed in certain areas, and for the most part I found these ranged for boring and unenjoyable to frustrating and unenjoyable.  I think at this point that I've finished all of the puzzles in the game, and I didn't find one of them to be enjoyable at all, and I enjoy playing puzzle games occasionally.
Hidden objects:  There are a lot of hidden objects to find in the game for 100% completion.  Fragments are mostly tied to quests but occasionally hidden throughout the game world.  There is an indicator to show you how many you are missing in a particular area, and I've been enjoying hunting these down.  I find them much more interesting than the less varied Ci'eth stone missions from the first game.
Then there are the wild artefacts which I ended up hating.  These are hidden objects that must be found to access certain areas.  Most of them I found during regular play, but after beating the game I still had a few that I hadn't found, and with no indicator hinting at which zone they might be in, I had to mindlessly comb every area I had been to looking for the last few.  I finally did manage to find them all, but I found the task very frustrating.  It feels like the developers might have been assuming that players would just go online for a guide for these, but I prefer to avoid outside assistance when possible.
Overall I enjoy it and if you enjoyed the first game you may very well enjoy this one as well.  It still has many of the flaws that drove away hardcore Final Fantasy fans, but some of those were fixed.

Despite the best efforts of Lightning and her crew, the world is once again in danger. Now it's up to Serah, mysterious traveler Noel, and moogling Mog to make things right. Despite putting 50+ hours into FFXIII-2, I'm about as equipped to discuss the plot as somebody who has never even heard of the game....or Final Fantasy.
I guess this title could be compared to previous Square games like Chrono Trigger & Chrono Cross. The player must pass through various times and dimensions, alleviating paradoxes, fighting monsters, and getting pushed around by some jerk named Caius. There are dark moments (like Chrono), but it sticks to 3-4 characters, instead of attempting to juggle 300 (like Cross). I guess that's part of what got me through this game. When the story doesn't make a lot of sense, at least you can watch the friendship between Noel & Serah grow, and realize that they're getting by despite the heaps of BS being tossed their way.
The battle-system is straight outta FFXIII, but with numerous changes. The most obvious is that the third party member is always a monster. Pocket Monster fans are going to find dozens of creatures to recruit throughout their journey. Monsters are strengthened via materials, and can be infused with others to gain additional skills. Admittedly, I was a little disappointed that monsters adhere to the FFXIII system. For example, I recruited a Giant Cactaur, but he's not going around using 100,000 needles on everything. He's a synergist so he sticks entirely to buffs.  I know I know, the paradigms are essential to winning in FFXIII, but I just...oh well. On the bright side, monsters tend to have unique skills that make them more effective in a given situation than Serah & Noel.
On the whole, FFXIII-2 is a fair bit easier than its predecessor. This is mostly due to the fact that you're actually not limited in how much you can grind. Since this game is non-linear, you could go to various optional areas and amass a ton of levels, making the story-battles trivial. Aside from a handful of post-game & DLC fights, you'll have to limit yourself if you want a challenge.
Speaking of levels, the Crystarium got a convoluted revamp. You cash in points for stat bonuses: +3 to magic, +20 to HP, etc. Over time you unlock and level all six roles, but your level 99 stats can vary. There's a "perfect" guide floating around to help you figure this mess out. While I ended up using guides to have a chance at 100%ing this game, I merely stuck to leveling what I thought would make sense. For Serah, I leveled Ravager on the large nodes to boost her magic, and with Noel, commando. I probably goofed somewhere and cost myself a good 30+ points in an essential stat, but I've done most everything in the game, so it isn't that much of an issue.
In order to get all 160 fragments, you're going to be doing a lot of exploring, grinding, puzzles, and stupid pet tricks. Mog is capable of finding hidden items, and can also be thrown to reach faraway objects (which you might need a guide to find). The puzzles are almost entirely mini-games. As anyone who has played FFXIII-2 will tell you, the clock puzzles SUCK. Most of them aren't that difficult and can be brute-forced. But there are a few that all but require a website for calculating solutions. Either take advantage of the tools the internet has made available to you, or watch in horror as the pacing dies a painful death, your choice. The grind isn't quite as bad as FFXIII, but expect to spend a lot of time in the Archylte Steppe fighting the same monsters for potent orbs, essences, & crystals.
After completing the game, all of the major DLC is unlocked. In the Coliseum, players will engage in battle with numerous fan-favorites, and a few characters from FFXIII. I find it amusing that one of the opponents should have been in a boss-fight in FFXIII, but it never happened because reasons. I won't spoil it, but if you played FFXIII, then you already know who I'm talking about. You'll want to fight these battles not just because they're quite good, but also because you can recruit everyone you defeat. The next DLC adventure is a solo battle between Lightning and Caius. Lightning has a specific set of roles, and is expected to switch between them constantly. For example, she can use the knight role to become impervious to damage, and it's necessary to avoid getting one-shotted by a handful of Caius's attacks. Since this DLC doesn't require Serah & Noel, you can do it immediately after completing the game to gain a powerful ally.
Sazh's DLC adventure takes place in a Casino. He's trapped in limbo, and his son is nowhere to be found, only by gambling can they hope to be re-united. While the concept sounds sufficiently dark, this isn't exactly Gambling Apocalypse Sazh. The goal is to acquire 30 fortune medals, which can be done in less than 30 minutes by playing Texas Hold'em. The casino is also available in the main-game, though all N&S can do is play slots and race their chocobos. Once I got the items I required, I never went back.
I'll admit, I enjoyed my time with this game more than FFXIII. Noel, Serah, and Caius are some of the better JRPG heroes and villains I've seen. Trying to make sense of everything is headache-inducing, but the revamped crystarium and monster-raising provided excellent distractions. The combat itself also recieved some slight improvements, like paradigm  shifting being noticeably faster. The various areas/times/dimensions being more than a narrow corridor definitely helped, though the quests tend to be of the fetching variety.
The port still could have been a lot better though. I'm not nearly as frustrated about it now as was when I started the PC version, but Square-enix isn't getting a passing grade for this one. FFXIII and its sequel deserve better ports, but I expect Lightning Returns to be at about the same quality as the previous two PC entries; superior to the console versions, and not much else.

Your career is slipping through your fingers, you can't afford to pay your rent, and the person you once thought would love you forever has walked out of your life. When things go so wrong so fast, it's human nature to obsess over what you could have done differently. Story-heavy RPG Always Sometimes Monsters asks what we can do instead, and specifically what choices we will make when we try to set things right.
Your character's goal arrives in the post on the second day of the main story: an invitation to the wedding of their now ex-partner, in one month's time. To make it there, you'll walk from place to place, visiting and talking to dozens of different characters via some basic top-down RPG interaction and managing a simple inventory of things like the food you'll need to keep up your stamina.
You'll have to balance the need for enough money or favours to get across the country with the time it takes to earn them, and face the consequences of that balancing act along the way. The day before the invitation arrives acts as a neat demonstration of that process: your landlord threatens to make you homeless unless you can bring him $500 in overdue rent by the end of the day, which you'll discover is only manageable if you do things like steal from your trusting elderly neighbour or pick people's pockets during a shift as a cloakroom attendant.
Later on, you'll be able to opt for low-pay but legal manual labour, which Vagabond Dogs has made deliberately slow and tedious for the player to ensure it's about as tempting as it is in real life. But most choices in the game are less obvious. Consequences are unpredictable in this world and aim to reflect real life situations to some degree, where chatting to colleagues at your temp job about the guy you've replaced might be enough to stop him from shooting himself.
Sometimes these options lack the choice that tally with your instincts or sense of logic, however. Always Sometimes Monsters cannot help but fall prey to this – you can't just phone a friend for help on that first day – but also uses it to its advantage in flashbacks that prevent progress until you make the choice your character has technically already made. You can't change the past, is the obvious point being made here, but it is dramatically effective. The flashbacks also play a crucial role in making the protagonist relatable.
The chance that you'll relate to your character is also increased by the additional choice of their gender, race, and sexuality. In a clever prologue scene set at a party, you choose from a range of potential protagonists via a publisher choosing which writer to sign, and while their backstories are the same the reactions of other characters will differ. Play as a black lesbian, and you might experience a doctor accusing you of playing the race card, a 'friend' ascribing your apparent lack of fashion sense to your sexuality, and plenty of everyday sexism. “I still expect a hard day's work from you,” says the warehouse foreman, “Even if you are a woman!”
The low-res RPG Maker aesthetic might seem at odds with the often stark subject matter, but the limitations of the tool help rather than hinder the game. Limited by little more than the amount of words the writer could produce and the player's imagination, Always Sometimes Monsters is able to tackle everything from homophobia to drug abuse to suicide with credibility. The focus is on the writing, sometimes overly dramatic but always engaging, and on the many branching paths down which your decisions can take you.
It's refreshing to see this kind of real-life subject matter explored in a choice-based game, and presented in a way that's competitive with the best written of those types of stories. Always Sometimes Monsters' vision of the real world can be painful to experience at times, but only in a way that demonstrates the level of craft in developing this strong tale about modern life.

Oh my lord! What an experience I just had with this game! The finest awesomeness ever! Unforgettable! I am so hyped, finally I completed this incredible masterpiece. I will quickly mention that my review is independent, honest and true and I was not influenced in any possible way to give a positive review. Mark Of The Ninja is everything that Assassin's Creed frenchise should have been. If I have to describe this game it is if Hitman, Assassin's Creed and Little Big Planet had a baby and than fed the baby steroids for extra boost. Yep, crazy, right! So you are this young ninja dude that is climbing up the ranks and with each completed mission you get a tattoo and new ability. You have to go trough the craziest ever mazes full of enemies and traps to get to your destination. You have a hot babe ninja for a guide and she constantly gives you tips and tricks, so you need to pay attention when she is arround. Along the way you become capable of swinging from post to post like Spider-Man, you can launch poisoned arrows, hallucinogenic darts with various side effects, smoke bombs, deadly beatles who will eat your enemies, you will lockpick, teleport yourself, slow time and many more. Oh boy, you will solve puzzles, avoid lazer beams, test your ninja skills and many more. The levels are very colorful beautifully hand painted and the animation of the npcs is very detailed and satisfactory. You get to play in various settings like The Metropolitan area, the Suers, The Metro Train area, The Arabic Desert, The Japanese Temples, The Beautiful Gardens and so forth. The cut scenes are in the form of an animated movie which is super cool! There are few characters that you really get to know and they have a complicated personas - nothing is black and white but various shades of grey. I am really fascinated with how well the space in the game is utilized - it is a sidescrolling game but the way the world is created leaves you with the impression that everything is 3 dimensional. One of the best games I have ever played. Super Mario, Little Big Planet and Mark Of The Ninja are the holy trinity of sidescrollers for me personally. I do realize that there are plenty more games out there just as good but these are my top 3 for now. Thank You and do yourselves the favor and play this game already!

I haven't played "Stealth" games before, because I assumed they would be focused on frustrating the player -- and I want my games to be fun. Mark of the Ninja, however, delivered just that: it wasn't difficult do play, owing both to the level design and the game showing you things like the range of audio events. There was really only one thing I couldn't figure out -- what exactly the guards can see in light.
The story wasn't the greatest highlight ever, but OK enough -- and I like having a story that somehow connects the levels and tells you why you start at one end and try to reach the other.
As far as gameplay goes -- if you can accept that everything has vents that nobody knows about, that guards are carefully positioned to leave a path for you, or that guards are generally dumb so they keep staring at a broken light hoping for a relevation or don't notice that their colleagues start disappearing, then the game has everything to make you feel like a sneaky ninja as you bypass guards and security systems, or take them down silently.
Presentation is also top-notch. The game may be 2D and generally set in dark areas, but it looks great regardless. Also, players can easily spot stuff they can interact with. The voice acting, music and audio is also great -- and the last level gives you a special music treat.

One of the best stealth titles out there, Mark of the Ninja holds its ground with its unique gameplay and overall design. The artwork of the game is blended perfectly with the polished stealth mechanics. With many devices in your ninja arsenal and the many ways to dispatch your foes, Mark of the Ninja will keep you busy and sucked in for a while.

One of the greatest PC RPGs ever made - and the fact that it sits right at the border between "old-school" and "new-school" Bioware generations makes it all the better. Combat is best done (especially in the harder fights) using the "pause and plan" method, which won't appeal to everyone. But the story is incredible (and seriously emotional by the end) and the voice acting is first-rate (Claudia Black is the stand-out as Morrigan). You actually CARE about the characters in this story, both good and "evil".
Even if you've played this on console before, buy the PC version - it was designed for PC, and the PC version is the only one Bioware themselves made. It's actually quite lovely visually on PC - though obviously time has made it look arguably "dated", it has its own unique art style that's miles ahead of the console-driven sequels. I'm especially fond of the intricate UI on the PC version, which is miles ahead of the "console compatible" UIs in the later Dragon Age games.
The DLC is not needed to fully enjoy the game, though if on one of the regular 75%-off sales, grab it for some extra diversion. "Awakenings" wasn't written by the same team as the main game and it shows.

Prince of Persia 2008. Absolutely stunning game.
The graphics still hold up extremely well thanks to it's style (and doesn't require a monster of a PC to run at 60+ frames per second). I found myself going "wow that looks gorgeous" throughout the whole game. The style features a wide variety of vibrant environments.
The OST in the game is also amazing and I did not find one track that I thought "meh I don't particulary like this one but I like the rest..." unlike most other games. The OST is for the most part orchestrated and fits with the vibrant graphic style perfectly.
The dialogue between the two main characters the Prince and Elika is for the most part very amusing and you ; I found myself grinning for long time after the actual conversations had ended. It consists of a lot of optional conversations which generally after you reach new area or have completed an action in that area. Other than the constant very tongue-in-cheek humour between these two characters, there are of course the serious talks that are related to the storyline and these are great too. The lore isn't exactly that original or creative but it's still decent and makes for a pleasant experience as you progress the story.
The story itself is not a linear story such as oh this happens then that happens all the time. It's moreso of there are four paths that you have to clear in order to get to the last boss. Each path has 6 areas (not including the intersection tunnels which really could be considered areas on their own I guess); you can do any of these areas you want at any time provided you have the powers available to progress those areas. Each area has it's own dialogue and specific OST track to go with it.
The platforming isn't generally hard but you'll find the bits that are "hard" are just literally a bunch of simple platforming but stringed together so that there is a higher chance of human error pressing the wrong button. As you progress each of the four paths you will get a new obstacle to avoid when progressing each new area. I personally like that there isn't anything that is "hard" that could possibly annoy you.
The combat seems a little left out really, there isn't much to it and many say that you cannot die, however this is false really because you can "die" it just plays a short cutscene when you are about to with Elika saving you. Once you "die", the monster or boss generally recovers most of it's hp so there isn't anything to complain about there. The combat just consists of blocking, deflecting (blocking at the right time) and then using combos which involve both the Prince and Elika which can do a LOT of damage to bosses.
10/10 for me, best game I've played in a while. I did not find anything that really bugged me and the "problem" many people  say about the difficulty wasn't there for me as it felt just right; it just meant for me that I didn't have anything that I constantly lost to and it was a smooth playthrough that I enjoyed. The dialogue is fantastic for people who love cheeky and sarcastic humour. The graphics are stunning even in today's standards which is very suprising for a 2008 game. The OST is great and the story is enjoyable.

I tried to like this game , I really did. But i cannot recommend it.
At its core it is a platformer with push puzzles  , traps and physics.
Problem is , the difficulty stems not from the game design but rather from the lack of it.
Some puzzles require you to jump on chains but the chains move without logic , sometimes catapultig you randomly around the room , into spikes.
There are purple mushrooms that act like springs , but they seem to ignore gravity and intertia and just catapult you as they will into spikes.
The final straw was a room of cannon enemies , their shots bounce like a pool ball , completely unpredictable , and explode on top of that.
I've had the broken mechanics work in my favor at times when i tried to push a treasure chest up a lift to distract some knights , it got stuck , bounced off a wall and crushed both of them.
Another time a cannonball took out three enemies for no reason , they all just bounced into one another and died without taking any fall damage.
If you can forgive frustrating mechanics the concept is unique enough to check out , but right now , as far as I am concerned , the challenge  is not designed as much as a chaotic physics engine that doesn't know whether it's coming or going.

Why should you play another puzzle-platformer? Because Goblins & Grottos feels genuinely fresh. The "but you play as the goblin" angle didn't fully sell me when I first heard of the game, though I was intrigued. But as I played the game, I realised the devs have really embraced that angle, making a satire of dungeon crawlers and MMO culture in general.
It's genuinely funny, witty, and it's very rewarding to drop an explosive barrel on heroes who are acting as obnoxious and ignorant as real players. The early "PvP zone" level stood out to me.
It's actually believable that you're playing as an NPC goblin inside an MMO game. A bit like Toy Story in that way. It feels believable but embraces the silliness at the same time.
If you want a few more laughs to your platformer, this is for you.

My measure of a great game is when it's buggy as hell, and seemingly unfinished in others, but it's still so original and fun you can't stop playing it.   As of writing this, they're on v 1.0.4 and, it's my favorite new platformer since Broforce.
Unlike BroForce or most other platformers, don't go into this one expecting to massacre enemies. I mean, you do massacre enemies (and friends) but in a long, drawn out sort of way, because you play as a tiny goblin with no weapons and only you Spiderman-like ability to cling to walls. (you're so weak, you can't even open up doors) It's basically Trapt or Tecmo's Deception, in platformer format.... with muffins.
There are pretty much only three ways to kill something in this game, crush them, make them fall, or blow them up. Every enemy in the game will one-hit kill you, but lucklily you can endlessly respawn at the beginning of the level or from restore statues scattered throughout (which gradually wear out and break, encouraging you to not screw up too often)
Pros:
* Fun stealth/trap-based platformer, where you play as the weakest monster in the dungeon.

* Very open ended exploration in a dungeon feels bigger than it is. There are lots of path choices, and it doesn't feel like the game locks you into a set course or holds your hand. You just keep exploring until you find the exit. It is possible to totally screw yourself by pushing the wrong crate or failing to take out an enemy with a barrel of explosives, but you can always reset and try again, and *most* of the time when you spectacularly screw something up, you're only depriving yourself of a cool secret area and some tasty muffins.
* Incredibly funny, and absolutely chocked full of secrets. Watching the other denizens of the dungeon interact is often nearly as much fun as playing the game itself.
* You can ride a sheep *AND* design your own levels!
Cons (as of v.1.0.4):
* Controls are slow and annoying in parts, especially with the "cling" and "throw" buttons on a controller, that can't be remapped (currently). It's also very hard to anticipate where objects will land with the throw mechanics, and there's no visual wind-up "tell" that you are actually about to throw an object, or how far it's going to travel. It would also be nice to be able to throw/drop while clinging, or when standing next to other objects. (being unable to throw or drop a bomb close enough to a brick you want to destroy because there happens to be a brick on the floor.) There's also no way to bring up the menu or restart the level from the controller.
* Physics/graphics fails. Mainly invoving projectiles, chains, and bombs. Nothing game-breaking but you do sometimes end up with explosions or projectiles flying off to get stuck in walls, or a perpetual sparking bomb animation that never goes away.
