This game is kind of deceiving. The first time you start off there is a long cutscene explaining what happened previously followed by another cutscene introducing a mission in Dubai. I had the feeling that the game would have a lot of these kinds of missions. The prerendered Dubai cutscene makes the game look "fresh" as you would expect a game from 2016 to look, the characters look more detailed, their hair looks more realistic, then you go to Dubai and the graphics look pretty good, there are subtle things like dust and pieces of cloth waving in the wind that give the game some more detail. After the mission is done you go to Prague and the difference in quality starts seeping through.
My first thought was, we waited 5 years and all we got was this? You're playing Adam Jensen again, which had me worried from the start. The graphics may look good, like the Prague itself and the different objects lying about the street, the furniture in houses, and the gun textures but the character models don't and it's very jarring. Everytime someone talks it's like watching a dubbed movie because it never looks like their voices are timed properly with their lips, and to top it off their mouths don't ever seem to move in a natural way. The further the game goes on I started to notice that they were using repetive character movements during cutscenes, this game is meant to be a big budget game yet they obviously never any motion capture to make human movements seem a bit more natural, like most games have been doing since 2014. Everyone starts to look robotic after a while and it makes the cutscenes extremely boring to watch, not to mention that it's made worse by the constant over the shoulder camera shots during dialogue, surely they could have put more time into adding some visual flare to these conversations.
These problems are made even worse when I started to notice the very prominent artstyle in the game, there is great use of lighting to add atmosphere at night, outdoors and in night clubs. There are a lot of stand out features throughout the city like monuments, shop fronts and some giant pills that lead into an underground metro. This is definately what the game does best, and the atmosphere is enhanced even more when paired with the soundtrack which accentuates the desperateness of Prague's citizens and adds a very cold, empty vibe to the city.
The combat is like Human Revolution again, though they changed something to do with energy so it's a bit easier to perform takedowns now. Overall the game feels very much the same as Human Revolution, there are a lot of the same abilities and weapons. Usually there is a big jump in quality or gameplay design between sequels but this seems far too similair for a game that was released 5 years later. It is more like a game that should have been released 2 years after the first with how little it has changed. It actually is more like an expansions in many ways.
The story almost seems non existant, I don't really remember much of it and the villain gets introduced half way through the game for whatever reason. It feels like they tried too hard to connect things to the original Deus Ex to a point where it came off as fan service. In comparison to Deus Ex, Mankind Divided's setting seems too serious since the segregation between Humans and Augs seems to be mirroring current events, like the writer was being very on the nose with his message. It's not that bad, but they decided to have more of a spotlight on the Illuminati this time around and it is very reminiscent of how they were in Deus Ex, which is bad for this game because it was always an over the top element to the original. It is very much like the Syndicate from the X-Files, which is great, and one of the characters in Mankind Divded even looks like the Well-Manicured Man. The problem is these 2 elements clash with eachother because they tone is so different, one is being deathly serious and the other is near satire.
Unfortunately there are only 2 other missions like the one in Dubai, they felt very new and something that these games needed, it let Jensen become part of a team and the integrate dialogue well without it becoming montonous. I liked the atmosphere of the hub, Prague, but I found it boring to play through due to the dialogue and the side quests, which felt more like something from a Bethesda Fallout game than a Deus Ex game, some of the quests were very surreal but it was yet another clash with the miserable tone set by the aug incident. One thing I really liked was the choices in the game weren't black and white, some of them had consequences and others prevented you from finding a way to complete both options, which meant that one choice wasn't necessarily the right one, but more about how strongly you felt about the choice. There was even a choice between which mission you wanted to take on, as it was time sensitive, so if you ever want to play that other mission you have to play a new game. This aspect was actually kind of bad because one of them wasn't really related to much of anything and the other has a lot of secret lore that is important to Jensen, and the series as a whole, It was really a dumb decision to make people choose between this, with the missable lore and the fact that people were complaining the game was too short.
In the end, it's hard to say whether I liked it or not because the game seems to have been worked on by people who put varying ammounts of effort into their respective fields, and it never ends up becoming a cohesive whole. I don't think I've ever played a game like this before, it's an anamaly, actually. I wouldn't recommend this as something fun to play, but if you're interested in experiencing how unusual this game is from a design stand point then it would be worth checking out.

If you approach the situation with more stealth it becomes much easier, but the game wasn't really built for a purely stealthy experience so it's not as smooth as you'd want it to be playing that way. I really want to like Ronin.  Its concept is unique and its presentation polished.  But its gameplay leaves something to be desired.  Its controls lack precision, and communication with the player is imperfect at best.
One of the ubiquitous "helpful hints" the game gives you continuously is "The jump arc is a lie," which is really the sort of thing that ought to be established up front and in detail rather than as a one-line random hint.  Sometimes the game will not let you project a jump arc onto a surface, obviously preventing you from jumping at all.  Other times it will let you project an arc, but when you attempt the jump you will be interrupted by the corner of a platform or an enemy.
In hindsight these limitations make sense, but in practice they are enormously frustrating, and representative of the sort of difficulty, rather than challenge, that the desigers of Ronin programmed into the game.  Because it is obviously intentional -- this is not a game that is rough-edged because of oversight or laziness.  Ronin is a game that is rough-edged because its developers wanted it to be rough-edged.
By the time you are ten or so levels into the game, you will probably begin to understand how to do what you want to do in Ronin perfectly every time, using the tools the designers have given you.  But if you have the will to get that far you are a more patient gamer than me.  Ronin is a whole lot of stick and not nearly enough carrot.  It's not that I hated the game -- I just don't care enough about it to keep trying to play it successfully.

This game started off well. It introduced me to mechanics and techniques that felt intuitive and fresh, despite being heavily inspired by the likes of Gunpoint. It put forward a nice challenge and trial and error gameplay where I still felt like I was learning. The plot seemed interesting, with targets that had personality and a backstory. Enemies were varied and interesting to approach. I enjoyed grappling most of all, swinging out of a line of sight remained thrilling throughout. Even the bonus objectives were fun to achieve and lead to good rewards that assisted with later levels.
However, my opinion on this game has drastically changed as of late due to one level in particular. The Officer level is actually the worst thing I've had to experience in a video game. I have not been so infuriated in my life. From my hours, I could guess that about 50% of those are from this level. Every once in a while I boot this game up to try again and leave more frustrated than before. Allow me to explain.
This level starts off normally, with clever platforming required to dispose of three or four guards. The second checkpoint is where this game loses its "innovative" mechanics and its "gripping" gameplay. Featuring upwards of ten guards, this courtyard has almost no grappling points besides the buildings on either side. This whole middle section is prone to being covered in bullet lines, with at least four being double turn shots. The amount of times I have been trapped in this part is almost impossible to count. It also features the "boss" of the level, the previously mentioned Officer. His attacks are telegraphed with a red line as per usual and yet he can only travel a set distance. For this reason, he may only travel 3/4 of the line before stopping and becoming vulnerable. This leads to a large amount of guess work as to whether you will die or not. Allow me to clarify, I have killed the Officer multiple times, opening up the exit to me. Yet, the bonus objectives prompt me to kill all the enemies, something I have yet to achieve. Even worse, this game has a Lockdown counter that starts when out of range or if a specific enemy is present. While this may not be such a big deal normally, the other bonus objective is not to trigger Lockdown. At this point I am seriously considering never playing this game again, and I feel anyone willing to unlock all the skill points will feel the same way after trying to finish this level.
Final Verdict:
The game is sound intially but later levels reveal its shortcomings in an infuriating way. People who fly through it without needing these abilities/skill points may have more fun, but completionists will likely find it difficult to perservere.

Parts of the game were really frustrating. For example, having to pay $10 for one sandwich and needing to eat 10 to fill up your stamina bar and the frequency you need to do that. I ate 5 sandwiches in the afternoon and when I went to bed in the evening it said going to sleep would be risky since I was starving. I figured, "Eh, people can live for several days without eating and I gorged myself like 3 hours ago, no big whoop." I died. I DIED CUZ I HADN'T EATEN BEFORE BED AND I HAD EATEN 5 SANDWICHES NOT THAT LONG AGO WUT?! T_T Save early and save often all the time. If you play this game, save like you've never saved before.
Another frustrating part was the repetition when attempting to earn money so buy bus tickets that rival airfare from North America to Europe and to buy the equivalent of Thanksgiving feasts for a midnight snack to prevent dying on someone's lousy couch. Getting shafted repeatedly by various characters in game and being blamed was also frustrating. For a vague example, Friend A makes bad choices because you didn't do something that wasn't really your responsibility but you get blamed for the tragic outcome even though it was really someone else's fault in the first place. Again, not sure if this is to illustrate life is really crappy or give you a headache. I think it accomplished both. Another annoying thing is boxing. Fisticuffs. Pugilism. Cuz some people just won't take money for auto parts and prefer punches to smackeroos? Alright, gonna do what I gotta do and hate it. I really got tired of playing about halfway through and just wanted to finish as fast as possible, survive all the BS, and after all that headache, win back the love of my life. The dialog is at times really awful. I can't say I enjoyed having my character called a "panty waste f*gg*t"or a &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; by an employer. I also didn't enjoy some turf warriors saying they needed to protect their turf from a "pack of n*gg*rs" despite one of said turf warriors having a dark complexion. Can't say I thought it was particularly necessary for some old guy telling the pawn broker he wouldn't let him "jew him". Seriously, you're not edgy or gritty. You're just awful at creating dialog. Yes, maybe they were trying to show how awful the world is again but I think the $10 sandwiches and having the metabolism of a hummingbird while being broker than broke and getting screwed by life repeatedly illustrated that just fine without the bigotted language for no actual story-defining purpose. Stop trying to be "edgy", edgelords.
That said, there were some pros. You could choose your character model and name as well as that of your partner. You could have a same-sex partner if you wanted and other than being called names becuase of it, that's pretty progressive. I'm partially curious if you get called that crap as a straight character. I'm skeptical the dialog varies that greatly between chosen character models given the overall execution of the  game. The premise of the game is really appealing, win back the love of your life cuz your life is an epic soap opera of the absurd. I'm so into that. Ending up in some of the dumbest situations ever imagined? I'm not as into that as I used to be after playing this game. There's a pretty thick line between dumb luck and living the Jerry Springer dream. The game shuffles across that line into Jerry Springer territory pretty quick. I'm really glad I got the ending I wanted and felt all the stupidity and random BS was at least mildly worth it. Closer to the end, I found a helpful community guide

Always Sometimes Monsters is a great little game on RPG Maker about moral choices and modern city survival really.

I don't want to spoil anything, but there are multiple life and death situtations that really just make you wonder who you are and how you deal with others.
This isn't a game for everyone, to be fair. It can become tedious in grinding if you're trying to get the "good" ending. (Which is why I have a new found love for Cheat Engine and the speedhack. ALSO, DON'T EVEN TRY TO CHEAT ENGINE MORE MONEY INTO THE GAME. I tried for hours and it just makes the game crash every time.) This is more of a game for people who like a sense of realistic life choices, and are okay with some tediously boring elements to get to an interesting, albiet also unoriginal, plot line. Really, I just enjoyed it for the moral choices.
I give this game a solid 7.5/10

-who are fans of games like Quake or UT

This game was the first game that I ever owned, and seeing as I was a fan of both LEGO and Star Wars at the time, it was perfect for me.
Time for my in depth analysis of this game that took away all my spare time.
Starting off with the controls, I found them to be fine, especially on a controller. The keyboard controls are kind of bad, but you can change them pretty easily if you want to, so I didn't have any problems. Each button has a function, meaning that eventually if you press everything, you'll get the gist of the game.
You start off in the Mos Eisley Cantina, which acts as the hub world for everything you do. At first there's nothing special about it, but as you progress through the game, you can buy numerous things in the shop, including hints (which are completely useless), characters, extras, and additional gold bricks to add onto your total. Additionally, all of the cutscenes that you view throughout the game will be unlocked for you to view at any time. All of the characters that you unlock will populate the cantina, making you feel like you've really progressed through the story. You can even enter cheat codes if you're lazy and don't want to actually work towards completing the game. There's also a 2 player arcade for messing around with a friend, a bonus area section, a character creator (limited to 2 unique "strangers), and an area outside the cantina that has a place to view minikits, and an area to show your total gold brick progress. This whole area outside can give you a small bit of practice with some of the game's core mechanics that will get shown off more throughout.
Despite all this, you're mostly blocked off starting out, so in order to progress, you need to go into Episode I before doing anything else.
If you weren't already aware, this game is actually a compilation of the 2 previous LEGO Star Wars games, LEGO Star Wars, and LEGO Star Wars II, each of which covered one of the 2 main trilogies that made up the saga. This game mashes these 2 titles and remakes some of the older stages, as well as keeping and reviving some older missions from the original LEGO Star Wars game, plus some new stuff. A majority of this content is in the bonus stages, but there are some additional things that also are unique to this title.
Now to talk about Episode I, this episode is the definitive tutorial chapter. At the beginning of the game, you're forced to enter this stage to continue the game, and within the first level, it introduces you to this games sense of humor, mainly through the cutscenes, which believe me, through my first time seeing most of these, I had a great time with them. It also does a great job of explaining many of this games core mechanics.
These include:
All of these are shown off via hints, but are fairly easily to figure out by oneself. As the stage progresses, it introduces you to tougher, and more versatile enemies that take multiple hits to destroy, and can even take away multiple hearts from your character. The stage isn't very long, only really consisting of 2 main areas, however it shows you numerous things about the game that will be of importance later on.
Upon competing each level you unlock all the additional characters you played as throughout the stage, as well as free play and challenge mode, which both allow you to go back through stages you've finished to explore them as much as possible. The game also shows your progress towards other individual parts of the level such as the minikit progression and if you managed to fill up the True Jedi meter. Completing the stage itself gives you a gold brick, with 2 additional ones being obtained via the minikit and True Jedi meter.
Once the first stage is completed, you are given access to every episode in the saga, so you're allowed to do each episode at your own leisure. You also unlock additional characters to purchase in the shop, such as the different battle droids and the famous Gonk Droid.
Speaking of episodes, they are each structured with six different main story stages, with 4-5 of them being ground levels, and the remaining 1-2 of them using spaceships as means of transport. Each chapter also had a bonus door, which has three options when you enter. One of these involves you using characters you've unlocked to collect 1,000,000 studs in under 5 minutes. The second option involves you using the completed minikits you've collected to do the same thing. Other than display and gold bricks, this is the only place where minikits will actually have an effect on gameplay. The third option is Super Story. Unlike the first two options, Super Story does not give you a gold  brick, but it does give you additional percentage towards 100% completion. In super story you're required to collect 100,000 studs and complete each level of the episode in under an hour. It's a fun challenge, and I find that it's still quite enjoyable.
Back to the Episode I, as it progresses, it continues to introduce more and more concepts that will be important throughout the game. I won't go too in depth about these, but here's a list of the main things it introduces.
Once each Episode is over, it gives you a final story cutscene and shows you the game's credits. Usually I skip the credits, but it's nice to watch it at least once. After this, it gives you your total percentage, and then finally boots you back to the cantina.
Now comes the rest of the episodes, which I'll group into one section mainly because there I ran out of room, and I don't want to have to link to a pastebin to express everything.
The rest of the prequel episodes don't add too much to the table, but give more in depth explorations of space combat like torpedoes, as well as different boss stages.
The original trilogy levels introduce levers and double score zones, each of which are not present at any point in the prequels. Since both trilogies are different games, naturally there are some new things throughout. The original trilogy levels are also longer and more puzzle oriented, allowing for lots more secrets to be hidden throughout stages. It also expands on the usage of torpedoes, using them for nearly every vehicle stage. Overall it has much better gameplay, with better puzzles, better bosses, and more creative and familiar stage layouts.
Once you complete every individual story stage, you are granted access to some of the last few unlockable characters in the game inside of the shop, namely the ghosts and bounty hunters. The ghost characters are invincible versions of Obi-Wan, Anakin, and Yoda that pass through most npc characters and take no damage.
The bounty hunters include Dengar, 4-LOM, and IG-88, which all are required to access the bounty hunter missions, a set of 20 levels outside the cantina where you enter random stages in order to track down random characters throughout the saga. It's basically a bunch of little games of hide and seek that can be completed in about a minute each.
There are numerous other secrets and easter eggs I could talk about, but to not ruin your enjoyment, I won't talk about them.

Wow!  This unassuming little gem is one of the best values out there.  It's a total steal even at full price as it's packed with an enormous amount of content and ship customization.
Ring Runners is essentially an isometric space ship shooter, but boy is it brimming with goodies.  The main campaign consists of over a thousand missions and each one is set up with 30 seconds of storytelling.  The missions have quite a lot of variety to them and only last maybe 5 minutes so this game is great for short bursts.
The ship customization is incredibly deep, yet quite approachable.  All other games should take notes from Ring Runners on how to build a great game with a very simple premise.
This game is quite linear and even when it "opens up" it's still extremely linear, so know that going in.  That said, the ship customization, writing and combat are all top notch.  If you're a fan of games like Escape Velocity or Space Pirates vs Zombies, you should buy this game right now.

Verdict: You're not missing anything, if you don't play this. If you can get it for cheap and are tempted, keep reading.
This is an enjoyable parcour platformer. It won't challenge you all that much, but that's part of the draw. It's more about the flow you experience when you flawlessly make your way around the level in a quick fashion.
The characters are fun to have around with their playful remarks every now and then, but it also has it's dark moments. The distinctive art style is nice to look at.
The combat is kind of repetitive and not much fun. Certainly not the reason to play this game. Don't worry about the widely criticised "you can't die" issue too much though. In earlier PoP games you had to press a button to rewind time, this time they do it for you... no big deal. Again, this is more of a laid back experience.
It sure is short. Most evidently, if you're good at moving around. You'll blast through the levels in no time - but again - it's fun to do so. Especially those parts leading up to the boss fights.
Technically: It doesn't support DirectInput gamepads, only XInput (XB360 pad). The story DLC was only released on consoles. Stereo 3D is bad (everything at almost the same depth).
If all this didn't put you off, do buy it. If you don't expect much, you'll be pleasantly surprised.

One mans opinion TL;DR at bottom.
Its a good game, I wouldnt say overwhelmingly so. Heavily inspired by other good stealth games. Enemies are dog♥♥♥♥♥♥stupid. It gets repetitive fast and its not really a skill game so much as a logical puzzle, once you have learned a level you can very easily beat it either violently or stealthily limiting replayability. Quite cliched. Nothing really unseen or amazing in the items/skill upgrades though whats available is well implemented and fun to use. There are some technique upgrades that could have been included in your repertoire right from the start rather than requiring an upgrade point, not upgrading increases challenge.
Artwork is simple but exquisite. Animation is fairly well done, in areas the movements are amazing and in others theyre kinda shoddy. An example is the flip animation when scaling a wall and mounting a ledge, which when entering a vent looks crap. Entering vents is an action you will be taking rather a lot in this game. So in areas the graphics could have been improved.
Sound - Competently acted, dialog is a bit crap, music is ok. It does the job.
Difficuly - Games biggest weakness, super easy from start to finish with what Id call extreme handholding. Enemies may aswell not have bothered coming in to work, slaughter them like pigs or fly past them like the wind, a mix of stealth and violence will help you get your best speed running time but dont expect any real challenge. Checkpoints are numerous, lives are infinite, make the slightest mistake and you can restart to checkpoint for a perfect run. There is no punishment in this game. Adding 3 lives and a continue right from the start would have been a great choice.
The story - You want a story you read a book.
TL;DR Fun -> Easy -> Repetitive -> Logic puzzle rather than skill -> Worth the money.

TeraBlaster has you controlling a small blue spaceship, shooting red space ships of varying sizes to an ear-throbbing loud techno beat. Even if you turn the volume much lower, the sort of music TeraBlasterpumps in the background gets you excited for your mission: destroying all enemy ships,
If that synopsis seems familiar to you, you may not be surprised to find that this game in many ways resembles Space Invaders and Asteroids; both games were simple in design, but got increasingly difficult as time went on,and the same can be said for TeraBlaster. It becomes harder and harder to stay alive as more and more enemy waves jettison towards you from across the small map. But beware, enemies aren't the only things that can kill you and cause your ship to have an introspective crisis with random quotes, from films like Fight Club or American Psycho. You can also be killed by explosive red boxes if you don't get out of the way in time, they function like red barrels in any other shooter game, though not made nearly as obvious as you're frantically flying across the blue grid like background. The grey boxes are for unlocking certain power ups like speed-ups, bombs and things of that nature. For some reason there's also a “Juiced” system that activates giving the player an area of effect explosion that clears the board of all enemies while you're hiding behind the fallen pieces of the grid. This is actually the best part of the game because it makes you actually think you're in another world, immersing you in this confined war-like setting. In many ways it resembles the film Tron, giving the player a sort of “We are locked in the grid” sort of setting, adding more atmosphere to what they're doing. If there's one thing the game does well, it's the atmosphere, which makes up for what can be an overall lackluster set up.

TL;DR first

Cons:

While the small playerbase is the most glaring issue of the game, it is typical of Arena shooters without a big name like Quake or Unreal Tournament. I believe Lawbreakers is a great game, but unfortunately this primary flaw is enough to stop me from recommending it. The cause of this invovles the non-existent marketing, the smaller-than-ideal market for Arena shooters, and the nature of the game scaring newcomers away. The competitive style often leads to one or two players repeatedly destroying every other player and games in which one team has no hope of winning. You don't have to be over-sensitive to appreciate the option to mute chat from other players as well; people can be annoying. This statement is not to say that the community is really all that toxic. Typically there's that *one* guy who won't shut up. The game would feel more interesting if there were more maps, and perhaps if the low-gravity zones moved periodically as well. The current map design is not bad, but makes the game a little more bland when you run into the same maps in a single play/run. Combined with the very poorly fleshed-out lore and personality of the characters, these issues end up demanding an amount of commitment typical of rogue-likes. That level of commitment works for rogue-likes because they are designed to be played as in and out, but this does not work for a game which requires a time investment for practice. This one is a small issue, but the customization sucks. Most skins are stupid-looking.
I bought the game as I wanted to support the efforts of Boss Key and do not think $30 is an unreaasonable price tag. Many were turned off by the switch from planned F2P to $30, but I wasn't too bothered by it. As a casual player and admitted ragequitter, Lawbreakers is incredibly fun to play. I do not have the reflexes or hand-eye coordination required to be good at this game, but I have noticed my ability improve over time. The game's speed and punishing nature produce a good amount of excitement. I have actually noticed that games in completely different genres feel slower after playing Lawbreakers. The feeling I get when I land a direct hit with rockets and grenades or a fully charged Omega headshot from far away is not one I have been able to get anywhere else. The game does a sufficient job of scratching my competitive itch, even if I have no intention on playing ranked games.
I may update this review later. For now, this is a great game ruined by a poor launch from which I do not see it recovering.
Buy it only if you really have an appreciation for this type of game.

Not the hardest game in the traditional sense of the word because of the known game's take on in-game death, yet in terms of gameplay, story, and artistic vision, it's topnotch. The game is divided up between two different characters. One that you directly control, the Prince, and the other that is a semi-controlled, support character, Elika. As for the gameplay itself, it is divided up into two sections: Platforming, and combat. The platforming is pretty much what you would expect from a 3D platformer, but at a more rhythmic, slower pace than a blisteringly fast one like most 3D platfomers out there. The combat more so resembles that of 3D fighting games such as Soul Calibur than what you would expect from a 3D action game. Yet just like the platfoming itself, the combat has a strict rhythmic combo system that makes it all come together, and a joy, when your combos string together properly. Besides the two main sections of the game, you also have the task of collecting the sole in-game collectibles called "light seeds". These light seeds more or less act as experience points: Unlocking new abilities, new areas, as well as progressing the overall story. While it may be tedious at times for those who don't enjoy collecting, it isn't too bad because of the game's excellent platforming making it a pleasure just to move around. The last noteworthy thing is the game's superb graphical style. Even today, in 2014, the game still looks absolutely jaw-dropping with an excellent artistic direction that makes the game looks almost like that of a living, breathing, painting. The same praise can be given to the game's soundtrack as well with it's relaxing scores, to the more active ones.
Overall, in my opinion, Prince of Persia (2008) is an excellent game in every sense of the word, and if you don't mind an easier, more relaxing game than it's predecessors, then there is a lot to love here. Yet even if the toned-down difficulty should turn you off, it still shouldn't deter you entirely from what is an excellent experience. Highly recommended.

It's my entire fault I didn't touch this game any time before like... 3 weeks ago.
I usually never let any game pass my radar and dismiss once I look at the name or the colour pallet like many self-righteous ♥♥♥♥s like to do. We're in an age everything can come at your doorstep, slap you in the face with a white glove full of solidified cement and make you learn to not "judge a book by its cover" (and... not open the door to random gentlemen).
"Oh it looks boring" ~ Me, 2010-ish.
But I digress. Had it in my steam library, was crying of boredom after wanting a deep RPG/Game experience and finding nothing to appeal me.
And here I am writing this review while I have lunch. What's the meal?
So let's start the epicness that is this party based RPG, shall we?
Best part of the game. The story is one of the very best that ever graced this planet. First of all, there's no introduction to tell you because of the background system, where you pick a background and that will be your "tutorial/introduction" so it depends on what you choose (there are 6 of them).
The very only thing in common between the introductions are the fact that in the end you are called to join the Grey Wardens, a group of elite soldiers with excellent combat skills that excell at repelling the Darkspawn, a faction of sort of undead, dark possessed beasts that just want the extinction of the human race.
And that's the core plot of the game. A Blight (absolutely colossal war between humans (and elfs, dwarves, etc.) and the Darkspawn. A loss would likely result in the extinction of the losing race unless re-population by fleeing losers happened) is coming, you join it at the right moment to let your sword taste some darkspawn blood (which will turn anyone into one OR drives people/animals mad with fevers until death strikes them) and time's drawing closer.
If only it was that easy as politics get involved and♥♥♥♥♥♥gets darker than the Darkspawn itself and we get to witness over 40 hours of the single best writing ever done in... everything, making quests, exploring, reading the codex and just the relationships with your characters so real and more interesting than anything in this age, same level as perhaps Game of Thrones, which is, sadly, the only medieval thing people like nowadays.
Now, I meantioned relationships. The dialogue with other party members , usually leads to either build affection with them, or... well... or not.
If the affection reduces to something close to 0, the party member will simply abandon you, because your ideas go against his/hers, depending on their vision, of course (I ended up threatening a chantry mother and lost 15 affection to one of my members and gaining 7 affection with another. It just depends if they approve violence or not, and especially against old chantry mothers :p).
This may seem simple but since there will be so much talking and hanging out with party members in common, some talks will lead to some building affection and other losing it at the same time, creating a very dynamic sense of relationship between all characters (and if you have ♥♥♥♥ed up moral values, some may end up fighting you, which will have permanent death in case you win the fight, obviously). Some will respond differently based on your choices, some even to your race and background, which makes the game ridiculously replayable! Testing all the story outcomes, all relationships with characters and witnessing all manners people and party members will look at you based on your choices through this epic adventure.
And there's more, such as the gift system, which is literally giving specific "gift" items you find in the world randomly to party members that will increase their affection with you (the same item may give one character a bigger affection boost than others so use logic to who you think would like a specific gift the most), some of which will even trigger a side-quest randomly and unique dialogue options (and even new skills!), making this feel extremely natural and organic, something I consider vital to an excellent adventure game, the sense of things happening because you came across them and not because you followed a waypoint like in 98% of videogames these days.
Released in 2009, Origins looked good for its time and it still looks very nice, aging pretty well and having better faces/hair than Skyrim or Deus Ex Human Revolution (which came out 2 years later). For 2016 standard it's not that great but I've played releases worse looking than it in recent memory and it runs like a beauty. It's good aging also makes graphic mods dismissable as the vanilla is still excellent.
Game world is extremely varied, between forests to caves to dungeons full of Indiana Jones style trap dodging and treasure hunting, to even snowy moutains, non creepy to creepy-as-♥♥♥♥ villages and even underground exploration mines with lava and such. There's way more than this still, thankfully. Environment variety is excellent and will hardly feel repetitive.
Audio is good. The voice acting is excellent for about 95% of it, the music is great and so are the environment sounds while exploring.
Besides adventuring and talking with interesting NPC's (which is about every NPC in the game), you'll be killing.
Combat can be played in real time or with pausing and tactically giving orders to each of the party members (which can go up to 4, counting with you). Each have their own abilities, depending on their class (mage, rogue or warrior, which then specializes in specific traits. Shapeshifting Mages, Reaver Warriors or Duelist Rogues are possible. Specializations are 12 in total, 4 every class and that change the core gameplay of that character quite a lot, making combat unbelievably deep), there is even a tactics screen that alters AI behavior depending on the enemies it's facing, the amount of them, etc. making the AI fully customizable to your liking.
Combat's deep enough to carry the game and make most encounters fun and tactically entertaining (when travelling between places, random encounters can get a bit annoying but passable).
Crafting is here as well, of course; ranging from poisons to buffing elixirs and runes to improve weapon performance, Origins never stops introducing the player to new and exciting moments, gameplay or story wise.
+ Excellent story
+ Phenomenal writing
+ Graphics and gameplay aged perfectly
+ Very deep and highly customizable gameplay
+ Immensely replayable
+ Great sense of natural adventuring through lack of waypoints and nice map and level design, making exploring a treat and not a chore
+ Relationship with party members feels organic and almost real, which is rare, if not unique in gaming.
+ Deep and rich lore/world
- Some battles can wreck your nerves, feeling sometimes a bit overwhelming for a 4-member party. I feel 6 would've been the best, I struggled ALOT on normal, especially against big battles vs. 20 darkspawn. Feels a bit BS-ish.
Overall... 10/10, definately one of mankind's masterpieces!

First off:
If you enjoyed BlOps, Quake Live/Arena, Unreal Tournament, etc., Buy This Game. Seriously. For 30 bucks you're getting one of the most seamless, fast-paced, twitch experiences with unique mechanics.
In a nutshell:
This game is not like overwatch. There is no rock-paper-scissors mechanic. What I mean by this, is that all of the classes are blanaced enough to where an experienced player can  1v1 any other class and come out on top. Movement in this game is surreal, and reminiscent of rail-gun matches in quake live or a Forge game with gravity turned down and movement speed turned up. There is very little focus on team composition (team comp). This game is for a skilled FPS player that is just looking to frag people and have a good time. There's no lore. There's no cute colors and things of that nature. No unlockable voice lines or particularly mind-blowing skins. It's a game to play as a white-knuckle experience. It will have you screaming and shouting and pounding your keyboard.
The Devs and community:
I have never seen a game with such a small player base receiving updates so frequently. The Devs are very committed to this title and it shows. Buying in now means being a part of a growing, evolving game that will reward your dedication. There are a lot of reviews mentioning this game going f2p. This could happen, it could be good for the game, BUT - the appeal to this game is an appeal to hardcore gamers -
This means that a lot of us don't care about RNG loot and skins. We want to win and frag people. For this reason, the game LACKS APPEAL TO YOUNGER PLAYERS.
It beats you over the head if you aren't intuitively skilled at a fast modern FPS. It's not bright, funny, and kid friendly. For these reasons, I love this game.
MY EXPERIENCE WITH MATCHMAKING:
I have gigabit internet (FiOS) and a reasonably quick PC (Ryzen 5 1600 @ 3.8GHz, AMD RX480)
- In group play: Matchmaking can suck. It can take up to 10 minutes to find a game when playing with friends. It has been a little faster as of September 12th or so.
- In solo play: I HAVE NEVER (until very recently) HAD A BAD EXPERIENCE. Seriously. With quick internet and a decent rig, I've never waited for more than a few minutes or so to find a match. Once with a group, no issues.
- Back to the playerbase: matchmaking will improve as more people pick up this title. I'm positive that the Devs have some sort of reward/free weekend in store to pick up more players. CliffyB has stated that he intends this game to have a course similar to Warframe (which I have only played a bit, despite my profile) in that the playerbase will grow as content is consistently and rapidly added to the game. There's a committment there that I respect, though time will tell if things improve.
All in all, I'd give it a 9/10 for all the aforementioned reasons, but in terms of sheer gameplay it'd be a 10/10

Upon starting up the game – besides seeing that the default settings for my hardware got 45fps – I looked around and found a hidden item, which gave me a proprietary QR code. Said app is also necessary for monitoring in-game stats like how many alarms you’ve triggered, etc. (This is necessary info for various achievements, etc.) This is not only a bit of a pain, but also reduces how future-proof the game is, as it is unlikely that SquEnix is going to maintain an App and the game, especially considering how poor the support is so far (see below).
This game also can’t be discussed without bring up microtransactions. This game is honestly really fun, especially with friends. WIth each match being around 5-6 minutes, its a really quick way for me to have some fun or loose up after a long day. However, this game is not without its faults.
Pros:
1. Very fast matches. Makes the game a really good way to loosen up and have fun.
2. Variety as there is an abundance of legends along with the Devs adding new heros every 3-4 months or so.
3. Very easy to learn. The controls of the game are very straightforward and the moves of legends are interchangable.
4. Friendly to all sorts of players, with different custom game modes as well as ranked and casual.
5. Everything can be aquired through grind and don't have to use money, besides cosmetics
Cons: Honestly, while there might be lot more cons, most aren't really that impactful
1. Server/Internet Lag. This is arguably the largest problem in the game. The servers clearly can not withstand the amount of players, espeically during the rush hour periods where there are the most people online. This is clearly a consequence of the increase of legends. The devs would rather push for a new legend rather than actually fix up or bolster the server
2. Inbalanced Ranked system. While this may not be a problem for casual fans, if you do decide to play the ranked mode of the game, be ready for some bullsh*t elo. You may be pitted against people who are 200 or even more elo higher than you, which will most likely result in your loss.
3. Toxicity. There is always going to be toxic players in game. Just don't let them get to your head
4. The mechanics are sometimes put into question. For one, sometimes when you can clearly see that you hit your opponents, the game doesn't register that you actually hit them. Or sometimes there is the hit sound but in reality, you did not hit them (mostly due to the lag problem previously talked about). There is also times where you don't physically hit someone, but the game registers that you did, leading to some really confusing and rage inducing moments. Also, some of the legends signiture moves have lingering hitboxes, in which the animation is already over, but you can still be hit by the move somehow.
5. The dodge mechanic. The dodge mechanic is something really buggy where it would work sometimes and other times just not do what you want it to do.
Finally, this is just a personal opinion, but the game was made 10 times less appealing to me when the devs decided to get rid of chain dodging and instead add a dodge function in its replacement. This leads to many 2v2 matches where the game just becomes who can spam signitures more instead of actual skill.
But all in all, really fun game and would recommend to people who are looking for a fighting brawl game and have a lot of friends to mess around in a custom lobby with. Otherwise, if you are one who is only looking to play this ranked, would recommend staying away as all the formentioned cons will make you more mad.

Devolver Digital
is a 2D turn-based action game developed by Tomasz Wacławek and published by Devolver Digital. This game looks very similar to
, one of my favorite indie games of all time, so I was instantly intrigued. However, this is a very different beast, and that isn't necessarily a good thing. This is the first Devolver Digital published game that I am not going to recommend.
Kill Bill meets Hotline Miami. In order to get revenge, the main character goes on a rampage to kill all those who wronged her. Simple, straight-forward, and (unfortunately) not the main focus of the game.
The 2D art style is pretty good, the animations are polished, and the level design is very well done. Unfortunately, there is little variety to the environments and you will face the same types of enemies over and over again.
Similarly to
, you move around mainly by holding a button to jump in the air and go on walls. However, the focus is on fighting rather than stealthing your way through, and when you enter combat, time stops and you must carefully plan your next move depending on where the enemies are going to shoot. The more hits you get, the more ability points you unlock to perform special actions like throwing your katana or teleporting.
There is a serious issue, and that's the controls: they are very awkward. Aiming your jump is very buggy, and you can't always hit the enemies even though you are standing right next to them.
The game is not really challenging, as much as it is frustrating: because of the afore metioned buggy controls, dying is usually the fault of the lack of escapes or the inability to kill an enemy. I died over 60 times in my walkthrough, which is even more than the times I died in
. But I have to say that finally clearing a room full of hostiles feels very rewarding and satisfying.
A mediocre soundtrack and lackluster effects don't help raising the enjoyment that this game might give you.
In order to achieve 100% completion, you have to finish each level killing every enemy and avoiding a lockdown. Accomplishing this tasks will give you ability points to spend in the skill tree. Other than that, there is little to no reason for coming back. There aren't even achievements that aren't story related!
Overall, the game had great potential, but its awkward controls and frustratingly punishing difficulty stop it from being enjoyable. I can't recommend it in good faith.

This is one of the best surprises I've had in gaming. It looks like a great game sure, but I didn't realize it was a classic.
Looking at the store page, its appeal is rather obvious. A ninja platformer, OK. Nothing we haven't seen before right? Well folks, there's a reason people get excited for Klei games. The maker of Don't Starve, Invisible Inc, and Shanks 1&2 has a reputation for tightly-designed games with a lot of character, and Mark of the Ninja is to me their greatest achievement so far.
I've never played a title that was so perfectly focused as this one. Every aspect of the game, be it the mechanics, story, graphics, sound, menus, etc -- everything seems to be perfect for the game, and complement one another, as if they have a genius project manager who knows exactly how much time should be spent on one aspect of the production or another.
The controls are freakin' magical. I've never felt I'd mastered a game's controls like this one. You'll be sliding and flipping and jumping and sneaking in no time. You'll never be unsure where you can land or hide or stop or go, and you'll never make a mistake that's the game's fault. But it's not just how well it controls, it's also how they combine them with the animation and level design. Everything feels so precise but so smooth... you'll never get stuck on anything or fall off a ledge that looked safe, you'll never have trouble aiming.. I used a gamepad as is probably the better control scheme, but also tried m/kb an found it suprisingly useable.
Each level has bonus challenges and a few collectibles to find, which really stretch out the level. But unlike so many games where these can seem like extra effort for unknown reward, in this game, you'll want to find all the things. And what's so cool about it is that although you'll have to work for it, you'll never need to google anything. You'll find everything if you look. I wish more games understood this.
On top of that the ending is decent, and there is replayability as well, since you can play one of a few characters that each have their own special move and loadouts.
So, in a nutshell- tight, polished stealth ninja gameplay with secrets, traps, projectiles, bladed weapons and challenging levels with variety and multiple paths, that never get frustrating or repetitive. Absolute classic, the pinnacle of indie gaming. You'll not find a more well-made game anywhere, AAA or indie.

Ballistic Overkill may look like your run of the mill trashy F2P FPS where players rely on cash guns to win. But it isn't.
The devs have managed to knock something special out of the park here. The movement has a fluidity which reminds me much of Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare. It's not a case of holding down LMB to win, when recoil is significant and requires a steady hand to control. Battlefield-like ballistics means taking long-range shots requires good positioning and judgment.
Weapons, while varied,  are surprisingly well-balanced. Unlike most shooters where 1-3 weapons are the meta picks and are used in every match, each weapon appears to be useful in their own way. Some may be mediocre in ADS but great in hipfire or vice versa. Assault rifles with short range sights have more ammo, and the same rifle type with long range sights have less ammo to balance things out. Grenade launchers, where available, are not one-hit kill noob tube affairs and are useful for flushing opponents out of corners, or emergency burst damage in close range.
And yes, there are stealth mechanics. While they may seem really boring to play against, they're not OP or impossible to play against. Shadow, the stealth character with the ninja sword may be cloaked, but his cloaked form is easy to see if your situational awareness is decent, and he makes a loud sound whenever he goes in and out of stealth. This is an obvious giveaway which makes him vulnerable, and any careless Shadow player can get rekt with a shotgun to the face.
Wraith is the sniper class who has an obvious yellow outline when in stealth mode, so he's also possible to go against. Because the game isn't hitscan and uses ballistics, being good at movement means you have a better fighting chance by dodging sniper shots.
The community, while small by multiplayer PC standards, is quite active and growing rapidly. Discounting the usual few ♥♥♥♥♥ who have yet to reach puberty, community members on the official Discord server are more than happy to welcome new players and will help with any questions. It's obvious that this game came from F2P roots, but the devs seem determined to want to deliver a polished experience without having to rely on microtransaction cancer to keep the lights on.
I can get behind that.

If you have ever been interested in playing Stealth games, but you cannot get past the montony of older titles, I highly recommend this game. As a veteran of the Genre, I personally find that Mark of the Ninja is the best stealth game out there. Why? Well, because it is the first game that I can recommend other to play if they want to try out stealth games without the admittedly mired barrier to entry for newbies to the genre that a game like the original thief might have had. In this game, whether this is your first stealth game, or you're a seasoned sneaker or phantom, this game will equally please you if you are either/or. This game is beautifully crafted, from art style to mechanics. Speaking of which, the art style even manages to enhance the game itself. The art is a beautiful "saturday morning cartoon" style, that while appealing, also manages to do away with all the more frustrating and alienating features of the more classic stealth game. For one thing, you will always know if an enemy can or cannot see you, you will always be aware of whether or not your movement or actions can be detectable, even something as simple as maneuvering is well crafted to the point where it is all up to you whether to pick using a controller or a keyboard and mouse. This game is, as far as I'm concerned, the best stealth game out there, giving newbies a great gateway to the genre and veterans a great challenge. If you have any slight possible interest in this game, buy it. Simple as that.

The good:
- Rich and well-developed world
- Cheap (I got it during a steam sale) - $1.50 for the game and $0.50 for the soundtrack that ruined my ears for the 20 or so hours
- Rob Hoard "I've got enough to eat at home" and James Starling cameo
- Branching story in an RPG Maker game - great for 2014
- Squaring tofus for money is surprisingly relaxing
The meh
- The story - B-movie standard
- The gambling and fight club sequences can get really tedious if you want to make extra cash (then again, maybe that is the point)
- The NPCs are really one-sided
- The worldview of this story paints an overly pessimistic and simplistic picture of corporate greed
The bad
- IS THERE ANY WAY TO TURN DOWN THE SOUND! The soundtrack is nice but is really annoying because it is in every single part of the game, often at INAPPROPRIATE times. Sometimes silence is the best soundtrack. Someone needs to shoot the person in charge of sound (not the composer, mind you) or pay the players back $10,000. It's not that I'm particularly fond of violence, but unfortunately sometimes circumstance makes it necessary. Which brings me to the next point:
- The dialogue is poorly researched and one-sided when representing landlords, corporate fatcats and casino owners. Often the dialogue can get so moralising it warrants so many eye rolls. It often feels that it becomes a mouthpiece of the writer's ideology. CUT DOWN ON THE NARRATION and let the player decide the moral of the story for themselves. SHOW DON'T TELL!
- The ending: You must love your ex or you'll become a bum, and I like the fact that you can get shot and resurrect later to publish your award winning book). So in life, we must never move on from our ex? What if I don't like him/her because they are just as selfish as most people portrayed in this game?
- Hitting the next dialogue often hits the first choice (which led to alot of hair-pulling moments) - perhaps having a confirmation stage would help
- You can't save or load during flashbacks and halfway during dialogues
- Achievements do not get reflected in the Mac version
Vedict: Buy in steam sale, BUT don't get your hopes up - it's in no way as good as To The Moon in terms of engaging the player in storytelling. Get ready for overly preachy and cliched dialogues. However, this game excels in world building and branching story mechanics, which is enough motivation for me to buy the game though.

The worst thing about most stealth-centric games is the ambiguity. Are you visible from your current location? Will your enemies hear it if you perform this action? It’s a niggling problem that even some of the best stealth games have trouble alleviating. However, Klei Entertainment’s contribution to the genre—
—uses both its side-scrolling perspective and easily recognisable visual cues to create a near-complete clarity that sets it apart from other, similar titles.
You play as an unnamed ninja, part of a clan that has survived until the modern day using tattoos with supernatural properties. As the story begins, you—as the “champion” who has accepted “the mark”—awaken to an attack on the clan by armed soldiers. While the plot does thicken substantially throughout the game, it’s not particularly outstanding. What really carries
is the clearly established rules that govern the stealth system, especially the visual representations of sound and light, which are simple and easy to understand.
The stealth gameplay itself is extremely polished, and the clarity that it presents makes you truly feel in control of any situation you may be in. The level design complements the mechanics fantastically, allowing for any combination of pacifist, ‘no kill’ runs and a straight-up bloodbath.
does rightfully restrict your ability to succeed in hand-to-hand combat, and while it’s certainly possible, it’s significantly less effective than stealth kills.
’s progression system gives you points to unlock different items and stealth kills based on the objectives you complete within each level, and it can take some time to unlock the majority of items it you’re running through without collecting pickups or completing optional objectives. It’s a nice incentive to be more thorough in your exploration of the game’s open-ended levels. On the subject of unlockable items,
goes for a sort of codex system in the form of audio logs, which are simple haikus explaining the backstory of the story’s central clan. It’s an interesting way of doing things, and it’s much better than the drawn-out voice readings from some higher budget games.
Aesthetically,
is pretty fantastic. The art style and animation is designed to look like traditionally animated films, particularly reminiscent of Disney’s pre-Pixar films. Everything just looks great. The character animations are fluid and the backgrounds look great despite the limitations of the binary lighting system. The gruesome variety of the stealth kills combined with the superior sound design really come together to make it a real joy to play.
My only criticism is the voice acting, which sounds like it was done in a hurry towards the end of production. Despite this,
excels in every field, to the point where I’d consider it to be the optimal stealth experience.

Well, to summarize things first: I've clicked on "Recommend", but you might
want to be careful. It's a somewhat weak recommendation.
It's a decent game overall, and it's also worth going through all the
dialogue. The look is pretty, the music didn't annoy me -- in fact, I
rather liked the rarer pieces.
However, the game is split into 4 main areas, each with 4 sub-areas to
"heal" and a final boss area. And this is where things get repetitive
-- a lot. All of these areas work the same, repeating the same
template over and over again, although they look different to some
extent.
There aren't a lot of enemies -- which is good, because you get the
same ones over and over again. In fact, by the time you get to the
boss area, you've fought the boss 4 times already, and the boss area
will just give you a longer fight of the same, usually split into 3
parts.
I also consider the combat to be annoying, but luckily it's just
tedious rather than impossible. Most fights need a lot of luck, and I
failed most quicktime events which means it drags on even
longer. Nonetheless, sooner or later, you'll succeed. The good thing
is that you don't die; when you do, the enemy merely recovers some
health but you can continue right away.
I liked the lightseed-collecting parts a bit more. After you've
finished the objective in an area, the dark and grim area turns
green and sunny, and you get to free-roam through it to collect
lightseeds.
There are 45 of these in each area, but you don't need to collect them
all -- you need 540 to complete the game, out of 1000 to be
found. Many of these are obvious and are just lined up along the way,
some are slightly hidden or require a bit of trial-and-error to
reach. Nothing frustrating, although I had to just take a leap of
faith in a few cases as I just couldn't find the last seed in an area
and started to just randomly jump into blind spots.
Having Elika around does provide the opportunity for dialogue, which
helps a lot to keep the game from getting boring. As far as her setup
goes, she's neither stupid nor comic-relief -- in fact, one has to
wonder why she even bothers following you around. I do see a potential
setup concerning the end of this particular series, though, so that's
ok.
Also, you character basically doesn't change at all. During the game,
you (or Elika, actually) gains 4 powers, but these aren't like spells
or skills -- they are more like keys to be used on specifically marked
spots, which will then move you to another fixed spot in the area. So,
by the time the end credits roll, you character looks the same and has
the same abilities that he had in the intro.
The story basically has two endings, with the first one being what one
would expect given how everything was set up. If you continue through
and past the credits you get to play a part that could best be
described as setting the stage for the sequel -- which never
happened. I played through it, of course, but I consider it to be
non-existent as far as the story goes.
So, overall, if you are looking for a not particularly difficult game
and don't mind doing the same things in slightly different scenarios
while getting a decent but not particularly unusual story, this one is
worth to consider. It also helps if you don't mind collecting some
lightseeds.

Mark of the Ninja is a compact package.  It does one thing and it's variants very, very well.  It's a stealth game, with an approach to design that reinforces everything that is exciting and tense.  Meanwhile, at least for the most part, it minimizes frustrations associated with the genre.
Visually and aesthetically, this game shines.   The characters and backgrounds are all very distinct and thematic.  Perhaps a bigger success though, the game play and design is weaved together so that no aspect of the game violates either artistic or logical sense.  As an example, you can always see the sounds you make in a visual manner with white expanding circles.
The game also offers a variety of game play styles, which helps add longevity to the rather short experience.  Terrorizing guards, slaying people silently from the shadows or just outright avoiding everyone, you usually have room for each approach in the often puzzle like levels. Each area has a unique niche that gives you both challenge and room to experiment.
Negatively, there are a few things this game suffers from.  Some of the upgrades won't be for everyone, and occasionally there are parts that feel locked in to certain items on replays.  Occasionally there's frustration at frequent resets, despite the game resetting so quickly you don't really feel punished for losing.  Honestly though, these would be less noticeable if it weren't for the bottom line.  This game is exceptionally well put together, from the tense beginning, to the truly climactic choice you have to make at the end.  Unless you despise stealth games, there's not really much reason to not at least play Mark of the Ninja once.

There seems to be a lot of hate for this game stemming from largely unimportant technical issues versus actual game quality, so let me give my two cents as an avid gamer with a very diverse array of games and technical knowledge.
Let me start off by saying that this is a console to pc port.  While this game, as all games are, have been developed on a pc, it was developed, originally, for an entirely different type of hardware, so you can't just take your pc dev source and throw that on a computer and call it a day.  While there are some technical issues, they are largely minor and unnoticeable with a few exceptions.  I'll cover all of that in detail below.
Gameplay:
This game uses a similar combat system to its predecessor, FFXIII, in that rather than micromanaging every move of your team, they learn from their combat experience and adjust their fighting on their own, you simply tell them what role to fill in the party by changing your party paradigms.  While this means a whole lot less button pushing and decision-making as far as battles go, it makes for a more casual gameplay experience and allows battles to be conducted in real-time.  For those of you that still want the final say in what is done how and where to what, you can select the abilities individually through the combat menus.  I don't suggest doing this on boss fights, as a note.
The game is split between exploring maps, battling monsters, and dialogue.  As far as the story goes, they have a lot of interesting bits.  There IS a solid story to be told and you are fed it through a myriad of time-jumps and side quests.  You could, of course, straightline the story and be done with the game in a few hours, but you'd be missing out on a lot of the depth of the story and information.  Take the time to explore the world, do the side quests, and you will be rewarded for the experience with a rich plot that is severely downplayed in reviews.  Once Serah grows a spine and takes up sword and bow for her sister's sake, she's a certifiable badass, and, something new from the previous game, you actually have a say in the stories, deciding what she says or asks at critical points to affect the information and reactions of the npcs.
The party mechanics are pretty different now.  Serah and Noel are your only real party members and you can swap between which of them leads freely.  The third party slot is filled by tamed monsters, each which has a specific role and can be evolved along the crystarium at the cost of item drops.  This mechanic is a bit odd, but not unwelcomed.  There's a lot to be said for a Behemoth mowing down your enemies along side the mains.  There are some battles where the characters from the first game assist, such as a battle alongside Snow fairly early on, but I wish there would have been some of that for some of the newer npcs, like Alyssa, who you run into repeatedly and even voices an interest in the party's actions and time travel.
Controls:
Don't use mouse and keyboard.  Sure, they work, and they will get you through some stuff, but they are a bit awkward and clunky.  The convenience of a controller is that all the controls for the game are easily accessible and don't require reaching across your keyboard and hitting the wrong button during a crucial moment, or simply losing track of where your fingers are on the keyboard.  I am very accustomed to keyboard/mouse controls....get a controller.  It will make your life easier and many games benefit from the ease of access of the buttons you need in your hand.
Audio:
I applaud Squeenix for this whole-heartedly.  For those of you who like the english voice cast (which they did do an amazing job of casting, I might add), the game offers the usual English release as seen on the consoles.  For those of you who prefer to hear the original voices, you can choose the original voice track from the Japanese version of the game.  If you know Japanese, you'll here some inconsistencies between the dialogue and the subtitles that are curious, but for the most part, both are solid and you won't miss anything one way or the other.
The music for this game is very easy to listen to.  Though the battle theme is repetitive and a bit obnoxious at times, especially as frequently as you end up in battles, the rest of the soundtrack during exploration is beautiful and well done.  Rather than simply extending the soundtrack a little from the previous game, there are only a few familiar songs from XIII, and most of the music for XIII-2 is new.  Nice vocals sung in English (for the most part) help add to the story as the songs are actually relevant to the plot in their weirdly Engrish way.  I wish the soundtrack was available for this on Steam as well.
Graphics:
Here's the bit where things get dicey.  The game is fantastically beautiful and well-worth exploring.  That said, the game's requirements are fairly punishing on most middleweight/moderate systems.  The game runs beautifully on my desktop (3.4ghz AMD Quad-Core, 16gb RAM, Crossfired 6870s), with no measurable issues.  All those people complaining about frame rates dropping to unplayable levels are either experiencing hardware incompatibility issues or other OS-related issues (such as background processes, viruses and malware, or everyone's friend, System Idle Process) ...or are simply first-worlders with no real concept of what unplayable is and are just whining for attention and because things aren't perfect for them.  Nothing is going to be perfect and this title is no exception to that rule.  It IS playable.
My laptop struggles a bit more with the game, on the other hand, but the issues are so minor that I still have no real unplayable moments.  The game engine is built with an internal frame-skipping mechanic that mitigates lower end systems, something I don't think many people have noticed.  While the game may not be running 30frames per second, it does it's best to keep it as close to 23 as it can.  I have no complaints with this.  Even when the count drops below this, the game is still playing smoothly thanks to the frame skipping with only a little bit of lag during the visually stunning spells, like Thundaga and Ruinga.  It's running a 3.2ghz AMD Quad-Core, 8gb RAM, and HD6650 video card.
In Conclusion:
This game is worth the money.  At $20, its not like Squeenix is trying to milk a new market, plus we get most of the DLC at no additional cost.  The only thing that they could have thrown in to make it a better deal would have been the soundtrack.  Sure, the game may occasionally drop in performance a little bit at times, but it's never bad enough that the game can't be played and the gameplay experience is not bad.  I'm playing Final Fantasy on my computer and I'm very happy for the experience.
As a side note, I do own both games on consoles, so I am aware of how they play there.  I can't pack up my console and take it on a roadtrip like I can do with my laptop, however, and as often as I'm on the road or in a position that I CAN'T play my consoles, this is a nice and welcome option.

I played this game in the betas a few months ago. At first I absolutely hated this game. I didn't get the mechanics at all and was just cannon fodder for the other team. I then tried looking up beta tutorials for all the characters. I found a few videos that were made by the developers of those characters where they explained all the ins and outs of a particular hero in a very detailed fashion. At this point, the game clicked for me and my enjoyment of this game went up immensely.
This game is EXTREMELY fast paced. Expect to fail miserably for a bit while you begin to grasp the mechanics. This game places a heavy emphasis on Momentum. In the middle of most maps, there is a zero gravity bubble. You move in the direction you are looking. You can also blindfire behind you (cntrl key) to give you forward momentum. There are several modes: Blitzball (take a ball voiced by rick from rick and morty to the enemy base to score a point. Get 8 to win), Occupy (take control of an objective that shifts position as the match continues), and others.
A lot of people online have been comparing this game to OW, but I feel the comparison is overdone. While they are both hero first person shooters that focus on objectives vs getting kills (at least until the Deathmatch mode comes out in a few weeks), they feel like fundamentally different games. Overwatch borrows many of its design philosophies from MOBAs. An example of this is how you always have to walk for a while back to the objective after dying, or how McCree's flashbang and Roadhog's hook stuns you, making your character unable to move. Compare that to LB, where there are no stun abilities at all (closest thing is Wraith's slowing ultimate, which doesn't render you incapable of defending your character) and it is easy to traverse the map with most characters. Another differentiation from OW, is that in LB any character is capable of easily killing any other class. In overwatch, there are hard counters (bastion can not kill genji as easily as genji can kill him).
Many people (mostly reddit TBH) have been screaming how this game is dead. I frankly haven't really noticed that to be true in my server region (US East). I almost always get matched in within a few min (longest I've ever waited was 7 min). While this game could be doing better, don't let gloom and doom influence your buying decision. Worst case scenario, just use the Steam Refund feature within 2 hrs.
One more thing I love about this game is the developers behind it. While the marketing at launch was lackluster to say the least, it has been steadily getting a bit more visibility on twitch. If you are at all interested in learning more about the game or want to find some chill people to play with, join the official discord server:
. The devs are very active on weekdays and are always willing to answer reasonable questions and take feedback (the 2 that are most active are lumos and IHoldShift). Where any other developer would have abandoned a game due to low player counts, these devs have doubled down on making this game as good as they can. They've recently announced a roadmap where they are adding a few new maps, a dedicated map for Blitzball, Ranked mode, Team Deathmatch and a new hero.
