I played this way back on my Xbox 360, and 100% it too, and I'll say that the game is great. It's better than XIII in every way really. I personally didn't like the first game that much, it was too restrictive and it took forever before you had some freedom but XIII-2 gets to the point very quickly compared to the first game and doesn't bombard you with as many tutorials. I would still recommend playing the first game or watch all the cutscenes on YouTube or something because this is definitely a direct sequel and you'll be very lost in the story if you don't check out the first game. The game does come with a XIII primer to help people who didn't play XIII to catch up so there's that too.
I was pretty happy to see this game coming to the PC. Unfortunately, the game has some issues. There are two main issues that IF fixed will help this port immensely. There is a TON of screen tearing and the frame rate is all over the place (the lowest I hit was 20fps). My rig has an i7-3770K, 16GB RAM and a GTX 670 FTW so it's definitely not my PC which can't run the game at a constant 60fps on its highest settings.
As for graphics options, don't expect a myriad of options. This is definitely a console port so don't expect advanced options like Tesselation, PCSS, and so on. You have resolution, shadow resolution and MSAA. The game is not ugly by any means though.
I will still recommend it. It's definitely the best in the XIII series, but buy with caution. I hope that Squeenix release a patch soon and/or someone releases a mod which fixes these problems.

Along with the other LucasArts games I've played from just a wee child to now from Grim Fandango, to Full Throttle, to the Tales from Monkey Island series and this Day of the Tentacle, I will always love the adventure games LucasArts has produced in its hayday. Day of the Tentacle was the third game I played after finishing Grim Fandango and Full Throttle as a child and now thanks to Double Fine Productions, Walt Disney Interactive and Lucasfilm we can now finally have another LucasArts adventure game fully remastered to its former glory
Funnily enough I did not know that Day of the Tentacle is actually a sequel to a previous LucasArts game known as Maniac Mansion and I have personally never played Maniac Mansion
Day of the Tentacle's story is brilliant. From its quirky characters to its lovable cutscenes and funny comedy. and the music (especially in the remastered edition) is absolutely brilliant! The cutscenes are lovable and fun to watch and are brilliantly animated, overall the game is brilliant!
The puzzles and game progression, although when I was young and I played Day of the Tentacle for the very first time I did not have any walkthroughs or guides, so the puzzles were a bit challenging and can be a bit too awkward for modern-day players or even newcomers to the genre. The game does not help you at all when progressing through and does not hold your hand when your stuck on a puzzle for too long, so be prepared to get stuck here and there, thankfully I remembered most of the stuff! Lucky guys with internet nowadays, you can simply type in walkthroughs for the game!
The remastered version, Double Fine have really done a job well done for remastering this classic. The music is spot-on and digitally remastered. The cutscenes, although not fully converted to HD are very watchable, and the new HUD system they implemented has made it easier for players to play the game. The addition of HD graphics, etc... made the game more stunning than it originally was (and if you want some nostalgia, you can play the game in its original graphics!)
Overall, Day of the Tentacle and its remastered version are simply brilliant and if you are a fan of LucasArts (like me!) or you like adventure games or you want to try something new, then I would highly recommend playing Day of the Tentacle and I hope that Double Fine will continue to remaster these old LucasArts classics!
Although no LucasArts classic adventure game will ever beat Grim Fandango, Day of the Tentacle is still a wonderful and one of my favourite adventure games to play even though nothing beats Grim Fandango, that's a legendary LucasArts classic game!
You can not do anything wrong by playing this game. Especially if you like classic adventure games.

As a follow up to one of the greatest point and click adventure games of all time, Maniac Mansion, Day of the Tentacle Remastered had a lot to live up to.   Maniac Mansion allowed the player to choose 2 characters from 6 friends to accompany the main character which means it had 20 possible teams to play as.  Day of the Tentacle had a standard 3 character set.
So does it measure up?  I think it does.  The story of the game is the team is trying to stop the Purple Tentacle that has gotten mutated and decided to take over the world.  The game starts with Bernard (a character from the original game, and a fan favorite) bringing two friends to help stop the Purple Tentacle.  He ends up traveling through time to yesterday and through a problem, the three friends are separated by hundreds of years.   The three friends need to find a way to fix their personal problems, and eventually work together to save the day.
So how is the game play and puzzles?   Well honestly, that's what really shines.  The remastered version of the game has the ability to choose between hot spots on the screen, which really helps.
At the same time there's a few puzzles that are hard, but honestly there's nothing that obtuse, and a few that are really clever.  There was a room or two I had to revisit with out realizing it, but overall a lot of the game is quite straight forward.  The puzzles work well and some of them are quite clever.
The story does shine as well, I love the updated characters and new characters for the original game.  It's not overly hilarious, but it's also not trying to be funny all the time.  The puzzles take precedence over the story, and that works.  So don't expect to♥♥♥♥♥♥yourself laughing, but you will get a couple really good laughs.
But wait there's one last thing to mention.  Day of the Tentacle also included the classic Maniac Mansion.  While the remastered didn't improve the classic game, it's still included in this version, which is a fantastic deal.
Overall I recommend this game as a great example of how an adventure game SHOULD be.  There's not a ton of frustration with it, and the story and areas the game explores are great.   The only thing I could imagine is this is a very American centric game.  There's a few puzzles that likely require a small understanding of American history, or colloquialisms.  It shouldn't ruin the game, but there was one point where I questioned if someone who didn't know a story would be able to solve it.    But still overall? Easy recommend, especially for anyone who is a fan of point and click adventure games.   And bonus points for having multiple different control schemes and the classic game included inside the game?  Hell yeah!

The game is 8/10 but this PC port is more like a 5/10. Out of the box on release day, this thing ran like a sloth on my ROG G750JM laptop (GTX 860M, i7-4700HQ, 16GB RAM). I had to open Nvidia control panel and manually adjust the performance settings (say INTEGRATED) before the game ran anywhere between 30-60FPS at 1080 (though it seems to be locked at 720 anyway), usually closer to 30. The graphics and even audio options are extremely limited (screen resolution, shadow resolution, aliasing, English/Japanese voice) so make sure you're at least close to the recommended specs. Once I had the settings down, the game was smooth sailing with no crashes so far but the overall experience could be more consistent. And for crying out loud, I would love to be able to adjust the background music level! That song at the beach was totally out of place when it kicked in!
The game just feels natural with a controller so I plugged in my PS4's dual shock FTW. One thing that irks me is that there's a silly bug that resets QTE displays from controller buttons to keyboard keys. You'll have to change it each time you boot up the game if you plan to stick to controllers or it could get very confusing during the QTEs. Either way, you can use both control methods at the same time.
As for the game itself, it's FFXIII made better in every way with a good dose of fanservicing. Oh and it's just Serah, Noel, your trusty Moogle, and a bunch of pets. If you heard bad things about this game's predecessor, well, XIII-2 more than makes up for them, at least in its systems. However, if you never played the first game, I strongly advise playing that before this because you'll sorely be lost in the story if you haven't.
There are reports of the story DLCs missing but that does not take away from the main story. It should eventually get patched up since they advertised the inclusion but who knows when that'll happen? Thankfully, the bonus costume DLCs work.
In spite of all that, I still recommend getting the game but with caution. In my own experience, the game is entirely playable and does not bog down. But there are some bugs and plenty of room for optimization. This release comes loaded with more things than the console versions came with and at a lower price to boot. Putting this game on your wishlist to wait for a patch isn't a bad idea though to get a fully fleshed out experience.

-Resolution: 1600x900

As a real life ninja, I found this ninja simulation to be woeful at portraying the realities of the Way of the Ninja. This is mainly due to two central design decisions. And you almost can't blame the game itself, because these come as standard in every other modern game.
Checkpoints
and
Achievements
Why do we become ninjas and stick to this path we have chosen? You will find many answers to this question, but a common thread is the adrenaline we get from putting ourselves in tense, risky, and frightening situations. When I am out on a raid, I'm often holding my breath as I weigh up my options, each decision momentous because of what I could gain or lose by the next action. There is no room to put a foot wrong, not even once.
In Mark of the Ninja, however, missions are segmented into many many checkpoints. If you make a mistake you can just restart at the most recent, never losing more than a couple of minutes work. No situation is scary in MOTN. No decision momentous.
When you throw in achievements into the mix, the game becomes more about experimentation and playing around with mechanics, rather than true stealth and survival. I'm not talking about Steam achievements, but in-game achievements, designed into the core of the game. You will get little sub missions, like 'complete this level without destroying lights', which add a gamey element and its reward. You are therefore encouraged to fool around, as opposed to becoming immersed. And all the moreso because there's a checkpoint 2 minutes back, so you have nothing to lose by trying something fun.
This is all wrong. Real ninjas like me are always focused on the mission at hand. We become truly immersed. We enter the zone. We do not entertain ourselves by seeing how many funny ways we can scare a dude.

Developer: Klei Entertainment
Publisher: Microsoft Studios
Mark of the Ninja is so brilliantly designed that, fittingly, its quiet revolution could almost go unnoticed. It’s a side-scrolling stealth game that allows for lethal, non-lethal and unseen approaches to its levels, and while the seamless nature of control, information and interface seem like they might have been refined for a generation or more, the game seems to have crept into the world fully-formed. Some of the ideas, such as the visible audio cues and lines of sight, have precedent in other stealth games, notably Metal Gear Solid, but Klei have reinvented or elaborated on every inspiration.
The game’s world throws high tech private military corporations and ninja dojos together – shadows, shuriken, explosives and laser tripwires. That allows for some tricky design but the game is rarely punishing, usually providing escape routes as well as weapons and tools that can put guards out of action. Visually, it’s a masterpiece. The slick cartoon graphics are only part of the reason though; the game’s main strength is its use of every aspect of visual feedback to inform the player. It gives you all the information you’ll ever need, tidily and attractively, and trusts you to play and experiment with that information as you see fit. If that involves unleashing a plague of flesh-eating bugs to dispose of a corpse, so be it.
Notes: Lead designer Nels Anderson is now working on the intriguing Firewatch at Campo Santo.
Where can I buy it: Steam.
What else should I be playing if I like this: Deadlight has a different visual approach, and zombies rather than ninja, but it’s another gorgeous and unusual side-scrolling game. Not as impressive as Mark of the Ninja but worth a look. Anything else by Klei is worth your time and money as well.
Simply a perfect, refined stealth game. Highly recommended.

Prince of Persia is, hands down, one of the most beautiful games I have ever played.
But first of all, it needs to be pointed out that this is not Sands of Time trilogy, and that you shouldn't expect a Sands of Time kind of Prince here.
That said, quality of this game is on par with Sands of Time. Everything about this game is amazing. The world, platforming, adventuring, everything is on exactly the same level as in any of the Sands of Time trilogy installments. If you are looking for a worthy successor to our beloved Sands of Time games, this is it. Look no further. I should point out that combat, while certainly interesting and visually appealing, is not as diverse as it was in Warrior Within or The Two Thrones, but the quality of this game is such that you will barely notice this slight flaw.
The aspect of the game that was the most beautiful to me is the story. I can't describe how immersive it is, how rich and deep it is. And you will love the Prince's new companion, Elika, just as much as you loved Farah. The interaction between the Prince and Elika is beautifully done. Their banter, small talk, discussions... it will keep you captivated throughout the game. You will find yourself rushing to defeat their next enemy just so you could hear them have another conversation, be that a philosophical discussion or a simple chit-chat between a guy and a girl.
And as the game progresses, the story will pull you in until the Prince's world becomes your own. By the time the game reaches its ending, both you and the Prince will find yourself enthralled by Elika's spirit and character that you will find yourself (both you and the Prince) profoundly affected by her and what she represents in this game's world.
And then the end will come. I will not spoil anything. All I will say is that it will send shivers down your spine. And please, this is not something that can be experience in a YouTube video. For you to really feel it, you need to play the game. You need to bond with the Prince and Elika. You need to care for these characters, just like the developers meant you to.
And then, once you play through the end, believe me, it will stay with you for a long time.

As a fan of the Prince of Persia™ franchise, I just couldn't miss this one. And it blew my mind.
This game was just what I needed. Like a ray of pure light it purged the ideas of blood, brutal violence, and gory deaths. This particular game was full of magic. And when I say magic, I mean it. The world is just beautiful. Filled with gorgeous landscapes such as: huge mountains, shining rivers, caves and caverns, flowery plains and other delightful sights. And that's just the "nature" part. There are also a large number of beautifully designed buildings. Some go deep underground, and others reach the throat of the world. Which is both beautiful, and impressive. Especially when there is a Day/Night cycle. And the nights are full of wonders.
The new protagonist is a nameless adventurer in search of fortune. Which, even though called a Prince, is not one. The adventurer is accompanied by an Ahura named Elika, whose race has forsaken the duty given to them by the god of light, Ormazd, and intend to set free the main antagonist, Ahriman. Ahriman is the god of darkness who was imprisoned by Ormazd. The game is a constant fight between the forces of Lights and Darkness. In order to entrap Ahriman and his 4 Corrupted followers once and for all.
Most of the gameplay is still intact. The player can use the Prince character's acrobatic prowess, sword, and gauntlet, as well as magic from Elika to perform combat and acrobatic feats variously throughout the game. Which not only looks stunning, but also causes more damage if you chain all the attacks together. The game features open world exploration that allows the player to travel to any spot in the game world at any given point, and lets the player witness the plot in any way they want. The traps are manifested in various forms of the antagonist Ahriman's Corruption. Black-colored blobs that coat the land and swallow the player if touched. The player can use acrobatic maneuvers to avoid these traps. And after they heal the land, the traps are purged completely.
The player can not conventionally "die" in Prince of Persia. Rather, when an enemy is about to strike the finishing blow, or The Prince presumably falls to his death, Elika saves him. But by doing this, the enemy has time to regain it's health. The combat is tricky at first, but when you get the hang of blocking and deflecting attacks, you won't go down anymore.
The voice acting is probably my favorite part of this game. As soon as the Prince started talking, I knew it was Nolan North. And the game would be full of jokes, witty comments, and funny remarks. And boy, I laughed my face off. Elika was serious about the imminent apocalypse, while the Prince was joking around most of the time, making this adventure less tensioned. Take a look at this:
Prince: I hope that hurt!
Elika: He can’t hear you.
Prince: He can’t?! And you're an ugly mother too!
[Elika gives him a look]
Prince: What?
Or this:
Elika: Tell me about your family.
Prince: I don't have a family.
Elika: Well, you come from somewhere.
Prince: Yes, and I'm going somewhere else.
Although I find Yuri Lowenthal's voice more charismatic and touching, I cannon resist Nolan North's. His voice created so many amazing characters...

I was even laughing while I was re-checking the text again. Ubisoft, thank you for choosing Nolan North.
Now the music. Stuart Chatwood and Inon Zur, my favorite composers. They created this amazing, vibrant music for the game. Both epic and fantastic. When you are roaming around the plains, and other healed ground. A soft, relaxing, light music is playing. And when a fight starts, the drums and flutes are pulsing and come crashing down. Both of these create the perfect atmosphere.
As I said, this game is just stunning. Full of adventuring, jokes, fights, flights, magic, beauty, and romance too. I had so much fun playing it, and I still do. I recommend this game to everyone who enjoys an epic adventure.

For a short game, it's worth the price. It's not meant to give hours of fun in a straight play session, like most twin stick shooters, but it's fun in short bursts. Let's move onto the pros and cons:

Catchy soundtrack
Nice style
Easy to run on most computers made in the last five or so years.
Fun in short bursts
No noticeable bugs
Cons:
Lack of enemy variety (They basically all rush you suicidally at varying speeds and health)
Once boxes on the arena are destroyed, it becomes the basic "box" shape as seen in many games of it's style
Field of view is a bit small to react to the fast rushing enemies
Lack of content (Enemies, boxes to destroy, two or thre powerups, that's it)
The shaky screen effect is a bit over done, and the machine gun is a bit loud in comparison to the soundtrack
The game is a bit bare bones, but it's decent for the low price. If you see it on sale and want a quick Geometry Wars-esque shooter, I'd recommend this one. I do hope some of the cons are addressed in updates, but time will tell, as this review was written a week after release. For now, I wouldn't recommend it to your average user at full price, but if the lack of content is addressed in future updates, I'll definitely change my opinion.

Prior to recent gameplay, I would experience severe stutter to an unplayable extent. As a result, I uninstalled and wrote the review below. I, on a whim today, decided to reinstall and the issue appears to be completely gone. The only change that I've made is using a wired third party xbox 360 controller (with a Boba Fett faceplate because... Boba Fett) instead of an xbox one s wireless controller that i was using before. I wouldn't think this would have any impact on performance though. Regardless of why, I'm glad that things are working perfectly now and I can continue to enjoy this game.
THE FOLLOWING REVIEW IS NO LONGER RELEVANT TO MY EXPERIENCE:
This game has a terrible stuttering problem that seems to be associated with Nvidia cards. After attempts to resolve the issue, search results have a majority of Nvidia card users sharing the same experience as myself. My specs shouldn't be the issue since I currently run a 7700 non k paired with a gtx 1080. I'm not sure if AMD users have a similar experience but for comparison, my sub $300 AMD a12 laptop was able to run this game with no stutter. I have yet to test the igpu of the 7700 to confirm if this is strictly an issue with the dedicated card or not, but regardless this should definitely be addressed by the developer. I've also seen claims that other Lego games suffer from the same issue with Nvidia cards as well. The components I have were a significant investment, and to see that a game from several years back with minimal requirements is causing an issue like this is a huge dissapointment.
If you have an Nvidia card, you may want to carefully research this issue prior to a purchase. Of course with Steam having an excellent refund program, as far as I've experienced, you can proceed with your purchase knowing you can always request your money back. You'll know in the first few seconds if you're experiencing this problem and want a refund.

This is a good game with good devs. Going to keep this short because I don't usually write reviews
+Pros
-The games gorgeous
-Controls are 'tight like a tiger'
-The Zero G effects are different and cool from a strategy view point
-It's unique. Yes I thought it was an Overwatch ripoff when I played it in Beta but once I spent a decent amount of time in game it's honestly not. The match types are different, in a good way, and there's not a 'winning' team class formula you have to adhere to.
-When the matches are close it's just frantic awesome chaos.... Yeah it's like 80's hair metal awesome
-For the most part it's balanced. There probably needs to be some class buff/nerf action happening but there's not one OP class that everyone picks.
-There's a decent amount of different playing classes / playing styles to choose from
-There's enough variety in the game modes but it could use more, this was addressed today with the roadmap
-Don't let the player counts scare you. Matchmaking is fast, and the absolute most I'll have to wait a minute to get placed is 1 minute
-Priced correctly
-Cons
-The matches can be lop sided. I want to chalk this up to the game being new and getting an influx of new players or it could be just how bad I'm at the game, the world may never know. Not going to lie, this was the first game to make me rage quit in a long long long time but after a few minutes I start it right backup and begin again.
-Needs a competitive mode, there was a timeline given for the game and it is coming. It's current offering might not keep interested
-No one talks in team chat. It's like your in a neutrino detector when you're playing the game. This might be a postive for some people but a bare minimum of human interaction should take place. This could also be attributed to my introvertedness.
-Semi steep learning curve. Again might be a PRO for some but things can get rough
That's honestly it. The PROS outweigh the CONS. The games good. If you're on the fence buy it. It's priced correctly. There's a lot of time you can invest into the game without it being stale. If the games on sale there's no reason you shouldn't be buying it.
TL;DR
It's good. Buy it.

For a person who was completely new to the Batman series, as well as 3rd person melee/stealth games (closest I've gotten is Uncharted 3, but that was mainly gunfighting), Batman: Arkham Asylum was a very good play. I'm sure there are very in depth reviews for this game elsewhere, so I'll just outline some of the pros and cons that I personally have.
Pro:
-Story is well done, I never really got bored of it. No glaring conflicts with accepted DC universe lore for a casual Batman fan.
-Graphics are pretty on point, never really got turned off by anything. Of course they aren't breaking standards or anything but the animation is well done for a 2009 game. Plus Poison Ivy still looked hella hot.
-Fighting mechanics are very simplistic and easy to understand. This is coming from a noob to Arkham and brawl type games so you can trust me on this.
Con:
-There is no way to change the mouse sensitivity in settings, you will need manually go into the games files and change some values around
-Minor glitches here and there, sometimes the camera gets stuck and you can't rotate it, making fights pretty annoying
-Possible awkward positioning of keys for some players. Using the Left-Ctrl combos  and having to hold it constantly for crouching cramped my pinky a lot
Overral the game is a very good classic, you should definitely try it out if you are thinking about playing this first before moving onto the other Arkham titles.

You can either kill every one you see or simply sneak past the entire stages utilizing all of the items you have for both Distractions items or Attack/Lethal items as you like. Unlock killing techniques and items as you play then make the best use of every situation.
I would highly recommend this to any platformer lovers who enjoy stealth games at the same time. 10/10

If you love playing action oriented videogames and you like Batman, you'll love this game.
Batman Arkham Asylum is a product of absolute value that can count on a cast of colorful characters to build a great game, really fun. The greatest strengths of the production lie in the gameplay built around what are the real capabilities of Batman, mixing action and stealth section, but always related with the universe from which have been extrapolated.
The story is engaging, the stealth mechanics are excellent, the missions are designed very well, and the voice acting is top notch. More importantly, though, it makes you feel like Batman. You can take on loads of enemies in a brawl, use a small variety of gadgets to help you through the levels, yet you are not invincible - this means you have to use Batman's traditional stealth in order to take on armed enemies.
The combat system, though good, can be frustrating at times, because the counter mechanic feels broken. There are no side missions at all and there is no open world feel, despite you having the ability to wander around the island as you wish.
Ultimately, this is a fantastic game but has a few flaws. Regardless, this game is top quality

The playerbase is terribly low, when someone rage quits a match rarely are they replaced with a new player causing for unbalanced teams and gameplay. Most matches seem to dive into team death match style gameplay with only a few players playing objectives. Ronin is a very interesting mixture of stealth, platform and puzzle mechanics. When the character is undiscovered by the enemies the game plays like a platformer, when the guards find out where you are the turn based combat phase starts. The enemies start to shoot at the player and/or call for reinforcement. The combat is based around carefully planned jumps and the use of the ninja abilities unlocked completing the missions. The game can be really hard until you understand how to stealthy pick off the guards without getting discovered by the remaining enemies. Many of the most difficult scenarios can be easily resolved if you manage to thin down the number of the guards, especially the heavily armed ones. Still sometimes not getting shot is a matter of luck, especially in the new game plus where the assault rifle guard becomes much more powerful. I have enjoyed this game very much since it's pretty unique but I understand that the gameplay may not appeal to everyone. Think about buying Ronin if you are not scared of a game that may require many tries before you can finally pass a difficult section.

RONIN would be a great experience--if it weren't so buggy. The gameplay is very enjoyable when it's working as desired, but when it's not, everything goes downhill.
Pros:
-decent art and music
-sufficient context for the game (why I'm killing people)
-enjoyable gameplay WHEN IT WORKS
Cons:
-First, let me tell you this is a turn-based game. THAT IS NOT A CON. The con is that this turn-based game only executes your desired commands 50% of the time.
-unaccurate player hitboxes
-player dropping down a ledge in the middle of a battle when you wanted to jump onto the ledge
-grappel is not easy to use in that it is difficult to tell where you'll go when doing small adjustments mid-swing
-buggy (enemy got stuck in a wall once and couldn't attack him)
-another bug: if you're standing on the edge of a platform and you want to drop down to a lower platform, there is a certain angle where it shows you can jump down but then your guy just stays at the same spot, wasting a turn and often getting me killed. You can understand my frustration.
-doing side-objectives, while not exactly difficult, are the only way to get much-needed upgrades
-final boss level has no checkpoints and in combination with the gameplay faults listed above, has created a frustrating experience which, in turn, has led me to write this review
To the dev--physics in this sort of game should be less prioritized than making sure the player's commands get executed. For example, if I was about to hit a wall but then I use my grappel to the opposite wall, my grappel should not extend and then make me hit into the wall which is what I wanted to avoid, instead the grappel should guide my momentum to the opposite direction.

Do you remember the game *EA SPORTS FIFA SOCCER '96*? I used to like it for the dumb simplicity of its mechanics & yet it felt convincing enough as a simulator. If you've been following this (in~)famous series of clone/reskin excersises from the very beginning, you might also feel that all the modifications & intrications till this day just cluttered the interface not really adding to the core gameplay which stayed rather schematic, full of grotesque artificial conventions & so very far from live soccer experience.
Pixel Cup Soccer 17 devs didn't try anything too fancy, in fact they got the process reversed starting from 96 (a 'demake' so to say) - they have further dumbed down the mechanics, abolished some unnecessary rules & implemented cartoony graphics, leaving all the initial clunkiness in place - the result is pure fun!
There is no such thing here as fauls or injuries (tackles always successful if not missed), no offside rule, no rosters or substitutions. Only 2 buttons left (pass/change & shoot/tackle) - it turnes out to be just enough with the contextual functioning & longer/shorter push mechanics.
Also the game boasts really jagged animations approximately reflecting what might have happened on the field, & that's cool with me as well.
The game feels sometimes like an old beat-em-up game with its rating based collision resolving. So it is a really cool party game & just relax time for soccer fans!

First, I have to say, the game looks great. Art style is extremely well done.
But gameplay is not quite up to snuff. They clearly were paying homage to classic arcade games, and they brought the issues those games suffered from along. The main two issues are defensive auto player switching and a complete lack of any kind of physics. Personally, I don't know anyone who actually likes auto player switching, and any game that gives the option, I think most of us would choose to turn it off. Even when the game does a good job of giving you the player you would want on defense (it does... Ok, here), it's the timing of switching that matters.
On the other issue, don't get me wrong, I'm not asking for an actual physics engine. I'd simply like to see a few frames of animation when a player starts moving in the opposite direction. Just like in SWoS, defenders are able intercept passes made in front of them, while being behind the passer, then immediately start running the opposite direction with the ball. It's possibly worse here than in that game, as I'm consistently seeing the AI intercept my passes in this way, when I press the button while the defender is still several steps behind me.
I think if they could marry this visual look with gameplay more similar to something like Stir Fried Games Soccer, they'd have real hit.

What will you expect from Final Fantasy XIII-2? (Strongly recommend to play through the previous game, CONTAINS SPOILERS FROM XIII)
(TL,DR: Read Pros&Cons and Overall at the bottom, I played on the console version)
„Why does mankind defy its fate?”
The game takes place three years after the events of Final Fantasy XIII, and depicts the story of Serah Farron's journey across time and space to prevent the end of the world while searching for her missing sister, Lightning.
Pros:
- Fantastic atmosphere
- The battle system expanded (you can catch monsters and they fight with you as third party member)
- Epic music (more vocals and remixed versions for pre-battle)
- ’More openworld’ than the XIII had, side missions, puzzles, casino etc.
- Returning characters and places (You can visit the areas in other timelines, these areas change in appearance)
- You can replay the chapters/missions anytime you want, and you can continue your journey (this is the NewGame+)
- Paradox (or alternate) endings
- Epic final boss battle with one of the best FF antagonist
- You will get all the DLCs (3 story, all Coliseum battles, outfits)
- Still an amazing story, but...
Cons:
- ...again linear and complicated (time travelling)
- Only two playable characters (the DLCs grant you to play with Sazh, and Lightning in their own story)
- Too easy
- Shorter than XIII
Story (AF timeline means After the Fall of Cocoon):
After the events of XIII, Lightning gets caught by a paradoxon and taken to Valhalla, the realm of death. While everybody thinks Lightning is dead, Serah is confident that her sister is alive. Lightning will be a knight of goddess Etro, and her task to save the future from Caius Ballad, who wants to destroy the time, he is Yeul's immortal Guardian and seeks to end the suffering she sustains by being endlessly reincarnated by killing the goddess Etro. Noel Kreiss comes from the Dying World at 700 AF, where he is the last surviving human in a world that faced destruction 200 years after the Crystal Pillar’s fall and Lightning ask him to find Serah and help her reach Valhalla. In New Bodhum (on Gran Pulse) at 3 AF Noel coming to find Serah. The two encounters in an epic journey through time and space to solve the paradoxons and save the world and Lightning.
What about with the original team? Fang and Vanille are still in the Crystal Pillar, Hope is now 24 years old and the leader of the Academy (the new capital city), Sazh and Dajh have mysteriously gone missing, Snow left to search for Lightning two years after her disappearance, and Serah stayed with the NORA at New Bodhum.
Battle:
The battle system returns from XIII, you are able to switch the party leader during battle, the third party member will be a monster that will fight along with you with their own role (One monster = One role) and you can upgrade them (new abilites, better stats). It’s okay because three monsters can be held at a time, and automatically switch to the role a player shifts to in the paradigm. The Crystarium system returns too, with levels not with tiers. A new form of damage, called Wound Damage, lowers a target's member's max HP during battle and can only be healed by items, giving further incentive to defeat enemies as quickly as possible. If the current party leader is KO'd, the party leader is automatically switched to the other human character. The defeat of the human characters in the party results in a game over.
Playtime (My first walkhthrough):
Story: 32 hours (ofc with cutscenes)
100%, All achievements, all (160) fragments, best chocobo for racing: 63 hours
Overall:
For me this game 10/10, if I need to compare to the other FF games then 8/10, the story not better than the XIII’s story, but the atmosphere is better and the battles are exciting, there will be people who like this game more than the previous.
If you loved the first installment, you will love this one too, if you hated you will be disappointed again, don’t buy it then. That's a pity, because I think it promises adventure not to be missed, despite its flaws.
If you liked the game, I can recommend the finale of the trilogy: Lightning Returns.
Thanks for reading!

- The maps are too small, and there is no spawn protection. This results in a lot of spawn camping.
- The game modes are basic and can hardly be housed in the small maps, resulting in gameplay that pretty much devolves into bum rushing a point over and over with very little tactics involved.
- The grenades get thrown with zero trajectory, meaning your years of aim and practice are thrown out the window.
- The classes are unbalanced, and the game holds your hand in automatically activating abilities.
Do not buy this game. You will be disappointed. Play Dirt Bomb instead. It's free, and good. This game brings absolutely nothing to the table. It's a waste of your time.

I was alone, and downloaded this as a joke a long time ago. I also had no internet recently, and eventually stumbled upon this in my library. I was against playing it at first, but after a few days of more boredom, I played it anyways. -And don't let my play time fool you. I might have very short time, but I have been offline for my playthrough.
I used timeskip with my Date and Time settings, and played through it twice after I wasted my crystals the first time. I actually racked up 8 hours a day average gameplay for 2 weeks in a row for the first playthrough, and another 2 weeks for the 2nd. Which makes it much more enjoyable for people who like variety and references.
Worth every cringe and laugh it brings with it. 8/10.

While I do find this game amusing, and will probably continue to play it as a time waster, there's a few gnawing reasons behind this negative review.
Starting out, I have to say that this is far from one of Telltale's best works.  The game honestly comes off as something they spent a weekend throwing together for a quick buck before they moved on to their next epic story.  It's poker, with some entertaining characters, and I realize that in itself has limits but this game had the potential to be a far better experience.
Getting down to the nitty gritty of the whole thing, the biggest flaw in the game is sheer repetitiveness.  Within the first half hour of playing you’ll quickly notice characters often become repetitive with their expressions toward your actions.  I swear, if I have to hear Sam say, “Great day in the morning”, one more time I can’t be held liable for the consequences.  Not to mention how often Claptrap brings the game to a solid halt explaining how he’s immune to bluffing, right before folding.  It was funny the first time, but the 300th time is just annoying.  That’s the biggest thing here.  All of these expressions were meant to be funny or amusing, and they are the first time you see them, but then it’s like watching the same joke over and over again.  It stops being amusing and just becomes dreadfully annoying.
The next least annoying feature of the game is, again, repetitiveness.  This time it takes the role of the introduction of each game.  Every time you start a new game a 3rd rate character announces the buy-in for the tournament at 20 thousand, the camera pans to show everyone putting meaningless and endless wads of money on the table, and after a short eternity you finally get to play cards.  This could have been completely left out, there’s no point to it.  Doesn’t matter how many times you play the game, everyone is still going to magically pull a stack of money out of their pocket and drop it on the table.  It’s not like a character is going to be $5 short, or reveal empty pockets, or something.  Everyone’s always got the money, so why waste time on meaningless “cut scenes”?  Going right along with that is the blind notification.  When GladoS comes in and talks about upping the blinds it seems really out of place.  It’s like felt they needed to make announcing a change in the rules enjoyable, but got the intern to do the job.
Aside from poker there are some other draws to this game, the most important being the unlocks for other games.  Having accomplished a lot of these unlocks I can safely say, they’re really not worth it.  From what I can tell each character has a “special item” you can win, by winning the poker game while they have the item up for grabs.  That means there are only 4 special items, each of which unlocks a few things across the different games the characters come from.  Most of the unlocks are simply cosmetic, and won’t actually mean much to anyone.  There are a series of these, again simply cosmetic.  You win points for playing poker and completing “achievements” that are assigned to you at the start of the game, like defeating 2 opponents in a head-to-head match.  These points can be used to unlock different cosmetic styles for the poker table, chips, cards, etc.  The unlocks are themed after the various games the characters are from (portal included).  That said, once you find and unlock your favorites there really is no further use for the points.  I had a bunch of the unlocks done within the first 3 hours, which really left me not wanting to do any more.
All in all, and I really hate to do it, I have to give Poker Night 2 a thumbs down.  At best it’s a gimmicky way to play Omaha or Texas Holdem poker (those are the only two modes available).  I went in hoping for more, and maybe that’s what led me to being so disappointed with it.  I’ll probably still play it from time to time as a time waster, but it’s not a game I’m willing to recommend.

While not directly building off of the last game, this is still a step in the right direction. The combat and stealth is just as riveting as HR, but these new graphics make everything
much better. The new aug menu really reveals just how much they did to Adam at the beginning of HR.
The experimental augs I haven't gotten to simply because I forgot to do the sidequest to get them without cost, so I was like "Let's not remove my current augs, thanks." The experimental augs are probably very useful for certain missions, but you can complete the campaign without them. Probably the only downside to them is not getting that sidequest done for them, which without would make you disable an aug PERMANENTLY, potentially screwing up any newgame+ you start with that save.
Another helpful feature for people, like myself, who haven't played Deus Ex in a good few years is the tutorials at the intro mission (which is strangely similar to the intro to DX:HR btw). Cover is no longer right-click, it is now F, and locks on to that piece of cover until you press F again. This takes away the cool run/shoot/hide mechanic that so many of us loved in HR, but makes it easier on your hand, I suppose. After adjusting and learning again, you can mimic it, but it's not the same.
The action buttons are now from F1 to F4, which is a much better reach than going from combat and looking over at your numpad going "Where the hell is the Typhoon one?!" as you mash your cloak, silent-pants and Superman-vision all at the same time, completly draining your energy as you stare your otherwise-would-be takedown in the face while he shoves buckshot into yours. Or that embarrasing moment when you meant to cloak but instead typhoon, killing the whole room of civies in the LIMB clinic and getting steam-rolled by local police. Fun times, right?
The UI is much more visibly pleasing than HR, and adapts well to large displays. The graphics are insane compared to HR (I just went back in to it and almost barfed at seeing visible triangles on the highest setting) and really set you in to Prague. Framedrops happen more often than not, but if you have the hardware, it's barely noticeable unless you pay attention to a framerate counter in the corner somewhere.
The story path I took didn't have Megan in it, but I saw her name and actor in the credits, so maybe she's in there somewhere? I dunno, but do something I didn't; DO EVERY DAMN SIDEQUEST. They say "sidequest" like you don't need to do it, but you DO. Absolutely, do every sidequest and POI, because there's some juicy isht in there. One of them I really liked, directly followed up on the aftermath of Panchea and.. well, not going to give spoilers here. You'll have to play it for yourself.

Similar to Mass Effect 2 this game provide a wide range of interesting characters that you get to associate with, in this case, you will have to bring the fight to darkspawn, ending the Blight. All the characters have traits, skills and personality that you would eventually have to get use to and stick with, and maybe fall in love with in the later time. The more time invested in the game, the more you understand the strength and weakness of each characters.
Character customization, this game allows you to choose your characters' race (human, elf, dwarf) and class(warrior, rogue, mage). All of those with different attributes and strength. Tinkering with the inventory is always fun. Deciding the types of weapons to equip depending on the class of the characters. Dialogues are cheesy, but still ok. The outcome and the consequences of the story depends on the decisions through all those cheesy dialogues that you make.
The story might seem straight forward, ending the Blight, reclaiming peace for Ferelden. True, that is the ultimate goal. The essence of the game is when you explore Ferelden through various quests while  getting ready to face the Blight. Deep and in depth backstory of characters and the plot itself. Solid first person shooter. It's different, fast-paced, looks great, and fun.
The characters are fun to play as. It's like Overwatch in that each character has 2 abilities and an Ultimate. And each character has a different way they can boost themselves, helping things move at a quick pace. There's a tutorial you can watch for each character, and you get in-game currency as a reward. The tuts aren't long either, they show you exactly what you need to know, that's it.
I haven't played long enough to have personally visited every map but so far, I'd say they're alright. They're very detailed and there's a lot to take in at first. I've seen all of the maps on YouTube and I just hope they add more with different themes to them.
The gamemodes are Blitzball (CTF), Uplink, Turf War (domination), Occupy (Hardpoint), and Overcharge. Uplink and Overcharge are the exact same thing so it's kind of dumb to have both. There's tutorials for each gamemode like the characters and you get coins for watchin each one (they're short).
The graphics are quite nice. I have an Intel i7-4970K 4.00GHz with an 8GB NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1070 and run the game on Ultra settings. I think there's a higher setting, can't remember as I write this. But at those settings the game runs smooth for me. No fps or lag issues.
It's not pay-to-win. There's Stash Drops that you get by playing the game. I got 3 Stash Drops from my last game. I got a lot of XP and did well so maybe that had to do with it? Not sure. But when you open a Stash Drop it opens 4 big cryo-lookin chambers. There's different quality tiers that many other games have. You get coins for duplicate drops. And with those coins you can buy character/weapon skins and weapon stickers. You can't buy currency but you can buy Stash Drops.
The skins for the characters/weapons look great. There's a lot of them. There's also a ton of stickers to choose from for your weapon. There's different qualities of stickers you can choose from, holographic being the best type.
Overall, I'm glad I got this.

If you were to ask me three years ago what I thought of Mark of the Ninja, I would bluntly state that I found it boring. And yet here I am now recommending you this game. I am going to tell you why both opinions should matter to you.
Basically, you're a ninja who is tasked with an impossible goal. With the use of a magical tattoo, you can achieve that goal. The game is a linear pathway of stealth tactics with a leveling up mechanic along the way. Solutions are numerous and continue to add up as you level up.  Art style is reminiscent of a saturday morning cartoon like Samurai Jack.
Let's start with my experience three years ago. I was looking for an atmospheric stealth game that could rival the quality of other stealth games such as Chaos Theory and Thief. When I saw the reviews, I bought the game without second thought and expected a game with the freedom of choice on how to handle situations. What I got was a game that offered you that freedom, but with a great amount of restriction. These restrictions included missing stealth kill techniques, something that should have been there in the first place since you are the *best* of your clan. You don't need some magical tattoo to do some simple kill technique.  It makes no sense to restrict such basic functions other than to make the player play *your way* . I also found the soundtrack and story to be rather boring and after that I stopped on the third or fourth level. I left irritated.
Three years later, I decided to give this game another try. I decided to play their way as I was sure they had a good reason for the restrictions. After adjusting my expectations, I played a game that was throughourly entertaining and intense throughout. Leveling up required you to play a certain way such as never being discovered or achieving three kills within 15 seconds. As you level up, you get new toys such as spikes and human eating insects, and boy was it satisfying using these items properly. When I played *properly*, the game had me hooked from beginning to end. It was great. But it's only great when you play *properly* according to restrictions.
Now for the score
Gameplay: 8.5/10
Controls are tight and gameplay is very satisfying when everything plays out. Yet initial restrictions impede the flow of your own tactics.
Narrative: 6/10
The story is there to give you an excuse to kill numerous security guards. The ending may have you talking, but you will never state that the story is part of what hooked you until the end of the game. Boring and uninspired with a lack of development for the protagonist.
Graphics: 7.5/10
The art design and graphics accomplish their goal of having you feel like you're interacting in a saturday morning cartoon. However, the graphics are really nothing special. In addition, aside from one level featuring stormy weather, none of these stages feature any eye candy or something to appreicate. But the animations are well done with tons of expression.
Sound: 7/10
Nothing to hear about folks. Audio cues will come in handy, but music and voice acting both present themselves as flat.
Originality: 9/10
Simply put, you will not find any stealth game out there that matches the fundamentals of the gameplay present here. Sure the idea of stealth is there, but the way these developers present their vision is great indeed.
Final Score
7.6/10

Probably. I'm not exceptionally nostalgic as I never played the console versions of this game but having played a lot of various Lego DS games I might have some bias.
It's also worth noting that it's not exactly fair to compare this game to other Lego games, as it isn't an original game. It's merely a compilation of the two existing Lego Star Wars games, so claiming it has more content than other Lego games is inaccurate.
But just because it doesn't have any more content than the average Lego game doesn't mean it doesn't have a ton of content in general. The game is almost a collect-a-thon in terms of things to find, from the main currency of studs, used to buy things in the shop, to Minikits, used to build models that can be viewed in the hub world, to Power Bricks, used to unlock extras that produce various effects on gameplay, to Gold Bricks, used to unlock entire levels. The amount of collection and replayability these introduce is astounding, and they rarely feel repetitive or tedious. The collect-a-thon aspects also make the game rather unique, as, rather being the typical 3D platformer, it's mostly an action game (though platforming is far from rare).
Well, two: The camera and the controls. The controls are by far the more egregious, though both can hamper gameplay at points. The controls, or more accurately the movement, are sluggish and make combat difficult. Some odd decisions, such as having to double jump almost immediately after the first jump, can make platforming difficult. Not being able to cycle through characters in Story Mode can also make it difficult to choose a specific character when multiple party members are in a small space. You have incredibly limited control over the camera, forcing the at times wonky perspective. This can make platforming difficult, as all you can do to line up jumps and see platforms is pan the camera rather than rotate it. These flaws, while far from insignificant, can be adjusted to and compensated for, though that doesn't completely alleviate all frustration.
And if you were looking forward to the multiplayer, I hope you have an extra controller. There is no online co-op, nor is there even LAN. The only multiplayer available is splitscreen, which is odd considering other console versions apparently had online.

Final Fantasy XIII-2 is a decent/good JRPG, but a subpar Final Fantasy game.  It continues to tow the line of deviation from what made the core series so great, interesting backstories and adventuring prospects and an overall cohesive main story.  Despite this it is still a better game than FFXIII, and its two main characters actually have significant character development (relative to FFXIII at least). This game although graphically stunning is lacking substance, and albeit improving on some of the linearity of FFXIII it is still not of the same caliber of  other Final Fantasy games and is a forgettable experience. That being said with the exception of some of the developments in FFXIII- Lightning returns aka. 3, much of this game can retroactively be ignored (FFXIII-Lightning returns is arguably the strongest installment in the trilogy, both gameplay and story wise). The story in this game is disjointed so much that playing Metal Gear Solid 4 before any of the others will logically make more sense than some of the components of this game.
Gameplay wise, its minimalist approach isn't all bad. You have two main playable characters, Serah and Noel and an captured monster that assists as a third member. The combat as a result offers more complexity than FFXIII-2 albeit still is rudimentary. The exploration involves a variety of areas, not bound by the linear connections that FFXIII's were, and as such you get more opportunities to adventure. You will have an enjoyable experience facing off against the classic assortment of FF foes and a few unique new ones. It should be noted, as stated prior that much of the cast of the previous game is not playable, and Lightning, whom I'd consider as the saving grace in FFXIII has behind the scenes role in this game, despite much of the plot relating to her. Overall the gameplay is worth picking this game up for alone, if you can tolerate the subpar storytelling and disjointed story.
I can't recommend this as a Final Fantasy game, but I can recommend it as a JRPG, at its core its still an enjoyable experience that you will find investing many hours in as you continue your adventure in the FFXIII universe.

Let me start off saying this. Before I played the Arkham games, I was not a Batman fan. That changed after playing Arkham Asylum on PS3. I soon bought Arkham City, then Arkham Knight. I also happen to own Arkham Origins. I have put over 200 hours into Arkham Knight, and while it is my favorite, none of the games capture the amazing Arkham atmosphere like Asylum.
Plot: The Joker attacks the mayor, and Batman arrests him. Batman brings him to Arkham Asylum, and hands him over to the guards there. However, Batman feels that something is wrong, and follows them as they transfer Joker to his cell. Before Joker is in his cell, he breaks loose, and manages to take control of the Asylum. With the help of his thugs(a fire at Blackgate transferred them), Joker is ready to unleash hell on Batman.
Controls: The game controls very well. I have found a couple issues with the freeflow combat, but overall, it runs very smooth.
Graphics: Many hiccups, mostly due to my sound card. However, with an update, the game ran fine.
Cons: The final Joker boss battle is pretty easy, and it seems unlike the personality of the Joker. However, it is satifying.
Overall, I would strongly recommend this game. The Batman Arkham games are my favorite games. That's saying a lot, considering I own about 210 games in total. Batman: Arkham Asylum: 9.7/10  Batman: Arkham City: 9.7/10 Batman: Arkham Origins: 8.6/10 Batman: Arkham Knight: 9.9/10
You need to play the Arkham games. Enough said.

Mark of the Ninja is the best stealth game since Thief 1/2. If you want a stealth game, you won't find a better one. Unlike the Thief games, MotN plays in 2D; however the transition from 3D to 2D doesn't mean it's less complex than the Thief games. You'll still have to be careful not to be seen, not to make too much noise and there are many side objectives in every level to keep things interesting.
All gameplay systems come together perfectly in the best stealth game in recent times. It's so good that I 100%ed it - MoTn is the first Steam game where I've completed every achievement and I've done everything there is to be done (it took me ~20 hours including the DLC level, so there's good value for your money). Besides GOAT tier gameplay, MotN also offers a simple but powerful story that complements the gameplay perfectly.
Graphics are nice, consisting of cartoon like sprites which are superbly animated. Sounds are deeply connected to the game's stealth system and are well implemented. And the level design is amazing. Seriously. Every level is built in such way to make you feel like the most badass ninja to ever exist (which in the context of the game, you are). Kudos to the level designer. There are also unlockables that you earn after each level/side objective. And after you complete the main campaign there's also a New Game+ mode, for that 'no kill run' you'll want to do.
When I was a kid, I used to play a lot on my ZX Spectrum and one of my favourite games was Saboteur, a game that made me feel like a ninja. ~30 years later, MotN reminded me of Saboteur, not from a gameplay pov but because it gave me the same "omg amazing best game ever" feel.
All in all, I have no bad things to say about this game. If you want to feel like a ninja, try MotN. If you want to play the best stealth game since the original Thief games, play MotN. It's truly a must play.

Bought it because I enjoyed Skyborn (by the same developers). This one sadly is quite awful. Not just in comparison, but in general.
- Some parts of the game has really good mapping, but for the most part it looks like it was thrown together in five minutes. This includes random space platforms in the middle of a cave for no good reason.
- There's a desert stage where the ground you can walk on the ground you can't walk on share almost the same colour, making it near impossible to see where any openings are. Doesn't help that it is one of the areas that loops around (guess the desert spans the entire world since if we go left for long enough we end up in the area we started).
- The writing was awful. After about 3 hours I started spamming through the dialogue because we didn't learn anything from it.
- There were several scenes that should have been left out of the game for they didn't add anything to the story or the characters involved.
- Balancing issues ahoy. Especially in regards to the final bosses, but also with a few of our own abilities. One of the final bosses has an AOE attack that almost one-shotted my party and stunned everyone. After we get stunned that one boss gets 2-3 more attacks before my fastest character gets to act. Now I had leveled enough to basically get no experience from enemies anymore, so I'm not sure what kind of level it is intended for... but apparently 60-65 is not enough for normal difficulty.
- Spell imbalances comes especially from Soha who has an AOE spell that can kill almost all regular enemies in the game alone on normal. The few that survive are generally taken down by everyone else shortly afterwards.
This game definitely should have gotten 1-2 more years in development to fix it up.
All in all, avoid this one and go play Skyborn instead.

So, I had experience with this dev team before. They make really good RPGmaker RPGs, On that note they do some weird things too.
Combat is grid based, has some learning to it,
Pros:
-Good turn base combat, much like Chrono trigger or FinalfantasyX if you want a reference.
-Really nice pacing on the story and combat, Only really slows down near the finale.
-A lot of freedom in building your stuff. Class specifics, Passives. You can very much so try your own builds of what is
given.
-Crafting that is fairly straight forward and doesn't punish you for trying to make new things.
-Every character has its place in the team, and then some.
-Exploration greatly rewarded. Every dungeon area has a dual box system where you get 1, then find 2. and you get a pretty good reward for it. Additionally most every map has EXP nodes which just give your EXP for walking on top of them further rewarding your for just walking about the map.
Cons:
-Lack of enemy information. Things like HP bars vanish after attacks so you do need to pay attention to what you have attacked, and not attacked.
-Some information is fairly lacking, for example most skills use TP, but don't tell you how much UNLESS you are in battle with that skill in your load out.
-No place to remind yourself of things. For the life of me, still don't know what the Shock debuff does.
-With instant dialog on, some text is shunted off of the screen before you can read it.
Neutral:
-So, like their other game SkyBorn. The final boss is super, super hard. I both like and dislike this since I played the entire game on Hard, and then this person just kinda slaps me down. On the other hand I really like that the final boss is actually hard, and isn't like so many games where the real challenges are optional.
-Hand in hand with this, there are a few areas you can revisit which refill chests and level up to you so you can farm. Issue with this, is there is a missible item system through out, one of the rewards for finding all of the items is an accessory that increases drops, and drop rates, which is not NEEDED, but very nice for the end game loop.
Over all, my time is some what boosted due to just leaving the game on often but I probably am near the 20Hr mark, certainly worth the money I paid.

RONIN is a neat action/strategy game about jumping on walls, swinging from grappling hooks, and most importantly dodging bullets as you slash entire facilities of mooks to shreads.
The game exists in two 'phases', spotted and not spotted. If not spotted, you move around with regular WADS controls, and can create leap arcs to walls, send out grappling hooks, choke people who haven't seen you, and pause time (with Space, super important for taking out several enemies before being spotted).
When spotted, the game becomes entirely turn based where you lose the ability to walk and can use leaps and the grappling hook to get around. Red lines will show where bullets are about to be fired so at your turns end you either need to not be near any of them or you need to kill whoever is holding the gun. There are mechanics that allow you to throw your sword and a few other powerups that aren't very useful. Being spotted but then disengaging from combat will cause them to call in a lockdown as well, making the rest of the level harder. Every level except the last has three 'bonus' goals: Kill all enemies, kill no civilians (useless, but can call in a lockdown), and don't allow a lockdown to occur. Getting them all in one level gives you a skill point to invest into upgrades.
There are quarks in the game to consider. The arc of your jump doesn't give you information like if you'll hit someone, if the glass will stop you (you need enough momentum to break it), etc, but overall the game is solid and gives you all the information you need to make an informed decision (as long as you realize reinforcements are always coming anyway).
The discussions page has a LOT of people complaining that the game is too hard, but nothing even close to unfair starts until new game plus, where a few modifications make the game boarder on the masochistic. On your first playthrough, though, you simply need to evaluate your straetgy and git gud and you'll have no trouble at all.
THE RUNDOWN: Kinda difficult, sometimes frustrating, but pretty fair- this game is the challenge you might be interested in. Fun gameplay, and is long enough to feel worth ten bucks or so without dragging on. Do recommend.

is an instant indie classic.  It is very easy to digest and has an alluring simplicity to it; but at the same time it boasts exciting gameplay and a very refined atmosphere.  Elements of 2D platforming, stealth, and action combine to create a distinguished and enjoyable identity for the game. If you generally appreciate this style of game, then you should consider checking out
.
The core gameplay is relatively simple and easy to dive right into.  The controls are mostly comfortable and intuitive, and the design style allows each person to tailor their play to their preferences.  Each mission allows for a little improvisation at times, as there are often different routes you can take to reach your goals. And as you unlock new items and abilities, you can experiment with new approaches to keep the game fresh.
There isn't much per way of the story, but there is enough information offered to give you a basic purpose to your actions. But even though the story elements are minimal, the game has an outstanding atmosphere.  The art style is very pleasing, especially the hand-painted backdrops. And the lighting effects are exquisite, particularly due to the importance of staying in the shadows. Add in the fitting weather effects and the soundscape and you are left with a truly pleasurable and captivating atmosphere.
also was designed to be challenging without being overly difficult. I personally felt that it was perfectly balanced to not be too easy and not be too hard, dwelling within that perfect “Goldilocks-zone” that allows the game to appeal to a vast majority of gamers. And since most people won’t be able to just breeze right through it unchallenged, it can take over a dozen hours to complete— even though it isn’t necessarily a
game. On top of that, there is also a NewGame+ mode to add some replay value for those who would be interested.
In summary, I posit that grabbing
is an easy choice for any true fan of the genre. And due to the high quality of the game design, I also would suggest that more casual fans of the genre give it some strong consideration as well.

Ballistic Overkill is a rather basic multiplayer first person shooter, leaning more towards fast-paced and arcade-like gameplay similar to Dirty Bomb, aside from having any special game modes.
+ Character and weapon handling is pretty nice.
+ Has a decent variety in character classes and a good variety in weapons.
+ Runs well on Linux, at least on my computer.
+ Has a pretty well-made loadout system.
- There are no major innovations in this game to speak of.
- Netcode could be better.
- Do we really need an unlock system for a purchasable game? Just having cosmetics as unlocks would be enough.
- Has aim-down-sights and sprint, which don't belong in arcade-like, fast paced shooters. You cannot opt-out of using aim-down-sights like in Dirty Bomb, because the impact to accuracy is much larger.
- A sad reality for so many multiplayer-focused games: The player base is not very large at the time of writing. Still, there are enough people to play with, at least in Europe.
- Just a minor thing: The animation quality could be better.
For the low asking price this game is worth the money and I can recommend it.

Let me start off saying this. Before I played the Arkham games, I was not a Batman fan. That changed after playing Arkham Asylum on PS3. I soon bought Arkham City, then Arkham Knight. Plot: The Joker attacks the mayor, and Batman arrests him. Batman brings him to Arkham Asylum, and hands him over to the guards there. However, Batman feels that something is wrong, and follows them as they transfer Joker to his cell. Before Joker is in his cell, he breaks loose, and manages to take control of the Asylum. With the help of his thugs(a fire at Blackgate transferred them), Joker is ready to unleash hell on Batman.
Controls: The game controls very well. I have found a couple issues with the freeflow combat, but overall, it runs very smooth.
Graphics: Many hiccups, mostly due to my sound card. However, with an update, the game ran fine.
Cons: The final Joker boss battle is pretty easy, and it seems unlike the personality of the Joker. However, it is satifying.
Overall, I would strongly recommend this game. The Batman Arkham games are my favorite games. That's saying a lot, considering I own about 210 games in total. Batman: Arkham Asylum: 9.7/10  Batman: Arkham City: 9.7/10 Batman: Arkham Origins: 8.6/10 Batman: Arkham Knight: 9.9/10

This game isn't a masterpiece.. But it is still fantastic. More open, good story, unique soundtrack, and amazing gameplay make this game great. The battle system of FF XIII-2 returns in a familiar yet more improved in some ways, resulting in my new favorite battle system of the entire series. Fights requires a mix of strategy, timing and a style that makes combat not only fast flowing but oozing with stylish flair giving each victory a satisfying feeling. You're never left feeling like you're grinding away in every battle. Quickly shifting to defensive paradigms when a boss is about to use a devastating attack or debuffing paradigms where you're setting up for the long haul. In fact, there are quite a number of improvements made to the system since the last game that make battles much more enjoyable:
• No longer will the game end when the party leader dies.
• Paradigm Shift animations are much more brief and in most cases, omitted.
• Paradigms can be tuned to focus on single or multiple targets.
• Six classes are available.
• Summons don't transform into vehicles.
• Shroud items (like Aegisol) have been removed.
• TP is gone.
Should I buy this game? YES.

I really wanted to like this game. It reminds me a lot of Gunpoint. However unlike Gunpoint, this game doesn't seem to understand what it is trying to be. The controls are clunky and imprecise, which for a tactical game is really not good. Playing with a controller makes it extremely hard to aim jumps, and the pause button on keyboard doesn't work (pressing space pauses the game for half a second, holding it pauses for half-second bursts?).
There is a pointed lack of accuracy in the prediction elements of the game. Bullets have to pass through some vague percentage of your leg to hit, but any percentage of any other section of your body. Enemies can never shoot eachother, while sometimes you'll be up against four or more machine-gun wielding guards. If you even tap an enemy body, you transfer momentum and your arc is affected. To that order, the arc predictor is annoyingly inaccurate.
The game tries to cover up various failures by telling you "Tips" whenever the game is paused. They often contain tidbits like "The arc always lies" and "This is not a stealth game, kill everyone." The former is obvious. The later, refers to various options to kill enemies out of combat. The game also actively requires you to avoid killing certain individuals, who will activate the alarm upon seeing any activity whatsoever involving the player. This includes broken windows, movement, dead guards, etc.
Your movement is also extremely clunky and awkward. When in combat, it is impossible to move in any way except jumping, meaning that even if you want to shimmy a little to the side, you must complete a full jump (often 2 turns) to accomplish that. With all the inaccuracies in the game UI, and the often haphazard hit detection, the combat eventually becomes extremely frustrating and boring.
I would say it has a very interesting idea, but is a poor sword-based clone of Gunpoint. It really needed to be tightened up a lot. Sorry, but give it a pass.

This game is beautiful, but bland. Most of your time will be spent parkour-ing around mini-hubs in search of enough collectibles to open up further mini-hubs to parkour around to collect more collectibles, and so on.
There is one way to play this game: each location has a set number of collectibles to find, that can only be accessed by taking a specific route. Failure to take the appropriate route - for example, by mis-timing a jump, or falling into a trap - means you get caught by your companion, and dropped off at the last flat terrain you were stood on. This means there's very little sense of scale to your surroundings: the only difference between being hundreds of feet in the air dangling from a cliff edge, or hanging from an archway above the ground, is the skybox. Fall off the edge and whoops, try again, you're back at the start.
The graphics are sharp and vivid, colours are vibrant, and there's a clear distinction between areas you've 'healed' and those that are on the checklist. There's even a nice subtle visual effect - what's it called? where the corners of the screen dim? - that appears when you pass from safe to dangerous areas.
There's not really a lot to the game, in all honesty. What kills it for me is the total lack of variety - enemies are few and far between, and generally exist as an obstacle to slow down your progress (as with the collectibles). Combat consists of waiting for the enemy to strike, parrying, and using a certain weapon to attack (that the game helpfully pauses combat to explain). Even the parkour isn't very interesting, as all the areas you are capable of traversing are marked with certain visual cues: 'wallrun here' areas are all marked with the same scraped texture, for example, and 'climb this ledge' areas have the same scuffed edges. So there's hardly even a sense of exploration, or experimentation: it's like you're told how to solve the puzzle before even attempting the puzzle.
Other miscellaneous points:
The player protagonist isn't either an obnoxious misanthrope, or a wisecracking cynic. Dude just wants to save the day and then go home with his donkey, which is admirable. The Princess is your standard warm-hearted 'i must reclaim my land from evil' archetype, but mostly exists outside of cutscenes to be dragged around the scenery with you and fed the collectibles.
The game itself is fully controller-compatible, but for some reason there's a launcher screen with a 'Launch the game!' option that you'll need a mouse for. Of course, graphics options etc. are also to be found in the launcher, rather than in-game.
The soundtrack isn't anything to celebrate: vague 'you are exploring an Arabian Nights-ish landscape' sonic wallpaper, nothing special or memorable.

Druid 1 & 2 on C-64 warped my fragile little mind many decades ago so when i first saw this i wanted to give it a try immediately. Time to re-open the scars i got then.

There are just so many glitches. Stand and fire? Not working if a enemy death animation frame was just in front of the player. It's now a invisible wall until you move a small distance. Sounds? none. Music warps (hopefully not intentionally?) like there is too much echo effect and bass. OST is ok i'd say but glitches make it terrible sometimes.
And then basically there is no game gimmicks like in D1 and D2 where the goal was to manage your ammo inventory and crowd control along with exploration. Now there is hard crowd control w/glitches and no other strategy other than knowing in which chest the key is.
So at this point i'll give this thumbs down until it gets more flesh. Too raw deal now to spend money on. Yet.
