The good:
The visuals look good, and the game flows wonderfully, making the Prince's acrobatic transitions from place to place a genuine pleasure to watch. The before-and-after transitions as you cleanse areas of their corruption are also enjoyable to see.
Elika manages, unlike Farah in Sands of Time, to stay out of your way and not shoot you with arrows, while still being there whenever you want to use her to enable a special ability (or to catch you when you fall). The byplay between her and the Prince is also enjoyable rather than intrusive, with the ability to prompt her for narrative on demand to flesh out the unavoidable bare-bones version allowing you to explore the setting and backplot at your leisure.
While the environments make little sense if you think about them too hard, taken on their own terms, they generally have an internal logic that can help you understand where to go and how to solve the various minor puzzles on the way.
The game also gives you a lot of freedom in which order you tackle its regions - you can explore most of the game's area as soon as you unlock the double-jump, though for most regions, healing them requires you to unlock one of the four special abilities, and in turn unlocks the collectible "light seeds" you need to unlock another ability. Each ability immediately gives you access to the associated sacred grounds (with a little travelling to get there) so you can choose which to tackle next.
The bad:
While some of the achievements are more challenging, including speed-running between certain landmarks, for the most part, the game lacks a sense of challenge - the boss fights are more like extended QTEs, and so are the journeys from place to place - while the paths themselves wind around, and parts may be visible from (in terms of travel time) far away, when you're actually travelling them, they're almost entirely linear - it's less a question of picking your route from A to B and more of launching yourself in the right direction, and tapping the right buttons at the right moments, as cued by chunks of environment.
When it comes to combat, there are fights against the four bosses, who you will face several times in their respective territories before finally eliminating them, each of whom has their own quirks, and keys to being defeated, but the only other enemies are boundary guardians between areas, who can be defeated either by traversing the route to them rapidly, or by facing them in combat - a good opportunity to work on your combos, but not so much for actual challenge.
The highly structured nature of the game also means that, while each area has its own minor quirks, once you get a feel for the overall structure, the only real discovery comes from uncovering new bits of scenery or solving some of the game's handful of puzzles. Even finding the few light seeds that aren't automatically collected as you follow the paths from place to place becomes routine after a while.
While the setting has a backplot and bits of history, the game's actual plot consists of meeting Elika and then going on a grand fetch quest to get the light seeds to restore the land and seal the great evil back in its can. There is some exploration of the characters history, but no development, and not much actually happens - probably mostly to support the player's freedom in choosing when to tackle each region, and whether to prompt Elika's narration.
The ugly:
The plot (such as it is) isn't actually resolved in the game - instead, you need to play the DLC, which isn't available for the PC version. Having to buy the endgame separately is bad enough; not being able to get it at all makes this a good example of how not to do DLC.
Overall:
It's a very polished game, which is more fun to watch than most, but ultimately hollow - all style and very little substance. That's not necessarily a deal-breaker, but the lack of an ending leaves me unable to recommend this. If the DLC ever comes out, or if you aren't worried about closure, then sure; otherwise, you're probably better passing on it.

Probably. I'm not exceptionally nostalgic as I never played the console versions of this game but having played a lot of various Lego DS games I might have some bias.
It's also worth noting that it's not exactly fair to compare this game to other Lego games, as it isn't an original game. It's merely a compilation of the two existing Lego Star Wars games, so claiming it has more content than other Lego games is inaccurate.
But just because it doesn't have any more content than the average Lego game doesn't mean it doesn't have a ton of content in general. The game is almost a collect-a-thon in terms of things to find, from the main currency of studs, used to buy things in the shop, to Minikits, used to build models that can be viewed in the hub world, to Power Bricks, used to unlock extras that produce various effects on gameplay, to Gold Bricks, used to unlock entire levels. The amount of collection and replayability these introduce is astounding, and they rarely feel repetitive or tedious. The collect-a-thon aspects also make the game rather unique, as, rather being the typical 3D platformer, it's mostly an action game (though platforming is far from rare).
Well, two: The camera and the controls. The controls are by far the more egregious, though both can hamper gameplay at points. The controls, or more accurately the movement, are sluggish and make combat difficult. Some odd decisions, such as having to double jump almost immediately after the first jump, can make platforming difficult. Not being able to cycle through characters in Story Mode can also make it difficult to choose a specific character when multiple party members are in a small space. You have incredibly limited control over the camera, forcing the at times wonky perspective. This can make platforming difficult, as all you can do to line up jumps and see platforms is pan the camera rather than rotate it. These flaws, while far from insignificant, can be adjusted to and compensated for, though that doesn't completely alleviate all frustration.
And if you were looking forward to the multiplayer, I hope you have an extra controller. There is no online co-op, nor is there even LAN. The only multiplayer available is splitscreen, which is odd considering other console versions apparently had online.
It's an old LEGO game so there aren't character voices, and everyone already knows the story. I like to set the music to mute, open up YouTube and stick some Bee Gees on.

This is my 4th Clicker game, and it really is the first of the 2nd generation of Clicker games!
Targeted Clicker game! You have to aim at different bricks, you cant just click anymore, you also have to hit them.... thats why you use guns in this game.
Sounds like a small thing, but really chances the whole game, great thing!
Also nice graphics!
Also, there are some decisions differnt to other Clicker games;
The Time Cubes you earn, in contrast to other clicker games, always count towards DPS once activated... even if you use them for upgrading of skills... this makes every run count... as you at least get stronger! Makes the mid to end game a bit easier to grind through...
The concept of differently colored blocks, which are worth different amounts of gold is also very clever!
Soon, there will be IDLE mode (currently you only gain very little money, but you dont progress in levels)...
NIce achievements give you a reason to get going and continue.

There is only one sentence that comes to mind after you play a few matches of this game:
"Why isn't this as successful as Overwatch?"
LawBreakers is a bloody brilliant game, something akin to a cross between Overwatch and Quake, which is very fast-paced and requires both quick tactical thinking and skill. It is easy to learn but very difficult to master - the high difficulty of the game, like with Dark Souls, compels you to keep pushing onwards until you become good at the game, until you can finally get revenge on that son of a ♥♥♥♥♥ who keeps killing you, until you can become the MVP. This is a game which highly rewards individual skill, but make no mistake - teamwork is still essential for victory. This is a game where you can pick any class you want with no worries, because there are no hard counters. Some classes are better suited for different gamemodes, but you will not have to change class because someone on the other team chose a certain other class, a problem which many games similar to this suffer from.
This is a game which really gets the heart beating and often leaves me physically shaking from all the adrenaline bouncing around.
The cons? Well, the maps, while well-built, are all a bit samey. The "heroes" are all bland and have no character behind them besides a few cheesy voice lines. The player base is small, which results in lengthly and poorly balanced matchmaking. It is also in the very unfortunate position of having to compete with Overwatch.
Those cons are fairly small relative to just how goddamn fun this game is, though. Fans of Overwatch, Quake etc will find this game thoroughly enjoyable and I recommend the hell out of it.

In my opinion, this is one of the best stealth games ever created and is almost mechanically perfect. Mark of the Ninja works because it combines perfect information, with a fantastic 2D artstyle and an incredibly tight set of controls as well. This is all successful because of how well Mark of the Ninja conveys if you are or aren't visible or capable of being detected by enemies. Any time you can't be seen, your character has a dark silhouette and this means that you're basically invisible to most enemies (unless they put a flashlight or other light source on you). When you're in full obvious color, this means that an enemy can see you at their maximum visual range and you're no longer hidden. This simple, but extremely effective mechanic is the key to making Mark of the Ninja an extremely fair and non-frustrating stealth game.
Combine this with the aforementioned extremely tight control scheme, excellent puzzle solving segments and compelling stealth kills (including an hilarious one from a box) and the overall package is incredibly well designed. The levels are also large, expansive and give you plenty of options for how you want to approach things. Just about everything you want to do is rewarded, including sneaking past and not killing anyone (if you choose). The sheer number of options for terrorizing, sneaking past, distracting or outright murdering guards can give a lot of replayability, as well as hidden scrolls and items to find.
Overall this is just an extremely fun and immensely well designed stealth games, that others in its genre need to learn a lot from. I can't recommend this game more if you're into 2D side scrolling games, with a bit of light puzzle solving and creative mechanics for trolling/murdering the AI guards.

I have my gripes with this game, but ultimately I decided to recommend it because I realize many players will not dislike what I dislike about this game, and the good things outweigh the bad things for an overall enjoyable experience.
I have played many RPG's, including many of the oldschool classics, which this game is very reminiscent of, and it certainly holds its weight when compared to them. If you're a fan of the classic FFs, Chrono Trigger, or anything along those lines, this game is definitely for you. Get it now!
The Good:
-Story. It's not groundbreaking, but it's interesting enough that you care about what happens next. There are also a couple points in the story that get very intellectual, and they are well done - much respect to the writer(s) for that. It's very rare to find that kind of insight in any media, let alone an indie RPG Maker video game.
-Gameplay. This is the meat of the game, and it really, really delivers. The battle system is different enough to keep things from getting stale, and there are a ton of options when it comes to strategy and customization of characters. The battlefield is a grid, and the placement of your characters matters; you can start with a formation and move them around, and enemies have skills that can move you around. There are a lot of different builds to try out for both skills and equipment, that broaden as you progress through the game. This is definitely the highlight of the game, as it should be for any game.
The Bad:
-Enemy scaling. Holy hell. The scaling towards the end of the game is atrocious. There are times where it is genuinely challenging and very fun (ie: some of the arena battles), but it's very easy to hit a roadblock and have few, if any, options for getting stronger, other than slowly grinding for material drops... And the devs have said themselves that grinding sucks! You practically have to play on hard past level 50 to have a chance at good drops, but good luck beating normal enemies past level 50, where leveling is actually BAD because enemies get stronger at a much faster rate than your party does. That's awful design. You could breeze through the final dungeon only to be stopped in your tracks by a boss, where the difficulty spike is insane and out of no where. And this isn't down to tactics; you could understand how to beat the fight, but just not have the stats to do it because your team is wiped out in two attacks. Frankly, the scaling makes no sense, and it's a questionable design choice from the devs. The scaling is truly unlike any RPG I've played, and I've played nearly all of the big titles and classics alike over the last 20 years... I could continue to rant about this, as it ultimately led me to quit the game right before the final boss out of frustration, but I understand that most players will just play through the game on Normal, so I will leave it alone by finishing that I was very disappointed and don't understand why this kind of scaling exists if the devs are against grinding, because it heavily encourages grinding.
-One final mechanic to note: leaving a dungeon erases all progress you made in that dungeon! A confusing mechanic I haven't seen in many (if any) RPGs, and it just seems anti-player with no real added challenge. If this mechanic didn't exist I would have continued, instead I am forced to lose 2-3 hours of progress because I didn't upgrade my equipment to the max that I could at the time.
I know the Bad looks bigger than the Good, but it's not so... This game is worth getting. I just hope the devs learn from the things they did poorly, and I definitely look forward to what they make in the future!

Fun game - Very entertaining to play. If you like JRPGs this will enjoyable. There are some minor gripes with the interface, gameplay, etc. but it is overall a good game and I am happy to have played it.
The battle system is a lot of fun and when paired with the number of skills per character make for a good experience as you play with different character builds. This really shines with the later solo arena battles which almost feel puzzle-like as you pick and choose skills and equipment to help refine your battle plan.
However, the difficulty of battles can spike - epecially for the repeatable missions - which leads to the biggest con for me: equipment & leveling. Equipment is more important than levels, but levels are easy to come by and monster strength scales beyond them. This mean you need crafting material. And for the higher end materials this mostly means fighting. But if you aren't already well equipped even easy battles are surprisingly difficult - even borderline impossible - which makes getting the materials frustrating. Instead of a cycle its just a wall you eventually hit.
Fortunately this was countered by rewarding your effort with said materials and the satisfaction of really beating a set of monsters not just grinding until you were unstoppable.
In summary I recommend Echoes of Aetheria to any interested. There are a lot of good ideas here. A bit of refinement - perhaps in a sequel(?) - would make the very good game this is into an unbelievably great game.

When I was a young person I've been spending a lot of time after school on drawing ugly things. I've had no console or PC back then, but my parents were buying me computer/console magazines each few months, so my imagination was in check and tune up back then. In one of these magazines I've read about Metal Gear Solid (first one in series), seen screnshots... few days after I've had three excersise books filled with 2D "puzzles" - cameras or guards with "vision cones", sliding doors (well, a bit thicker lines touching thinner ones, walls, but that still counts!)... generally, labirynths, but from the side, not top view. That was around 15-20 years ago.
And then, few months ago, I've read a review about mark of the Ninja in one of the game magazines. Should I add anything more? It's my exact idea from childhood... well, instead of Snake there is a ninja, but idea is the same... served as an incredibly playable game. Visuals are very pleasant, especially climatic backgrounds, graphic in overall a bit cartoony, but definitely NOT rubbish... sounds and music fitting and dynamic in right moments. My only complaint is visible FPS drop in "desert" levels because of the sand storm effect, but hey - I'm on a  years old laptop!
Currently best game in its "sneaky-2D" genre.

Well for the singleplayer experience alone the game is worth getting. That is solid fun.
However on PC, especially since the launch was delayed compared to consoles, people mostly get it for the multiplayer component.
It feels like a cheesy MMO in many ways. You just grind the money. You do a lot, and I mean a lot of work, for very little pay compared to the prices of everything.
Many things are clunky and rough on the edges. Higher level players love to bully everyone out of boredom. A lot of the missions are designed in such a way, that they can be easily interruped by other player for no real benefit to them.. So people just destroy each other's fun. Plus a lot of missions are a terrible chore. Like you may not believe.
There are hackers in the game, not so common nowadays, but it used to be a huge problem. So again - no fun.
And now imagine my day today: I'm tired, last months were tough. So inbetween all the Xmas stuff I log in to play with my friends. Nick says, that I should clean up my garage and get the discounted Kuruma (armored vehicle, extremely useful), and a free Hermes. OK, I help him out with the missions, I'll buy the cars later. And so in the evening I get into the garage, to sell one of the cars, I get inside and.. a helicopter spawns inside, I can't get out... OK, finally I buy the Hermes, it says "FREE". That substracted 535,000$ from my account. So I'm 12,000 short of a Kuruma. For the last delivery mission (that's my biggest source of income) I was paid 168,000$. And I need a crew for that, and hopefully an empty session. Yeeeees. I feel very done.
It's some weird kind of rat race: more money, better cars, bigger houses, and the way you get there is through boredom and pain. Get a job instead. It will help you pay the bills, interact with people face-to-face, good stuff. It will keep you sane. This is like a bad job - slowly drives you insane.
Basically baited me for christmas. I'm a newer player and to have 535k taken away is like taking away life support from a cancer patient.

The stealth kills in this are so freaking badass plus the animation for it is just beautiful to witness like how the main character moves, the environments and the kill animations. Plus their is a mechanic where you can terrify your enemies by breaking lights, dropping a dead body in front of them etc and then they will start panicking and just generally freaking out. The only con that I think is with this is that the story seems so far kind of simple and not that interesting but hey I have not finished yet so it could get better. Plud there is tons of replay value here by collecting poems hidden throughout the levels, optional objectives, High scores and different costumes that actually give you different abilities. In conclusion, BUY THIS GAME

Did I enjoy it: Yes
Is it a good game: Debateable, but I'm going to say yes
Cons can basically all be pointed back to the choice of RPG Maker as the engine. However, if you can look past that you'll find a game that tackles some interesting topics in a novel way.
How many games allow you the opportuntiy to be homeless and unemployed? Or face discrimination based on your race, sex or sexuality? Even the minigames in which you make money are an exercise in dealing with boredom - probably an artistic choice on the designer's part, but not a smart mvoe when making a game.
All in all, I found it engrossing. It's basically a road-trip movie that takes itself seriously, and wants to explroe the darker side of the modern world. Dialogue can get incredibly preachy and go on too long about simple philosophical concepts, and some people feel they were rail-roaded too much in the latetr part of the game after the initial 'open world' experience of the first act, but these are minor niggles. The fact that most NPCs treat you differently based on race, sex and age are all commendable, showing that these choices matter.
Always Sometimes Monsters delivers a good story, has some solid points to make and dares to do something different.

I really really wanted to like this game. I did. I got it, I was super interested in it. It held my attention well for the most part. . . Until the ending. I know others have stated it but I absolutely loath the ending. Hands down, I really enjoyed this game until you got near the end. I enjoyed going through the turmoil with my character, watching them grow as a person, seeing the effects of the choices I made. . . But the ending is such a slap in the face.
Spoiler alert for anyone wishing to play the game. Do not read beyond this point:
So I pick my character, I have my love interest, I lose my love interest and my life spirals out of my hands. Not a bad start to a game. It was definitely unique so I did enjoy that aspect of the game. Then I played on and I found myself getting immersed. My character gets a job  at an advertising place, while there though I save a young man from commiting suicide simply by being honest and not judging someone I don't even know. Kudos to you game developers. I liked this.
I get to the next time. I continue helping people from a transgender man to a hungry young boy to even my "friend's" marriage all while being reminded of my choices and what to do when I meet up with my ex.
I think hands down my favorite level is with my 'uncle' whose now a pastor. How finding out that his love for me as his own child turned his life around and how he wanted to be a better man. I dunno. I really liked this part. I also liked the part where he asked me what I wanted to do. Was it to reconsile with my ex. Was I going to finally let go? What was I doing. . . Now at this point in the story my motiviation had gone from 'get back with your ex' to possibly letting them go (In my eyes the relationship wasn't that good if it ended in the direction it did) and to make a better start.
and then Vegas/Ending. . . The game PUNISHES you for not going with your ex. It really does. I don't care what anyone says. I played through it and even though I had a high compatibility with my ex I decided to let them go on with their life and Bam. SHot in the head as a hobo. WTF?! Seriously. I was finally making amends with an old friend, seeing them marry my ex and I get shot in the head as a hobo cause I couldn't get over it?! FLIPPITY DO DAH AH! I hated that. I absolutely hated that. So I reload and interupt the wedding and profess my love. Get accepted, undo everything I had done (Making amends, learning to stand on my own two feet) and even that ending wasn't really rewarding. I just.  . . I hated the ending so much. I still do. It's been months since I last played it but that ending has stayed so vividly in my mind because of how much I had enjoyed the first 2/3's of the game until the end.
That's basically the end of my rant. If they've updated the endings I may give the game another shot but as of right now, no. I regret owning this game and that's really sad for me to say as again I did enjoy a good chunk of it.

This was a very strange game, and yet in a way I think it set out to do what it was intended for. The game is about ways people struggle, about what we could do to help with problems that arise in the world. We have three separate ages going through some patchy areas of life. First there is a child whose parents are fighting, then we have a adult that runs into a person assaulting a woman, then a elderly man who sees children fighting.
The gameplay is pretty simple, use the arrow keys to move your character forward, use the E key to interact with the world around you, and use the mouse to move the direction you want to look. The problem that arises with this is that there were many times that I could not turn all the way I wanted to go, the character keeps going when you let go of the keys, and its rather hard to figure out what you can interact with. This made the game rather difficult as I had to fight with the controls or sometimes get stuck with not knowing what the heck I was supposed to do next. They could have at least had a way for you to figure out what to do next. The movement of the old man was really annoying too. It was so slow, not just from the walking, but even looking around was really slow. The hub world was also very hard to work with as it felt unfinished. It was a pure white room with many doors, and yet only 4 of the doors actually worked to get into the areas you were trying to get into. We had the ‘credit room’ where we had characters that were standing still like statues with the names of the creators, a exit door to leave the game, the start game door, and then a door that I guess was supposed to be for settings and yet when I went into it, there was nothing to interact with.
Sadly, because of how annoying the controls were, especially for the old man, I didn’t really explore as much as I did in the other two areas. I was ready to be done by then as I was seriously frustrated.
The artwork is alright I guess. The characters and the world around them are a bit blocky with single colors, much like that of Unturned in fact. I was never really a fan of this style as it has nothing much to it. Even the movement of the characters felt unfinished. Every movement they made felt rather stiff or they wouldn’t even move. It’s not that I am against this sort of style, I would be fine with it if the story was good. In this case though, the story wasn’t all that interesting to make up for the artwork. I do like however that the different ages had a different style for each of them. The child’s world is bright and had many colors, the adult’s world was gray and depressing, and the old man’s seemed to have a filter that was sepia toned. That made it a little better but not by much.
The scripting is a bit cheesy, almost sounding like an after school special rather then normal speech. I don’t think an old man would say, ‘Oh now the children will never fight over that toy again’ the way he does in the game. I did like that the words were in different fonts depending on who was talking, and actually smiled when the old man’s script was in a really beautiful script style. The sound was… was their really sound? I just never really paid attention with that because it was just sort of bla.
Basically, you can go play this if you want to as it’s a free game, but I wouldn’t actually pay for it. It definitely didn’t end up like how one of the trailers was with the sugar rush place. I would think that that would actually be a bit better then what we did get. If you do play it, prepare to be frustrated with it at a couple points.

Not a very well balanced clicker game.  Nothing helps the grind, because of the gigantic periods of time you have to spend progressing through "Training".  You simply have to reset every time you hit Training until you can blow past it because of all the Artifact bonuses you've been stacking up.  But wait, most of the artifacts are near-useless for their price after purchasing them only a few times, so even after a few thousand time cubes you're just stuck on the second round of Training.
The cooldowns on the active abilities prevent most of them from being useful for anything except pushing past bosses, ESPECIALLY the one that gives you a stacking permanent bonus.  Eight hour cooldown?  Seriously?  If you're not looping every eight hours you're not making progress, so you're just going to use it once when you first buy it and then never again.  It might as well not stack at all.  This isn't like Clicker Heroes where you can boost your DPS by 5% every 45 minutes via the right order of ability use and the right ancients purchased.  It's just useless.  Most of the enemies are flat which means the piercing ability is mostly useless, the crit bonus abilities are mostly useless because crits tend to one-shot cubes anyway, and the shot-spread ability has buggy targeting-- it will just fire straight through cubes without hitting them sometimes.  Actually I'm not sure how the hit detection even works, since the gun is angled so differently from where you're looking.
The buyable helper types are unbalanced too.  You'd think that each successive one would be more powerful than the last, but that's only true for base DPS.  You have big boosts to damage from time cubes after looping, so a large portion of the next loop will involve your helpers one-shotting everything.  This means fire rate is king, and the last two helper types have low fire rate.  The last one is the worst offender, being single target AND low fire rate.  What winds up happening is that it only comes into play when you start slowing down, and its bonus ability winds up overkilling everything when it triggers so it's mostly wasted... unless you're going so slow you should just loop again.
On top of the fire rate issue, the upgrade system for the helpers involves purchasing a "rank up" which resets their fire rate and special abilities in return for boosting their raw DPS.  So when you're one-shotting things it's actually a BAD idea to rank up.  Although this does does result in interesting decision making, I feel it is unintuitive and possibly not even intended.  After the rank up, you wind up purchasing basically the same base upgrades again on your way to the next rank up once you're past a certain point in the rank up system, which frankly strikes me as boring.

Mark of the Ninja is a side-scrolling stealth game, developed by Klei Entertainment. It was initially released on Xbox 360 in September 2012, before being released on Steam in September 2013. You play as a nameless ninja in current times.
Mark of the Ninja places a high emphasis on stealth. You are able to see how much noise your character makes by moving, or carrying out a certain action by a circular area showing so. Noise can be used against you, or to your advantage, such as creating a distraction to enemies to allow you to pass by. The game does have a combat system, but it is on the basic side. The combat is essentially a small QTE, requiring you to press the button shown on screen in order to carry out a clean kill of the enemy. You are able to use the environment against your foes too, such as cutting a chandelier to fall onto your enemies head, turning on electric wires to shock them, and many more creative ways to cull the bad guys.
Throughout the story mode, you are able to unlock extra mechanics to use, such as sliding kicks, hanging attacks or new tools to use out in the field like smoke bombs. You can upgrade these at any of the upgrade points in the game, using the talent points you have earned.
Visually, Mark of the Ninja ticks all the boxes too. Even though it is only 2D, you can see how much care and attention has gone into making this game look as good as it has. The backdrops in which you are in are gorgeous, plenty of awesome looking characters and bad guys too. Every single bit of animation looks spot on too. All of the characters move so fluidly it is almost perfection. The narrator and all other voice acting are done to an extremely high standard as well.
This game is by no means easy. You will at times find yourself almost rage quitting at how difficult certain stages are. Some points almost feel impossible until everything just clicks into place. That is what I loved the most about this game. Whilst there is an element of luck involved in a lot of situations, the main points always come from how skilfully your carry out kills, and distractions. If you practice enough, you will eventually heighten your reflexes and senses to allow you to progress. Upon completing the game, you will unlock the New Game+ mode, which is seriously one of the hardest gaming experiences you will have. Enemies become more intelligent, they will kill you in a single hit, your line of sight is limited to which ever direction you are facing and you no longer have the radius area around you to show how much noise you are making. If you want a challenge, this game mode is certainly going to be for you.
The single player story mode took me just a little under 16 hours to complete. This is spread out across 13 levels. Each level has three different challenges/optional objectives for you to complete such as finishing the level in a certain amount of time, finding some special loot or even something as simple as killing a certain about of enemies. This all adds to the replay ability of the levels and gives you something different to strive for. Even though I have only just started the New Game Plus mode, I can see it taking almost double the amount of time to complete due to how high the difficulty ramps up, whether it is something I see through to the end is another thing though.
Mark of the Ninja is a technically sound game as of now. I was able to play in high resolutions with all of the settings turned up. The game needs to be played with a controller though. I tried with keyboard and it just isn’t as reflex friendly compared to a joy stick sadly. Whilst there isn’t any so called multiplayer aspect to the game, you can always take part in the leader boards for each level, which is a nice little touch.
To sum up, Mark of the Ninja is a seriously must play game. In my opinion it is one of the saving graces of the Stealth genre’s recent surge in popularity. It does everything right, and you will struggle to find another stealth game that is as polished and fun to play as Mark of the Ninja. The indie price tag on the game sits perfectly too; at €14.99 being an absolute bargain of a deal.

Mark of the Ninja is an incredible 2d stealth game, that has a fantastic gameplay and a beautiful art direction. With the stealth focused gameplay, there's also platforming sections and puzzles that are very enjoyable. It's levels are so carefully designed and so awesome, that it's foolish to call this game not smooth, because it is incredibly slick. It has this Metal Gear Solid style of gameplay that never gets old, and with the variety of tools which you can use to distract, kill and manipulate enemies, it's a game that has replay value. And, through the campaign, the pacing is so good, because there's also some levels that involve only sneaking from enemies without having weapons equipped, and using your environment to survive. There are also some optional challenges that involve solving well designed puzzles. It does have a story, and it is, for the most part, simplistic, but it has some cool plot twists that were unpredictable. It has this comic-book vibe to it, that makes it really charming. I really can't say anything bad about this game, because it's almost flawless really. It's a must-have indie game, and one of my favorite indie games for sure. It gets a 10/10.

'Big bad' God Ahriman is breaking out of his tree-prison and covering sidekick Elika's kingdom with 'corruption'. To put the cork back in his bottle you must bust out your very choicest pakour and cleanse all of the 'fertile lands' across the impracticality designed kingdom. For reasons that may or may not involve Elika's hip to waist ratio, our #Edgy Prince decides to tag along.
You're left to explore a relatively non-linear overworld. You're free to choose in what order to clear levels, but ultimately they must all be cleared and they all follow an identical structure. Climb to fertile land, fight boss, cleanse land. All too quickly, you settle into this routine, and the cycle goes unchallenged throughout the entirety of the game. So much so that you get diminishing returns; no matter how satisfying it is at first to return a fertile ground to it's prettier, greener version, after cleansing 20 areas they all begin to blend into one and each feels less rewarding than the last.
Levels do their best to stand out. Sometimes the stage's boss will interfere, flooding the level with corruption, destroying structures around you or polluting the air. This would've added texture to the game but none of it ever has any impact on gameplay, and amounts to nothing more than decoration. Nonetheless, during these sections Elika and the Prince will dutifully play along with the developers, acting as though these facades are serious issues.
You can't die, Elika will save you no matter how bad you ♥♥♥♥ up. This completely undermines any potential tension. My play style soon veered towards recklessness as there was no reason to be attentive or careful, mistakes are never punished. On the other hand, this feature means the flow of the game is uninterrupted and creates a relaxed and pleasant mood when parkouring across the land.
Combat is stiff. You never deal with more than one opponent at a time. The prince has suddenly lost all acrobatic ability and is fixed to the ground, confined to four attacks and combos. Compare to The Sands of Time wherein combat was more intrinsically linked to the prince's parkour abilities, and there was often space to get creative when tackling many foes. The combos look great though, and parrying attacks is satisfying if sometimes unreliable. When you screw up and need Elika to save you the enemy regains health meaning if you're struggling these fights can go on for a long time.
Once you've cleared a level, 'light seeds' appear across that level, requiring you to backtrack through the area once or twice to gather them. Despite the transparent effort to extend the game, the most immersive platforming takes place during these searches. Unlike the mindless tunnel platforming throughout the rest of the game, you must occasionally pause, examine your environment and plan your actions. You'll require exponentially more and more of these seeds to unlock four-colour coded powers that each unlock access to more fertile grounds. Unfortunately the powers are indistinct and unsatisfying to use.
The red and blue powers are identical and simply propel you from a suitably colour-coded plate to another point (usually another plate). The green power is the most fun, propelling the prince in a straight line up and across walls and ceilings, leaving it to the player to strafe left and right to avoid oncoming obstacles. By far the most obnoxious part of the game, the yellow power propels you into a stiffly-animated on-rails 'flight' around the map on the longest route conceivable to man. If you can see through the ugly obtrusive special affects that border your screen you must dodge corners of buildings and whatever other last-minute obstacles the developers decided to try to run you into. Other times it blissfully propels you across short distances... so works exactly like the red and blue powers again.
Elika handles world building exposition throughout a frequent scattering of cut-scenes, explaining what the different sections of the kingdom were supposedly used for before they became interchangeable slip'n'slides. Her descriptions are inconsistent, vague and fail to lend any much-needed depth to the setting. Character development based dialogue and exposition are confined mostly within optional dialogue snippets available at the press of a button.
This is an odd way round to do things since the narrative success of the story hinges on you developing an attachment to Elika, and so character development should be the primary focus. Regardless, initiating a conversation on your own terms is fairly immersive and I only wish that the feature had been used more widely to reduce the number of expositional cut-scenes that break the flow of play.
The final battle is much like any other stage, unsurprisingly. The game's narrative twist lies in (SPOILER ALERT) forcing the same choice upon the Prince as Elika's father when he brought her back to life at the cost of freeing Ahriman in the first place. This was a nice opportunity to allow the player to make up their own mind. However, the Prince decides that getting his♥♥♥♥♥♥wet is the prime directive and the game ends with a disappointing fizzle as you're forced to walk around doing some tree-prison gardening and undoing everything you've achieved in the space of a few minutes. (SPOILERS END HERE)
Apparently there was DLC for the console versions which layered an additional unsatisfying ending over the top in a desperate attempt to reach for a conclusion, but they didn't release that on PC so ♥♥♥♥ 'em.

If you play games for gameplay mechanics, then you might not like this title unless you're a fan of QTEs. This game is essentially one long QTE with a bit of running around intermixed. This title was more enjoyable for me than the previous PoP titles, because there was less focus on combat. The combat is pretty simple as long as the player can time the counters correctly, and there are hardly any enemies to fight. There were literally 20-30 fights in the entire game, IIRC. This title reimagines the "rewind time" mechanic from PoP:SoT as a magic-using companion that essentially just saves the main character whenever he falls to his death and returns him to the last solid ground he was on without any interaction from the player or limit on the number of uses. Prince of Persia is a beautiful game and it's a lot of fun to play. The controls are simple and make all the well animated jumping and running easy to pull off. The graphics are very beautiful, almost like playing in some kind of painting.
The game is rather easy, since you can never die. If you fall or miss your jump, your partner Elika will pull you back onto solid ground. If you start to lose in a battle, she will pull you to safety, knocking the enemy back. However, the enemy will regain some of it's lost health for doing so. To me, this is a really great option. Sometimes games are just meant to be fun, and not so much to provide a hardcore challange that will only end up frustrating.
Combat is fun and smooth, with great attack animations. You can attack with your sword, you can grab an enemy, and you can let Elika attack. You can combo all sorts of beautiful moves together to make for an awesome fight scene. None of the bad guys should really give you too much trouble, especially since right before you would "die", a button will pop up and if you press it in time you avoid the "final" blow, so that way Elika doesn't have to save you and the enemy's health stays where it's at.
The environments are great to look at. The world starts off all dark and dreary with corruption, but as you heal the lands, everything becomes bright and green and lush again.
Most of the time you'll have to go through an area twice, once to get to the fertile ground so you can heal it, and then you'll probably want to go through it again after it's been healed so you can collect all the Light Seeds lying around. You collect Light Seeds in order to "buy" special powers that Elika can use for platforming, which allows you to get to new areas.
The voice acting and script of the game are not top-notch, but are certainly passable. Personally, I found the soundtrack and plot incredibly pleasing.
Overall, Prince of Persia is quite fun; however, it is not for those who don't want to relax. Challenge-seekers will be severely disappointed, and those looking for excitement will also be let down. For those who seek a fun and relaxing experience in a richly textured world, on the other hand, Prince of Persia is the game to play.

Mark of the Ninja is a side-scrolling stealth game, developed by Klei Entertainment. It was initially released on Xbox 360 in September 2012, before being released on Steam in September 2013. You play as a nameless ninja in current times.
Mark of the Ninja places a high emphasis on stealth. You are able to see how much noise your character makes by moving, or carrying out a certain action by a circular area showing so. Noise can be used against you, or to your advantage, such as creating a distraction to enemies to allow you to pass by. The game does have a combat system, but it is on the basic side. The combat is essentially a small QTE, requiring you to press the button shown on screen in order to carry out a clean kill of the enemy. You are able to use the environment against your foes too, such as cutting a chandelier to fall onto your enemies head, turning on electric wires to shock them, and many more creative ways to cull the bad guys.
Throughout the story mode, you are able to unlock extra mechanics to use, such as sliding kicks, hanging attacks or new tools to use out in the field like smoke bombs. You can upgrade these at any of the upgrade points in the game, using the talent points you have earned.
Visually, Mark of the Ninja ticks all the boxes too. Even though it is only 2D, you can see how much care and attention has gone into making this game look as good as it has. The backdrops in which you are in are gorgeous, plenty of awesome looking characters and bad guys too. Every single bit of animation looks spot on too. All of the characters move so fluidly it is almost perfection. The narrator and all other voice acting are done to an extremely high standard as well.
This game is by no means easy. You will at times find yourself almost rage quitting at how difficult certain stages are. Some points almost feel impossible until everything just clicks into place. That is what I loved the most about this game. Whilst there is an element of luck involved in a lot of situations, the main points always come from how skilfully your carry out kills, and distractions. If you practice enough, you will eventually heighten your reflexes and senses to allow you to progress.  Upon completing the game, you will unlock the New Game+ mode, which is seriously one of the hardest gaming experiences you will have. Enemies become more intelligent, they will kill you in a single hit, your line of sight is limited to which ever direction you are facing and you no longer have the radius area around you to show how much noise you are making. If you want a challenge, this game mode is certainly going to be for you.
The single player story mode took me just over 18 hours to complete. This is spread out across 13 levels. Each level has three different challenges/optional objectives for you to complete such as finishing the level in a certain amount of time, finding some special loot or even something as simple as killing a certain about of enemies. This all adds to the replay ability of the levels and gives you something different to strive for.  Even though I have only just started the New Game Plus mode, I can see it taking almost double the amount of time to complete due to how high the difficulty ramps up, whether it is something I see through to the end is another thing though.
Mark of the Ninja is a technically sound game as of now. I was able to play in high resolutions with all of the settings turned up. The game needs to be played with a controller though. I tried with keyboard and it just isn’t as reflex friendly compared to a joy stick sadly. Whilst there isn’t any so called multiplayer aspect to the game, you can always take part in the leader boards for each level, which is a nice little touch.
To sum up, Mark of the Ninja is a seriously must play game. In my opinion it is one of the saving graces of the Stealth genre’s recent surge in popularity. It does everything right, and you will struggle to find another stealth game that is as polished and fun to play as Mark of the Ninja.  The indie price tag on the game sits perfectly too; at £10,99 being an absolute bargain of a deal.

A game that really needed some polishing. Absolutely fantastic concept, really poor execution.
I started off with no knowledge of the controls, and was thoroughly confused when attempting to do basic movement. I am told that others got a prompt with controls, but I somehow skipped it unknowingly.
Next, I find the escape menu that tells you some challenges. No alarms, kill all enemies, kill no civilians. Right then. I immediately find an inaccessible enemy, and, assuming I want to complete the challenge, get frustrated as I see no way to access this enemy. He doesn't count apparently.
Next, the movement system sucks. It never feels like the character is doing what I actually want it to. Even when out of combat and just using WASD, the main character just doesn't feel good to control. Would it kill you to put in a "jump" button? Maybe I don't want to do a time-stopping leap across the room. I just wanna jump a few feet up.
The platforms are terrible. The actual platforms are mechanically obnoxious. You can't grab onto them, despite the game seemingly relying heavily on the wall latch system. In combat, you can't go up a wall, you are required to jump off. Can't reach that platform from the place you are at on the wall? Better try again. You won't reach the platform unless it shows the landing marker on the platform, despite how important it may be. I had a battle (right before quitting) that was just me jumping around a room for a while until I could get high enough to kill the enemies only slightly out of reach.
Finally, combat. The second introduced enemy acts out of turn. Kill me immediately on his turn, fine, but I expect his turn to play before he slashes me. They don't even follow their own lines of action, which is the entire pillar of what the game relies on.
And when I want to jump off of a platform, land on a marker behind an enemy, kicking him in the face, I expect to do exactly as the line of action tells me I'm going to do. I don't expect to jump two feet and get shot in the face, which is not what the game told me I would do.

It's interesting to see the reviews for this game as mixed. The reason for me saying that is because I would have thought more people would hate it. RONIN is a specific type of game for a specific type of person. You might at first think that this game shares an audience with the game Gunpoint, a game similar to this one, but this game is much different. The turn based combat with an emphasis on nonstealth and stealth at the same time is a mixed bag of emotions. The situation is similar to a girl you meet at a bar and says she only wants to talk to nice guys, but whoever buys all her drinks will sleep with her in the end (For most of you this is unrelatable, but hear me out).
Some of the more interesting parts of the game come from the things it makes you do. In some of the hints, which tell you that you can't disable them, it tells you that this is not a stealth game. That statment really gets to me because ITS ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥T. To fully complete a level, you not only have to complete the main objective but the side ones as well. The side objectives are the same everytime and include not killing civilians and killing all guards. So to be able to do these things you HAVE TO stealth through the game. You might be saying at this point that you do not need to 100% each level and only complete the main objective. To those people I would suggest you go play Nintendogs because you don't understand how games work. You have to 100% each level to recieve a skill point to gain acess to skills that should make the game easier. So if you don't fully complete the level, well lets just say I don't envy your position.
I am currently on the way to 100% the entire game, which for the most part is not that hard. but all the same problems for the first time I played the game are still in play. Btw, the only difference I can see for the new game plus and regular game is that the guys who shoot semi-automatic weapons move their aim while firing. So if you like threading the needle like I did, then tough luck. But like I said in the beginning, this game is for a certain type of person and I am one of those people. This does not mean I think the game is great or that it has no problems, because I have raged so many times. But it's not a bad game for the simple reason that its beatable. This does not mean some parts are poorly designed and are bad, but overall its not in its entirty bad.
I have played levels over and over and over, but still have found the right way to go about a level that will grant me completion. This game for 12.99 USD is an ok buy, but I would highly suggest a sale. I purchased this game from a humble bundle, just for clarificaton.  Now you might be asking me, you said there were things that make it a poorly designed game, what are those things. And my answer to you is I don't know. It could be the difficulty, but thats not a good enough answer because it's beatable. I don't know the exact thing that makes it hard for this game to be enjoyable, but when you finally beat the level that you have been strugging with, its a nice sigh of relief. You could also point out the level design, but I would not complain TOO much about it because I don't think I could do a better job. Most of the problems can come from how a level is laid out but my retort to that is, get a better solution for that level.
All in all I would reccomend this game to anyone that wants a puzzle of an action game. For someone seeing if their interested, buy the game and return it if you don't like it. Simple solution.
Side note, just saw someone saying that you can feel unstoppable while playing this game, THEY ARE DUMB AND WRONG. You could be playing on the lowest difficulty and still be wrong.

Echoes of Atheria is a great and entertaining old-school 16bit-era JRPG style game. Really, it is!!
Dancing Dragon Games have outdone themselves this time and raised the bar to new heights concerning what can be achieved with RPG Maker. There are indeed moments while playing when you will forget that this game is actually made with RPG Maker VX Ace.
Let's look at the game in more detail:
The STORY, following the adventures of Lucian, a member of the Veridian Army, starts of with a wedding where just at the end of the ceremony the bride gets abducted. Immediately our hero sets out to follow the abducters and finds himself soon in the midst of political power struggles, intrigues and events that might even bring forth the destruction of the world. While this may not sound new to RPG players, it is the way the story works. It is totally coherent and logical, and only knows one way and that is forward. The pacing is just perfect, there is never a dull moment. Twists, turns and surprises happen regularly enough to keep the player engaged.
Same goes for the CHARACTERS. Each of them feel unique and their actions understandable, considering the circumstances they find themselves in.
The WORLD itself is vibrant, colorful and alive with nice little decorative gimicks like squirrels and birds.
One DRAWBACK for some RPG players might be the fact that the progression in the game is linear and there is no open world. However there are a few repeatable areas that can be selected from the world map, where you will find yourself after finishing a story segment.
GAMEPLAY is where things get interesting. While it does feature the usual exploration and search for hidden treasure chest, it is the battle system and especially the crafting system where the game gets very interesting. The BATTLE SYSTEM is the feature where you will start to forget that this is "just" an RPG Maker game. It is turnbased and introduces new features, e.g. strategical character positioning on a grid based area, area of effect spells and skills, where the area of effect really matters and staggering enemies to just mention the most noticeable. Throughout both of my playthrough (one on medium difficulty and one on hard) I found the battles to be fun and at times quite engaging; especially boss battles, even on medium difficulty. These boss battles really deserve to be called boss battles, and while they are quite challenging on medium already, on hard they will leave you with a sense of accomplishment after you have taken one down.
The second striking gameplay feature is the CRAFTING SYSTEM. There are a huge amount of weapons and gears to be crafted and each can be fine tuned enough to fit your playstyle for each of your party members. I have wasted literally hours on crafting and experimenting with equipment. Items are crafted from a base material, a reagent, stat enhaning gem, a third element for armor or damage enhancement (crit or armor bypass) and schematics that can raise all stats of the item from 10% to 40%.
In CONCLUSION Echoes of Aetheria is indeed a great and entertaining RPG experience that I'm sure RPG fans can and will enjoy. And even RPG Maker haters should give this a try, as it shows how much is possible with this game engine.

Dancing Dragon Games is probably what I'd list as one of the top two RPG Maker developers out there, if not necessarily the top. Their focus is on good, solid, technically impressive creations with the software, featuring enjoyable stories, memorable characters, and good music. Graphically, they tend to produce a slightly awkward mix of generic RPG graphics with assets of their own design, and in this last area, Echoes of Aetheria is their best showing, since it presents its battles in an entirely customized and animated isometric perspective reminiscent of such titles as Super Mario RPG and the early Persona games. In fact, on a technically level, Echoes is head and shoulders above their previous offerings, with the only recognizable "recycled" assets that I've visually picked out being recycled original assets from their own previous games, which is totally fine with me.
Like the Deadly Sin games and Skyborn before it, Echoes focuses on smaller, tightly-designed, and pleasurably simple-to-traverse dungeon areas as its main gameplay venue. As such, Echoes of Aetheria (and by extension, previous Dancing Dragon titles) is a very good pick-up-and-play RPG, but for players who prefer a more expansive and ponderous experience, other titles such as the five-part Millennium series by Aldorlea Games would probably do better (although their games are generally more "vanilla RPG Maker" in design and appearance than Dancing Dragon's).
To any readers who have made it this far and are pondering the idea that RPG Maker instantly means a game is shovelware, don't. RPG Maker is a fantastic tool in the right hands, highly customizable through scripting if a good programmer is on the team. Dancing Dragon makes good use of that, as does Aldorlea to a lesser extent. I'm going to enjoy playing through Echoes of Aetheria from where I'm at, but the hours I've clocked so far have already convinced me that this one is well worth playing for fans of turn-based role-playing game.

I wish the game hadn't done that honestly, because if you get there too soon and your equipment is sub-par, you're kinda screwed. Thankfully most of this is in the optional missions, but it still can put you into an issue of needing to do the optional missions to get the better equipment, but I can't survive the optional missions because I don't have the better equipment: 5/10
Magic and Combat: The game's weakest point I'm afraid. Early on, battles are will put you to sleep, as it is all waiting for TP to build up, then unleash an ultimate attack. It gets more interesting late game when you get your full party of 5, but be prepared for some ridiculous difficulty spikes late game. And speaking of which, developer, can you tone down the ridiculous HP of some of those monsters? I felt like it was HP spongue after HP spongue once I hit the level 50 monsters (I mean what do they have, 99999 HP? That's what it felt like! And this was on normal difficulty). And don't get me started on the final boss, which basically two shot killed my party on normal (level 62 party, mostly obsidian gear, one ultimate weapon). To add to it, I felt like late arena battles were pray to the RNG goodess, because if that enemy counterattacked me I was dead. I serously lost count of how often I had to redo an arena battle just due to an unlucky counterattack wiping me out. 2/10
Equipment: Pretty well done, the game has a system of improved gear that is pretty easy to figure out. Within each type you have to decide on light vs medium vs medium/heavy vs heavy, each with different advantages and disadvantages Only quirk I noticed is for some reason I got better stats on Obsidian gear, yet my party talked like Aeatherian (however you spell it) gear was better? 7/10
Economy: Well done. You start off struggling for money, then you'll spend about 50% of the game with more money than you need. Then, late game you'll get access to very expensive items which permanently increase your stats, which will force you into some hard decisions. 10/10
Graphics: Standard RPGMaker graphics, though well polished and used well. 7/10
Main Quest: I thought the main quest was pretty interesting, though early I did start to cringe when I heard the lines "Things are afoot which you have no idea about" for about the seventh time. Felt like early game tried too hard to keep me in the dark. Then when it started to come together, prepare to change goals faster than some NFL stars change teams. I do feel some areas had holes in the story, and sometimes I did find myself wondering why I hadn't heard anything about them until now, if they are that integrated into the world? But those quirks aside, it's still a fun story to experience: 7/10
Gameplay: Overall, decent, very few bugs. Just wish the battle system had been better. 6/10
Total: 67/100. That puts the game into recommended territory. With a better battle system the game would be outstanding, but as it is I say play it for the story, and if like me the battle system annoys you in the end, drop the difficulty to easy and enjoy the ride instead.

I fell in love with this game from the moment Lucian came running into the wedding to avoid the fangirls, and enjoyed every part of it. There is so much to do and customize, from training quests to customized weapons and armor, to setting the skills and levels of said skills to make each character not only ideal in the team, but also great soloers. On top of that, there were three different levels of difficulty to choose from per level, so you don't need to restart the entire game if you find it too hard or too easy. Personally, I played it on normal, then backpedalled to some of my favorite levels to try on hard mode.
The storyline followed pretty closesly with other fantasy RPGs- save the world, insert a twist, save the world again. But it was the characters, especially their interaction with each other, that was wonderful. A good deal of the game is based on conversations that happen in the base. These are encouraged through little boosts of exp gained by conversing with these characters, and make even the support character that much more important to the characters and the player. It also made the game that much deeper when *spoiler spoilers IwarnyouIcriedthough* Banter between the main characters built a strong connection, which made the tensions when things weren't going smoothly really stand out. But what really got me was the end. Alternative endings. I'm not even sure I got all of them. The game over ending in particular caught me so off guard that I had to put the game down before trying again.
Overall, an awesome game that allows you to play multiple different ways for hours of fun. Definitely recommend.

I've been playing FPS since wolf3d.  I was in at the ground level on things like dwango, and deep in when QuakeWorld with it's amazing mod scene came in.  Over time my excitement for shooters has started to die off with a lot of the same old being stamped out over and over again.  Low skill floor, slower play style, and turning the game into a grind for the next reward rather than an experience that wraps you up and wants you to do more.  Lawbreakers brings out the friggin kid in me again and has me dying for my next match.  This takes me back to the same exhiliration I used to get playing games like rocket arena(1/2/3) or the Unreal Tournament series.
That being said this game is absurdly addictive.  Matches are intense, and the skill floor is extremely high, which means a lot of gratifying moments during play.  Every match is something different.  There are some things that might be worth retooling in terms of balance, but overall my experience in playing has shown me that it really is just a difference in player skill that offers the most imbalance.  This game can draw comparisons to a lot of things, but it's an entirely unique experience.  I really can't emphasize that enough.  I hate I didn't hear about this game sooner (wtf marketing) and when I did, like most of you I read reviews and watched videos and tried to put this game in it's right place.  Every notion I had about the game, how it would play, etc were wrong.  I'm glad that I ultimately I pulled the trigger and I haven't regretted it at all.
So, what are the down sides?  Off prime time, match making can take a while.  Honestly, this is probably the biggest disappointment to me.  I can get plenty of matches in, it’s not like I’m waiting ages for a match (US-East player pool); but there are times when it can take a while.  The thing that makes this so painful, is less that it takes time, but that a game with such tight mechanics and fast paced chaos is being missed by a larger audience.  At this point it becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy as people see that it has low pop, they don’t take the plunge and buy it.
What do I have to say about that?  Look, if you're reading this review, take the chance, spend the $30 and get in here with us and play.  I can assure you, if you like fast paced, skill based shooters, this is the game you need to buy.  The more players we have, the more games we have.  Stop sitting on the fence.

This is very close. Another game I wish I could give a neutral rating.
Its a push your luck card drawing game with each suit triggering a different mechanism and along with your traits you can combine them in to more or less devestating attacks in order to collect cards that bolster your score.
Contrary to some of the reviews Ive seen nothing to suggest that the AI is cheating, it does pull off some last minute nasty moves at times but keeping my cool I can think back to the many times I have done the same thing. How much this actually matters is debateable, if the game makes you feel like it is cheating then whether it is or it isnt, the frustration is always real. I think this will be the biggest sticking point for most people, at first it may not be quite so apparent but as things go on you will see through to the luck component of the game increasingly easily and more and more you will feel robbed by complete chance regardless of how well youve played a hand.
The traits and the combination of traits can be fun to toy around with, but this leads to a scoring issue. The game considers high scores to be good, not a difference in score between you and your opponent. This means that the many aggressive tactics put you at a horrible disadvantage; even when winning regularly with your strategy if you have not defended your high score you will end up winning tournaments tens of points away from the three stars you are aiming for. Its kind of a punishment just for picking a style of play.
You can unlock more and more traits as the game goes on, but also portraits which are quite dull. Id have preferred them just to stick to a lower level and give the portraits for free along side the traits.
Each tournament has a set of rules, and some of them really shake up the game format, unfortunately they repeat the rule sets two or three times due to the huge number of tournaments there are. Again, I would have preferred fewer more focused tournaments, as the gameplay simply isnt varied enough to support the huge number of what are essentially the same games over and over. (60 tournaments in all, with about 3 games on average in each.) The tournament scores are also very harsh, some require you to be within 5 points of maximum score in each of 3 or 4 games, it can lead to _a lot_ of repetition. (Cards go from 2 to 7 so a single lost card is more than enough to bring about a failure.)
and of course. A big issue for many, no multiplayer. I can understand this to a degree, they have a boardgame to sell as well, and this is about a third of the price of it, but the different use cases really should take care of this. A lot of people buy boardgames even when they have a digital version on an iPad or some such to hand. In fact there are plenty of people who play computer games who dont board game and vice versa.

This review will be from a Linux user's persepective, and for anyone on Linux interested in playing this game.
I meet all the reccommended system requirements to play this game except the supported platforms. I use Solus as my desktop os, and Lutris: Wine 2.19 staging to get this working. Everything works out of the box except for a gamepad controller, which I'm sure there are ways to get that working.
I've sunked a decent amount of hours into this game, and have only played the free side of it. The free aspect limits you to only 6 characters of their entire roster, which are rotated every Wednesday during their updates. During these updates the game becomes breifly inaccessible for online play.
Brawlhalla is a Super Smash Bros type game where where 2-8 players can duke it out on floating platforms in various game modes (2v2, free for all, 1v1). Once a week there are special missions that you can play in order to get more in game currency. There's Brawl of the Week and 1v1 missions that will reward you the most for completing them.
I would say the game is entertaining. The basic gameplay mechanics are fairly easy and fast enough to get into, while the more advanced combos will of course take some time. The playerbase seems quite healthy as I'm able to jump into a game within about minute. Characters selection while limited to only 6 does change once a week, offering you variety and time to try out new characters. The in-game currency that you are rewarded with from completing missions, or playing ranked, are used towards purchasing new characters. If you rather you could also purchase the entire character roster and receive all current and future characters.
Onto what I dislike about this game. The in-game store offers a variety of items to customize your character, as well as loot boxes. The in-game currency I described earlier cannot be used to purchase these asethetic items. Seems that only real currency will apply. The in-game currency will only apply to Legends (playable characters), and that' about it. If you're the type of person whose into customization then you're going to have to shell out the money to do so. If you're like me then the free version is enough, and with the currency earned will be able to unlock other characters later.
While Brawlhalla is a Super Smash Bros type of game, it lacks all the charm that Smash Bros has. For example there is a severe lack of items. In game you'll be presented with a weapon which each character will have only two types, usually a short and mid-long range weapon that will enable you to do more combos. Then there are the bombs which consist of a standard throwing bomb, and a landmine. There is nothing else. No gimicky or goofy weapons, so the game heavily relies on using the character's weapons to dish out damage.
Something that may be a Wine specific issue that I've experienced is the lag. Now I've already stated I meet all the requirements for this game including the bandwidth needed. My inputs to the game have often been delayed causing my character to perform a few seconds after I hit the buttons, or not at all. As you can imagine this is a terrible thing to have in a fast pace fighting game. Due to lag sometimes my character will run off the platform to their doom, or I'll see the other player fall to their doom to actually be my own, or the game will lag and I'll instancely be dead. The performance of the game itself is noticeably laggy. Their are quite a few threads in the Steam discussions on the topic of lag, so it may not be an issue specific to Linux or Wine, though Wine may be a cause.
Overall I would say the game is fairly entertaining and for a free game it's definitely worth trying out. Though if you're going to be spending a bit of time with this game, then be warned that the lag often makes for an unpleasant and frustrating experience. The game is definitely playable but nothing like native/ported games to Linux. If I were to use WineHQ's compatibility rating then I would say Gold, because while everything works the lag is a big issue. As of the current status of this game on Linux using Wine I would not reccommend it, unless you are willing to stomach the lag. I'm sure on the supported platforms performance is probably significantly better. I would wait until Brawlhalla is either ported to Linux or Wine compatibility is improved.

For anyone deciding to try out this game, the only thing you should be worried about is how much of your time it's going to take up.
In only a few months, Brawlhalla has very quickly taken up 280 hours of my life, and I can see it taking up hundreds and hundreds more in the next few. If you really want the most bang for your buck, this game gives a hell of a lot of bang for zero buck. It follows a true F2P model, meaning you can only buy cosmetics with real money. It also runs at only 60 Frames per second and has pretty unintensive graphics, meaning nearly everyone can play on even ground: No huge gaming PC required (I play on an old Macbook Pro and it works perfectly).
Speaking of cosmetics, everything about the design in this game from the Artwork of each new character and skin to the sound effects is so clean and stylistic that it's one of the few games where it's actually worth your money to buy the majority of the skins in the store. The game is seriously customizable; I can't imagine how much time it took to make all the colors for all the skins for all the characters and weapons.
What really hooked me in was the gameplay, though. With that 60 fps cap, everyone can reach frame perfect gameplay. It's ridiculously hard to explain how much variation and creativity you can put into your combos with just the basic six light attacks, recovery, and ground pound for each weapon. Then you have three unique heavy attacks for each weapon on each character, momentum dodges, gravity cancels, and all kinds of complicated tech that seems impossible to do at first but that you pick up on before you know it. The skill ceiling is almost limitless, with so many weapons and so many characters all with different signatures and attacks. Plus, you can always change it up; if you get bored of playing a certain weapon or legend (character), you can just try out a new one.
Finally, what I consider to be the best part of this game, the community. While yes, there's quite a bit of toxicity in the game, especially at the lower levels, the overall community is amazingly supportive and active. In particular, the devs are more responsive and helpful I've found for any other game. They listen to the complaints and wants of the players and put updates and hot fixes so quickly that the game is more balanced than any other I've ever played. No single gameplay style reigns supreme (being passive used to, but guess who essentially changed the entire game just to fix that?) and no legend or weapon is broken. If you don't believe me, looking on any stats website for Brawlhalla shows that the winrate on all the legends only varies by about 4% from 50/50 ever, and most are within fractions of percents from eachother. The people that play are amazing and provide so many great resources to learn and improve. Brawl League in particular has Gold and Under tournaments for new players that want to play a tournament against people that aren't way better than them and tutors that will actually get in a game with you and teach you how to play a certain legend or weapon.
And it's free. I know I already said that but seriously, a game this high quality for free?

This is a tactical assassination game with some stealth elements. Essentially, you're supposed to kill every single combatant in pause-based combat while avoiding detection by non-coms.
It *is* quite as interesting as it sounds, but also extremely frustrating at times due to a few design problems.
1. During combat, you will occasionally end up in a position that affords no good jump trajectories (e.g., clinging to the side of the building you are assaulting). When this happens, you do not have the option to simply climb up and continue your attack, forcing you to make a bad jump.
2. If you kill all nearby mooks, you snap out of combat mode even if you are in view of a farther away enemy. The moment or two you need to realize you're no longer in pause mode but are in real-time mode can cost you a perfect win.
3. The single-auto-save system doesn't always work well. It sometimes saves at an inconvenient time (e.g., after a civilian has spotted you), causing you to have to replay the entire level.
These three problems may not seem so bad, but I promise you they will cause you to hate the game from time to time. Overall score: 6.5 / 10

Great concept, poor execution.
This is one of those times where I wish Steam reviews gave a "maybe" option instead of just "yes" or "no".
Nice music and atmosphere, kind of a "cyberpunk Samurai Jack" thing going on.
Where everything breaks down is with the terrible controls; it seems that the devs were going for a "simple and streamlined" approach, but instead they just ended up with something that only works some of the time.
Turn-based tactical/strategic gameplay should be precise, not semi-random. Half the time, it seems like taking an action is like playing Russian roulette; things don't always do what they say they'll do, and it's hard to tell when the game will switch between real-time and turn-based at times.
Possibly worth picking up for cheap (on sale/in a bundle), especially if you're the patient sort (can get quite frustrating, have to redo things a lot), but I certainly wouldn't recommend paying full price.
