Don't buy into all the negative reviews, this game is treated unjustly. Why? Because alot of people just could not grasp the concept.
RONIN is an interesting blend of platforming, stealth, turn based-strategy and action game unlike anything you have played specifically, but reminscent of many games you have. All of it comes together nicely with a simple yet effective art style, music and level design. The story has a thin narrative but it does the job well enough establishing a cyber-punk samurai tale of revenge.
The controls (I used Mouse+Keyboard) were responsive and tightly tuned and they really let me sink my teeth into the finer nuances of combat such as letting bullets graze me and threading those jumps.
The game poses a moderate challenge even for a veteran gamer as it is not a simple hack+slash stealth game, but actually requires you to think ahead and attack at the right time or even the right angle. The learning curve is real and you will die until you ~GET GUD~ but not as much as these negative reviews would have you believe.
The players have all the advantages in the wonderful combat of RONIN, they only need use them!
Highly recommended

Mark of the ninja is an excellent stealth game.
Unlike many stealth games nowadays which merely give stealth as an option, and let you go in guns blazing without a care in the world (think Dishonored and the Assasin'ns Creed series), Mark of the Ninja remains a "pure" stealth game in that you are severely punished for making mistakes. It values stealth and caotion, making it one of my faviourite games.
Asides from that, the way Klei entertainement have used a platformer concept to create a compelling world that you can interact with is astouding. The visual affects are amazing, and the game perfectly blends ancient japanese art with lasers and electronic tripwies.
The controls, tools and just motion in general are extremely fluid and make it a joy to play. They may feel a bit fiddly sometimes, but overall they do an excellent job of immersing you.
Overall, Mark of the Ninja is a must try for anyone who is a fan of stealth games.  9/10

I'm all for free little artsy things like this. But this has nothing to offer. This review will contain spoilers if you want to play it before reading, but there isn't really much to spoil.
The boy's section, with really ill fitting music, just has you finding things around your apartment to show to your parents so that they'll switch from an awkward 'fighting' animation to an awkward 'hugging' pose. Then it ends.
The middle aged man's section is really deep because it's in black and white because his life is dull. So deep. (Sarcasm) You walk a bit until you go down an alleyway where there's a couple fighting. You can intervene and there's a really terrible joke of an excuse for a 'fighting system'. You click the icons with questionable effect for a while until an ambulance (?) arrives and the character explains that it was the right thing to do to intervene and society is bad if we don't intervene or something to that effect. Then it ends. Not really deep, thought provoking or well written.
The old man's section has you stumble upon a couple of boys fighting over a toy. You buy another toy for them. Then it ends. Probably something else you could have done here but there was seemingly nothing else around to 'interact' with. The controls in this section are PARTICULARLY awful, so I didn't fancy wrestling with the controls in order to try and see if anything else was hidden away.
Controls weren't great in the other sections either. The low FOV, which you can't change, made me feel ill while playing.
Whole thing completely lacking in substance. Took absolutely nothing away from it, did not evoke much of a reaction besides mild irritation and illness. Only good thing I can say about it is I like the visual style.

The Way of Life is an experience, a small piece of art with a melancholic subplot whose impact remains even after you make it to the end (which will take few minutes).
It's a series of short episodes where you will be actively take part, part of everyday lives, episodes that may happen to everyone, in whiche we are sked to put our imput.
You can choose the character you want to embody: a child, a business man and an old man.
Every character has his own perspective and view of the apparently decaying world, with his own priorities and morale. As you progress in the exploration you can interact with ceratin objects and people to see what they think about that/them, having a general view of your character's ideas and beliefs.
I won't spoil some interesting features of this game, you need to find them on your own. The Way of Life is free and takes a moment to install, why don't you get it already?

Echoes of Aetheria is an awesome game if you loved the old school NES Final Fantasy (which I do). The story is engaging and the characters are interesting and well written. I particularly enjoyed the forging and augmenting feature for weapons and armor and find myself going back just to see if I can do some fine tuning. Some of the characters may seem cliche, but I find them comfortingly familiar; the damaged hero, the wise-cracking sidekick/love interest. There is very little not to like about this game. Old timer here, one who grew up on Quake Arena and UT where strafe jumping and bunny hopping got you frags and prevented you from being a constant victim. While I'm not going to compare to what was and what will be in the gaming world ... I can easily say that LawBreakers filled in the void for a fast paced and most importantly skill based arena shooter (with a little twist). Yes I die a lot, but I do have some awesome kills too. I am impressed how much skill (think aim, and movement) is important in this game. You have to aim well, move well, and with practice just like me you will start earning some goodies.
So lets get to the good part:
This is one helluva fast paced game, and its a good thing. While some strategy needs to happen while playing most of the objective based matches, being good with navigating the map and being quick on the trigger is key.
This is not your father's arena shooter (and it isn't mine either) ... but that's a good thing. On top of fast movement, and precision aiming you must learn how to use your characters abilities to exploit the map (arena) you play on ... from the zero G areas to knowing where you can recharge this game will challenge you every single time. The movement in this game is unlike any other I've experienced. It's sort of rocket jumping and mid air headshots on steroids.
Now here are some bad parts:
I'm afraid some newbs (and I'm a newb myself) will get quickly discouraged by getting matched with really good players on the opposing team, but I understand that if the player base is a little low you'll get matched with really good players out there - that being said - you must train to get better, this is not one of those games where you "get better" with cards, buffs, etc. You've got to stick to it and practice in order to kick♥♥♥♥♥
With the above in mind, I wish there was a custom bot arena that would allow us mortals to practice. The first handful of matches were brutal for me to the point where I wanted to quit ... so having a custom bot match where I can play alone vs AI or maybe have a friend playing co-op vs AI would be awesome ... I guess what I'm trying to say is that some of us like to practice before we go out there and get our egos bruised.
One of the total let downs for me here was the fact that unlike in any other game I can't just causally sip my jack & coke ... the entire match is a run around, jump around, fast trigger action mayhem ... but maybe that's a good thing :)
Here is the hope part:
Firstly I am hoping for custom bot matches where I can be against the AI with a friend or solo.
Second I want more maps. Yea I know it's easier said than done, but with what the devs did on the current stellar graphics and gameplay maps I am hoping for more - in short - I want more!
Lastly, I want more character customization ... male to female, etc. I know you have your character classes set up, but who doesn't want to play a wraith as a hot harlequin piece of♥♥♥♥♥
See you in the zero G.

I played this game before it came out on steam and had the opportunity to speak directly with the lead developer. Although the game has charm and will give anyone who has played Runescape nostalgia, you will quickly run out of things to do and realize the game's problems. This mostly the fault of the main developer and his incompetence. Being a newly created game, there are a plethora of bugs and glitches, even problems that sometimes cause the whole server to crash. While very frustrating, this is expected and should, I hope, go away with time as long as people continue to work on the game.
Some of the major issues:
If a mob spawns on the same square a player is on, that player and the mob is trapped there until another player comes by and kills the mob. This can even happen in the wilderness (which functions exactly like the Runescape version), and could easily let other players set up to kill them.
The combat styles are totally imbalanced in pvp. Archery is by far the strongest combat style due to being able to infinitely kite players while firing arrows. Magic spells have too long cast times and too short cast distances so that players can simply run away if they see someone start to channel a spell. Melee is by far the worst because both the person attacking and person being attacked have to remain TOTALLY STILL for attacks to land. This means you can just run around if someone is trying to melee you and avoid everything.
There simply is not enough content at this point for the game to be interesting for an extended period of time. If you party with other players to get group xp you will be able to kill the strongest monsters in the game in the matter of a few days. At this point, it's not even worth trying to kill other players because the only reliable way is to exploit bad mechanics.
Duplication glitch. I know of one duplication glitch in this game. There are probably more...
If any of these mechanics get fixed I'll remove them from this review.
Finally, lets talk about ResBak Online. If you've played Orake, you've probably had your game crash at some point and might have seen the message "ResBak Online has stopped responding." A quick Google search will reveal another 2D MMO project that failed. The server and client for ResBak is available Online and after playing it, is IDENTICAL to Orake.
Literally the only difference are the sprites used. The source code for ResBak is available online for $30 is very obviously how the developer was able to produce Orake without knowing anything about or understanding his "own" game. The best part is that the main developer I referred to earlier explicitly stated "I created 99% of the content in this game.".....

---TL;DR AT THE BOTTOM---
This game is really fun, why is it so dead? I bet this question has been asked a million times but I seriously don't get it.
I just purchased this game last night, and I even bought it for my girlfriend and we both love it, I don't regret it.
I thought about it ever since it's release with the low player count and I just said "♥♥♥♥ it" and got it. Turns out the player count doesn't mean a lot. I've played multiple games, even and fun, never the same player in a different lobby and the queue time took 1:53 at 1:00am PST.
If you have thoughts about buying this game, but the player count is holding you back, I'd say just do it. It appears dead but doesn't feel dead. You'd even be contributing to it's growth.
Also, this game seems like it's got a high production value. It's not half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥looking or feeling. It doesn't feel like any other game I've played, except for Unreal Tournament when I was a child which I loved. It's got a high level of creativity and detail. The character's do some-what lack personality and depth  but they're all pretty unique. The skins and camos are really nice and detailed as well.
I see a lot of people criticizing the game for it's price. It's just baffling. The game could EASILY be priced at $59.99. How can anyone complain for it being $29.99? I've seen a lot lower quality games be priced way higher that you'd most likely play only a handful of times.
For anyone feeling this is a copy of Overwatch, it's really not. It's far from it. Play it, watch a review and find out for yourself, like I did, that it can't be anymore different.
This game does have downsides as well, such as the game modes can come off as confusing, even after the tutorials, since they all have their own "Twists" which frankly I enjoy, it's unique and different. The characters are also slightly hard to get used to at first. The tutorials really helped understand them better.
Honestly, if you're on the fence about this one, just really consider all i've said here. Get it on sale if the price is too steep for you. If you're a fan of the kinda FPS game, this one does it very well. I'm frankly afraid for this game's future. It could either have a few sales or free-weekends and the player base skyrockets, or the game will stay the same or slowly decay. I don't see the decay happening for a while since the devs appear to be RIGHT on top of this game and it's development which isn't too common and I really appreciate that.
TL;DR:
-Plenty of lobbies and players to play with. Definately playable with short queue times.
-Very fun, face paced, shooter with unique character's and abilities with more on the way.
-Great looking cosmetics, easy to obtain.
-Price is very good for a game with this kinda production value. Easily could be $59.99.
-Dev's appear to be involved in the community, active updates etc
-Does need more regional servers for more players to easily play
So far those are my impressions of it. Hopefully the game will pick up with future sales, such as the Winter sale.

OK, let's get this out of the way. There are two things that are a problem with this game at the moment, but doesn't effect how I feel about this game. First of all, the most obvious problem with Lawbreakers is the low population count. The game had a terrible launch, and at it's peak had only 2500 players. It's now down to about a third of that. This in itself is the fault of whatever marketing team Nexon has. The game itself is superb and needs more players. The other Critical issue is the fact that this game has a learning curve and new players may get discouraged when the begin to join their first few matches and get annihilated by a Wraith(My main class lol), who moves so damn fast when a skilled player uses it. The only issue presented with that takes us back to the low population count. If those who love it are playing it all the time and vets are all newbies get paired up with, the population won't grow.
Like I said, those two issues are a problem but don't effect how I view the game. So now, to the game itself.
The only critique I have with the game is that it has no lore. Well it does, but it requires you to pay attention to the character's outbursts and also to do a little digging. It's by no means game breaking, but to someone like me who enjoys a grand story, the lack of a complete back story is a little irritating.
Now, the good bits.
The greatest thing about lawbreakers is the sh*tstorm fire fights that can happen. For example, in the game mode, Turf War, if Zone's A and C are captured by either side, B, the one in the middle, becomes the only objective and it becomes an all out brawl to capture the zone. If both teams are balanced and on equal footing when it comes to skill, the fight can last for a long time.
The air combat is a unique twist on the arena shooter genre. The anti grav zones take some getting used to, as do the movement/jump skills of the classes. But once you get used to them, it becomes insanely exilerating. There's been a few times I barely escaped by the skin of the lower part of my ballsack, when a Vanguard used their Starfall ability right above me, and as a Wraith, I slid out from under their divebomb, jumped and then proceded to use his walljump ability to get above her, use the Stinger(Explosive dart fired) skill and opened fire in mid air to kill her before she even completed the the explosive fall.
The Game Modes are Incredibly fun. as stated above the fire fights can get crazy, but for the first time while playing any shooter, I don't feel like I'm just killing over and over again. The simple objectives in the modes actually make you feel like you have purpose in the match other than the "kill everything that moves" outline of most competitive shooters. My favorite is Blitzball. Not to be confused with Spira Blitzball. This blitzball has no water(at least no giant glob of water), the ball talks and explodes if you hold it to long, people are trying to kill you, and it's actually fast pased and fun. No turn based water kicks or cringe worthy laughs after the game.
The classes are actually varied and suited to the maps and game modes. Whether it's the Assassin's Grapple ability that allows you to Spider-Man your way to death or a blood soaked victory, or the Enforcer's classic military archtype, there are many ways to play each character. Some of them tend to shout things that give clues the world in Lawbreakers and can sometimes lead to a few chuckles(Especially the previously mentioned talking ball).
In my opinion, the maps are where this game shines the most. The design of each arena is well suited to every game mode, and all of them present challenges to overcome on your way to complete goals. They are neither to small or so big that you cannot find anyone. The antigrav sections are well placed and depending on how you play, can be a huge help or hillariously frustrating. There was one match I was in that I was escaping from the whole enemy team, sliding and walljumping my way clear with the blitzball and just about made it, but I got caught by one of the antigrav globes and was slingshot around it so fast, I didn't react quick enough, and landed right in the middle of the guys pursuing me. I honestly laughed at my own misfortune.
So, bottom line is this game is insanely fun, fast paced, and honestly made me feel like I was doing something in the matches. Don't listen to the naysayers who say it's dead. Give it a try, get past the learning curve and enjoy the chaos that is Lawbreakers.

Absolutely scratches the Unreal Itch. Low grav, high speed. The amount of mobility is unparalleled, even relative to games like Titanfall 2 and their mobility system. Lawbreakers is an extremely polished FPS. It is not for the faint of heart. Playing this game feels like being tossed in a washing machine for 20 minutes. You will be exhausted. Yet there's very few experiences in gaming that are as satisfying or rewarding.
It's a hero shooter that's core is its gunplay. You move with a variety of high tech gadgets...teleporting forward, jetpacks, thrusters. Everyone's fast. Headshotting a target that's soaring above you at 100mph is Lawbreakers in a nutshell. It hearkens back to the arena shooters of old, like Quake, and at times feels like Tribes' distant cousin. The hero elements are secondary to its hardcore FPS roots, yet abilities have their place and feel impactful.
There's a nice contrast with Lawbreakers...in the age of the kiddy-glove FPS, the F2P shooter, the 'team comp matters more than your ability to aim' shooter..it's nice having something as honest as Lawbreakers. They tell you it's going to kick you in the teeth and it does.
It's a fantastic game and I couldn't reccomend it enough to anyone who enjoys FPS and a challenge. Now if you'll excuse me, I have the sudden urge to go get my teeth kicked in.

Always Sometimes Monsters is one of those games most people probably won't get. And that's okay. If you thought To The Moon was interesting, then you will love Always Sometimes Monsters, because it is better in every single aspect by a multitude of 10.
I don't remember another Indie game which was able to make me emotionally respond in such a way. Actually I remember very very few games which actually ever managed to to do that. Some bad reviews talk about things being monotonous within the game. And that's true. But the game isn't about fun. The game is about the at some times crushing futility of life. We all have had such moments, and ASM does catch them in it's own way. There are some funny parts, but most of the game has a very serious and grim tone. This is a game, which is a depressing story, not told, but perceived by the player itself.
ASM is an experiment of sorts and while not always executed all too well on the technical side, it is a game where the choices you make actually do have an impact, contrary to all Telltale games I have played so far.
There's a lot of heart in this little gem and anyone who can look beyond the dodgy retro art style might be able to have a very worthwhile experience. It's one of the games I would have never played if I hadn't been victim to a random sale impulse purchase. Or it was part of a Bundle somewhere. But it's really a hidden gem.

One of the best stealth games I’ve ever played, fluent gameplay, non-linear level designs, good game mechanics, very immersive once you get the hang of it. Players often have many gameplay options, whether to be a ruthless sword wielding killer who slices and hangs his victims along his path; a light armoured runner who utilizes tunnels and hidden pathways to sneak past his enemies; a masked phantom who snap off lights and teleports between shadows; an assassin who use spike traps and smoke bombs to distract and pick off his opponents one by one; or even a sparing martial artist who hang up and knocked out guards to terrify other guards while taking no lives, the choices are many. There are also achievements and side quests to make the levels more interesting and the exploration more worthwhile. Once you finish the storyline, NewGamePlus unlocks which provides further challenges, new DLC is also great fun. The game has a great art style and the sound tracks are outstanding.
Story was a bit basic, and ending was a bit anticlimactic for me. But overall the game is a definite must buy.

This is a very basic card game where the objective is to form a better hand than the computer opponent.  You form hands by taking turns drawing from a deck, each turn ending when you/AI collect the cards drawn, or bust by uncovering two cards of the same suit.  When the deck is depleted, the round is over and the winner is the player who has the better hand.
There you have it.  If that sounds interesting, go ahead, but that's all you'll be getting.
Sure, there are special card abilities and other razz-a-matazz to make the game seem more interesting but those don't change the fact that it's basically a simplistic luck-based game with a little bit of decision-making thrown in to make it seem like your skill factors into it.
Good graphics, good presentation, good user interface and reasonably smart AI, yet stupid enough to make conspicuously bone-headed decisions, which breaks immersion.
Maybe I've played too many card games in my life, or maybe I've programmed too many, but this game doesn't offer me what I want which is a skill-based card game with a little luck thrown in.  Instead this is a luck-based game with a little skill required.

Mark of the Ninja is really good. I just finished the game and for sure will play it on the New Game Plus mode (the harder difficulty mode unlucked after finishing the game on the normal one).
Pros:
-Climatic, you really feel like your character is a Ninja.
-Never too hard, there are no moments when you just have no idea what to do.
-...but not too easy, you have to think, about what you are doing. Not everything is obvious.
-Ideal for achievments, there are plenty of them and if you finish a level finding scrolls (hidden treasures, 3 per level) and doing additional challenges, you will be able to unlock new stuff.
-Awesome ending!
-Game is really well done, music and graphics are good.
Cons:
-It is too dark. Yeah I know it should be, but it was TOO dark and yes, I know that I can change brightness but it isn't the thing. Sometimes rooms are just too black. You can't see walls.
-You can find some things that are not perfect. For example you can unlock killing enemies that are right over you, but in game you are able to sometimes kill enemies that stay close to the "perfect place" and they will be teleported.
-If you are not a fan of doing game for 100%, you may end it too fast.
-If you play just for 100% you may just end up runing around the level seeking for a scroll, or doing stupid things to complete challenges
-Later you unlock a power that... makes game boring and way too easy (the Final Mark), but you don't have to use it.
-Controlling your character can be hard sometimes, especially when you try to jump high on a celler or a wall, or close the door.
-Maybe it's only my bug but game won't close after exiting it in main menu. I had to restart computer to close it.
Even if it doesn't look good, I really recommend "Mark of the Ninja" to everyone looking for a good sneak game with an option of additional challenges (like in Assassin's Creed for 100%). Also it can be a really good choice for speed runs.

It seems like I've made a habit of collecting really cheap shoot 'em ups that focus on a single unique trait to make them stand out from the endless number of competitors.  SPINGUN (hereafter referenced without all caps) didn't break that trend.   But let me say up front that this game's 'unique trait' is one that takes some getting used to and may be pretty unappealing from the start.
Spingun uses two buttons exclusively.  Not just in the gameplay, but in every piece of the game.  Even navigating and selecting items in the menu.  The game instructs you to use the left and right arrow keys of your keyboard for this, but I found out soon that many other keys are representative of “left” and “right” and that it was most comfortable to use “A” and the right arrow key so that my hands were reasonably separated.   Navigating the menus involves left and right to go up and down and pressing them at the same time to select the highlighted option.  Once you start the game, left and right will not only turn your ship left and right respectively, but it also produces forward thrust.  This means pressing a direction will not just turn you that direction, but will have you traveling forward in a circle.  In order to go straight, you have to use what I'll just call the “canoe” method of swapping quickly between left and right.  This also steadily increases your speed, so everything gets a bit touchy as the enemies start stacking up.
As those enemies do pop in to existence, you'll need to fire on them.  This is done by pressing both left and right at the same time.  Of course, in doing so, you lose the ability to turn or move forward, so you have to line up your shot while you're moving against a moving target and fire without being able to change your movement along with the action.   So while you have a game that looks a lot like a twin stick shooter, it doesn't play like one.  Along with the strange movement scheme, you'll be collecting pickups in the form of weapons and health.  As soon as you pick up a weapon, the ammo starts draining, so there's no holding on to a good one and firing it sparingly for maximum effect.  Though firing the weapon does drain your ammo faster, so it's still important to do more than spam it as soon as you get it.  Weapon pickups also increase your total amount of ammo for your base gun.  Your health starts out with a handful of blocks that are replenished by health kits.  Health kits, similarly, increase your max health if they're picked up when you're at full health.
So that's far too many words to explain a game so simple, but I suppose the real question is, is it fun?  Well, yes and no.  You definitely have to get used to the control scheme and it's one that can make a big difference in how you perceive the game.  At first I found it extremely frustrating, but with some practice it seemed very rewarding to be successful using it.  When I found some success in the game mode Endless Classic (I made it to 19th on the leaderboards!
I suddenly started enjoying the game.  However, my experience with the “Boss Fights” game mode just felt like I was playing something that didn't really belong in the game.  Repeatedly losing to things that take up most of the arena with a very limited control scheme and being punished for touching them annoyed me.  Yet I suppose the idea of having game modes that are distinct serves to potentially appeal to different people.  For those reasons, I recommend Spingun because at the very least, you may find one or more game modes that deliver a worthwhile experience and justify the $2 base price.  However, if you're like me and picked it up for under a dollar, it's a little easier to say it's not wasted money.  Good discounts can do a lot for the overall value of a game, and Spingun is not an exception.

Mark of the Ninja is really good. I just finished the game and for sure will play it on the New Game Plus mode (the harder difficulty mode unlucked after finishing the game on the normal one).
Pros:
-Climatic, you really feel like your character is a Ninja.
-Never too hard, there are no moments when you just have no idea what to do.
-...but not too easy, you have to think, about what you are doing. Not everything is obvious.
-Ideal for achievments, there are plenty of them and if you finish a level finding scrolls (hidden treasures, 3 per level) and doing additional challenges, you will be able to unlock new stuff.
-Awesome ending!
-Game is really well done, music and graphics are good.
Cons:
-It is too dark. Yeah I know it should be, but it was TOO dark and yes, I know that I can change brightness but it isn't the thing. Sometimes rooms are just too black. You can't see walls.
-You can find some things that are not perfect. For example you can unlock killing enemies that are right over you, but in game you are able to sometimes kill enemies that stay close to the "perfect place" and they will be teleported.
-If you are not a fan of doing game for 100%, you may end it too fast.
-If you play just for 100% you may just end up runing around the level seeking for a scroll, or doing stupid things to complete challenges
-Later you unlock a power that... makes game boring and way too easy (the Final Mark), but you don't have to use it.
-Controlling your character can be hard sometimes, especially when you try to jump high on a celler or a wall, or close the door.
-Maybe it's only my bug but game won't close after exiting it in main menu. I had to restart computer to close it.
Even if it doesn't look good, I really recommend "Mark of the Ninja" to everyone looking for a good sneak game with an option of additional challenges (like in Assassin's Creed for 100%). Also it can be a really good choice for speed runs.

Very late last night I finished this. The story is not very deep or interesting but what makes it stand out is the story-telling. The atmosphere is filled to the brim and the many collectibles do a great job at fleshing it out. I did learn a lot about the world of Batman so it was a little disappointing that so few bosses were in the game. Oh well, there's enough future games to rectify that.
The combat is the right amount of challenge but it's more on the easy side. Leveling up Batman wasn't very satisfying. It's the gadgets you upgrade and acquire during the campaign which add for nice new gameplay mechanics. Getting access to previously unreachable places makes for a nice sense of progression.
While neither being a classic open-world nor traditionally linear, the mixture of both elements worked very well in the end. There is minimal backtracking unless you have an itch to complete all Riddler Challenges - which I did - but thanks to compact levels it didn't get tedious. I'm interested to see how this changes with future Batman games that went open-world.

While this game has the distinct appearance held by most RPGMaker titles, it stands out in every other way. The soundtrack is great on the standards of big production games, let alone independent titles. The gameplay does something unique for a JRPG, drawing inspiration from titles like Lunar and Suikoden where position of your units have real value. There are a lot of different ways to optimize each character with skills and customizable equipment, offering a great deal of potential variety and allowing you to create your own strategies and gameplay style. The story really caught me off guard, going in a direction that most media isn't willing to. It caught me off guard a couple times, a big point in its favor to me.
If you are a serious RPG player, make sure to play it on Hard difficulty. At this level, battles actually require strategy and thought. Later in the game, you may find yourself getting the swing of things and going on cruise control, but don't get too comfortable. Even well-leveled and with high-end crafted gear (which takes some work to get), the end game presents a reasonable challenge.
One other point worth mentioning: the amount of backstory presented in this game is huge. There is a lore catalog that you can choose to read if you so desire, and the amount of world building put into this game is impressive.
There are still some minor bugs, but judging by the frequency of updates thus far, the creator is addressing them as they are brought up (including things like balance issues, which is above and beyond as far as I am concerned).

Fans of traditional jrpg, especially from the SNES/PS1 era, will find Echoes of Aetheria a nostalgic throwback and at the same time a breath of fresh air.
A classic story about war and ancient superpowers is supported by likeable characters and entertaining dialogues (although sometimes a bit cheesy), and while it's presented a bit naively, it does have its nice moments, clever ideas and a satisfying, well thought ending.
What really shines in Echoes of Aetheria is the gameplay, faithful to traditional, old school jrpg but also very refreshing and, most importantly, well designed.
The battle system takes ideas from many different games: it has grid positioning, a "time bar" for turn order and casting times, which includes tactical interruptions and stuns, skills with either a cooldown system or the use of points shared by the whole party, which is a nice take on the classic "MP" resource, and it's overall fast paced and engaging.
Each character has (many) unique skills which allow for different and satisfying builds, and the player is encouraged to experiment since choices and points can be reallocated as necessary. Moreover, characters' skills synergize very well with each other, and this coupled with the tactical grid/formation allows for deep customization of both the characters and the party as a whole.
Speaking of customization, there's a pretty straightforward but nicely done crafting system which really shines at the endgame, where rare resources can be used to either forge new, unique equipment or to greatly strengthen existing ones: flexibility and experimentation are the keywords here.
Lastly, but even more importantly, these mechanics are well implemented into the game: on hard difficulty battles are challenging, some endgame optional fights are tailored to specific characters and builds, requiring full understanding of each one, and all this preparation is not wasted at all because (finally, a game does this right!) the final bosses are just as hard as they should be.
This is the high note defining Echoes of Aetheria for me, a game not only having a deep enough system, but also encouraging the player to make full use of it, tailoring the challenges to what the player can realistically achieve and prepare for.
If you can go past the raw, generic interface and overall cheap-looking presentation of the game (sprites are actually cool, though), there's much to discover in Echoes of Aetheria. A seemingly traditional game with a nostalgic feeling to it, yet able to turn nostalgia into a new appeal for classic gameplay elements, thanks to a masterful mix of everything we loved about the genre.
Dancing Dragon Games proves once again that they can make a fun JRPG with a great story.

Before I start, let me give you three fair warnings :
- first, Echoes of Aetheria is an old-school J-RPG in the most traditional way. If you've ever played games like Final Fantasy 4-5-6, Breath of Fire 1-2-3, Chrono Trigger, Suikoden 1-2,...and didn't like those, this game isn't for you.
- secondly, this game has been made with RPG-Maker, but do not judge it solely on this, because this is the prime exemple of how RPG-maker can be used to make a good professional game. There is a LOT of production value in this, and not some basic use of the default assets that come with RPG-Maker : original, animated sprites, original character portraits, original musics, original battle system...you get it.
- thirdly, Dancing Dragon, the devs of this game, are also known for making some other good J-RPGs, the most well-known being Skyborn. While this game is superior in almost every way to its predecessor, it does re-use some of the assets of Skyborn, a music there, the sprites used for making the maps, etc, etc...That being said, it's not detrimental at all, and keep in mind that we're talking of an indie game made by a couple people, sold for a somewhat low cost (especially if you compare to the price of similar games in the "good old times")
With that being said, how is this game?
One word : solid. It takes the old formula of J-RPGs of the SNES era : an epic story revolving around a party of heroes, punctuated by some tactical combats.
The story is good, very solid (can't repeat that enough), and has a catching intro, a good amount of twists, and a quite satisfaying ending. While it's nothing ground breaking, the characters are likeable, do have some amount of depth, and the world is believable, which is, in my opinion, quite important. It's very close to reach the heights of some of the classics of the genre (the likes of Chrono Trigger or Breath of Fire 2), but I felt that some dialogues could have been a little more developped and that some cutscenes were a little too implicit, and let you rely on your imagination to fill the gaps. But just the fact that it can be compared to some of the most renowned J-RPGs should speak for itself about the quality of this part of the game.
But Echoes does not rely solely on the exemple of its elders, and offers very good and fresh ideas in the gameplay department : the battle system is not exactly turn-based, but closer to a Grandia, where you can interrupt/slow/anticipate the ennemies actions. There are lots of skills available for each character, with quite some amount of customization. The gear can also be customized for your needs, and the crafting system is well-thought and allows experimentations with a minimal amount of consequence (every consummable ressources can be bought/farmed at some point or another) Overall, you can't screw your party, and while some tactics may be more efficient than others (especially on Hard), a good amount of flexibility remain, even in the hardest challenges.
In conclusion, if you're looking for a solid old-school J-RPG on Steam, Echoes of Aetheria is totally worth its price. It's a well-crafted work of passion that does its best to keep the old J-RPG vibe alive, and, in my opinion, succeed with flying colours.

Echoes also features some neat twists, like a small crafting system and the use of refundable skill points to enhance the abilities of your party members, allowing you to change their skills on the fly. While some of these ideas could be better fleshed out, what's here is certainly worth your time.

Cons:

Dialogue
First the good, it's funny and well written, with lots of references to the characters' source material. However, after about an hour you've pretty much heard it all, and then it can get really irritating. The issue is the fact that a lot of it is unskippable, poker night 1 at least had an option for minimal conversation, however this seems to be absent in 2 as far as I've found. And whilst muting dialogue helps, it still leads to long, boring pauses where the pace is slowed in favour of conversation you've already heard 100 times before. This is also where the issue with Claptrap and GladOS come in, whilst the quality of these characters' dialogue is subjective (I've never been a fan of claptrap) it gets incredibly annoying having to sit through their dialogue, granted claptrap isn't the worst (it's more how his voice sounds than what he says a lot of the time) GladOS is present throughout the game and will constantly interrupt to berate you, which whilst at first humourus and definitely in character, it gets annoying fast, especially due to the fact that her lines can be fairly long and she talks very slowly.
In conclusion of this point, dialogue is both the main draw and its main drawback. An option to minimize interrupting dialogue would've helped the replay value greatly.
Cosmetics
The Borderlands 2 ones are decent compared to the standard of the title, although the TF2 ones are definitely the main draw, the necrinomicrown and long fall loafers can easily go well with other cosmetics for their respective classes, also the samson skewer goes well with the brock locks heavy hair, essentially letting you cosplay as Brock as Heavy, also he has other military theme cosmetics it can go well with.
As for in the game itself, this is where the incentive to keep playing past the other game cosmetics comes in, After every tournament (unless you are the first knockout) you will earn credits which you can use to either buy drinks or buy cosmetics to change the theme of the inventory. This is a clear improvement over the last where you could only change the decks and felt, in 2 you can change the decks, felt and chips, choosing from a borderlands, sam and max, venture bros, army of darkness, or portal theme. If you equip all of the same theme, the background of the inventory changes, along with the music, and will also have special scenes for player knockouts and winning.
Gameplay
It's poker. The only other poker games I've played is poker night 1 and the minigame in new super mario bros, easy to say it trumps them both, also I'd say it's likely a step above any free browser/flash one you'd find.
However, the game can often feel unfair. Now whilst this may just be a case of poker being based on probability, but you can never tell with a game just by playing it that if it's following the same rules you are. I'm definitely not the only one who experiences showdowns that seem like a sure victory, but the ai manage to either get really lucky, or just completely trump your hand, like for instance one time I had two pair beaten by three of a kind, then a three of a kind beaten by a straight, then the next I had a straight beaten by a flush, at that point where it's beating it with the winning hand one station higher consecutively it feels incredibly unfair, and like the game isn't being honest or even following any kind of rules.  This is mainly an issue if you're going for the achievement of having $1,000,000, as sometimes your losses can feel very forced.
Final Conclusion
The game is good, and worth it even if you only want it for cosmetics. I'd maybe say wait til sale but at £4/$5 it's cheap enough for what it offers. The game is only hindered by the dialogue getting repeaty and the game sometimes feeling unfair, however PvAI card games will almost always feel at least slightly suspect no matter if it's based on gambling or not.

Win ugly TF2 hats
Win ugly Borderlands cosmetics

A great example of a stealth game done right Mark of the Ninja plays exactly how you would expect it will - the player can navigate levels in truly acrobatic style, while taking care of the hazards with an array of special 'gadgets' and a plain good sword.
From sneaking through vents through hanging off the anchor points to casually jumping over the enemies (you can actually pull this off in the darkness, jump from just outside of enemy's sight-range and land behind him) - the ninja can do it all, and there is little that can stop you, save for getting too cocky or careless. The movement and animations mixed with game's visual style make beating every level feel good from start to finish, and the freedom of approach given to the player allows for even greater satisfaction.
while you do start with quite humble tools, progressing through the game and succeeding at optional objectives will allow to quite rapidly upgrade protagonist's capabilities. By the endgame, you can treat enemies with a whole array of nastiness: from as tame as simple distracting sound to as horrific as having them devoured by bugs. Mix in a chance to set-up a trap or inject the guards with a fear-inducing poison, and it is quite easy to feel bad for them. You can do whatever you wish, nobody is going to question it - they may challenge you to take a harder path, but it will be yours decision. And with the alternate costumes that modify the rules, one is sure to find just the style for themselves.
Two special shoutouts go to the visual design and story. Starting with visuals, not only do they build a very specific atmosphere, fitting the point in narrative as well as the current location, but also leave nothing to be guessed. Each important spot or indicator is just organically there, making sense and being very easy to read.
The story is a strange but attractive creature: for the most part, it seems linear and inconsequential, until the game reaches its final stages. Suddenly, everything that was seen before and every little dialogue snippet will come back to you as you face the last level. At that point, it is not about gameplay but a choice - and one that can leave you sitting and thinking for several minutes even.

I would say that the main asset of licensed Lego games has always been the soundtrack. In this game, which was the first large licensed Lego PC game, the soundtrack by John Williams, all hail John Williams, is used extraordinarily well. It underscores in-game situations properly but of course, it can't compare to the genius of the films' score. Without the soundtrack, the game would be devoid of most of the SW atmosphere with only the iconic lightsaber and blaster sounds to back it up. The gameplay is much more combat-oriented than the newer Lego games. There are many space battles that have their magic but are horrible to control. When the chapter description informed me of an impending vehicle level I was horrified what would await me. You will die a lot because the camera and controls don't make it easy for you. At one point when I was running away from the lava, I died 15 times just because the camera angle was stupid. The original trilogy has overall better level design than the prequel one because the developers learnt a lot from their mistakes after releasing the prequel episodes. The original trilogy is more graphically advanced, has longer chapters and more memorable cutscenes. However, the dreaded vehicle levels make a comeback. Without achievements, there is little to no reason to 100% this game because it would require you to play each level two more times to get all the collectables which is more daunting than it sounds.

+ soundtrack, visual rendition, occasional laugh

I want to like this game. A RPG in a contemporary setting, that doesn't involve saving the kingdom or mechs (as cool as those are). A RPG that examines the modern condition, its ups and downs, and the choices people always sometimes have to make. In some parts, it can be illuminating and daresay enlightening. The music is unique, each city and town has a subtle feel. The artwork, though not masterclass, is quite good. I almost, almost mind you, forget that I'm playing a game made in RPGMaker. I played it all the way to the end. I got every achievement (though they are checkpoint achievements, so not the greatest accolade). So, I want to like this game, but I don't. I find it interesting, promising, and quite unique. Indeed, this Toronto-born award-laden project makes me proud to be a Canadian gamer.  But at the end of 10+ hours, I am unwilling to recommend this game.
For about 50% of the journey, there are interesting twists and turns. Interesting characters, insights, and questions raised. Your choices are, if not at least an illusion, actual choices. Then it comes off the rails in the final chapters. For all the choices made, the detail in people and places, the mood and atmosphere: the story begins to make less and less sense. Given certain paths in the story you choose: the ending can make a lot of sense or no sense. The storyteller's conceit from the top of the game can be brilliant or just downright bizarre. For all the great beginnings, the meat of the story before it: the ending is just a miss. This is not a gamer lamenting a bad ending that he didn't manage to avoid. Even on the "good" ending (or one of them, depending on your point of view), I was just confused. This is a game with a message, trying to tell us something we don't often hear. It is a game trying to do something that isn't a nostalgia trip to bygone JRPGs of yesteryear. Yet, it all falls apart.
So, do I recommend this game? No, not to everyone.
Do I hate this game? No, I am disappointed.
Should they have not made it? Better to fail ambitiously than to succeed in mediocrity.
I cannot recommend this game because, I feel, that it missed the execution of the ending. A story with a poorly handled ending is just the death of story-driven tales like ASM. Yet, I cannot bring myself to hate this game. For all the ending had failed; the promise of a great modern-day RPG that stands apart from all rivals: that is well worth trying. I would rather the boys and gals at Vagabond make the attempt and miss; than for no one to ever try. I cannot condemn this game as something that should never have been.  There is too much promise and hope in such a title. Even if you don't get the happiest ending possible (if one could call it that.)
This is an interesting game that I hope Vagabond makes a similar attempt at. This is a game that other developers should strive to perfect. This is the sort of game that modern gaming we see more of and not less. So if you want to have a little inspiration, a little glimmer of what a unique game could be like, then buy this;  play it; and make it better. Indeed, keep an eye out for future games by this studio: they have a masterpiece in them: they just have to make it.

So, disclaimer first: Lawbreakers is only the third FPS I have played since the original Unreal Tournament (also by Cliff Bleszinski) came out. Left 4 Dead and Left 4 Dead 2 are the only other ones I have played in the meantime. Shooters just became too generic and more of the same for years.
That being said, I have been following Boss Key from the moment it was founded so I always knew I would play this game, whether it would suck or not. Guess what? It doesn't suck.
I think Lawbreakers will be the FPS I have the most fun with since the original Unreal Tournament, thus overtaking Left 4 Dead. The game is fast, like epicly fast and brutal in its demand of its players. That is a good thing though! Lawbreakers is about teamwork and player skill, in that order. You might not be the best player in the world but if you are a good team player you can easily be MVP every round. The rating system does not just count kills but awards you for assists, heavy assists, objectives completed or supported...it is probably my favorite part of the game's design. Next part would be the playing styles per 'character' that is way less weapon/ability based but much more movement based; the entire game encourages you to keep moving at all times, there are no snipers (thus no campers) and no support-only jobs.
TL:DR; if you like a game that awards team play and player skill, and (so far) lacks a toxic community, get Lawbreakers...you will not regret it.
To be fair: the biggest downside is that sometimes people are inactive or drop out of a game and the balance of the game is such that that probably means you will lose. Although dropped players are refilled fast and on the spot, sometimes it is not fast enough and 3 vs 5 is not maintainable.

My hour count is high because I left the game running (whoops). For the record, I finished it once, and it didn't take me that long.
The whole point of this game is to get back with your ex. Problem is, he's getting married. Winning requires you to tear apart a pretty happy existing relationship. It's a fun game through the middle if you're not expecting it to be too serious. But the main arc of the story and some of the people who are supposed to be main characters are so ridiculously juvenile, it's not even funny. And the ending turns out awful for someone no matter what. I don't mind games with no "happily ever after"--but there should be an option where a core character doesn't end up wishing they were dead.
Trigger warnings for suicide-, drug-, and death-related stuff. Crops up a couple times, and although it was kind of hackneyed, it's worth mentioning that if that stuff pushes bad buttons for you, this game isn't worth it. Ending aside, there's this one pretty early on:
If you're still interested in playing, there's a really good step-by-step guide here that tells you what to do to get the 'good ending' (scare quotes) or in case you get stuck. It doesn't spoil the actual plot just by reading the guide.
I used it loosely as I played, so I did get the 'good ending', but had I made my own choices, that wouldn't have happened. By the end I was pretty disgusted with the three main characters--they're all kind of jerks. MC does some questionable stuff over the course of her (or his, it was her for me) adventure, and then chooses to stop a wedding during the ceremony when she could have literally spoken up days before it happened and saved a lot of expense, drama, and effort. Aaaaaarrrgghh. Your ex strings Sam along to the point of almost marrying her when he actually wants you, and then ditches her when you show up and just say that you wuv him and he should stop before he makes a Big Mistake because you two are ~soulmates~. And then Sam--oh, Sam.
She invited you to her wedding just to shove it in your face that she was marrying your old flame, and brag about her huge book deal. Either that, or she's an idiot. There's no indication that the main character and Sam kept in touch or were still friends in any way. MC did kind of "steal" her crush (he chose MC over her, if you call that stealing), and MC got a book deal that was supposed to be for both her and Sam but cut Sam out of the deal, and ended up taking it anyway (it was a sticking point).
I got really annoyed when Sam got held at gunpoint over her gambling debts and wanted your manuscript so she could cash in on her book deal and pay off her debts--and I mean annoyed at both characters. I was really irritated with Sam, of course, but I was also irritated because where were her friends when she got carted off to play high-stakes cards? Sam has a reputation for getting drunk at parties and wandering off to get into trouble, so why weren't they watching her a little better? Can't someone around here act like a responsible adult? (Preferably Sam, but that was never going to happen.) And then Sam's life is in danger and MC gripes about what giving her the manuscript will do to MC's career. This is the same MC who blackmailed a doctor because "a life is a life"--remember? Anyway, you can pay it off without giving up the book, but it requires major minigame work or gambling or one of a couple other options that are pretty boring.
So, either you take your book/crush and become happy and successful and Sam ends up in the gutter, or vice versa, because apparently nothing is more important than Marrying Your Soulmate, and success is a zero-sum game. (eyeroll) What happened to Sam's giant book deal, anyway? How... never mind, I'm going to stop trying to make sense of this.
There were parts that were fun, though.
In the second town, I ditched both the union job and the protesters and joined the detective instead. He was obviously a Superman reference on legs, really boring, but he didn't stick around long. I got a kick out of the computer scenes. Snork. Pixel Cup Soccer 17 has been released in Early Access recently, but already has a lot of content.

Dead Man's Draw is a fast paced (disable animations in the options menu) card RNG game with a slight peppering of strategy involved.
I'll get right down to it, I absolutly loved this game. This was an obsession on the level of something like Teris or Puzzle Quest. That equated mix opf luck and skill that just keeps pulling at you to do more, play more, unlock more, win more.
Is it hard? Not at all. You can figure it out in about 6.5 minutes give or take 30 seconds and once you've gotten it you question if it'll be fun to play. Then you play a few more game and you are solidly invested into unlocking characters and abilities like it's in a time constraint. But it's not. The game is so simple it's almost laughable how much time I put into unlocking everything.
The game is a simple card draw with the general rule of negating all cards drawn if you have two of the same face cards or numbers depending on the game. Every game lasts for a few minutes. A tournament is several games with a simple overarching rule such as: first player to X points wins, player with most cards at end of deck wins, player with lowest score wins. These ensure you tweak your character's abilities and playstyle to win consistently. Sometimes you lose solely out of bad luck but sometimes it may be a bad pairing of abilities that simply doesn't jive with the tournament rules.
I think it's only worth a few dollars and that makes sense for what you get. Graphics are nothing amazing. Sound is kind of corny. I usually play this while listening to some sort of podcast on YouTube (Tested, Google Talks). All in all its worth the money. Get it, get deep into it, unlock everything then sit back and wonder why you spent  24 houurs playing a 3$ card game.

Batman Arkham Asylum still holds a very special place in people's hearts. Back in 2009 the Batman had had his ups and downs in regard to videogames, and then suddenly there was this one which came somewhat out of nowhere.
It had its very own fighting system, tried a different approach to the game making it feel closer to the comics and additionally it didn't stop there. As Batman's greatest weapon is fear and striking from the shadows as he is almost always outmatched, the game added predator encounters, in which you should avoid fighting the henchmen head on and insteadt jump or swing from vantage point to vantage point and pick them off one by one.
Basically, Rocksteady took a risk and gave us something new. Completely new gameplay mechanics, a new story...
Additionally, they topped it off with tried and true voice actors and I have to say, Kevon Conroy and Mark Hamill are just perfect for this.
This package worked perfectly. Arkham Asylum is still the masterpiece it has always been and has aged well.
This is a great game for everyone. For Batman fans, however, it is a must-have!

A simple shooter game where you only have two buttons to do three actions: Spin rightwards, spin leftwards, and thrust forward. The goal is to survive as long as possible inside a small, sort-of-rounded square room where enemies constantly spawn around, manier and stronger each second.
Even though the objective is simple and straightforward, what makes this game difficult is the limited controls. The physics of the ship plus the game's gravity makes it difficult to maneuver the ship in the way you want it to be. Go too fast and you'll bounce around in unexpected directions, move too slow and you'll probably get hit by enemies or projectiles.
It's very addicting if you're into hardcore games (not that I'm hardcore. I'm just an averager) with the global ranking encouraging you to keep playing and try harder.
There are many game modes as well, which all provide interesting mechanics and separate global rankings. Some game modes are for casual and fun, while some are even harder than the original game mode. Choose what you like!

Good, but not as good as it should be.
Mankind Divided is an great sequel to Human Revolution, and helps to bridge the story in HR to the original game. However, it seemingly stops short. After completing the game it felt more like I was left with a cliffhanger than a satisfying conclusion.
I really liked the how the game mechanics have been expanded along with aug abilities, truly letting you tackle objectives in so many more ways than before. The map design also reflects this attentiveness.
However a few things stuck out negatively. There is an obvious shift towards modern gameyness with the collectathon of items to access things outside of the main game as well as the notorious microtransactions and tacked on DLC (all of which could have been integrated into the main game). It's rather immersion breaking to see that stuff pop up in game. Other things like the points of interest I felt were also a bit too open world like. Major choices in the narrative also are geared towards replayability. It's obvious with the ending Picus report cinematic which goes down a list of choices made and their effects. Oh and New Game+. Why not just construct a very strong narrative? Being linear is not bad, especially not in a series like DX. I know you could end up with different results in the original and HR, but it was not this obvious forced Choice A vs Choice B.
The character animations, namely the expressions in conversation seem worse. Everyone seems to bounce around and shake a lot, throwing theirs hands about. Some reactions are rather melodramatic. I wonder if they used some sort of automated software, but it's definitely not on the same quality level as Human Revolution where the movements and expressions looked very natural and even subtle expressions could be read.
Also, it seems to be a bit buggy. I had graphical glitches and some crashes due to the interface, but thankfully they could be worked around.
It's a shame this didn't set the bar even higher, but that seems to be more the fault of the publisher than the devs who otherwise delivered an amazing narrative. I was on the edge of my seat, especially when seeing the bridges being built to the original Deus Ex. I hoped for so many more answers and exploration. But sadly it cut short. Hopefully they do decide to create one more game to complete the bridge and make it a masterpiece.
Would I buy this game at full price? No, not with the poor practices in place. But on discount it's not a regrettable purchase, especially if you enjoy the Deus Ex franchise. Funny thing is that I personally would buy this game full price if they just had more integrity instead of chopping it up.

A Great addition to the DEUS EX series

It's a great game. The gameplay and level design offered are a more refined version of those found in Human Revolution.
It features two hub worlds, Prague and Golem City, with singular missions taking place in Dubai, London, and a facility in the Swiss Alps. Prague changes throughout the story, opening up new locations and side missions. Though the levels are not as BIG as the levels in Human Revolution were, they are designed with more emphasis on density and environmental storytelling. For example, while in HR you could run past entire buildings and streets without having anything interactable in them except for a few barebones apartments, in MD, you can break into almost every single apartment and shop, all of which utilize datapads, emails, and uniquely desinged environments to paint a lived in world with it's own history.
The detailed world doesn't go to waste and is where the side missions are where a significant amount of content has been relegatred. They are essential if you want to know more about the world Jensen inherits after the Aug Incident and they also provide many opportunities for you to test out your augs and weapons. You will solve a murder mystery, you will help out an underground conspiracy magazine, you will catch with characters from the past, and you will get tangled up with the Czech mob.
The main story is also more focused compared to the ambitious globe trotting adventure that was HR. Personally, I found it to be slightly more enjoyable than its predecessor because the narrow focus allows the game to maintaine a grounded story while still shedding some light on the secret Illumaniti conspiracy happening behind the scenes.
It took me over 80 hours to experience most of what the game had to offer. The game welcomes multiple playthroughs by offering different pathways and solutions to the mission objectives and on more than one occasion I went back and did missions differently just to satisfy my curiousity.
If you like these kinds of games then you must give Mankind Divided a chance. It's one of the best examples of its kind.

This game has so many flaws.
-Terrible servers and high ping players. Lag and poor hit registration.
-Poor map design. Spawn camping is the standard for almost every game.
-Awful weapons. Small mag size, high rate of fire, and low damage mean if you miss any you are going to find yourself constantly dying while reloading. There is very low potential to take on multiple enemies. Maybe the guns at higher level are better, but I can't force myself to grind for them.
-Ninjas with swords that are also bullet sponges. Miss any shots on that guy running around a corner at you with a katana and you are going to die while reloading.
-Tiny health packs. If you take any damage you might as well just forget winning another gunfight. No health regen on most characters and the health packs are tiny. Oh and you don't even regen health in spawn. If you're lucky, there's a large health in there, but it's different on every map.
-ADS sensitivity is garbage. It seems different for each gun.
-The game is full of players that are absolute garbage or sweaty and play this game religiously. Because of the small mag size, no health regen, and tiny health packs it's very hard to stay alive long enough to hold control points/objectives, therefore you can't carry the bad players on your team.
-Leveling up is a pain because some of the weapons are complete trash.
This game looked like a lot of fun but just doesn't cut it. Go play black ops 2. Better weapons and map design, better hit registration, overall more enjoyable experience. And that's even with the occasional camper using an LMG with target finder. So that's saying something.

Soundtrack is raw.
Rest of the game is going to depend on personal preference.
Movement and fighting are very fluid, though from what Ive played of the beta and now on release there is going to be a steep skill curve for anyone new to fast paced arena shooters to reach that feeling.
Biggest step is finding the character to match your playstyle and mastering it.
If you like UT or quake then you'll probably enjoy this game alot but be prepared for some small class balance issues that you will have to be good at playing around.
The game is teamwork based, if you want to carry then you need to know how to play off your teammates and what their class does. That said, there is alot of room to shine individually since the core of the game does not revolve around team comp but rather individual skill of the players on either team and how they play around eachother.  There are no hard counters or stun cc, the main factors in your performance will be your aim, movement around the zones, and use of your abilities at the right times to support your teammates or stop/secure obj scoring.

This game is fantastic, but it could stand to have some glaring, frustrating issues fixed:
* Collision detection while jumping is spotty - if you have a white arc showing you where you're going to jump to, but a small slice of platform stops you from getting to your destination, maybe turn the arc red to let you know it's not viable?  It Is KILLER frustrating knowing you have a perfect line of sight to your target and are about to make a miracle kill with a domino effect... and then you get a "bmph" noise and you only skipped 3 inches, and then get machine-gunned in the face.
* Platform detection is also goofy - sometimes my jump-arc lets me land on a platform, sometimes not.  There doesn't seem to be a logical reason why.  Maybe mark platform surfaces during the jump-arc pause with green if they're reachable, red if not?  It sucks having to launch towards a platform you think is within easy reach, fall through... and get machinegunned in the face.
* The pause function needs to be SPOT ON - jam space, game STOPS.  This is more a puzzle game than anything else, with a series of tight and logical moves required to defeat a level.  I don't want the pause function to only work when I"m A. not moving, B. not in the air, C. not swinging from the grappling hook.  Timing the pause is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ because the game auto-pauses on a dime, but you sometimes negate that and swing face first into a machine gun.
* I would LOVE to see some kind of flowchart on your moves, to show what options are available the NEXT time you can do a thing - I know part of the fun is to jump headfirst into combat and see where it takes you, but the cheap kills are a bit too frequent if you miss a mark by a millisecond, and simply having a radius around you with icons showing what gameplay options were available would be a huge help.
* Contextual movement trees would be lovely, as well - maybe I don't WANT to jumpjumpjumpjump kill jumpjumpjump for 20 minutes before I have enough downtime to smack that dude in the eye before getting machinegunned in the face.
Don't be fooled - there are funny prompts during the game that say "This is not a stealth game - kill everything."  But if you run in guns a'blazing John McClane style, you're toast - this IS a stealth game with puzzle gameplay, more than anything else, if you want to not only succeed during the levels, but also complete all the pass/fail objectives.
I do recommend this game quite a bit, it's a lot of fun and even with the INCREDIBLY FRUSTRATING cheap kills, I find myself coming back - and for someone with a HumbleHoarded Steam gamelist of 500+, that's saying something.  It's tight, mostly responsive, has a great theme and feel and succeeds as a hybrid action/stealth/puzzle game.

A tentative "yes" recommendation for Ronin, in that the princible of the game feels so fresh and exciting that I can forgive the rest of its negatives.
Yeah, the jump arcs aren't accurate, yes there are some really madenning bugs, yes the final level in insanely frustrating, no there aren't enough skills, no there's no real story other than a lazy attempt at a Kill Bill revenge plot with a few words and a single photo.
So why then do I like the game? Firstly, I love turned based games. This feels like an X-Com platformer, and by God that's a beautiful mix. I really wish this was a new genre, because turn-based action feels like a massively untapped market (if you're excluding troop command war and building games from the list). Some of the skills blend so well together, such as rope swinging, throwing your sword, jumping up onto a wall and leaving behind a decoy, and then recalling your sword and watching as it ricochets into two different guards who are shooting at the hologram you dropped. That♥♥♥♥♥♥is beautiful, man.
If they'd worked on adding a story, fixing a few frustrating glitches and oversights, and added a few more skills, this would have been a classic indie game. Doesn't deserve quite as much of the harsh reviews as it's been getting, but it's also not worth £10.

Ah yes, the one that started it all. Batman: Arkham Asylum. Or as I like to call it, Batman: Begins. Begins to actually make good Batman games that is! Man, I remeber playing Batman on the SNES and whoo boy, that a pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥ I mean, it was pretty damn bad. You didn't know what to do half the ♥♥♥♥ing time and the graphics looked liked somone was trying to make an homage to the earlier Mortal Kombat games(I thought they were better to be honest). So granted, my first experience with a batman game with 2-D fighting controls was a bummer. Lo and behold though, it would be years later when the DC franchise would pull itself up by the bootstraps and finally implement a fighting scheme that would not only complement the amount of enemies on screen, but also give inspiration to other games later as well. Not saying it's wholly original, nothing ever is, but it did refine it and give it nice shoe polish. Punching feels good and your attacks have impact. You actually FEEL like a super-duper detective in a skin tight suit(Schumacher fans will be disappointed), enacting your hero fantasies of yore. I never really thought stealth could be done in a batman game, but Rocksteady has proven me wrong. Takedowns from the highest perches to the lowlyest floor grate always feel smooth and satisfying. Snipers feel a bit cheap though, even when you're busy doing doing full nelsons to avoid enemy fire, or when you unexpectantly got shot from the back because you didn't see somone line up a perfectly placed shot in the guard tower adjacent to you. In short, it's a short game; took my only about 7-8 hours to beat, but well worth the experience. If you enjoyed Kevin Conroy in the 90's Batman animated show, bleed your fan-boy heart out.

This game runs smoothly on most PCs, which is nice and helpful. So, the gameplay, like I said, is your destroying cubes like crazy. The game mechanics are simple, yet they can easily get complex. Also, like most Clicker games, this game gets you money even when you aren't in the game. That's a really nice feature for a Clicker game to have.
Anyways, as you get further into the game, it gets even more satisfying knowing that your DPS (Damage per second) is high enougn to destroy EVERY CUBE.  You upgrade your weapons to get high DPS and you learn Active Abilities, which are very helpful abilities (Duh) and really make your pistol and other weapons very powerful.
Like Clicker Hereos, you progress by waves. I feel that that is a great way to gain levels without feeling overwhelmed when you suddonly are screwed. I appreciate how hard it is to create a card game with new rules. Well, there are books around here with rules for hundreds of Solitaire game and 2-player games made with regular cards, so you can always get inspiration from those, I guess. This one game uses a custom deck with many more suits, each being associated with a power-up.
The hardest part is balancing it out, I guess. DMD doesn't do it with flying colors, though. You can only unlock tournaments one at a time. If you really suck at a particular set of rules, you're screwed, you just can't finish the game. I'm only halfway through it and with about 12 hours of playtime, I'm guessing there's at least 25 to 30 hours of time to play. It's all very artificial, though... After a while, new tournaments are just variations on the previous ones, with harder AI, etc.
My biggest issue with the game is the complete lack of a story. There are characters; tournaments all have a title that supposedly draws from pirate lore. Great. But no one has anything to say, you just play against them and I guess you have to make up your own story.
The soundtrack is very limited, too. There's a quasi rip-off of the Pirates of the Caribbean score used in the main menu (at least it's longer than the very similarly PotC-themed single track from Clicker Heroes), and a more ambient song used during games. Overall, it looks like most of the development time was spent on refining the game rules. To each their own.
I'll also note that some of the special rules are self-contradictory, and as such the AI appears to be cheating, when it's just not applying the rules properly. I don't know what to say about that. This game is getting old, I doubt it'll ever be fixed.
If you're into hard casual games, walk the plank and give this one a try. It's well worth its price on sale. Maybe even at full price. I don't know, I'm not used to buying games full price any more... I'm so scared they'll get bundled the following week for a buck. Yes, it has happened before, and it will happen again™.
EDIT: I finished the game after 25 hours. In line with the last of story, there is absolutely no ending. No even a congratulations message for finishing all 60 (?) tournaments. Gosh, I wish it weren't so addictive... At least, now I can move on. Game isn't too hard because it relies so much on luck, and getting XP on losses means you'll eventually unlock everything, including unbeatable combos like Misfire/Parry or Plunderer/Davy Jones' Locker, etc. The fun comes in trying to find the right combo for each duel. Unfortunately, after the first half, all of your adversaries start using the same usual combos, so there's nothing new to see beyond the first dozen of hours. Still, well worth its price.
