Ring Runner: Flight of the Sages blew me away.
it  had looked interesting for a long time, as if the gameplay would be different and something i could really enjoy.
after trying it, boy was i right. but i got a LOT more than i bargained for, from an Indie Developer i've never heard of, and the pretty bargain bin price.
this game, has downright absurd depth and attention to detail.
the gameplay is very skill based, controlling your ship takes practice and mastering of Inertial forces.
Gameplay is not just point and click, you will be required to think your actions out to control your ship well and survive. Controls are numerous and will take some getting used to, but i find are very rewarding to invest the effort to do so.
the Story... doesn't suck. i know, that's weird, a Video Game with a story that isn't garbage.
to build on this story you get from the Campaign, there is ample flavor text on just about everything - which ties into the story.
and boy, the customization and variety. as you play through the Campaign, you are given the opportunity to try out many ships and get a feel for them. eventually though, you're given free Hangar customization freedom. i was already loving the game before that, and as soon as i saw the Hangar, and all of the customization available.... just wow.
browsing the customization, i was instantly overwhelmed with buckets of unique parts and ships. there's a playstyle for everyone. hell, there's probably 20 playstyles for everyone, because there's just so many different ways to play.
an enourmous plethora of Weapons, special Abilities, Ship classes and Hulls in each class to choose from. every single Weapon, Ability and Hull does a spectacular job of standing out from the rest, and being unique. no cookie cutter content here.
Ring Runner will also run on just about anything, while still looking very nice and can be an enjoyable visual experience for both low end and high end users.
the Options allow for wide customization of Video, Audio, Controls, as well as Gameplay related features and settings. if you're a power user, you will not feel left out if you prefer things a certain way.
playing Ring Runner, i can feel as if i'm in a living Universe. Characters have personality, and the backstory of this Universe is more than sufficient for your mind to build the world around you.
the only complaints i could possibly have, are all very minor. the Menu UI could be built a little better, and the game HUD could be easier to see against the background of the game. a couple of the colors blend in with the background of the game a little too well, and can therefore be hard to read.
all in all, i am blown away by this little gem i've found. Ring Runner doesn't deserve the meager existence it has, this is a much, much better game than it appears to be. it is a shame that Ring Runner is not well known of, as this game should be much more popular than it is.
a very well presented product, Triple B Titles has a very well put together game here. the name Triple B doesn't even do justice, this is a higher quality game than that.
Ring Runner is now one of my favorite Space Games.
if i was forced to rate Ring Runner, i would rate no lower than 90.0/100.

A time killer, just realize there is NOTHING random about the cards. At one point you will play numbers instead of suits. You will notice that you are pulling 3 card doubles about 80% of the time. Let's see, 2 cards drawing a third, 7 numbers total. That's 2 cards of 7 that will cause a double and 5 cards that won't. Does it seem like you are playing those odds. Now add the 2 card doubles. This game also has tension builders that are not needed. You have to rush your discard pick because it moves right away. The computer's is figured before the graphics even shows but the screen pauses and slowly scolls like it is choosing at a relaxed pace. Creating what seems to be an unfair illusion because the computer does not need that relaxed pace. Now the "Busted" graphic does get old but it is also creating tension. First, you are being told repeatedly that you have failed. Next, clicking the mouse should remove it and the cards, starting the next hand. It doesn't work, you have to press the mouse a second time to remove the cards. Thus you try to match the timing of the double click or wait for "busted" to disappear on it's own. As that tension builds you are now button mashing thinking that will speed it up. One click should finish the process but they want that tension there. It helps the AI appear to be a tougher opponent. Actually the AI follows a pretty basic set of commands. In the end the Devs ruined the game by adding these things so I cannot recommend it.

Being a big fan of the JRPG since the SNES and having loved Skyborn, I had to play this game. When it first begins you're pressented with a beautiful wedding being used to unite two waring nations to gain peace. Not unlike anything we've seen before. Then, the bride, who happens to be the Princess of one of the nations gets kidnapped. Oh no, not the concept this again. But that's okay; our young dashing hero Lucian is on the chase. Though when we meet Lucian, he has the look of a hero, but early on we see emotional depth. He's to some degree socially awakward, which is something you wouldn't expect from a guy like him. It's espeically funny when he tries to hide it behind his bravdo but the next unlikely companion see's right though it.
This would be Ingrid; built from the same mold as the main herione Claret from Skyborn. She has has the wit, street smarts and pragmatism to see her job though. What was great about her is that she can seem like she's presented in a light that would seem tomboyish but I didn't feel like she was a one note character. In the brief time that I've known her, she's shown a great gift for ingeunity and engineering. I don't know how rare it is for a character to build an airship from the ground up form scraps but she did.
Lastly Soha, who should be more aptly named as a "Warrior Princess". Turns out this girl needs no saving. While some might think she has questionable attire choices, she makes up for it by using a combination of sharp wit, mind control and swordplay to mow down her foes.
After completing the first mission, I felt like I wanted to know these characters more. I wanted to see how they dealt with the hard times as well as the good times. Match that with a very enguaging battle system and a world where swords and guns still intersect in battle, I think this ride will be one to enjoy.
Check it out, you won't be sad you did.

Just completed the campaign and must say this is a very well done game, solid 5/5 as my complains are trivial compared to the quality of everything else.
It does take a bit of investment to get into as the ships have A LOT of controls which is just plain confusing and disorienting until you get the hang of it, but the depth when you do is impressive.
The story is also surprisingly deep and well thought out (and long in a good way).  The maps in each segment of the game are quite small with not a lot to do besides fight (you could say it is designed around pure tactics with no strategy) but that aspect is so well done that I wasn't bothered by it.
A complaint I do have is that restarting when dying in the campaign is often annoying because it sends you through the dialogue each time.  There is an option to skip the dialogue, but it only skips a section, if there are multiple (with camera animations between), you have to wait until the next pops up to skip it, so it can take many seconds to retry (which might not sound like much but when you are on a difficult mission with lots of dying, it is quite frustrating).  On top of that, the loading of each mission is quite slow, and something as simple as returning to the hanger to switch ships for trying another approach requires waiting for the loading again despite your ship being the only thing that changed.
I also experienced frustration many times with the turret deployables that cause friction as well as those that grab hold of your ship.  These can cause you to get "stuck" in the middle of a huge swarm of opponents, putting you at nearly hopeless odds with very little you can do, so I think the presence of these "weapons" does more to detract than enhance the game, though with enough experience you would probably learn whatever subtle tricks are needed to avoid them.
Overall, though, very high quality, very well thought out, lots of depth, and plenty of fun to play, certainly a gem to have found.
I haven't played multiplayer but I would imagine it would work very well with the design of this game.

Echoes of Aetheria follows the standard RPG tropes, but that's not entirely a bad thing. It was great to play a game that hearkened back to the snes era of RPGs, but still stands strong as its own new age title. Even though it was created in an rpg maker engine, it's battle system makes it unique and addicting with some impressive sprite work. Battles are active and by using your array of skills you can control the flow of battle and make sure your party comes out on top.
The difficulty level starts out easy, but then battles get tougher with more confusing dungeons near the end, but it's all appropriate as the game helps ease your way into learning how to play and you can also choose your difficulty before each dungeon so you can play at whatever level you're comfortable.
I personally enjoyed the crafting system, using the materials I worked hard to find in dungeons to make "legendary" status equipment. You can choose a blueprint of a weapon or armor, but it can be customized and crafted into a large array of options that fits to your playstyle. Higher magic damage, defense, or physical attack? It's up to you to decide which of your characters needs what.
I loved getting to play this title. Echoes of Aetheria is a solid entry in the rpg genre.

Unfortunately this sequel does not meet the bar set by its predecessor, Deus Ex: Human Revolution. The biggest issue for me is the story. Human Revolution had a great plot with interesting characters. The overall themes of a world adapting to a technological renaissance are far more interesting than the “augmented apartheid” presented in Mankind Divided. You’ll also notice the pacing in the sequel to be far off from what is expected. HR had interesting developments and plot twists throughout and an ending that felt like a good payoff.  MD will have you chasing multiple story lines that don’t seem to connect or have a large impact on Jensen’s goals/motivations. The ending also comes far too soon and makes you feel like they either shipped the game without its proper, planned ending or that they were going for a stunt cliffhanger ending to lead into the third game, which never plays well in the video game medium. All that said, I still recommend the game to fans of the series. It’s fun to continue your adventure as Jensen and I love having another modern immersive sim to play. If you are new to the series, start with Human Revolution.

If you're looking for a casual arcade, 10 minutes to waste and unique game controls SPINGUN is a fun indie game.  Once you get use to the control mechanic you'll have a blast.  There are plenty of powerups and health drops to keep you going and to shoot down advancing baddies.  There is a few modes which includes practice, endless, zones and boss rush.  You are limited in a small arena which makes the game more challenging and maneuvering and shooting with your ship takes skills.
For the price it is well worth your time if you're into shooters.

SPINGUN is a retro style arcade game where you must survive by avoiding, and destroying various different enemies in a small enclosed "arena" environment. This may sound easy, and perhaps even a bit cliche except for one important feature; there are only two buttons to control your ship.
At first SPINGUN may look like just another retro arcade shooter in an over saturated genre of cheap indie games, but it offers up three things a lot of the others in said genre don't; a unique control scheme, a surprising amount of customization/content and it's actually fun!
The controls might seem simple, but it's really quite hard to master. You can use either A/D or < / > arrow keys to boost and turn the ship simultaneously or press both at the same time to fire your gun. You can't turn without propelling yourself in the direction you push which makes for some interesting flight mechanics in such a simple game; so if you want to go up, you must alternative Left and Right quickly. Whenever you aren't propelling yourself you slowly fall back towards the bottom of the screen. This all takes a bit of getting used to, especially when you have to both kill enemies, and dodge them and their projectiles!
There are five different game modes in SPINGUN; Practice, Endless, Zones, Boss and Ballpit. Practice is just that, a practive mode where bullseye style targets randomly spawn and give you a chance to practice flying and try out some of the many different weapons/powerups in the game. Endless is the traditional survival mode coming in both classic and hardcore (hardcore spawns more enemies, and has you playing with just one health bar and no health pick-ups). You have to survive as long as you can against lots of different enemies, some that chase you, others lunge at you, some shoot, etc., all the while health and weapon pick-ups appear to help you out. Zones are challenges that each consist of 5 waves where you have to progress and survive using a specific weapon for each zone. Boss has three different challenes where you face three very difficult and unique bosses. Lastly, ballpit is a fun mode where you spawn in an area full of "balls" that break into smaller ones as you shoot them, your task being to destroy them all as quickly as you can.
Along with having a good variety of enemies, there's a good selection of weapon power-ups including a flame-thrower, homing weapon, spreader and a few others. One of the other interesting features of the game I like, is being able to boost your total health. If you have max health, for example 4 bars of health, and you get a health kit, it then gives you a 5th one that is empty which you can then fill with another pick up. It allows you to grow your health bar and have longer surival times when you build it up.
SPINGUN also has a surprising amount of customization considering what the game is and consists of. There are 50 different ships you can pick from (all of which are only visual changes), many which have to be unlocked by suriving a certain amount of time, or reaching other milestones. You can also change your weapon colour from a slider so you 100% control over what colour weapons you want to use. Lastly, you can select from 15 different boost visuals,  which is the colour of the flame that projects from your ship when you fly. I was quite surprised to see all of this added in to a game like this, customization is always welcomed as far as I'm concerned regardless of game and genre.
All in all SPINGUN is a really fun game for cheap. There's a lot of content for such a simple seeming game and I'm glad I picked it up on the release sale, and would gladly pay full price.

An exercise in repetition and tedium, Prince of Persia ignores the properties of risk and reward in favor of battle mechanics that amount to button mashing and canceling out whatever color of defense the enemy has up with no fear of death. I got Prince of Persia 4 (the 2008 'reboot') in a pack with the other PoP games for $10. It seems safe to say I've got my monies worth. Although this one lacks the sheer "wow factor" that the first PoP had upon its release, the 2008 reboot does ambiously innovate in its own ways. There are gameplay mechanics that will frustrate, even irritate you at times, and by the end of the 15 hour campaign it begins to border on repetitive--but other aspects of the game really stand out. Amongst these are the unique water-colour graphics, the incredible sound-track (one of the best I've ever heard), the excellent voice-acting, and an exceptional ending; probably in my personal 10 best of all time. I don't want to give anything away, but it had me thinking, and that's something few games accomplish these days. It's not the best game I've played in the last year, but it does some things better than most, and it is one of the most ambitious and unique, something that I respect in an increasingly saturated "appeal to the lowest common denominator" market. Thank you Ubisoft Montreal (makers of  Assassin's Creed) for taking that chance. The gaming industry needs developers to take more chances on games like this, even if they aren't a complete success in every regard. If you get the chance, pick it up. You'll be supporting creativity, and treating yourself to a pretty excellent game too. 8.2/10.

PROS:
-Despite being free, the only things that cost real money are cosmetics

CONS:
-Rewards you for spamming (At an MEH level, you have to be OK or GOOD to avoid and counter spammers)
-Super passive agressive gameplay, I find myself spending almost a minute to get 1 hit on someone because of their dodging. (games are 8 minutes long max) In game you can use shift to dodge any attack, and this can be reset by hitting the ground. Unfortunately, this can cause up to 7 minute games, especially on some maps
-Not a variety of weapons, this may be considered good or bad but there is 10 different weapons in the game. (Katans, Axe, Canon, Hammer, Gauntlets, Sythe, Spear, Blasters, Bow, Sword) Every character can switch 2 depending on their weapons they have. This can cause not a lot of variety, besides a special move that they have with each weapon, which is called a "signature" move.
-Bad maps for beginners. The "down" button is a huge part of this game as it lets you do tons of attacks that you need for comboes. However, it also lets you go down on platforms. Some maps, have these platforms taking up most of the map, so if you click down to combo, (along with the attack button) you will fall through UNLESS you do it in this small pocket of time. This is very difficult and leads to most beginners' deaths.
Overall, I do recommend this game. However, it is very difficult to get into and can be extremely boring and hard sometimes. I really do hope they do something about how passive agressive and long the gameplay CAN take, and add more of a chance to punish spammers.

If you've never played a Far Cry game, Blood Dragon is a fabulous place to start.
Far Cry as its core is an Open World 1st Person Shooter. You start in one corner of the map, and have to proceed to different areas to either advance the story, or unlock side missions that allow your character to become stronger. It's a formula that while initial successful has started to grow stale.
Blood Dragon is short as far as Far Cry games go, but this is not a knock on its quality. It's the perfect length for someone wondering what it's all about, and the price can't be beat. If you like the GAMEPLAY, then this should be seen as a spring board to other Far Cry Games.
What makes Blood Dragon unique is it's utterly bizarre and totally self aware. It mocks everything but most notably cheesy 80s action movies, SNES era cut scenes, and, yes, even Far Cry itself. There are bad one liners, action hero tropes, and memes galore throughout the game. If you've ever seen the Indie movie "Kung Fury" this is thematically identical, only in video game format.
So in summary: Never played Far Cry before and want to try? This is a good start. Love 80s action movies? Welcome aboard.

It's astonishing to see Rockstar & Take Two get away with such a heavy microtransaction-based system. If you fall into their trap, you would only be supporting their shady behavior to expand in the next installments.
It's not like this is a cooperative online game, either. No. There is hardly any collaboration between strangers. All everyone does is mindlessly kill and bully each other on free-roam mode. Missions are not great either. Granted, the gameplay feels awesome. But the implementation of a leaderboard system in which only the winner gets the spotlight ruins the feeling of accomplishment if you don't finish on the front. Oh and let's not forget about the half of your time that was spent on the loading screen.
I rarely feel like I made a mistake by purchasing a game. But I wish I was able to refund this one.

After putting in almost 200 hours into this game, my impression has sunk into a new low. At first, it was a great game to kill time whenever you had it and a chance to build your charatcer in more ways than just mindless combat. From being a melee tank to a greedy merchant, you pretty much can do what you like in this open world type game and develop the skills you like on a day to day purpose. In other words, you make the story of your adventure.
Now the controls aren't the best in the world, being that the same button to melee is the same button to also interact (causing many issues when you need to access a door or a chest). Also, the npcs move quite a bit to the point where you need to play cat and mouse to interact with them. There's also no targeting monsters in this game, but you can target players for the purposes of pvp (which I think this is where the game is heading towards.). That's not all to the controls of course, but I believe those two points make it quite clear that there needs to be some thought put in if this game hopes to make it past early access and towards open beta.
Graphics wise I like the simplicity this game has because it feels like a game, and not a grueling chore or obligation. Unique animations with spells and unique monsters which leaves room to think back into the past when you played your first mmo. Also the soundtrack of this game are borrowed melodies from other games, but again adds to the nostalgia factor.
As for the community, there couldn't be a better one. Quite a dynamic and helpful community that welcomes all kinds of players, and makes you feel right at home. Admins are quite vigilant and will assist you in more ways than one. Surely there are some sore spots, but usually comes to a halt when it comes to helping a new player or someone asking a question.
Finally, the gameplay of his game is again (and sorry for repeating this word constantly) nostalgic. You fight enemies, level your combat accordingly, and proceed to the next step. Skills like mining or gathering as of a similar fashion, requiring lots of patience in order to make the gold necessary for purchasing spells or armor.
Now you maybe asking, why I feel a new low with this game after all the praise? Well, it comes to the instability of where the game stand. Gold wipes have been happening quite often, and lots of disconnecting issues and running the game. There seems to be a lot more bugs than what the devs and admin are overseeing, and with the current higher leveled players demanding for content they neglect to see the bigger picture. Sure everyone wants new content and want access to new maps and features, but those players make up the minority of what is to come with the influx of new players coming in. The principle of the matter is making the server stable enough to where the servers are running at a constant pace, and the need for maintenance is limited to at least once a week. Constant changing, wiping and having the server down can bring lack of trust to players, and the competency of the admins who run this game. Also, the controls need tweaking big time and mods need to moderate come of the potential issues that the community can fester up through frustration and inpatience, and the assistance of new players to catch up. Only then will the game grow and improve with a wider range of support and ideas.
Other than that, this game on my end receives a 7/10. Not quite there yet, but I am hoping and I do recommend this game despite the negatives I have pointed out.
.P.S. For the love of Orake, stop encouraging people to use discord and adding features through that venue. Instead, implement a mail system so the players can reach out to you efficiently, giving you the time to view them at your pace.

Think of this game less of a VN and more of a quick puzzle game with some VN elements and excellent voice acting. The story, while short, did pique my interest long enough for me to clear the whole game (which takes around an hour or less). It also provides some decent backstory for its sequel, Unhack 2. It's nothing deep, however.
Gameplay is basically sliding block puzzles. You move across a maze of sorts with WASD and try to get the other side, sometimes while avoiding lasers and killing enemies through use of timed shots. The game isn't hard at all, and Easy mode even gives you infinite lives. It does get a little stale though, and I would've liked to see more intricate hazards.
There's no saving feature. That said, you're allowed to choose which "episode" you want to play at the title screen, so the saving isn't really needed (each episode lasts around 5-10 minutes depending on how fast you clear). I would've liked an indicator of what episode I was currently playing, but it's not that hard to quit and choose a different one if you select wrong.
The voice acting is superb. Probably the biggest name here is Xanthe Huynh of K-On, SAO, Persona 5 fame. That's not to say that the other actresses didn't do good jobs. Aimee Smith, Skylar Davenport, Rachael Messer, and Xanthe all performed wonderfully at bringing the characters to life, despite how short the game is.
I really do recommend Unhack. Maybe not at the 3.99 price point for something this short and a bit rough around the edges, but at a lower price I do suggest buying this game.

OK for all those unable to run the game I have finally found a solution. Anyone who is able to run the game must already have the Micros*ft C Runtime Library installed and have the needed .dll files already on their system.
To fix the game without downloading the whole runtime library; Google for and download msvcp120.dll and msvcr120.dll. Place these two files into the root directory of the game C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\Geared and you should be good to go. No compatibility mode or running as admin needed.

My main complaint is, that with only 30 puzzles (and half of them only being tutorials which explain/introduce game mechanics in my opinion) the game  is very short and not very complex. Most of the puzzles can be completed without thinking by randomly dropping the wheels in various places until everything starts moving.
The game mechanics are very limited. There are four types of gears:
The levels also contain varying amounts of green pegs, which prevent your white gears from falling through. A few of the later levels also include glass "walled" areas where direct placement of gears is not possible (but gears can fall into and through those areas if placed outside and moved there by other gears/gravity).
The only puzzle that I spent more than 2 minutes on was the last one, which actually did require some thinking and planning to complete. All others were simply too easy.
Beyond that, there are many other things to criticize:
Ultimately this just feels like a test application for a simple physic engine, not a game. And the physics aren't that great to begin with, as the gears tend to jerk around and even have their teeth move through each other, when you create a lock-down situation which forces two interlocked gears to rotate against each other instead of with each other.
This "game" is, in my opinion, just a very simple tech demo. Which was very disappointing, because the game mechanics could be vastly expanded upon with (what should be) little effort:
It really isn't hard to think about ways that could make the simple "place cogs to cause motion" game mechanic a lot more engaging and allow for more complex and difficult challenges. But until then:
If you like challenging puzzle games, search elsewhere.

An interesting and fun, if flawed, semi-roguelike. There's a variety of different offensive spells you can equip yourself with and a decent difference in how different character races (effectively classes) play, very pretty environments to explore and music, and most importantly the core gameplay (fighting monsters and exploring) is very fun. But it is flawed, mostly in that they had a lot of half-baked ideas they didn't implement properly. Virtually everything to do with the town, townsfolk and constructing buildings is a pointless mess that should have been cut from the game. One or two of the random modifiers on spells can make the spell worthless. You can't switch classes until you die. And most importantly, even though you do gradually unlock new foes and the difficulty scales up as you do New Game +s, it does get repetitive after a while.
Still, while flawed, it is fun. And isn't that the part that really counts?

I recently reinstalled all my ARCEN games, and wanted to make a review of AVWW1,because yes, while it is mostly a 2D sidescrolling game (most reviews will tell you it is), to understand the game completely requires a different mindset.
A Valley without Wind 1, is a Real Time strategy game where your character is both the worker and the only unit you have.
There it is. That's what makes the game special.
You have to balance exactly three things perfectly in order to win against the overlord and go to the next continent. Do I have enough resources? Are my spells high level enough? Have I pushed the wind far back enough? These questions entangle themselves beautifully in the actions you are going to make and the choices you can make for grand strategy purposes. Gathering resources requires exploration, and completing missions. Doing this requires the appropriate spells, having the right buildings on the map, pushing the wind back so you can build more and explore even moreso.
And so on.
The main complaint to have about the game is that, to really be two feet into how it works, and have a bit of challenge, you need to beat the first continent, which is about 10 hours of play. Though you can start the game, when creating a new world, to the second continent, which is greatly appreciated.
Everything is procedurally generated, the exploration is nice, there is a bit of a melancholic feel to the game that I appreciate as it makes it more a relaxing experience than anything. The graphics are not top of the line, but are quite pleasing, and ARCEN games are not about graphics in the first place, more like niche gameplay mechanics you cannot find elsewhere. The replayability is literally endless.

I've been playing Dancing Dragon's RPG's since Deadly Sin 2, and let me just say that with each major game entry this developer just keeps getting better and better. If you want to play classic, old-school RPG's that don't feel like "knock-offs" but real, traditional, successors to the greats like Final Fantasy IV and Suikoden II, then I highly suggest you look into this developer, and more specifically, this game right here... Echoes of Aetheria.
Here's a video review that's more your speed:

The full (German) review can be found
I had no real interest in playing Echoes of Aetheria, as most of it looked like standard rpg-maker fare. The battle system was the only thing that stood out, but that can't save a game that is otherwise lacking. So why did I play it anyway? Because someone sent me a key even though I didn't ask!
And what can I say? The game is solid. Neither mediocre nor particularly memorable. Perhaps better than Skyborn, which I never finished, but still not as good as some of my favorite rpg-maker titles.
The encounters are where the game truly shines. It uses an active time battle system where some skills can be used instantaneously while others need to be prepared. Some consume no resources, others drain the user's blood, and then there are those that demand a certain amount of TP. Those can be gained throughout the battle or through equipping certain items. The higher the cost, the more powerful the skill. They also employ a cooldown system, so you can't just spam them.
Another thing you need to pay attention to are formations. They can protect your characters from harm (by someone in the front taking the brunt of all damage), but the same applies to enemies. So you need to take care of the front if you want to strike those at the back. Unless you use ranged attacks, magic, or skills with a certain are of effect.
Problem is: the battles are too easy (especially since most skills are available before half the game is even over). Playing on normal provides absolutely no challenge until 10+ hours in, and that's after skipping hordes of enemies. So you might want to play on hard while ignoring easy from the get go. It can be changed every chapter, so you're never locked in. But there's one thing you may hate: the party is healed after every encounter and you can save whenever you want. Only two areas are different, but those aren't a problem if you make a beeline for the boss.
I personally didn't mind, as something else was more annoying: the crafting system. It's nice in theory, as you can combine lots of different items to equip your party however you please. Thing is: you don't have a choice. Most equipment that can be bought is already out of date. So you have to craft every single piece, all while making sure not to go over capacity (if a character wears too much, their other stats drop). Kinda tedious, if you ask me. Would have preferred a more standard system with crafting being optional.
And that's mostly it. The characters are well presented (especially if you talk to them after every chapter), the mouse controls are solid, the dungeons okay (except for the last, where most enemies can't be avoided), equipment can be improved with accessories, skills can constantly be changed to suit ones needs ... but the antagonists are boring (I remember three, two of which aren't even worth mentioning) and the story would have benefited from a more gripping presentation. Sure, it uses animations here and there, but I've seen far better games made in rpg-maker. For free no less!
So, would I recommend the game? Sure, if you dial down your expectations. It's nice enough for 13 - 14 hours (the rest of the time was spent outside the game), but it's nothing I'd remember for long.

Greetings fellow gamers! This is Gamer Guy (In a Suit) from the Echo Army YouTube channel! Today I am bringing you a review of the brand new RPG Echoes of Aetheria. Echoes of Aetheria was released today, January 15th, 2016 by Developer Dancing Dragon Games and Publisher Degica.
(NOTE: This game was reviewed using a key provided by the Developer and/or Publisher)
Video Review:
The "Too Long, Didn't Watch" Review:
Wow! Fantastic little RPG. Great feel & story! 4/5
The "Meat & Potatoes" Review:
Well, now. Heh. There are TONS of little RPG Maker games that populate the Steam store these days, and no, that is NOT a bad thing. Granted, they aren't all the best, but having options is good. I'll cover that some other time. For now, Echoes of Aetheria. Wow is this a fun game! Upon being asked to review it, I admit I was a little hesitant. It looks like some "blah" RPG Maker game, but I gave it a spin anyways. WOW. I am SO glad I did! This game has a GREAT story that hooks you in right from the beginning AND gets moving and twisting early and it does so very well. It does not feel forced or cheesy at all, it is solid writing. The gameplay mechanics are very familiar RPG-style mechanics. Nothing special. For me, it's the characters (there are several good ones!) and the story in this one that really engaged me from the get-go. Particularly Ingrid, she's a fantastic character! AI sincerely haven't been this engaged in an RPG since I used to play FFVI back on SNES. And yes, I am serious. This game and it's story are sincerely hooking me like that one did. Not as deep or as rich with supporting cast, but super-solid storytelling is here and you do not want to miss out. It's the kind of game you're thinking about while you aren't even playing, the story is that good. If you dig RPG's, make sure to give this one a try.
Happy Gaming!

Retrospectively,
is the high point of Rocksteady Studios'
trilogy. It's a tight, focused experience with a deft tonal awareness, shaping a dark, grotesque setting for a plot that hits all the 'edgy
story' notes, relying on spectacle - supplemented by some pretty top-tier action and stealth gameplay - to see it through.
Similarly to the way
itself is the pinnacle of the
series,
's third-person melee combat is quite easily the best to be found within this genre. It's fluid and functional, with solid ability variation supplemented by superb animation and sound design shaping an experience that is - at its core - quintessential to the cheesy, ridiculously one-sided combat of superhero comic books. Despite the borderline omnipotence of Batman's combat ability, the fights never became overly unchallenging, as the game introduces new enemy abilities frequently enough to keep you juggling knives, stun batons and giant experimental abominations. Regarding stealth gameplay,
utilises mechanics that necessitate a predatory approach - if you're spotted by armed enemies, you'll be dead in seconds. Creeping around in the shadows and picking off burly, shirtless men until they start to panic is great fun, but it tends to be even more one-sided than the combat. It's almost as though there's too much freedom to just hang out on a rooftop with the x-ray vision constantly turned on until a specific enemy moves far enough away from the group for you to drop down and take him out, and then rinse and repeat. The endless functions of the x-ray vision makes it almost irresponsible not to keep the thing turned on, despite the fact that it replaces pretty much all textures with various shades of dark blue. The somewhat 'Mary Sue' nature of most superheroes is probably the cause of troubles like this - people would complain if Batman didn't have tons of ultra-powerful gadgets like this. Regardless, it doesn't totally ruin the game's balance, it just tends to make a lot of encounters a touch too easy.
is pretty aesthetically brilliant. Voice performances by long-time Batman and Joker voice actors Kevin Conroy and Mark Hamill adds an air of authenticity to the dialogue, as does top-tier animation and some genuinely creepy underground sequences. While the plot is more of the same stuff you'll find in a lot of
comics (
is primarily based on Grant Morrison's 1989 comic
), it's still good stuff. Not because of the storyline itself, which is samey and tedious, but because of the amount of work put into the various villainous characters, particularly the Scarecrow, whose subplot features some pretty interesting surprises along the way. It's in the depictions of established characters that the story shines, coming close to the 'definitive versions' that the endless superhero film reboots seem to be going for.
really ramps it up towards the ending with some fancy setpieces that are actually very enjoyable. In general, the game shines as a rare example of a popular IP being adapted into a video game that actually manages to gel the elements of the
franchise with what makes video games inherently fun.

An excellent party based RPG with an uncluttered, intuitive interface, nicely rendered graphics and quality audio. The storyline is VERY strong with in depth characters and interesting side quests. For me the only real blemish is its linear progression that results in a few compulsory, overly long & in the end rather tedious quests.
It is a game I ended up with a love/hate relationship more than any other game I've played. The highs were truly excellent but there a few lows too. But all in all taking into account I've been playing video games for around 35 years DAO is probably one of my top 10 games of all time
This is a strange game in that initially there is so much to recommend this game, there then came a period around 20 hours into the game of real frustration during which I came close to abandoning the game. However, I kept playing and was duly rewarded  with one of the top 10 games I have ever played. Yes, there are some nagging issues kept irritating me during the game play but in the end they were relatively minor.
In this game you control a party of up to four characters, one of which you create at the beginning and who must always be in your party; the other characters you pick up along the way.
You have the option to render in first or third person with the game cutting into quality audio video clips for important character interactions.
The storyline is particularly strong and is one of the main selling points of the game.
Usually you have a number of options displayed in text at the end of the interaction and choose which one you want to action. Whether the choices actually make a difference to the storyline I couldn't say but they certainly made me believe that they did. The members of your party have their own personalities and will make their opinions about your choices known.
The game uses a levelling system based on experience points for character progression, the characters gaining experience points by performing tasks. As each new level is achieved a character may increase their base attributes, and increase or select new talents and skills. This is easy and straight forward to accomplish and there is enough variety without overpowering the player with choices.
The combat system is well implemented. I initially struggled to get used to only being able to see the battles from a player's perspective (as other games of this ilk I had played had allowed the player to move the view about the battlefield) but I grew to appreciate this not as a restriction but as an addition to the game play.
There is a quick access bar at the bottom of the screen where skill icons can be dragged to for use within battle. Battles can be paused at any time and character commands issued or changed.
Characters become unconcious when all their health has been taken. Death only occurs if the entire party becomes unconcious and characters that become unconcious in battle re-spawn at the end of the battle, albeit with some restrictions that can be nullified via certain spells or potions. If the party dies you can restart at the last save point.
New items acquired, quests updated and new background information are all clearly displayed as messages that can be clicked on so that the player is taken directly to the relevant entry in the inventory, quest log or journal.
This is game where, at least for me, party death was common. I found I could rarely rely on brute force to win battles. Nearly always I had to ensure I maximised as much as possible all party member abilities.
The main weakness in the game, as in any linear adventure like this, is that if you get stuck at a point then it's game over as there is often no way to get around that point. Sadly, there are a number of points like this in DAO. I find it then becomes tedious trying different "random" things to try and get passed the point. However, this was parcticularly noticable around 20 hours in and I found more familiarity with the game mechanisms seemed to resolve this.
I can definitely see myself playing through this again as a different character race/class.

Dead Man's Draw is a deceptively simple game based on both skill and luck together.  In all honesty its about 40% luck 60% skill.
The core game is based on 1v1 drawing from the same deck, once the deck is gone the player with the most points win. How do I earn points you ask? Well, let me tell you. There are 10 suits which have numbers on them 7 to 2. Each card in your hand adds to your point value. However only the highest card in each suit counts. Each suit has a specific ability once drawn which are slowly introduced and pretty easy to quickly grasp. But a few examples are the canon suit makes your opponent discard a card or the mystic suit allows you to see what card is next in the deck.
You can pull as many cards from the deck as you want each turn unless you pull 2 of the same suit, then you bust and all the cards drawn are discarded. However further into the game there are modifiers that may change this function.
There is no multi-player which is a little sad but its still very enjoyable against the AI. The game is also slightly RPGish in that you earn experience points even if you lose, though not as many. It'd be cool if it had some tech trees or something to tailor your own progression but you earn XP fast enough where that doesn't really matter. The games aren't very long either, probably 5-7 minutes if I had to guess. The XP earns you levels which at each level unlocks either a new character portrait or a character trait which is essentially an additional modifier to the core rules. Using the example from before, the mystic trait would change when the mystic card is active, it would reveal the next 3 cards in the deck rather than just 1. The other traits are similar in this fashion. Once multiple traits are unlocked you can choose from them before each match to attempt to thwart any rule changes that may make you play more defensively or cautious rather than an all out attack or risking a bust.
The game is split into tournaments, each having their own modifiers on the core game as well as each opponent within having modifiers of their own. Which leads to what is a very simple game into something that keeps you on your toes and keeps you switching tactics to progress.
A fun casual card game.  Recommended.

Batman: Arkham Asylum is a third-person action game casting you as the Dark Knight himself. The title opens with Batman racing back to Arkham, Gotham's home for the criminally insane, with the Joker in tow. Batman was able to track him down and re-apprehend the baddie. However, things are never what they seem with the Joker, so after getting the maniac back into the building - a building stocked with hundreds of the Joker's goons after a "mysterious" fire at their prison - Joker breaks free with the help of Harley Quinn, takes control of the penitentiary, and releases all the inmates.
From there, you're off on an adventure that ranks right below The Dark Knight movie in terms of awesome Batman experiences. The actual Arkham campus is a loony bin spread across multiple buildings on one massive rock. With the Joker in charge you're going to have to swing over rooms filled with gas, save doctors, rip vent covers off the walls so you can make a path around locked doors, and move as fast as Batman can to stop the Joker from releasing an army of monsters on the people of Gotham City.

...
Arkham is not tied to any specific property other than the characters than have populated the Batman universe for over 50 years. Seeking inspiration in all of the media that has come before, the game references the Christian Bale movies, the Tim Burton movies, all of the animated series and the comics themselves, weaving these details into a claustrophobic, atmospheric story.
Penned by animated series and comic creator Paul Dini, the pitfall found in Wolverine is avoided by casting voices from the animated series, namely Kevin Conroy as Batman and Mark Hamill as the Joker. As fully committed to the performances as Jackman, they create familiarity to fans of character without jeopardizing the verisimilitude of the presentation. Had Arkham been tied to Dark Knight, it may well suffer from some of the issues facing Wolverine.
The seemingly ubiquitous Unreal 3 engine makes a spectacular appearance, rendering large colorful worlds that appear open but are quite limited in scope. Once again, the decision to set AA on an island and solely within the facility grounds serves the game well, motivating the linear aspect of play.
I found it amusing that expositional scenes revealed through off camera radio transmissions are in full force in the game, as apparently that is a feature built into the engine. The animations for these sequences are identical to the ones uses in Gears.
What I found most striking in the difference between these very similar games was the presentation of the main character and their interaction with the environment through gameplay. Batman uses his familiar bag of tricks from his utility belt, resulting in a cavalcade of gadgets and upgrades. Platforming is restricted to using a grapple gun and a glide ability, referencing both the movies and the animated shows. Puzzles are integrated into a detective mode as Challenges left by the Riddler.
Combat is an integral part of the game and  Batman’s combat is a far more nuanced and cerebral experience, playing much like a real-time Bruce Lee movie. Counters are used to intercept attacks, allowing the player to chain together attacks and build up multipliers, which unleash finishing moves. Strategy must be employed and it is a far more satisfying experience.
Against the odds, junior developer Rocksteady created a tour-du-force experience in AA, while Raven managed what appeared to be impossible prior to AA’s release: create a good comic book game. Wolverine is a very entertaining game but it pales in comparison to the masterwork that is Arkham Asylum.

Excellent game and one of the best single player titles in recent times.
You can probably split the appeal of this game into two categories-
Gameplay
Story/atmosphere
Gameplay-
Combat: Addictive and great fun, easy to use but difficult to master.
Predator (Stealth): Incredible fun, you really feel like batman stealthily wiping out hapless henchmen one by one. Possibly a bit too easy when you get good at it. However they made it harder but ruined it (imo) in the later titles.
Both elements make you feel like Batman when you pull them off, which is just so damn awesome. There's not too much more to say about them, but the hours of fun they provide cannot be understated.
Story/Atmosphere-
Amazing. This is not an open world game like the later titles and from my perpective actually benefits massively from it. The story is dark and mature and the 'feel' of the game is oppressive and even scary at points, this feels much more impactful than swinging around Arkham City and randomly dropping in to beat some thugs to pulp (which is entertaining, but ultimately feels much more like GTA and the masses of other titles which emulate it). This recreation of batman is better than all the film versions, and damn, that Kevin Conroy Batman voice is perfect.
If I had to criticise, then my first target would be the bosses, especially the poor final boss which mostly seem to be copy pasted across the game in a predictable mould. Don't get me wrong, the titan fights are great. I just wish that there was more variety and more good stuff.
Overall this is a very good game, I would argue that if you are a remotely a batman fan (I wasn't) you should definitely get it. If not it applies to anyone who wants to sink some hours into an absorbing story and experience the thrill of being batman.

Okay, this is going to be a long one, so i'll start with the obvious : take what you'll read in this review with a grain of salt. It is my personal opinion on this game, and if after reading you still want the game, or think i'm a moron, or that i'm over-critical, then by all means, go ahead and buy the game. And make your own opinion on the game.
I got this game as part of the Humble Devolver Bundle of April 2016, and suffice to say that RONIN basically was the reason for me buying the bundle.
Oh boy, was I in for a world of Pain and Frustration.
Because yes, RONIN is the most Frustrating video game i've played in the 23 years I've been on this planet. Never had I ever insulted a game out loud like I did for RONIN. Never before had I wanted to punch my screen after the N-th death on the same level. But RONIN has this special quality about it that, after a few dozens of minutes with the game, you'll have forgotten you're human, and you'll be screaming at the screen like a beast each time the game tricks you.
That game made me ashamed of a behavior IT incepted in me. Shame on you, RONIN, Shame *bell rings 3 times*.
Let's start with the main loop of the game : You have to kill a bunch of people, for some reason. The helmeted character you play as has an old picture of a group of people, and he/she circles the heads of his/her targets on it. When he/she has killed one, he/she crosses the head, and circles another, until you've killed them all (Kinda).
Well... here comes the first negative point of the game. I still haven't explained what the basic gameplay principle is, and I already have something to point out : You'll never know why you go around and kill these targets. It is just never explained. But let's forgive this, a game has a right to be myterious.
At the start of the game though, you start assuming that you'll kill everyone on the picture, but only 5 heads out of 9-10 ever get circled. Why some are killed and others not, you'll never get the entire truth (though you'll get pointers on some of them). Which means that early on, the game makes you think there will be more levels than there actually is. So if you like the game, you'll be disappointed by the early end of it.
Thank god there wasn't more levels, though.
So onto the gameplay. For each target on the picture, you get several "info-gathering" levels, in which you go to buildings to which the target is linked in some way, to find out their location.
Then you get a final level where you kill the target.
New target, rinse and repeat. The rinse and repeat part is in no way a problem though. The problem come from the levels themselves.
If you've read up to here, I'm assuming you've seen images or footage of the game, so i'll be short.
The game plays in real time, but switches to turn-based when encoutering an enemy in the level, putting you in combat-mode. This mode, i'll add, feels more like a strategy game than an action game. Here's why.
In combat-mode, enemies will try to shoot you, lunge at you with katanas, or report your presence on their phone, subsequently ringing the alarm.
Not ringing the alarm is one of the optional challenges of all levels, so if - like me - you like to do everything perfectly on the first try, you WILL get frustrated really fast, because it is really hard to prevent the guards from ringing the alarm. Guards inside or outside of your view will ring it, civilians wil randomly ring it atfer seeing you, or after you broke a window in their general vicinity. And I could swear the timer on them is broken, it feels like sometimes it is not displaying the lowest alarm timer, so if you think you have 7 seconds to down a dude, well sometimes you're in for a reset because another dude has a 4 second timer on him.
Because the game is turn based, the enemy attacks are - mostly - preventable. You'll be presented with a series of red and white lines showing where the bullets will hit at the end of the turn. Your job is then to kill the guards while, at the end of each turn, not colliding with any of the lines. On the ground though, your character wil auto crouch and avoid bullets, to a certain degree (it is never actually shown when you'll avoid the bullets, but you build up a sense of when it will happen, which is actually one of the good points of the game).
The main problem with this is that the red lines represent several types of attacks, making it very confusing. Here is what a red line could represent :
- a single bullet shot at the end of a turn;
- a flurry of bullet shot all throughout the turn;
- a katana lunge.
While white lines represent a second turn of bullet flurry. It would have been easy to give all these attacks a differently colored line, but that wouldn't have been as frustrating, would it have now ?
On to the actual combat. The only way to move in combat-mode is basically the jump arc. It is a prediction of where you'll land if you aim your jump a certain way. In theory, it gives you a precise representation of the jump you're about to make. In practice though, it rarely is that precise. Here's why :
- It is quit common to try and jump down a platform to avoid incoming fire, but instead of jumping down where the arc showed you would, you just jump forward on the platform a few pixels, taking all the incoming bullets in the face.
- Sometimes you'll be close enough to an enemy to kill him, but you'll want to jump away instead, because of incoming fire. Instead of jumping properly like the ark showed you, though, you'll bash into that enemy and send him flying, resuting in a tiny jump at the end of which you're still on the path of the bullets.
- In a lot of cases it is impossible to jump up a platform from under it, which just sucks. So if you planned to do that 2-3 turns ago, well congratulations you just trapped yourself. Have fun dying.
One important thing to note about the arc, is it will show you, by turning part of itself red, when during the jump the turn will end. This is a pivotal point of the gameplay because in many cases it allows you to kill a guard with minimum risk. Ideally you'd want to jump in way that, at the end of the turn, your jump hasn't finished and has put you just over a guard, so that other guards aim at you in the air. Killing the guard under you then puts you under the bullet lines, out of harm's way.
The problem with this is that the arc is REALLY inaccurate, meaning sometimes (and this happens a lot) you'll do the method I mentionned before, expecting to float at the end of the turn, but despite the arc telling you you'll stop in the air, you finish the jump and end up on the ground anyway, usually to dye (the floor red).
Some would tell me :"Saucisse, the jump arc IS an approximation, and you have to play around that."
The developers even put a tip in game saying "The arc jump is lie". Yeah, thanks a lot.
But the matter is that the combat-mode of this game is more strategy than action, and it requires precision. And when a job requires precision, you use precision tools.
That game is like being hired to nail nails (heh), and on your first day on the job your boss gives you a hammer with a foam handle, telling you : "That'll get the job done!" Non, it won't.
I'd have a lot more to say on this game, but I  can hear you yawning. So here's a little conclusion.
There's a reason why I bought the Bundle for that game. It has potential. Heck, it was even fun at times. But ultimately the implementation of everything that made the game interesting in my eyes was just short of "good enough".
I'm okay with brutally difficult, punishing games, but when you make a game like that, make sure it's oiled well, or your games loses all fairness.
From cool turn-based action cinematic goodness to die-and-retry strategy, the promising RONIN in a nutshell...
Too bad.

Alright Unhack, we need to talk. I like puzzle games. I like visual novels too. I think we both like both of these things. So why on earth did you take the most boring tropish components of each and mashed them together? No, no, I don't hate you. You're a good kid and I know you mean well (your art is nice for what it is), but it felt like you made this game with cruise control turned on. Now I know you have a lot of dlc and a sequel, but I have never played an easier puzzler, nor gagged harder at the forced harem and the general tsudere/mary sue dynamic pressed upon the story. A forced harem, mind you, with literal digital girls who are programs who somehow can go super saiyan but are also programs but can also feel love.
I'm not faulting you for any of this. It's the easiest story to write, the easiest game to conceptualize and execute on. Even then, I think there's potential. Maybe the sequel makes better use of the genuinely charming idea that's presented here, or the dlc. All I know is that I rolled my eyes far too hard far too often playing this, and I'm not want to play it again. I do think there's a winning formula hiding somewhere in Unhack, however. Somewhere in it's DNA.

I speak condescendingly because the game itself felt like a condesension; when I hear puzzles, I hope for challenge, and when I hear Visual Novel, I cross my fingers for an engaging narrative. Neither were achieved here, instead giving us the barest minimum to achieve mediocrity. Unhack is not a bad game, nor is it a good game; it simply made me feeling nothing except a distant pang for a missed opportunity. A guilty pleasure at best for me, if that. (I love your other stuff Invert, this one just didn't click.) Pass.

This short kinetic visual novel feature an anonymous male protagonist referred to as The Unhacker. As the best unhacker of Smash Security, the Unhacker attempts to investigate the source of the 5K Worm virus infection that is spreading across cyberspace with some help from his AI companions Weedy and Miss Debug. Suspecting their immediate competitor ACME Antivirus to be behind the creation and spread of the virus for financial gain and profit, the Unhacker attempts to hack across multiple different security systems in the form of 10 arcade puzzle/action minigames which involve moving a square icon across a maze to an exit without being destroyed by various environmental hazards and uncovers a sinister past on Smash Security and The Unhacker himself before confronting the source of the 5K Worm.
Although the arcade minigames can be played at varying difficulty with infinite retries and infinite health in allies at the easiest difficulty, it would be nice if the game allows the take screenshot button on Steam to work, as well as a gallery to list and show all unlocked CGs instead of having to replay a particular chapter and its minigame to obtain the CG. Having dialogue over various parts in the arcade minigame which often automatically skip when moving across the arcade minigame quickly to avoid the environmental hazards which move in real-time draw attention away from the storyline and plot. Soundtracks and overall game presentation is good after factoring in soundtracks and voiced dialogue. Recommended when at sale or in bundle discount as it takes less than 10 hours to finish all arcade minigames and read through the entire visual novel.

The AI's however are the focal part where the Unhacker is a catalyst between the interaction of characters. It's one of those games where the you find that the AI are the one's that you sympthize with.
Speaking to the charm, this game really embraces the anime feel in an mostly (in my experience) American way. The game makes use of many emoticons (or whatever you call them these days) that lend a very light-hearted tone, even when by the end you start to think it was Nakige (Emotional story).
I'll keep it brief, as much as this game actually, and point out that this is worth the $4. I payed way less on sale and wish I could pay more to support such an awesome game that made my day. There was love given to this project and even though the gameplay feels very simple it plays more like a story game with a mini game that drives the story..
In short, If you don't like the culture of the internet, you might not like this game; if you like games that are a little self aware and act silly, you'll like this game; if you like anime and visual novels, you'll LOVE this game. If you're the latter, Buy it, Sale or no.

2-) AI is weird and for both sides. The auto switching of the player chooses the sub-optimal targets, the enemy team freezes up and doesn't move (in friendly matches) etc.

There are a few other problems but all in all the game is a fun experience for those who don't want to deal with all the buttons and technicality of soccer while playing the game.

This is a fun puzzle game. You can play it for an hour or two unutil you get bored. Casual.
However, the game has an extremely annoying mechanic. The opponent player prioritizes removing your card over everything else. For example, let's say he can play a key card and there is already a lock card on the table. So playing that key will get him loads of cards from the deck. But instead he's going to play a cannon to remove 2 points from your deck instead of gaining 15 points himself.
And this trait makes it a very very annoying game as you see over and over again in each level the same underhanded tactics being used by the opponent.
Another annoying thing is that the opponents can use advanced-level abilities and you can't. And it makes the game quite unfair. I wanted an easier casual game where I don't have to repeat the same level over and over again.
But if you can overlook both these points then everything else in the game is positive. The graphics, the puzzles, the simplicity, the variety of powers.
I still can't recommend this game because I had to keep playing thanks to my OCD else I would have quit a long time back.

I can't really think of anything this game does wrong.  Mark of the Ninja is a very enjoyable stealth platformer that incorporates pretty much everything I'd want from a stealth game.  Levels are varied enough that you don't feel like you're doing the same thing over and over, and, unlike many other games in this genre, this game doesn't force you to progress through each level at an unbearably slow pace as you wait for the exact moment to move forward.
You can "see" where enemies are both by sight and sound (their footsteps appear if they're walking).  Various actions will cause loud sounds and nearby enemies will react.  You can run so that your footsteps draw attention, or you can throw daggers at lights, walls, bells, gongs, and even enemies in order to draw attention.  Sounds are indicated by a blue circle that shows how far the sound travels. (Sound circles go away in New Game Plus if you want the extra challenge.)
Levels reward you for achieving perfect stealth kills or for not killing anyone at all.  You need to be careful if going for no kills, though, because if an enemy accidentally walks into a trap and dies, you get credit for the kill, even if you did nothing to attract the enemy to that location.  Each level also has artifacts to discover that boost your score and scrolls that both boost your score and further elaborate the story.
I particularly enjoyed the challenge levels, though I admit they do have a bit more trial and error than I would like to see.  Some of the later levels also require speed and precision in movements, which I find difficult to perform with mouse and keyboard.
The special edition includes Dosan's Tale, a fun and challenging level that occurs chronologically prior to the events of the game and explains a bit more about the tattoo ink.  The special edition also includes developer commentary spread throughout the game which can be turned off if you don't care to see it.

Now, I've had to change my review because, to their credit, the developer more-or-less fixed my initial key complaint in their biggest patch, namely in the balance of the special traits. Unfortunately, as time has gone on, other complaints have replaced this one, even if they're not QUITE enough to merit another thumbs-down. I'll detail them here so that buyers can make an informed choice. If you'd like details on how the game actually plays, the descriptions and some other reviews/threads should give you the gist.
Needless to say, the lack of multiplayer is one gaping flaw, although it should be noted that a good chunk of the player abilities would have to be disabled or revamped for this to work, since some of them do too much to cancel out others to make for consistently balanced matches. And there's no point allowing players to see each other's selections beforehand, since this would just lead to a cyclical bout of power-switching as they keep trying to counteract the other's selections. Still, doing this would make multiplayer perfectly doable.
The next complaint is that there is an incredible need for some kind of counter or image to give the player at least some idea of how many cards are currently in the discard pile, which is currently off-screen. Some players can apparently keep track of this mentally without disrupting their experience, but the rest of us often have no idea what to expect once the pile starts to get low, and when choosing whether to take from the discard pile or do something else, it would be nice to be able to tell whether there were many - or even any - cards in the pile altogether.
And the final gripe is that, as much as people dismiss the mere suggestion, I think there is some genuine unfairness in the AI's knowledge of the draw deck. I don't think it's deliberate stacking or cheating, but rather a partial failure to partition what the AI SHOULD know (i.e., nothing) from what it actually does. I base this on the sheer number and proportion of cases in which the AI will take unreasonably high risks (namely drawing when it already has four, five, or even six cards on the table and the chance of a bust is high, even though there is nothing protecting most or all of the current cards from loss in the event of a bust) only to be rewarded with exactly the right card or even succession of cards it needs to get the most out of its current hand. I understand the effects of luck, but this particular bit of grand (and situationally specific) "fortune" has played out a few too many times for me to be satisfied with that explanation. Combine this with the AI's being generally aware of what's in the discard pile (unlike the player), and there are times when what should have been a fair bout turns into an infuriating, unbroken string of losses for a perfectly completent player. Now, to be fair, the program does sometimes make less-than-efficient or even self-defeating plays thanks to other holes in the programming, and luck does indeed play its role in all cases, so this doesn't really break the game. But it sure makes for a less enjoyable experience than it might have been.
Still, for a cheap, renewable diversion, you could do worse.

Dead Man's Draw is a slick and polished head-to-head card game, played against an AI opponent. The rule-set is initially very simple, with more rules and features introduced as the player progresses, providing a smooth introduction to the finer points of playing the game.
As with many card games, luck plays an enormous factor in your success or failure, but there is also a significant degree of skill that can be applied to influence the outcome of a game.
A single round of the game takes only a minute or two, meaning that this is an excellent "filler game" for when you only have 5 minutes to play something quickly. That said, there's a reasonably long campaign-style progression, which continually offers new opponents with various abilities and tweaks to the rules to keep things interesting over many hours of gameplay, and it's easy to get sucked into "one more round".
Overall, it's a splendid little game.

Let me start by saying that not only is this game free, but there are NO MICROTRANSACTIONS!
I have lost a lot of hours to these free clicker games.  It started with AdVenture Capitalist and then Clicker Heroes.  Time Clickers is my favorite by far out of these.  All the other clickers seem to just want you to check in and play them for a few minutes and then leave them alone.  With TC I actually want to stay in the game and play it.
The biggest difference with this game is the fact that you're not just clicking on things to kill them, you have a gun that shoots cubes to destroy them.  Different colored cubes have different ammounts of health.  You get to hire more shooters and upgrade them as well as yourself.  There are is a mini boss every 5 levels and a main boss every 10.  After defeating any type of boss the game will activate any special abilities you have unlocked for free and let you used them for 30 seconds.  Every 100 levels you get Time Cubes.  These are the main objective, you use them to permanently increase stats that persist over the course of your game after your resets.  Even after you spend them, you still get a 10% DPS bonus for each cube.
I think they thing I love most is that the enemies are built out of cubes.  You can see from watching the video how everything looks, you shoot the enemy and slowly chip away at it.  I can't begin to tell you how satistying this is, it's what keeps me in the game and actually playing it.  I really feel like they want you to play and have fun, not just mess with the game for awhile and then let it idle or only check it a few times a day.
I did my first reset after only a few hours of playing, with most other clicker games, this may take DAYS.  If I stayed in the game, I think I could probably do it this time in 30 minutes or so.  If you're a fan of these games at all, and you want to feel like you're not wasting your life clicking your way to carpel tunnel, then play Time Clickers.

A Valley Without Wind is definitely not a game for everyone, but it's a game everyone should probably try.
In the tutorial, you might notice that the game tries to discourage you from over-exploring. It mocks you a little bit for going into caves without much in them and suggests that you made a mistake going in them.
If you're like me, this isn't going to stop you either way, but there is a good reason for why the game does this and I will elaborate on why.
I started playing this game again the other day after a 3 year break. I did the tutorial, messed around in my settlement and decided to go and do my very first mission. There was a grid square with a mission very close by on the world map so that's where I headed.
The area where the mission start was located had a cave connected to it which I decided to check out, on the off chance that I could nab some resources before doing the mission. This cave ended up being massive, and I went into every. Single. Room. The game gives you a rough idea on what kinds of things you can find in each room by simply hovering over the dungeon map but I didn't care, I thought I'd explore the cave and move on.
Here's the kicker, this cave had 3 sub-dungeons in it. All of them put together made up about the same room space as the entirety of the cave itself. Furthermore, at the lowest point of the cave was a passage into a LOWER cave, which housed higher level enemies.
I wasn't too sure about going lower but I did it anyway. This cave was about half the size of the previous one, but it ALSO  housed another lower passage. The lower passage seemed smaller still, but at this point Level 3 enemies were far from merciful to me and I decided to back out. Not without noticing however, that there was another passage to a lower cave that I could take. This doesn't account of course for any sub-dungeons that could exist in the Level 3/4 cave, since I didn't explore that far.
In total, my venture in this cave and its sub dungeons took almost two hours. Once I finally scrambled my way out of it, I started the mission. That took just 4 minutes.
I like this game.

Despite loving the Sands trilogy, I always felt like I was following a very specific, very controlled path, which had only one way of completion. Even so, it was all very fun, most of the time.
Prince of Persia takes that kind of platforming to the extreme. It's much more streamlined, but still very enjoyable most of the time, thanks to good (not perfect) controls, stellar animations and beautiful levels (and graphics in general, really).
The combat system has cinematic confrontations in mind first and foremost, and allows only for one on one combat. At times it is fun, at times it is frustrating and sometimes it's simply there.
The Prince is Nathan Drake this time around, but that's not really a bad thing, considering that particular character archetype is easily enjoyable. Also, you will appreciate the relationship him and Elika develop throughout the game (if you're the kind of person to appreciate that stuff, anyway).
As for the story, or rather, the ending, my interpretation is that how it ends is up to the player, so keep that in mind.
Overall, good game.

Update: 2014-12-26 0823 AM
Galactic Arms Race is another game attempting to be an ARPG shooter. Space pirates and zombies is also highly recommended for having an arpg/shooter set of elements and an infinitely better control system.
I didn't hate this game, far from it, it just deeply disappointed me expressly because of how much I liked what was there. The story is truly excellent, the dialog text is magnificent, the music is awesome, and the graphics are unique and understated in a very stylish and pleasant way.
But trying to appease players that would honestly be happier shooting each other in COD for 17 hours a day is a gargantuan strategic mistake if you assume anything other than profit is the objective.
This game has a deliciously unique futuristic melancholy feel that would be astoundingly well suited to a real ARPG. But given the rigidity, this game effectively is more fighting game and APM trainer than ARPG.
"Do you recommend this game?" is a hard question. Ultimately I say no because I would rather not encourage gaming to evolve in this direction because you can't please the try hards and casual gamers at the same time and were it up to them ALL games would cater to them, which means freedom itself becomes undervalued and synonymous with "cheap" or "lazy."
I feel morally obligated to oppose this trend, so I must answer no for the record. However, as a totally selfish appraisal I would at least recommend a play though on easy for the story, music, and atmosphere. But due to poor design and rails and walls everywhere, there is no meaningful replay value unless you're a try hard, in which case my opinion is totally counter to yours anyway.

Apparently at least one other team is trying to do it right. Search: Drox Operative for a true ARPG shooter attempt.

For example: you are hanging on the ledge in combat, but you can't just climb up. You have to jump and graple to something higher. This action can fail, in which case you have to do this all over again. All this while someone is shooting at you.
But the biggest issue lies deeper. There are two kinds of games: stealth and non-stealth. I enjoy games from each of that category. But this game tries to be both. Not in terms of giving you choice. You have to play stealth and loud at the same time. Too much for me, I'll stick with the mark of the ninja (brilliant game btw).

Here are the problems with the game as I see them:
1. Constant screen and sound stuttering.
2. Quality of Life improvements aren't even an afterthought - they don't exist. For example, you can't ctrl + click or Shift + Click to get items to and from your stash. The vendor where you buy items, you can't sell there. - How counter intuitive is that? It does have this nice feature where you can just sell anything from your inventory - ok, neat, but again counter intuitive. You can't use your mouse scroll wheel to scroll the item boxes at any vendors.
3. This game lacks polish all over. Tooltips aren't helpful. The buff bar only gives you icons, if you hover your mouse over them, nothing indicates what that icon is doing. The "auto attack" feature in the game interferes with your ability to use skills. The UI is also clunky and the games does little to explain it to you, so this is why it feels clunky.
4. Where is the lore, story, plot? Anything that I could use that might give me a reason to be engaged is missing almost entirely.
The only nice thing I will say about the game is that I like the art direction. I like the eastern theme. I do not recommend anyone throwing money at this game until they fix some of these issues.
