Purchased via a humble bundle, so no refund in my future. But this game had a great idea - turn based action, dodging according to sight lines, planning out encounters - and really sank it all by being very fiddly and unpredictable. This game really should have had more playtesting and care put into designing areas, encounters and the basic platforming. What became the breaking point between 'this is kind of aggravating' and 'this game deserves a bad review' is the in-level tip, that 'The jump arc is a lie.'
That really brings home all the problems. When it's about precise attack dodging and knocking down enemies, doing little frog hops instead of leaping into someone aiming a gun at you means resetting. Trying to jump onto someone near a ledge sometimes means knocking in just underneath it, and there's no helping you if all you need to do is go up instead of jumping around aimlessly to do a simple climb. The jump arc is essential to playing the game, but is unreliable and frustrating; that's not funny, that's just poor design.

Deus Ex Mankind Divided is a very fun game to play. It would be easy to suggest that Deus Ex Mankind Divided is a bad game through its first playthrough until the end. I had a succinctly decent experience when I leveled my Adam Jensen until he was his very own MachineGod from the third and fourth playthrough after recognizing all the smaller details of a level, as well as traversing through Prague's many apartments.
--
Though I thoroughly enjoyed most of Deus Ex Mankind Divided, I am glad that people are starting to consider Square Enix to not be that brand we can trust from the nineties. They've tried so hard to implement this kind of shameful monetization method with Triad Wars by NaughtyDog, and while Triad Wars had its own troubles insisting PC users to use console controllers, this example was a push for a proof of concept.
If this game really is the last of the series, I'm glad that they will be sealing away plenty of positive memories instead of using the brand as a way to mock itself in future installments with microtransactions.

*Queue the: Another Overwatch clone...*
This game plays NOTHING like overwatch. The only vague similarity between the two is the fact that there are classes/heroes. Overwatch's class base relies on hard countering a certain class with another class, LawBreakers class system merely gives you tools that cater to your playstyle and doesn't require you to change class mid game to counter an opponent. Lawbreakers leaves it more up to skill, movement, aim, map knowledge rather then depending on your team to pick a certain composition to win the game against the enemy team's compostion. (Not to mention it's an arena shooter)
Is the game perfect in it's current state? No, every game has it's flaws, including this one, but the dev team is talented and dedicated to support this game with fine tuning, balancing, and new content to make it better every update. It's a unique and refreshing take on the genre and has massive potential. Graphics, artstyle are fantastic, and it preforms and feels really nice. If you're on the fence about it, you won't regret buying this at all. Don't let the currently small player base be the factor that keeps you from buying it, give it a chance and help it grow.

Without a doubt the best stealth game I've ever played. In my opinion the only way to make a successful and enjoyable stealth game is to clearly define the rules of the game. The player needs to know what does and does not lead to being detected, and has to feel confident that they are playing within the rules. Mark of the Ninja clearly defines and communicates these rules to the player, so the game never devolves into trial and error. It is a consistent and enjoyable experience.
Sound and graphics are good. The art style is crisp, and the game runs smoothly. If works very well with a controller (Xbox360 controller in my case). Neither of these are mind blowing, but both are very servicable.
As for gameplay, this is a 10/10. I've beaten this game multiple times on Steam and GOG and I can confidently recommend it and I rank it near the very top of my favorite games of all time, with Super Mario Bros 3, Rayman Legends, Demon's Souls and the original Doom. The unlockables and upgrades are fun and the game has great pacing throughout. There is a meaningful difference between the different stealth tactics - "ghosting" through the level unseen and leaving the enemies undisturbed, killing enemies, or knocking out enemies. The first time I beat the game I immediately started again so I could do a no-kill playthrough.
I really can't recommend this game enough and I think anyone who likes stealth or sidescrolling platformers even a little bit should experience it.

Dead Man's Draw is a pirate themed card game that you play against an AI opponent.  There are 10 different card types in this card game, each card type has it's own unique abilities.  The game further allows you to equip two traits before each match in order to form a strategy going in that could best counter your opponent.
Even though I gave this game a No recommendation, it doesn't mean that this game is bad.  It's can actually be quite fun at times.  The problem comes in when you put in more than 5 or 6 hours in the game.  The first bunch of matches were really fun, you were unlocking new card powers and then new traits to augment those card powers.  Each game felt really unique and it was fun to learn how each new power interacted with the ones you unlocked before it.  However the tedium started to set in after about 6 or so hours of play into the game.  Unlocks became very slow and instead of cool new traits now you were getting cosmetic hero potraits which further slowed getting new traits.
The game does try to combat some of that tedium by introducing a different set of table/map rules for the matches as you further progress into the game.  And yes the first time you play those rules it again brings you back into the game.  Instead of just having more banked points/gold than your opponent you have to beat him and have less than a certain number of points/gold, or instead of just counting the highest point value cards in your hand it counts total value of all cards currently held (which can get kind of crazy with some of the traits that you or the AI can have).  But once again the tedium sets in.  Once you've played through the rule sets twice, it's no longer that fun and combined the fact that you've progressed so far in the game and nothing else has really changed each match feels more like the ones before it and there doesn't feel like a really big need to keep playing
And then there is some randomness that needs mentioing.  The randomness is mostly contained to only the drawing of cards.  After the draw is done based on how the cards interact with each other and the traits you can equip you can control the randomness of the drawing a fair bit by comboing cards together.  However that still wont' stop you from drawing a key and drawing a second key and busting your turn without being able to do anything.
Lastly since this is against the AI only, I'll mention that the AI isn't exactly the most polished.  They do make some questionable moves at times while at other times pull off perfect combos and that inconsistancy can add some not needed frustration on top of game that kind of feels like it's to long.
I'll finish up with saying that I'm not giving this game the thumbs down because it's bad.  It's not a bad game, it's actually quite well done and the card mechanics are quite fun.  It's just that I can't recommend it to everyone, it's a very niche game and for someone looking maybe to kill 10-20 minutes here and there it can be fun but playing for longer times in one sitting shows the weaknesses the game has.

This card game is similar to 21 (Black Jack), in that players draw cards (10 suits, 6 per suit) increasing their score until they stay and collect, or bust by drawing 2 of the same suit.
This is an unusual video game, because a player experiences 3 different phases that are completely different.
Phase 1. Honeymoon: You love it. You are winning most games. You get half the achievements in 2 hours of play.
Phase 2. Frustration: Now the games are evenly matched you each have 2 traits. Your opponent is better than you. They have a computer program that instantly calculates odds on inceasing the score risk. Now the rules change often and your AI opponet never forgets them. The AI has all the best card play sequences for every situation stored in its memory, you don't. You are still winning games, but you are losing 4 times as many.
Phase 3. Resolution: Out of your frustration to proceed you look for a guide and read the forums. You learn about a bug that gives you an unfair advantage. It is merely an undocumented key board stroke. No 3rd party. You use it to slaughter your opponents now scoring huge wins. You feel elated and take revenge on the opponents that hve been consistently beating you. You feel justified because you have convinced yourself that the deck is stacked in the AI's favor (even though it is not).
Few other games have brought out more emotions in me as I played it. Both thrill and agony.
Get it on sale for $2.49
Don't get it if you are a purist strategist, this game has too much random luck for you.

A very solid VN with light-puzzle elements (all of them potentially super-simple if you crank the difficulty down), Unhack excels in the areas where it counts; the writing is a pleasure to read and creates a great sense of character and place, and although you can blow through the whole game in a couple of hours, it tells an interesting and engaging story without any filler. I honestly felt much better about spending my time here than I have when running carbon-copy fetch-quests in some AAA titles.
If there's a downside it's the puzzle/hacking elements, which are functional, but perhaps a little too simple both graphically and in terms of substance- It's pretty hard to suspend your disbelief enough to imagine that shuffling a coloured box around a Pac-Man maze equates to hacking super-secure corporate IT infrastructure. Again, it's a testament to the characters and writing that they manage to sell it regardless.
In any case, a very solid buy. Get it, play it, remember it. Then be disappointed that so many other games with 1000X times the development budget aren't written with 1/1000 of the charm or heart.

Without a doubt the best stealth game I've ever played. In my opinion the only way to make a successful and enjoyable stealth game is to clearly define the rules of the game. The player needs to know what does and does not lead to being detected, and has to feel confident that they are playing within the rules. Mark of the Ninja clearly defines and communicates these rules to the player, so the game never devolves into trial and error. It is a consistent and enjoyable experience.
Sound and graphics are good. The art style is crisp, and the game runs smoothly. If works very well with a controller (Xbox360 controller in my case). Neither of these are mind blowing, but both are very servicable.
As for gameplay, this is a 10/10. I've beaten this game multiple times on Steam and GOG and I can confidently recommend it and I rank it near the very top of my favorite games of all time, with Super Mario Bros 3, Rayman Legends, Demon's Souls and the original Doom. The unlockables and upgrades are fun and the game has great pacing throughout. There is a meaningful difference between the different stealth tactics - "ghosting" through the level unseen and leaving the enemies undisturbed, killing enemies, or knocking out enemies. The first time I beat the game I immediately started again so I could do a no-kill playthrough.
I really can't recommend this game enough and I think anyone who likes stealth or sidescrolling platformers even a little bit should experience it.

Coming from an e-sports heavy background, (COD 4 Promod, CS, Quake etc), I absolutely love the game. Getting good with 1/2 characters is really rewarding, the variation in characters means you can play whatever style of game you like.
However there needs to be a big bump in the playerbase for this game to last more than another few months. Be it through marketing, promotions, free weekends etc, this game NEEDS more players.
Oceania matchmaking can take upwards of 10 minutes in the evenings and often games are incredibly one sided due to unbalanced teams.
Pros:
-Satisfying combat
-Wide range of characters that lets you play your way (tanky, stealthy, melee etc)
-Rewards system is straightforward enough and doesn't affect gameplay
-Raw skill is rewarded. Team comp makes next to no difference, I can play the weakest hero in the game and if I'm good at them, win the game singlehandly.
Cons
-Minimal playerbase
-Lack of real practice. I want to get better with a specific character, let me go into some form of DM to practice how to play with them, every major competitve game has this and getting stomped in quickplay when you're trying to improve is incredibly demotivating
-Runs like♥♥♥♥♥on old machines. Whilst this is a minor gripe, it does isolate a lot of players with machines that aren't from around 2016+. On low my game runs at 90FPS with a lot of drops meaning easy shots are missed, and on a 144hz I need to be pushing above that.
Overall I really love it, it's definitely worth picking up and playing.
Tl;dr
Quake+Overwatch for hardcore FPS players but minimal playerbase and not much chance to practice.

An amazing stealth game. Most stealth games seem to try to put you in the eyes of a ninja, or spy. They try to fully immerse you in the experience. Klei's gem does away with this P.O.V and the game is instead a sidescroller.
In fact, id argue this is more immersive. A "ninja" in the traditional sense, is a master of stealth, and knows where everything is and how to use it. This 2d point of view sets this immersiveness up perfectly.
Many stealth games I've seen fail to make being caught just as engaging an experience as being a master of badassery. The fighting and running (especially from later enemies such as stalkers) when they find you, FEELS satisfying, even though you dont WANT it to happen.
This game also advocates multiple playstyles. If you want to be an ultimate assassin (kill all) you can fulfill the Assasin fantasy. You can also be the puzzle solver, if you want. And if you want to be a whisper in the night (not being detected or killing anybody).
For the following reasons, the game has unique stealth mechanics that make it more satisfying, that failing to remain 100% stealthy has a consequence that [while] making it so you dont want it to happen, but it's still satisfying when you do; and that you can play the game with a number of different playstyles; I strongly encourage you to play this game.

You can disregard any reviews that compare Lawbreakers to Overwatch as they are so unlike one another that to do so only reveals one's narrow experience with shooters in general. Instead, trust authors who come from games like Unreal Tournament, Quake, and Titanfall. My personal perspective is shaped mostly by years of UT, and I can say with confidence that this game captures the feel of old school arena shooters - fast-paced, high skill ceiling, an emphasis on movement, and a grungy, realistic art design. But the game isn't strictly an arena throwback. It distinguishes itself from the dying genre in its ambitious attempt to smoothly incorporate roles (basically hero classes) into the fundamental design, and it does this with only varying levels of success.
In lawbreakers, just as in classic arena shooters, a proficiency for movement control within very specific playing environments is an essential part of the skill curve. This is a layer of complexity that is missing from most of today's popular titles, and it makes LB refreshing and fun. However, the introduction of role-based abilities as the primary engine for movement has added an unfortunate barrier to accessibility. A legitimate and common complaint is that players feel "stuck" playing only one or two roles because of how awkward the game has made it to switch between them.
For example, there are several roles that gain jetpack-style movement from a LSHIFT ability, but each design is so different from one another that you find yourself fumbling over the controls once you get used to doing it a certain way and then try to switch. The Vanguard's jets go forward, but the Harrier's jets go up. The Enforcer can glide
the ground but the Battlemedic needs to be
the ground. And one of those pairs requires you to hold the key down while the other pair requires you to toggle. It's as if the desigers deliberately implemented every possible permutation of function and all for the same key - abilities that are similar enough that you intuitively want them to behave the same way but not similar enough that any of them actually do.
An added complication is that there is no way to custom map your keys for each class. If you want to swap your primary and secondary fire for Gunslinger, as many Gunslingers are wont to do, then you must rebind your keys every time you switch to and from the class.
The use of low gravity environments can only be understood as a successful implementation when one consideres that until LB they've been little more than a gimmick. It's a nice change of pace to find that the low gravity doesn't ruin the game, but it doesn't add much to it either. The ability to blindfire for forward thrust through 0g is a great idea, but it turns out that your typical 1g movement abilties - sliding, grappling, wall dodging, rocket jumping, etc - are still more fun and more consequential.
The game lacks adequate environmental movement features that might help the less mobile roles get around. The tanks, in particular, feel too slow to play. There are no portals, lifts, or vortexes, and jump pads can be found only rarely. The gravity balls are fun though.
In summary, Lawbreakers often feels like an excercise in the frustrations of awkward controls and the playing environments leave some things to be desired, but the game is fun, albeit difficult. Would I have preferred a more traditional arena shooter that ignored separate roles but focused more on making low g actually work? Probably. But the game is good. It might be the best shooter of 2017 and if it fails to maintain a playerbase then it will say more about the sad state of gaming culture than it would about the design of the game itself.

At this point, every new game is going to steal a little (sometimes more) from a title preceding it.  What is used matters less than
it's used.
- How does the game stand apart from its competition?
- In what aspects does the game focus on: gameplay, eSports, skins, community, campaign?
- How much fun is the game as a sum total of its features?
LawBreakers stands apart as a mature, quick-moving, hard-hitting first-person shooter.  The hardcore attitude reminds me of the fighting game community, where bravado and style mean as much as damage and defense.
LawBreakers hones in on the multiplayer-only experience.  It pulls you in to its upside-down world of low- and no-gravity, of chaos and skill.  The game is not intersted in wasting your time with needless exposition or choosing overpowered weapons or unlocking new archetypes: hop in and play!
Is LawBreakers fun?  If you're up for the challenge, if you have friends to banter with, if you don't mind getting your face stomped into zero-G, yes:
While price shouldn't matter much, in my opinion, $30 is a more than fair price, considering its competition.  LawBreakers is a lean, mean, great idea for a game, and if you were unfortunate enough not able to try it before release, $30 will NOT break your Steam Wallet.

OK, first of all, this is NOT a stealth game. It's a puzzle-platformer, masquerading as one. In addition to lasers, traps and enemies, you're also dodging enemies' vision cones and play with lights. That's it. It has everything that's bad about stealth games (like sitting there for ten minutes, waiting for those two guards to sync their patrol cycles), put it into a complicated 2D environment (complicated because you can run on some walls and ceilings) and gave it crappy controls. That's your biggest enemy - SPACE is used for almost anything from jumping to opening trapdoors (but not normal vertical doors) to changing from wall to ceiling. Except it's not always apparent what will happen when you hit some keys (usually SPACE + WASD). If the ceiling above you is "climbable", you will stick to it. If it's not, you will jump right in front of that guard you're trying to avoid.
Story-wise, you're the chosen one of a ninja clan, who gets the "mark" - a magical tattoo that gives you some powers, but turns you insane/demon/whatever, so you're expected to kill yourself after your mission (go watch Claymore). Of course, this looks like a very nice way to ged of a goon that's no longer needed, so, SPOILER ALERT, you don't kill yourself but run away and try to find yout what your leaders are up to. Helping you is a ninja-girl who points out plot-critical points and acts as a tutorial, but she's kinda annoyng. She's not helping, but shows up after you've cleaned half a level, just to tell you what to do next. The game lost me when, after killing a major bad guy, you go somewhere infested with some high-tech bandits (without explanation as to who they are and what they are doing there), who seem to have better security than your previous mark - a wealthy noble/CEO. No, thanks, I think I'll go back to the original Thief.

Since I didn't have many other PC games at the time, this was the one I played the most. Bear that in mind when you see my 75 hours playtime. I bought this since I'd played Neverwinter Nights by BioWare and enjoyed it greatly, liked Knights of the Old Republic well enough despite its shallow and predictable story with flat characters, but was disappointed with Jade Empire -- it seemed rushed and incomplete.
For the longest time, playing this gave me vague hints of deja vu. I knew that the interface and gameplay reminded me an awful lot of World of Warcraft, so that wasn't the source of my unease. After 75 hours of suffering my irritating emo companions and doing fetch and deliver quests typical of MMOs, I finally realized: it was the same plot setting as Jade Empire, and to a lesser extent, KotOR. "You are the last jedi/martial artist/gray warden of the council/dojo/demon-blood-drinking-cult, and it falls upon you to save the galaxy/empire/world!"
Okay, so it's not an uncommon setting, but BioWare just does such an astounding, jaw-dropping job of rehashing stereotypes and making them even more bland and hackneyed than previously believed to be scientifically possible. In a sense, it's an amazing achievement, but I can hold more appreciation for "World's Largest Ball of Dryer Lint."

This is DLC done right. In first place, it isn't exactly DLC, but a standalone expansion to Far Cry 3. It uses the same game engine and mechanics, but it's a completely different game, a spin-off if you will, meaning that you don't need to own or had played Far Cry 3 to enjoy this game. And if Far Cry 3 was great, Blood Dragon is awesome. This game may have been a gamble for Ubisoft, but it was a great one. For me, there are 2 things that make this game great: first, and obviously, it's the setting. The retro-futuristic theme is brilliantly executed, from the style, the colors, the music, the menus, the enemies, the weapons, the cutscenes, the story, the mission design, the world map, and of course, the humor and references; secondly, the balance between a linear and an open world game. The game is open world, with a small but very alive map. The game is also short but it works to it's favor. Completing 100% in Far Cry 3 was a chore to me. Here, you do the same stuff, but it's more condensed and interesting. Beating the story takes around 5 hours, and for 100% another 5 hours. The progression here is linear, your character gains levels that unlock new abilities. And you unlock attachments for your weapons to make them stronger. And you'll notice this progression. The game incentivizes the player for 100%, and i also recommend it. It isn't a chore and you'll get the most of this game. But get it on sale, since the game is a bit pricey for the amount of content included. But it's definitely quality content.

Failure to Launch, Houston we may have a problem.
Lawbreakers a great game that for an unknown reason hasn’t generated the traction it deserves, zero-G arena-based shooter sounds awesome and frankly is as awesome as it sounds, but despite mostly positive critic and player reviews the concurrent population rarely peaks at 1000 and sits somewhere around 650-700.
Is The Game Dead? Dying? Dead on Arrival?
I could sum up the answer to all 3 of those with a simple no, it has a small but dedicated player base, with 5 aside matches even 500 players online would give 50 matches running at any given time of the day, the queue times are often under 60 seconds and one you are in a game often the following games instant fill for any drop out and you can easily play back to back matches for hours.
The longevity of the game will depend on how the dedicated player base grows or retains its numbers, an eventual Free to Play version would bolster numbers, but with it would come an even larger issue, a mass influx of farmers, bots, and hackers.
Gameplay
Maps and Mode
The Game is split into multiple maps and modes, while most maps take the form of a space age asteroid colony environment, there is still variety in them, some of which have appearances of different cultures and countries, the game offers multiple game modes, a variation of capture the flag is played in reverse in the form of blitzball, where you capture a ball and take it to the enemies base, other modes focus around area denial, capturing and holding data/batteries as of yet there is not a dedicated team Deathmatch mode.
All maps offer zones which have reduced gravity allowing longer and more exciting aerial duels, giving you an opening for attacks from any direction.
Roles and Characters
Lawbreakers is a role-based shooter, and as such, each faction (lawbreakers vs law) have equal roles portrayed by different characters which fulfill the same role with only cosmetic differences.
We will be focusing on the main weapons/tools, as most classes have some form of basic sidearm which all fulfill the same function, a weapon when your main needs reloading.
Hellion / Kitsune – Assassin: Melee focused DPS role, limited ranged ability in form of a shotgun.
Tokki / Feng – Battle Medic: Support/Healer with Aoe provided by the grenade launcher.
Axel / Kintaro – Enforcer: DPS/Tank Ranged DPS role.
Abaddon / Faust – Gunslinger: Tactical DPS Role.
Sunshine / Baron – Harrier: Support/Sustained DPS role, focusing on sustained damage vs burst.
Aegis / Nash – Juggernaut: Defensive/Tank Role.
Bomchelle / Cronos – Titan: Shock DPS, Defense Breacher role.
Maverick / Toska-9 – Vanguard: Arial DPS Role/ Support Role.
Deadlock / Helix – Wraith: Agility based Melee/short ranged combat role.
Community
The community is the standard shooter community, some of which will be toxic and downright immature, but overall the majority of players are helpful and good sports about wins or losses, the steam forums sadly has an active troll contingent who love to constantly post versions of “ded gam” “game is dead” “LOLZ no playzer” and the like.
Pay to Win?
A question asked of any game which has a store/transactions "is this game pay to win?", the answer is a resounding no, the only “win” would be functionally useless cosmetic items, which while look good provide no stat or ability change to weapons/gear.
Lootbox and Rewards
Gaining levels grants you stash crates which provide cosmetic items, avatars, and credits, personally, while I think they are cool, this aspect of the game does appeal to me, as cosmetics are not my interest in such games, collectors of skins and cosmetics however, would enjoy this.
In Conclusion
Lawbreakers is a great game worth a purchase, however all buyers should go into it knowing they won’t find Overwatch or even Paladin player numbers, if you want a great game which has fast ques and good gameplay this scratches your Quake/retro itch, fans of old time shooters will feel at home here and as well as newcomers to the genre will find they can pick it up fast and enjoy the  Zero-G frag fest.

Very fun game, almost completely overshadowed by horrible controls. When you're in the turn-based combat system, the Start button, rather than pausing, skips your turn. As far as I can tell, there's no way to "Pause" while in this mode. On paper, that's fine, because the action is effectively already paused, but when the non-turn based portions of the game do use the Start button for pause, this trains you (on top of decades of it being the standard) to press Start in a situation when you might generally pause the game. For example, I was at the very end of a very long and difficult battle, having killed probably a dozen enemies, with only one to go, when my dog started barking to go outside. Of course, without thinking, I hit start, and that stupid effing ninja sliced right through me, and I had to restart the entire battle. That's not the only issue, which is arguably one of personal preference. Right from the beginning, on the main menu, directional controls to select an option are unresponsive, sometimes requiring multiple presses, no matter whether I use the d-pad, stick, or keyboard. In-game, when jumping or using the grappling hook via the unified right-stick control, about 15% of the time, the game will just ignore what I've chosen and leave me on my current trajectory / in my current position. This may be because the cancel action is triggered by clicking the right stick (another control design flaw, in my opinion), but it seems to happen even when I'm certain I haven't clicked the stick. These issues persist whether I'm using my Xbox 360 controller, which has a more sensitive stick-click action, or my Dualshock 4, which takes significantly more pressure to click the thumbstick in. The game is difficult on it's own, clearly by design, and I'd be fine with that, if it weren't for all the "cheap" deaths that have come not by the AI besting my skills, but by faulty controls.
Oh, one other issue I encountered, which seems minor by comparison: I had one of the samurai/ninja dudes get stuck in a wall, no longer able to attack me or be attacked. Initially I was cool with that, because those guys are evil ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, but when I finished the level and realized I failed the "Kill all enemies" objective because of that, I was somewhat annoyed.
All-in-all, I can't recommend this game due to these game-breaking problems, but if they get patched out, I'd definitely turn around on that conclusion. The game has great potential, and an innovative mechanic that holds much promise.

Ring Runner: Flight of the Sages is the center of an emerging story-telling universe, and is possibly the best new game I've played since VVVVVV.  If you're a fan of arcade spaceship combat set in a detailed SCI-FI universe, then Ring Runner will likely hold your interest for a while.  The story telling is well thought out and moving to the last line.
The core gameplay is built around several different types of ships, from traditional shoot and scoot play ala Freelancer, to stealth tactics relying on precise timing of your abilities, to more devious physics based attacks reminiscent of Half Life's Gravity Gun.
Played it through and I want more!  Help support these guys, they started from the ground up in college and finished the game out with a kickstarter campaign for funding.  Would love to see them come back with a second installment of the game detailing the Extinguishing.

Highly, highly recommended to anyone who is a fan of stealth games.
Its strongest aspect without a doubt is the level design, allowing the player to clear each stage of the game in a variety of ways (note that unlockable moves and throwable distraction/attack items further add to this throughout the game). Having tried to clear levels in several of those different ways during my playthrough - from only distracting guards (without killing anyone) to only getting rid of those in my way to making sure every single last one was dead before moving on - I can conclude that all of those options felt viable, challenging and satisfactory (once completed) in their own way. You're also rewarded as a player for pretty much anything positive you do (killing an opponent, staying undetected while an opponent passes by, successfully distracting an opponent, etc.), so no complaints there.
Furthermore, the game does a good job of throwing in new types of enemies or other obstacles (e.g. poison gas, explosives) whenever you think you've seen it all, and although the story for the most part is not overly impressive the ending made me appreciate it a whole lot more (dw, won't spoil anything).
As a final sidenote, I should note that I found messing with guards and leaving them in a state of terror (usually happens when they see another guard step into a trap and die in front of their eyes) absolutely hilarious, 10/10 would do again.

Mark of the Ninja is, comfortably, the most satisfying stealth game I have played. It has opportunities for multiple ways to achieve goals, all of which are fun to try. The mechanics are great and the game offers decent challenge without seeming unfair.

Quick pro/con summary here, longer explanation below
Pros:
-Absurdly fast gameplay and movement mechanics
-Relatively easy to pick up but still difficult to master
-Really solid netcode and hitreg
-Stylish and highly polished
-Weapons and abilities feel really rewarding to use properly
-Process of skill mastery is enjoyable and long lasting
-Devs actually give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about their game and community
Cons
-Community is on the smaller side
-Some class imbalances, fairly minor in the grand scheme of things
-Maps can be awkward on certain modes
-Overcharge is essentially obselete with the addition of Uplink
-Cosmetic (loot box) microtransactions
I really can't stress enough how good this game is. I mostly come from a background of casual TF2 and I love fast movement and movement mechanics in FPS games. I'm also no stranger to TF2's very backwards learning curve, which punishes new players until something clicks and they get vastly better at the game over 20 hours in, then has incremental skill mastery from there. I tried to get in to arena FPS games for their speed but the skill floor was even higher and consistently getting ♥♥♥♥♥tomped by people who've been playing for 15+ years isn't very enjoyable. A large number of people are falsely equating this to a hero shooter, and while it does share some elements it plays nothing like most other games on the market. The closest comparison I could draw is UT or Quake, but even then Bosskey has made significant strides in making their game accessible- without greatly sacrificing skill ceiling. Lawbreakers is much more intuitive and far less punishing for new (average, non arena fps vet) players than Quake, UT, and even TF2, but still highly rewards mechanical mastery, strategic knowledge (including map mastery), and effective team play.
That and the devs actually give a damn about their game. They had launch issues (Which weren't in any of the betas and were mostly on the PS4), but they were resolved by a hotfix before the first actual patch. They are actively listening to their communnity and trying to improve their game (and that includes people who have stated they are outright done with the game due to complaints, which is a refreshingly mature stance to take), including nerfing 3 classes that were overperforming within a week of launch. They've also made development goals clear rather than leaving them to the last second for players to deal with.
All of the glowing praise aside, the game does have issues and I wouldn't be comfortable leaving them unaddressed. I have not personally noticed the same players in any of my matches (where I have requeued rather than staying in the lobby) within my time playing the game- both in betas and release. That being said, I am in one of the most populated regions IIRC and concurrent player count isn't amazing. Bosskey is a relatively small, new studio so it's unsurprising that their player count is low. It's not quite DOA levels but if this concerns you and you don't think you will get 30 hours worth of gameplay out of this game before you think the community will die, then I can't say I reccommend it for you. However, I do not think this will be an issue in the long term. Once Bosskey has built more of a reputation thanks to their community interaction (and once the really awful and misplaced vitriol about the game dies down) I'm sure more people will look into this game- but again, this is your call on what you're comfortable spending money on. There's a redundant game mode (Overcharge) in the game- and it is rather annoying as it is nearly identical to another mode (Uplink) but due to a minor change is far more swingy and more fundimentally unbalanced. Some of the modes also aren't as well suited for some maps as they are for others, but I personally haven't found this to be much of an issue (there are people who will disagree and they have some very valid points. I would advise you to hear them out as well before you take my word for it). There's also some annoying dialog but it's far less grating than a lot of contemporary multiplayer shooters in my opinion. The game does have cosmetic microtransactions, but the only thing I personally dislike about them is that they're a loot box system (which while I care less because they're cosmetic, it still annoys me. You get a ton of drops if you play regularly though).

Where do i even begin...
It just... hits the right spots. All of them. At once.
is so great, giving you the chance to play the character with the playstyle and mechanics that suits you best.
You wanna be so agile, fast and lightning-quick that your target will have a hard time tracking and following you? You can.
You wanna reign over the skies scanning the whole battlefield? You can.
You wanna dominate the ground with some of the toughest moth******ers you've ever seen? You can.
You wanna exterminate your opponents with surgeon-like precision while floating in zero-g? You can.
Whatever your playstyle is, you can find your match here.
From the faster-than-light moving class, to the more slow ones, you will enjoy moving throughout the whole map no matter what. It never gets you tired, it never gets boring.
Once the match starts, you'll gain the momentum that will accompany you for the rest of the game.
Speaking more of the technical side, i find all
to be original, yet some of them old-school... Timeless classics. It's a great mixture of what we didn't want to forget about the past, melted down with the FPS' innovations of our times.
The abilities are awesome and tons of fun. Great cooldowns management and sinergy. They can literally subvert the entire game if used properly and at the right moment.
are very well made. Featuring diverse areas that might give advantage to some classes over others, and vice-versa. You've got your big open spaces (most of them in zero-g) where a Vanguard or a Harrier would feel very comfortable. But then you also got tighter spots where a Wraith, an Assassin or a Titan would dominate over their opponents' carelessness.
modes are more or less something we've all already seen, but with a touch of LB itself. You also got unseen ones, like Blitzball (shown in the game's trailer).
P.S. The "ball"'s voice actor is the guy who dubs Morty in Rick & Morty. Imagine Morty saying "Thanks for picking me up! We're running out of time" or complimenting you on your kills while you're carrying it. I mean, come on! \m/
The game offers a customization section where you can make your characters look more badass.
Everytime you level up you acquire a stash. The stash contains 4 items. These items can be a character skin, a weapon skin, a sticker to be applied on weapons, or a kick decal (to clarify, everytime you kill someone with a kick, your footprint appears on that guy's screen, like a foot in the face).
All the items also have grades, like in most RPGs. You have Base (White), Advanced (Green), Superior (Blue), Exotic (Purple) and Boss (Orange).
Items can be found in stashes or you can buy them with coins. You obtain coins when you find something you already had from a stash.
The game also gives you the opportunity to buy stashes for money. Keep in mind that in NO WAY can someone spend money in order to become stronger than others. There is no chance to P2W here.
I'm not going into detail regarding each class, since a bunch of other people already did a great job doing that... but they are so insanely fun you won't know until you put you hands on them.
For Nvidia users, once ShadowPlay detects LawBreakers, it'll ask you if you'd like to automatically record every highlights in your games. At the end of each game, you'll have the chance to watch your highlights, trim them, save them locally, or upload them on YT with a single click. All very smooth and fast.
Your profile has a bunch of usual FPS statistics, and it also has a Match History section, where you can recover your recorded highlights in case you forgot to save them at the end of that match. (Unless you wiped out your temp folder of course :P)
Remember, this game was made by some of the best FPS veterans in the history of videogaming.

Let me start this review by saying that I'm not only a huge FPS fan, but I also love good racing simulators. So there is nothing weird if I love Need for Speed series. I mean really love them. My first Need for Speed was Porsche Unleashed. Because of that and because I'm a BIG Porsche fan, NFS Porsche Unleashed is my favorite. Even so, I also love Hot Pursuit 2, Underground 1 and 2, Most Wanted and Carbon. All of them are great games, my second favorite being NFS Most Wanted. I never tried Pro Street, but until Need for Speed Undercover came around, for me this series was divine. Undercover is the worst NFS I ever played. It loses all the greatness other NFS games had. It ruined my favorite racing simulator series.
In this game you no longer play the role of a street racing outlaw, but a police officer gone undercover… in the world of street racing of course. The game starts with you driving a Nissan 370 Z and trying to lose the cops on a highway. When you hit the first roadblock, you are rewarded with your first cinematic. You'll be getting plenty of those throughout the game. So in the first cinematic your superior officer is talking to a hot Asian woman about you going undercover. After that, you are reintroduced to the game and driving a Nissan 240 SX. Your job is to keep racing and build your wheelman reputation. This reputation attracts the attention of other street racers, that will offer you jobs and if you win races against them you'll get pink slip cars. Also, the more your wheelman reputation grows, the more of the city, cars and tuning parts are unlocked. All of that is important in order to beat your opponents.
This game has a different perspective than other NFS, because you will steadily increase you driver skills and you can win races in two ways. Every time you start an event, no matter if it is a sprint, circuit, cost to state and so on, you have a certain time to beat. If you finish the event over that time, you'll simply win, get cash and reputation. If you finish the event under the time, you'll dominate. By that you'll get more reputation and your driving skills will improve. Every time you advance a wheelman level, you'll get additional driving skills. These skills are available for every car you drive. If you can dominate all the events, your skills will increase to the max.
The cars of the game are well designed and have good handling in general. There are 4 tiers of cars, in three categories: American, European and Japanese. These tiers reflect the cars performance: 4 being the lowest and 1 the highest. Unlike NFS Most Wanted, you can't get a Volkswagen Golf with performance stats as high as a Bugatti Veyron, through upgrades. You will have to change your car to match the other cars you opponents have. Which is good, because I doubt a Golf can reach 400 km/h without breaking up...
So far so good, but for me it's obvious that the producers of this game don't know many things about cars, because there are some serious errors. For example: The McLaren SLR 722 is in tier 2 when it should be in tier 1 without a doubt. The Corvette Z06 is in tier 1, while other cars like 911 GT 2 and Dodge Viper SRT-10 are more powerful and faster in the real world and are included in tier 2. The Nissan GTR is also a tier 1 car, which is not correct, because it is slower than a GT 2 for instance, which is a tier 2 car. And last but not least, why in God's name are the NFS producers so impressed by the Audi R8? Why are they including it tier 1 and make it go faster than a Carrera GT and SLR, when the real R8 is slower on track and in a straight line that a 911 Carrera S. The R8 has only 420 BHP, not 600+. What's so damn good about his car? The looks don't make it a Batmobil. The producers need to check out some car sites before making a game.
Modifying cars is nowhere near as fun as NFS Carbon and Most Wanted or Underground 2. You have fewer possibilities and most of the body kits and rims look bad. Performance upgrades are cool and seriously improve the stock car. You can also tune your engine, transmission, drivetrain, suspension and so on in order to adapt your car to different situations. More horsepower for straight lines, more grip for twisty roads...you get the idea.
The graphics are ok, nothing too special but not bad either. The world looks good, but the cars really steal the show. They look very good and on high details they look almost lifelike. The sounds are also pretty good, although the will repeat in similar cars. Music is great. You no longer get stupid heavy metal tracks that sound awful and when you are in the main menu, tuning cars, the tracks are very relaxing, clearing your head after tough races.
And now let's talk about the bad and so damn annoying parts of the game. NFS Undercover has plenty of bugs and annoying moments. On many occasions, this game will make you throw your computer out of the window. How can a 2 meter wide Bugatti Veyron tip over in a corner??? How on Earth can that happen? Also, I was doing 380 km/h on a highway and the police SUV caught up to me and passed me like they were jet planes? What the hell is that about? Physics are really stupid. Your car will sometimes hit invisible obstacles when in a corner, it looks so NOT realistic when flipping in the air and other very frustrating things. Also, the highway battles will make you freak out, because even if you have a Zonda or Carrera GT, in some races opponents with inferior cars will give you a hard time. And let's not forget about the almighty Audi R8, which is like a rocket, when the real life car is total crap compared to a Veyron, Mclaren F1, Carrera GT or Zonda and so on.
As a conclusion, this NFS is the worst I played. It does have some good parts, but in the end it will make your brain go wild because it is so damn annoying and stupid. So thanks EA for ruining the best racing simulator series!!!

Far, far too luck-based for my taste. I'm not opposed to certain types of randomness in games (especially card games) as far as the initial dealing of the cards, but once you play your cards, they should be played. Dead Man's Draw doesn't feel that way, though.
It's essentially just regular old "War" where you and your opponent draw cards and whoever draws the highest card wins, but DMD just puts off the score tally until the end and has you "test your luck" each around by drawing additional cards and trying not to bust. Essentially, it is a combination of blackjack and war.
What I don't like about it, though, is that the game is overflowing with random occurrences of upsets and reversals. Imagine blackjack or war where every number between 1 and 10 has a special effect, where if you draw that number, a certain thing will happen every time you draw that number, no matter what. This goes for both you and your opponent. Drawing a 1 reveals the next card to be dealt (note: it doesn't give you the OPTION to look at it; it just shows you). Drawing a 2 forces you to remove a high-scoring card from your opponent's discard pile, dropping their points. Drawing a 2 and a 3 on the same turn automatically doubles your score for this round. Drawing a 5 forces you to steal any card from your opponent's discard pile. As these effects are turned on, they can be chained together into combos by you or your opponent. Draw a 5 and steal a 1 from your opponent (lowering their score), which allows you to see that the next card is a 2 and won't bust you, which you draw (raising your score) and use to destroy another one of your  opponent's cards (lowering their score). When you are chaining these combos, it feels like "strategy", but the only reason you got to perform this combo was luck (you happened to draw a 5), and deciding which card you are going to steal or destroy is a bit of a no-brainer. So it is a very shallow sort of strategy as far as I can tell.
The net result of every drawn card having some kind of game-upsetting effect is that even when you score points, you can't count on the fact that you simply scored those points. Your opponent will randomly draw a huge combo opportunity on the next turn and drop your points from 50 to 10 while raising his points from 7 to 48. The score upheavals and reversals can be so random and large, it's enough to give you whiplash.
Ultimately what this game feels like is if the game gave you and your opponent each a bag full of random effects, and each turn you both randomly draw an effect out of the bag, which makes some random stuff happen, and then one of you ends up having more points than the other. Whoever that turns out to be is the winner. End game.
Also, the game has the most superficial and meaningless use of XP I have ever seen. I don't know why it is in there. For a feature brag, I assume.
The art is great, though. The game looks and sounds fantastic. The test-your-luck blackjack element is a great aspect of the game and probably my favorite thing about it (and the gameplay element that persuaded me to give the game a try). Unfortunately, the torrent of forced upheaval effects on the cards just turns the whole thing sour for me. It feels like a game of interesting decisions getting overruled by a steady torrent of RNG interruptions, which just turns me off.

However, people feel it necessary to complain about prices of content like facilities and bunkers and hangars. Next, players. Yes you get griefers who travel Los Santos with the aim of making your gameplay as little fun as possible. But there is passive mode. If, unlike me, you don't like to fight back so they don't bother you again, enter passive mode via the interaction menu so they cannot touch you. Sound simple? Because it is.
Futhermore, a common complaint is the amount of modders. In fact, I ran into one yesterday - he was spawning trucks onto players faces. This is exteremely irritating and has a right tot be complained about. If passive mode doesn't work, I would recomment reporting the modder and joining a new session. The likelihood of a modder being in the next one in minimal.
I have also read people complaining that the recent updates have been all to similar. True, they have given a very "give a few million to start another business" kind of vibe, but again, if that's not your thing, you don't have to buy or play it. Period.

A short game with simple gameplay, but a nice distraction when everything is said & done.
It's inexpensive, moreso when on sale (full disclosure, I got it on sale, so under $3 for the game & it's extra content) but it also only took me about 2 hours to go through the game.  Still, that's a better dollar/hour rate than going to the movies, so I'm not going to say much else about the length of the game.
The gameplay is simple, which is kinda nice in this insatance (especially considering it's a simple graphical representation of you being a super white-hat hacker [or, as the game calls it "unhacker"] via a colored square moving along a path)  You use WASD, clicking with your mouse (I do not suggest using the mouse for the "unhacking" bits) or the number pad to control your little square, moving from point A to point B (though you usually stop along at points C F and P along the way) to achieve whatever goal the story put before you during each segment (episode)  Sometimes there are enemies to avoid, sometimes there are traps to avoid.  There are some pickups, and eventually some things you activate to move things along.  Simple in execution, but with enough added as you play to keep it interesting (I was interested enough to blow through in one sitting, so take what you will from that)
The story is solid enough for what it is.  It's all given through conversations between your character & the various AI's you work with (and their conversations with each other) and all the AI's have full voiceovers, which are pretty nice.  It's a simple story, and I think that works in it's favor here.  The story & gameplay mesh pretty nicely here.  There were a couple little twists here & there, but with how things progressed they weren't terribly suprising.  Not bad, but nothing to write home about.
As far as the art goes, it's nice.  It sticks to standard VN art with the characters having only a few images during gameplay, with most changes simply being expressions, but that art is clean & seems to fit well with everything else in the game.  After each level you get a screen that somehow relates to what just happened in the story, and they all look well done for a title from such a small group.  I didn't dislike anything that was presented to me on my screen.
The music works very well as game music.  It never gets overly distracting, fits the mood of the levels well, and is able to go on for a while with a smooth loop that won't suddenly jolt you with a harsh transition.  I will say that the stage cleared music (played while the cleared screen image is up) doesn't always feel right with the story elements of the game.  Not a deal breaker by a long shot, but just me stating my opinion.
All in all, I'm satisfied with my purchase and will keep an eye out for other stuff from these folks.  It's short enough to play in a single sitting, and interesting enough to keep your interest long enough to achieve that.  I'll probably go back and try a playthrough on the hardest mode in a bit (I only played on Hard, since it was midnight and I had just gotten off of work) but that'll be for another day.

Great twitch shooter. If I had to describe it in one sentence I'd say that "It's like a class-based Unreal Tournament, except the classes don't matter that much." The zero-g movement and combat is absolutely fun and adds more to the general skill ceiling.
There are a few balance issues, but the game's still pretty fresh so that shouldn't be too surprising. Mechanical skill trumps class choices for the most part anyway.
Don't get turned off by people saying it's dead, that's the kind of attitude that'll kill it in the first place imo. The playerbase is healthy enough, but the amount of people playing on each server depends on their respective time zones. (e.g. I tried finding a match on SEA last night and it took a significant amount of time, so I had to switch to US-West to quickly jump into games)
EDIT: Also, I wouldn't really compare this to Overwatch. While they're both class-based shooters, this Lawbreakers is more focused on pure skill while Overwatch is more about optimal team compositions and knowing when to press the ult button. I'm a Master-rank player on OW and I love both games, but I think the comparisons are a bit unfair.

Unhack Destruction is an interesting mix of VN + Puzzle/Strategy/Action game. Regardless of the devs inexperience when putting this title together, as they state it was their first one on steam, the game flows pretty well and isn't too long or drawn out.
Some games you feel they could have just stopped and you would have been happy, or they continue to make insane challenge after insane challenge. That's not the case with Unhack. It feels just about the right length for the type of game that it is.
You are an unhacker (think Whitehat I suppose?) and your job is to fight the 5K worm and clean it out of systems. As you progress and revel the story that makes up our world, you learn about greed, sure as the description says, but really there is more there in terms of friendship, loyalty and sacrifice.
The game is very short, to be sure, and because of that, I'm not sure the price is right, but I picked it up in a bundle.
For the Otaku: No nudies for you, in fact the 'girls' will recognize you for who you are.
The artwork is pretty good, and the mix of tech with Anime doesn't clash as one might think originally.
Interesting concept and I'd love to see where the dev will go with this in Unhack 2.
Overall, Unhack is entertaining if short. Worth the hour long play through on Normal, and if you want a challenge, try it on it's other settings.

The 2008 entry in the Prince of Persia series has a strong visual aesthetic and an impressive pedigree, but lacks gameplay worthy of either. At first glance, the ruins-crawling action seems to be on par with other standouts of the genre, but the gameplay quickly begins to feel repetitive and linear. The platforming is especially limited by the removal of the death mechanic - as soon as you miss a jump, you are transported back to the begining of the obstacle. This has a profound limit on the choices available to the player, as all paths are essentially reduced to on-rails quick time events. Combat is sparse and incredibly shallow, and since you can't die, it feels like more of a chore than anything. Most of the difficulty in this game comes from cheap tricks rather than clever design, and the handful of puzzles are all variations on using a lever to rotate things until they line up. Toss in an underwhelming story to boot, and you've got a frustratingly mediocre game.  C-

In short, better in every aspect than Human Revolution except story.
For the longer version, read on.
Firstly, the positives. They absolutely nailed the atmosphere. This game has a much darker and decidedly less cyberpunk tone than Human Revolution, fitting in perfectly with the change in attitude toward augments due to the events in Human Revolution. Graphics are fantastic, some of the best I've seen in a game. Gameplay is good, takedowns are satisfying and the augments provide some interesting ways to progress through the game meaning you never have to tackle the same problem in the same way twice. However there are a few things that keep it from being great which we'll get to in a moment. Lastly, the characters were done well; each one felt unique and real. Their motivations were believable and their actions understandable, which increases the immersion of the game. Where the narrative shone was in the side missions, specifically one involving the murder of augmented people and a female witness - one which still sticks with me months after playing the game.
Now for the negatives. The story was lackluster; it seemed incomplete. This is explained by the inclusion of important story elements as (paid?) DLC later on, which really should've been included in the base game. Furthermore, the story felt like it was cut short. Just when I thought, "Oh yes, now we're getting somewhere" the game abruptly rolls its credits. Apart from the beginning, there was nothing truly memorable about Mankind Divided's story. In addition to this, the negative gameplay element, namely the infuriating cover system (I found myself jumping over rails and straight into the enemy's sight quite often when all I wanted to do was round a corner), hampered the experience somewhat.
In conclusion, Mankind Divided seems to suffer from middle game syndrome. In the same way that a middle child is conflicted over his place in the family, Mankind Divided is conflicted over its place in the Deus Ex universe. Is it supposed to advance the story? Is it supposed to keep the audience entertained just long enough for the final game in the trilogy to arrive? It doesn't know. And that, ultimately, is the achilles heel of Mankind Divided.

This game actually deserves a better rating than it has.
Because it is highly enjoyable, and delivers what it promises.
There's several points of criticism, and I'll address those.
1.: Most of the story takes place in Prague, too few other locations and visiting those too shortly.
While it is true that the game does not have the scope of Human Revolution, that does not make it a bad game. Prague does feel more fleshed-out and larger, and while a change of scenery would have been appreciated, it is only ever something one notices in a direct comparison, not something that stands out as 'missing' from the game.
2.: But it has microtransactions and those are bad!
True that, they are there and it's probably the most stupid marketing/monetization strategy they could have come up with. They are utterly unnecessary. I think I got some stuff from the Season Pass, and never even bothered to activate that. For all matters and purposes, you can consider those microtransactions about as necessary as cosmetic DLC. If you want, get it, but there's absolutely no need to do so.
3.: The season pass is bad, and some of the unlockable stuff there is active only for one playthrough.
Ok, that 'only one playthrough' instead of 'get it on each playthrough' is another stupid decision. But then, you can decide yourself if you want to pay the extra money for the season pass - those who bought it previously, at full price? Yeah, I can understand the complaints. You reading this? You know what's in there and what you pay for. You don't like it, just get the base game.
In summary, the game is highly enjoyable - and what's important is value for money. Right now at the sale, there's a -85% discount, and at that price, it's a great deal. Full price? I would not recommend it. But then, I only buy stuff when it's on sale and often wait for a discount, so your mileage may vary. Still, for the reduced price, you will definitely have a better time than the 'all reviews' rating would suggest.

GTA online, whilst once an interesting and fun new idea... Is now an unambiguously cynical pile of rubbish.
A griefers paradise, where the rich/lifeless pay/grind their way to the biggest and best toys and proceed to ruin any fun anyone else might be having.  Make no mistake, this is a toxic community, and it makes perfect sense why it would be when R* are so happy to sell the tools to make it so.

People like to argue that you can easily ignore this new content, but if you don't buy it you get spammed with messages and phonecalls from in-game characters reminding you that you haven't ponied up for it yet.  Almost makes you miss the days where they were just pestering you to play a bowling mini-game and go see "big American ♥♥♥♥♥♥s".
This is a great way to crash a plane/die in a gunfight too since your controls get hijacked until you've dealt with the phonecall in one way or another.
The glory days were when the heists were just out, but there's only a handful of those and they do get old (cool as they are...).
The singleplayer is pretty good, but you probably knew that.  This is GTA 5 we're talking about afterall... It's bigger than Jesus at this point.  I only really write this to communicate the frustration.  GTA online was a pretty good thing with a lot of promise, and it's been thoroughly, thoroughly... thoroughly buggered senseless by the forces of unashamed greed.
They killed the magic.  It turns out when you do that it makes it far more obvious what the shortcomings are in the driving, the shooting and the godawful community.
If you have a time machine and can go back a couple of years this is recommendable.  Right now I'd stay clear unless you're buying at a heavily discounted price to do the singleplayer content.

Look, I'm sorry, but I thought this game was a waste of time. I downloaded it because I thought it was a cool premise, and it looked beautiful. I love that art style, and that is one of the things the game definitely has going for it.
I will now discuss the game's meaning in its three sections. I will only mention the gameplay briefly in each. Spoilers ahead, but, I'll be honest, there's only about 5 minutes of gameplay to spoil.
Section 1- The Business Man.
This man sees the world as an ordered machine, with people moving one way only. When you get into the building, all the names on the doors are blurry except for yours, and it just says office. Also, you can't run or jump, making this section a little bit annoying, but not at all bad. This section was actually quite a cool idea, but could have been aided with further explanation.
What does this mean?
Well, it means that the pursuit of money takes the fun out of life. When you pursue one goal, all other elements fade away, and you lose the wonder of the world, as it is replaced with clockwork movements of 'unimportant' people.
Section 2- The Old Man.
The old man is slow, and sees the world as faded, and is only in shades of grey. THIS SECTION IS AWFUL. I know the slow controls are part of the message, but, goddamn do they get in the way of the gameplay. This section was absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥ I make no apologies.
What does this mean? I honestly couldn't give a damn. I didn't take in the message because the gameplay made me so angry. I guess it's that, after a long life, life once again has lost its magic, and, as you get tired, you become more apathetic.
Section 3- The Kid.
This section was pretty cool. At last, some colour, and, by god, it is beautiful. It's great- vibrant and tangibly childlike. However, there were some mild performance issues. Not game-breaking, but noticeable. The jump section was annoying, because I kept getting knocked by birds into the lava, and there was a bit of a collision detection issue on the last step until I restarted the game, but that's not really a problem.
What does this mean?
You should look at the world as a child, and your end goal should be happiness (the giant donut). It also means you should never lose your childlike wonder. However, this game does not seem to encourage maturity. It's almost like the 'Toys 'R' Us Kid' commercials. Also, the message was lost a bit here due to the fact that the path is different.
Look, I'm sorry, but this game has its head up its♥♥♥♥♥ It thinks it's saying something new and profound about life, but it's not. Conveying its message with no dialogue was great. WELL DONE! You should be extremely proud, and I think that the idea could make an awesome game. The message is so superficial due to the game's limited playtime that it can't convey anything truly meaningful or original. If this game allowed you to see the rest of the world the people experienced, it would be SO MUCH BETTER. I really want to see the child's view on the adults at work all day, and the old people sitting in the park or crossing the road. If you could see until the end of the day and possibly even have some internal dialogue, it would be brilliant, but, honestly, at this point, I wouldn't recommend buying it. If I were you, I'd add it to your library now and wait for it to be out of early access.
TL-DR: I like the idea. It could say something great- it could have a message that turns out to be really interesting. I love the art style, and the child's viewpoint is beautiful. FIX THE GRANDPA SECTION. Currently, in my opinion, it suck balls. I'm sorry- I know the slow controls communicate the message, but the message SHOULD NEVER get in the way of the gameplay. A very unique and experimental asymmetrical game.  The concept being that you are either playing as a baby who's sole purpose is to kill themself, or a daddy who's purpose is to prevent the baby from killing itself by babyproofing the house and stopping the baby from doing things that would result in it dying.
The game maintains a balance by allowing both babies and daddy's have several different ways to complete their goals and the maps are somewhat randomized to prevent the same exact game from happening twice.  Anything the daddy can do, the baby has a way to deal with it.  And similarly, the daddy is capable of preventing the baby's death in their own regards (Assuming everything is working and not buggy).
In the current build, playing a daddy is downright infuriating.  The selection radius for picking up and using item's is microscopic at best, resulting in you often trying to click a single object in order to pick it up, but you end up doing nothing or picking up and dropping it immediately afterwards.  And given the fact that the baby is capable of ending their life in a split second by either bringing a fork/knife to an outlet, or using a hammer on the glass table, the daddy has alot of work cut out for them the moment the game starts.
This frustrating factor of the daddy is not shared with the baby, who only ever has to search for a method to kill themself either slowly through poison, quickly through electrocution, or a mixture of things to make the daddy's job extremely complicated as the daddy has to find the baby, cure the babie's poison, maybe raise their health, and prevent them from instantly dying all at the same time.
This makes the daddy millions of times harder to play than the baby, and results in most players prefering to play the baby over the daddy.  Anybody that wants to play the baby in public games, quickly realize that almost nobody wants to match up as a daddy.  This is compounded by the fact that daddies not only have to be extremely alert, but they also have to be precise with their clicks.  There are preventative measures that daddy's can do to make their life easier, but the time they have to actually do these is both extremely limited, and determined by luck.  The outlet covers spawn randomly in the house, and the outlets are randomly placed in several assorted locations.
Examples:
Covering each outlet will prevent the babies immediate death by electrocution, but the time it would take to create this prevention might allow the baby to kill themselves either a different way, or by just electrocuting themselves before you manage to cover every outlet.
Locking the cabinets containing poisonous materials can be done as well with the cabinet lock, but the lock must first be located and then used on the cabinet's all while the baby is at the same time searching for a single or multiple way to kill themself.
In all, this is a good game for it's price.  A great game to play with friends if your just interested in either creating a dominantly controlled environment as daddy, or causing serious mischief as a baby.  The graphics may appear very hideous too look at, but the substance the game offers is pretty enjoyable.  I personally find it surprising that this game is released as a completed game, because clearly it still has that work-in-progress Early Access feel.  Hopefully this can get changed with updates so that daddy's don't have to get seizures to perform their simple tasks, and the graphics can appear at least remotely decent to look at.  Additionally, the game is missing any ingame instructions or tips on how to do alot of the stuff you have available to offer, so if your interested in playing then expect to learn alot of how to play by searching wiki's and the discussion boards.
And in case your wondering why the multiplayer is dead, it's because only good players play daddy, and the daddy players get exhausted quickly (Just like good parents)

What is there to say really? This is a phenomenally good game.
It has an interesting story, great villains, good combat system, sweet gadgets, enticing collectibles and is actually pretty bug free from what I can tell.
You play Batman in 3rd person and you're here to stop the Joker (and various other super criminals), who has taken over Arkham Asylum. On your mission you will be able to explore a relatively open world (The Arkham Isle as well as several enclosed "levels"), in which you can find well hidden trophies and solve riddles by the Riddler, which unlock more lore information and give you some points for your next level up, but nothing really essential. It's a great way to break the monotony of "run, fight, repeat". You will also get several gadgets over the course of the story, unlocking even more ways to fight your enemies and reach new locations.
The combat system is just fluent, attack, block, special attacks against certain enemies. A good player would be able to not take a single point of damage in this game, since the system is pretty much flawless and any damage you take is definitely your fault. There is no cheese here. Enemies attack you in succession, but don't swarm you, so you can always block. This is how the system is designed and it works very well. Fighting better and upgrading your combat capabilities means taking out enemies faster.
The upgrades usually provide some quality of life changes and some new ways to play the game or make you more resilient. It's not spectacular, but not bad either.
You also have access to a "detective mode", which lets you see things you can interact with, such as destructible walls or trophies, etc. The problem is that this mode is so important to actually seeing stuff that you're basically playing the whole game with it being activated and that kinda screws the pretty nice graphics over...
My biggest gripe would be with the Batclaw (upgraded), because it takes ages to take down a barrier, while tapping A like a madman, and the "challenges", which are just a set of "fight this for x rounds" or "knock out all enemies in a room as fast as possible". There are about a Dozen of them or so, and they're not that easy to get a good grade on, but I found them rather dull, so I left them out. Apart from that the game is 100% for me, which happens very rarely.
A must buy imho if you're either into Batman or 3rd person fighting games with some Metroidvania aspects.
