Ho-lee♥♥♥♥♥♥ This game is excellent. If you're at all a fan of Overwatch style class-based games, you'll love this. And if you want the most fast-paced experience available, this should be in your library. Lawbreakers is an extremely well-made game. The classes are balanced. The variation between normal gravity and low gravity changes the dynamic entirely. Many of the classes can be extremely mobile in the low-gravity environments. The music, sound design, and graphics are all very solid. Get ready for a bit of a learning curve, as the tutorials for the characters are only YouTube videos, so I'd recomment playing around with them.
Thank god they didn't decide to make this free-to-play. I thought the trailers for this thing were too good to be true, but they give a pretty decent reflection. All I can say is get this game immediately.

My phone chimmed with a notification from a friend simply saying "you're welcome", he followed this up by saying "Check your Steam". Upon logging in I saw he'd gifted my a copy of LawBreakers.
My first hour or so with the game was...confusing, the zero G sections felt slow and impossible to control with any precision and I struggled to move around the map, however with some time and looking over some tutorials I began to learn what this game is all about. One of the chief skill to learn is using Blindfire (bound to LCtrl by default) by shooting behind you you can generate speed, change direction and even give the occasional pursuer something to think about. This coupled with learning your roles movement specific skill and how to apply them make for some truly unique. Simply put, once you learn the basics of movement in this game it's really becomes something special.
The game modes and maps are decent to be sure but I like most will tell you that Overcharge and Uplink are WAY too similar and we'd be much better off with another mode. Blitzball is a lot of fun but with the speed of certain characters like Assassin and Wraith a turnover can result in a goal in only a couple seconds so it's imperative to have some sit back on defense which can be a little boring but if you've ever played any sports you'll know that defense more often than not will make or break a team.
The characters (Roles) are unique as is the case with most games in the "Hero Shooter" genre but unlike games like Overwatch there is less of a need to counter particular characters but the occasional midgame change up can be useful if your team is lacking a heavy hitter like Titan or in need of some healing from Battle Medic. It should also be noted that while the Medic does heal it's all very passive, there is no real support in this game, everyone needs to be doing damage and killing.
The main thing that most people ask about is whether or not the game is worth it, I would answer yes! The player count is definitely not as high as a lot of other games but not such that you wont be able to find full matches. At the end of the day this game is a lot of fun especially with some decent team mates or a few friends. So to my buddy who gifted me this copy I want to say thanks for making me try this game, it's one I'll be playing for quite some time I imagine.

LawBreakers is honestly the most fun I've had with a first-person shooter game since DOOM last year. I'm usually not the best at competitive FPS games and I admit to giving up on a few in the past because the interest to get better just wasn't really there, but LawBreakers manages to make me
to get better at it, which surprised me in a big way.
One of the things that makes LawBreakers great in my opinion is that you can pick pretty much any class in the game, and you can do very well with them against pretty much any other class; they're all distinct in how they feel, and even classes that you'd think wouldn't do much for damage (tanks, medics) can hold their own with their dependable weapons. It's still a team game of course so you can't go full-on Rambo and 1v5 the enemy team, but there's obviously a lot of individual skill involved.
Another fantastic part of this game is the anti-gravity mechanic, where a designated area will have less gravity than normal and will radically impact your ability to manoeuvre in it. These are usually located near a central objective so will be a regular place to fight in. Learning to use your weapons to give you momentum to move in these areas will be really important to success, and the game is well aware of this and allows you not only to fire your weapon forwards but also backwards. It can feel a bit clunky at times, but once you get the hang of it you will be flying at break-neck speeds towards objectives or winning fights on low HP thanks to successful dodging. Easily the most unique part of the game, and I'm not sure the developers are properly conveying this part of the game to either the people who've yet to pick the game up, or even the people playing right now as this mechanic is only briefly brought up in-game in a tooltip.
If I were to voice a major complaint, it'd probably be the amount of leavers I've seen. Seemingly every game there is at least one, and it easily ruins the flow of the game and there are currently no punishments for it, but it is something that is being discussed by the developers. Another complaint I have (which is more of a personal thing) is that certain maps just aren't that well-designed for some of the modes the game incorporates, either too small in size, having predetermined locations for objectives that are placed in little rooms that lead to some really clustered and awkward fights, or one map in particular having no main anti-gravity zone which makes it a bit dull in comparison to the rest.
Overall however, at its current price and state I would definitely recommend this game if you are in the market for a fast-paced objective-driven FPS. The game delivers on many fronts and has an unbelievably solid core, and I feel like too many people are ignoring it because it's not exactly thriving with its player count (personally haven't had any issues finding any games at most times of the day). If it at all looks interesting to you, you can't go wrong with LawBreakers.
EDIT: OK, so I think I need to make an update to this review since I last wrote it. While the above mostly stays true, the playerbase has simply fallen too low to consider the game healthy. Matchmaking wasn't too bad when there were about 600 - 1000 players on at a time, but now it is going to not only take a long time to find a game, but if you do get a game it will be matchmade against anyone that happens to be queuing at the time.
Oh, and for some reason the developers decided to add health regeneration out-of-combat to
classes, in a game where you already had health stations to fall back to and health packs placed around the map. I am completely against this addition, and I am especially not happy that both natural regen and the existing health options are in the game.
To put it bluntly, avoid this game if you can. It has been enough time for me to realise that there is no coming back at this point for LawBreakers.

I owned this game on release back in the day and played the heck out of it. I loved it, it was a revelation back then to play a Batman game...no a SUPER HERO game that didn't suck. Each hit felt like I was a real super hero, the voice acting was stellar, the story was excellent, a real upgrade system and collectibles which added extra layers of story.
First of all the
. It's not really a story which will have you on the edge of your seat, the game does an excellent job of weaving a lot of characters into the plot as possible, but you will not really be playing the game for the in depth plot. It's pretty standard fayre for a super hero game, bad guy does bad thing in bad place, beat side bad guys to get to main bad guy to stop bad thing. However what the game excels at, is the amount of sheer effort it puts into character development and little easter eggs of story along the way. Aside from the main plot you will find a sub-plot of collectibles involving the Riddler, he will "challenge" you to find and solve all his riddles. These unlock character bio's for a lot of the Rogues gallery. The story is littered with villains(being set in Arkham Asylum that's no surprise), what I enjoyed was the particular attention paid to the "lesser" villains, not just the major ones. Killer Croc getting a huge look in, The Ventrilloquist having a hand in proceedings through Scarface(allbeit very minutely). The story at the time was excellent, but for those of you playing in 2016 and beyond, Arkham City is the game you want to play for story.
How did the voice acting hold up? Amazing. Not much needs to be said about this, its Mark Hammil as the Joker. It's the guy who voiced Batman in the animated series as Batman. It's literal voice acting perfection. The only gripe is during the stealth parts of the game, sometimes the random thugs voices can get a little bland. Not enough to detract from the fantastic performances of Harley Quinn, Batman, Gordon and The Joker.
How where the graphics
? I'm not the best person to tell people about graphics, I thought they were all right, obviously not as good as future incarnations. However I'm not a graphics ♥♥♥♥♥, I like games for gameplay, so long as the graphics are decent I'll take it. The characters looked good, it wasn't blocky, I had no frame rate issues.
? This is where the game excels, and some 10 years later its still amazing to play. Each movement flows with such ease and it involves one button click. The slow addition of extra enemies keeps the gameplay fresh, wanting to add to your combo score keeps you coming back for more. There is slow addition to the maps without you even realising and a decent size for free roaming without the maps becoming dull. There is collectibles galore with interesting riddles along the way. The game is crammed with Batman easter eggs(personally favourite, go find Clayface). If you hate combat, you can try and stealth situations with a very good stealth portion of the game. Bosses feel fresh and have different mechanics to fighting them, not the awful "fight this guy" mechanic that previous super hero titles had given us for years. There is an upgrade system which isn't borderline ridiculous, you never get seriously overpowered but your gadgets slowly unlock portions of the game you wondered what they where for earlier. The main thing this game got right was the combat, beating enemies felt epic but never ridiculous. Too many superhero games get this so very wrong, Iron Man wouldn't struggle to beat a random guy with a gun, Superman shouldn't struggle to beat a generic thug. At the same time, it shouldn't require a 30 button combo for me to feel epic beating them up. Batman Arkham Asylum did it perfectly, LOTs of enemies with easy but satisfying combat. One button hits people, that's it, press x to hurt people. You flow from one enemy to the next, it looks and feels epic. However if you mess up, sheer numbers may hurt you, which is believable, Batman after all is naught but a man and he is often depicted in the comics as being injured after fights.
Overall in
I can still suggest this game, after finishing it multiple times years earlier I still went back into it and loved it, getting every achievement. 9/10 a MUST own game. The only reason it doesn't get 10/10 is because Arkham City is better.

In MotN, you control a Ninja on a mission to stop a technologically advanced enemy. It's about infiltrating their multiple complexes, and along the way you have to sneak by guards, dogs, movement-sensitive cameras, laser beams and so on. What makes MotN such a joy to play though is the expressiveness of the gameplay. It differentiates itself from games like Splinter Cell in the way that it rewards every single Ninja-type action with points. That means if you hide behind a vase and a guard passes by, the moment he does it (for the first time), you get some points. When you knock out/kill a guard, you get points. When you hide a body in a dumpster, you get points, and when you dangle a body from up high and a guard sees it and freaks out in terror, you get points. The beautiful thing here is that this system encourages and rewards all these stealthy actions with points equally. You don't need to adhere to being super aggressive or super sneaky. MotN wants you to find your own preferred style and play it your way. It's not like in Deus Ex: Human Revolution for example, where the game ultimately wants you to play in a more pacifist way.
All this wouldn't amount to much if the controls weren't up to snuff. But they are. I played it with a gamepad, and once you wrap your head around the context sensitivity of the button layouts, you feel in total control. Other than that, level design is also hugely important. While to objectives are quite linear, the environments allow for a good degree of free-roam. Often you'll find yourself with the task to get to a room, but there are multiple paths to get there. And even within one path, there are a multitude of ways to bypass obstacles. So in that way, MotN is a real sandbox of stealth gameplay. There's a lot of room for experimentation, and because of the way it rewards it, it feels like a breath of fresh air compared to other titles in the genre.
The beautiful 2D art looks good in screenshots, but it's much better in motion. And even better when you're actually jumping, climbing and sneaking in these environments yourself. The animation is top-notch, especially for the main character. You inevitably will feel like a ninja. In that way, MotN really appeals to the inner child in me. I would run around, grapple-hook on top of chandeliers and do somersaults over unsuspecting guards just for the heck of it. It's a joy.
Story wise, you get a pretty bare bones setup that really just exists to give everything a fictional frame of reference. The story really doesn't impose itself on the game too much, and there are few cutscenes. The ones that are there are brief and actually quite entertaining to watch. You're a ninja from a ninja clan. Some mercenary corporation attacks your hidden compound. You are sent to kill their leader. It does get more interesting at the end, and the finale was actually really well done. All in all, MotN knows that it has such great gameplay that story purposefully takes the back seat here, and it's not really any worse for it.
My verdict would be that Mark of the Ninja is a great stealth game that seamlessly takes its place alongside the genre greats. The beautiful presentation, tight control and - above all - expressive stealth gameplay make it a joy to play. It's got great replay value because achievement hunting and exploring different playstyles keep the missions fresh and interesting even if you know their layouts by heart. It's light on story, but that is a purposeful design decision. The fact that this game single-handedly invented a gameplay formula for 2D stealth gameplay that works this well impresses the heck out of me and reminds me of the design brilliance of the original Thief. If you're a fan of the genre, you really should've played this by now. And even if you're not, it's accessible enough for newbies to give it a good shot.

It really puts things into perspective. While it tells that same old thing about childhood, adulthood, and being elderly, it does it in such a beautiful way, that it makes you feel like you are the character.
As the child, you feel like you're a thrilling adventure, and you reach an awesome gift at the end. As an adult, it's just mundane, and you are only set to go to your destination. As an elderly person, you are slow, weak, and even need to take a rest just to progress.
Each level has its own unique challenges and atmosphere, all of which adds to the overall emotions shown through each character.
For a Game Jam project, put on the free market, lasting no more than 5 minutes, it holds itself up wonderfully, and then some. I highly recommend it to anyone wanting to experience a magnificent piece of art, witness a beautifully told story, or just play an intriguing and quick game for the fun of it.

It was disheartening to see nothing related to Red Riding hood, or any of the Grimms tales like I was promised.  I bought a game that is probably going to simply sit on my account.  It has features belying it to an MMO, but they're missing all three letters.  Massive - The game seems rather small, in what I can figure are up coming areas I've yet to be. Multiplayer - It certainly WANTED to be at some point, but it fell short in the fact that... you play by yourself.  Sure the character creation screen is limited due to them wanted to be online, and sure they have a number of purchasable features in game, but I came into this expecting a single-player action-adventure rpg.  What I got was some kind of purgatory between a Multiplayer game and a Single-player campaign.  Online - When you first get onto the game you're greeted with a "Connecting to online" screen briefly.  This surprised me as nothing I had seen said anything about it being online.  You then go to your typical MMO character creation screen and, subsequently, build your character.  Then you have to create a name, and anyone who's played an MMO before knows how arduous a task this is... I digress, but after several different tries I got one that worked. Then I connected to the game.
And I was alone.
There was not a soul to be found, save the NPCs that eventually show up in town.  The little chat box at the bottom lay barren, devoid of any purpose as there was nary a soul to talk to.
The game-play itself isn't bad, it plays a lot like guild wars.  The story seems to be there, but the awash of MMO features seem to render it bland and leaving of a bad taste in ones mouth.  Purgatory seems a good way to describe it.  Like a sort-of Limbo, never will you feel more isolated and alone than if you were to play this game.

A truly creative mixture of Asteroids, Street Fighter and Disgaea.

It takes the frantic, but still highly tactical combat from Street Fighter by making it possible to kit out a ship with a small selection of abilities that have a mind-bogglingly wide range of effects and then asking you to apply them in high-speed and close-quarters combat.

This is one of the great games of 2013. Let's go in order.
First of all, the gameplay. In an individual mission, the gameplay is smooth, and once you learn it, almost brilliantly intuitive. You'll be using a grand total of as many as 14 abilities at a time, some of them obvious, and at least one- The Archetype ability- implemented in a way that should've been involved before. Used in a variety of ways, either through a flick of the mouse, or holding a specific key and then flicking your mouse, this ability is, to my knowledge, entirely unique to this game, and is based around the precision- occasionally- of your mouse movement, allowing you to fire rockets, dodge, teleport, or do any number of other, exciting things to move in a given direction. It's unique, it's awesome, and it's a very fun addition, that gives you unprecedented mobility in this kind of game.
On a broader scale, the gameplay is similar to most space-shooters, but innumerably more diverse. Where most shooters are content with perhaps a spread gun or a few other things, a single class from this game will allow you to summon meteors hurtling towards you, paving anything in their way over, generate mathematical fields of energy projectiles, fire gravity-altering balls of dark matter, and generate powerful waves of force impulse. There are a total of five classes, each oriented towards an entirely aspect of gameplay, from the Fighter's straightforward ace style, where maneuverability, heat management, and being the quickest-witted Valkarian in the sky is the key, to the Arsenal, a tower defense game in disguise, and the other three only get weirder from there, in all the best ways.
In the metagame, you have research. New hulls and equipment are researched, and you could have a lifetime of fun with a single class of hull, since each one is capable of great variety. There are even some minigames, usually based on various old arcade games, which are fun- Though Particle Command may see you yanking your hair out- and sometimes downright thrilling. Personally, I love the Brick-Breaker game played on a subquantum scale. Research takes a while- It's intended to be a long-term investment, and it'll take you at least a couple of playthroughs to complete. There is a double-unlock system; First, you research a broad category- Like a kind of node- And then, you must purchase your researched component. Thankfully, the best way to accrue the currency of the game is either: Set your game to paid research and go to work, as the research continues while you are not playing the game, or play through campaigns, which will speed up your research and deliver the necessary plex; Either way works, really.
One thing that may trouble you at first is the camera; It tends to zoom in close, so you need to learn how to tab to the map to show you the shape of the area you're moving through. When you get close to an enemy, it pulls back, exposing more of the area, but situational awareness is always tough; You'll want to practice learning how to keep the map coming up occasionally to watch your surroundings, and be aware of the shape of the battlefield.
Graphics. The graphics are interesting; While they're not designed to be ultra-realistic, they are stylized in the best way. Ship hulls are distinctive; Each breed of hull tends towards the distinctive, and with a little study, you should easily be able to tell the silhouettes apart. The graphics for the backgrounds, the large structure models, and the explosive graphics are where the game shines, however. With a little practice,e very ability will be obvious, which is good, because knowing the difference between a friction-enhancing trail of glitter and a field of red glowing mines may well save your life. In the quiet moments during missions, the background graphics can give a feeling for the majesty of space, and the fantastic world in which you inhabit.
Story. The story is told primarily through incidental explanations, and brief conversations. It starts off with you dealing with a pair of feuding galactic garbagemen in a small nebular galaxy, and ends with you facing off against what can only be called a god, and the best part is that it introduces this change gradually, and with great appreciation. There were moments that made me grit my teeth with anger, that filled me with a righteous fury to make things right, and then the game provided the chance to do just that. There is one character whom you meet, who you know you're going to have to kill before the end of the game, and who you know is going to be an incredible challenge. They manage to make the character fit that challenge perfectly, and provide one of the most thrilling boss fights I've ever seen in this kind of game. And then, they manage to top that. The dark hints in the backstory, at a galactic empire that has displaced humanity and has left its mark throughout the world, the gradual introduction of the nature of Anchor Drives, the nature of sages and the question of who has created them, fills the story; There is a novel series, which I have not read yet, but fully intend to. And throughout it all, the game adopts a tone of blithe comedy, in the best traditions of Terry Pratchett and Douglas Adams, where the grave stakes do not mean that people can just sit around being gloomy and serious. And in a delicious turn, at least for me, your character is openly contemptuous of the bandits that so frequently waylay characters, pleasantly explaining that they're not getting one dime before proceeding to tear said enemies apart. Never has a random encounter been so satisfying.
Music: This is perhaps the most striking, for me. The music has been well-made, and is perfect space opera fare. You will learn to associate certain themes with certain feelings; I could not spoil it for you, but the music will become a companion, exhorting you to fight harder, and to savor your surroundings. There are 20 tracks on the soundtrack, and they will become dear friends to you before the end of the game.
is one of my personal favorites, and will serve as a reminder that you're about to fight something that has dedicated its whole life to being able to destroy you, and has no idea what it is in store for.
When I first played this game, I made it partway through the first galaxy before giving it up. When I started playing again, I kept playing, and I have not stopped since. It provides that most unique of science fiction game experiences, akin to the best space opera out there, of starting with nothing, and learning of a world that defies your imagination, to face all that it has to offer, determined to find out why you are. You must push through, as the first galaxy could take as much as a solid ten hours to get through, and is largely a tutorial, but it will give you a solid versing in the play-styles of all five classes, a background of the world you're exploring, and the gameplay mechanics, and when you break free of it to the world beyond, you'll find it the most magnificent thing you've experienced in quite a while, I wager.

If you really don't know this game you probably didn't play any games in the early 90s.
This game is a classic point-and-click adventure, so it's almost entirely controlled with mouse. It is the classic adventure "Maniac Mansion 2: Day of the Tentacle" in a remastered version with higher quality, a reworked GUI and - of course - lots of Steam achievements.
Day of the Tentacle (also called DOTT) originally was conceived by Tim Schafer for LucasArts, which sadly was eventually bought by Disney and closed only recently. In the late 80s and early 90s, LucasArts was THE high quality studio for adventure games, although some competitors such as Westwood managed to make similar great adventures in this style.
I won't go into the details of this game but one thing is very clear: This game is hilarious! The way it tells its story (underlying plot of time travel!) and how you will have to solve puzzles will stick with you for many years. I still managed to play through this game without any help 20 years later.
Recommended: For anyone who enjoys adventure games. In fact, everyone else should also try it on a good sale.

Always happy to see popular card games getting a PC port. The game mostly runs on plain luck which can be in your advantage but mainly will be running against it. The tournament conditions adds a very nice variation to the game, which gives a nice boost to the replay value. If your a fan of RNG based (card)games then Dead Man's Draw is surely a game to pick up.

Warning! This game is incredibly luck based. If you can not take losing in a graceful way I would recommend skipping it.
That said, Dead Man's Draw is a very polished card game with a decent learning curve and simple gameplay you can easily get the hang of. You can make a lot of combos with a lot of cards and you will probably have a few good hours with it.
While it may seem the AI cheats, to this point I have not found it to do so. In fact, for a large part of the game the deck is stacked in your favour by giving you two traits at once while the AI has only one. The AI though is incredibly agressive, prefering to use cannons to blast your hand over potentially winning moves. This is quite annoying if you're just starting out, but often it leads to the AI impotently blasting away your 7 score card to reveal a 6 underneath, barely doing anything.
The AI does not seem to be able to really understand the game, it's functional, but feels very much like it follows a flowchart rather than that it plays the game. All opponents are the same as well, all following the same AI.
Luckily, where the AI does not change, the traits they use does, and the game has interesting ruleset changes after every 'tournament' (A string of a few matches) you play to keep things interesting.
As much as it looks like it may be enjoyable with a friend, it does not have multiplayer at this point. To continue on with its flaws, the game needs you to play a lot to unlock things. To the point where it begins to feel like grinding, and that the randomness begins to get annoying after yet another loss to an AI using a trait that you haven't even unlocked yet.
Is it polished, entertaining, and an interesting game?
Yes
Worth 10 euro?
I'd be sceptical. If you can find it on sale you're sure to get a few hours of amusement out of it, but otherwise it might be hard to get your money's worth.

Do you like card games?  If so, then this relatively unknown gem is one that you need to add to your collection.  The game was so well-received that Mayday games (in conjunction with Stardock) made a physical version of the game that can be purchased at Amazon and other retailers.
Dead Man's Draw is a pirate-themed  card game with an interesting rule-set that changes each game.  Each of the 10 suits has it's own unique 'ability'.  Additionally, players can choose up to two 'triats' each hand that invariably change the gameplay and adds to replay value.
There are some things that the game could have done better.  The lack of multi-player is the biggest thing missing from the game.  Another thing that would have made the game even better would be a 'free-play' mode; the game is very structured -- which is great for learning the game -- but that 'structure' means that the game will decide who you play, in what order you play them, and any special rules for that particular game/hand.
Dead Man's Draw is an entertaining card game that can be played for 5 minutes at a time or 5 hours at a time.  If you like cards and you see this on sale ... get it.

Unhack is a bizarre game. It's a mix between a visual novel and a puzzle game where you go from point A to point B.
Unhack, story is pretty bizarre as well. You play as the unhacker and you have to go through data streams to stop the 5K worm.
The gameplay is you moving a square through orbs, but you can only place your square on the orbs. There are viruses and lasers that will destroy you on impact.
There are boss battles where you have to shoot at the AI core to destroy them.
The visual novel aspect is not really there as you can't choose what to say and there's no decisions to impact the story. So why they advertise the game as a visual novel is beyond me.
The art style is quite mediocre. I felt that the characters look ridiculous and I can't take them seriously.
The voice acting is also mediocre and some of it, is just beyond terrible. I can't take some of the characters seriously, just because of the voice acting.
The game is really short, only around an hour long and there's next to no replay value in this title. So don't expect to replay it after you are finished with the main story.
The game is also pretty easy and there are difficulty options, if you want a bigger challenge.
Overall Unhack is an okay-ish title. It's not bad, but it's not that good either. It barely get's a positive rating from me, because I enjoyed the gameplay.
Final Rating:
6/10 - Okay

I came into this game really, really wanting to like it. I adore games that mix sidescroller style games, survival, and RPG elements together. They're refreshing, offer a challenge, and are generally very addicting.
The very first thing that caught my attention upon entering the game was the art style. I am literally the last person on the planet to allow my opinion of a game to be built on how the game looks, but holy cow - the art is genuinely bad. It feels rushed and lazy, and gave me a bad first impression. I shrugged this off, however, as the gameplay could have more than made up for it.
There are some things I genuinely found to be pleasing about A Valley. I loved the way they handled dungeons, for example. The dynamic way they added in secret rooms really made me want to explore the world to the fullest extent. I also really, really liked the idea of respawning with a new character every time I died. It made me feel more attached to my characters, and made my actions feel like they had a lot more weight.
The spell system was also worthwhile. I really dig the idea of different spells being used for different aspects of the world instead of only combat. Using a spell for harvesting, instead of just pressing E? Oh hell yeah!
Yet, there's just an overwhelming amount of stuff I didn't enjoy. I am all for games that don't hold your hand, believe me. I've beaten Dark Souls, and Might and Magic from 1988 is my♥♥♥♥♥♥ Yet, those games are all intuitive. This game, however, is a little too complicated to simply pick up through intuition. You need a guide - which, I guess, isn't really that bad of a thing - and although there is somewhat of a tutorial, it's just not enough. Because the learning curve is so high, early gameplay is akin through wading through mud - slow and arduous, and leaves you feeling like you haven’t gotten anywhere.
I do own the second game, and I do look forward to giving the series another try through its predecessor.

Yes, the game is a very ackward child of several different genres. Yet, even though all of these elements don't blend together into a focused gameplay experience, I would say AVWW is greater than the sum of its parts. It's a game best played when you don't want massive amounts of stimulation or tough decisions to make. It's slow. Peaceful. Bizarre. Simple. Deep. Calming. Additting. Demanding. and totally hands off at the same time.
Serveral points:
Graphics:
For many people this ruins the game for them. While I do acknowledge the stiff animations and strange blend of styles I find thay they add to the game more than it distracts from it. This uniquely strange artstyle helps instill the player with the game's mood- mystery and wonder. The setting of the game takes place in a fractured reality where all times and places converge (think Land of the Lost 2009) the juxtaposed visuals help with this suspension of disbelief.
My one complant with the graphics is that some of the backgrounds in indoor areas don't mesh well with the indoor patforms, causing confusion.
Music: Arcen Games always has good music and this game is no exception.
Gameplay:
Platforming- Excellent controls and physics make jumping around a joy and an ease.
Combat- It's repeatitive yet satisfing. There are many different missions which help shake things up a bit.
Exploration- Strangely mystical... The proceedurally generated worlds seem souless yet full of mystery, terror, and quiet beauty at the same time. It reminds me of playing Dwarf Fortress survival mode.
Progression- In my eyes, this game is less of a Metriodvania as it is a Dungeon Crawl. It's as if Diablo or Fate had a child with a proceedurally generated Metriod. It is satisfing to level up and improve one's inventory in this game.
Final Words
I disagree with the assertion that AVWW is an experiment gone wrong. It's an unpolished gem, sure. Yet its beauty comes with its strange lumps and bumps. It's polished, but not for an museum or a lab.
I'll be coming back to AVWW from time to time to feed my imagination, but also to feed my desire to float above a pack of velociraptors in ancient Egypt on a carpet of air bubbles whilst bombarding them with boulders and summoned rhinoceroses.

You start off on the bottom.
Rock bottom.
Your life is in pieces and you set out to put it all back together.
And from there, the adventure is up to you.
With the theme of desperation always lingering, will you resort to doing immoral things to add some bills to what little money you have?
Will you invest some of your precious time into making friends, or would you rather be a lone wolf in the world?
How far will you go to win back the love of your life and have a complete restart in your life?
There are some choices in this game which I find to be irrelevant, and some mechanics I found to be useless
But if we go storywise, I'd consider this as somewhat of a masterpiece
It's not the first of it's kind to have dark themes
It's definitely not clear of useless parts in it's story
But it opens your eyes a bit
In the numerous towns and cities you go to in your journey, you will see many disturbing things that are actually things that happen in real life
There are some characters that you might grow to hate, their sharp tongued, selfish and hypocritical
They're human
If theres any word that can summarize my whole take on the plot, it's human
Whether you like it or not you will definitely make choices in this game that would give you second thoughts
Another thing I'd like to add is how realistic the ending is
Even if you try and think you made all the right choices, you're probably going to get the bad ending
You have to work really hard to get a "Good" ending, or at least where your character is happy
It's human in that the end will always leave someone on top and someone rock bottom
It's a human world, and humans are Always Sometimes Monsters

Dragon Age: Origins is a role-playing video game developed by BioWare's Edmonton studio and published by Electronic Arts. It is the first game in the Dragon Age franchise. The game was released for Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 on November 3, 2009, and for Mac OS X on December 21, 2009.
Set in the fictional kingdom of Ferelden during a period of civil strife, the game puts the player in the role of a warrior, mage or rogue coming from an elven, human, or dwarven background who must unite the kingdom to fight an impending invasion by demonic forces. BioWare described the game as a spiritual successor to their previous Baldur's Gate and Neverwinter Nights franchises. The game is played from a third-person perspective that can be shifted to top-down perspective. Throughout the game, players encounter various companions, who play major roles in the game's plot and accompany the player throughout the game.
BioWare described Dragon Age: Origins as a "dark heroic fantasy" set in a unique world. Its setting was inspired by The Lord of the Rings and A Song of Ice & Fire, and was described by BioWare as a mix between high fantasy and low fantasy. Development of the game began in 2002, and lasted over six years. BioWare employed more than 144 voice-actors, and hired Inon Zur to compose the game's music.
Origins received critical acclaim upon release, with praise mostly directed at its story, setting, characters, music and combat system. It sold more than 3.2 million copies, and 1 million pieces of downloadable content. Its multiple year-end accolades included Game of the Year and Best Role-playing awards from several gaming publications. BioWare released an expansion pack for the game titled Awakening in March 2010, and two sequels, Dragon Age II and Dragon Age: Inquisition, were released in 2011 and 2014 respectively.
Dragon Age: Origins is an action role-playing game. The player is a Grey Warden, part of an order of elite fighters, whose task is to defeat the Archdemon and save the world from a disastrous event called the Blight. Players create their own Grey Warden character, customizing gender and appearance as well as choosing a race and class.The available classes are warriors, who perform strong physical attacks; rogues, who carry out stealth attacks and steal items from other characters; and mages, who cast spells on enemies, create combo spells, and support other party members. The three choices of race are human, elf, and dwarf. The combination of class and race determines which of six different origin stories the player experiences: Dalish Elf, City Elf, Dwarven Noble, Dwarven Commoner, Mage, or Human Noble.This affects the way other in-game characters perceive the player's character; for instance, a Dwarven Commoner would receive hatred and discrimination from other dwarves. However, all classes follow the same plot after the completion of the origin story.

Ring Runner Review
I bought the game on sale for $8, which works out to be pennies an hour worth of game play.  It’s hard to tell how many hours I have put into the game because the last Steam client update wiped my hours played, but before the wipe it said about 118, and since then I have put on 54 according to the current count.  I spent about 8-10 hours perfecting three ship builds, which involved mostly sitting in the menus with a calculator doing math, add in another few hours reading mission info, setting up random ships and looking at equipment.
I figure actual playtime through the main campaign took about 40-50 hours; more then what was listed in the product description.  This is probably because on several missions it would tell me things like quickly leave the battlefield or I needed to lose the fight so it can show me what happens when I die;  instead I decided to stick around and fight for long periods.  Couple this with flying around exploring environments [when possible] and sitting back listening to an amazing sound track.  Figure 30-50 hours for the main campaign which will also vary based on your difficulty setting.
The game was an impulse buy, one that was triggered by watching the trailer and hearing the amazing music tracks, watching the trippy explosions, and all out chaos of the ship battles.  I am not a fan of top down arcade style space shooters and prefer 4x stuff like the X Series or overly complicated, hard to learn and brutally unforgiving games like Eve Online.  With that said, Ring Runner had far more depth then any arcade style shooter I have tried.
For a game made by a small handful of people, I was shocked at its production value.  You will have a hard time telling it’s made by a small team of people.  It’s too bad the main stream [un]professional donkie-hole full time game reviewers seem to ignore indie games, because Ring Runner has not gotten the publicity it deserves.  I can only assume because they are a small team that does not have the capital needed to bribe the broken, deceiving, lying, incompetent main stream game review websites that only exist to sell ads and ruin gaming by coddling to big corporations that are increasingly taking a crap on a plate and charging you for the “privilege” of having it shoved down your throat.  I can assure you that spending $10 on this game, like it or hate it, will not leave you with the taste of feces in your mouth that comes from spending $60 a game on the typical horse $hit you are probably used to by now coming out of corporate America.  It’s worth buying Ring Runner just on principle IMO, but as a bonus you are getting an amazing game which should lead to many hours of fun game play.
The best way to describe the game is to think of it as a fantasy RPG with your typical fighter, Mage, Rogue, etc class system but with the ships you fly determining which “class” you are playing.  Just like in your typical RPG there are different item slots that hold different equipment which do different things.  Pretty standard for an RPG, not so standard for a space shooter.  The combination took me [pleasantly] by surprise when I finally figured out the game mechanics.
The dev is active on Steam and responds quickly to requests, questions, and concerns.  You can tell the game is a labor of love and a lot of time has been put into getting things right.  I have only had a small handful of black screen crashes, though they did require a forced PC reboot, overall the game is very stable, in fact looking at a lot of big title releases I would say it’s far more stable than Battlefield 4, X Rebirth, Rome 2, etc.  It’s hard to believe considering those other games have millions in production costs and far more people working on fixing problems.
The following are some negatives though I do not expect these to get fixed because IMO I have already gotten far more then I paid for and I know the dev is working on another project.  The game is already “complete” so the following is just for reference when making choices on future games.  There are some minor annoyances like AI ships picking up already scarce “plex” [money] in scenarios like death match, which will probably anger some people when trying to farm.  I noticed several AI ships flying around not shooting; rather just intentionally heading to the plex drops and picking them up before I could get over and do it myself.  This does not happen in missions, but when you are at endgame and trying to play with different builds which all cost a lot of plex, it makes things very obnoxious.  I understand AI characters picking up power-ups and would expect nothing less, but plex should not be something they can take as the AI has no need for in game money.
Post Game expect grinding for plex; a lot of grinding.  If you did the math from the first paragraph of this review you are probably wondering where the other 50+ hours went; the answer is playing [mostly] one mission over and over grinding for plex so I could buy different ships/equipment to try different builds.  The dev stated they were working on a minor fix, but it’s not hard to figure out why there are not a lot of Steam workshop builds online as its pointless to post a ship unless its set up properly which takes a lot of in game money.
My last gripe is that 95% of the equipment can only be used once per build.  This makes sense with some heavy hitting guns but not other very weak ones.  It makes it very hard to create a balanced build with anything other than just a few setups.  My guess is this is also why there are very few builds up on Steam’s workshop.  Sure, you can pile 8+ different crappy weapons into a ship, each with a different cool down timer, different amounts of heat or energy, each doing a different effect, but at the end of the day you will be doing nothing but button mashing for less DPS, more heat, and more energy use then you would get out of one decent weapon.  Oh, and good luck timing those 8+ weapons to actually hit your target as the game is very fast paced with flying feeling like you are on a rubber band shooting through space.  I am not saying it’s not fun to play with different builds, but at the end of the day you will probably just stick to one or two main weapons to max out DPS with the least Heat/Energy consumption.  A lot of things may look great on paper with a calculator, but in practice you can easily break the game with a few well thought-out builds.
Lastly, equipment descriptions are all over the place with some giving damage per second and others giving damage per shot, and still yet others give no description of damage leaving it to trial and error.
I know I ended this on a slightly sour note, but the game is anything but sour.  It took me over a hundred hours to break things, which was a lot of fun in the process.  That works out to less than ten cents an hour which is the cheapest you will probably ever pay for a game.  I don’t expect the devs to do anything else with it as again it’s a complete game.  If you are on the fence about buying it I highly recommend spending the $10 and having some fun.  The story is not bad [better than most high budget games today] and the dialog will defiantly will put a smile on your face.  By the end I was sitting on the edge of my seat swearing at the “bad guys” and loving how I was just wrecking them for the crap they pulled earlier.  It’s not often anymore a game will pull that emotion out of you with its story.  Again, fun times.
Thank you VERY much for an amazing game and I will be keeping an eye out on Kickstarter for your next release.

Ronin is essentially an action-oriented Mark of the Ninja with turn-based combat. And it is

I got this game on the humble bundle for about a dollar, and I'd say it was worth it cause god DAMN this game. I dont know how to feel about it.
As it states, it is a turn based ninja combat game, where you have to dodge red lines that indicate enemy attacks while at the same time trying to kill off the enemies. Thats, pretty much it. No variety and stealth is pretty much needed because, well, you're a ninja. Unfortunately you have to deal with enemies much more then you do actual ninja'ing stuff. This game is fun, I wont lie. But its the fact that it outright FORCES combat onto you is something that annoy's me greatly. I've been stealthing as much as I can for the sole purpose to avoid fighting, because after a while it is VERY repetitive. Absolutely no thought went into the gameplay as a whole, which even though it goes for something new, its ironically one of its few weakest points in the game. There's an upgrade screen, but even that feels lackluster in its attempt because its just "Spend a point on nothing to get closer to that one particular skill". It makes me feel I'm just wasting points just to get to that one specific skill. All skills, by the by, are useful. It just doesn't feel very fun to level up because you spent a point on a node that does NOTHING. Thats just my view on it.
The story is.....something. You're a ninja that must kill off five people in a photo. The thing is, I dont know the whole backstory, and probably never will because the SPECIAL EDITION apparently locks away the story behind a paywall! What kind of fair business is that? I have to spend an extra 20 dollars on a game just to get story, which I will find through other means, thank you. Overal, the story IN THE GAME is lackluster. I'm not counting the digital comic because when I play a game, I expect a game with a story implemented into it. Not locked away over a "Special Edition"
The music is quite repetitive. I mean, its cool and all, sounding pretty dark to fit the mood and such, but its the fact that you hear two (or three) of the same track, with the only different moments being when you've just (Or about to) assassinate one of the five people. Those are the only times that the music sounds any bit different. Everywhere else is the same couple or so tracks that have always played.
All and all, the game RONIN is another one of those games that provides something interesting, but bores out in the end probably because they just lost interest mid development. It feels pretty shallow, and doesn't really hold up to be what I was hoping for. Luckily, I got this on a humble bundle for a dollar, so at least I felt I got the money's worth of the game. Only buy this game when it is SERIOUSLY cheap, because this game doesn't really feel like it earned 13 or even 20 dollars due to its repetitiveness, and story that just flopped because you didn't spend the money needed JUST to get some context.
Too addicting guys. I havnt played a game that got me worked up as much as this game does in a long time. Brilliant, and loads of fun

I really like the concept here and badly want to like this game, but the execution leaves a lot to be desired....simple design decisions, such as being unable to pull yourself up a ledge or even MOVE (other than jump) in turn-based mode are only the beginning of the problems....
Ultimately, this is a shallow action combat game that has you "pausing" (turn-based) the combat so you can time "perfect" jumps all over the place (remember, you can't move during combat other than jump).
PROS:
-Action sequences are fun (non-turn based gameplay)
-Art style
NEUTRALS:
-Mini RPG / ability unlock system was ok but felt slightly out of place (not sure how I earned the ability points, seems like you get 1 per level)
CONS:
-The turn-based components are there, in essence. However, the core of the game is built around an action game (dodging the shots, etc) and with little to no stealth mechanics or other "strategy" component, it leaves for a very confusing and frustrating turn-based experience.
-Can't MOVE in turn-based mode. WTF? You can ONLY JUMP, so if you are hanging off a ledge, you cannot pull yourself up.  NUMEROUS times there will be combat areas with excessive edges. During these sequences expect to die+restart countless times because your character automatically grabs ledges, and once she does, you are basically a sitting duck unless you happen to have an arc you can jump away from since you cannot do anything else. Frustrating and extremely stupid design.
-Many actions simply disappear when you are (forced) in turn-based mode. For example, those stairs you just climbed down? Sorry can't climb them in turn-based mode.
-Lockdown mechanic: If an enemy loses sight of you, they will automatically initiate a lockdown in 10 "turns." Since not triggering the alarm is an objective in every mission, and since you CANNOT MOVE during turn-based combat, this means you have to "jump" (1 jump = 1 turn) over to that enemy so that he does see you and stops his 10-turn countdown.....in almost every instance of doing this, some OTHER enemy will now lose sight of you and immediately begin na 10-turn lockdown counter.....extremely annoying.
-Atrocious level design and pacing. Most of the level is reasonably easy and then out of nowhere a room that is near impossible. Several places in the levels have ledges which grossly interfere with gameplay due to the inability to move properly during combat.
-TERRIBLE documentation. Absolutely abysmal. Virtually nothing is documented.
-No UI information for a "turn based" game (for example, the robot looking minigunners appearing in mission 3 shoot their gun for 2 turns, but the only way to know this is by trial and error).
TIP:  The game bugs out at resolutions above 1920x1080 but it is hard to tell that it is bugging out. If your combat icons do not appear above the enemies, and you are having a hard time with the controls, try running in windowed mode or reducing resolution.

Although it can't compete with the classic NFS titles like the original Hot Pursuit and Underground, and doesn't match the exploits of its predecessor Pro Street, Undercover nevertheless is still a good NFS entry, and the last meaningful one to feature car customization.  The story and characters are forgetable, but it makes up for it by having a large selection of cars from humble coupes and sedans we all know and love to the greatest of supercars:  to all-American muscle, Japanese tuners, and European exotics.  And the cosmetic customization options are incredible.
Race types are what you'd expect.  There's circuits, sprints, and checkpoint races.  Outrun is decent for freeroaming while racing, and the Escape, Cost to State, and Cop Hunter events are great fun if you can stay wily enough to avoid getting pinned by the super-aggressive cop AI.
Unfortunately, there's also one Carbon-esque race type.  Highway Battle.  It's like Carbon's Canyon Battles, but if they took place at high speed on a stretch of highway where, instead of falling off of the cliffside, the danger comes from traffic speeding past you.  To make it worse there's a lot of RNG to Highway Battles itself, with you hoping your opponent will crash hard and you'll avoid crashing long enough to outrun him, and with your camera angle locked to the front bumper of your car.
I've seen some reviews complain about the controls for mouse and keyboard.  It isn't that bad, but I do recommend switching them around  a bit to make racing that much easier.  Unfortunately, you can't get a 1600 x 900 native resolution in the graphics settings, so you'll have to make do.
Finally, upon startup, it'll confront you with that idiotic Punkbuster anti-cheat.  It'll let you play without having to agree to Punkbuster's terms, but you'll have to deal with pressing "I Disagree" every time you start it up.
To sum it all up, it's the only decent Need For Speed title on Steam.  If you're looking for fast cars, then you've come to the right place.

NFS: Undercover is pretty decent. It's a fun arcade-style racing game that has a good variety of race modes. It is "open world" in the sense that you can drive around in a massive open world, but there is almost no point to that. You can immediately start races from the main map screen, with no need to drive to the physical location.
My least favorite part about the game is how dumbed-down it feels. I grew up playing the late 90's / early 00's NFS games like Hot Pursuit and High Stakes. Those games were a challenge. Undercover is not so much... The handling of the cars in Undercover is ridiculously easy and unrealistic. I win most of my races in Undercover without a fight, whereas in High Stakes and others, you had to fight hard to do well consistently. I am also disappointed that Undercover doesn't have a damage system that hinders you for your poor driving. It is also impossible to run your opponents off the road. Smashing into them at high speeds has very little effect and these "takedowns" were always a fun part of playing NFS growing up.
The cutscenes are also hilarious. The game shows its age (2008) with its live-action cutscenes that try to be really "gangsta" while actually coming off as extremely lame. The soundtrack is a solid mix of electronic, rock, and hip-hop, however. I was excited to hear Pendulum, From First to Last, and other great artists while racing.
One of my favorite parts is how good this game looks for being (at the time of this review) 9 years old! Sure, the landscape leaves a bit to be desired, but the cars are gorgeous. It doesn't compare at all to modern racing games, but it looks pretty nice for its time. And being old, it runs amazingly well on modern PCs.
The only issue I've had with running is that on occasion it will revert my graphics settings back to the lowest, opening my game is 640x480 resolution instead of the 1920x1080 that I had set it to. But this is a minor bug that isn't really annoying.
For a solid arcade racing experience, I totally recommend NFS: Undercover. It is a great casual racing game if you just have a few minutes to kill and are looking for something quick and fun.

Unhack is a game that combines the aspects of puzzles and the elements of a visual novel to bring a unique experience to the gamer.
The game itself is very short. It is definitely intended for one sitting (I got 50 mintes of gametime). Though you might feel that a short game is not good, Unhack is actually not bad for its length. Although there are better games available, Unhack is a nice game that can get you a bit emotional.
The puzzles in the game a bit mediocre, well at least in the beginning. It is extremely basic at the beginning, however, as you progress further into the game, the puzzles become much harder. It is not difficult, and you can easily formulate a plan on how to solve the puzzle and progress further.
The characters in the game are all voiced by English voice actors. Although it looks like a game from Japan, this was not made there (I believe) and therefore the creators could enter the English-speaking market easily. You get to discover a new world in this game. The voice acting is funny at times, as Miss Debug always says "*Yawnies*". The voice acting is on point.
The DLC for this game is even shorter than the main game, with only three levels to complete. It shows of a sad story of ACME Security's history, and actually made me feel a little bit emotional for the characters. The gameplay here is basic though, with this focus being on story. If this DLC were to be longer, I would have definitely cried from the sadness.
Overall, an excellent game. And for the price, it's a good game. You should only play this game in one sitting, as you may lose track on which level that you are on. The game is just for the story.
I recommend this game to people who are trying to get into the visual novel market. 8.5/10

So I have played the game for a couple of hours now and I am very satisfied with the state of the game being in such an early phase of development.

-Community is small but amazing.

-PvP is fun and has rewards/risks, there is a specific zone that has good loot but is open pvp with a level range in which if you die you lose your items (which I like VERY much).
Things I did not like about the game were:
-Couple of interface and functionality things like not being able to withdraw stacks of items or lock into nearby enemies.
-Clunky combat controls but the game being in such early phase gives me hope it will be worked out before full release.
All in all I believe if the game gets polished and frequent updates are a thing it will garner a big niche community.

I'm going to be honest here. When I first saw the screenshots for this game, I wasn't that impressed. The only reason I decided to play was because I literally had nothing else to do.
What I found was the kind of MMO that you'd see 10 or so years ago, and I mean that in a good way. This started as one man's labour of love. He's no expert at game development, but he laid the framework for all the non-coding stuff in the game.
Orake looks and feels like RS Classic but with a more experimental interface. Bugs often occur (in Early Access) but they're fixed within the day. Content is shoved out like planks from a lumber mill, but it's good content.
This game is not going to be one of your top 10 favorite games. It's not going to try to beat the competition. It's not going to bleed you dry of your money and laugh in your face.
Orake is what it is - a Work In Progress of a game that's going to end up being what Stardew Valley would have been if it was based on RuneScape instead of Harvest Moon.
The absolute best part is that the staff members are active and talk to players all the time. It's the best customer service I've ever seen, and it's the first time I've ever felt that my opinions and suggestions were actually valued.
Speak and you will be heard. This is a truth you won't find in any other MMO.

Hello all!
I found this game on Steam while searching for a new MMO to try out. I'm a disgruntled Runescape vet that turned to raiding on World of Warcraft about 4 years ago. So far I've clocked 15.5 hours on the game (I started 5 days ago) and I'll share the pros and cons I've observed.
Cons-
1. The graphic quality is low, and is indeed 2D as stated by the game title. Personally I don't mind sacrificing asthetics for gameplay but it may deter new players.
2. The story is minimal. It's implied that we need to defeat the powerful monster named Orake, but we don't have anything else to go on. Quests are simple tasks that don't give any backstory or context for what our character is doing in the world. This is the area I feel the game could use the most improvement in.
Pros-
1. Gameplay is simple, but fun. There are several noncombat skills, which is great because I appreciate MMOs that have a signifcant non-combat component. There are also 3 different styles of combat- melee, archery and magic. If you feel like using a different style, it's as simple as changing up your gear.
2. The mods are online often, friendly, and are always willing to help. It's the first thing I observed about this game. This possitive attitude is continued by the community, which is also very friendly. I have not had a negative experience.
3. The Dev is actively involved in the community he has created. By this I mean he is not only online and plays with the playerbase, but also considers their feedback when adding/changing content.
4. The game is fair for non-members. There is a "member" system for the game, where players that pay have access to more content. So far the two differences I've seen are access to an additional map (area of the world) and cosmetic items. The Dev has mentioned that non-members have access to all non cosmetic items that members do, which means balance is important to him.
Overall, I give the game in its current state a 8.5. It's very similar to Runescape Classic. It's still in early access which means we will be seeing improvement. I definitely recommend giving it a try. It's F2p and is a small game file, so you've got nothing to lose! If you're also someone that's been let down by changes to Runescape2, this is the game you've been looking for!

I debated for a while whether I should give this a recommendation or not - and ultimately I have to say no, it doesn't deserve it.
This IS a great little card game and I really like the way it plays.  Mechanically it works well once all the different card abilities have been unlocked, and I like how it eases new players in to the game.  There is some strategic decision making to be had, and there is also a 'push your luck' aspect which mixes things up nicely.  The graphics are good, but the pirate theme is pasted on.
There's two things that stop me giving this a recommendation:
1. There is no multiplayer.  If this game had online multiplayer for 2 players I would not hesitate to recommend it.  As it stands this omission makes the game feel a bit pricey for what it is.
2. Unbalanced AI.  Far too many times the AI will manage to put together a combo that is just amazing (it's not uncommon to see a significant lead wiped out in one hand), or will draw in such a way that it doesn't make sense (for example sometimes the AI will stop drawing after 2 useless low value cards and bank them; this could be a strategic decision, but every time it happens the next card turned over would have made the AI Bust).
It all leads to too much frustration for what should be a fun time waster.
Enjoyable hybrid card game with plenty of various game modes to proceed through and unlocking extra abilites and avatars as you progress.

Unlike most RPG's ASM takes place in the real world, dealing with more 'mundane' real world issues in more conventional ways. Instead of a story interspersed with combat sequences your main concern is simply gaining enough money to progress the storyline, paying off rent, getting money for a bus ticket, and things like that. Naturally the way to gain money is through work, and completing odd jobs throughout the game becomes its homologue to combat sequences and grinding found in other RPG's. Unfortunately the job aspect of this game is extremely tedious, although it doesn't take up a huge amount of the game seeing as it's the primary way to earn money I would've liked this process to be a bit more enjoyable.
Luckily the work minigames are the only real portion of the game that disappoints. The story is refreshingly original, and tackles a lot of real world issues that were competently handled with a surprising amount of choice and consequence found in the games decisions, which can lead to several different endings. Morality is great here as well, with most of your choices leaning on the gray side of the morality scale.  The characters were well done but sadly the game is short,  so you don't get enough time to really care for the characters except for perhaps the protagonist.  I also enjoyed the soundtrack, which was better than what I expected for an RPG Maker game. The same can't be said for the graphics though, it IS an RPG Maker game after all, and it shows.
Overall I'd definitely recommend this game for any RPG fan looking for an unconventional take on the genre, it's not perfect, and it leans on the short side (although it does boast a fair amount of replay value). What it does provide however is an interesting story that tackles tough real world issues with equally tough choices that actually matter, and that's a formula that inevitable leads to a great RPG.

Overcomplexity.
This is the one word summary of the reason this game is bad. Do you need a longer summary?
Ambition. Miscalculation. Over shooting.
What is the problem here? There are many. Maybe you checked out the screenshots and already feel bad about the game. I am not such a guy. I spent 20 hours to understand what is going on, since as all of Arcen's games, (maybe with the exception of Bionic Dues), you really can feel the love developers spent for the game here. Go to wiki of the game, spend some minutes to see that those guys, really love what they are doing. Even though they have many games now, they still do this with an amateurish enthusiasm.
While this is a good thing since they really make unique games, when it comes to knowing their capabilities as a 2 man show company (except visuals), they horribly suck. "Overcomplexity" is a well put summary for all of their games (except Skyward Collapse and Shattered Haven).
-> AI War: A combination between 4x games, supreme commander, wave based tower defense with some implemented arching story.
-> Tidalis: A casual AND not casual puzzle game with two almost completely different submodes, billions of different block types. This is the only case where overcomplexity did not hurt.
-> last federation: A space Europa universalis but a shootem up at the same time. Wait there is more! This shootem up part is also turn based.
-> Bionic Dues: A roguelike, but not a roguelike. Something nearing 50 missions pasted after one another, not finding the time for balancing stuff properly.
->  Stars Beyond Reach (upcoming game): A full fletched 4x, AND a semi full fletched city building game.
-> Starward Rogue (upcoming game): A sci-fi Binding of Isaac merged with sidescroller space shootemup.
Do you see a pattern here? I see one. They are really ambitious about making unique games. This is not a bad thing. BUT. But there are only 2 people working on this. So there is a trade off in their games. Because of overcomplexity together with limited labor force, in all of their games tutorials are walls of texts, since no one is willing to spend some time for making one. Another point is they really spend almost no sources to represent their game world, be it animations or sounds or UI. What else, all of their games are a mass of intricate mechanics thrown one after another without spending time perfecting individual mechanics.
A Valley Without Wind mostly suffers from the last one. It tries to be a metroidvania, a city builder, a randomly generated sandbox game, a spellcrafting game, a party based RPG, a roguelike. It succeeds in some, it horribly fails in others. For example during my first continent which took me something like 15 hours to complete, NONE of my party members are good enough to not die in simplest of the missions. Although there are many spells, they are not well thought, just picking two long range damage spells with different elementals as a warranty to some resistant boss types is enough. Even though there are many many mission types, they do not feel different that much, since you can just use running and jumping together clumsily to reach the end boss, spam your best spell and done. They try to randomly generate buildngs and stuff with materials hidden, but since they are not differentiated enough you dont need every spell, and most of the ingredients you will already find doing some quests, so it really serves no purpose, other than making the world look bigger.
Another weak point is, they left too much options for the player. While they really think this is a good thing, it is not. It IS the developer's job to design a cohesive game with each part's role and weight assigned properly. They just put some difficulty sliders for each aspect of the game and leave you with the designing part. To me, that seems really lazy, not everyone wants to be a modder to play a game. And even that is not doing a good job, since for some normal slider is easy, while normal slider for party is nearing impossibility. This ambition of freedom also has consequences in gameplay: There are many things you can do, most of which has not got any purpose. Occam's Razor has not been invented in this alternate timeline.
What else is bad? Story. This is also a common negative side for all of Arcen's games (except Skyward Collapse, since it is pretty straightforward). They are not good writers, and they dont believe in outsourcing. And what is worse, they really dont see when a game needs a story and when it is not. This game does not need a story. What they present is fairly weak, and not believable, and actually hurting the fun. World design also helps the feeling of mish mash, even though I know that they intentionally made the world look like a mish mash, this does not mean that I cant complain about it.
I really dont like giving a thumbs down to this game, since I know they really care about their products. They care too much actually. You can see this in their move of giving away Valley Without 2 to owners of the first game. This is also bad for them financially, since this overreaching has hurt them in the past too. In development of this game, they overdid it, and was about to go bankrupt doing so.
But here is the deal, if a developer got too ambitious and forget that they are an indie company with limited capabilities, I may also forget about that and compare their games to games with higher budgets. Sometimes, less is more, and this is a general remedy for all of Arcen's games.

The first Poker Night was a middle-of-the-road for me, but on the bright side it has taught me a lot of the basics of poker. Poker Night 2, however, seems to take that logic and throw it out the window.
Before, your experience mainly depended on your skills with the element of chance that all card games have to offer. However, in Poker Night 2, the odds seem to be stacked against you. (Or at least is a buggy mess, but considering the types of glitches I've come across it's likely the former.)
As I mentioned above, this seems to be a buggy mess. For instance, during a showdown against Claptrap, the odds meter on the top of the screen read my odds as 51%.... and Claptrap's as 52%.
I've also been the victim of "lesser readings" as I call them, where the game interperets your hand not as the highest it possibly can, but rather as the lowest. For instance, in a 1 on 1 showdown with Max, a Flush that I had was read as a single pair of 2s; still technically right, but ♥♥♥♥♥♥ nonetheless.
All in all, Poker Night 2 is a terribly broken trainwreck that pales in comparison to the original. Sure the new opponents are a nice change but I feel that the glitches and bugs it presents make it unworthy of most Steam libraries.

This game might be the best WW2 game ever made, at least for the European theater during the war. This game is like a cross between CoD and Battlefield, but with more battlefield as in the combat system is realistic (to a point). This game is still having a rough time with updates and new features being added, but it has a crap ton of potential that is slowly surfacing with each update.
One thing to note: this is a pay to win type of game. I've been playing without Membership since about a year back and it has taken me a very long time to even acquire a few guns for my soldier. Memberships aren't expensive, but most people don't like spending money on a game that is free. It being free is one reason why it does take so long to level up and progress. The micro-transactions in the game are what keep it free and keep the content coming.
One thing to note about playing is where to start with your soldier. Do you want to be an infantry, tanker, pilot, paratrooper, or recon? Here is my description of each.
Infantry: backbone of the army, has the most customization and flexibility. Basically can take down anything, anywhere but require support depending on the situation. They also have a total of 9 (or maybe 8) vehicles per faction, which includes trucks with AA guns and amphibious cars.
Tanker: The spearhead of the advance. Tanks are impenetrable to all bullets in the game. This gives them the ability to roll up to a point unopposed. Tankers do require support, which makes them and infantry a great combo! The tanker doesn't come equipped with any gun to my knowledge (it's been awhile since I got another tanker) but you can unlock weapons. There are currently around 12 tanks available for each faction. Also note of advice, Germany has the best tanks in the game right now. So you should start a tanker with them.
Pilot: For those who love a birds eye view. Planes in this game have two purposes: killing other planes and bombing the f*** out of a point. There are 3 ways you can configure your controls so that you can fly with ease. Currently each factions has 3 planes, a recon, a fighter, and a heavy fighter. Also to note, America has the best all-round planes, so start a pilot with them.
Paratrooper: The sky infantry. These guys can freely drop onto any point. They come equipped with the standard issue rifle for the faction, but can be upgraded for better weapons. Be careful of your para-plane, as it will get easily shot down by enemy pilots or AA guns on the ground.
Recon: Kind of a glorified sniper-infantry but with an armored car for a vehicle. These guys come equipped with a scoped rifle and can have basically any weapons in the game later on. Each faction has a different armored car for their recon. Personally I think the Germans have the best armored car in the game, it has an auto cannon and can be a very good get away car.
Anyway I hope this review helped. I know it's long, but I tried to put in a lot of details. Have fun!

Pretty decent little game.  Plenty of quick fun, especially for the price.  I really liked the voice acting, as well.

I really liked the basic idea of the gameplay, but it was much too easy.  New gameplay mechanics were introduced in each chapter, but none of them were fully explored.  The timing sequences didn't really get any harder from the beginning of the game onwards.  My suggestion would be to add in some puzzling elements to spice it up and make the game longer.  The playtime is definitely too short (about 40 minutes to beat once) when compared to the price.
Art was fine.  It wasn't spectacular, but none of the characters looked super awkward or anything.  I liked the art style of the hacking game better than the character art.
The story was okay, though it was predictable.  The dialogue was neither good or bad.  The voice acting was okay, but pretty flat.  One thing I did like about was the way the dialogue advanced during the gameplay sequences.  It felt more natural than just having cutscenes all the time, and gave you something interesting to read while playing.
One final thing is that the lack of a save system is pretty bad.  The only reason it didn't completely ruin the game is that the game is so short that you can beat it in one sitting.  You can choose to load the game at the beginning of each chapter, but the game never tells you what chapter you're on, so you just need to choose chapters at random until you find the right one.  Even just having the load screen show what chapters you've already completed would be a big improvement.

On one hand, it's a fairly easy but amusing action puzzle game, at least if you're not playing on Insane. I don't think it really ever puzzled me except during the very last mission, so much as it required me to time doing the obvious thing properly, but eh, I still had enough fun with it. It also has some decent voice acting, though I didn't particularly like Weedy's voice as much as the others, which is awkward since she's more or less the main voiced character.
On the other, the entire game is 40 minutes long and I didn't really feel like it developed itself as a game much at all. It told a complete (if rushing from one plot point to the next at breakneck speed) story, I suppose, so I'm not really criticizing the narrative as much as I ended up feeling that the gameplay part could have used quite a lot more fleshing out.
All in all, I have to say this one is pretty skippable unless you manage to get it in a bundle or for free or something.
