Remember there is a free demo that covers 40% of the game.  If you are interested, just play that first.
In any event, this game just... underwhelms.  It's basically a visual novel with some basic gameplay thrown in to appease those people who claim that simply reading text "isn't a game", but the problem is that all it does is create a minor obstacle course to slow the player down in between text segments.  Since all you do is use the arrow keys, it basically amounts to being told to push the same couple buttons with some general sense of timing to avoid the bad things, but since you're more focused on the WAITING than the timing, it lacks all the appeal of a rythym game.  It's more like those stealth games where all you do is wait for an immobile guard to just turn a different direction, and where you have no tools at all.
But this surely leaves the stronger point of the game, the story in the visual novel, right?  Well...
There's two parts of the plot of the game, the actual unhacking part, and the character drama part.
Unhacking gives you zero sense of actually being the master hacker the characters all seem to think you are.  There isn't any discussion of getting past firewalls, no vulnerability exploitation, at one point, your character is apparently hacking into a computer without even realizing he wasn't invited, because apparently, hacking is so like signing into an instant messenger service that even a pro can't tell the difference. You delete viruses by stepping onto green tiles to fire "blasters".  It's not even presented as an abstraction for actually doing real hacking, the way a lot of games throw in hacking minigames, they're telling you to "defend the core by firing those blasters".
As for the characters, well, they're undermined by the stilted dialogue.  Weedy has stiff, formal, and frequently awkward English.  The dialogue is written like someone still learning English as a second language.  And oh God, Ms. Debug's catchphrase is the immesurably irritating "Yawnies".
The plot relies heavily upon being invested in the characters enough that you care when yet more "shocking swerves" you could see coming half the story away are revealed.  The problem is, the dramatic points are so cheesy and predictable that you can't help but roll your eyes and know that everything will be OK at the end, because there's just no way they're selling a really gripping story of loss like this.  Since the story is so short, there's also basically no chance to develop the characters at all outside the first chapter or two, and that's only Weedy and the player character.  You can sum up the characters with just a couple gags or catchphrases they continuously repeat.  (Weedy: Forever declined, A2: It's A-squared!, Debug: Yawnies, Unhacker: costume mod.) The only thing I could remember about A2 beginning to end was just that they apparently just put Hatsune Miku in skimpier clothing for their rival. They aren't even two-dimensional personalities, they're bullet points.
To be honest, I think it would have been better without the gameplay elements, so that they could have spent more time actually giving this thing a story and setting up a way to actually deliver the drama.  Everything is just the same character portraits in front of purple hexagons with flatly delivered "I will destroy you all," "Oh noes!"-type dialogue, and at least showing some variation in artwork would have done SOMETHING.  The entire "game part" of this game is just a timewaster distraction to pad out an anemic story.  That's... really saying something.

So annoying. Just so annoying.
Listen, devs. I want to feel like a badass ninja assassin. It's not a stealth game? That's fine, nobody watched those old ninja movies to see people quietly sneak around. Killing's great. So why did you make it so, so stupid? Why do I have to spend so much time bouncing back and forth between enemies, gently knocking them to the ground so they can get up and shoot me in two turns? How about, you know, letting me kill them? A room of 9 enemies who can shoot the floor? Great, just let me kill them instead of pushing them around. It's just tedious. So, so tedious.
I won't describe the game, the gameplay's unique, go watch a video of it. But I will complain. You spend the majority of your time in turn-based mode, hopping around in arcs. You might think that since you're a badass assassin with a huge sword you'd use those hops to hop on enemies and stab them, but oh how wrong you'd be.
Your hops are for either knocking guys over or for avoiding 4 or 5 frozen laser beams representing enemy aim. Your hopping goal is not to hop ON the enemies to stab them or break their necks or anything, no that would be stupid. Your goal is to hop in such a way that the end of the turn finds you in the air somewhere NEAR an enemy. Should you achieve that, then next turn you can actually do the killing IF, and only if, none of the other 7 enemies are aiming somewhere that'll get you killed. Knowing THAT is complicated by the fact that where you end up after making a kill is somewhat random.
Actually your movement in general is a little random, particularly if you bump into an enemy but also for other reasons or no reason. Where exactly the enemies aim seems to vary a bit, which for better or worse adds an element of randomness to the levels which would otherwise play out the same way every time were you to use an identical approach.
Whatever. I'm sure it's a fine game if you're one of those people who find difficulty inherently fun. It's stylish and unique-ish. I just found it to be more annoying than enjoyable, and it made me want to stop playing real quick.

Much of it is trying to deal with the weird controls, lack of knowledge on what's actually going on in the level and poor level design.
The game isn't hard because it's strategic, it's hard because pulling that strategy off without your character moving an inch forward, instead of jumping to the ceiling like you told him to, or stopping in the middle of enemy fire for some reason, or the character just straight up not doing what you told him to - is a constant issue.
In order to make a strategy, you need to react to the information provided, the problem is that information is wrong most of the time. The game might tell you that if you jump in X area you're in the clear, but then you do that and get shot anyways because your character jumped a few feet back from it and got shot for no good reason. And in a game like this, where responsiveness is absolutely essential since you die in one hit, these problems are fatal for the game, and are reason enough for me to not recommend it.

In MotN, you control a Ninja on a mission to stop a technologically advanced enemy. It's about infiltrating their multiple complexes, and along the way you have to sneak by guards, dogs, movement-sensitive cameras, laser beams and so on. What makes MotN such a joy to play though is the expressiveness of the gameplay. It differentiates itself from games like Splinter Cell in the way that it rewards every single Ninja-type action with points. That means if you hide behind a vase and a guard passes by, the moment he does it (for the first time), you get some points. When you knock out/kill a guard, you get points. When you hide a body in a dumpster, you get points, and when you dangle a body from up high and a guard sees it and freaks out in terror, you get points. The beautiful thing here is that this system encourages and rewards all these stealthy actions with points equally. You don't need to adhere to being super aggressive or super sneaky. MotN wants you to find your own preferred style and play it your way. It's not like in Deus Ex: Human Revolution for example, where the game ultimately wants you to play in a more pacifist way.
All this wouldn't amount to much if the controls weren't up to snuff. But they are. I played it with a gamepad, and once you wrap your head around the context sensitivity of the button layouts, you feel in total control. Other than that, level design is also hugely important. While to objectives are quite linear, the environments allow for a good degree of free-roam. Often you'll find yourself with the task to get to a room, but there are multiple paths to get there. And even within one path, there are a multitude of ways to bypass obstacles. So in that way, MotN is a real sandbox of stealth gameplay. There's a lot of room for experimentation, and because of the way it rewards it, it feels like a breath of fresh air compared to other titles in the genre.
The beautiful 2D art looks good in screenshots, but it's much better in motion. And even better when you're actually jumping, climbing and sneaking in these environments yourself. The animation is top-notch, especially for the main character. You inevitably will feel like a ninja. In that way, MotN really appeals to the inner child in me. I would run around, grapple-hook on top of chandeliers and do somersaults over unsuspecting guards just for the heck of it. It's a joy.
Story wise, you get a pretty bare bones setup that really just exists to give everything a fictional frame of reference. The story really doesn't impose itself on the game too much, and there are few cutscenes. The ones that are there are brief and actually quite entertaining to watch. You're a ninja from a ninja clan. Some mercenary corporation attacks your hidden compound. You are sent to kill their leader. It does get more interesting at the end, and the finale was actually really well done. All in all, MotN knows that it has such great gameplay that story purposefully takes the back seat here, and it's not really any worse for it.
My verdict would be that Mark of the Ninja is a great stealth game that seamlessly takes its place alongside the genre greats. The beautiful presentation, tight control and - above all - expressive stealth gameplay make it a joy to play. It's got great replay value because achievement hunting and exploring different playstyles keep the missions fresh and interesting even if you know their layouts by heart. It's light on story, but that is a purposeful design decision. The fact that this game single-handedly invented a gameplay formula for 2D stealth gameplay that works this well impresses the heck out of me and reminds me of the design brilliance of the original Thief. If you're a fan of the genre, you really should've played this by now. And even if you're not, it's accessible enough for newbies to give it a good shot.

I was looking for a game that would give me a pretty good ninja experience and this one didn't disappoint. This is a cool side-scrolling stealth platformer where you get to unlock and use all kind of ninja tools to sneak by guards in each level, or dispatch them in any number of ways. The game has cool mechanics; you can climb walls, hang from the ceiling, run, sneak, traverse air ducts, knock out lights, terrify guards, kill them, distract them with noise makers, hide behind or in things, glide, and all kinds of other ninja-like things. You have to be careful not to be seen and you have to be careful of noises you make. All of these mechanics are well-implemented in a 2-D world. You can go completely pacifist if you want to; you'll just have to be extra sneaky as you traverse each level. There are puzzles that make sense as you navigate buildings and take out security systems. The story is just so-so and I wasn't crazy about the "Samurai Jack" cartoony style of look to the game, but the game is really fun to play. There is full controller support, but it was a little wonky at times; specifically when trying to aim some of your thrown weapons. Other than that, I recommend this game if you think ninjas are totally sweet.

This left me with mixed feelings but since I played through it, I think it's recommendable.
This could have been a really great game but has a couple of issues
* Unreliable jump arc: You can't be 100% sure that the suggested path is really what happens. Stumble in an opponent and you will more or less stop there. Sometimes I got stuck at something and did move only a pixel. Most of the time this led to an unfortunate (and theoretically avoidable) death. This made up for about 50% of my deaths ...
* Limit system and special attacks: Stumbling into or killing an opponent gives you a combo point. You need those for your special attacks (like sword throw etc). However having 5 points deletes all of them for a free move. This sounds good but normally all special would have been better thant the free action. So you try to get not too many combo points ...
* Checkpoints: Most of the time the checkpoint system works fine. However there some of them are placed ... unconcenient.
* Bugs: It happened quite often that I got an enemy stuck in a wall meaning I couldn't kill them any more. Since you get only a skill point for killing all enemies this could be a problem. I haven't checked if they count as defeated at the end of the level but rather reset to the last checkpoint.
In the end it's a fun little game with some issues.

A Valley Without Wind. AVWW is a 2-D, side-scrolling, procedural open-world, action adventure game with elements of metroidvania, roguelikes, crafting and strategy all mixed into one game. It puts an emphasis on exploring, tactical combat, and strategic planning. This is a very experimental game and has some wonky mechanics and a weird graphic style that can be polarizing for many. That said, it was well polished and can be fun to play. Especially with it’s procedurally generated world that adapts to the player’s actions and power level.
The overall goal in AVWW is to create a valley without wind by bringing peace to the world. The continent you're living on is ruled by an oppressive Overlord and his lieutenants who subjugate the world. To make matters worse, there are harsh windstorms, many strange monsters that roam the lands, Skelebots from a future time, raging oceans and many more dangers in the land. How you bring peace to a tumultuous land such as this is entirely up to you. That, is the point of A Valley Without Wind.
When you enter the game of AVWW you choose  from a variety of humanoids to be a glyphbearer,
. Glyphbearers have a glyph that follows them around, allowing them to wield magic from the various elements of nature. These Glyphbearers are assigned by the enigmatic Illari, who are giant floating crystals, to bring peace to Environ. Environ is the world around you, shattered by an unknown apocalypse. The world has forever been changed and contains lands of many different time eras all crammed together in one place. The moon itself has also suffered from the apocalypse, the damage to it is easily seen in the night sky. Once you make it through the intro-mission, you'll find yourself in a small settlement with NPCs and a floating Illari. They protect your settlement's small population & buildings as well as heal your wounds when needed. With you, their hopes and goals lie.
As a glyphbearer, you have the forces of nature at your command: fire, water, earth, air, light, and entropy. These magic spells fill your arsenal of weapons to damage, protect or heal. Your spells cost mana to cast, though your mana pool regenerates quickly. You can be several different kinds of glyphbearers from different time eras including Skelebots. Different characters in the game comes with their own uniquely generated stats. Though you wield a powerful arsenal at your command, you’re very likely to die quite often in the game. Which is intentional with the game’s perma-death system. It isn’t the end of the game when you die, as your items and spells will transfer over to the new character. The only thing that doesn't transfer over are your base/upgraded stats from upgrade stones that you can find while exploring. It should also be noted that dying also causes you to leave behind a vengeful ghost that will attack you later. Which you can kill ghosts, but they can possibly throw a wrench into your plans. Especially if you died in a boss room. So, you’ll want to avoid dying as much as you can. Saving, by the way, is done automatically in the background. That means "scum-saving" is an unavailable tactic in progressing through AVWW. The world of Environ is a harsh and unforgiving place in more than one way.
Exploration is one of the main features of this game and this is the first game where I didn't question why I was exploring. I simply wanted to. I could and have spent an insane amount of time exploring the depths of Environ. Finding all sorts of goodies, new places to see and monsters to fight. The exploration is so good that it might be a little too too much for its own good. You'll feel the need to explore each and every building or cavern that exists. But the game was designed for you to explore only necessary buildings and you could potentially burn out from exploring everything. That's where the encyclopedia comes in to help point you in the right direction. The encyclopedia is heavily detailed with a glossary of terms, useful tips and a to-do list to keep you on track.
Combat is the second staple of the game. The combat is surprisingly engaging. Being a side-scroller means a lot of dodging enemy attacks while simultaneously throwing spells back at them. All of your spells are instantaneously cast, giving combat a frantic and fast tempo. Especially considering there are few ways to protect or heal yourself. There aren’t any traditional potions in the game. So, you're encouraged to defeat the enemy as quickly as possible while avoiding damage. The assortment of enemies won't make this easy though as they cast their own spells and touching them causes you to be knocked back, taking damage. Add in fall-damage, a lot of hostile mobs and surviving can be very rather difficult. But if you die, it’s not so bad. So long as you don’t mind facing the ghost(s) of mistakes past that rise to make sure you don’t die too much in the future. The permadeath mechanic in this game is properly balanced in my opinion.
Settings for AVWW1 are pretty much feature complete for a 2D title. Multiple resolution options, V-Sync, controller support, audio sliders and options to turn down the intensity of the graphics are here. Key rebinding is here as well and is quite in-depth. The graphics and animations are a major polarizing feature of this game. Some like them, other’s don’t. I personally liked them but I'm definitely an odd one. The up to eight people Multiplayer is ok but I found that most would go off on their own and do their own thing It doesn't really encourage being on the same screen.
A Valley Without Wind (1) was a fun experience. However, fun in an experimental idea sense. This won’t appeal to everyone between its odd collection of game mechanics and it’s polarizing graphics. In my opinion though, its open-ended gameplay makes for a very rewarding exploration and city-building experience. Even if the combat is a bit lacking sometimes. The exploration is very satisfying, allowing you to explore huge levels. It goes on and on and is well paced to keep your interest going. If you like weird metroidvania experimental games, then you should definitely give A Valley Without Wind a chance to win you over.

This game is exceedingly well executed, and is an example that I give when talking about games that have been done "right".
Pros:
-The art style fits very well, and even though it's reminiscent of old 90's cartoons, the game it still very dark in tone.
-The controls are some of the tightest I've dealt with, and this is a very big deal for me, as I often find controls aren't anywhere near responsive enough in games like this.  Note though, that I'm using an xbox gamepad, I have no idea how this game handles other controllers or KB+M.
-The puzzles are well thought out and well executed; and where a lot of games it feels like the developers actually utilize questionable design choices to make puzzles harder artificially, this game feels more old school in that the puzzles work with the game mechanics to be challenging without frustrating.
-You can play the way you choose.  There are a variety of options within your loadout and within the game mechanics that let you decide whether you want to use stealth and deception, to sneak through a level, or slaughter everything from the shadows, or any combination of the two.
Cons:
-There isn't enough of this game.  It's a little short and you'll find yourself still wanting more when it's over.  Opening this game up to the steam workshop and letting people design challenge levels would greatly increase replay value.
-There are a handful of random difficulty spikes in a select few areas that can be frustrating to get through, but they are few and far between, and don't detract from the experience in any meaningful way.

The Way of Life is somewhat troubling to me. A game with a lot of ambition that keeps me endlessly optimistic.. but cautiously optimistic nonetheless. The decisions made for the game are unnerving, but they don't seem like outright bad ideas for the game being made. Or even like cheap or pretentious ideas. Just ideas that seem to point to a cheap and pretentious mind-set of game development, that makes me genuinely concerned, but still kind of open to the idea of this experiment.
Seeing it's transition from three seperate people walking down the same street with different viewpoints of that street, to three comepletely irrelevent stories about those same three people from before seems like a sudden change if not simply inoquous at best. And the personality of these three characters seems out of place from the beta that I played in the beginning.
Gone are the days of childlike innocence, playing adventure down a street to get some ice cream. Now the child is collecting love memorabilia to convince his dad to stop beating his mom. The suited man is now trying to go home from his job, instead of go TO his job, and his nightmare deals with his family in peril on a floating space rock. And the old man dreams of death chasing him down a temple run arena. My point is that this game is worry-some even if it'll all turn out alright. And it doesn't help that they set up a money campaign the moment the game came out.
Although I'm ever curious, I still think this game is worth keeping your eye on.

The Way of Life is a short hgame that wants to send out a message. That message is glaringly obvious to any normal human being however, and what's worse than the game's bad setting are the controls.
Controller support does not exist -- you can make the camera go ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, and you can make the character's movement twitch. Finding that out, I reached for my mouse and keyboard only to realize the characters (the first and last, but I'll get to that later) slowly move to the right. It's comparable to a gamepad's left thumb stick being stuck halfway to the right.
The gameplay is ruined by the bad controls and glitches, but that's not all. The second playable character, the elderly man, is a mess as you barely have control over his movement and vision. Some of his short screentime is scripted, so you have no control over him at all during that, but what's worse is that you're never told when the automation ends. With the slowly-walking-to-right issue I mentioned earlier, this only leads to death and it took me a while to realize when I was supposed to take over.
The last playable character, the child, is supposed to be a lively one -- mouse sensitivity jumps to unbelievable heights, which is a shock coming from the old man and his barely moving FOV. The child's level is supposed to be a simple parkour one, where you jump from one step to the next. The walking-to-right bug, high mouse sensitivity, and the fact that this the camera is first person are all things that make the last level (last out of three, mind you!) impossible to beat.
In short: don't install the game or you'll end up being irritated enough to write a negative review.

This game gets ridiculously addicting once you get the hang of it. If you like fast paced shooters that require you to have good movement and aiming abilities, then you will likely have a blast with this. There is definitely a skill curve here, but it is very rewarding as you notice yourself improve over time. The variety of classes offer a range of play styles, while also all being plenty capable of scoring kills and working towards objectives. There are no pure tanks/supports (for instance, the battle medic has a grenade launcher that is plenty useful while also being able to put down health packs for teammates), so you can be useful with whichever class you choose to practice and play. This means that teamstacking a certain class isn't as big of a deal as it would be in other class-based shooters, but still isn't necessarily recommended either.
This game plays nothing like Overwatch at all. It only initially appears similar due to the unique character cast and the loot box system. While the characters in this game do have their own unique abilities, including an Ultimate, they are not as critical as they would be in Overwatch. Your expertise in using your weapons as well as utilizing movement will determine whether or not you win most fights. Your abilities are more secondary, but are still definitely useful in playing your class to its fullest.
Loot boxes are unlocked when leveling up, but can also be purchased with real money. They strictly contain cosmetics (player and weapon skins along with decals) with no competitive advantage. Duplicate loot seems to award currency that allows you to buy a specific skin. All future content/dlc will be free to everyone who buys this $30 game.
While the playbase is quite small, I haven't ever had an issue getting into a match (on US West servers at least). The devs have stated that they have no intention of abandoning this game any time soon. They've also been good about communicating with the community and putting out good patches.
If you do decide to try it out, put in some time and try out different classes. It took me a couple hours before a certain class really clicked for me and its been insanely fun since then. There unfortunately isn't much of tutorial for new players, other than a solo practice level with stationary bots and general tips, so it really helps to read up on this game a little. There are small critical mechanics such as the Blindfire ability (shooting your gun behind you to gain momentum; mainly in zero-G areas) or bunny hopping (repeatedly jumping across the ground in non-zero G areas to keep most of your momentum) that aren't explicitly explained, but are definitely necessary in performing well. Even the slower/heavier classes can really get moving around by just utilizing those two abilities.

Here's what I think of Grand Theft Auto 5's singleplayer.
It's a phenomenal experience. From the streets of Los Santos, to the dry, arid desert of Sandy Shores, to the northern fishing town Paleto Bay, the game is incredible throughout. The driving mechanics are a near perfect blend of arcadey and realistic, with car performance being realistically simulated, but with speed and traction altered to make the cars handle more easily. The radio stations are unique and varied, all with incredible music and funny satire. The game world is magnificently detailed, no two locations could possibly be mistaken for eachother, even out in the wilderness or the desert. The story is fine, but it serves as a suitible wrap around the wonderful anarchy that makes GTA's gameplay so fun. The gunplay is fine, not more. Overall, the singleplayer alone is well worth the $60.
Now, here is what I think of Grand Theft Auto Online.
Like an estranged younger brother, GTA Online seeps off of the success of it's cohort, borrowing the best mechanics and twisting them into something darker. While the driving, shooting, and open world from the singleplayer remain, the story is replaced by basic missions with menial tasks to complete and worthless rewards. The free, open anarchy is replaced by opressive, unfair tyranny by the players who have more on the players who have less. In GTAO, you're either in freeroam being killed by some b*stard with a fighter jet, or an armored truck, or a sniper rifle; or you're in a mission, grinding out cash and xp, so you can some day be the one on the other end of the stick, with the fighter jet, and the armored truck, and the sniper rifle. Or, you could take a shortcut and purchase your way to the top. The loading times are atrocious;' just loading in to the game is 3-5 minutes or longer, and between every single mission there's at least a full minute of loading in or out of freeroam. There is no substance to this game, and the only motivation is to have more than other players. That kind of toxicity is what fuels this games' success. So unless you want to be a part of that cycle, turn away now.
I can't deny it, I've spent more than 1500 hours in this game, most of which are in online. This cruel system has sucked me in; don't let it suck you in too.

I give it an "eh" for effort. Nothing special here.  The gameplay is a series of platforming "chains" that must be completed or you need to restart.  You get a couple of fights along the way, but its all platforming for the most part.  And by "a couple", thats what i mean. Literally one "minion" as you enter each new area, (which you can "cancel" if you get to the warp-in fast enough" and boss fights.  It's like combat was an afterthought.  The platforming was amusing, but it rarely gets tough or tests your reflexes. Your main character does most things automatically, just waiting for your input based on special triggers.  Someone obviously thought this would be a fun game, and built an intriguing storyline, but then the execution utterly failed.  Don't be fooled by the pretty graphics, playing Prince of Persia: Sands of Time trilogy would be a much better use of your time.  And yes, the ending is terrible.

I really liked this game when I started it. The grapics are cool and unique. The user interface is simple. The fluid dicipline system is a good bonus. Being able to go through a 'hunt' or dungeon once (before I had to grind in order to gain enough in-game money to continue) and get gear I could use was refreshing. I first tried the standalone client, then the browser and eventually switched to Steam. This game has a lot of potential to break the norm. I  have experienced some bugs that did not totally hinder my game.
What I found dissapointing was finding out that the game has been abandoned by most players and that an active community does not exist. Upon first deciding to try out the game I was banking on it being an MMO only to find out it will have a co-op feature in the future.
I thought overall the game was good, still needs fine tuning and attention. I don't know if after this long it's going to succeed unless somehow enough resources are accumulated (through Spicy Horse or a different company that potentially takes it over) and it's really given some TLC.
Some suggestions I thought of while playing:
-Bigger inventory or base storage.
-The option to use they keyboard to move and fight.
-More character customization.
-More tutorial/walkthrough in the beginning on more complex concepts than moving and attacking.
-Make dropped items easier to see and/or pickup, perhaps with an auto-pick up option.
-Be able to preview multiple pieces of armor at once (esp. with special items.)
-Because the game is dungeon-based make some aspect of that more in-depth, original and unique. Something
different from all the other dungeon-based games out there.
I'll hold onto the hope that development begins soon, it being 2015. However, until then, I don't know how much longer I will play.
Finally, I would reccomend the free versions of this game for first time players, if any. If you like it a lot, buy it on steam. Otherwise, wait.

The fact that it's held strong at a 95%+ approval rating by the overall community is largely owed by its strong attention to story, character detailing, a cohesive and intuitive combat system, and environments so grand and intricate that you won't hate going back and fourth between them (as the missions will make you do).  The collectible system is truly unique to the series, and was a treat to stop and pick some of them up because of how useful they were to the upgrading system.
Aside from the mystery of how Batman's cape is immune to gravity when hanging from the occasional gargoyle, I just can't get over how beautifully detailed the character models were. I do wish that there were more of them to see in terms of having more diverse enemies. The "puzzle" elements that require you to go into Detective mode were far from any sort of challenge that should make you label the game as a puzzler, but I will commend the use of Detective vision as making the game more interesting to play. It helped me make the most of the environment in stealthier portions of the game. The fighting can get a bit more repetitive, but is countered by putting upgrade points into combat improvements - if you're not into beat-em-ups, this isn't the game for you. I cannot recommend this game enough for fans of the franchise - it was a strong start with a series that came into the gaming world with the best intentions, and certainly lived up to the hype.

I hate stealth games.
Well♥♥♥♥♥♥ here I am, recommending one that I love.
MotN is an atmospheric 2D stealth side-scroller game with a gorgeous art style, reminiscent of (ninja) Shank. In it, you can feel as a stealthy (ninja) predator waiting for the perfect moment to strike at your prey from above (or below) and bring end to their miserable existence (or not).
I won't spoil the story, which is okay, but also sorta meh and not really of much importance. What it boils down to you as a player is that your job is to infiltrate a series of buildings, overcoming a large number of armed guards by any means you choose. Over time and via completing goals in the missions, you unlock an array of tools, abilities and costumes which all alter you playstyle. You can only bring a couple to your mission, making hard decisions, and this presents one of the many strengths of the title.
You are never bound to progress in one way or another. You can choose to be a silent intruder, not raising a single alarm and progress through the whole level without anyone knowing. Or you can choose to go all out, kill any guards you encounter, and use their bodies as grim reminders of your presence - to instill fear in the few remaining survivors. Do this enough and such terror strikes them that they go mad and start shooting anyone they see, including their own.
The controls are crisp and, very importantly, with enough practice you can tell the outcome of your actions in advance and plan. This is the one thing that typically bothers me in stealth games - that you don't have complete information - and you are thus making guesses and relying on random outcomes being favorable. In MotN, all the necessary information is relayed via a set of audio-visual clues, vision reticules etc. Be observant enough, and you see predictable patterns in the guards' actions, which you can exploit. Be hasty, and these petterns will come to bite you a bit later when you are chased by a billion other guards. There are ways in which the game makes this harder for the player later on, but all present an enjoyable challenge to overcome.
As such, the game is in essence a sort of a puzzler, where you are trying to find the flaws in the defense and use them to your advantage. This style reminds me a bit of the old Commandos games, but with only a single highly mobile directly controlled guy.
But much better :)
Overall, this game is a definite must have, nice to look at, loads of fun to play - grab it, play it, enjoy it.

Mark of the Ninja is a 2012 2D stealth game developed by Klei (Pronunciation pending) Entertainment, previously notable for the Shank games, and who have gone on to develop Invisible Inc and Don't Starve.
Every major point there is to judge a game on, Mark of the Ninja hits off the tee with flying colours.
It's gorgeous, somehow managing the make the typically sore-looking "puppet" models animate smoothly, and the emphasis on hand-painted backgrounds blends in perfectly with the silhouette foreground. At any moment, you could stop and be treated to one hell of a view, or immediately start and be treated to one hell of an animated snack.
Supported by the sound design and aesthetics alike, the mechanics - not just the responsive controls, but everything from the unconventional and instantly readable UI to the array of distraction and indirect attack devices - are beautiful. Far from forcing you to wait for the AI to make its rounds, Klei took advantage of the scenario and gave the player an insane amount of maneuverability and control over the situation.
You play as a ninja, it's in the title, you get the idea.
It's also worth noting that the Special Edition is worth getting - it adds a new level with an old-timer, a more unique playstyle to mess with, and a ridiculous amount of commentary. That was well worth reading, awkward history lessons and all.
Now a game doesn't need to be perfect to be worth playing, and while that's the case, Mark of the Ninja ain't perfect. There's some annoying bugs regarding checkpoints and awkward (sometimes disastrous) spawns when respawning at those checkpoints. Climbing over and around crates is tip-toeing on eggshells else seeing your ninja throw himself across the room, and some weird, but frustratingly reproducible, lack of the Focus Effect doing anything to offscreen entities.
It's an incredibly short game - 12 levels and 6 hours for a reasonable first playthrough. It gets shorter on each extra playthrough, once you know the "solution" you either execute that or bypass the "puzzle" entirely. Infinitely shorter on NG+, which smears half your screen in vaseline at all times and is horrible to play. I recommend rushing to the exit and then never playing that mode again.
Now this wouldn't be bad in itself - at least the shortness itself, NG+ can go suck a tattooed egg - and it definitely lends itself to the game's pacing over, say, double the amount of the same levels.
There's a distinct lack of narrative climax throughout the game, however. Despite all the commentary, the repeat playthroughs and the trippy ending sequence there's only a handful of characters who barely interact and mostly just show up, react to the player character, then die. While the story ends well, staying invested in the tale of these characters during the bulk of the game was a struggle.
The odd decision to make the protagonist completely silent and then have a side-character speak for him anyway certainly didn't help. Then to simultaneously insist that the unnamed, silent character is a full-character and that you should be invested in his perception.
That side-character was so boring. All the characters were boring and one-note. I didn't care. I still don't.
Fortunately, Mark of the Ninja is a mechanics-focused game. That's what matters, and that's what it does well.
Despite wearing its inspirations on its sleeves, referencing other stealth games constantly in commentary and supplementary material alike, Mark of the Ninja completely fails at its dreams of derivative mediocrity, and with its elegant execution of bringing such an established genre to the second plane, manages to be both one of the most unique and one of the best stealth games released in recent years.
This game is well worth your time, no matter what you're into. I'd recommend it to anybody.

NOTE: This is a review for a free to Play game as as such, you should not take it or any other review seriously. Play it for yourself, it's better that way. It does costs you nothing after all.
Time Clickers is like Clicker Heroes, only in an FPS perspective, simpler and easier to get into and executed atleast 3 time better.
Let's start with my #1 gripe with Clicker Heroes; Prestiging and Prestige Tokens.
This game has those, Time Warps and Time Cubes. Time Warps are only unlocked once you get some Time Cubes and have unlocked every ability.
Time Cubes give you a permanent 20% boost to DPS (5 of them gives you a 1x boost and so on for example) and this boost stays if you spend them or not. You can buy things from the ability to start at later waves upon a reset, start with more money upon a reset, or doing a very large variety of things into categories of Gold, Damage, Abilities and Clicks.
You can buff individual weapon's DPS by 100% per upgrade, or you can decrease ability cooldowns. If you want, you can increase how much gold you get per box by buffing gold find, and even you can upgrade the number of time cubes you can get.
These Artifacts, as they're called, have anywhere from a single level to 500 and they're all wonderful, not a isngle one is useless.
Gold is given when you kill cubes which are all that enemies are, jsut a collection of cubes, only you slowly destroys parts of an enemy, effectively de-atmoizing them.
Upgrades are often-appearing, 5 being for every range of 100, and a promotion at 100s to gain access to a new range of upgrades in the next 100 levels.
All of these allow for Time Clickers to essentially have no progression walls, which every other idle game and clicker game has. There's more or less just... slow parts, at which poit you should just time warp and get a higher DPS boost so you can power through it.
The game's progression is only fast if you actively play it and is infact designed around it, many abilities buffing the click pistol in ways that make those abilities the most devastating, such as punchthrough, which allows you to ghost-shoot through an unlimited number of cubes, hitting all of them equally in the same line your shots are in.
The game actually feels rewarding, never will you wonder "Should I spend my cubes, or jsut hold on to them" since... their bonus is never lost. Ever.
All in all, I could rant and rave about this game for literally hours on end, jsut play it yourself, it is literally like any game similar to it, only it does everything better and... it basically makes Cookie clicker and Clicker Heroes look completely boring.
I give this game a 10/10, it is Legendary, what should be the standard for future Clicker/Idle games. Once I get to the highest point, I shall determine if this recieves Godlike status.
As far as I know, there's no bad parts to this game, nothing to gripe about legitimately.

TLDR: Great gameplay, fast gameplay, skill based gameplay - With gamemodes that does not cater the gameplay. Too complicated for its own good.
The game feels great, it runs great and mostly its just really satisfying getting kills. Most classes are fun and no class i like another, very diverse class choices. Most roles can be taken, tank, assassin, healer and it usually work in that way too, requires some teamwork to shine though.
What makes this game "bad" is the gamemodes, they are competing against overwatch and therefor all the gamedoes are objective based. The gamemodes are good, domination, capture the flag, king of the hill - all gamemodes they put twists to. What it is lacking though is just a pure team deathmatch were killing is the objective. The gameplay is fast, killing is quick and getting killed is quick and mostly that is what you want to do most. Kill. It needs a free-for-all or a team deathmatch to really let casual gamers get into it.
Now classes, the classes are great, for what they are. However they try to make most classes work in many ways regarding range and mobility. There is no pure sniper class, there is no true shotgun class and that is for me a big deal. They do have the gunslinger, half sniper and half close range burst, this makes for a versatile class but both sides feels weaker than what you expect.
Wraith is probably the class wich is pure close-ranged, running and gunning class. It is what it is and doesnt do much else. Most other classes has a sencond weapon to cater close range or long range combat, wich they in my mind dont need. If you want to play close range you switch class not weapons to get a weak side arm that might work.
To healing, healing is very weak in this game, wich is probably a design choice. Healing is clutch and doesn't really help in the heat of battle, you have to run away to grab health packs or go somewere silent were your healer can throw you stuff or give you a shield. The healing classes do deal alot of damage wich makes them feel great playing but the healing feels weak.
To summarize, fun game that needs more simplicity.

Look at the hours played of all the reviewers and you'll see very few over 20.  The question is why does a game that looks great and has so much potential end up with the game play hours of an RPG Maker game?
The reason is that Birthdays is a fishbowl maker.  You put down terrain.  You fill it with water (temperature / moisture).  It chooses what fish you get based on the your choices.  Once you've done that, you can watch an unchanging world.
You have fun up until that last step.  Every creature in the game is a representation of a number under the hood.  It walks around and makes noise, but it doesn't actually do anything.
And that's when you see your limitation in the game.  You can only affect the terrain.  The only way that the animals live or die is based on terrain you make.
You end up with an expensive terrain editor with creatures that are check boxes with pretty animations.
Was it fun?  It was INCREDIBLY fun.  Was it worth the $40?  You need to ask how much 10-20 hours of an incredible game is worth to you.  For me, it's not worth $40.

One of my favorite games from the last few years. The game is absolutely bonkers ridiuclous and I love it. It is very much an homage to action films of the 1980s in every aspect. The visuals, the narrative are heavily influenced by classics like James Cameron's The Terminator, Paul Verhoeven's RoboCop and John Carpenter's Escape From New York. The gameplay can be wonky at times, mainly due to the mechanics being the same that are found in Far Cry 3, but what is lost in wonky mechanics is made up for in the increased abilities you gain by playing as a human-cyborg hybrid voiced by Michael Biehn (Kyle Reese in the original The Terminator). Like I said, the game is one big homage to 1980s action cinema, and the campy tone compliments both the narrative and the gameplay. This game would be almost completely insufferable if the tone were serious in any way. I won't get into specifics because if you haven't played this game, there's quite a lot that's better left to be discovered for the first time.
As far as game soundtracks go, this one should have definitely won some awards. It is completely complimentary to the game, again with many influences from the synthwave soundtracks of 80s action cinema, which is not surprising since the soundtrack artist is Power Glove. The soundtrack seamlessly flows between tense Carpenter-esque beats into more modern tracks, all of which sound consistent and enhance the overall experience. I totally recommend the soundtrack, it's a great listen both in and outside of the game.

GTAV Single Player is still a worthy addition to the Grand Theft Auto series after all those years, even though it never got any expansions besides the "next gen" launch. GTA Online is the single worst online experience I ever had in my life, on top of a shiny AAA polish. By all means buy it if you want to play the story mode, community mods, or modded online dedicated private servers, but I urge you to stay far away from GTA Online. Don't get addicted to it. It's not worth it.
Let me show a rundown of what your GTA Online experience will be. I'll assume that you saw the Deluxo (flying Delorean) on the trailer, and you really want to play just to get it and have fun with it.
The first thing you'll notice after making your character is how long the game takes to load online, even after loading all map assets. That's because it uses a peer to peer architecture, instead of having any dedicated servers (like they don't make enough money to host them...). It has to connect to every single person in a session before dumping you in, and it takes very long to make everyone stays in sync. And you are constantly jumping sessions, between doing different jobs and modes, getting out of them, to connecting to your friends, to getting randomly disconnected all the time and having to do it all again. Expect 10% to 20% of your time in game being wasted on load screens, depending on the quality of your internet. Loading screens between interior areas and exterior areas are also unusually long for whatever reason.
Next thing you'll notice is that most of the stuff shoved in your face is extremely expensive, and how little content caters to new players. It urges you to buy the expensive Criminal Enterprise Starter Pack, or else you are going to be grinding missions for days in order to get an expensive enough apartment to do heists, a car, and one of the criminal enterprises, in order to start making money for your Deluxo. While you do that, you will have to deal with people in public sessions that already play the game for a long time, and are going to grief you with military cars, jets, explosives and powerful weapons, spawn camping you for hours without end, since you can't do VIP and enterprise missions on a private session. Public sessions in 2017 are a warzone. To top it off, until you get to level 100, you will have much less HP than other players, which is a stupid game design decision.
The heists (not doomsday) are the life blood of GTA Online. They were the most anticipated DLC, are the most fun piece of content, and gives a lot of money in missions that are done in private sessions. But even then, you are going to have to deal with some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t game design. First, you need four people to do then, and they can't be completed if even one person doesn't know what he's doing, harming everyone else in the process. Then there's the long unskipable cutscenes after some really difficult checkpoints that are going to demotivate you even more. Then there's the fact there's little variety to the stuff you'll be doing, and you will see yourself relentlessly grinding the same, most rewarding one if you don't want to deal with public sessions. Did I mention that the loading between tries is extremely long?!
Then you will realize that in order to make enough money to rival the microtransaction option, you will have to own one or more of the criminal enterprises. You will then come across the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t public session mandatory missions, with it's ridiculous AI that can headshot you all day while you run, and civillians that ram into you on purpose when you come across then, and the fact that everyone else in the session gets a huge blip on the map showing where you are and are rewarded for destroying you and disrupting your missions. You can spend a whole month grinding $2,000,000 in crates, just to have this one guy in a jet or with an orbital cannon destroying everything you worked for. Your stolen import/export cars can even expontaneously explode in your face if everyone else disconnects from your session (and it happens a lot, the online is unstable). It's blatant frustration being induced to make you buy money through microtransactions.
Now, you did one of two things: you caved to the microtransaction option, or you painfully got through everything to get there. It's time to buy your Deluxo and customize it! Not so fast though. You will then come through some of the content paywalls. While you can store your Deluxo in any cheap garage (some of the cars can't, they need one of the expensive enterprise options), you will need a MOC ($1,165,000 cheapest bunker + $1,225,000 MOC) or an Avenger ($1,250,000 cheapest facility + $3,450,000) on top of the Deluxo ($3,550,000 trade price), and some more (sometimes $500,000) to customize it. Considering how an $8,000,000 shark card costs USD $100.00, and the Deluxo is not even that good, you can see that this is NOT worth it at all. And there's a lot of money dripping that is going to make you lose a lot of money in the long run, like insurance costs and daily expenses for every single property and enterprise you own. Leave your game running overnight to let your product be ready to sell by the time you wake up, and you can lose up to $200,000 when you were not expecting.
And that's only some of pieces of content in the game, there is a lot more to buy. A random boring piece of clothing can cost up to $100,000. Every couple of months comes out a car that blows other cars out of the water so you need to buy and customize it in order to stay competitive in races, and there are a lot of different types of races and car categories. Couple this with the fact that Rockstar loves to put cars in categories that are obviously not meant for them. It's a ♥♥♥♥♥how.
When you are at the top, you will come to realize that no one around you actually plays fair and square. There are money glitches coming out every new DLC, and on PC there are a lot of people using mods online. Rockstar has proven to be very bad at banning those people, and when they try to, they end up getting people that had nothing to do with it. So they just don't bother. Don't be surprised if all your expensive weapons are wiped out, or if you start to explode inside your own house.
That's everything I have for now. This is what you are signing into when entering the world of GTA Online. And that's the kind of stuff that you should expect from future Rockstar games, so always wait for it to come out before buying.

So I've never written one of these before, but I feel that a warning for prospective buyers is in order.
I've played this game a lot as you can see, since (very) early access. Clearly I liked it in the past, but now I'm not so sure. Why?
There is very little, if any, testing of a new update before it gets pushed out. Crippling bugs like the game not launching on Mac and/or Linux, black screens and other such delights are often missed and unleashed on unsuspecting players. I seriously wonder if any testing is done at all, these bugs are so bad and so obvious they surely would have found them by just opening the game once. This was somewhat acceptable in early access, but by now it's ridiculous.
Class balance is handled in a haphazard way at best. Obvious problems are often ignored or "fixed" by doing the wrong thing. Some classes are cleary more powerful than others.
Developers have recently added a system that helps friends play together. Fine I suppose. But in the process they removed all automatic team balancing. Apparently it clashed with their new system. This is incredibly stupid. Matches are now wildly unbalanced by default, players switch to the winning team without penalty and teams aren't even scrambled between matches, which is hilarious when half your team leaves between matches because you now face the other full team with just two mates. Again, this is incredibly stupid.
A competitive mode has been promised. Last year. Still haven't seen any of it beyond a few second hand rumours. On the other hand, this is probably a good thing because playing competitively with the problems I already mentioned is a bad idea.
The hit detection is all server side, so I hope you like dying in cover. Because you will. A lot.
If you don't care about any of this, go ahead and get this game. You will probably enjoy it for a while, enough to get your moneys worth out of it. But if you care just a bit, I would stay away for now. Plenty of other games out there after all.
Update 16 June '17: a new update was released today and guess what it did? It made the game not launch on mac. Hard to ignore the urge to yell "I told you so" at the screen.

In concept, it's a great game, in practice, it's F****ing awful. I managed to get through the first few levels, despite the game doing its absolute best to make that an impossibility. Now, when I say that, I don't mean the game is hard, in fact, it's really easy, or it would have been if ANY of its mechanics worked properly. I found myself redoing fight after fight after fight well over 10 times each, and not because my plan didn't work, no when my plan worked, it went swimmingly, but the game makes it SO hard to implement any plans  I might have that it's largely irrelevant whether I have a genius plan or if I just win it.For instance, the jump arc that appears when you're setting up your jump has a tendency to be innacurate to a startling degree. I'd line up a shot for the floor below me and end up moving less than a foot on the floor I was already on then getting shot because every guard had his gun trained on me. There's a "hint" in the game that says "The jump arc is a lie", and that annoys me more than anything else, because it's true! if the devs KNEW the mechanic they implemented was fautly, why did they leave it in? Not only that, but there's NO WAY to move in combat unless you jump, so you'll often find yourself screwed because you tried doing something that SHOULD have worked. Beyond that, this game is tagged is a stealth game, not only is it decidedly NOT a stealth game, the game even says it isn't! The devs are marketing one product and knowlingly delivering a different one. There's no way to avoid combat, and the game isn't great at telling you that until it's too late. I bought into the stealth kill tree early on, hoping I could avoid encounters that way, but no, the game forces you to deal with its janky jumping, no matter how hard you try to avoid it. Hell, even if the game DIDN'T force you into combat, every time you manage to escape with any guards in the room left alive, you only have 10 seconds left before they sound the alarm, and if that happens, you miss out on an ability at the end of the level. I'm not talking about piddly little concept art packs, or a new costume if you complete X objectives, I'm saying that every combat ability you get requires you to accomplish all 3 tasks on every level to get one. Which of course only compounds the issue. Sure, I managed to get through the combat after 20 tries, but now I have 10 seconds to find a guard and LET HIM SEE ME so that the alarm countdown will stop. So counterintuitive it hurts.
tl;dr: You have no control over your playstyle, and even if you did, the controls are so **** that it's irrelevant.

I picked up Ronin for 1 euro on the Humble Bundle, although the pick of the crop was "Gods will be watching" which turned out to be♥♥♥♥♥♥
I took a brief look at Ronin's description and heard that it was turn-based, which is usually a bad sign, and after coming straight from Gods will be watching, I wasn't expecting anything great.
The game proved me wrong pretty damn quickly.
I'm a massive fan of games like Gunpoint, Hotline Miami and Superhot, so when Ronin came along with the same mechanics, but then made them time-based, it pretty much tipped those mechanics on their head. Combat is fluid and responsive, I get into crazy situations where I barely escape by the skin of my teeth, and to top it all off, the game forces you to improvise rather than plan.
There's nothing quite like smashing into a room through a skylight, landing on one motherf**ker, throwing your sword at another motherf**ker, then diving past the sword to grab it just in time so you can cut another motherf**ker. It's all so goddamn satisfying.
That being said, as the levels progress, the game reaches an annoying level of difficulty. The final mission had me tearing my hair out for an hour straight.
Further on the topic of flaws, the story really doesn't mean anything at all. There's no explanation for who the main character is, no explanation for why she's hunting down five guys. She has a short monologue before each assassination, but it doesn't tell you anything. And then the ending offers two choices, neither of which make any difference at all.
Then there's the skill point system. You can only earn a skill point if you ace a mission, as in, complete it without killing a civilian, raising an alarm and without leaving any enemies alive. That being said, it's impossible to do that on certain missions without specfic upgrades. That means if you don't upgrade yourself in a certain way, you can quite literally be locked out of skill points.
Say for example, there's a part where an enemy is standing underneath a light, and a civilian is watching him. You can stab the enemy, after which the civilian will see his body and raise an alarm. You can attempt to knock the civilian down, after which he'll raise an alarm, or you can kill the civilian, after which you'll lose the objective of not killing civilians, or you can leave the guard behind, which will void the "kill everyone" objective.
Turns out the solution is to get an ability that lets you drag bodies up to the ceiling and hang them there, but that costs a skill point, so you're going to be screwed in that mission unless you've gotten that skill beforehand.
Other than that, it's fine. Movement is a little janky at times, but the game is pretty good. It really needs an endless arena mode where enemies continually attack you until they eventually beat you. Also, the design on the Officer's level and the Boss's level is terrible. Just gotta say that. Expect lots of frustration on both.

I'm a very casual multiplayer FPS gamer, but I do enjoy multiplayer FPS from time to time. Quake 2/3, Unreal Tournament, Overwatch last year and now LawBreakers.
LawBreakers is fun, simple as that. It's similar to Overwatch - you get different classes with each their distinctive abilities mapped to LSHIFT/Q/E - but it's not as cartoony and with faster gameplay. There's also the zero gravity zones that make the fight go vertical, which is a nice strategic addition.
With 5 hours I've only sratched the surface of this game, but I briefly played all characters and they seem well thought and (more or less) balanced. The maps invite strategic gameplay for the different modes. It's not too difficult to get into, but as with all multiplayer games, you'll have to invest a lot of time to really get good at it. Last but not least: the random people I've played with were all friendly, even when things went haywire (on the other hand: it's a new game, so that could change when people become better and feel more 'elite' compared to others).
It does not have the polish of Overwatch, but the devs seem to be in it for the long run though so they'll get the rough edges off in time. At time of writing there's unfortunately no way to practice the maps on your own, as you can in Overwatch. There's only 1 map playable in tutorial-sandbox mode and that's it. So basically you'll have to learn the maps by playing.
Overall, if you like team based multiplayer FPS like Overwatch, you'll like this one as well.
Summarized:
Pro:
* it's fun, simple as that :)
* good characters and abilities
* 5 fine gameplay modes
* vertical combat
* friendly random people (for now)
(* not as cartoony as Overwatch, which is a very personal opinion of course)
Con:
* no single player practicing different maps / gameplay modes
* not as polished as Overwatch

I won't try to convince you of anything so I'm going to give you some information.
- The game is fun, competitive and has a great community. Nearly everyone is nice and appreciates the competitive nature of the game, but most don't get cocky.
- The game has original game modes that are very refreshing from your average TDM or CTF. However TDM would be nice, could increase the interest of the average consumers.
- The game is very balanced and has enough maps and characters to have you entertained well past the next map or character update.
- The game is pretty much bug-free, apart from one bug that I've had and some others as well, where your character's ragdoll when shot can fall through the map. This isn't gamebreaking and isn't even disctracting IMO.
- The game has a problem where people leave a match. This issue has not yet been adressed and people can leave a match without getting any punishment. Your team can become outnumbered and the enemy can have already taken such a big step ahead before new players join that it's a lost cause already. I did mention this before in a discussion thread and one of the developers took notice of this issue and said they've taken it into account.
- There's still some a-holes in the game, but what did you expect? It's a given with any online game, but comparing it to CS:GO or something, they're very rare.
- No hackers, the game is new. However as pointed out by someone to me, there are already aimbot services for LawBreakers. This sucks and I recently found out, but I have to say that I've not seen a single person that I even remotely suspect of using aimbot. Most players are just looking for a fun and competitive game.
- The playerbase is low, but not dangerously low. Matchmaking on my server (EU) tends to take less than 30 seconds, but of course on off-times, (like if you were to play at 2am on your local server) you can of course expect to find no match, but I believe you can change the server easily.
- The game isn't losing players fast. It was, but that's with every game, but with larger games you don't see it. If, say, a new Call Of Duty has 40.000 players on launch, that will probably drop by at least 2/3 within a week, and then it'll decline slowly. Same thing here with LawBreakers, it's pretty steady now. - Some new players play as Wraith or Assassin and tend to not focus on the objective, but focus on kills. Please, please, please, if you buy it, do NOT be that player. You can play as either of those classes, but just play the objective. It'll get you more XP and it'll get you and your team to increase your chance of winning.

A solid game that I enjoy a lot. It shares a lot of similarities with Overwatch, which is not a bad thing at all, but at the same time it feels a lot faster and more action-soaked. I really, really enjoy the "gravity-defying" concept - basically you're not limited to the ground at all, and in fact you'll spend most of your time flying in this game - which adds a lot to the already fast-paced feeling of the game. The classes are varied and have a lot of uniqueness to each one gameplay-wise, and the game itself is very well-made and mostly bug-free.
As far as queue times, I've read a lot of reviews saying they are too long, but I never really experienced that myself. Finding a match takes no longer than a minute for me in most cases. So I'm not really sure what others mean by that.
Other good points I would give to this game are the fantastic soundtrack accompanying it and the lovely level-design that I personally really appreciate. It just feels fun and well made.
As for cons: balance is still not perfect, mostly because the game is pretty new. Some classes can out-perform others, but not to the point where it breaks things. In addition, players leaving the match can become a pain because the refill system takes very long to find a different player to fill that empty slot, which in turn tilts the match in one team's favor. However, these two issues will probably be solved in the future, and I can definitely say they shouldn't be a reason to skip the game completely.
All in all, this is a very solid and fun title. I was positively surprised by it and I enjoy it a lot. If you like fast-paced and skill-based games, this one is definitely worth a try.

The game combines turned based combat and real time stealth that allows you to control a ninja out killing a limited variety of enemies. The game is rather difficult if you don't adjust your playing style to what the developer intended yet it's very entertaining and rewarding to figure out the alternate strategy to get around.
Frustrating yet satisfying. Definitely not an easy game, it does have challenges that will make you retry several levels a LOT. The designer clearly had a short list of intended ways to beat a level and if you don't realize them it can feel nearly impossible; figuring it out can be half the fun in the game. The game suffers from several glitches and inconsistent mechanics that'll make you die randomly which does ruin a few things. It's almost like a 2D Splinter Cell game in both that it really encourages stealth and how frustrating it can be that your plans will fall through for any number of "unfair" reasons.
A lot of reviews say this game can be really unfairly difficult to which I would agree there are glitches and poorly designed mechanics making it harder than it needs to be. Bullet paths aren't always accurate and the fact that if a machine gunner can be shooting just over your head it means you just can't move as most movement involves jumping up into their firing path. If you understand these mechanics you can definitely avoid them and I think that's part of the challenge.
There were however several points in the game I could barely pass or couldn't get past until I realized how to take advantage of the game. Use the right mouse button to look around, it can help find alternate paths or enemies that'll catch you off guard. A huge thing is holding the spacebar to pause time which can let you do tricks like swing through a window, grapple to the ceiling and stealth kill a group of enemies before being detected. And note sneaking is a lot more important than the game lets on because if a room has 6 enemies you can usually bring it down to 2 or 3 to make it far easier.
Special note for The General, sneak over to the right side of the map and clear them out first, then clear the left side. That'll make it so you only need to fight 5 guys rather than 10+ which I found impossible at first.

Coming from a background of someone that loves sim games, I honestly didn't know what to expect with Always Sometimes Monsters. In the beginning of the game, it felt really weird and I felt as though the game didn't know which genre it wanted to be. After getting past the introduction; however, that is where the real drama happens and I was pleasantly surprised by how great the quality of the narrative is.
Basically, you are trying to get to the wedding of your ex in the next 30 days, but you are broke and have no family or any other means to help you get to where you need to go. Fufilling jobs, getting favors, and doing side missions, all the while keeping your stamina needs up are key to winning the game. There's also a choice system as well, and depending on your actions, you can change the ending of the game.
Honestly, Always Sometimes Monsters felt as though I was binging a Netflix series. The game is just beautiful in terms of how immersive the storyline can be. I made myself the main character and my partner as the ex and things got real pretty quickly!
Also, I have to give the creators a round of applause for allowing not only interracial relationships but also same sex relationships as well.
Pros:
+Excellent narrative with real customization options to make the story your own.
+Game play that really keeps you on edge, clock ticking anxiety makes it exhilarating.
+Mini-games are really fun and quite symbolic to life as well.
+The soundtrack is really good! Very memorable soundtrack.
Cons:
- The choice sections come up really fast. I wish there was a delay or something before the choices come up, because there has been numerous occasions where I would hit the space bar to progress dialogue and accidentally make a choice that I didn't want to make!!! Please somehow fix that!
Overall, I would most definitely reccomend Always Sometimes Monsters. I just finished the game and I'm still emotional at the ending I got. Definitely worth the time and money. It's like reading an interactive book. Highly, highly recommended!

Sure this game, The Way of Life, isn't the longest game and it is pretty short. So to all you gamers who love long games this might not be for you. Where a boy wants only to have fun, imagining dragons and a candy fortress while running around and being crazy. While a man only wants to beat traffic and get to work and an elderly man just wants to be safely enjoying the rest of his life with his friends and family. This is a very short game true, but it has a lot of meaning. The graphics are surprisingly good considering this is a free game and the controls are like any other game. I highly recommend this game if you want to see life on a different level.

I want to start off that this is an awesome WW2 game. Its universal - you can play as tank crewmen, fighter pilot, paratrooper, Infantry or a Recon Unit - but does have its issues. I shall list some pros and cons and a summary...
PROS:
- Universal War
- All units involved in high ranks
- Great atmosphere
- Great maps
CONS:
- Toxic players
- Games are usually one-sided
- A very big grind (Expect a few days to get a gun or vehicle)
- Some guns are OP
- Repetitive
- Long waiting times at low player level
SUMMARY:
If you are able to grind without ripping your hair out and are a very dedicated gamer and play a lot, go ahead, but if you only play about and hour or two a day, expect to think suicidal thoughts and uninstalling it. I indeed recommend you give it a shot, but don't be surprised if you don't enjoy it after a while. Very fun to play with friends though, especially when performing an attack.
FINAL VERDICT: 7.5/10

What is "Day of the Tentacle Remastered"?
It is the classical adventure "Maniac Mansion 2: Day of the Tentacle" in a remastered version with higher quality and a load of Steam achievements, but also a reworked GUI.
As the game is a classical adventure, it is controlled almost entirely with the mouse. As I knew the game already and had finished it in 2011 for the first time over the course of a few days, I just rushed through the Steam version to get the achievements, so my time should not be an indicator for the time with "normal" play.
The game originally was conceived by Tim Schafer for LucasArts, which sadly was eventually bought by Disney and closed only recently. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, LucasArts was THE high quality studio for adventure games, although some competitors such as Westwood (Legend of Kyrandia) managed to make similarly great adventures in this style.
There is a comic style to the entire game, and it is comedic in nature with an underlying plot of time travel. Purple Tentacle is a purple tentacle (thanks, Captain Obvious!) who drinks industrial waste water and then aspires to conquer the world. The three anti-heroes to stop him are teenagers: A crazy girl, a nerd and their overweight friend.
The game includes its predecessor, Maniac Mansion, entirely to be accessed via an ingame computer. Following however the story of this game, Purple Tentacle becomes the leader of the world in a tentacle ridden future where humans are held as pets. With a time machine, two anti-heroes land in different stages of history, while the other one stays in the present. Arriving near a few founding fathers of the United States of America, ready to sign the Declaration of Independence, the past has to be altered to provide means in the future to fight against the tentacle oppression. Thanks to the flush technology of the time machine, almost all items can simply be sent to each time period, so the three characters can use them as they please.
As the plot advances, it becomes clear that this lovable game still is one of the best adventures of all time, deserving very well its plalce in - of course! - history.
The downside is that the voice actors don't sound very professional at too many times. In fact, if anything about this game is to be criticized, it is this point. Maybe a new set of voice actors would have improved the game, with options to switch between the voice sets, just as there are options to switch between the new and old graphics.
Recommended: For anyone who enjoys adventure games. In fact, everyone else also should try it on a good sale.

After 420 hours I still can't seem to get my head around this cluster♥♥♥♥ of a platform-fighter.
My Elo fluctuates between 1700-1900. Every game feels like a coin toss. Sometimes I dominate high level players, other times I get slaughtered by low level players. It never feels like I've won or lost fairly.
It's often hard to even comprehend what's happening on screen, mainly due to the many new ways that players can approach and evade with the current dash mechanic.
The hit detection is so inconsistent it hurts. Often times a successful attack or dodge will be canceled out for no reason. It's immensely frustrating when you can predict exactly what you're opponent is going to do, account for it, but fall for it anyway due to some inexplicable variable not working in your favour. My attacks always seem to just barely shave the hurtboxes of other players, and whenever I get hit it feels like my hurtbox teleports into the oncoming attack.
It always feels like there is a constant delay on inputs, particularly with dodging, which often results in me having to sit and wait patiently for my opponent to finish their combo while I'm powerless to do anything, or wait patiently whilst falling off stage before I can begin recovering, as if my character is stunned or something. It's also very easy to misinput the wrong move, and given the twitch-based nature of the game, this can cost you dearly.
Brawlhalla is a great game to play casually with friends, but it's an absolutely appalling competitive experience. It may be free, but it will cost you your sanity. There are things you can practice and learn to improve your chances at winning, but there is no mastering Brawlhalla.
