Deus Ex: Mankind Divided continues on after the events in Deus Ex: Human Revolution, where augmented individuals were secretly given a implant that would take over their body and cause them to become extremely violent - the "Aug Incident".
Adam Jensen is now part of a Interpol task force TF29 - a group that handles augmented terrorists. He would be sent to Dubai to take down a weapon smuggler. The plan goes awry when augmented mercenaries ambushed both his team and the weapon smuggler's men. They now have to figure out who are these mercenaries and why were they ambushed. After Adam returns to Prague, he would be caught in another incident that now involved innocent lives - a terrorist bombing at the train station. More questions are now beginning to pile up - who are behind these attacks?
The gameplay mechanics in Mankind Divided are much more polished and improved compared to Human Revolution. You have more options to upgrade your augments - giving you more abilities to use during combat, stealth, or exploring areas. Not only that, you have more options as well to upgrade your weapons and customize them on the fly.
Side quests are actually impressively, making it fun and interesting to the game unlike a few games where side quests are more like "Go to A, go to B, grab X items" etc... They have their own unique story apart from the main story line, which actually adds a few more hours to the game if you take the time to do the side quests.
The game also looks very pretty, with huge improvements in graphics compared to Human Revolution. You need a decent computer in order to get the most out of the graphics.
For DLC's, the "A Criminal Past" story add-on is a great DLC to have - where Adam Jensen goes undercover as a dangerous augment individual in a high-security prison meant for augmented criminals.
Overall, Mankind Divided is a great game to play. The plot is great - though cut short if you don't do side quests, gameplay mechanics are amazing, as well the graphics. I recommend to get this game when it's on sale, along with "A Criminal Past".

You could easily rename this as "We Had Lots of Ideas: The Game" because that's honestly the best way to describe it. A mashup of numerous ideas, art styles, and gameplay mechanics.
Let's start with the first and most easily noticed one, the look of the game. It's fairly inconsistant. This is compounded by the gameplay, too. At times it's trying to be Terraria where you're gathering resources like wood to make platforms, at others it's trying to be Diablo with a Mana Pool for spells and skills and exploring buildings you come across. There's blocky, almost placebo-esque objects, but they're mixed in with lumpy, mishapen boulders.. slender trees.. and even animated portals.
You start off with four randomly generated and barely customizable characters, and there's a very limited number of character designs to boot. This means when Sykdemo Thargbiscuit dies, there's a very good chance that Archibald Roundabout will take their place and look exactly the same. Except their stats may be slighty different, and depending on how far you were before you died, a lot worse. This also means you may have to go from playing a ranged mage to a melee meathead with little say in the matter.
Unlike, say, Rogue Legacy which does this with a charming upgrade system and consistant, yet progressive stats, A Valley Without Wind just kinda.. well, tosses the player into the wind. Oh, and you'll die a lot, to be sure. If not from actual mobs (which is very likely as you have no clue what you're doing, and the User Interface is clunky and unhelpful), then you're sure to die of boredom as you repeat the same handful of tasks over and over again.
I got the game ages ago as part of a bundle because I thought it'd be a fun Metroidvania sort of title, and at first glance it definitely seemed like it might be. Unfortunately, the other thing AVWW reeks of is the feeling that it's unfinished. It's pretty clear the developers got partway through progress of making the game, given it's bizarre title screen which features "asking for your key", a blurb about the aforementioned progress which hasn't updated in forever, and a scrolling storyline summary which is about as much as I ever got for plot.
Even free it didn't feel worth it. I just hope the bundle came with other games I actually enjoyed, but it was so long ago I have no idea anymore. I can definitely tell you that unless the sequel is made out of ♥♥♥♥♥♥s and maybe chocolate, it probably isn't worth the $15 it's currently sitting at, either.
As an aside, I've read that there is eventually city building. Sadly, the game just couldn't keep my interest long enough to actually make it that far. From what I understand from a friend who has played it, and a few other reviews.. you don't get the sense of progression you ought to in a game like this. Once you "complete" an island with rebuilding, bosses, and so forth, you just go off and repeat it and this happens ad nauseum. Given how the general gameplay was so unpolished, I can't imagine the rebuilding stage of it to be any better.

Birthdays the Beginning is an interesting game about building a world and letting life evolve, an interesting concept that is poorly executed. Whilst the initial hours of the game are enjoyable for those who are creative (like myself,) it quickly gets bogged down by wonky controls and tedious world building.
First of all, the story is something slapped together in a few minutes, and actually a bit cruel if you think about it. There isn't much to say about it other than the fact that it is uninteresting. This game even goes out of it's way to explain what a food chain is, so you end up wanting to skip a lot of the dialogue the red avatar tells you. Speaking of skipping, that is something you wish you could do with this game's cutscenes. Not only is the story's cutscene lengthly, but there's also a dragged out dialogue every time you start the game.
That red avatar that guides you has a voice that quickly gets old, but other than that, the sounds are charming and there isn't much unneeded music. In fact, music changes depending on how you have shaped your world, which is a nice touch. When it comes to world building --the game's main selling point-- it does it decently. Building the world is cumbersome and time-comsuming, even with the larger brushes. However, the world does feel alive and it's very satisfying seeing lush forests where there was once rock; and you were the one who cultivated it. I feel like if there was a "smooth terrain" item, it would make things much, MUCH less tedious. The lack of any smoothing tools is what keeps me from recommending it.
The UI and controls are flat out terrible; even the most basic actions in any game are somehow made complex. This is quite obviously a console port, as the controls are unoptimized for the keyboard. For instance, moving your character is done using WASD, but moving the camera is with the arrow keys. Also, pressing [Esc] does not bring up the menu, but a weird submenu that could have easily been made into hotkeys. Although if they were, they could have been just as badly placed, like holding down C to sprint (try doing that while trying to use S or D.) Some hotkeys overlap, most noticably the item hotkeys with brush size. I found myself accidentally using items on multiple occasions, which can have drastic consequences on your world. By the way, there's NO autosave either!
Overall, Birthdays the Beginning is a niche appeal game, poorly optimized, unengaging, with some moments of satisfaction.

What a fun Viva Pinata Garden Evolution game!
I've been waiting for a game like this for quite a while, and it delivers in all the ways I wanted! That being said, if you're not into simulation games, this is likely not for you, but i'll give a basic rundown of the game to help explain what it is and what you do.
Birthdays the Beginning revolves around you, the player and your avatar, doing one of two basic things: making oceans or making mountains. Doing either one is done by controlling the elevation of the landmass and will affect the temperature, which in turns affects moisture levels, and all those factors determine what can/will evolve or spawn on your world. When a new creature appears, you can register it and get a picture and basic info on what it needs to appear and its name. A lot of the creatures are scientifically accurate, but some artistic liberties have been taken to keep the aesthetic of the game in tact.
Now for some pros and cons
Pros:
- Lots of creature variety! Over 150+ at least, and that includes dinosaurs, mammals, birds, humans, ect along with many plant species
- The tutorial is pretty useful and quick to grasp, if you pay attention then freedom mode is easier to manage and understand. There are also scenarios that help you get the feel of how to spawn in the origin species for dinos, mammals, humans, ect
- Very cute aesthetic, but this is subjective I suppose. Look at screenshots of the game, if you hate this style, this may be a con
- Atospheric music that fits the game very well, sound affects are not bad either
- Items you can use/find that act as anti-frustration mechanics and help raise/lower temp, moisture and sometimes force mutate/evolve creatures if they aren't doing so naturally for you
- Freedom to mold the world as you please! You can creature mini to huge worlds with a huge variety in creature and geological permutations
- Varied camera modes, you can look from above, first person, there's even a camera mode where the UI is switched off to help you take screenshots if that's your thing
- Easy to export your level, items, creatures to a brand new world if you hate the one you made but don't want to lose progress. You can continually level up, collect animals/plants/items and just migrate all of that. Easy to save/load as well
Cons:
- Campaign's story is not really....sensible? It's pretty obvious only there to give some kind of context asto why you're doing what you do but if you're looking for a very long campaign and missions and things, there's not too much of that. The game is more freeplay, this may be a con for some
- Controls take some getting used to initially, and if you lack a controller and don't want to use one, you're out of luck since the game's pretty optimized for controllers
- For some reason, can only exit the game while you're not in the main menu?
- Some people get lagging, glitches, ect, but this hasn't happened to me and the devs are working on helping those it IS happening to. Make sure you have a good video card and that it's used when playing, it might fix most of your issues
- Price tag is a bit much. For me, this is worth the money because I am enjoying myself and can comfortably spend enough hours on this game to feel satisfied, but this game is infinitely cheaper on PS4 and most people don't feel comfortable shelling out 40 bucks for sims. Price rarely goes down too
- While there are lots of animal/plant varieties, many of the different species are just palette swaps, which while understandable, can cheapen it a bit for some
- The game is very precise about what some creatures/plants need in order to appear, so it's not very easy to make a creature spawn sometimes, even if you meet the criteria for it
Overall, the game is great if you don't mind the price, like the artstyle, like freeplay games, and like trial and error as the main method of progressing. It's difficult to really get it going, but the tutorials help and once you have the hang of it, it's easy to make the world you want and get the cool creatures to spawn in
I adore this game and really hope we get a new one in the future or some more creatures to evolve via DLC!

Having finished the whole thing more than 12 times, have to say. It is OK. don't be deceived by the 465 hours on record, most of those playthroughs were outside Steam.  Definitely do NOT buy the standard edition, but hang out for the 'Ultimate Edition' because there is LOTS of DLC and you want it all. Dragon Age Origins is something of an enigma. It is a great RPG that brought together most of the good things that Bioware had achieved with Baldur's Gate and the Neverwinter Nights games, but it falls just short of perfecting them. All the content is superb except for the absence of an explorable world, (something Bioware has never even tried to achieve). Sadly the series turned South after this. Edmonton seems obsessed with the idea that video games need to be interactive movies where players marvel at the studio's voice acting talent and cinematic cut scenes. They forgot along the way that role-playing is about the players creating their own stories. In time all of the once numerous class and race options that players had enjoyed with the AD&D based system disappeared, along with any real moral or narrative choices. Dragon Age Origins was the last Hurrah for the old-style feel. I would say that every RPG fan NEEDS to own and play the Ultimate edition of Origins. Enjoy all that is good in it. Also observe the key ways in which it fails. Origins is a great case study in RPG design.

I usually never do a written review for steam as I would prefer to produce a video review. As im typing this, I realize that I more than likely will create a long overdue video review for Ballistic Overkill which you can view on
. With that being said, lets get into why this game is one of my favorite first person shooters in quite some time.
I remember reaching out to the development team looking to acquire a review code so that I could share my opinion. I saw some gameplay online as well s the realease trailer on Steam. I thought, "This could be a rather interesting game and I can't wait to see what it has to offer." I was not disappointed at all as every match was fast paced, colorful enough to not feel like a modern day fps and fun enough to keep me wanting more.
POSITIVES
The game features several character classes that have their own advantages and disadvantages. While other games in the genre do this, the one thing that felt different was that each class levels up and earns new weapons and abilities that extend your play time. This incentive helps with longevity and creates a great sense of game padding that drives me to come back and continually play.
The graphics are rather well done as there are some really good effects and interesting locations. Lighting is pretty good and best of all...the game isn't too demanding for people with PC's that aren't that powerful. While my personal computer is somewhat powerful, I have seen this game run on medium settings with a moderate rig and it still looked pretty good.
The audio isn't the best but it gets the job done where it counts. While wearing a headset, I was able to quickly distinguish if there was an enemy nearby thanks to the sounds of footsteps and the visual aid that accompanies it. Overall nothing spectacular, but more than welcome when it comes to a game like this.
The price point is also very appealing for anyone looking to have a well made first person shooter that doesn't want to spend $40-$60.
NEGATIVES
The game maps are good but when playing it doesn't feel like there are too many of them. It also feels like match variety is pretty low. So with the limited amount of maps and modes, it feels as if there isn't enough variety.
Some of the characters feel a bit more overpowered than others and that falls in line with map design and loadout design.
There is no single player experience what so ever. I knew going into this game that it was predominately a multiplayer focused shooter, that is fine. The only thing that I wanted was the ability to play bots offline so that I could (A) learn the map layout and (B) play casually without relying on other people.
There is no controller support. I have heard that it will soon be patched into the game. I was told that when I first started playing the game and it still hasn't happened. While I am fine with playing mouse and keyboard, I have friends who are making the switch from playing games on console for years and they would like to transition into some games with a controller. Not necessarily a deal breaker, but in many instances it is.
CLOSING
In closing, if you're looking for a game that gives you an arcade feel with a modern twist then this is probably the best bang for your buck. It's not perfect by any means...but what it does do is offer hours of fun that is hard to shy away from.
SCORE
8/10

The game combines turned based combat and real time stealth that allows you to control a ninja out killing a limited variety of enemies. The game is rather difficult if you don't adjust your playing style to what the developer intended yet it's very entertaining and rewarding to figure out the alternate strategy to get around.
Frustrating yet satisfying. Definitely not an easy game, it does have challenges that will make you retry several levels a LOT. The designer clearly had a short list of intended ways to beat a level and if you don't realize them it can feel nearly impossible; figuring it out can be half the fun in the game. The game suffers from several glitches and inconsistent mechanics that'll make you die randomly which does ruin a few things. It's almost like a 2D Splinter Cell game in both that it really encourages stealth and how frustrating it can be that your plans will fall through for any number of "unfair" reasons.
A lot of reviews say this game can be really unfairly difficult to which I would agree there are glitches and poorly designed mechanics making it harder than it needs to be. Bullet paths aren't always accurate and the fact that if a machine gunner can be shooting just over your head it means you just can't move as most movement involves jumping up into their firing path. If you understand these mechanics you can definitely avoid them and I think that's part of the challenge.
There were however several points in the game I could barely pass or couldn't get past until I realized how to take advantage of the game. Use the right mouse button to look around, it can help find alternate paths or enemies that'll catch you off guard. A huge thing is holding the spacebar to pause time which can let you do tricks like swing through a window, grapple to the ceiling and stealth kill a group of enemies before being detected. And note sneaking is a lot more important than the game lets on because if a room has 6 enemies you can usually bring it down to 2 or 3 to make it far easier.
Special note for The General, sneak over to the right side of the map and clear them out first, then clear the left side. That'll make it so you only need to fight 5 guys rather than 10+ which I found impossible at first.

Definitely worth playing if you like Gunpoint and Mark of the NInja. I even got some Half Life 2 vibe from the soundtrack.
My main gripes with the game are:
- you can't jump through enemies. You'll always stun them and be slowed down yourself, which makes some deaths unavoidable if RNG is not in your favor.
- the marker showing where you'll land does not always tell the truth, which is even acknowledged in the game tips. It's pretty annoying to think that you can successfully jump over an obstacle only to hit it mid-air and have your tactic completely destroyed, forcing you to restart.
- when flying into an enemy who's group will certainly spot you, there is a split second before the turn-based combat mode starts, during which you can kill off the closest enemy. This means you have to spam the button for stopping time until you get a prompt allowing you to kill that enemy. If this is by design, then it's an annoying design.

Grappling Hook only works when the game randomly decides that it will. I was about to escape out of a window and had the grappling line all set up and the game said, "You know what? NO! You're gonna fall into those electrical wires!"

Fantastic concept, but as is, it's basically a 7-7.5 / 10 game. Could've easily been a solid 8.5 with some extra polish and refinement. Some design decisions are a bit baffling... An excellent summary can be found at good ole RPS:
(many of the caveats he mentions in the early access review still exist in the game -- specifically the bits about the jump arc and the lack of a manual checkpoint / additional player quicksave slot)
Awesome:
- I haven't played anything quite like this! When I started playing for the first time, I immediately thought "man, this is so cool!" It felt strange that I hadn't seen another a turn-based game quite like this, since the concept grabbed me pretty quickly and the tutorial bits are integrated well into the initial level(s). It's pretty awesome when the game is firing on all cylinders and everything works as you expect.
- Solid music in some levels, simple but effective art style. Would've been nice to have a few more animations for various kill strikes, but everything that's here fits.
- Cool abilities that go well with the ninja theme. Thrown sword kills, a dash strike, and a suspended garotte kill. To save yourself some possible aggravation, I'd suggest going with the Stealth-ish based skill tree at the bottom first. It definitely seems to have the most useful abilities (Shuriken stunning most of a room, dash striking someone 50 ft away based on line of sight).
Neutral:
- There's a loose framework of a story there, but I don't expect it to really go anywhere beyond a loose sketch, which is fine. (I'm a few chapters in -- maybe halfway through the game?)
- Even when the game is super annoying, it's still solid enough to want to try, try, try again! It my be frustrating at times, but it's definitely got a bit of an addictive hook. It's almost like a combat puzzler in that sense, and even when the game works against me, it does make getting that perfect combo feel that much more rewarding.
- Thankfully the game has an automated checkpoint system that is fairly sensible. It hasn't triggered for me at some horrible, non-recoverable moment that forces me to start the level over again. That said, some of the checkpoint decisions are a bit puzzling. (Why would I want to checkpoint before an elevator ride? The doors don't open automatically when it arrives at its destination, pausing to let you plan ahead...)
- Controller support seems pretty solid (tested with my standard Xbox 360 pad with a generic wireless adapter off Amazon). I played the first few levels with it, but found myself wondering if the mouse / keyboard combination would be better. I think the issues I was noticing are probably related to inconsistencies with the game itself (see below), but I can't tell, so I'm going to put this in the neutral category. I switched to M+KB and haven't looked back.
Annoying:
- The jump mechanic is inconsistent. You might expect to be leaping onto a platform, but the arc isn't quite high enough, so you end up missing it or falling back to the floor. The game handwaves this away by saying "the jump arc isn't reliable!" in the hint section repeatedly, which is... kinda lazy.
- Every movement in pause mode has to be a leap or attack action. You can't walk or crawl on the ceiling or scale walls, and switching to real time mode seems a bit flaky. Most of the time this is fine, as you're better off leaping at someone to try and kick / stun, but if you're leaping up to a platform in the middle of a room, you'll have to take more jumps to get there, as you can't hit the wall or underside of the ledge and simply climb around. Definitely more irritating in some rooms than others!
- Unclear / inconsistent "action point" mechanic. I found some instances where I'd perform basically the same action sequence to enter a room, and sometimes I'd get two ticks on the "action point" bar (it's called "Limit Break" -- some kind of Final Fantasy reference I think?), other times I'd get three ticks. I guess it's like a charge meter... I think it gives you more ticks dependent on how consistent and efficient you are (executing multiple kills in the fewest turns possible). I seem to be figuring out, but I couldn't tell you exactly what's going on.
- It would be really nice to have an additional "quick save" or player set checkpoint. I think one instance after every automated checkpoint would suffice, allowing the player to fall back to the automated checkpoint if they end up making a critical mistake after their own custom checkpoint marker has been set.
- The skill point system is a bit harsh. You have to complete all three objectives per level to get a skill point. (Kill all enemies, trigger no alarms, and no civilians killed.) As the RPS review I linked above indicates, it's a bit backwards... you're more likely to need MORE abilities if you're having trouble completing these objectives! I suppose if I get stuck on a few of them, I could go ahead and beat a level or two and come back and do them later (assuming I am able to get skill points from later levels, but they only get harder). It's somewhat at odds with the theme in that regard... You can't just stealth through levels. The only "stealth" aspects are sneaking around civilians and maybe picking off the occasional guard when convenient, but that's about it. No pacificist style playthroughs here! It's a bit unfortunate, but understandable. Just know what you're getting into beforehand, I guess?
I just picked this up super cheap in a Humble Bundle, and I'm very happy with the price I paid for it! I wouldn't pay more than $4-5 Canadian, personally. Try the demo, and if you like it, grab it on sale or get it in the bundle now. Just make sure you're willing to grit your teeth and put up with some annoyances and inconsistencies. (I assume the demo will give you a good idea of what the main game is like... I haven't tried it, so I can't say for sure.)
I understand this game was made 4by a solo developer, which is pretty impressive! I'm sure quite a bit of work went into the game. It's well done, but would've benefited from a little bit more polish and tweaking. I assume this is easier for small teams to do, since there are more people to help with testing or helping with development, but it's a solid game as is. I'd definitely be interested in a sequel or even updated "director's cut" style tweak for a nominal cost upgrade for existing owners.
Verdict: Soft recommendation -- definitely try before you buy! Pretty neat concept, and a fun game if you're not put off by a bit of inconsistency and minor fits of apoplexy. Expect to swear at the game a bit, followed by a pleasant hit of dopamine when you beat some ridiculously finicky or tricky sequence.

One of the hardest games I've played and that's without exaggeration. Maybe it's just getting used to it but the game is really designed in a way to make it incredibly hard for you to adapt to any situation it presents... And I... like this.
It is very hard to explain how RONIN works but it's a mix of real-time platforming and turn-based combat. What made the game hard for me is that I wanted to 100% all the stages, which meant no civilian kills, no alarms raised and every enemy in the stage has to be dead. Having to do all of this and keeping your sanity is very hard as the game constantly throws unfair room set-ups at you. I swear, had it not been for some of the more useful skills like the stun or the shadow strike (teleport), this game would be only for the most hardcore of masochists, and even then, they may give up on it. Having to repeat the same level over 40 times, figuring out the best way to kill everyone without setting off an alarm and keeping track of every line aimed at you or your surroundings and the one who's aiming it (could be a one shot, could be a rifle guy who fires for 2 turns or worse: a samurai that dashes through everything in his path).
I will admit, I did ragequit several times, which was a big mistake since the game doesn't remember checkpoints in the level if you leave it, so i had to start over again. All of the missions are varied in terms of stage design, not so much in objectives. The level is usually "hack these terminals, kill the target, leave" and that's fine. It follows Gunpoint's example in that regard and it shouldn't be a surprise, seeing how it's from the same person, after all. And even though the game has such a high difficulty if you decide to take it seriously, and that I hated it every moment of the last few missions where the checkpoints were just unfair, I can recommend this game for you hardcore completionists and casual indie action platformer fans alike. RONIN is a game I picked up without any expectations other than a Gunpoint-like experience, but what I got was something almost completely different that was worth it all the way through. Lots of props for the level design and game overall to the dev and hoping for more 2D games from him. (Just add a difficulty option for the next one)

Those are some high quality promo items.  Grand game.
...But in all seriousness, Poker Night 2 is a very entertaining poker excursion.  Before this game, I had no idea how poker functioned.  Now, when...or if...if I ever participate in an actual poker tournament, I highly expect witty banter from interesting characters, nostalgic yet distinguished jazz-like music and fascinating themes.
Either that or I will be instantly disqualified and forced out.
It's the perfect education tool, it teaches all the world about the joys of poker!  Such as buying alcoholic drinks to slowly but surely sabotage other fictional players or using a cheat sheet.
If any sentient being is still alive after reading that, then good, now I can accurately assess my opinion of the game.  Really, Poker Night 2 is a simple "video game" at the end of the day.  After all, it is what it is, poker.  What makes it so entertaining are the characters and their conversations with one another.  Poker Night 2's cast of characters is comprised of several fictional video games, animated television series, and even film characters.  Though these celebrities are hardly the most obscure of competitors, I admit that I had little idea of a few of them.
However, the way they interact with one another manages to crack a smile on my face.  The act of Brock Samson, the deadly assassin bodyguard from the Venture Bros. snigger at a profile of Sam, the bipedal dog detective from Sam & Max is a humorous conversation to listen to while looking at one's deck of cards.  Same with the adventurous Ash Williams and the slightly annoying yet semi-endearing CL4P-TP robot talk about his life story or attempt to put the moves on the dealer, a female A.I. by the name of GLaDOS and instantly be dismissed is nice to listen to.
...The first few times.  While the charm of the conversations can last for quite some time, if one plays this game for hours on end, they will inevitably listen to the same dialogue line they heard sometime an hour or two before.  There unfortunately is only so much variety in one playthrough.
Luckily, the game does not rely on characters chatting your ears off to keep you playing.  Not only are their incentives like the promotional items for Team Fortress 2 and Borderlands 2, but the soundtrack is a pleasure to groove to in one's seat.  Songs like "Still Alive" are reprised in a smooth jazz version to fit the calm, calm mood of having one's virtual wallet face the equivalent of being suctioned in by a vacuum.
Of course, that seems like a hefty toll.  Fret not, for your ears do not have to take on the entire burden.  For your dear optic nerves, there are several card and chip themes for your playing pleasure that can be used to customize your tournaments.  You can combine card themes, chip themes, and table felt themes of your favorite franchise (as is represented) like Portal.  Unlock the themes and deploy them and watch as your poker table is immersed in an Aperture Science simulation.  Alternatively, employ a Borderlands 2 theme set and get the gritty, casino feel or the Sam & Max themes and unlock a black and white detective mystery movie-esque setting, originally meant for Sam & Max's 25th anniversary.
However, at the very end of the day, Poker Night 2 is just that, a poker game.  A poker game featuring the stars of video games, a television show, and a movie series.  I recommend it, not just for its incentives, but for its fascinating, entertaining themes and dialogue around the poker table.
...And because those promo items are really good looking.

I wrote an amazingly long review that glitched out and didn't post, so I'll keep it brief.
DISCLAIMER: I played the game with a friend the whole way through, and we were goofing off from the very beginning.  That might color my views a little bit.
This game was responsible for both my best experience in gaming, and the hardest I had ever laughed at anything.
This game is not a good story-driven game.  The choices you would expect to matter don't, and the choices you would expect not to matter do.  For example, you can steal from a rich old woman who trusted you or literally murder a man in broad daylight with no consequences, but selling a dog results in it being trained as a boxing animal that you have to fight later on, which makes things much, much harder.
The game doesn't give you enough time with it's characters to really feel bad for them.  This makes sense given the setting of the game, but it's still a point against.  You need to develop a character if you want people to appreciate it when they get broken down.  You can't just introduce characters and then instantly have them kill themselves or get shot and expect me to feel sorry.  If I felt sorry for those sorts, then I would also feel sorry for every random enemy I shot in an FPS.
It never made me feel sadness or remorse even though it constantly tried.  In fact, it was how hard it tried that made me laugh most of the time.  Some parts are obviously intentionally funny, and are funny due to being outright ridiculous, but most of the games humor came from it trying way too hard to be tragic in a way that made me feel like I was laughing with the game, not at it.  It is hard to explain.
There's no way to describe all the times the game made me laugh without spoiling it, and even then, it needs context for you to really understand.
If the developers were trying to make an amazing comedy, they succeeded and are absolutely brilliant.  Humor comes from the unexpected, and this game is paced and marketed perfectly for that.  If you think about the hardest you have ever laughed, chances are you aren't thinking of a joke a comedian told.  You expect comedians to be funny, and you expect funny games to be funny.  You expect sitcoms to be funny.  That expectation lowers the potential.  It can make you laugh, but not quite as much as things that aren't supposed to be funny.
If this game was developed to be funny, it is the greatest work of comedy ever devised.
It has just the right amount of soul-crushing, boring gameplay where nothing interesting really happens.  The majority of the game is walking through towns and talking to characters you will never see again, about things that don't really matter.  It's that drought of fun that makes the bright spots all the better.
I can't even tell if it was developed to be funny or to be an interesting story.  The perfection of the pacing leads me to believe its supposed to be funny, but the marketing, and the amount of people who apparently didn't think of it as a hilarious experience make me think that maybe it wasn't supposed to be that way.  Maybe I only think of it that way because I played it with a friend the whole way through and got it for free off of a humble bundle without really knowing what it was or what it was supposed to be.
In short:  Play it with a friend and expect nothing.  Forget you ever read this.  You can use skype screen share while the game is in windowed mode to play it with a friend and talk at the same time, that's what we did.  (sorry steam but your steaming service is bad at the time of this review)
If you do that, you might just have as much fun as I did, which will make it well worth two feet of subway sandwiches.

Alright, I think it's been enough time since I've played this game to give an accurate review of it. To preface this, I went in with high expectations due to watching Jesse Cox play this game on Youtube, expectations that were MET in the BEGINNING of the game anyway. The game looks good, the writing is solid, and the minigames to get money are fun.... BUUUUT the entire game is hamstrung by a time-constraint that you need to be at your Ex's wedding by a certain time, on top of which the 'variety' of choices you have really boils down to two equally unappealing prospects, which you pick the one which sounds the best. To make matters a bit worse, there aren't even many apparent consequences OF your actions beyond what you can imagine.
That normally wouldn't be a deal-breaker, but then, due to my neurotic nature, I looked up how to best play the game and what I needed to do, willingly spoiling the ending for myself and.... Seriously? The entire point of this game is to go through trials and tribulations so that you might be able to achieve SOMETHING right? But no, spoiler alert: No matter what you do, the ending will suck. That is a deal-breaker for me, when you build up a game that is actually REALLY good starting off, but then you decide to give a bad ending no matter what? That's just... Terrible writing on the dev's part. The game has its moments, and if you're in it for the mini-games, or some of the decisions, then good, but if you are wanting a good ending as a sort of payoff for putting in hard work and becoming attatched to your character, then you'll be in for a big disappointment. Hopefully some people liked this game, and it's a good try for the devs, if they do make any more games, hopefully they'll think ahead and see that setting up every ending as a kick in the groin ISN'T a way to please fans.

is one of those experiences that would make you stop in a random moment of your daily life, and reminiscence some irrelevant happenstance from long past. You'd ponder, you'd sweat. You'd ask yourself if you did the right thing back then, or how your life would be turned out if you'd do otherwise. You'd feel uneasy for no relevant reason to your actuality. The only relevant reason is that your conscious decided to pay you a visit and you just got a hit on home.
On a rainy night, a furious young man with a 2000 dollar suit and an Italian accent slams the door behind him as he proceeds towards the dark alley. In mere seconds, a shaky middle aged gentleman with spiteful features does follow him, and orders the Italian to come back that instant. The Italian refuses, and declares that he is done. They start to argue, as the Italian keeps walking away and the other man keeps throwing threats around like Halloween candy. Suddenly, their argument is cut short with the appearance of a faceless hobo who asks them to listen to a story, with a .45 at hand. As his ex-boss keeps yelling for the Italian to shoot the hobo, he keeps the hobo on gunpoint and makes a choice... This is the defining moment of
, and as you make your very first choice, the camera rolls to tell you the hobo's story.
is a story of someone as real and as ordinary as you or me, who'd hit rock bottom and take a journey to redefine their place and worth in this world. The narrative is excellent and compels you to take every little aspect of the game personal. I've emphasized with my character so deeply and invested in her achievements, her choices and her personality so thoroughly... I found out that I've been playing the game as myself all along. Considering the whole display of the game consists of 16 bit graphics, a repetitive techno soundtrack and a text narration, such atmosphere is a great feat by itself.
The world you play is as uncanny and as simple as the real world, and nothing is sugarcoated. The game is a contemplation on human nature and the element of choice. By definition, the storyline forces you to make choices and live with their consequences at every given turn. There will be moments that would make you, and moments that would break you. You will be forced to face the ugly, cruel and downtrodden part of reality; nuances and topics that we'd better left ungazed in our daily life. Sex, drugs, language, immoral and unethical, even violent actions are only the beginning of the content you'll be forced to deal with. By the first hour of your gameplay, you'll become familiar with the term "lesser evil".
As you may have guessed so far, the game has multiple endings and huge replay value. You are given an open world with limited time for one conquest. The journey in between is what would define you in the end. One thing that I've appreciated the most is that there are achievements only relevant to plot progress. As you'd complete one casual playthrough, you'd have every achievement. This encourages the player to experience the game with honest choices and make his/her own decisions: play the game as it is intended to be played.
Bold in tone, bare in nature, ordinary in content and extraordinary in achievement,
is an experience. Take out a can of beer, pick your headphones and start the game. By the end, you'll discover more about your own self than you'd be comfortable with.

A great space flight RPG with plenty of content. Ships have basic control similar to the old "Asteroids" PC game (you thrust to go forwards, and turning does not stop your momentum) and have plenty of hull types,  weapons, and abilities to customise with. The game is story-driven with light humour, but has a rather slow-paced intro galaxy that may put people off (however, it can be skipped!)
Missions are basically set in closed arenas where you perform the task required, so this is not a fully open space sandbox (which wouldnt even make sense with a 2D game in space anyway).
The graphics are nice and tidy, and when the combat gets going you can end up with great little light shows.
All in all, RR:FotS has enough to get you addicted, and very few real drawbacks considering the price it can picked up for.

Ring Runner follows FTL into the illusive zone of flawless indie game glory.  It is almost criminal that it took this game as long as it did to get on Steam.  Addictive gameplay with an incredibly smooth UI, and a staggering amount of flexibility, with a depth and sophistication that will continue to surprise you.  There are countless ships, with a fitting system of a quality you will be hard pressed to find outside of EVE Online.  The story and dialogue is surprisingly good, at times goofy, often trippy and surreal and almost always hilarious.  The graphics are absolutely beautiful, proof that it is not always necessary to melt your video card.
One comment which might be helpful, and which is only negative depending on your preferences, is in regard to how episodic the game is.  I did not necessarily expect an "open world" but did expect some greater degree of openness to the campaign than I encountered.  There really is none, the campaign is very episodic.  Initially this may seem like a significant down side, but it gradually picks up and at least provides you with a little bit of choice.
A campaign and maps with significantly more "openness" I think would easily have pushed this onto a short list of some of the best games ever made, but as is Ring Runner is truly a jewel worth far more than the measily $10 they are asking for.

You begin as a middle aged working person. The final stage you play as a child. The enviroment changes completely, The zebra crossing turns into white slabs you jump to leading to a sweet heavon kind of thing. After 420 hours I still can't seem to get my head around this cluster♥♥♥♥ of a platform-fighter.
My Elo fluctuates between 1700-1900. Every game feels like a coin toss. Sometimes I dominate high level players, other times I get slaughtered by low level players. It never feels like I've won or lost fairly.
It's often hard to even comprehend what's happening on screen, mainly due to the many new ways that players can approach and evade with the current dash mechanic.
The hit detection is so inconsistent it hurts. Often times a successful attack or dodge will be canceled out for no reason. It's immensely frustrating when you can predict exactly what you're opponent is going to do, account for it, but fall for it anyway due to some inexplicable variable not working in your favour. My attacks always seem to just barely shave the hurtboxes of other players, and whenever I get hit it feels like my hurtbox teleports into the oncoming attack.
It always feels like there is a constant delay on inputs, particularly with dodging, which often results in me having to sit and wait patiently for my opponent to finish their combo while I'm powerless to do anything, or wait patiently whilst falling off stage before I can begin recovering, as if my character is stunned or something. It's also very easy to misinput the wrong move, and given the twitch-based nature of the game, this can cost you dearly.
Brawlhalla is a great game to play casually with friends, but it's an absolutely appalling competitive experience. It may be free, but it will cost you your sanity. There are things you can practice and learn to improve your chances at winning, but there is no mastering Brawlhalla.

Lighthearted and fun. I played the first three Episodes years ago on the Playstation 2, so when I saw a version with all 6 episodes I knew I had to pick it up.
The game is great both for adults and kids, the story is slightly modified to keep it understandable in this format (the game features no voice acting - everything is grunts). I played it solo here, but I know that when I played it years ago, the co-op was great fun (the game was designed to have two players at all times - if you play solo the second player is replaced with an AI who automatically does their part in the teamwork puzzles but does nothing else).
The game is broken up into 6 episodes (the original triology and the prequel triology) with each episode having 6 levels. Each level has a story mode. Upon completing each level, you also unlock the "Free Play" version of that level which allows you to revisit the level using any characters. Each level has a number of secondary objectives, most of which require you to visit the level in Free Play mode to use characters with certain abilities to access hidden areas, so once you finish the game on story mode, you still have a lot of content to explore!
If you have kids, putting two of them in front of this is a great way of getting them to learn teamwork and puzzle solving.
All in all, an extremely fun game.

Dragon Age: Origins is definitely in my Top 3 for favorite Bioware games, coming close to KotOR 1 and ME2. It definitely has some of the most memorable companions (imo). I don't usually like to do pros and cons, but it's hard to break down this game any other way. so:
Pros:
- Incredible story. You really can't find a better underdog story than this, especially if you go the City Elf route. Not to mention that this could probably compete with Game of Thrones with all of the scheming and backstabbing.
- Six unique backstories. Sure the general plot stays the same, but with six different introduction stories, the game becomes very re-playable.
- Companions. Aside from the dog that you'll probably forget you even have, your companions are very unique and interesting. From Alistair to Zevran, they all have a personality that is hard to forget. Well, except for Sten, but he's memorable in other ways.
- Engrossing. The first time I played this, I was so involved in the story, I could hardly believe it when I checked the clock and saw that 3 hours had passed like nothing.
-Content. It will take a while for you to finish this game, no doubt about that. I generally average about 30 hours to finish, and that's without doing half of the side quests.
Cons:
- Combat. Don't expect the combat to be very exciting. It's a bit slow paced, and you'll spend most of your time watching your party take their sweet time to swing their swords while you wait for their abilities to cooldown.
- Dungeons. A lot of the dungeons are really drawn out. You'll spend so long fighting your way though the quests that you'll probably forget why you're there in the first place.
Overall, I'd give this game an 8.5/10. You won't be wasting your money here.

I was one, of many, who preordered the, rather dissapointing, Arkham Knight (I got it cheap from a friend, don’t blame me). However, Warner Brothers decided to be a bit empathic and give us all the older Arkham-games, which, to a certain extent, made me forgive them.
Enough about that, let’s get to the review.
The gameplay is really good, flying using the grapping hook is surpringly fun and the combat, while in reality not too advanced and arguably a bit too automated, feels great and is really fun. Batman has a vast arsenal of moves and gadgets to use, many of which need to be unlocked through leveling up, hence keeping the combat fresh and interesting.
The game also contains a lot of puzzles, none which are too advanced nor time-consuming to complete, but they do add to the gameplay. Kind of reminds me of the “The Legend of Zelda” games. You might find this comparasion a bit bizarre, and I can’t blame you really.
Collectibles are plenty in the game, and while I know that everyone isn’t a fan of them, I find them quite fun to find here, having The Riddler mock you about not having found the rest hardly gets old. That, and the fact many of them require some creativity and/or puzzle solving keeps it interesting. You also get XP from finding them.
About XP, as mentioned, the game features a leveling system.
It’s quite basic, you gain XP from combat (amount depends on how many moves you managed to do in succession and how varied they were), solving riddles and finding The Riddler’s throphys, plus a few other things.
During my playthough I neverfelt like I was under nor overleveled, the game went on at a good pace without any moments were I got stuck.
Coming to the controls, I’ve only been albe to try the keyboard/mouse ones, and they work well, could be better, but far from bad. I never felt like they caused any problems, to put it that way.
The story is good. Not too advanced so that it gets in the way, nor too mediocre so that everything feels unmotivated. Because it doesn’t, not at all. I’ve played a few games (*cough* Borderlands (1)) where everything simply felt unmotivated and forced, simply because I had no idea on why I was doing this. Before you tell me that I should’ve read the text boxes on the quests, this was co-op. But, enough about that.
Where the game really shines is its charatcters, especially the villans.
Sure, none of them are original, but they all fit well together in the game, and manages to feel unique, even though they’re high in quantity. While the normal thugs you’ll encounter mostly stay the same, some carry different weapons and/or have armour, which does shake things up a little bit. It’s nothing that ever bothered me playing through the game though.
Runs great on my hardware (specs can be found on profile), for the most part. It does stutter a bit while loading things off the harddrive and
utilises PhysX a bit too much, leading to a framerate cut in half (from a near constant 62 FPS, which is the cap, to a unstable 30 FPS), and even after the fight it dropped even lower (4-5 FPS). Restarting fixed this though.
The graphics hold up well despite their age, and the artstyle is nice. I found no obvious pixelation on any textuers, though you’ll probably be able to find some if you actually look around. The lack of any anti-aliasing aside from MSAA is a bit dissapoining, but not really a problem with today’s hardware.
The soundtrack is good, nothing memorable, but it sets the mood well and does well in the background without disturbing you.
Same goes for the voice acting, though perhaps a bit better than the soundtrack, so perhaps I'd go as far as to call it great. No complaints here really.
Sounds for actions, such as Batman hitting someone or him grappling up to a ledge are excellent, no complaints here either, not that I'd expect otherwise.

The soundtrack to this game is on par with Jet Set Radio. The sound effects are so realistic, you will end up turning around in your seat to make sure [said effect] wasn't happening in real life behind you. This game is also amazingly stable- it runs at a steady 60 FPS on a potato and runs extremely well on a higher-end PC with very little CPU usage. With graphics, mechanics, and taxing physics this high, WAR does a truly remarkable job in denying any bugs, crashes, or issues. Look at PUBG. It doesn't even look as good as WAR and crashes every couple of minutes on top-level, state of the art gaming PCs (according to trustworthy people who own PUBG). For $3.99, Wild Animal Racing is ridiculously underpriced and the steal of a lifetime. This review can merely understate the graciousness of WAR.

2 aspects of the controls stink.  These make you character do things you arn't trying to do.  In a turn based game, that should not be an issue.
Aspect 1: special action icons
One would think you hover over a special action icon, it highlights (enlarging in this case), you click, when time resumes you do that action.  Well no.  You hover over the icon, it doesn't highlight, you click, and you jump (default mouse action is jumping if you aren't clicking an icon).  Instead, if you would mouse off the icon by the better half of an inch, then it gets big and you can click on it.  You could almost adapt to this wonky control if not for aspect 2.
Aspect 2: pausing
Press space or hold down mouse button to pause.  Mouse button also makes you do something, so when you just want to pause, space.  However, sometimes it's paused while you hold down space, and sometimes the space down press toggles pause.  This would almost be fine to introduce some reaction time and not make it entirely turn based, except when you are planning on it being turn based, and except for when combined with aspect 1 (real time clicking an icon, but you were supposed to hover, then move around until it gets big, and release before you move it more accidentally and make the icon small).
I think this would be a good game if the controls weren't all mucked up.

Those are some high quality promo items.  Grand game.
...But in all seriousness, Poker Night 2 is a very entertaining poker excursion.  Before this game, I had no idea how poker functioned.  Now, when...or if...if I ever participate in an actual poker tournament, I highly expect witty banter from interesting characters, nostalgic yet distinguished jazz-like music and fascinating themes.
Either that or I will be instantly disqualified and forced out.
It's the perfect education tool, it teaches all the world about the joys of poker!  Such as buying alcoholic drinks to slowly but surely sabotage other fictional players or using a cheat sheet.
If any sentient being is still alive after reading that, then good, now I can accurately assess my opinion of the game.  Really, Poker Night 2 is a simple "video game" at the end of the day.  After all, it is what it is, poker.  What makes it so entertaining are the characters and their conversations with one another.  Poker Night 2's cast of characters is comprised of several fictional video games, animated television series, and even film characters.  Though these celebrities are hardly the most obscure of competitors, I admit that I had little idea of a few of them.
However, the way they interact with one another manages to crack a smile on my face.  The act of Brock Samson, the deadly assassin bodyguard from the Venture Bros. snigger at a profile of Sam, the bipedal dog detective from Sam & Max is a humorous conversation to listen to while looking at one's deck of cards.  Same with the adventurous Ash Williams and the slightly annoying yet semi-endearing CL4P-TP robot talk about his life story or attempt to put the moves on the dealer, a female A.I. by the name of GLaDOS and instantly be dismissed is nice to listen to.
...The first few times.  While the charm of the conversations can last for quite some time, if one plays this game for hours on end, they will inevitably listen to the same dialogue line they heard sometime an hour or two before.  There unfortunately is only so much variety in one playthrough.
Luckily, the game does not rely on characters chatting your ears off to keep you playing.  Not only are their incentives like the promotional items for Team Fortress 2 and Borderlands 2, but the soundtrack is a pleasure to groove to in one's seat.  Songs like "Still Alive" are reprised in a smooth jazz version to fit the calm, calm mood of having one's virtual wallet face the equivalent of being suctioned in by a vacuum.
Of course, that seems like a hefty toll.  Fret not, for your ears do not have to take on the entire burden.  For your dear optic nerves, there are several card and chip themes for your playing pleasure that can be used to customize your tournaments.  You can combine card themes, chip themes, and table felt themes of your favorite franchise (as is represented) like Portal.  Unlock the themes and deploy them and watch as your poker table is immersed in an Aperture Science simulation.  Alternatively, employ a Borderlands 2 theme set and get the gritty, casino feel or the Sam & Max themes and unlock a black and white detective mystery movie-esque setting, originally meant for Sam & Max's 25th anniversary.
However, at the very end of the day, Poker Night 2 is just that, a poker game.  A poker game featuring the stars of video games, a television show, and a movie series.  I recommend it, not just for its incentives, but for its fascinating, entertaining themes and dialogue around the poker table.
...And because those promo items are really good looking.

This is an entertaining and interesting mix of a puzzle game and a visual novel. It is short but masterfully paced. The short running time enables the creators to keep surprising you with changes and with delightful interplay of mechanics, story, art, voice acting and music. They all develop together and play off each other in smart and satisfying ways. It also helps that the game is very easy so you're never stuck in one place.
There is no one aspect of this game that is very good. The story is clichéd, the mechanics simplistic, the art repetitive and the humour juvenile. But they all work together perfectly and reinforce each other. The game is so full of smart ideas and genuine enthusiasm that even its flaws become charming. This is a short, unique experience that's easy to recommend.

Short but sweet.
Unhack features simplistic puzzle gameplay over a backdrop of visual novel -esque dialogue and character interraction.  The dialogue is the main "pro" of the game, but it also acts as its main "con."
The three AI characters are all voice acted, but the protagonist isn't  This means that while you're progressing through the puzzles, you'll need to look down to read the protagonist's dialogue in order to gain context for what the AI voice actors are saying to you.  This really takes you out of the puzzles in the worst way.  It would have been better if the protagonist had been voice acted as well to create a better flow between the puzzles and story.  WIthout this, you have to tackle to puzzles slower than you would normally in order to experience the full story as well.  This disn't prevent me from having fun with the game, it just stood out as a main issue that could have been prevented.
All in all, it's still a fun little game that's worth the price if you're looking for a casual one-off experience.

The characters are cliche' and have shallow, if not non-existent, character development.  Characters appearing for the sake of appearing, villians being there solely for being a conflict rather than anything that feels menacing, etc.  Plot is very simple, you'll see pretty much everything from a mile off after the first 5 minutes or so.  Nothing is explained and there is little to no worldbuilding.  Many things just happen for the sake of happening, especially with character and villian appearances.
Gameplay is essentially navigating a linear maze dodging obstacles all with timing-gimmicks.  Simple stuff, got kind of boring after the first hour.
Voice-acting was an interesting addition, and I admit I bought into the game because of the premise of amateur voice acting in an indie game.  However, it was too monotone; I never really felt any emotion come out of the characters, it was as if they were just reading the text that appeared on the screen to you.  Nevertheless, I have to give them points for trying.
At the end of the day, the game felt like a poor time filler and I expected more replayability, but I knew what I was buying into.  If you are bored and want something to fill an hour or two, go ahead and get this game.  However, its experience is short lived and forgetable.  There are many other cheap games on steam and ways to fill your time in them.  As such, I do not recommend this title.

Prince of Persia is way too easy because the protagonist is virtually invincible, there is no dead, game over or any punishment. Combat is so climatic and cinematic with memorable and distinctive enemies. You can make a chain of combos similar to free-form combat even though it's always one on one fight, it's still fun. From the beginning it's easy to fall in love with this game. The opening cinematic shows us that Joker has been up to his usual mischief in Gotham, and has been apprehended by Batman. Almost immediately afterwards, we are put into the shoes of the Dark Knight himself, as we walk with a chained up Joker through the Asylum to his cell. This scene is perfect in the way it sets the games mood, atmosphere and the tension that there is just something wrong. It also captures how great Mark Hamill's beautifully twisted Joker is, paired with the writing of Paul Dini (Batman The Animated Series, Batman Beyond), his performance is consistently brilliant throughout the game, and the opener is our first look into it. I should also mention the voice talent in the entirety of the game is fantastic, Kevin Conroy and Arleen Sorkin are especially great as Batman and Harley Quinn respectively.
After the Joker is unchained and walked off to go to his cell, he escapes and we learn that he has been planning this for months, with the help of his sidekick Harley Quinn. We're then introduced to the games fast paced and fluid combat system, where you'll be battling it out with up to thirty enemies at a time. The combat can be a fair challenge at first but as you level up and make your way through the game, thirty thugs will be nothing to you. This game excels in pacing throughout and that is clear, with the way it never makes you do one thing for too long. Aside from the meaty combat system the game features stealthy sections where Batman will be put into a room of armed thugs. Considering Batman doesn't have any super powers, he isn't safe from bullets and after some exposure to them, he will fall like any man. These stealth sections, will have you picking off a number of enemies in a number of ways. You can hang them from gargoyles on the walls, you can pull them off balconies or just get up close and personal, then choke them into a peaceful slumber.
Aside from hunting down criminals, you can also hunt down the games collectibles, consisting of Riddler trophy's, which are small question marks that are hidden in every nook and cranny throughout the Asylum. Or try your hand at his riddles. The beauty of Arkham Asylum's collectibles, is that they never feel tedious to collect. Collecting them will unlock concept art and character models to view from the main menu, they also tie directly into the story as collecting them all will help you capture The Riddler.
Other sections of the game will require you to manually climb and jump around vertical mazes, which offer a nice break from hurting people. Pressing the X button will also put you into a handy detective mode, which allows you to see through walls to locate thugs and at some points set up crime scenes for tracking criminals down.
My main problems with this game lie in the boss battles - Scarecrow and Killer Croc have fantastic encounters, with the former putting Batman into a nightmarish state which houses some very interesting sequences that flip the game on its head. However the other bosses feel very boring in comparison, the rest are like normal combat sections with a boss added, and it doesn't help that the game ends on one of these fights, which felt like a let down after around 10 hours of a near perfect experience.
Even with the games small faults, the rest of the experience more than makes up for it. In total, Arkham Asylum is the current game to beat in the superhero genre. Its fantastic performances and writing make the narrative a memorable and mostly satisfying experience, with solid gameplay that makes you feel like the bone-breaking Batman.

Wow... Almost 7 years old and this game feels as great as it did the first time I played it back in the Peasant Station 3's golden days. It's a game that never bores you from beginning to end and it encourages you to find every unlockable.
What to say about Arkham Asylum? This game revolutionized the way we play games. It brought so many innovations to a time when games were starting to feel so repetitive, uninspired, buggy and generic. The surprising thing was that this game was based on a DC superhero world; something that was considered a stigma in the gaming world. Almost no superhero game has ever been good, or interesting enough to engage people who are not into comics. Yet Batman Arkham series threw this misconception away and brought a magnificent piece of gaming software at the same time.
So many games have tried to copy the Free-Flow system, but non have succeeded. This combat system is the 'pièce de résistance' of the Arkham series and will have you craving for fights. And I love how the game does so well at not overdoing it. It gives you just enough fights throughout the game so it is always exciting, without falling into repetitiveness. And still,  at the end, it rewards you with a mode were you can beat as many henchmen as you like.
Appart fromt he wonderful combat system that it's such a treat to watch and perform, the game also engages you in stealth as well as playing the detective. It manages to wrap all this into an immersive story with a very dark style never seen before in a Batman game. It even manages to sneak some horror elements, which does fantasticaly well! Definitely a surprise for the first-timer.
I really can't find any negatives on this game. It plays brilliant, looks wonderful for being a 7 year-old game, amazing soundtrack and sound effects. great voice acting (we've got the official Joker's voice: Mark Hamill), gorgeous and badass character designs, engaging story even for the non comic fan, and the list goes on.
This game is a classic on its own right and it will go into history as one of the greatest and most influential games of the past gen.
Graphics: 8/10 It's a 7 year old game but it still looks fenomenal. The PC version benefits from sharper textures, light effects and 60fps. It almost does not look as old as it really is.
Sound: 7/10 The soundtrack alone is epic! But it suffers from volume spikes. Cutscenes are too loud. Something that many games suffer from.
Controls: 9/10 You got to play this with a controller. Once you do, you find yourself with one of the most responsive, smooth and intuitive controllers there is. Developers really put an effort in them.
Gameplay: 9/10 This game is in a league of its own. Back when it came out, there was nothing like it. Brilliant fighting mechanics! Great ballance between stealth, beat'em up, exploration and even horror, making this game feel interesting from beginning to end.
Story: 8/10 Simple, but engaging. That darker, more mature Batman game no one really asked for, but oh boy, thank the gods we got!

The world has been obliterated by an undying, supernatural wind that causes temporal anomalies to reconfigure the land as a patchwork of different eras. With an astonishing degree of organization these monsters are led by an overlord and its lieutenants, who  are intent on keeping man down. Your character is one of the few that can survive the challenges that stand in the way of restoring the world.
The story is supplemented by journals you find through missions. But don't expect to be blown away by it (pun intended?).
This game is pretty much a love letter to the SNES classic ActRaiser. You're a glyphbearer (i.e. wizard) that used glyphs (i.e. spells) to upgrade your character or lay on the damage. The game plays in two stages: first, you select an area from the procedurally generated map (procedural being the buzz word used in every other game nowadays). Then you're transported to a 2D view of the area, where you can loot a place for valuables or find randomly generated missions.  Rewards can survivors, new spells or buildings that you can use to improve yourself and/or your group.
Missions are somewhat varied in their objectives, but none of them are mandatory besides killing the lieutenants and the overlord. You can play them in whatever order you desire and drop missions as you wish. The game even allows you to go straight to the overlord...but it being the final boss, it vastly overpowers you at the beginning. Killing its lieutenants effectively lowers the power of the overlord and unlocks higher level spells, making that the overall game progression.
In the topic of spells, the game employs an elements system whereas some enemies are resistant or weak to certain spell elements (a handy feature for figuring this out is that you can check enemy attributes by pausing the game and mousing over your target). As previously mentioned, you can get new spells by completing missions, but the game also has a crafting system. Sometimes useful if no missions have the spells you want, but in gameplay terms it tends to be superfluous. Spells start out pretty basic, a fireball here, a slice of wind there, but higher level spells allow you to summon effects or monsters to fight at your side. The trend overall though is to shoot at things until they stop bothering you, and strategy only goes as far as choosing which element to use.
Rounding out the spell system are enchantments and a series of spells that allow you to interact with the environment easier. Enchantments can't be crafted and are only unlocked through loot drops. You just plug enchantments in a separate menu and that allows you to increase some stats here and there, or give you the ability to double jump.
The game features a perma-death system. If the character you're using dies you restart with another survivor. Characters are nothing more than a collection of attributes though, so the game expects you to go through them if you wish. Just don't lose them all!
The game uses early PS1-esque graphics. They don't look horrible on a 2D environment, but don't expect to be dazzled.
The music is nostalgic, using bit tunes reminescent of the SNES era. There isn't much variety though. After a couple of hours you better bring your own mix or turn the music down.
Strangely enough characters in the game don't make noise. Spell effects do. So you get into rooms full of silent monsters and all you can hear is the music and spells being thrown. Compared to the music though, sound effects are not annoying.
A Valley Without Wind is a fun, practically endless arcade game. What it lacks in depth it makes up by constantly throwing enemies to destroy at you. It doesn't pressure you, so you can pick up and drop missions as you wish, with no real penalties. Get it if you miss ActRaiser but wish it didn't end, or nostalgia is not enough to make you play it again. While it doesn't have a lot of variety, replay value is insane. If you can get it on sale it's a heck of deal.

I heartily recommend A Valley Without Wind.
In true Arcen fashion this is a different kind of game. It is quite unlike anything else, it's a 2D sidescrolling exploration game with an incredible amount of spells, each of them different and fun to use.
Arcen also went ahead and developed a sequel, which supposedly fixes the problems of the game. This is because the original didn't turn out as they had originally intended. However I must say that I disagree with them (and apparently many others as well), I think the original game is far superior to the sequel. It is much more interesting, it gives you more freedom, there are many more possibilities and it also looks better (although the visuals in this game are certainly something you need to get used to)
The best way to realise whether or not you want to play this game is to check out the screenshots or watch a video, and if it looks like it might be something you'd enjoy then you really should go ahead and play the game because this game really is unique and you owe it to yourself to experience it. However if you don't see anything appealing here, then just move on to something else because it is unlikely that the game will win you over.
This game definitely isn't a crow pleaser, but I managed to find great enjoyment playing it and I hope you do too!

I will start this review by saying this:
I have played through Arkham Asylum roughly 10 times on Xbox 360 and once on my old HP laptop (circa 2011). I just recently built a gaming PC and pushed a new 1070 into it. This review first includes my reaction to playing this game the way it was meant to be played in all its graphical glory. Later on, follows a concise review of Arkham Asylum.
This was one of the first games I fired up after completing my new gaming PC. Playing this game on all the highest settings at 60 fps really opened my eyes to modern PC gaming. It had been far too long. As many times as I have already played this game, seeing how much better the graphics were has opened my eyes. And this is a game that is going on 8 years old.
I have not had any problems running the game and it's running buttery-smooth at 60fps on an LG ultrawide monitor. Using the Steam controller has been a joy and I am slowly starting to prefer the "mouse pad" which replaces the right analog stick.
If you have any doubts from a hardware standpoint I can fully recommend this game off my current build which includes an i5 6600k Skylake, MSI 1070, MSI mobo, 16gb GSkill ram, EVGA 750 PSU.
As far as a review of the game itself, well-this game started the Arkham franchise and still holds up after all these years. Gameplay, story, graphics, replayability-it's all there, and then some.
If you are a Batman fan and enjoy gaming this is a must buy. I can sum up the experience in one sentence. This game makes you FEEL like you are Batman. It has minor stealth play, excellent combat, detective skills-all the things that make Batman feel like Batman. And don't exclude the Rogue's Gallery of villains. Beyond the many you encounter, there are a plethora of easter eggs thanks to the narcissistic Riddler. If you like collectibles in games, this will be right up your alley. If you don't like collectibles in games but you want to "Be the Batman" this will be right up your alley. Collecting Riddler trophies and solving Riddler riddles was some of the greatest parts of this game in my humble opinion.
If I had to grade this game overall I would give it 5/5.
Simply put, Arkham Aslyum is a must buy.

This game is without a doubt a hidden gem. As an avid MMORPG player of over 12 years, I have spent many months and many games trying to recreate the feeling of awe and excitement I experienced during my first steps in the MMORPG world. This game is the first time that those feelings were recreated for me.
To start, this isn't a AAA game. Don't come in to the game expecting amazing graphics, flawless game design, lack of bugs, amazing AI, and interesting in depth lore. If that is what you are looking for, you should turn away now. However, if you're looking for a charming little game, with a vibrant and friendly community, helpful and cooperative developers, and exciting game play that reminiscence of the past, please check this game out.
Some pros:
-Decent graphics, if you're in to old-school 2d games.
-Extremely active and helpful developers, who are very open to feed back.
-A fun non-toxic community. Honestly this game has the nicest community of any MMORPG I have ever played.
-Very frequent updates (you can expect an exciting medium to large scale update every week)
-Very frequent bug fixes/balance updates (every day the devs work hard fixing issues reported to them)
-A classless skill system (think Runescape stat system)
-Tons of things to do! Explore, train fishing, wood cutting, craft gear, enchant items, kill bosses, fight other players in PVP, kill regular mobs, become a merchant, do quests, chill and chat with other players etc.
-Loot based pvp system. Kill another player and you can collect their gear as reward.
-Guild/party systems.
-The game is ENTIRELY FREE! No need to spend ANY money to enjoy this game.
-As a result of the above point... There is NO Pay To Win aspects. Finally a game where your real life wealth doesn't affect how good you are in the game. No pay to win, pay to progress, pay to advance... Not any form of advantage at all can be bought.
-Probably more that I am forgetting.
Some cons:
-The control system is... tedious to say the least. The game could use a major re-design in terms of the way controls are handled. Unfortunately the devs are currently very much against re-designing the control system so it looks like we may be stuck with it for a while.
-There are a lot of bugs, however devs are working hard on fixing them as they pop up.
-The servers are unreliable. Expect to be disconnected at least once a day until this is fixed.
-Dev team is small and indie. Due to this, certain updates/changes to the game may be put on the back burner for long periods of time, and take a long time to fully develop.
-UI is hard to grasp at first (and honestly it IS a little confusing... hopefully they re-design this to be more intuitive).
-The community is really small at the moment.
Over all this game is a 8/10. If they fixed the controls then I would easily change my rating to a 9/10, but the controls do hold the game back from its full potential quite a bit. Hopefully this is changed soon and I can update my rating!
Hope to see more players join this game! If you need some food feel free to hit me up in global chat - I play as a fisher/cooker merchant.
