Don't get me wrong, I did enjoy this game, but it didn't wow me the way I expected it to. After years of hearing praise for the story, combat system, etc, I decided to give it a try, but I'd say it's only about 40% fun and 60% frustration.
Pros:
-Decent graphics that still hold up 7 years later.
-Good looking designs for Batman's rogues gallery, especially Joker who, looking more like the classic version, was a welcome change from the now stagnant Heath Ledger version everyone was obsessed with at the time.
-Believable story (even with the body sized ventilation shafts and conveniently placed gargoyles).
-Hearing the voice actors from Batman: TAS was pretty cool.
-Cool gadgets
Cons:
-Navigation was a royal pain. I had to constantly check the map to see where I was going, and backtrack every 5 minutes.
-The Riddler challenge is a distracting side quest that I ultimately gave up on.
-The fighting mechanics gave me a headache. Countering only worked half the time, and it would constantly go into slow motion, which is hard to control. To be fair, it did set the standard for other combat styles, such as Shadow of Mordor, which requires a bit of strategy but actually works if you know what you're doing. Here, I basically just spend the whole fight clicking and mashing the spacebar, because I'm not in control at all.
Overall, I did enjoy it, but I would not put it in my top 5.

Dragon Age: Origins is easily one of the best games I have ever played. No other game has made me actually care about the characters on such a massive degree as this game has. Combine the world class Bioware writing and worlds with a pretty good but not perfect combat system and you have truly an epic adventure to behold. The world itself isn't really open world but that doesn't stop the land of Ferelden from being an interesting realm to explore. Graphically the game is quite dated now and lip syncing/animations are at times awkward (oh god the sex scenes ._.) but there is a very large mod database for improving visuals and despite looking old the game is still very much playable. (Also I'm pretty sure anything can run this game in this day and age)
Having many important choices actually matter and have a huge impact on the story makes this game incredibly replayable and a wetdream for roleplayers. In many situations you can be the good samaritan or evil incarnate. This leads to a level of immersion  rivaling that of other high fantasy rpgs such as the Elder Scrolls games. Everything from the various dialogue/party banter for the smallest of details to your companions actually having opinions on every choice you make really sells Dragon Age: Origins as a living breathing believable world which you can get lost in for hours on end.
The combat is very traditional dnd/baldurs gate style combat which some people who favor tactical combat with many pauses will enjoy and those who enjoy something like traditional hack n slash may not. Also the game starts off very slow so you have been warned. It picks up a few hours in when your party actually has a variety of skills.
My playtime (5% being me alt tabbed out) is for a single playthrough so there is definitely a ton of content in this game.

Dragon Age is a kind of game that is becoming increasingly rare: a deeply immersive single-player RPG with an interface clearly designed for the PC. It's easy to sling around the word "immersive" at any game that looks pretty, but DA isn't messing around - the world of Ferelden shows a unified sense of design and depth that blows even famously vast games like Oblivion out of the water. Coupled with consistently excellent writing and across-the-board quality character design even down to relatively unimportant NPCs, the game truly does feel like it's reacting to your choices dynamically from the very beginning, and how you play your character can have amazingly subtle effects on the way the story unfolds.
Graphically, the game's a little uneven. All the design elements are there, and it has plenty of high-quality textures and strong environmental visuals - particularly fire effects. The polygons themselves, particularly on character faces, are a little simpler than you'd expect from a 2009 game. Overall, the game looks about on level with Oblivion, although the visual distinctiveness and design ethic of areas and characters are significantly better. Animation stands out as a strong suit here, particularly during the game's frequent dialog sequences, with none of the dead-eyed staring or bizarre walk cycles that plagued other RPGs like Fallout 3.
Gameplay is pretty straightforward, and very much in keeping with previous Bioware titles like Knights of the Old Republic and Mass Effect. You control a party of up to four characters, each of whom develops a plethora of useful abilities to keep track of. The inclusion of a minor programming element (very much in keeping with the gambit system from Final Fantasy XII) will let you set up a few default actions on each character so you're not stuck frantically switching between them to make sure they drink their healing potions, but battles frequently require some degree of tactical planning. Setting up ambushes and planning your party strategy to play to strengths is necessary to get through some tougher areas. The interface is, shockingly, clearly tailor-made for the PC (the console versions have their own interfaces designed from the bottom up and are apparently easier games to allow for the sacrifice in easy access to skills). You have an insane number of quick-access slots, and nearly the entire keyboard is bound to one thing or another. It's the kind of interface that hasn't been in vogue since before the PS2 came out. The game is extremely linear, although the frequent and varied dialog options give it the feel of a more free-roaming game, and it's very tempting to go back and replay huge chunks of the game just to see how the complex and dynamic conversations will play out. The main downside is that there's no easy way to level-grind, which is to the game's benefit to a point (no tedious circling around killing wolves) but occasionally means you can get in over your head.
What the game sacrifices in terms of sandbox free-roaming it more than makes up with in the excellent writing and characterization. An absurd attention to detail and across-the-board excellent voice acting breathes a lot of life into the game's conversations, which make up a significant chunk of gameplay. Characters are extremely varied and the interplay between them is a major draw, a trademark of Bioware's games, but Dragon Age has some of the most likable characters I've ever seen in a video game and the excellent performances from talents like Tim Curry, Kate Mulgrew and Claudia Black really put the game a notch above. Even the game's fairly generic-on-the-surface fantasy world is livened up by a few critical details - for example, the elves in Dragon Age are a massive underclass of servants.
It's actually difficult to find things to level complaints against in this game. One petty gripe is Morrigan's visual design - her character is one of the game's strongest, and she has great personality and some very clever writing, but visually she's a pair of giant breasts with a cloth draped improbably over them. Other women in the game are treated with a bit more restraint, though, and female armor is gratifyingly sensible. Another issue is that it can be difficult to manage battles on the fly, and accurately targeting enemies with skills frequently requires tactical pausing just to line the cursor up over their relatively small active areas. It's a petty annoyance, but the game clearly wasn't meant to be played Diablo-style anyway.
A few other things to know about the game:
-The game is mostly DRM-free, and ships only with a simple disc check. EA has a reputation for fouling up its customers' computers with DRM malware, but DA seems to be free of those problems.
-If Dragon Age were a movie, it would be rated R. I don't remember ever seeing any swearing, oddly, but the game is rife with violent imagery, extremely dark themes and frank sexuality (including a handful of relatively tasteful sex scenes and occasional demonic nudity). The game handles all of it with maturity and depth, but it's clearly not meant for children, and even parents of younger teens should be cautious.
Overall, Dragon Age is one of the strongest games to come out in recent memory, and is another installment in Bioware's increasing resume of superbly-written RPGs. Players looking for a fast-paced hack-and-slash "rpg" should look elsewhere, but anyone who likes deep and elegant plot development, memorable characters and excellent role-playing will love this game.

Ronin is a semi-turn-based stealth-action game in which you play a katana-wielding, motorcycle helmet-wearing ninja seeking revenge. Now that my hyphen quota is out of the way, I can address the real question: how the hell did they screw this up?
The central mechanic to the game is, somewhere deep down, solid or even excellent. Movement is real-time when you're undetected -- which is rare -- but when combat begins, time freezes and you enter a form of turn-based combat that I can't say I've ever seen before. Your only form of movement during this phase is through jumping -- using the right stick to control the arc and direction of your jump as you dart between enemy lines of sight and between bullets. As you plot your next move, time freezes with your enemies' laser sights visible to show where they will fire between turns. There are a few variations on this basic bad guy type -- some enemies fire continuously, others wield swords and utilize a lethal dash instead of a firearm -- but by and large, you're dodging bullets.
Sounds cool, right? A turn-based Mark of the Ninja with a little Gunpoint thrown in is, in theory, a fascinating combination. Unfortunately, things come undone very quickly and in a variety of ways. For starters, the visible arc of your jump is often inaccurate or misleading. Too often I fell short of the marked landing spot, bumped into an enemy the arc showed me I could clear, or had trouble discerning if the path of my jump was or was not clear of enemy fire. As this jumping control is the ONLY method of movement during combat, the lack of tightness and poor tuning are unacceptable.
Combat also often devolves into tedium due to the quantity of enemies. As you progress through the game, you'll take on rooms packed to the brim with gun-toting baddies who rarely give you any time to do more than continually dodge. This is fine to an extent -- there's absolutely a certain thrill that comes from bouncing from floor to ceiling to wall while your opponents fire helplessly at your previous position -- but there came a point where it felt nearly impossible to get into a position where at least one guard wasn't aiming at you at all times. The poor level design really hurts this area of the game since the vast majority of your conflicts take place in large, generic open rooms that offer little room for improvisation or enemy separation.
When RONIN clicks, it feels damn good. Dropping onto an enemy agent, throwing your sword into another across the room, and then grabbing it from the floor while bullets whiz by is the sort of rush that few games can offer. But the hours of tedium separating these flashes of brilliance are simply too much to ignore.

Mechanically it's more Deus Ex: Human Revolution, but far better. Better mantling, better augs, better weapon customization, and better energy management. The one boss fight in the game can be handled like Anna or Gunther, much to the shock and horror of the newer fans who didn't play the original, and he can even be handled non-lethally if you so desire.
However, the length is a concern. It's about 2/3 the length of HR, but with more binary choices and more replayability. I also think the DLCs were better. Therefore I suggest buying on sale. Performance/optimization is a concern (unlike HR), and don't even think about running this game at a Very High Level of Detail without 16GB of RAM. I thought the game was great, but being both better and worse than HR makes it a hard sell as anything but more HR. It's also the only game I've seen to do a dialogue wheel that was in no way inferior to a standard list of dialogue options and still have excellent dialogue options and voice acting to match.
Would I recommend this game? ♥♥♥♥ yes. It's no VTMB, but it's still a great game, and Squeenix can burn for what they did to this franchise.

This is one of those that I wish Steam allowed for more than a rigid "yes or no" for reviews. I, personally, have problems liking this game and getting immersed enough with the story and mechanics (which actually at some points seemed off putting and monotonous)
Of course it's hard not to give the game props for its visuals, though as stunning as some of them are there are still a few small errors where one resource doesn't quite look like it matches with the rest of the objects of the map (unfortunately a few of the tiles they used from the Futuristic tile pack looked like this for me, but I'm not sure if it's because I know those tiles or because they actually do have a completely different look from the drawn looking resources made for this game)
There are other reviews that summarize the story so I'm not going to get too into deconstructing that, but I do have quite a few issues with how things are setup and certain writing through out. Many of the characters (including sadly enough some major characters) come off as very flat in the writing. I also noticed a few minor grammar errors (unfortunately I forgot to note them down since I usually play games through Stream to unwind) but it wasn't anything that really detracted from the intended meaning and took maybe a second longer to process.
I do typically like stories and games that try to look or deconstruct moralistic views, but this many times felt a bit like some kind of agenda was being pushed and instead of feeling (as a player) free to pick whatever path I wanted; it seems very clear a lot of times that there's still a very right or wrong option.  Because of this, I don't quite feel like it achieves precisely the level of control over ethics and consequence that the game devs pitched (or maybe I'm just looking at it wrong)
Really, one of my major issues and a problem with the game that I don't like at all is it suffers from making a lot of maps just way to big, or at least it feels that way due to not being able to run on some of them (heck, even on the outdoor maps where you are able to run they just feel way to big sometimes; especially since most of the time to get the story you'll probably only go into about half of the buildings available making the rest just extremely large pieces that take up space)
Actually, overall it suffers from the wrong kind of padding; as mentioned before the maps are a bit too big occasionally meaning you'll be walking over them many times and many of the actual gameplay elements are either RNG to the point of being annoying or just monotonous actions and possibly prompts. Removing or changing these to a more understandable setup for to the player might have been better, except the game wouldn't have been near as long (I'm up to about 5 hours [that's the total on the save file] right now; that's just for one play through and I haven't even actually reached the ending yet) or probably have as much gameplay.
Also, as nice as it is that the game has its own music, the tracks all get rather annoying pretty quickly; it's pretty unfortunate that there's no way to just turn off the music after awhile.
None of this is to turn others off from playing, though; clearly even though it does have these problems there are still quite a number of people who absolutely enjoy what the game devs managed to create with this game and it's still quite possible that you could, too. It just happened to not be a game I enjoyed and that's perfectly okay.

The greatest thing about this game is that there isn't an illusion of choice, as most choice games seem to revere. It questions the player's morality, it was easy to make the wrong decision, thereby encouraging a higher replay value. However, that brings me to the pacing of the game. For one thing, I spent SEVERAL HOURS working in a tofu factory making tofu products for extra cash and then gambling for another hour just to make a little more; makes me hesitate on picking up the game again...unless of course I can find an easier way to make money. The story makes up for it for the most part and while grinding is technically realistic, it felt a little too strenuous.
Secondly, there are quite a few points in the game where you, as a player, feel very isolated and the game seems to be going nowhere - but I'd say that's pretty typical for an RPG-maker style game. This would happen if you miss a certain point in the game such as miss a job opportunity or skip the bus to get to the next town. It seems as though you can almost just stay in your home town and let the wedding go and while that says 'CHOICE', it also says boring.
One weird side quest in the second town over (or the third; I can't remember) that I'd like to mention, has a fishing kid who asks you to fetch some lake crab. This felt incredibly 'RPG' and far-fetched from reality and to top it off, his sprite turns into a black kid after you finish it. I didn't know if this was just a joke but I laughed with a questioning look on my face. You gained almost no benefit from it besides gaining more fishing spots to get free food.
Something I really adored about the game is the choosing your character and partner mechanic. I didn't get it at first but when I did, I was very pleased. It was unexpected and surprising but very clever.
In regards to the story, it was interesting, dark, romantic, intense, sad, silly. It makes you think, it rewards you, it beats you up and kills your insides. No matter what, in the end, you'll feel like a bad person, regardless of the 'good decisions' you make. You're selfish and subtly (or not so subtly) mean and rude but in my opinion, that's realistic. The cameo of the developers, Jake and Justin, was a bit of a weird meta stretch but their conversations were pretty entertaining so it wasn't all that bad. However, it did seem a bit over confident.
I'd recommend this definitely, especially if you're into a choose your own adventure visual novel-like game. If you're into the Louis CK 'local man's life gets progressively worse' theme, this is the game for you. And despite the little small weird details to the game, I can't wait until the sequel, Sometimes Always Monsters, which I got to play the demo at PAX'15 and got super excited with Justin over it.

A gorgeous, and somewhat casual, experience.  This is a shining example of how far the 'norm' of game design has evolved.  Once an brutal game untimely demises, then a game about rewinding said demises, now a game where you cannot die whatsoever.  This is definitely a game more about an experience than a "game" in the traditional sense of the word; 'Passive Beauty' is a good way to put it.  There isn't any real urgency felt as you deftly navigate the worlds and bosses, but it lets you absorb more of the visual artistic grandeur that lies in this world.  The characters begin to show some semblance of depth and witty banter, but I wish the story-telling matched the artful execution of the world.  In the end it's as lighthearted as the death-free combat, which is too bad, because it's the weakest link in this otherwise stellar reboot.

Well lets start by saying one thing about this game,how shall i put it "GOD THIS GAMES ADDICTIVE".
Ok got that out of my system now on with the review,this is one of those casual games that just creeps on on you grabs you by the shoulders and says "HEY PLAY ME I AM A REALLY GOOD GAME" and trust me it is just that.
You start the game with a normal hand of cards and when you first start you have no special traits that can be applied to your deck but you earn these as you play and earn points and level up.
Now the object of the game is to win and be in front by the most points come the end of the game,now this is on some games a lot harder than it sounds depending on what special objectives are applied to that game and what special traits your opponent has equipped as these can spell success or failure depending on which ones are equipped.
Some special traits make you draw 3-4 more cards,some let you take an opponents card from any set you havent got and some further still let you play a card from your hand over again and there are many more for you to discover.
The graphics in game do there job (although this game is'nt about graphics to be honest) and the sound does its job also (again not really an issue as this games not about the music either) but its the play mechanics and the actual simplicity of the game that drags you in by the scruff of the neck and wont let go.
Start to play and you'll see why hand follows hand and eventually you realise that you have been sat playing the game for what seems like no time at all and yet 2-3 hours have passed.Now let me say that things start of nice and easy but (and this is where the game gets you) things soon pick up and eventually you end up at one of those pull your hair out moments that a lot of these deceptive games allways seem to posses ("I NEVER GET LIKE THIS I PROMISE" "OH YES YOU DO YOU LIAR" "OH OK THEN I ADMIT I DO OK,HAPPY NOW").
Dont worry about this though and dont let it put you of because as you play the game you will eventually start to learn the little Intricacies this game has and all the little tricks it throws at you and eventually you will wade past that difficult point you were stuck on,to only then get to another point thats just as annoying and just as tricky (but allways in a good and entertaining way).
So in closing if you like your games to be simple yet at times throw you with its twists in gameplay styles and also have the time to learn to play through all that the game throws at you then jump on in "ME BOYO",if not then i would suggest you look somewhere else as this game wont be for you,and remember why are pirates such dastardly deceptive blighters-answer "BECAUSE THEY AAARRRRRRRRRRR" (GOD THAT WAS SUCH AN AWFULL JOKE)

A Valley Without Wind is a unique game. The combination of randomly-generated levels and metroidvania-style platforming gives it a great deal of replayability. Something that I find interesting, however, is the game's emotional impact. While the game's story isn't particularily impressive, the combination of easily-learned gameplay, beautiful graphics, and incredibly memoriable music give a profound sense of solitude and loneliness. As a Glyphbearer, you are one of the only people in the now-shattered world who can survive outside the scant few villages spread across the continents, and the loneliness and sense of hopelessness that accompany sich a role are palpable. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, though. Personally, the mood of the game feels very quiet and reserved. Unlike many other games, A Valley Without Wind truly gives the feeling of being a wanderer, passing through dead towns and snowy forests with nowhere to truly call home.  If you're familiar with the concept of Catharsis, then this game is a brilliant example of it in action. The game provides a memoriable experience that I have never found in any other game, and I would heartily reccomend it.

I really wanted to like this game, but its inexcusably shoddy controls make it impossible.
Break your way into a facility to hack computers and assassinate people, with a turn-based combat system? It sounds wonderful.
However, in combat, your primary method of movement is jumping. The game gives you an indicator to tell you where your  jumps will go. The problem is that the indicator doesn't work. You will line up a jump, ready to dodge bullets and tackle an enemy... and your character jumps into the floor and stays still. With a major usability issue in the game's core mechanic, I cannot recommend it to anyone under any circumstances.
Let me use a metaphor to explain why this is such a problem. Imagine playing a turn-based RPG where you had to use a cursor to select one of four combat options. While hovering over an option, it would glow. However, the actual area you had to click was different from the area that triggered the glow. So when you clicked on the left side of a glowing button, you'd choose the option to the left. You might learn how to adapt, but no game should ever make you. This is unacceptable, and tarnished a game with a great concept.

But superficial similarities aside, it's a very different game, as the tutorials keep reminding you ("This is not a stealth game! Kill everyone!) Where Gunpoint was a stealth game in realtime, Ronin is a turn-based action game with some stealth elements, and in that respect it has more similarities to Superhot or even chess than Gunpoint. All that insane fight choreography you see in movies and other games, it has to be meticulously planned in this game. That's not to be miscontrued as something boring: there's a certain thrill in having to plan ahead for where your position will need to be a few rounds ahead for that fatal blow to land, knowing full well that you may need to adapt your plans and moves depending on what the enemy AI chooses to do. Not sold on this at all. Decent idea: seeing the same world through the eyes of a middle-aged person, a frail old man, and an energetic child. I know it's just a demo, and I appreciate that it's free, but it's like if a book had a 'demo' that just gave you a stack of blank pages and some words on the side.
You have to cross the road three times, with slightly different visuals and control balancing every time, and that's about it in terms of gameplay. Of course, it's not the gameplay this game is about, so I'll focus on the story. Okay, there isn't a story either (it is just a demo, so I'll let that slide), and instead talk about the statement the game is making.
Selling itself as an art game, the lack of depth is my main issue with this game. It does have a tiny bit to be gleamed from the experience (The way the old man has to time the crossing of the road to avoid the cars running him down could be a symbolic statement about how modern society moves so quickly it has no patience for those slower than themselves, and having to jump on the zebra crossing to avoid lava is something I remember doing yesterda-a few years back), but that's about it. While the child's outlook is lively and colourful, the other two are almost exactly the same. They both walk down a grey, lifeless path, the exception being that the old man has hazy vision and a swaying camera, representing his frailness. The only message I can take from this is that life gets steadily worse as you age, an outlook I've heard some of my relatives object to. It doesn't really say why it gets worse, or have any solutions as to how one can keep his from happening. The one thing I consider kind of insulting about this is that it assumes that all people are the same. I'm sure some people live in this predicament, but it's not universal, it's not the same all across the board, it's not, as the game puts it, "the way of life". Not all children have twinkly-eyed magical adventures through the early stages of their life, and not all middle-aged people are lifeless, superficial shells of people. For all it's artistic pretentions, it doesn't have anything big to say. Although, guessing from the charity-appeal violin music, it thinks it has something big to say.
Having the double criticism defense of being an art game in early access, I could always be called out with either "It's not a full game, it's too early to say", or "It's about art, not entertainment; you just don't get it." But this isn't fine art. Art has insight, wisdom, depth and a new spin on something familiar that can engage us in a topic. This hasn't. It's a cynical, bland, simplistic experience that acts like it has some higher meaning, exemplifying the worst elitist attitude that some minimalistic indie games have started coming dangerously close to in the past few years.

*UPDATED REVIEW FOR LATE DECEMBER 2015*
When I compare this game to its previous version(s), I see a big improvement in development. The game starts to somewhat take shape and the old incomplete game fades away. However, it's clear that the game is still not even close to being finished. Why? The game still adopts its original (yet ironically unoriginal) concept of age-influenced perception. As stated by myself (in my previous review) and by others, it's simply NOT MEANINGFUL, NOT NEW, and NOT SPECIAL IN ANY WAY.
The environment of the world(s) in the game is incomplete (such as the cut-off street in the old man talking scene) and the graphics are very basic, even for its low-poly style. There is no introduction, you just get straight into the blank world with a numerous amount of doors (horrible beginning). No drive is seen to be implemented into the game, causing the player to have no motivation in completing the BASIC and LONG "puzzles/objectives" the game offers. It's seriously odd that the developers of the game chose to put cheerful music in moments of shock (such as the husband strangling his wife in front of the child); it completely ruins the mood.
The game is incompelte in all aspects of game-making and its core subject is a bore. In fact, the only thing that is good with this game is its free price tag. I do, however, see a big improvement from before. I hope when the game finishes its early-access stage everything will improve greatly to the point where it can let players have a reason to play the game.
TL;DR: Game is still incomplete and is completely lacking in all aspects of game-development. Recent updates with the game has, however, been somewhat promising. Unless you've got ~30 minutes to waste (and I mean you've REALLY got 30 minutes to waste), then you can go ahead and give this game a go.

The game has a nice balance of both melee combat as well as stealth sections that allow you to utilize Batman's various gadgets and tools. See a guard walking underneath where your perched on a Gargoyle? Drop down and sweep them up and let them hang.

Batman: Arkham Asylum is a top rate Batman action game. Firstly, I'm a huge Batman fan, so maybe a little bias coming in there, but this game absolutely get's it right in the look and feel of playing Batman.
I first played this game about 6 years ago and completed it and have just finished my second run through. I'm really impressed with how the graphics have held up, despite being released over 6 years ago. You can still get a lot of visual enjoyment from the game.
The gameplay itself is engaging, the combat is a highlight - the flow, the animation and the feedback leave combat an untterly enjoyable experience. A game like this could run the risk of combat feeling very stale after a while, but that is not the case - they have absolutely nailed it with the mix of move, combos and visuals.
What I also love about the game is it's not daunting. I recommend playing with a controller but you will get the hang of the controls easy enough and it will become second nature, without getting overly complicated.
To me they also have got the challenge and pacing just right. Some people may criticse that the boss fights arent challenging enough, but I disagree. I don't want to spend hours on a boss fight. The main thing is a boss fight, feels like a boss fight and again they hit the mark for me with this.
Throw in all the bonus content such as challenge modes, solving the Riddler's puzzles and finding trophies and there is a huge amount to keep you interested in your play through.
Highly recommended.

I watched a few You Tube Let's Plays (Wanderbots and Aavak) of this and it looked interesting. Reviews (and the Let's Players) mentioned issues with the game and that's why I bought it on sale (still a hefty £26).
As I can waffle at international level, I'll do a quick review then a longer one with bullet points which I feel the developers need to address before doing anything else to the game like DLC.
Short version:
- You'll either like the graphics or not, you don't need to buy the game to figure that out, check You Tube
- Play the beta version; it has more adaptability to the key configuration if you're using a mouse and keyboard
- The controls are abysmal and the tutorial does not in any way help you with learning the controls because it ALWAYS assumes you're using a controller. This is really shoddy work on the part of the developers and should have been fixed before release
- The mouse cursor is laggy; presumably down from a bad console port. Also should have been fixed before release
- Has great potential but the lack of polish just screams "can't be bothered" by the developers
- Absolutely not worth full price
- Definitely wouldn't purchase DLC until the quality of life issues have been addressed
Yes, my play time is short. Because I got fed up with the controls and the game ignoring that I've got a PC version not the console version. And I'll be honest; at least 30 minutes of my play time was me using the wiki to find out how to do what the tutorial insisted that I do (EG open a certain menu). Which says a lot about the game.
Long version:
I saw Let's Plays, I read reviews and as it was on sale (still a hefty £26), I was very torn whether to buy it. I'm torn whether to return it because it has such great potential.
However, the start of the game is so unhelpful, so badly presented and generally so poor, it doesn't engage you, just frustrates you.
The intro story and graphics are lovely. The music (at that point) is atmospheric. But once you get into the 'tutorial' it all goes wrong.
- The entire tutorial presumes you're using a controller. So it doesn't give you any idea of what to press if you're using a PC. I had to use the WIki
I've been gaming for 30 years (before mice were a thing), I always use a mouse/keyboard (I have a HOTAS and a Logitech G13 and I prefer the mouse/keyboard). I play a lot of games where there are lots of key combinations and I don't have an issue with that. Usually I can remap them in a way they make sense to me and I'm good. But this game's controls are an incomprehensible mess.
- If you remap the keys, it doesn't tell you that it's still assigned to something else
- It isn't clear what each button means
There are a lot of menus and options. It isn't clear what each one does. So you remap "Pan Left" in Macro mode to A and then have to find out how to get the camera to do the same when in View mode. Why? Am I likely to want the latter bound to B and L shift?
The tutorial is not helpful. And you can't break out of it and just press random buttons to find out what happens ... you are literally STUCK until you hit upon the right combination of keys.
- The tutorial doesn't know what it's doing
It isn't teaching you the controls, it isn't teaching you how to play the game. It a long winded hoop-jumping process which basically caused me to give up.
I really want to like this game. I really want to play this game, but I am not going to spend three hours sorting out key bindings and playing 'guess what the tutorial wants' because someone couldn't be bothered to actually port their game properly. That was incredibly lazy. I wouldn't accept it from a £5 game and from one at £32 full price, it's inexcusable.
I sincerely hope the devs do update the tutorial. That the game shows what controls are required if you're using a PC.
- They need to have pop ups on screen when you hover over icons
Until then, this game isn't worth it.
And I just made up my mind to go for a refund.

As a fan of anime and manga (who also happens to be broke) it was inevitable that a Steam user such as myself would stumble across this game. It starts off a bit slow, and admittedly it can be a bit tedious at times. However those two facts have been somewhat remedied by daily/weekly events. In a world where the harem setting in anime, manga, and visual novels is rampant, it's refreshing to find a game that pokes fun at it. The game doesn't take itself too seriously, which I enjoy (expect fourth-wall breaks from more than one of the gals; Neptune and Deadpool would be proud of some of the comments they make).
Those anime cliches you see everywhere? They're here too, but can be hilariously lampshaded and poked fun at. Almost every girl is a tsundere for a while (as a tsunderephile I love this), but Cassie takes the cake. If she was real I would VERY much like to read the book she mentioned wanting to write "Attracting People Through Hostility". I won't get too much into spoiler territory but the other -dere types I've run into are kuudere and yandere (and the latter actually made me a fan of a certain psychotic cutie). And the references and shoutouts?
... Well, I'll let YOU find them. If you're an otaku like me you'll enjoy those little moments and go, "Aha! So Sad Panda is a fan of this? :D" I enjoy it a lot.
In summary, I recommend this. Just a note: it's all cutesie, but the raunchy humor and double entendres come into play later in most relationships, and a certain character is pretty much a living embodiment of "Anything That Moves", which can be pretty damn funny.

A lot of people throw the term "ninja" around the internet like they're trying to repaper the walls with it. People claim to be "ninjas" after watching a dozen or so episodes of the wrong cartoon, after they buy an unsharpened aluminum samurai sword at a flea market, or just whenever they're trying to impress people anonymously.
So when I point out that I write this review "from the standpoint of a ninja," I'm aware of how half-witted and watered down the term is. But a ninja is nothing if not determined to overcome tough odds, so here goes; time to♥♥♥♥♥♥up this rope.
Mark of the Ninja is possibly the best ninja-themed stealth game I've ever played, and I've played nearly all of them.
The first major note to its credit is, Mark of the Ninja favors gameplay over realism or historical accuracy. The player can always tell how visible they are based on the tone of the character's graphic. Enemies can see things which are in the light and can't see things which are in the dark. Walking footsteps are silent, and running footsteps make noise in an area around the character; the distance they can be heard from is indicated with a graphic on screen.
Open combat is virtually nonexistant and, most importantly, avoidable. The code of the Hisomu family demands that their sword be used only on an unaware enemy, and as such every patrol of guards can be outwitted and avoided or eliminated by surprise one at a time. And that's how and why the game *really* starts to shine; Mark of the Ninja is, at heart, a puzzle game (as most of my favorite stealth games are), inherently one where there are multiple solutions to most of the puzzles.
As such, it's not an exaggeration to say that it lives or dies based on the level design. The levels are linear, with distinct starting and ending points and few branching paths, but each section can be approached from numerous directions. The addition of hidden areas and collectable scrolls I could take or leave, but being able to unlock new equipment and "Paths" (suits of armor granting special powers) means that the already variable gameplay sprawls out even a little more.
So it's linear, yes, but with a huge amount of room for creative puzzle solving for players who have good awareness. Nervous guards can be tricked into shooting their team or tripping and falling off ledges. Killing a sentry or sniper and leaving his body somewhere others will discover it can lure them away from your objective. Often times, clever use of cover can remove the need to confront or eliminate guards entirely.
In summary, from the standpoint of someone 20-ish years deep in what's left of the real ninja tradition, Mark of the Ninja is a spectacular ninja-themed game because it rewards awareness and patience, promotes creative and variable problem solving, and most importantly always puts the important task at hand (in this case gameplay) first in terms of priority. Anything missing by way of historical accuracy is made up for on all points with the spirit, method, and feel of what the way of the ninja is *really* about.

I guess i'll start by saying that i've played games such as Cookie Clicker and Clicker Heroes before, in this review, you'll notice that i'll compare this game to Clicker Heroes quite often, as i find them to be similar in some way and i'm sure many others would agree.
To start off, i'll say that there was just one thing that i felt as if it was missing from the game that i really liked about Clicker Heroes, and that is the ability to revisit previously finished waves/levels. Just a small thing i really liked about Clicker heroes, but i guess to some extent it wouldn't suit the whole "wave" system they have in place where you need to destroy a certain amount of cubic structures to progress to the next one and each 5 waves, you must fight a boss to progress to the next, but you do have the ability to go back to the previous wave in order to earn gold to be able to break the boss before the timer ends. I haven't found this useful most of the time, since you do receive gold from some of the other easier to break blocks that i have mostly found myself just using those to strengthen my team and increase dps and dmg per click.
Pros:
-Its free, you do not need to pay to play the game nor are you able to purchase something in game as you play. No
ability to purchase gold, none of that crap. You wont think you're playing a free to play game that there's no need to
pay for anything, but yet get the feeling as if its being forced on you, in order to progress in the game.
-A great "Time Cube" feature, that adds cubes to the game which you are able to collect once you've reached wave
100, but they don't make it easy, they set a challenge in-front. In order to use these cubes, you must use "Time Warp"
which resets your progress and then you'll receive your cubes, along with 10%+ dps for each cube. You will be given 10
cubes when you reach wave 100, but to get more you'll have to progress and fight more bosses which sometimes have
these "Time Cube" cubes. These cubes can be used to purchase artifacts once you've used the "Time Warp" which can
give you a nice but balanced game changing advantage. I recommend using "Time Warp" at least once while playing.
-A nice organized five "bots" system i guess i could call them that are referred to as your "team", rather then having
around 10 that you will have to upgrade. You will only have to focus on five of them, along with upgrading your
clicks(there's a limit that you'll reach quite quickly, but you get more dmg per click as you upgrade your team) and
abilities that are purchasable which come with cooldowns.
-There's a leaderboard which requires you to register on their website and pair your game with the account, but luckily
its a very easy process. So if you're interested in being listed on their leaderboards, you can easily do so.
-Nice bright colors to keep you awake, along with some nice effects to go along with it.
There are many more, but you'll just have to try it and find out :)
Cons:
-Like i said before, there's the wave system which i would love to be able to change to waves i've finished. Its not a big
game changer to be honest.
-While i was playing i noticed some frame drops which have stopped after some time, they don't really ruin the
gameplay, but definitely something to take note of, as i am not running this on a bad computer that shouldn't easily run
the game. Then again, this issue might just be occurring on my PC.
As a conclusion, if you like addictive clicker games, this is what you need. The wave and Time Cube aspect of it, just opens up almost an unlimited number of playtime hours if you wish to progress in the game further!

At the time of writing this I have about 120 hours of playtime put down in this game and as much as I would like to recommend this, I simply cannot do it since doing so would be tricking people into spending money (although 30€ is cheap) on something that wont pay off.
The game has no real playerbase, there's maybe 4-6 hours a day where there's a "peak" of players and by "peak" I mean roughly ~1000 players active at the same time and it's also the number of players counted on all of the 5 regions/servers (US-east, US-west, EU, OCE and SEA) together and this number is steadily dropping. I believe the week after I write this, the peak will most likely be down to a three digit number.
The game has no competitive mode, it's aimed at casual players who enjoy quickplay and there is no penalty for leaving a game, which has led to most of the matches you play having a high chance to have atleast one or two leavers either on your side, the enemy side or split between the two (but 8 times out of 10 it'll be one-sided 4v5 or 3v5).
The developers also seem to highly favour some of the roles above others, promoting people to play for example gunslinger over assassin, wraith, enforcer, vanguard, etc. (I have no source on this being fact, it's merely an opinion made from observating the changes made in patches throughout the betas, the launch and the first official patch after official release)
The fullscreen mode is broke and forces you alt + enter until it enters fullscreen (you'll have to do this everytime you launch the game)
It's with a sad heart I give this otherwise unique game a thumbs down and recommend everybody to either wait for a discount, a free weekend or the game going f2p.

On the other hand, the graphics are really nice, the girls are adorable, and it's a genuinely good way to pass a little time or take a break. It also has some genuinely entertaining dialogue, ie "If there were no women in the world, it would be a pain in the butt" from Nutaku, which took me a second, but once I got it I couldn't stop snickering.

It has potential, that much is certain. As it stands now though, the game feels like nothing more than a Free-to-Play MMO, quality wise. The stages follow the mobile method of finish one numbered area then move to the next which you will be scored in with gold and exp. Each single stage has three levels of difficulty which is unlocked when the previous difficulty is completed.
While this system works in mobile titles, it suffers here because it severly hurts the games ability to tell a story. Right now, before each stage, you are only given a small slideshow of pictures explaining the events leading to it. Very dissapointing considering the "story" is actually what I looked forward to in this game. Red girl background and all.
All these said, the game is still in production and while I don't recommend it now, I will, hopefully, change my mind once the game is more complete.

I was surprised to hear that the game has a lot in common with Bastion, but after seeing how they did the town I can see it.
At this point in early access the game is designed to start sending you back to the earlier areas at higher difficulties to allow you to grind xp and items. Enemy variety has been good for the early part of the game, but the maps appear to be static. I have always felt that randomized areas help give dungeon crawlers longevity so it'll be interesting to see what they do.
I suggest starting with the Fortitude character, currency is shared as well as the stash so if you decide to have multiple characters it's easy to pass stuff between them.
It also appears that you can summon an ally, even if offline, and they will get rewards for it. Very cool concept.

This game is in some sort the prototype that shaped the whole action genre in all these years. So this means it is a well done game. Mediocre:

Bem o que podemos falar de Brawlhalla?
Brawlhalla é um jogo de luta criada pela Blue Mammoth Games, ele lembra bastante Super Smash Bros, nosso objetivo é jogar outros jogadores para o vão para fazer com que ele perca vida ou perca pontos!
Também podemos fazer com que a defesa fica com pouca durabilidade fazendo com que seus socos ou suas armas de corpo-corpo fazem com que o jogador seja jogado para o vão, ou seja quanto menos defesa é hitkill para você meu amigo.
Bem, no Brawlhalla tem vários modos para os jogadores.
Modo casual é o modo que há mais pessoas jogando
Modo Competitivo: Modo onde você ganha rank, lembrando bastante Counter-Strike, caso perca você perde rank..
Modo Vs2: Modo aonde forma time de 2 pessoas, única coisa que muda que adiciona uma pessoa..
Modo Competitivo²: Esse modo forma time de 2 pessoas, tendo friend fire caso use algum tipo de soco forte no seu amigo Bye, Bye!
Modo Personalizado: Modo aonde os jogadores fazem sua própia sessão com vários mudanças.

Right, so the games works great and is a lot of fun. I've beaten the campaign three times, however, when my stock XBox 360 controller died I replaced it with a Thurstmaster GPX, which is made under liscense as a 360 controller, and the game became unplayable. Turns out that unless you have an actual, wired, Microsoft manufactured, 360 controller the game doesn't recognize the correct inputs and there is no way in the game to remap the controls. Well, that's not true; you can remap the controlls, it just won't do anything. So unless you have an original 360 controller or don't mind using B to accelerate and A to break and not having a Start or Select button, you should probably give the game a pass. Which is a shame because the game still looks good and is a lot of fun.
So far I have tested it with wired/wireless XBox One controllers, NVidia Shield Controller, the aforementioned Thrustmaster and two other 3rd party 360 controllers with the same results. A quick Google search will turn up a bunch of other peopel with similar complaints and for a nine year old game there is zero chance of EA patching the problem. Oh well.

Need for Speed: Undercover is not the abysmal mess it's often made out to be. It is not an unrecoverable piece of garbage with no redeeming qualities; if anything, I'd sum it up as sort of like a last-gen/mobile clone of Most Wanted (2005). However, it very clearly isn't done. The driving physics seemed exceptionally odd at first, not requiring braking, and then I booted up 1998's NFSIII: Hot Pursuit and found this game actually closely matches the old games' physics with the newer games' open world and style.
However, it's just... worse. This game feels like a low-budget knockoff of Need for Speed, or, more likely, a very hastily rushed product that could've been at least decent. There's polish in some of the wrong places; vehicles are slippery messes, while police dialogue has an incredible number of new lines and is excellently acted. Cutscenes are sparse, incoherent, uncomfortable (I'm trying to play a racing game; being abruptly told "you can be my pet anytime you want~" by an NPC is not a fun addition to this, nor a rambling thirty-second cutscene trying to make talk about Wile E. Coyote chasing the Road Runner somehow sound like a seductive proposition), and don't line up with gameplay (being told "meet me at the docks at 6" and the game jump-cuts to a highway at 8), leaving me to think they were originally longer but got chopped up to fit what little game was finished. Most obviously, you're once given a job to collect six cars around the city, and the quest ends as soon as you get four (it's implied other members of the gang got the other two, but then why harp on six the entire cutscene?).
The actual Hot Car jobs are phenomenally fun, throwing you right into a police pursuit with some absurdly beautiful and expensive supercar. These are awarded as part of story progression, and story progression only comes with leveling up, which comes with experience earned from races. These races go from absurdly insultingly I-can-win-with-my-eyes-closed-and-heart-not-beating-and-literally-deceased-and-collapsed-on-the-accelerator easy, to controller-smashingly infuriatingly impossible, with AI brazenly picking up speed by hundreds of miles per hour as soon as the finish line is around the next corner. They don't
win by a long shot, it's
picking up an absurd amount of speed right at the line. I once even saw an AI car take a shortcut, crash at high speed, and then just
to the finish ahead of me by ping-ponging off of the invisible walls along the map.
Which brings me to another point. I used to very much enjoy messing with NFS:MW with memory editors and trainers, messing up the physics and screwing with the game's logic. And the problem with Undercover is, it behaves exactly like that out of the box. Traffic can spawn in going over 100mph, in mid-air, so you just kind of have to get used to sedans breaking the sound barrier above you. You harmlessly thunk into AI cars while they can easily pit-maneuver you. Speedbreaker now hits you with such a massive speed penalty, you come to nearly a dead stop if you try to use it to turn instead of in a pursuit situation. Police cars are paperweights that can be battered around with ease, and spike strips are still a death knell of any escape. Shadows of buildings and trees frantically rotate at high speeds in a desperate attempt to catch up with the time of day. Every time something appears, it's out of place, and it makes sure you notice by hastily scrambling to get into place and making it all worse.
Essentially, this game is a shame, because it's clear some people worked very hard on it. However, it's not even the fundamental failures of gameplay, uninspired map, or clumsy forced plotline that make it bad. If it was terrible and fun, I was still going to recommend it. But a massive difficulty spike around level 14, combined with the game forgetting all my settings and resetting to 640x480 for the third time, finally were the last straws for me. If you're going to buy this, do it as part of the EA Racing Pack, where as it's part of a discount, you're essentially being paid to own it. That would probably be a comparatively acceptable way to end up with this.

I played this game before it came out on steam and had the opportunity to speak directly with the lead developer. Although the game has charm and will give anyone who has played Runescape nostalgia, you will quickly run out of things to do and realize the game's problems. This mostly the fault of the main developer and his incompetence. Being a newly created game, there are a plethora of bugs and glitches, even problems that sometimes cause the whole server to crash. While very frustrating, this is expected and should, I hope, go away with time as long as people continue to work on the game.

Some of the major issues:

If a mob spawns on the same square a player is on, that player and the mob is trapped there until another player comes by and kills the mob. This can even happen in the wilderness (which functions exactly like the Runescape version), and could easily let other players set up to kill them.

The combat styles are totally imbalanced in pvp. Archery is by far the strongest combat style due to being able to infinitely kite players while firing arrows. Magic spells have too long cast times and too short cast distances so that players can simply run away if they see someone start to channel a spell. Melee is by far the worst because both the person attacking and person being attacked have to remain TOTALLY STILL for attacks to land. This means you can just run around if someone is trying to melee you and avoid everything.

There simply is not enough content at this point for the game to be interesting for an extended period of time. If you party with other players to get group xp you will be able to kill the strongest monsters in the game in the matter of a few days. At this point, it's not even worth trying to kill other players because the only reliable way is to exploit bad mechanics.

Duplication glitch. I know of one duplication glitch in this game. There are probably more...

If any of these mechanics get fixed I'll remove them from this review.

Finally, lets talk about ResBak Online. If you've played Orake, you've probably had your game crash at some point and might have seen the message "ResBak Online has stopped responding." A quick Google search will reveal another 2D MMO project that failed. The server and client for ResBak is available Online and after playing it, is IDENTICAL to Orake.


Literally the only difference are the sprites used. The source code for ResBak is available online for $30 is very obviously how the developer was able to produce Orake without knowing anything about or understanding his "own" game. The best part is that the main developer I referred to earlier explicitly stated "I created 99% of the content in this game.".....

It's dark, it has bat-toys, it somehow manages not to kill despite pulling enemies into a crazy long fall, it is batman!
Okay so this is a great game, with lots of references to batman villains. Far from all his villains, since he does have a massive gallery. Since my batman knowledge mainly comes from the cartoons, and not the comics, there were biographies for a lot I didn't know of, but there was also some missing that I really liked. But of course all the big guys are at least referenced to or make an appearance. You just can't be certain your favorite is mentioned, if you have one of the smaller villains in your top most wanted list. My personal favorite characters all made appearances though, but they are also some of the bigger names.
The combat is nice and easy to control for the most part. The only parts where it really had me angry was during some of the boss battles, where the camera was locked in place... Which was really annoying, after having had full control of it during the rest of the game. While the bosses all looked cool, there was only one I liked. Since who the bosses are spoils who is in the game, I will let it be in spoilers for those you don't want to see it.
The second annoying thing was the riddler trophies/challenges for collectors. Not that there was too many, even though there were a lot and many could have been removed. No, the problem was the way some were made. Instead of making sure you could find a way to reach every trophy in an area, before moving on with the story, several of them were locked behind places where you were unable to reach them without a gadget you wouldn't get way later in the story. Some of them you could even SEE sitting there taunting you going. "Oh hell no! You have to come back here near the end of the game if you want me! Even though it will make no sense in the story to return here." Like really? Really? There is nothing wrong with having to return to an old area later if you want to pick up stuff you might have missed, as long as it is the player's choice. But forcing them to return because you don't give them the tools to reach everything before the story pushes on, is just low. Especially taunting them with the things they can't reach...
But the story was fun, and beating up enemies outside of boss encounters was also a lot of fun. Flying around and surprising your foes gave you a feeling of being the fighting batman. Overall it was a really great game, which is why it is so annoying that the boss encounters and riddler stuff left me frustrated. I recommend it to any fan of batman and action games.

This game is very deep, over whelming, confusing and complex. That is why it is simply just a fantastic game, there are barely any boundaries to what you can do within the game scope. You do literally progress how ever you want, with your settlement and advancing character(s), you will defiantly loose a few when playing. The game is not linear at all.
The game has a combination of RPG and platformer elements, which opens up to some crazy combinations of abilities, spells and gear enchantments your characters can use. For example, flying through the map at insane speeds while exploding fire every second. Why do you ask? Just because you can really.
The world you live in is all randomly generated, so each play through won't ever be the same. What else could you ask for? Content around the same skill level as you? Sure! Monsters scale to your playing abilities, so there is always a constant challenge. Don't think the game will let you off that easily.
From what I've played, I've barely scratched the surface to what this game offers me. But from what I saw, it was quite over whelming and made me question what the hell I was doing every second. And I loved it. But the main jist of it all is that you need to save your continent from an evil overlord. Once that's done, you just move onto an even bigger continent with a much harder overlord!
This game is truly an ultimate character customisation game, where there is pretty much no limit to how you kit out your character. But as well as that, you get to do the same with your settlement with saving, upgrading NPC's you find on your adventures, build buildings for them to live in and turn your home in a flourishing city! It's just going take a while to do so...
I would recommend playing the demo first, before you decide to pick this game up. And if you find it a bit too much and over whelming, I hear the sequel is a bit easier and simplified a bit for people to get into. But if you like a challenge, being over whelmed with information, go into insane fights with enemies and have no limit on what you want to do, then this is the game for you.
In conclusion:
7 / 10, Don't fall down deep pits, you'll regret with what you've found.

An excellent game once you get in there and really dig into the game's many mechanics. Lots to explore, fight and build. The graphics are generic looking, yet crisp and clear at the same time. The game is polished for the most part and the general controls are good, controller support is definitely a plus for a Metroidvania game such as this (and customizable support at that). The soundtrack is one of the best game soundtracks I've heard in recent years with lots of the tracks occasionally getting stuck in your head. As for the in-game mechanics, there are A LOT of them surprisingly for a game in the Metroidvania genre. It's highly frustrating at first having all these mechanics thrown in your face (crafting, building, etc.) and with a literally endless world to explore (you simply will never completely explore your world, it's that large). Yet once you get a grasp of them (took me a long while), they all turn out to be welcome additions to a game with otherwise simple core gameplay.
A big one for me is modding. You can do everything from literally changing the character sprites themselves, to designing your own levels and so on. Although, unfortunately the modding community never really hit it off, so there isn't much pre-made mods to choose from. Yet if your like me and your fine with making your own, then your golden.
In short, this is basically one of those games where either your the kind of gamer who just wants to sit down and enjoy a game, and that's it. Else your the kind of gamer who doesn't mind doing a little work to really learn a game. So if your part of the latter who likes to learn, experiment and most importantly loves Metroidvania-style gameplay, then definitely pick this game up. Highly recommended.

A Valley Without Wind is a good game that suffers from obvious design mistakes that tragically prevent it from living up to its potential. So instead of a great game that can be played endlessly we get a game that's good for a while but runs out of steam once you've seen everything it has to offer. The tragedy is that it was clearly aiming to be played endlessly with it's endless ocean and bottomless caves, and people clearly put a lot of work into creating a wide variety of weapons, enemies, and mini-games, but they were putting their effort in the wrong direction.
When exploration is done right in a game, it can keep you busy for as long as you care to spend exploring. In principle it's not complicated to do it right. Just look at Minecraft or Terraria and do something like that; give people a huge and varied world, scatter prizes around like Easter eggs, and let people wander. The hard part is generating the world. It seems that A Valley Without Wind wanted to be an exploration game, but couldn't figure out how to generate a world so they took a shortcut and generated a endless web of interconnected rooms instead. They worked so hard to build a good game around that web of rooms and they succeeded, but it's still no substitute for an actual explorable world.
The saddest thing of all is when this game shoots itself in the foot because of its own good intentions. They have a map, but the web of rooms is too complicated to represent literally on a flat map, so you get an abstract view that shows only the connections and doesn't show relative positions or sizes. The game explains this very carefully because it could easily be confusing. They explain that to represent the rooms with size and relative position you would need a 3D map, which would be difficult to read, which is very true. The map they give is very easy to read and an excellent tool for figuring out where you are and where you want to go. It's so good that it shows you explicitly the real truth of what you are doing. You're not exploring a cave or a dungeon; you're exploring a graph, a set of nodes connected by edges. The rooms aren't parts of a larger building; they are just mini platforming challenges that you overcome to get to the next room, and the map makes this so very obvious.
I usually find myself wanting to get through a room rather than wanting to explore it. Why explore a room when I know it's just a meaningless node in a graph that I will never have reason to return to? No room has anything that I can't find somewhere else. As soon as you find yourself skipping rooms that you know won't lead anywhere instead of going in to every room just for the fun of it, you've realized that this game is not an exploration game.
There is no RPG in this game and there is no strategy. The exploration is very week. It may be technically a sandbox, but it's a sandbox where all you can do is run, jump, and shoot. What is good in this game is pure platformer with mouse-aimed shooting, and it's strength is in the wide variety of weapons and enemies. It also has tons of stuff to collect and several mini-games where you have do to things like get down a long hallway of monsters without taking damage or protect a village from a meteor storm by knocking the meteors off coarse.
This game is probably worth its price, but that's hard to judge. You might be best to wait for a sale. It's not one of those priceless games that you'll keep playing forever. It should be very entertaining for quite a few hours, but once you've done everything you're going to want to stop. The game won't tell you when to stop since it is endless, so eventually you'll stop because you've stopped finding new things and you're bored, but that doesn't mean it wasn't really fun in the beginning.

The game that started it all. Of course, compared to the rest, this game is sorely lacking some features that creeped into the later Arkham installments, however this game's rock-solid mechanics and amazing attention to detail alone make this game worth your time and money.

There are alot of things I like about this game, and may I don't. Let me go into a little more detail.
What does it for me in this game is that it has the perfect atmosphere for a Batman game. It's dark, gritty, relistic, disturbing, etc. In other words, it is everything that a Batman story should be. Everything from the voice actors, to character design, to art style, it all perfectly encapsulates what I think of when I hear the word "Batman" or sit down to watch/play something related to the Dark Knight.
Where this game really frustrated me, though, was the actual gameplay mechanics themselves. I have many gripes with it. I will organize my complaints into neat sections here.
I felt the gadgets were rather lacking. There are only 5 main ones with others that you can get by buying special upgrades. However, they're all related to movement, mostly. First of all, you get the batarangs. The problem with them is that they suck. They can't be used to take down an enemy, only stun them for half a second, which isn't enough time to take enemies down before they recover and shoot you to death. It would have been much more fun to throw the batarangs like B-man does in the tv shows and movies: disarming henchmen or flat out knocking them out. Obviously this would make the game too easy because the batarangs are infinite, but an easy fix would have been to make the 'rangs limited in quanitity, and you pick them back up after a fight or something. This also would have made the game more realistic and added an element of strategical item management.
The second gadget is an explosive spray that can be detonated at will. The problem with this gadget is it's rarely usuable in combat or stealth sections. It's pretty much only used to open up new areas for finding stupid riddler trophies or other pointless unlockables.
The remaining gadgets I have no problem with in and of themselves. One is the batclaw, which is a firable hook that can pull objects or enemies to you. It's phenomenal when trying to carefully take out groups of gunmen, or even in basic melee combat. Another is a sonic sequencer, which can be used to hack things, is very useful, as well as provides a fun mini-game to counter-point the action. Lastly, there is a horizontal line gun which is solely for movement. Cool, but nothing spectacular.
Overall, the game could have used a lot more gadgets, especially ones like the batclaw that have multiple uses in and outside of combat. I would have loved to see bolas, throwable smoke or flash pellets, or maybe that goo he throws on faces in the movies. Basically, stuff that breaks up the monotony of combat and provides alternative ways to take down gunmen without getting shot full of holes or just give an extra edge in melee (more on that later). What I'm getting is that I want to be able to do all the cool things that we consider iconic of Batman, rather than costing by soley on the batclaw.
Which brings me to the next thing: melee combat. There are a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of parts where you're in a room and can't leave until you beat up all the thugs (like an arena shooter). I hated these parts because they aren't very interactive. You just click left mouse repeatedly to have Batman kick/punch guys. The game auto-manages all of this for you, having Batman jump wildly around the arena doing complicated moves and such. The only time the game requires player input is when you need to block (at which point an enemy gets a blue thing above his head and you're supposed to press right mouse to counter). Half the time though, Batman won't counter even if you do press right mouse, leading to some quite frustrating deaths or loss of combo points. The other problem with this system is because the game manages the combat for you, Batman could end up moving across the room to punch someone in an area you didn't want him to go (such as some kind of enviormental hazard you need to stay out of). Overall, you're going to get really frustrated at times due to lack of control, as well as just being bored. The only times this combat was fun was when they introduced special enemies that you couldn't take down just by left clicking, you have to do other things that require player input. However, these enemies were few and far between, the game electing to throw hordes of zombie-like regular henchmen at you most of the time. None of the gadgets were that useful in these sequences. Mankind Divided is the sequel to Deus Ex: Human Revolution, the popular prequel to the classic Deus Ex.  This is the first game in the series to star an already established protagonist (Adam Jensen).  Set a couple of years after the events of HR, the incident at the climax of the game that saw augmented people lose control all over the globe has increased tension between normal people and the augmented.  The latter are now treated as second-class citizens and discrimination against them is rampant, to the point that a law that bans augmentations is in danger of being passed.  Not helping the situation are terrorist attacks being blamed on a pro-aug organization.  Adam most now investigate these attacks and get to the bottom of it before his own life is deemed worthless in the eyes of the world.
MD has the same gameplay style from the previous game.  Choose your own path, customize your augmentations to your preferred playstyle, etc.  While the game does a good job of explaining these sytems to you, it's better to have played the previous one in the series to get a better handle on things.  New "experimental" augmentations are added, with a temporary setback forcing you to shut down an old one or suffer issues if you want to use one of them, so you need to make some careful choices.
Unlike the previous game, that had a couple of hub zones and smaller, linear areas, there's only one hub zone here (Prague), but it' pretty big.  If you decide to explore around it can take you hours to even start playing the first main mission.  The "3D metroidvania" nature of the hub area means that some sections will be unreachable until you unlock certain augmentations, so even after that you won't be able to see everything the first time.
Characters in this game are well written, deep and interesting, and some of the sidequests are very good, but the main story isn't very good.  The game tries to compare discrimination against augs against regular racism, and it just doesn't work.  As seen in the last game, people have very good reason to fear the augmented.  On the other side of the spectrum, the discrimination reaches cartoonish levels at some points.  I really wish the main story had had an entirely different approach.
That being said, the game is still a lot of fun.  And it works pretty well in my PC, but, there are a few caveats.  I've suffered a few crashes and slowdowns.  It becomes evident that the more the game is being played, the more strain in the memory it causes, and at some point it just runs out.  I only have 6GB of RAM, though, which is less than the minimal requirement of 8, so that's probably on my end.  Still, you have to wonder if that minimal requirement is only there because the people in charge of the port couldn't bother to make it work with less.  There is one problem that's not related to my PC, though, and it's the loading times, as they already were large enough in the PS4 version, which I also played.
In any case, just know that the game does work with only 6GB of RAM, but too long play sessions (4+ hours) are discouraged.
Despite the flaws, I definitely recommend the game, particularly if you're a fan of the series.  It never reaches the greatness of the prequel or the original, but it's still a lot of fun.

I really enjoyed this game, the rules are really simple to pick up, it's fun to play, the characters are memorable and consistent in 'who they are' with the trait combos they use. The AI is really good and not overly cheaty, there were a couple of times I thought you wouldn't keep drawing like that or you'd have had to have known that card was there to have carried on or to have played that card, but this didn't happen often enough to make it a concern. It is incredibly fair the majority of the time.
Basically cards in your hand are banked, cards in the draw pile are the ones that you play with.
There are 10 suits and each suit has a function.
You're trying to beat the characters and usually you need a score of 65 at least on each game to get 3 stars on a tournament. (It will unlock the other tournaments on just one star though which just requires you to win each game with any score. I was going for the achievement which is why the 65 was important to me.)
You play cards from the draw pile, if you get a duplicate suit you lose all the cards in play to the bust pile (unless your opponent has a trait that puts bust cards into their hand instead)
Only the highest card from each suit is counted towards your score (although there are a couple of tournaments that count every card towards your score)
* Anchors lock all previously played cards so you can't lose them
* Hooks let you play a card from your hand
* Clairvoyant lets you see what's next in the deck. (The mystic trait will allow you to view the next 3)
* Swords lets you play a card from your opponent's hand as long as you don't already have the suit in your hand or currently           in play.
* Chest combines with a key card to give you a selection of cards from the bust pile based on how many cards you drew that turn (or your ops hand if you have the plunderer trait. The treasure hunter trait will let you triple the amount of cards you get given)
* Cannon makes you discard a card from your hand which goes to the bust pile, or you can take the misfire trait and you can discard a card from your ops hand instead....if you combine misfire with the scavenger trait, the card you blasted goes in to your hand.
* Kraken makes you draw 2 cards to play so you can't choose to bank the cards you have until you've drawn them. If your op has the beastmaster trait you'll have to draw 4 cards.
* Mermaid lets you replay a card currently in play....Sir Lovesword sometimes uses a trait that banks the card you replay (you can also unlock this trait)
* Maps lets you take a card from the bust pile and put it in play. Ordinarily you get to choose between 3 cards, but the navigtator trait lets you pick from any card in the pile.
You don't have to memorise the suits to play effectively, if you hover over a card it will say at the top of the screen what the suit does.
There are loads of traits to choose from which you unlock as you level up (much more than the ones I've mentioned here) which allow you to manipulate how the suits work for you or against your op.
You can choose 2 traits at a time to use.
I completed the game with 3 stars on every tournament and I tended to stick with the misfire and scavenger traits. I only occasionally swapped one or both of these out for something else.
Here's a tip if you're going for the 3 star achievements....you can only get 70 points in total (unless you're in the tournaments that count every card towards your score) and you normally need 65 points per game, so I played to get five 7's and the rest as sixes if I couldn't get 7's (obviously any extra 7's will allow you to have another suit at lower than 6 and still get the 65 points you need), all lower numbers are dross and can be gambled with. The cannons trait combo will let you steal the 7's you need from your opponents hand. There are a few times this trait combo doesn't work as well, or you'll find it's better to negate your opponents traits instead but for the most part this method worked brilliantly.
There is no multiplayer, which doesn't bother me, I prefer single player games for the most part, this game would be great as   a multiplayer though.
