Pretty amazing, endlessly mutable procedural Mario Hell platform speed runner with oodles of game-changing modifiers. Absolutely terrific couch co-op. Quick player customization with some funny props helps differentiate your guy on screen so you can better follow him in the chaos.
Simple to play, will evoke screams of frustration at the many deaths, but never really rage-inducing or friendship-ruining, because the squawks and shrieks this game will pull out of you as you nimbly dance through whirling death corridors will have you laughing too hard to stay mad. Also getting someone to the end of the level often becomes a cooperative effort. Respawns are generally quick and the action just keeps going such that, besides a quick moment at the end of a level, sometimes a death is a welcome breather while you try to figure out what you are supposed to do.
On top of what appears to be a Story Mode with hundreds of levels, there are Arcade challenges also with hundreds of levels, and if that's not enough, there's a custom level tweaker thing where you can dial in all of the various elements to your satisfaction, including all the way up to 11 to create a limitless variation of absolutely insane but completely possible challenges.
That's the really neat thing about this nutty game: even the most nightmarishly wild level it can throw at you is somehow constructed by whatever clever algorithm they came up with to have a PROVABLE SOLUTION. Don't believe it? Spend a few gems (the only collectible in the game) to see it for yourself, and then try it again.

Dont know what to write, so I will write a recipie for pancakes.
ingredients
100g plain flour
2 eggs
300ml semi-skimmed milk
1 tbsp sunflower oil or vegetable, plus extra for frying
pinch salt
Method
Blending in the flour: Put the flour and a pinch of salt into a large mixing bowl and make a well in the centre. Crack the eggs into the middle, then pour in about 50ml milk and 1 tbsp oil. Start whisking from the centre, gradually drawing the flour into the eggs, milk and oil. Once all the flour is incorporated, beat until you have a smooth, thick paste. Add a little more milk if it is too stiff to beat.
Finishing the batter: Add a good splash of milk and whisk to loosen the thick batter. While still whisking, pour in a steady stream of the remaining milk. Continue pouring and whisking until you have a batter that is the consistency of slightly thick single cream. Traditionally, people would say to now leave the batter for 30 mins, to allow the starch in the flour to swell, but there’s no need.
Getting the right thickness: Heat the pan over a moderate heat, then wipe it with oiled kitchen paper. Ladle some batter into the pan, tilting the pan to move the mixture around for a thin and even layer. Quickly pour any excess batter into a jug, return the pan to the heat, then leave to cook, undisturbed, for about 30 secs. Pour the excess batter from the jug back into the mixing bowl. If the pan is the right temperature, the pancake should turn golden underneath after about 30 secs and will be ready to turn.
Flipping pancakes: Hold the pan handle, ease a fish slice under the pancake, then quickly lift and flip it over. Make sure the pancake is lying flat against base of the pan with no folds, then cook for another 30 secs before turning out onto a warm plate. Continue with the rest of the batter, serving them as you cook or stack onto a plate. You can freeze the pancakes for 1 month, wrapped in cling film or make them up to a day ahead.

I like clicker games and I use to play dating sims in high school. Saw one of my friends play this and figured I could use a good idle game to pass the time while I have been a binge of classic RPGs lately. This game fills that spot perfectly after the first 10 hours of playing it, before that it takes a bit to get into though.
Now for the nitty gritty.
Graphics: 10/10
The main artist did a great job with the girls and other things as well. Everything is nice and bright. I have one complaint and that is the date/milestone scenes, a few girls look a bit strange compared to their standing there portrait. But that could be me.
Music: 3/10
The one song they have on there is catchy at first, but will quickly make you want to turn it off.
Gameplay: 8/10
You click on things for a good while, there is a button that you can click that is way better than clicking the girls themselves which makes the game easier, the problem it has a cooldown but when you soft reset you get a speed boost and that includes a cooldown reduction. I have it now where there is no cooldown and so I have a clicker macro just do it to get the girls to like me. Otherwise you will have to wait quite awhile for progress until you hit certain thresholds. I don't mind the waiting because I work almost 50 hours a week anyway so it's great to come home click a few things and then start doing something else while letting that do it's thing. One more thing is the timeblocks mechanic, it adds some planning and strategy all the way through the game. (That was way longer than intended.)
Plot: 5/10(It's a clicker game there isn't much for me to say.)
I'm actually talking about the story. For a clicker game this has some story to it, not only in how you meet the girls and the like but I mean there is an actual end to the game!  So, the game doesn't have much story until you unlock the wizard job, then some weird stuff starts to happen and it will be up to you to save the world with your love power!
The Girls: 10/10
You have your normal sterotypes, and they are nicely written with plenty of humor and references everywhere. I mean come on, one of them is pretty much Rainbow Dash even down to being an athlete. I will say that each of them probably will have some place in your heart when you play the game as long as I have. Except Pamu, f*** her.
Best girl: +2
As a D&D player, Luna made me smile the most with her quotes. But Elle is my favorite girl, she is so cute and reminds me of a friend of mine that I have a crush on.
A minor gripe: -1
I don't mind that this is free to play and whatever you get the premium currency as you play, but damn without using a lot of it you will be waiting a long time for some things. I do throw 20 bucks at a F2P game if I get to at least 100 hours and will still be playing for quite awhile. I put my 20 in early(maybe about 20 hours in) and was really glad I did the wait times in this game get ungodly rediculous.
Overall: 8/10
Good clicker/idle game if you are into those and pretty decent dating sim for the simple fact that the girls are varied and interesting and still follows the same kinda formula.

Unhack is a short little puzzlegame that can be quite tricky at stages.
The main goal is to move your block to the goal, some goals are simple "get there" stages, some are bossfight stages where you have to repeat a more or less simple (but still harder) mechanic 3-4 times in a row.
The puzzles at its own would be not that awesome, but they pack it in an quite tempting story where you take the role of an "pervy" [wants to try out his costume mods on the AIs, he gets "forever declined"] unhacker (someone who destroys viruses) that tries to do his job. He gets accompanied by AIs that talk to you at checkpoints. Those AIs are fully voiced in english.
Pro:
- Puzzles are fun
- 3 Difficulty stages (Normal with unlimited lifes, Heavy with 3 tries and Unbelievable with 1 live only)
- Fully voiced AIs, with cute voices.
- Actually has a story in a puzzler
- Cheap price
- cheap dlc
- music
- trading cards (cause many want cards...)
- great comedy moments
- for DLC: +1 for the troll ^-^
- Cute drawings of the AIs
- Soundtrack included for free.. like srsly i dont get why companies charge extra for them most of the time >.<
Con:
- dlc though has not much content (3 puzzles with story), fast finished, but still fun so i considder it not too bad

A cute visual novel story combined with simple but engaging puzzle mechanics. The short length of time it takes to play through the game (2~ hours or so) is a good thing, not because the game isn't fun, but the short playthrough keeps things clicking along and minimizes the "fridge logic" of overthinking the universe's take on AI. The game's story is about the interactions of the characters, and the underlying mechanics of how the actual world works don't bear up to too much examination.
The voice acting was also cutely done and kind of a surprise for a game at this price point.
The game is not without its flaws and questionable design choices, of course, including tying dialog steps to literal moves on the puzzle board, which can result in flipping past dialog and having to back up through it if you go 'too fast' or fail to notice that the (unvoiced) viewpoint character 'said' something. It's inconvenient and immersion breaking. Also, the game has no save function, balanced by the fact that you can jump to any chapter - BUT the chapter numbers aren't shown to you during play so if you have to stop for some reason you just have to guess at how far in you were. This isn't exactly game breaking though considering the game can be fully played through in a single evening.
If you play while being mindful of not tripping yourself over those two problems, though, it's a short, fun little game at a good price.

Ronin is a 2D platformer/sort-of-stealth game with an interesting core mechanic. Pros:
+ Interesting and unique combat system
+ Good level design that makes use of lights, glass, and platformers for the occasional stealth section
+ A few interesting special abilities that are unlocked through completing optional tasks in the missions
+ Checkpoints happen just at the right time to prevent too much frustration
Neutral:
* Okay enemy variety. A few different mooks to fight with.
* About a 5-6 hour single player campaign
* Story is a little lacking, but the developer was obviously moving his effort toward the gameplay.
Cons:
- Remember those "optional tasks" I mentioned before? There are only three of them, and they're the same throughout all the stages.
- The checkpoints can sometimes put you in awkward positions. For instance, if you decide to backtrack and hack a terminal from earlier in the level, your checkpoint will keep respawning you at that earlier point, forcing you to advance everytime you respawn.
RONIN isn't for everybody, but I think I got my money's worth, and I'm glad a demo was offered to help me make my purchase decision easy.

Takes a little getting used to the controls, but I think it was worth it. It's hard to succinctly describe how this game plays. While nobody sees you, you can move freely. When an enemy can see you, time stops and a pseudo-turn-based combat system kicks in. You will see where enemies will shoot on the next turn, and you must use this turn to reposition yourself so that you both remain unharmed, and are in a position to kill one or more enemies.
The "story" in this game is very thin, despite setting itself up as a lone swordsman dismantling a conspiracy. It consists of one photograph, and the protagonist monologuing at the start of some levels. And the photo has people in it who remain unaccounted for, even taking the supplementary material into account. It's as if someone was starting to design an intricate plot and got bored 20 minutes in.
Cutting to the chase; the fun in this game is in methodically, a turn at a time, slaughtering dozens of people while never taking a scratch. Having all the upgrades in the final level didn't make it easier, but it did make it very fun.

Addictive little card game, like Uno in that every card has an "action" that occurs when you play it (steal cards, be forced to draw two more cards, allow you to "protect" your existing cards, etc) , but you draw cards until you either decide to bank them, or you draw two of the same suit (in which case you lose all the currently drawn cards).  The idea is to get the most points, and the highest-scoring card of each suit from your hand is all that counts.
Nice, steady introduction so you don't get confused, calm progression so you don't notice that you're learning the full game, and occasionally a spin-ball thrown into the rules to keep you thinking.
Ignore the comments people make about it "cheating" - as far as I can tell, it's the usual gambling fallacies where you remember bad luck that happened to you, but not your good streaks.  It's as random as any other card game, but unlike a lot of others this would actually make quite a fun two-player card game with a real deck.
Would be nice to see a multiplayer mode (even if only two-player).

Reasons why I loved this game:

1. Story and Character development: In this game you meet the basic characters that are mainly focused on in the comics (Joker, Harley Quinn, Killer Croc, Poison Ivy, Scarecrow, ect.), but you feel like you know them after you played the game or a few scenes with them. Not only that, but you can listen to tapes that are found all around the game, containing background information of the character. Whether its Killer Croc's moody attitude and the passion he has to kill Batman (and every other person who helps run the prison), or Harley Quinn's bipolar disorder and her over affectionate personality toward Joker. All and more can be found in the game. It does an excellent job of doing this, slowly revealing every character's strong suits, or weaknesses (Joker's desperation and depression).

2. Easter Eggs: There are so many Easter eggs in this game I can't even count it...
From characters to plans for the next game (Arkham City), anything you can think of is in the game. Changes in simple things (like a mannequin) can be leads for where the game is going. Even three different alternate endings to the game if you watch the credits. There are so many more but I don't feel like listing them all...

3. Gameplay: Simple controls tie in really nicely to the game.
Combat is simple, and you don't have to really know all of the quick fire actions to get the job done. Playing with a controller (Xbox One) is highly recommended though, remembering everything on a keyboard is considered impressive to me.

4. Vent Simulator: 2009.
There are so many vents in the game you have to climb into, it should be considered a crime, but it's not a negative. You don't have to climb into all of them all of the time. Sometimes vents are used for strategizing your next move or plan. Although annoying, they're useful.

5. Great for people who follow the comics. This game has been praised several times for being accurate to the comics. I personally never read a Batman comic, just followed the old TV shows and movies, but after playing this game I want to read one, badly.
6. Graphics on the highest setting it can go for, plus constant 60 fps for a game that was released in 2009, makes the game looks like that it just was released yesterday. FYI: If you can run it on the highest settings, you don't need the remastered version of it (Batman: Return to Arkham).

First before i get to the actual review, I just want to state how i found out about this game: To set the record straight, i watched Cry's playthrough of it on youtube. So i played this game knowing most of what would happen because i had watched the playthrough (i stopped watching it after a while to play the actual game). Granted with games like this that allow you to take different paths depending on the choices you make, you can never watch the same Let's Play twice and whatever the Let's Player does shouldn't be the exclusive path you take. In general i LOVE games that allow you to take different paths with the story. I also love writing and want to be a writer and turn most of my works into webcomics. So because this game was about a writer trying to mend their relationship with a former flame, my interest was almost instant and Cry's let's play let me get a preview of what i could expect from the game.
Ok, now onto the reivew:
As stated above, the game is about a writer down on their luck in life and living near-poverty in a run down town called Dubstown. They're down on their luck and taking whatever jobs they can get to earn enough money to pay their rent or risk eviction. On top of that, they also find out that their ex (who they still have feelings for) is getting married in 30 days. So that puts your character on a quest to make enough money as possible and get to the wedding to mend their relationship with their ex. This concept is very good. It's rare we see games and media in general dealing with a character trying to fix a past relationship with this much effort (going on a road trip to see an ex one last time is usually something saved only for the romantic comedies, which the majority of are just chickflicks made with no effort at all). On top of that this is one of the rare oppertunities in media that we see and PLAY as a character in or near poverty, another nice change from the norm.
But while the concept is well and good, it's all about the delivery that makes or breaks a story... And honestly i feel rather dissapointed...
Pros of the game include:
- A new perspective to the world of writing
- a new perspective to the world of mending relationships and what love and romance mean
- a new perspective by playing as a character in or near poverty
- self aware and meta humor
- good set design for an RPG Maker game
- The game can get pretty philisophical when it comes to the theme of choice, which is very much appreciated.
- The NPC dialouge is unique for the most part, even random ones walking around on the street and not the major ones
- The choices you make in this game are pretty impressive seeing that you're playing as a writer in poverty. You're essntially homeless for a lot of the game because you're on the road, forcing you to sleep in the street and do whatever you can to find a bed at night should no one want to give you a home. Making money is also realistically hard as it would be for someone in that situation. You can help your friends or completely break people and possibly yourself in the process.

Always Sometimes Monsters is an interesting game, to say the least. It has story, choices, and an ending that changes based on the choices you make, so it's already a step above most games, as well as having 8bit graphics that fit perfectly with the style of game Vagabond Dog made. Pro's and cons:
Pro's
+Art style fits the game perfectly
+Choices effect the ending
+Your gender and your (ex)significant other's gender are up to you. There is no discrimination here.
+There is however, discrimination elsewhere. Depending on your sexuality and gender, people will treat you differently.
+Game is short. This makes it so you can sit down, enjoy yourself playing a game, and finish it. Adds replay value.
+The story made sense. It wasn't a huge jumble like in some games.
+The Music is very nice, yet it does get repetitive.
Con's
-Since the game is short, it does have replay value, but only because it is easy to forget. If the game was longer, it would have less replay value yet it would be a more memorable experience.
-The ending doesn't change all too much , because...
-There's really only a handful of endings available.
-In order to get the best ending you have to farm for money. lots of money.
-this^ gets two cons because you need $10,000 in order to get the best ending. shame.
- In my opinion, $10 is too much for a game you can finish in a few hours.
Overall, Always Sometimes Monsters is a good game, but suffers some flaws, just like most games. If it ever goes on sale, I recommend it.

This game is AWESOME!
PROS:
-Combat system and Stealth system is easy to understand, but takes awhile to truly master
-Stealth Missions make you think and can get very challenging. This is easily the best part of the game.
-Combat and Stealth is equally spread accross the game.
-Character and level design is perfect. Every character sticks to the original character design while still being new and refreshing.
-Voice acting and music is a huge aspect of this game. Every voice is exactly how imagine each character to sound like. Every line and song sets the tone for the level (especially during Scarecrow levels).
-Game does not restrict you enough to feel open, but still gives you enough direction to make it feel linear.
-Collecting all the trophies, solving all the riddles, and looking for every other collectible is definitely a tedious but rewarding task. Each riddle is cleverly crafted and does take quite a bit of thought.
-Boss fights are very interesting, clever, and difficult. Bane, Harley Quinn, and The Joker are your typical beat-em up style bosses. Scarecrow implements a stealthy platformer level at the start of his boss fight. Poison Ivy is like a Legend of Zelda style boss. The Croc is the most creative fight, you need to navigate a maze while avoiding him.
-There are a lot of bonus challenge maps.
CONS:
-Literally nothing to do in the aftergame. No post story or anything.
-Scenes when Batman is talking to characters are like Fallout talking scenes and it looks very derpy.
-The world, although it feels open, still feels a bit small.

After a year, I still have work to do in all facets. That, along with the developer's frequent additions of content gives me hope there is still a lot of game left as well. The striking thing about this game is how well organized it is. Information is easy to find, you're never left wondering what to do next, and there is a good balance in the types of gameplay, so you're always doing something new.
The story isn't much, but serves its required function of explaining what you have to do, and why. There is significant dialogue between the characters, which is mostly for humor (which it does successfully), and little else.
Puzzles are a primary feature of the game. They are just challenging enough to be fun, and no two are alike.
Quests come in the form of islands. When you recieve a quest, you unlock that island on the map. The game has four seas full of islands to explore, with a nice balance of required and optional quests.
Progress through the game is nice and tidy. Nothing takes too long, and you always feel like you have a choice of which quest to take on next.
Overall, this is a very well made game, and I recommend it highly.

One of the best games I've seen since the Aveyond series. There are many "Pros" to this game and very few "Cons" in my opinion. I've played MANY of these RPG maker games. Most of them I wind up giving up halfway through. Either I lost interest in the storyline, characters or the game in general. The biggest CON for me in some RPG maker games is that the mobs are invisible and you never know when you're gonna be attacked. Random frequent accounters will make me stop playing some games in 10 minutes (or less). I'm happy to say that is not the case with THIS game. You can see your mobs and easily decide whether to fight them or not. So if you are just trying to do a specific quest and get in and get out then you can avoid them. However I recommend fighting all the mobs in this game b/c there really are NOT that many and the fighting is pretty evened out. Meaning that you are not extremely overpowered and kill them in one hit and likewise the mobs are not so overpowered (as long as you keep killing them and not avoiding them) that they kill you very easily either.
I like the storyling. I'm about 8 hours into the game. Now, I like to take my time and do all of the side quests before moving on to the next area. The mobs, once you kill them, do not repawn. So once you kill all the mobs in a specific area, you are free to roam the area at will. The quests are unique and the story line is intriguing. The menu and fighting style is pretty standard of RPG maker games. There are save points literally EVERYWHERE so at any given point you are only seconds away from a save point which I like. I like the Atlas style map and it is comes in very handy when I'm not sure which island is on what seas. I check the Atlas very often.
Now the only CON I really found is that not one of the people have a healing skill. You have to reply on strictly potions for all healing. You do find a ton of potions but it's not nearly enough so you will have to buy a lot of them. The equipment is not outragiously priced or frequent so you will have plenty of money left over for the potions. It's harder in the lower levels to have enough money though. The people are all pretty much the same. The characters are the only unique facial features. The looks of all of the shop keepers and town residents are pretty much recycled from town to town. Overall I like this game very much and if you are a fan of the rpg maker games then I think you will enjoy it too.

Crush Crush is a free-to-play clicker/idle game about dating girls and resource management. Our little, intentionally non-descript, marshmallowy hero encounters various girls that he initially causes great trouble to, and must then atone for as he wins their affection through gratuitous volumes of materialistic purchases, excessive numbers of dates, and prerequisite amounts of experience in certain hobbies and occupations. Work your way from "Nuisance", all the way up to "Lover" as you unlock more girls whilst balancing the amount of time you have with the amount required to level up character traits, work proficiency, and actually taking girls on dates.
Resource management comes in the form of "time blocks", limited quantities of which must be allocated to your various hobbies and jobs to level them up as required by each girl. The number of time blocks you have increases as you hit certain progression landmarks, but so too do the demands of the girls. Thankfully, help comes in the form of prestige resets, which allows you to restart your conquest with multiplier bonuses based on progress as well as having acquired time blocks carry over.
From moment to moment you'll mostly spend your own time clicking on gifts to buy or dates to go on, but an awful lot of your time will actually be spent out of game as you wait for money to build up from all your jobs, or for your hobby experience to rise. It's the type of game you'll be active with in bursts as you build up your requirements or rebuild your status after you reset, then leave for a while as the numbers do their thing. Early game can be pretty active, but late game you'll maybe find yourself playing a couple times a day or maybe even once a week or so.
The game can technically be finished without needing to spend any real money on it, but the time to do that is so long (most likely well over a year, possibly even longer) that doing it in any reasonable time will require diamonds to be spent on upgrades and boosts. Diamonds are the game's premium currency, you can get quite a few just by playing, but realistically you'll probably have to buy some to get things moving at a satisfying pace, which, understandably, might not be an option for everyone.
Personally, I've greatly enjoyed my time with the game; with its loveable cast, its cheeky, playful sense of humour and the quality of its art, and was happy to return the favour and spend money on it. It's also encouraging to see the game be continually supported with new (although somewhat infrequent) content and the promise of more to come. I'm also forever in its debt for teaching me that the way to a girl's heart is to spend a vast fortune on nice things for her in order to make her like you. And if these kinds of life lessons aren't worth real money then I don't know what is.
Oh, and FYI, the best girl in the game is clearly Quill, and anyone who says otherwise is a filthy, rotten liar (though Ava would also be a relatively acceptable answer).

Underrated Triple-A Quality Arena Hero Shooter at Half the Price.
This game combines the best parts of arena and hero shooters with its own unique twist, really making this game stand out in a time where we have a pretty good selection of competitive shooters at our hands, LawBreakers has to be the one that has sold me the most out of all of them.
The gameplay itself has a high-speed feel akin to Quake 2004 featuring classic competitive shooter game modes that most should be familiar with, but with a twist to bring more dynamics to the gameplay. Instead of weapon spawns on the map, you have classes and each class has its own unique loadout, skills and movement abilities that are extremely diversified between all of the classes you have to choose. It's this aspect in where LawBreakers really got me hooked. That and the Zero-Gravity combat.
The Wraith, for example, has an automatic pistol, a knife that lunges him forward when used to attack with and can propel you around Zero-Gravity zones in maps, and a slide. The Harrier, on the other hand, has an infinite range laser beam rifle with a projectile secondary fire that marks an enemy for increased damage, a healing pack station that can be dropped to heal you and teammates, jet boosters in the feet to propel you around the map that you can also kick with to boost you(and enemies in front of you) around the map. Each hero plays and feels completely different, and I personally look forward to seeing what other classes are in store for us.
I have a lot of hopes for this game, and it's great to see how much it has improved already since playing it back in Beta. The team at BossKey seem really dedicated to making this a quality and balanced shooter with how quickly they balanced some classes after the game's release, on top of bringing us a new class.
There's a bit of a learning curve between the speed of the game, the classes, and zero-g, but once you get the hang of it, it's an incredible experience. They provide tons of tutorial videos you can watch in-game, and I highly recommend it, to learn about each class and game mode, while also earning you some in-game currency to buy cosmetic items.
The graphics and designs are top-notch running on the Unreal 4 Engine. There's tons of achievements you can earn in matches that give you xp towards level, which earns you some stash drop loot boxes for each level.  There's a grading system at the end of every match that's based off the amount of points you accumulated in a game, which then becomes your XP, there's Discord and Twitch integration, and so much more.
If you're looking for something different to add to your shooter library, if you like arena shooters like Unreal Tournament or Quake, this is a game that you just have to play to see why it's so fun. Videos cannot do it enough justice alone. Give the folks at BossKey a shot and download it, play it for two hours and see if you dig it and if not, return it. Chances are, if you're into shooters, you're gonna fall in love just like I did.

Unhack (2014) is the sort of pleasant surprise you’d never pick out from a glance at its simple artwork, seemingly basic mechanics, and emoticon laden dialogue.
Rest assured Unhack isn’t complex, nor does its artwork ever emerge as much more than it first appears, but the game is carried by an infectious charm and a recognition by its developer of their limitations (which are then subverted by played as a strength). By the end I was rather taken aback just how much I had enjoyed myself.
Unhack casts you as an unhacker (which is exactly what it sounds like), a security specialist paired with an AI assistant and tasked with hunting down viruses before they somehow destroy the world. Naturally everything quickly goes entirely out of control, rogue AI and viruses alike running amok, and you’re left at the center to try and fix the mess while trying to convince your partner to try your TOTALLY PG costume pack (did I mention your character was a pervert? Perhaps it goes without saying, but thankfully it never goes beyond a few tame jokes). Sure, it’s a predicable, melodramatic story in a lot of ways, but Unhack is carried by its not-quite-self-aware but still firm understanding that it is going to come off as silly no matter how serious it tries to be, knowing just how far to go without becoming obnoxiously heavy handed while still having a lot of fun in the process.
It definitely helps a lot that the voice acting (which was unexpected in and of itself) is more than decent, with appropriately chipper voices all around that refrained from the grating tones so often given to AI in media. There aren’t a huge amount of emotions needed from the script, but I was legitimately impressed at the cast and couldn’t help but find them as endearing and adorable as the charmingly amateur artwork they’re drawn with.
I can’t remember actually bursting out laughing at any particular line, but I was definitely smiling the whole way through as the cute AI bantered back and forth with the oxymoronic lovable ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ protagonist. Unhack also manages to pull off a very internet tone with its dialogue, with phrases and emotes that will be familiar to anyone that’s ever made the poor decision of glancing at a comments section, without coming across as just a writer having trouble disconnecting from their texting habits. I’m sure some will still think it’s dumb (for which there’s an option to disable emoticons entirely), but it was strangely charming to me and felt natural in this landscape of super hackers and sentient computer programs.
There’s not a whole lot to say about how Unhack actually plays, aside from that it does a fantastic job of not outstaying its welcome. Navigating mazes as a little cube of code is fun while it lasts and new mechanics are introduced regularly enough to give you something new to consider with every level, keeping things simple but engaging and wrapping up in a brief but satisfying hour or thereabouts. Unhack knows what it is, it knows its strengths, and it doesn’t lean on any of its weaker points long enough to become tiresome. For the price of a burger and less of my time than I spend looking at pictures of cats on any given day, I doubt I could be anymore happy to have given Unhack a chance.

Unhack is by no means a groundbreaking gaming experience. There are a few technical issues that may hamper your experience. The game will last under two hours, all told. All those gripes aired though, I can say I did find the game moderately enjoyable.
The gameplay of Unhack somewhat reminds me of Chip's Challenge, though much simpler, with more of a focus on action than puzzle-solving. There's nothing particularly interesting or challenging about it and it serves mostly as way to pass the time while serving up dialog, though difficulty modes with limited lives exist which change this into a very different experience, where you must play carefully and skillfully or fail the mission. That may or may not be your thing. I was mostly in it for the dialog and so stuck with the normal difficulty.
The visual novel portion of the self-described "visual novel x puzzle game" is similar to the gameplay portions in that nothing massively original or special ever happens, but nonetheless it's not a bad way to spend a few hours. The jokes are a bit cliche but manage to entertain nonetheless. The plot's pretty generic, but that doesn't matter either. It does a good job doing what it does and doesn't overstay its welcome (in fact it could have stood be just a
longer). The art's not entirely to my taste, but it's good enough. I was surprised by how much I enjoyed the voice acting, and most of the lines in the game have voices (your own character does not).
Now, about those technical issues. The game is built on a web engine that really isn't designed for gaming. It's forced into full-screen mode with no resolution options and no ability to play in windowed mode. There's no Steam overlay support, and consequently no Steam screenshots (barring some nasty workarounds). There are no Steam achievements either. The game doesn't save any information, so it won't show you where you are in the story, and it won't remember any settings you change. The lack of saving may be the reason there's no gallery of the CG's that appear at the end of each chapter, which is a pity because it'd be nice to be able to go back and see those all in one place.
Unhack is not a game without it's flaws, but again, I enjoyed it nonetheless. "Good enough" would be a fair descriptor of it. There's a demo which you should absolutely try if you're interested in the game. It'll let you see how well your computer deals with some of the technical issues and get a feel for game's content yourself. You should be able to figure out if the game's right for you by the end of the second level.

The game is something unique. The game is fast paced, and avoids a lot of the faux pas that plague most modern PC FPS failures. The gerneral combat can also be quite fun.
But the game has several glaring issues.
The class balance relies on pigeon holing classes and making them overly strong in 1 area and gimped in other areas. This not only robs the combat of a lot of depth but makes a lot of kills feel cheap and unskilled; you killed them at the range your class was good at and their class is helpless at it. The pigeon holing becomes especially problematic without a class limit, (this game doesn't have class limits) because stacking a bunch of long range classes can make it next to impossible for melee focused classes to get into short range or stacking defensive classes can make it next to impossible for anyone to score and will drag the game out. Or you can stack multiple enforcers and have their group dps and speed buff nerver fade.  The game also focuses on movement, but has 3 long range focused hitscan classes that penalize you for using the movement the game is focused around.
Every single game mode promotes a snowballing effect. Comebacks are difficult if not impossible and games usually feel like they're over well before they are.
Lots of maps just don't work with certain game modes.
A lot of basic options are missing like custom crosshairs or smaller view models if not being able to remove them alltogether.
The game also relies on the weapon viewmodels to display information such as how much ammo you have left, which can be frustrating especially with long weapon animations and weapons moving when you're running. Some guns don't even have a number showing you how many rounds left, but like so many lights left on the weapon as an indicator.
Also there are obnoxious UI decisions like every time you join a match your screen is flashing red.
Finally, it takes forever between matches. You'll have 2 full teams after the match and it will make you wait like 90 seconds before it will load you into the next match.
In short, the basics of combat is good. The balance is bad. The game modes are bad. The maps are at least bad for the current game modes. The game feels rushed out the door, and i have doubts the current team has a good enough understanding of PC FPS to properly balance the game.

The one that started them all and the third one I played. Having played Origins and City I came into Asylum with reasonable expectations - it was the first game in the series after all. There's no DLC. There's no alternate armor or costumes. Getting a copy that lets you play as Joker is a headache and pretty pointless since - by and large - most of that content is just as much fluff as most of Knight's dlc.
Much of it felt easier than City and Origins - especially the puzzles which were far more intuitive. In fact; the much smaller map made Asylum the first one I actually beat Riddler on funnily enough.
The gadgets - like Asylum itself - are in their infancy and most of the combat moves are far more limited and lacking than City, Origins or Knight. But the atmosphere of Asylum is right up there with Origins and City itself. This is Batman in his prime being driven to insanity by the very monsters he not only defends his city from - but that he (in many cases) helped create.
Mark Hamil is disturbing as the Joker and there are so many jump-scares in Asylum that you would be hard-pressed to play this game for the first time and not squeal at least two or three times. There is just so much fan-service in this game that you could almost call it porn for Batman aficionados. Forgetting that this is a Batman game for a moment leaves you with a remarkable realization - because this isn't just a good BATMAN game... it's a good game period. They could have called it Bowsers Castle and had the lead character be Mario and it STILL would have been an achievement. The fact that they brought all this material together makes this game a phenomenal achievement and well worth a look despite it's age.

Someone in a forum asked if they would still enjoy playing this game as they had already played the later Arkham games first and heard the combat mechanics in this were clunkier, so I decided to turn this into my first review.
Yes, it is a little clunkier, but still enjoyable once you get into it and the overall atmosphere is still probably the best in the series. Because the world isn't as open, it's a more focused story and running around in the Asylum is often a claustrophobic, nightmarish experience. Scarecrow is actually scary here instead of the annoying, glorified Hugo Strange type character he plays in Arkham Knight. Being in the sewers with Killer Croc is still freaks me out when I've had to replay it - recommend you turn your volume up!
It also has some of the coolest NVidia physx effects additions to the series if you can run them, such as interactive leaves, breaking floor tiles and stretchy cobwebs  (still haven't had any cobweb effects in any of the other games despite them being in every airduct you crawl through - it really enhances the experience).
Biggest differences in fighting are the countering is much less forgiving (You can't wait a whole two seconds before you counter like the other games), evading over someone's head doesn't automatically make you untouchable and there's no sliding (I usually like to open combat with this). Also, if you were a fan of the remote batarang, forget about using it here. While it exists, piloting it is probably the last thing you want to be doing.
Also, as it's the first game in the series there's a lot more instruction as you begin, whereas the later games tend to treat Arkham Asylum as the learning point for the series and instead drop you straight into the action. If you can get over all of this and liked the later games, I think you'll enjoy the game, it has a nice tone, some fun Joker commentary and feels much more intimate overall.
8/10, would play again if I lost all my achievments due to Windows Live closing down and rendering my older copy useless (B@stards).

Hey all,
I'm normally not writing reviews, but in order to help this game I will try to summarize some points here:
Pros:
- Fair price / In-Game Cash shop is there but purely cosmetic and not required unless you really want that stuff
- Great graphics, high FPS even on a bit older rigs. The game runs fluid as hell
- Combat is fast and frantic, really fun to move around and use the abilities. Overall, regarding the amount of keys that are required, I would say LawBreakers is easier than Titanfall 2 for example / However, the real challenge lies in properly moving you character through the map/air and combining everything together, which is really hard at times
- Decent amount of roles and maps are already in the game and they are great so far
- Brings back old school FPS gaming like Unreal Tournament, Quake etc. and mostly abandons current hero shooter design seen in many other games
Cons:
- Currently a small community (Let's keep it growing)
- Matchmaking only has a single queue, you can't choose which mode you want to play (I really do like 4 out of the 5 modes but so far I don't like Blitzball and there is no way and letting me choose not to play it)
- Characters and Maps might not have the personality as in some other triple A titles (However, in my personal opinion this is not so much of a problem, it is about the fun for me not about back stories of characters etc.)
So, if you have not yet bought the game, you really should do so, if you like great FPS games and if you want that old school feeling back. I really think the price point is quite low and new maps, characters and even modes are in the works. I would not compare the slow start of LawBreakers to a game like Battelborn, which had a better start but quickly declined after that. The main difference to that title is that Battleborn did also not have good reviews (to some parts that was justified) whereas LawBreakers sits at a very good spot and therefore I believe now that summer ends, and with Boss Key and Cliff Blezinski behind it, the game should be there for a long time to come.
Have fun!

An excellent introduction to the Arkham series and for superhero video games in general. While not completely canon with the animated series, the game acts as a spiritual successor of sorts (though if you discount Arkham Origins, the Arkham series follows very well after the animated Batman series). Most iconic villains of the Batman franchise appear in this game, with Batman fighting many of them during the story.
The best part of the game is definitely how you play; you feel like you really are Batman. The grappling hook, his gadgets, the movement are all great and fluid. The combat is fairly simple but fast and very entertaining. And the predator encounters always make me smile as the mooks before me wet their pants the more I take down using planning and strategy, and their reactions are priceless.
The voice acting is great too; not only did they get most of the voice actors from the animated series to return, they are very much in character and very entertaining to listen to. Kevin Conroy as Batman and Mark Hamill as the Joker are definitely the best and wonderful to listen to.
The music sets the rather dark and creepy tone well, both from Batman's point of view and his opponents as you hunt them.
The collectibles are fairly enjoyable via the Riddler. Simple enough to find, not frustrating to the point of giving up, and giving you substantial rewards with XP used to upgrade your abilities. Riddler maps are a must, if you plan to get everything. And towards the end you'll want to hunt for that last air of annoying Joker teeth to make the Riddler cry.
I don't really have many complaints. There are only two minor ones; the first is how easy it is to upgrade to the max level well before the end of the game. Then again, I'm not sure you can farm for XP so maybe it's for the best.
The other is more related to the animated series, actually; in this game you see the dead bodies of innocents everywhere as a result of the Joker and the other super criminals escaping, but the game and Batman just seem to ignore them for the most part. This doesn't really fit with Batman's character all too well in my eyes, as he should take some responsibility or guilt for the deaths of innocents. Thankfully this gets better further into the franchise.
Overall a wonderful game and recommended to anyone who likes a good action game; whether they're a batman fan or not.

Synopsis (via Steam):
This exploration game has 3 main characters: a business man, an old man and a child. They find themselves on a road which is apparently the same, but changes upon their perception of reality.
First Impression:
The download through Steam literally took like 30 seconds. Upon opening the game, the three different fonts, while I understand goes with the three different characters, does not give off uniform impression overall. As far I can tell, there is no option button, and you click the person to start the game.
Gameplay:
While the game gives you no instruction on what to play, the keys are easy to figure out. WASD to move, space bar to jump, and mouse to move the camera. The objective is pretty simple - get to the other side of the road. In any stage, should you fail the objective, you restart from the beginning of that life.
Artwork:
I'm not a fan of the artwork, but I will give a nod toward the uniformity of it through each life, and the correct impressions of how each life sees the road. I will admit that the child's life made me smile. I do have to say while I do understand that that is how the road is seen through the child's eyes, I wish they had made the "road" more... road-like. I can also understand, after finishing the game, why the child's life is last and why the game was not set in chronological order. (I still wish it was...)
Music/sound:
The music fit each life, and it was decent to my ears. It's nothing that I would want to play over and over again, but for its purpose, it worked.
Storyline:
There's no real "story" here, which is fine. If you want, you could say that the game progression itself is a story through each life, but that would be considered null and void due to the fact you start your life as an adult first.
End Impression:
It's a quick play, and the child's life does bring back nostalgic moments of childhood while the older stages make you think about them (if you want to take it to a deeper level.)
Parting Words:
If you're looking for a quick game to play, this is one of those less-than-10-minute games.
SCORES:
Artwork: 6/10
Gameplay: 6/10
Music/Sound: 5/10
Storyline: N/A
Overall score: 6/10

OK, So before I even talk I'm going to warn you, this is a hard review for me to write. Don't get me wrong I LOVE this game but I have trouble explaining HOW it is so good. Especially since now I've start Arkham City and that seems completely different but better. Anyway let's get started, shall we :D (Corrine VS Pin)
First thing first, The game looks SO good for it's time. It actually definitely holds up to today's standards. The controls for this game are perfect and I acually MUCH prefer a keyboard over a controller. Into the gameplay, the game's unique fighting system is really nice! it isn't perfect but the idea is great. You can see that in Arkham City they had the budget to polish the fighting system but here it is still good. The only imperfections within the fighting system are just things such as not being able to counter straight after a takedown/attack. This just slows down the gameplay and doesn't make it feel very smooth (Arkham City fixes this though :D). Another gameplay feature that I love is the gliding! Oh how I love gliding around. And the Stealth sections also!!! Love it, Love it, Love it! It is very fun to BE the dark knight and takedown people like a total badass :D The gadgets are also what makes this game so great and unique.
Other great gameplay features worth mentioning is the detective mode, the riddles and the riddler trophies! All great feature that just really make this game all the more unique and absolutely AWESOME!
Onto the setting, the entire game is set on the Arkham Asylum. For some people this may seem repetitive but for me I love it! The mood and atmosphere of the island the the constant 'announcements' made by Joker make this feel ALOT like Bioshock's atmosphere however imo it's WAY better than Bioshock's world and atmosphere (Bioshock fanboys INCOMING!). The map is used great for evey scenario and I love the many hidden riddler trophies in every corner of the map. The characters in this game are AWESOME! I LOVE the Joker and the BATMAN! The voice actors for both were so perfect. Honestly I've never liked any of the film batman's (that was my only knowledge of batman as a kid) but this Batman is the perfect batman!!! The Joker is also the TRUE JOKER! I personally still prefer Heeath ledger's joker but I like that more as a realistic Joker. THIS, THIS IS THE ORIGINAL! Love it! Another great charcter that had some of my fav moments in the game were the Scarecrow scene.
Onto the story :D How do I explain the story in this game?... Well, this at first seemed like one of those mvies that are good because of everything on screen but the story wasn't that great. AT FIRST it seemed like that, however now I realise this story is actually REALLY GOOD for a start up Batman game series. There are no plot twist like I said but still, the scenes with Killer Croc and Scarecrow are amazing! This kind of leads me into the boss battles. This game had a lot of good ones and a few bad ones. To start off, as long as you've actually completed one single game before, you should set the game to 'Hard' difficulty at the beginning. I didn't do this but I should've since the game is really easy and it also saves a LOT of time when gathering achievements.
Ok so now onto the boss battles. First I will talk about the good ones which inlcude the Bane boss battle, Poison Ivy boss battle and of course the Killer Croc boss battle. In my opinion the Killer Croc boss battle was the best but the Poison I vy boss battle was the hardest. The Bane boss battle was ok but there were MANY more boss battles that used the exact same mechanic which got old and boring quickly. This leads me to the bad boss battles which mainly include all of the Titan X bosses and the final Joker boss. As I said the Titan X bosses got boring but the Joker boss battle was a huge let down as it was so EASY! I FINISHED IT ON MY FIRST GO!!! That is not something to be boasting about because it is actually quite disappointing :( I was expecting more but it was so... simple :((((
Overall, the great graphics, characters, area, atmosphere, story and overall great gameplay makes this game a true masterpiece that will NOT be forgotten. It really makes you feel like the dark knight and the completely unique gameplay give you so much control :D
To one of my fav games ever :D

-The riddler trophies and plethora of bonus content
-The immersion
-The enjoyment you get from playing!!!
Cons:

So I've invested a lot of time into this game when it originally released on the Xbox 360 in 2009 and here I am in 2016 playing it again. The game runs much better with also being the GOTY edition the extra content makes the replayability last a little longer.
Batman: Arkham Asylum, in many ways a great Batman game and especially bringing the series back to having good games after a long time of horrible releases, but there are some flaws as well that many people may not like. The flaws really just derive from the gameplay, meaning that there are some things you may not like about the game (these flaws however were improved in the sequels. Combat is fun, but can become boring quickly if you do not like beat em' up style combat, which this game focuses heavily on. The "Free-Flow" combat system refreshes the beat em'up style of games by providing a fluidity of movement as if everything works within a rhythm and as I mentioned it can be good or bad.
The collectathon aspect of the game is primarily its biggest side quest (it's the only real side quest), you must collect all of the Riddler's trophies, figure out all riddles, and much more. The journey can be rewarding but taskful as there are 240  collectibles in the game. It's your choice to task yourself that role.
The length of the game is about 10 hours, maybe less if you rush through it all and overall a nice experience. If you're a fan of Batman, you'll surely love this game along with the other Arkham games.
Performance is great, I stay at a steady 62 fps, due to the game being a bit older the port isn't as great as people would think but textures are improved, but other than that there are no huge differences between the PC port and the Xbox 360/ PS3 version. The only issue I have encountered though is during my second encounter with the Scarecrow. After "defeating" him, my game dipped to about 8 FPS and remain still for a few seconds during the transition of getting out of the Scarecrow nightmare so be wary of that if you encounter this issue.

Always Sometimes Monsters was a nice game about being homeless and scrounging up money to get to your ex's wedding, that I received as a gift.
The game starts off at a party, you are Larry. You go around talking to your guests, which all offer a drink. Whoever you pick then becomes your character for the rest of the game as you decide their names by what you write on his birthday card.  It's a more interesting than the usual selection menu and while it may feel like a small detail, I really liked how this was handled.
I very much enjoyed this game but I'm going to come across as negative review - the game is made on the RPG Maker engine, which I have used but don't particularly like. You press space-bar to progress dialogue but also choose your decision so if you're reading quickly you might occasionally select the wrong thing if you don't expect a dialogue box to show up or talk to a character again once they've finished speaking. They aren't bad but I'm not a particular fan of the engine's graphics either - individual environment sprites look very nice and the title screen is gorgeous but you can always tell that RPGMaker uses a square tile-based grid because grass instantly turns into a pavement with no overlays or curves. These are all personal grudges however and ones I'd apply to more games than just this one.
The writing isn't perfect - None of the characters converse like real people, but this is a video game so I can forgive it and the overall plot was interesting enough that while I noticed it frequently, I wasn't particularly bothered by it. I actually felt kinda bad for my character, although some of the choices made would definitely make them unsympathetic. A lot of the decisions are fairly big and really interesting - there's one right at the end that I loved and seriously struggled with.
Always Sometimes Monsters is set over a course of 30 in-game days, doing certain tasks will move time forward and at the end, you need to sleep. I enjoy games that use time as a mechanic and there was a genuine thought of ♥♥♥♥♥♥I need to get moving, I might actually miss this wedding' while playing, so I feel it's done well.  The idea is that each day brings different tasks, certain shops are only open at x times and it's appreciated, because it gives you a direction to go in.
The initial task is to get money so you can pay your apartment rent and get the key back. When the game has things going for it, choices to make and new things occurring, it's a lot of fun to see you're taking the story and I seriously got into it. The game doesn't have enough plots/choices for all 30 days so sometimes, while it starts off very strongly, the flow can get broken and you'll wake up from your bed wondering if there's something I'm missing somewhere or if I should just spent the day making money.  For example, a certain character offered to give me a lift, which was great, they said they'd contact me in a few days which I then spent killing time because there didn't seem to be any objectives left.
On a different engine with more experienced writers, this game has a potential to be a lot better, which isn't to say it's bad. I stuck with Always Sometimes Monsters to the end and I'm glad I did - the ending was good and the journey was worth sticking with. It deserves praise for trying new things and bringing fresh ideas, not all of which work, but it gets points for trying.

for short) is a first-person stealth-action role-playing game. It offers a lot of content to the player who enjoys such a mix of genres and it certainly gets a lot of things right, but unfortunately, it also gets some things wrong. In the end, I feel the good things far outweigh the bad and I'd rate this game very highly as it offered me dozens of hours of immersive fun.
After the protests and riots as a result of the polarization between the augmented and the non-augmented humans that was the focus of the story of
, which climaxed when a terrorist organization triggered all augmented people to go into a murderous frenzy (now referred to as 'the aug incident'), the world is even more divided. Both groups of people are extremely suspicious of each other and basically, the whole situation is a powder keg.
A couple of organizations claim to represent the interests of their respective group of people and they either demand equal rights for the augmented or a limitation of those rights in the wake of 'the incident'. Some of these organizations are extremist groups or even terrorist groups.
When a train station in Prague gets blown up by one of these extremist groups, an augmented Interpol agent called Adam Jensen is sent to investigate. He finds himself in a city that's increasingly weary of augmented people. The local authorities even have augmented people shipped off willy-nilly to a seedy housing complex called 'Golem City' by its inhabitants, adding to an already explosive situation.
is mainly meant to be played as a stealth action game. But you can play it as a first-person shooter, too, if you prefer a more aggressive and harder route.
Don't get me wrong. Gun combat in this game is certainly enjoyable. There are different types of guns, skills to enhance your shooting skills and defense, different types of ammo and upgrades for your weapons. However, in the first part of the game you won't be equipped to survive more than five seconds of actual combat, so you'll automatically turn to sneaking, at least partially.
The whole sneaking system, which is pretty much the essence of
's gameplay, is exciting and fun. You analyze the opponents' positions and patrol routes and try to single out one of them to sneak up to without being seen by his comrades or by security cameras. You then press a button on your keyboard/controller to silently eliminate him. Finally, you drag the body out of sight of any remaining patrols or security cameras.
The main thing that makes
enjoyable is its impressive level design. The main hub, the city of Prague, is huge by comparison to the two smaller hubs in
. There's also much more exploring to do as the Prague hub has a lot more optional (i.e. not quest-related) areas.
The areas you're supposed to sneak (or fight) your way through have been designed with the utmost care. There always seem to be at least three ways leading to your target. Which ways are available to you depend on your creativity and the augmentations (skills) you decide to invest in. You can crawl through vents, move aside heavy objects that are blocking the way, jump down from great heights, punch through weak spots in walls, remote-hack cameras or turrets to give you time to pass them undetected, hack locked doors, hack computers to disable security systems, use your resistance to gas or electricity to pass through corridors that would otherwise be unpassable, and more.
It's too bad the hacking minigame is based on luck. You can increase your chances by investing in skills and by using consumable items, but it remains a minigame based on luck. So you will be reloading a lot. I would have preferred a minigame that relies on logical thinking or on dexterity, especially since you play the hacking minigame a couple of hundred times.
Another piece of bad news is
has a lot of bugs. They're all minor bugs so no game-breaking issues, but they're annoying by themselves and even more so because they are plentiful. We're talking about clipping issues, rendering issues, problems with scrolling the map, no mouse scrolling during the hacking minigame, controls sometimes not responding, drawers that are shown as lootable but you can't interact with unless you reload, quest markers that point to the wrong place, merchants who keep saying you're wasting their time when you only sell items (and later on even when you do buy stuff from them), and so on. Together, all these small issues make the game feel unpolished, especially after a couple of patches that already fixed a bunch of bugs.

The game's graphics look good enough for a current-gen game. Still, I wasn't overly impressed with the graphics but that's probably because I ran the game on 'high' settings, so maybe that's a far cry from the 'very high' and the 'ultra high' settings.
Speaking of Far Cry, the voice acting is top-notch. Especially Elias Toufexis, who voices protagonist Adam Jensen (and who has voiced main characters in Far Cry, Splinter Cell and Assassin's Creed). He delivers a voice that's a cross between Doug Cockle's Geralt of Rivia and Christian Bale's Batman, and he manages to put some humanity in an otherwise cool-as-ice Jensen, who is more machine than man, after all.
The music sounds wonderful. It's subtle and atmospheric, exactly as it should be.

The equipment DLC add a few weapons that you can easily do without, and some consumables that are one use only, so you can only use them in one playthrough.

Arkham Asylum, at the time of this review, is a bit aged (released in 2010, this is 2016), yet still manages to hold it's own admist the newer generation of gameplay and graphics.
Already being a fan of Batman and DC since a child, I was extremely excited to try out the first real Batman game, and I was pleasantly surprised with a game that actually is better than many other games, even given it's semi-un-original content and linear storyline based on plot information that most people, even non-DC/Batman fans already know.
The game takes place in Arkham Asylum, an island in the city of Gotham, Bruce Wayne/Batman's domain.  The island goes under quarantine after Joker escapes his captivity and leads the various villains and criminals to control the island.
As previously stated, the story-line, is semi-unique.  It hasn't been told exactly before (afaik), but it's fairly predictable if you're familiar with the universe.  Even so, the story is rich, characters have backstory and development and well-done voice acting and dialog in general.
The combat system is the classic Assassin's Creed II combat system.  Lots of hand to hand and "press Y to counter" combat, with lots of gadgets, specials, combos, score multipliers and other abilities.  The combat is very fluid and fun, but may get a bit repetitive for some after a while.
The game world is semi-open.  You have free reign over the island and it's buildings to do the missions, or go explore for collectibles (a lot of these by the way).  This is of course permitting you've reached the story points that allow access to the locations in question.
The collectibles, while there are an abundance, are all useful.  Collectibles unlock backstore to the creator of the Asylum and it's history, cell-tapes from various villains, backstory on villains or important characters, concept art and challenge maps.
The graphics, for a 2010 game in 2016, are still pretty damn good, so nothing to worry about here.
Keyboard and mouse controls are a bit clunky/confusing and don't work to well, due to the console -> PC porting of the game, unfortunately, but with a controller, the gameplay is stellar, and goes without a hitch.
Definitely worth picking up, although at $20 for a 6 year old game, personally, I'd wait for a sale, even though the game is very good and still likely worth $20 for most.

tl;dr - This is a fantastic game, don't let the reviews put you off from buying it.
Playtime as of review: I have 5 hours on record on Steam, and about 8 on PS4.
B:TB is a game about evolution. You set up the environment on a large voxel cube, and then sit back and wait for life to appear on it. There are hundreds of different creatures to evolve, from single celled organisms that arise through abiogenisis, all the way through to human beings. As you set up the environment for the various creatures, you have to think about things like temperature, elevation, water depth, moisture, the food chain etc. It starts simple, but birthing some of the more "complicated" animals has several layers of complexity attached to it, and requires creative solutions and a good bit of thinking.
The game is extremely laid back and relaxing. If you are the kind of gamer who appreciates a games that doesn't ask much of you, and allows you to tinker away with complex machinery, or even if you are just like me and are looking for a break from the constant violence that seems to be inherent in video games these days, this is a great choice. Although not entirely noddy, the game is never stressful, and certainly never punishes you.
In my opinion, the best thing about this game is the visual style. The models and environments are beautiful, and the animations on the creatures is awesome. You only have to look at the screenshots people post in the community thread to see what I mean. If you get the collectors edition, you also get access to a HD scan of the games artbook, which has dozens of adorable art samples of the games creatures.
It was pretty obvious from the get-go that this was going to be one of those games that divides people. A large chunk of the video game buying public really dislike games where the "fun" comes from winding up your toy and then watching it go. With the occassional outlier (like Gratuitous Space Battles), most of the games of this type on Steam do not have good reviews.
The big issues currently plaguing this game is the performance. On a 970M laptop with a latest gen i7 processer, I struggle to maintain a solid frame rate. and the game suffers from some heavy lagging at seemingly random moments. However, this isn't a game that really requires a lightning fast frame rate, and if you are playing with a controller, it is far less noticeable. The developers are already working on patches to sort out the performance issues, and it runs much better on PS4, so it seems the problems aren't engine-inherit, and can be sorted out.

The game itself is very interesting. It goes through evolution in a unique and entertaining way. Highly educational. However, the UI has not been developed for the PC. The lack of an EXIT button is evident of than, as well as the multiple key binding to the same action. Which is a shame as it destroys the emersion of the game. It is therefore with regret that I am unable to recommend this game.

Arkham Asylum, at the time of this review, is a bit aged (released in 2010, this is 2016), yet still manages to hold it's own admist the newer generation of gameplay and graphics.
Already being a fan of Batman and DC since a child, I was extremely excited to try out the first real Batman game, and I was pleasantly surprised with a game that actually is better than many other games, even given it's semi-un-original content and linear storyline based on plot information that most people, even non-DC/Batman fans already know.
The game takes place in Arkham Asylum, an island in the city of Gotham, Bruce Wayne/Batman's domain.  The island goes under quarantine after Joker escapes his captivity and leads the various villains and criminals to control the island.
As previously stated, the story-line, is semi-unique.  It hasn't been told exactly before (afaik), but it's fairly predictable if you're familiar with the universe.  Even so, the story is rich, characters have backstory and development and well-done voice acting and dialog in general.
The combat system is the classic Assassin's Creed II combat system.  Lots of hand to hand and "press Y to counter" combat, with lots of gadgets, specials, combos, score multipliers and other abilities.  The combat is very fluid and fun, but may get a bit repetitive for some after a while.
The game world is semi-open.  You have free reign over the island and it's buildings to do the missions, or go explore for collectibles (a lot of these by the way).  This is of course permitting you've reached the story points that allow access to the locations in question.
The collectibles, while there are an abundance, are all useful.  Collectibles unlock backstore to the creator of the Asylum and it's history, cell-tapes from various villains, backstory on villains or important characters, concept art and challenge maps.
The graphics, for a 2010 game in 2016, are still pretty damn good, so nothing to worry about here.
Keyboard and mouse controls are a bit clunky/confusing and don't work to well, due to the console -> PC porting of the game, unfortunately, but with a controller, the gameplay is stellar, and goes without a hitch.
Definitely worth picking up, although at $20 for a 6 year old game, personally, I'd wait for a sale, even though the game is very good and still likely worth $20 for most.

If you don't want to read the rest of this review, the takeaway is this: the game rocks and you should be playing it. Here's why. The gameplay is fun and charming. Keeping in mind, I'm not a gamer or an expert in that field, more serious or professional gamers could take my review with a grain of salt. But I'm an everywoman. I like what I like, and I like this game.
If there's one thing that I know pretty well from my near-decade of loneliness before I met my current girlfriend, it's dating simulators. I play almost exclusively dating simulators. Now you may look in my library and say "oh, there's HuniePop, but you have 8k hours on Skyrim!" Wrong. I have 8k hours on Serana Volkihar Dating Simulator. "You have a lot of hours on XCOM 2!" Got the mod that let your soldiers date. You get the picture. Crush Crush is a delightful dating simulator that allows you to be a lesbian that dates other women that are, from the writing, written to be explicitly bisexual AT LEAST. In fact, in my hours of meticulously combing through every girl's dialogue click by click, there are several references to being attracted to other women and only one or two referencing specific attraction to dudes.
Which leads us to the writing, the real meat of any dating sim. It's charming and sweet and while there are a few spots where it's immersion-shatteringly obvious that the dialogue is written by a man and a line or two here and there that get too meta/self-depricating, for the most part I'm happy to say that it's host to some of the most delightful characters that I have ever come across. It's easy to cringe at first - during the early relationship stages, most girls are one-dimensional stereotypes - but as your relationships progress and the girls open up, each one is pretty true to the type of woman they each represent. Spoilers here, but I found myself begrudgingly nodding along during the Dark One's later-stage dialogue. Exceptional mechanic for a boss fight and a cute, relatable goth. I felt called out (in a good way)!
Speaking of individual characters, my girlfriend and I both became endeared towards certain characters. I do feel a bit bad, because while my girlfriend is an athletic gamer (I know, what a freakishly powerful human that I love and fear) it was Bonnibel that captured my heart and earned my Diamond Ring with her tender and romantic dialogue. My girlfriend is smitten with Nutaku (who we affectionately call Nut) which is a relief for me because that's pretty much how I flirt anyway. Point is, there's really a girl for everyone; they're not just cookie cutter tropes. Okay maybe they are, but those cookies are baked with meticulous care and decorated creatively.
And how can we talk about decoration without talking about the beautiful detail and care that went into these girls' art? I'm actually not that big of a fan of anime-style artwork but this game's art style took my breath away. There's not even a hint of same-face syndrome in the game and even a lot of the nsfw art (easily available on their website for dirt cheap if you're not an idiot and can operate a search engine) is diverse and realistic. Well, as realistic as anime style can be. They all still suffer from the unfortunate boob size ratio of big-bigger-biggest (srsly Elle ily darling but my back hurts just looking at you) but as my girlfriend wisely says, all boobs are good boobs. All in all, though, the artwork was an absolute breath of fresh air from the stale quagmire of media with naked women drawn by talented artists that have never seen a naked woman in their lives.
On the subject of stale quagmires in media as well, I have to go back to the writing. I know I'm picking over the writing in depth, but as a storyteller myself, it's really important to me, especially media that is conscious of three audiences: typical, target, and potential. Typical audience is gonna be cis straight men, probably gamers. Target audience is... actually hard to tell and for that I give credit where credit is due, because that means that they're mindful of their potential audience. I'm obviously a lesbian and I really enjoy dating games where I don't get broken from immersion by having to say "aww, this is for guys." Instead it is masterfully written in a way that the protagonist could be any gender and find something that seems quite natural to them in a way that I haven't seen since I read Jeanette Winterson's "Written on the Body."
The story, as well, is something new and exciting. I won't spoil it, but there is a story. And no, not just the typical "wow! you're lonely! Have sex with these women! Now you're still lonely in real life haha so meta!" that I see as the plot of a lot of romance games. These girls actually seem to care for you, Marshmallow seems to care for them, they all know about one another and are happy and comfortable with it (for the most part) and the plot draws you in and gives the game a solid, satisfying ending. Even after that, there's still the best part - spending those sweet, sweet diamonds on a wedding dress to give to your waifu. And then scooting over to let your girlfriend drop your diamonds on hers. Everybody's happy.
My biggest complaint by far is something nobody but me even really cares about - Marshmallow. She gets SO few customization options (and I like what hobbies do to her, btw, that's genius) but I put my dumb lil ponytail on her and pretended it was an undercut and worked my butt off to get her somewhat nice looking and still she was the exact same in all the cutscenes. I don't know what I really want here - a broader range of customization, for my customizations to reflect in-game, whatever, but I still found myself really wanting more from that. I imagine that would be a thing if they had a bigger budget, so... let's get them that bigger budget!
All in all, it was a beautiful, charming game and I'm still loving it after I finished it. I cannot wait to see what more comes from this studio and these developers. Also if Sad Panda Studios is reading this, I'm begging you to bring back Bonnie in the visual novel. Or even Nina? Please? XOXO, Emily.

Ok. So this will be a quick review. This is the first Batman game in a trilogy by Rocksteady. I played the second one first so I knew the type of gameplay to expect. The game has some of the most seamless combat in its genre. It can be simple to understand and get into yet difficult to master.  Its not a true open world game because you're not really roaming the world. You simply roam the asylum, albeit a large one, its still a very confined area with the city off in a distance that is visible but not reachable.
The graphics are pretty good with very low system requirements, I play this on a Surface pro 3 (I3 processor) with the settings on medium.
Is this the greatest super hero game ever? No, its not even the best batman game currently on steam. Arkham CITY is better in almost every way, but its very good in its own right. I would give this game a 9/10 during its release and a 7.5/10 today. Lets face the facts games have caught up with Arkham Asylum in its vastness, story telling, and graphics but it can still hold its own today.
Bottom line:  If you're looking for a semi-open world dark heroic adventure, this is a great place to start. If you've played part of the series and are considering buying this game, it is worth it, especially on sale.
