A Valley Without Wind is a Valley Of Pure Boredom.

There's a lot to love in A Valley Without Wind - freedom and exploration in a randomly-generated world, crafting and upgrades, lots of perilous platforming challenges and a Rogue Legacy-style new hero system - but the experience is somewhat marred by the fact that the game looks like something that would barely pass muster for freeware back in the 90's. If you can past the somewhat dated visuals (although it can hit 60FPS, which is always nice), there's much fun to be had.
Just be mindful that this isn't really a game that holds your hand - as each playthrough is never the same, you may be frustrated at the fact that there's no real direction or point in the beginning. Stick with it, and you'll learn to love it.

It pains me to see the low playerbase so shortly after the release of LawBreakers. I feel like this is the kind of FPS we need in today's current market of casualized FPS games. LawBreakers is all about raw skill, and that's whats so amazing about it. It isn't too difficult to pick up if you are new, but the game has an incredibly high skill ceiling. Unlike Overwatch, this is a game where you will want to stick to one character and practice them. The different character classes are much more in depth and have more complex mechanics to master. You will also need to master the fluid and quick movement system, and your aim of course. Again, I hope to see more FPS games that harken back to pure skill based gameplay like LawBreakers. It's a great game and more people should support this type of FPS. Buy it please!

Whelp, I guess that was all of Unhack.
At a full 61 minutes of playtime, do not mistake this for a long game.
Should you get it though? Eh, why not.
Gameplay consists of guiding a small orange cube through top-down levels representing the insides of computer programs. You travel by means of nodes, so there's no real exploration element, it has more of a puzzle vibe to it.
On its own this would be boring, you're playing this for the story. The story is that of an unhacker (...the term is never really explained in the game either. I guess a security tech person? Because that's sort of what you do) and his companion AI uncovering a conspiracy where one of the IT security companies is behind the recent influx of worm viruses in an attempt to grow rich off of the fallout.
this AI and the various other AI you encounter all happen to take the shape of cutesie anime girls, yeah one of those games...
Don't get me wrong, this isn't a full-blown visual novel, you are never given any conversation options or relevant branching paths in the gameplay, you follow a linear story divided over 10 chapters in which you will hit every anime trope and stereotype you can think of.
Technical execution is very bare, with no way to see which of the 10 chapters you've actually finished so far, leading to some awkward restarts if you click the wrong one from the menu, and there's no sense that you're unlocking anything (most games with this amount of VN content at least have a gallery mode that you unlock when you clear the game...).
Yet, here I am recommending this game... so what am I not telling you?
This game has heart. It's flawed in its execution, but it never seems to be because the developers did not want to bother. The story is rife with clichés but in the very end did manage to draw me in enough to care, a big part of that credit goes to the solid voice acting that was delivered.
If you don't go in expecting too much, and at that price you really shouldn't, you might come away charmed like I was.

So... When's the sequel?
Unhack has a very... Unique style of humour. For instance, the MC, you, use emoticons during dialouge. It's quirky and stupid, but really enjoyable for some reason.
Also, having FULLY VOICED characters (and in english, no less!) really makes the 2 hours of fun all that more enjoyable. Xanthe Huynh, from Sword Art Online even makes an appearance. So if you love her performance, you won't be dissapointed. The gameplay in this is fast, but 'puzzle' really isn't the right term for it. It's a lot like the impossible game (the one you control with the arrow keys, not the musical one) but you jump from point to point instead of free movement. Also, in the last quarter or so of the game, your movement speed is increased and so is your health. But honestly, I reccomend you play on the hardest difficulty, which allows NO DEATHS, simply because the game lacks a little in difficulty. Around the only times I died was when I accidently hit a movement key and went hurling to my death. I still want to see a speedrun of this game, though.
In summary: It's quick, cheap, funny and all around entertaining. Fun for the whole family. I can't wait to see more from the developers.
Which puts me back to my first line.
So, when's the sequel?

I remember first getting this game for Christmas as part of the original "Lucasarts Archive" collection, which had Sam and Max Hit the Road, Fate of Atlantis, and a bunch of demos.  At the time (I was ten, maybe eleven?) Sam and Max was by far my favorite, but over time that has become...Day of the Tentacle.  Let's be honest, if you're even looking at this you've probably already played the game in the past, so I'll touch on just a few key points.
1) The remastered graphics is probably the best balance between keeping the old style while cleaning things up for the "modern player."  Things don't change radically - really, at all - between the original and new style, which is more than Secret of Monkey Island can say.  Having played this almost annually for twenty years, I think I now prefer the updated graphics.
2) The developer's commentary is great.  I mostly play this on muscle memory (without being cognizant of it in the game), so the commentary on its own would freshen things up.  However, the fact that most of the original team (key players at least) were available makes this worth listening to on its own.  Say what you will about Tim Schaffer, he knows how to keep discussions interesting AND educational.
3)  The new controls are good, definitely streamlined, but I think this is one case where I prefer the fake "freedom" of the original SCUMM verbs.  Still, if you don't care about such things the new controls are very intuitive.
4)  You can no longer access Laverne from the start.  The commentary explains why, and although it's not how it was designed in the original I actually think it's a good call.  You couldn't do anything anyway...but at this point it's probably only going to be appreciated by new players.
IF you've played the original and still own it, this is definitely a must buy.  For those who - shocking - have not played the original, this is definitely the version to get.  Without a doubt my vote for standing the "test of time."

I wish there was more than a binary rating system for recommendations; I am very mixed on this product. I'm going to offer a /very soft/ recommendation. If the premise interests you, it won't disappoint; it is still rather flawed all the same, with a weak visual novel pigeonholed into a puzzle game which has a lot of good pieces here, but could be fleshed out more.
For its pricetag and relative experimentation with two genres, it could be a valid purchase for anyone who's a major fan of VNs and puzzles, if you belong to that niche group like I do. Its flaws are apparent for most of the game, but has considerable payoff towards the end. It's very short, even for its posted pricetag.
Fundamentally, I feel the VN and the puzzle halves are, for the most part, acting in opposition to each other. To its credit, dialogue usually pipes in while you are in safe places (at which point you may be compelled to sit and listen to the voiceacting or read along). Because the protagonist is unvoiced, you have to split attention between the two parts of the game while puzzling. It feels as if the puzzle rarely has a factor on the plot or interactions of the characters, as the protagonist and the given AI girl are usually bantering with one another. There is one particular moment at the end of the game (avoiding spoilers) where there is a meaningful change in gameplay that supports the plot, and I feel that's enough of a payoff to take from the experience.
All in all, as an experiment in providing a VN with light gameplay elements, I feel it stumbled, trying to pigeonhole VN elements into a straightforward puzzlegame without recognizing the VN's inherent strengths as a genre. It is difficult to focus on the emotions of the characters when you would rather deal with the puzzles presented to you.
Another strength of the VN genre is dictated by the strength of its writing, and I do not feel that it is present here. The story lacks worldbuilding and context - there's something to be said about suspension of disbelief, but without proper establishment of setting, you get lost on what is happening, especially with regards to the integration of the digital and real worlds (something that is never attempted to be explained). You never leave the monitor, but real life actions will occur to your protagonist (up to and including time in the slammer). Things generally happen because it has to happen to have a coherent plot.
The general banter between characters isn't especially interesting, compounded by the fact that the voice acting of the AI universally sounds flat and robotic. It fixates on repeated tired jokes regarding perversion. I didn't get much out of it, and it compounded to a general feeling of going through the motions to get to the end of most levels.
All the flaws laid bare, the plot is solid, with a good amount of twists even for a short product and a climax that pays off pretty well. It throws in enough variations to the puzzle gameplay to keep things fresh. The background music is solid, the art is passable. There is nothing outright bad about the game, and a lot of what can be considered weak or tacky can be phased out via options.
It's a nice little time killer for an hour, that's about all that can be said about it.

This is the idle game cousin to Time Rifters (a FPS that you play with yourself), and as a result various shared traits make it stand out from the rest.
For starters: enemies aren't just one piece of massive HP but collections of blocks, each with their own HP with some having more than others.
In response your click gun can target them and your "allies" have various traits beyond higher DPS, like the rocket launcher's spread damage or the particle ball's crit
there's some level up settings for quicker leveling without holding down a button and leveling and abilities for your allies are on the same track, (you level then get the ability, then level some more); this ensures passives aren't missed.
As far as your active abilities go those are learned separately and have hot keys, including Space which activates all the ones you current have for a nice Alpha strike effect.
Want an shooting/FPS flavored idle game? This is for you.
It's a great game, shame that there just aren't enough people playing it.

If you were ever wondering how it would be to pass one day in Batman's life, this game may could help your imagination.
Batman: Arkham Asylum is a third-person action game where you cast the Dark Knight himself. The story is about, like the title spoils, the Arkham Asylum. The Arkham Asylum is the place where all the crazy and evil opponents of Batman are held in, including the Joker. With the help of corrupt guards in the asylum, Joker can escape from his cell and take the whole island, where the asylum is on, under his power. He kidnaped Commissioner Gordan and threated to detonate hidden bombs in Gotham City if anyone tries to enter the island, so Batman has to come alone on his self without any help. As a result, Batman came to the asylum to defeat Joker, to free Gordon and to save the city. In the progress of the story there will come more surprises, but I won't to spoil to much...
The gameplay of this game is made really handsome, so you can play the game without any disturbings in the control. You see your character from a third person view, so you have the overview. In corners or in other situations you can change the point of view in that way, that you can see everything. The map is an open world, so you can explore every angle of the island, provided you have unlocked all areas. The exploration of the map goes on very well, Batman can run, jump, climb, crouch, glide and use his inventory with some great gadgets. All in one it's fun to explore the island, especiallly the riddles which you have to find and solve.
The fights between Batman and his enemies are also made interesting. In many cases you can choose to sneak by and let the enemies in ignorance of your presents or to fight them face to face. Also after every chapter you have to fight against a boss, who is one of Batman's enemy known from the comics. The boss fights are really challenging if you choose the hard gameplay mode.
Let's talk about the graphics. This game has, considering the date of the release, a really nice graphic. The atmosphere is dark and tense like you know it from the Batman comics. The characters also looks nice, but the proportions aren't looking real. But that's just a side effect. The environment and the map fit the atmosphere, so you can't gripe about the graphic.
All in one it's a really good game, not just for Batman fans. One negative point was, that I had some issues with the graphic card and the game was lagging on some points, although my graphic card fulfills the requierements. An other negative point is the GOTY extra content, which is getting really boring after a while.

One of the best casual card games I've played -- and I've played a lot of them! The deck consists of 10 suits of cards numbered 2 through 7, and your simple goal is to get the highest single card of each suit you can, with lower-ranked cards you collect functioning as backup for when (not if) your top card gets stolen.
Each suit has a special ability tied ingeniously to its thematic element.  For example, swords allow you to steal and play a card from your opponent's hand, while anchors "lock down" all previous card in the current play to protect them from a bust. (A bust occurs if you draw a second card of an already-played suit in the same turn.)
The artword could not be better, and there are tons of special abilities ("traits") to unlock.  Achievements are gained by playing a series of tournaments using special rulesets (e.g., "Swords and cannons target the lowest card of a suit instead of the highest").  Even though it's a completely casual game, I find myself enjoying it for hours at a time.  If you like card games, you MUST get this one.

I AM COMPLETELY REWRITING MY REVIEW.
RONIN/RONiN (however you want to write it) is a neat game with a nice concept. The turn based combat mechanic is something that will do one of two things. Hook you in, or drive you to near suicide. Personally, I find this cartoony art style to be extremely appealing, and the animations to be nice and fluid (thankyou Vanripper!). The soundtrack of this game also echoes a dark, grim tone, and suits the bleak tones and contrasting reds of the game (which I feel gives an emphasis on blood and killing). The story, however, is virtually non-existant in the main game, with the exception of some words over the backdrop of a photo which I presume is the last photo of her father (oh yeah, the protagonist is female). If you really want to know the story (like I did) you'd have to do two things. Purchase the special edition with the digital comic, or scourer the internet for forums and the like (which I did, and which made me want to purchase the digital comic too). The special edition comes with the digital comic (which I have yet to read) and the soundtrack. The soundtrack alone, (to me at least) is well worth the $6 upgrade price, and couple that with the digital comic that has that art style I love, means to me it is well worth the price.
Now, if you didn't already see I like this game from the big blue thumbs up at the top, then you should by now know that I like it. A lot. But that doesnt mean the game is perfect. A lot of the gameplay revolves on trial and error, which can be at times irritating, but the pay off and satisfaction of finally pulling off your ninja fantasy is a great feeling. Another issue is that the jump arc can be misleading. This wouldn't be as big of a problem if the game developer hadn't put in a tooltip recognising the flaw, and then just ignoring it! Other than those two things, and the lack of in-game story, there's no real major issues that I can think of that are something to put in the review.
If you want a more detailed review by someone far more suited to this kind of thing, watch TotalBiscuit's review of the game on YouTube titled "WTF is RONIN?"

I've seen RONIN's creator refer to the game as a Gunpoint rip-off, but that really doesn't adequately explain what RONIN has to offer.
It's also a Mark of the Ninja rip-off.
I kid, somewhat, but if you're going to take inspiration, it's probably a good idea to take it from two of the best games on Steam. RONIN successfully emulates Gunpoint and Mark of the Ninja in a way that is noticeable, but sufficiently original too. Unfortunately, RONIN also takes the flaws from both of those titles, and despite being - spoiler alert - worth a purchase if you enjoyed either of those games, it also doesn't quite earn the right to be ranked amongst them.
Let's start with the good. The game's art style and music are both done very well, keeping the game dark and moody, but colourful and interesting too. The controls are simple and easy to understand, and while there's a mandatory tutorial level, it's not easy to enough that it wastes one of the games 15 decently-sized levels. And if you can make it through an entire level without raising an alarm, harming a civilian, or letting an enemy escape un-stabbified, you can unlock bonus abilities, like the ability to hang enemies from ceilings, or throw your sword.
But this is just stalling - the real MVP is the combat. The combat in RONIN is the kind that makes you think 'Holy crap, why has nobody else ever thought of this until now?' It's turn-based, and every turn you have to avoid to fire from enemies (helpfully highlighted thanks to the laser-sights of their guns) while making your way closer, killing them all, and stopping them from raising the alarm. You can jump, grapple, swing, attack, and after upgrades, teleport, stun, and throw your sword. Enemies are resilient enough not to die if you just knock them over a few times, but kicking them straight out of a six-storey window is just as satisfying as it sounds.
While the combat system is great enough that the game understandably doesn't want you to ignore it and sneak past everyone, it can lead to a few levels that make you wonder 'Why was this tagged 'stealth'?' But what stealth there is is still wholly enjoyable, and there are a few highly-populated areas you can clear our by picking people off one at a time, with no one the wiser. And while the combat has a few annoyances - enemies are capable of shooting straight through each other while aiming at you - it's also very gratifying. Jumping into someone takes them out of the action for at least two turns, and it's possible to kick them into each other, distracting whole crowds while you get started with the killing.
One trick that it's best to learn as soon as possible; if you're jumping towards an enemy, try to arc your jump so that your turn ends with you still in midair, but close enough to kill them. Every enemy will aim at your midair position, and you're free to kill your target, fall to the floor, and avoid all fire. That's all I'll give you though, you have to learn the rest yourself.
As for the bad, well, as I said, the game takes its flaws from its inspirations, and, sorry to say it, amplifies them. From Gunpoint, it takes a fun, interesting concept that could let players tackle levels any way they want, but more often than not, the only path forwards is surprisingly linear. And much like Gunpoint's batteries, RONIN gives you lots of gadgets that you can unlock, but you honestly can't use them very often. The 'teleport to another nearby enemy' ability is always incredibly useful though, so I would make that a priority.
From Mark of the Ninja, the game takes a New Game Plus that really doesn't need to be there. It's a nice optional feature that isn't really optional if you're looking to 100% the achievements, where you start with all of your gadgets unlocked, but enemies are more frequent, bodyguards with assault rifles can change their aim while shooting, and getting an alarm means it's game over. It's not impossible, but even though I beat the 3rd level of the 4th chapter, I honestly couldn't tell you how. Far too often on NG+ the game becomes dependent on trial and error because you're tasked with taking out 12 enemies at once, while not letting a single one count down from 9 to sound the alarm. It's extremely difficult.
That being said, the only other problems that come to mind are the occasional glitch and the almost non-existent plot. Every once in a while, while using the grappling hook to zip towards a wall or ceiling, you might just go straight through the wall or the ceiling. Sometimes this is a funny surprise. Sometimes this can even be helpful. More often than not, it completely ruins your chances at a level. As for the plot, there really isn't much to talk about. There's a minimal amount of white text over a picture of some people whose faces gradually get crossed out at the beginning of every boss chapter, but it doesn't really explain anything. Am I the good guy? The bad guy? An ex-pizza-delivery girl who got disgruntled by a lack of tips? I don't know, but it doesn't have that big an effect on the game.
And that's the final verdict here; a fair few problems, none of which have that big an effect on the game. I don't know if the developer plans to make a RONIN 2, but if they ever do, I'm happy enough with this game and confident enough that they'd try to improve the things that need improving that it would be an auto-buy.
Bottom line; RONIN is a good game.

Ronin has a very interesting and uniqe set of game mechanics, but the overall game design is not so good. There are many examples of the game being unfair, rather than callenging. What i mean, is when playing this game, you are going to get punished for making a mistake, that certainly is not yours, because the game is misleading, or because the mechanics are inconsitent.
You are going to waste a turn (and probably die afterwards), because the character didnt jump the way you aimed the jump. You are going to get spoted by an enemy who is standing on the opposite side of a wall. You think you are going to be able to jump down through a platform, since you could do just that with all the other platforms that looked just like it, just to find out that it didnt work, and that you are still standing on top of the it (and you wasted a turn, which probably caused your death).
The fact that this game is a turn based strategy game just makes this worse, because if you cant count on consistent mechanics in a strategy game, if the rules of the game just change in the middle of it, there is not really much strategy to it.
That being said, i really think that the core mechanics in this RONIN could make a pretty engaging game, it just does not feel like the game has been polished enough.
I could also make a long list of ideas for gameplay improvement, since i feel like the game needs a lot of changes made to the controls and gameplay. but i realize that this is not my game, and that this is not about my ideas, but the controls definately feel clumsy and just not right for a strategy game.
All in all, this game has potential, but it has a lot of holes, that a finished game should never have.

Arkham Asylum was the first superhero game within the recent years which wasn't a simple license-cash-grab, but a fully fleshed out and mastercrafted action adventure with brilliant story, great voiceacting, extremely great art design and an atmospheric soundtrack. On top of it, the gameplay was well thought out and there were more and more mechanics introduced throughout game progression.
As it stands, Arkham Asylum is probably one of the best entries of the entire Rocksteady Batman franchise, as while being linear compared to the other titles, it has the most story impact due to less distractions.
11/10 because Batman.

Batman Arkham Asylum is a perfect game for those who are looking to get into the Action-Adventure genre, or even those who are just fans of Batman. Filled with interesting riddles, maps, and level bosses, the game is surely going to give you 5-6 hours of great gameplay, plus at least 2 more hours of gameplay to complete each of Riddler's Challenges and to obtain each one of the Character Trophies. Add in 1.5 hours for challenges and Steam achievements, and you have yourself around 9 hours of gameplay that will surely leave you wanting more.
Gameplay mechanics are simple, yet many exist. Several gadgets from WayneTech are necessary to progress, so be sure to purchase those, along with the armor upgrades before anything else. Riddler's Challenges can be ignored (except the first one) until you beat the final boss (Joker).
The game includes a wide array of DC Villains, including Zsaz, Harley Quinn, Poison Ivy, Bane, Scarecrow, Joker etc, and each boss battle is sure to keep you on the edge of your seat.
You might want to play the game in Easy if you are not experienced with Adventure games, Medium if you are good at Adventure games, and Hard if you think you can take it.
A worthwile purchase for the price, and I'm looking forward to playing Arkham City

Batman: Arkham Asylum is developed by Rocksteady Studios and published by Warner Bros. At first, I am not a huge fan of Batman or pretty much I am not a fan of comic books. Surprisingly, this is the Batman game that met its expectations for fans and comic book alike. The game sets in Arkham Asylum, playing as Bruce Wayne or Batman (state the obvious). The story starts where Batman is taking and apprehending Joker to the Asylum, causing it was a setup and controlling the asylum by Joker. I am not going to tell you much about the story, it's better to play the game to know about the story. Trust me, it's such a great Batman game to start with. The combat system is based on combo, score multipliers, dodges and counter attacks. There are gadgets to tackle obstacles throughout the story. You can upgrade your abilities by leveling up. Collectables all over the map (Riddler's Trophy, scarab wall and searching the answer for Riddler's challenge), like the backstory of Arkham Asylum, the interview tapes, the concept art and character bios to learn about their orginality.
The verdict for this game's honest review is a must buy, like come on buy this game and you will love it every second, even if you are not a fan of Batman like myself. The story, the atmosphere, the voice acting, combat system and unlockables. You can find all of the extras after you finished the game and play some challenges. I don't find any game's technical flaws (unless I am a blind bat or not paying attention to details). I definitely recommend this game, just go buy the game.

This is a thought provoking, original, well written, incredibly human game with a lot of subtle humour that really reflects on its own nature. I was positively surprised by it.
Character choice is interesting and new, although at first I didn't quite understand what I was meant to be doing. This later turns out to be the absolute purpose of the game, I guess. You're down on life, your love has left you, and you know nothing as certain as that you have to get her back.
So you go on a long, sometimes brutal journey to reach him/her, making ethical decisions on the way, deciding how to make the days count.
The game can at times be slow, but it gripped me from the start with its writing. Events happen frequently and keep the pace just fine. I honestly cared for some of the characters and found myself sometimes going back to a previous safe just in order to amend a bad decision I made. Although I imagine going with your guts at first and sticking to them is also really great in this game. And probably makes more sense for what the developers intended.
Here your choices really give the impression of mattering, and you have a large impact on the lives of the other characters in the story. Be good, be bad, you can be always a monster, sometimes a monster - you get the idea.
Can really recommend this game. Worth several playthroughs I reckon, because one playthrough is definitly not enough to see all the options there could be if you had only done something different. Always a few other people to side with, or other decisions to make that determine how you feel about the person you made the character become in the end.
Ending is probably a bit deterministic. From what I can see so far there is about three or four different endings, but they dont necessarily rely too much on all the things you have decided during the journey. I enjoyed the ending nonetheless, although it wasn't the best written part in the story. Something a character in the story says comes to mind "are you prepared for your happy ending?" well we might not even want it. Or something like that.
Anyway. Graphics are charming. Music stays in the head but is always well fitting. Few minigames to break the old mold, some of them pretty fun. Real interesting concept. Can recommend wholeheartedly.

Greetings, comrades! I really, REALLY wanted to like this game. I mean, who wouldn't? A randomly generated "Metroid-vania" style game with RPG-heavy gameplay, what more could you want? Well, the answer lies below, if you dare to enter the rabbit hole.
Pros:
As I already stated, the concept is amazing, and the RPG elements are simple yet complete. Unlike most RPGs, this one gives you a very strong weapon right off the bat. Not the best, but good enough to be a constant companion throughout the game.
I found the graphics to be a refreshing change from the standard "drab-&-dull" that older Indie games are known for (not all Indie games, calm down fan-people). The world is bright and sharp, with clean angles and stunning detail.
The custom difficulty is nice, allowing you to set your own pace.
The controls, while a bit quirky, are responsive and imaginative.
Cons:
While the RPG elements are all there, there really isn't a temptation to level up. I mean, my character could "tank" all of the early bosses with ease, the only challenge being when a boss is resistant to a certain elemental-type weapon, and you have to use another element to kill it. Even then, the challenge rests not in the boss itself, but rather in finding the new element required to kill it.
While I like quick weapon progression, as it allows you to do other stuff instead of trying to get a new weapon, this game suffers from a lack of other stuff to do. The quests are the same, the enemies are the same, the graphics are the same, and the gameplay style is the same. All the same. All the same. Did I ever tell you the definition of insanity? (Heh, see what I did there? Ha ha! No? Ah, forget it.)
As I said, the world is very realistic, but the characters are not. It's almost like playing one of those old CD drive games in which the people look like cut-outs pasted onto a background. This is actually a fatal flaw, as it throws off jumping in an odd way. It makes you unsure of what is in the background, or what you can jump on. I really can't describe it, but if you play it, you should see what I mean.
I really hate to say it, but this game's lack of creativity and excess of imagination bring this game down from the heights it could have achieved. It's almost like they were so focused on the imaginative idea of the game that they forgot to flesh it out into something workable. Plenty of people like the game, and I can see why, however I just couldn't bring myself to do the same.
Thanks for reading and have an awesome day!

WHAT A SHAME...(ᵃˢ ᵗʰᵉ ᴰᵉᵘˢ ᴱˣ ¹ ᶠᵃⁿᵇᵒʸˢ ʷᵒᵘˡᵈ ᵖᵘᵗ ᶦᵗ)
BUT:
I personally really enjoyed this game - There are so many more options to rate a game on than just its ending.
Take for example:
I understand why some people complain about the sometimes spongy movement, but for me it is still fine, since you are either running or mostly moving from one cover to another.
Talking about that, i think the developers did a good job at the cover system: the new ability to "crouch-run" from one cover to another can often prevent you from getting caught if you want to move a little bit faster but still go for stealth (and don't have the glass shield cloaking aug yet).
You are also now able to mantle up edges, which improves moving around a lot, and made it possible to design the levels more vertically.
The other augs (at least the ones i have used) are great as well:
(ᵂᴬᵀᶜᴴ ᴼᵁᵀ, ᴳᵁʸˢ, ˢᴾᴼᴵᴸᴱᴿˢ ᴬᴴᴱᴬᴰ!)
You still have all the loved ones from Human Revolution and that's good, since you obviously are still playing Adam and you don't have to adapt a lot.
However, the developers have also added some new augs, like the ability to mark NPCs and track their movement, or the Typhoon, which allows Adam to shoot a 360-degree burst of projectiles.
As I have mentioned before, you obviously still have the stun gun (which I believe has changed mostly compared to the other guns, but honestly, I liked the design from HR more; it felt a little more compact and stealthy) and the tranquilizer, but also most other weapons from Human Revolution, only with adjusted looks and different names/brands.
They are incredibly detailed and a pleasure to look at.
On the other hand the weapon feeling has been changed a lot by increasing the camera shake and some additional effects. To me it is a little bit too much, but that's probably just a matter of taste.
There also has been a big change of the upgrade system: weapons now often can have different firing patterns and ammunition types, but also more attachments like different sights/scopes and a silencer.
By collecting and using crafting parts, which can be found literally anywhere, you can upgrade a weapon's properties like damage, accuracy and fire rate, but also build certain items, like biocells and mine templates
.
I really love the game's level design.
As its predecessor, Mankind Divided's environment is beautifully designed. Prague sometimes even gets a little Half Life 2- vibe due to the great mixture between traditional and modern buildings and elements and some autumnal trees.
And just like Human Revolution, the new Deus Ex really achieves it to draw you to hidden paths making you explore the environment and maybe even come up with some new ideas on how to solve your problems (ᵒᵏ, ᴵ ᶜᵃⁿ ⁿᵒᵗ ᵍᵘᵃʳᵃⁿᵗᵉᵉ ʰᵉʳᵉ ᵗʰᵉʸ ʷᶦˡˡ ˢᵒˡᵛᵉ ʸᵒᵘʳ ᵖᵉʳˢᵒⁿᵃˡ ᵖʳᵒᵇˡᵉᵐˢ, ᵇᵘᵗ HEY, ᵃᵗ ˡᵉᵃˢᵗ ᵗʰᵉ ᵒⁿᵉˢ ʸᵒᵘ ᵈᵉᵃˡ ʷᶦᵗʰ ᶦⁿ ᵗʰᵉ ᵍᵃᵐᵉ...).
In addition to Prague you will also visit some other locations, which look very good as well.
To me, golem city looked the best due to the incredible amount of detail the developers put in.
Like Hengsha in Human Revolution, this part is probably the most cyberpunk looking area in the game.
Of course, the developers haven't missed out the iconical air vents from Human Revolution;
inside them you can now move faster, and also more verticality has been added to them providing a better switch between different floors.
The Graphics look really nice on ultra, but probably require a modern computer to enjoy them smoothly. Turning down the quality to lowest obviously makes the game run better, but affects the atmosphere quite a lot, since all the fancy effects making Cyberpunk visually intresting, like bloom, screenspace reflections, volumetric lighting, ambient occlusion and tesselation are now turned off.
I personally own a AMD Radeon RX470, on which the game runs acceptable (about 50-80 fps on medium).

While Batman Arkham Asylum lacks many of the gameplay improvements and larger environments that later games in the series introduced, its linear design and single story thread offer something that later games in the series lost over time: focus. Arkham Asylum is a dense and highly detailed setting that is ripe for exploration. Tucked away everywhere are mysterious hidden rooms and passages which contain references to the Dark Knight's history and offer the player alluring tales about the dark secrets hidden within the asylum.
The game's general art and character designs are also more true to the comic books' outlandish and extravagant art than previous games in the series are, as they opted for more gritty and realistic designs. This gives the game an exciting and somewhat fantastical tone that highly effective in making you want to progress through the plot, which itself is a highly well written and performed tale, that will hold your attention throughout the duration of the game.
Neither the freeflow combat nor the predator encounter systems are as tight or varied as they are in later titles, but that isn't to say they're dull. They are both still rock solid in their handling and execution, and form the backbone to what I believe are, to this day, the game's strongest gameplay feature: its boss battles. In comparison to other games in the series, Arkham Asylum's boss battles are grand and have a sense of immense scale. Many of the bosses themselves are presented as gigantic titans which need to be brought down in some amazing manner, thus making the task of doing so a tense and highly rewarding experience. Other games, with maybe the exception of Arkham City, largely abandoned this style of boss fight making Arkham Asylum's maybe the best in the series.
So while Arkham Asylum may not feature all the great gameplay advances achieved in later games, the manner in which it progresses in such a highly focused way, in terms of both its world and story, insures that players will have a superb gaming experience.

Hello lads and gents. Welcome to my review of NFS: Undercover. Please note that I'm going to talk about the game's cons first, because, the game has more pros over cons in my opinion.
We play as an undercover police officer of TCBPD, allied by Chase Linh (Who is actually a corrupt police officer) and Liutenant Jack M.Keller. The game starts with player driving a custom 370Z while TCBPD is on his tail. After the prologue, we start with a stock blue 240SX, which is...um.. fine for a starter car I guess. As we win more races the street racer gangsters starts to get to know us. And to prove them that we are not a cop, we outrun and challenge against cops (our colleagues lol) as well. As we win more races, we go deeper and deeper into the characters that'll be friends with us (or enemies?)
Please note that this is the fifth game that contains heavy story plot and characters. We even have a love interest (still not sure but..) which is Carmen Mendez. You'll notice it :D Now lets get over the spoilers and talk about the game itself.
Firstly, lets talk about the cons.
Cons'n cons. Damn you Black Box, damn you EA. You just wasted your own game..
Firstly, the ''heroic driving engine'' ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t is not fine for a such beautiful game like this. Physics are terrible, cars feel extremely heavy or extremely light and this is actually amazingly disturbing the player. I mean, isn't there a middle point between it? Well. In UC, there's not.
Second  one is the graphics. I'm not talking about the ''graphics for that date'' thing. It is decent for a 2008 racing game but. Even in a powerful computer the game just keeps laggin' and laggin. Stutters, graphical bugs are flying all over the place! This is extremely annoying. Also the game's ''yellowish'' environment and effects are overwhelming. So, if you're ever gonna buy and play it, I highly recommend to play with ENB series that has settings that makes the game darker and more ''bluish.''
Now lets move on to the pros.
The cars. Man. This game has some extremely great additions to the series. Especially Veyron 16.4, BMW M6, R8, GT-R, McLaren F1 and many many more.. man, I just can't count! Imagine you're an undercover police officer and free to grab one of these. Amazing. The car list is almost double of Most Wanted!
Secondly, the story, plot and characters are really good. Missions, storyline, races, highway battles... just doubling the fun to play. I'm not gonna lie, I can harm my several hours into it. Also, Tri-City Bay looks really good. Not good as Rockport imo, but still great to drive in, especially the highways where you can fly over 350 km/h!
And, the soundtrack. Man, this NFS had the best OST that NFS series games ever had. Drum and Bass and Electronic Rock genres took over and they did a hell of a good job. The Qemists, Airbourne, The Prodigy and of course.. the fathers of dnb, Pendulum! I met Pendulum in 2008, in this game by the track ''Granite'' and its still my favourite. Seriously, grab your steering wheel and enjoy driving your monstrous car while Pendulum plays in the background! This is what I call fun! The pursuit music and chatters are also very successful. Now cops do chat to each other unlike just reporting us like in MW. It's very fun to listen to them, some of their lines are pretty funny XD, they also refer to Ryan Cooper :> they thought about anything!!
So thank you all for listening and reading this long review. It's my first long♥♥♥♥♥♥review, so I hope that helps! A classic. Get it while you can, sometimes on a discount! But as I said before, I highly recommend playing it with ENB. By the way, if you bought the game, add me and if possible we can play together (I dunno if the servers work already so dont blame me pls)
Final : 8.5/10

Unhack is an indie puzzle game with a story that is delivered in visual novel style. For a rather decent price, you'll get a hour or two of very nice story, well made backround music with anime styled sprites dubbed by english voice actors.
I will try to avoid all spoilers in these few words I'd like to share about my impressions.
First of all, for such a short game, the story is very nice. It has everything from a nice start to a well done climax. The characters are nice. To my suprise even the english dub is nice as the voice actresses are doing much more than just reading a script (although if I hear "Yawnies" again I'll probably go crazy...) I can't find praise for the humour in the game. I really enjoyed it, with all the crappy puns to various other surprises which are very pleasant compared to other indie VN games.
The main character uses a lot of emoticons in the conversations making them lively and with the humorous replies it makes the main character unique and memorable. Most of them are rather complex so understand the meaning, but there is no shame to look it up, or simply turn them off in the options, which in my opinion shaves a lot of uniqueness from the main character.
I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who wants to relax while enjoying a short story with a simple puzzle gameplay and backround music which fits nicely the setting.
As for gameplay, it is very simple. You simply move with WSAD (heresy to call it ASWD!!! *shakes fist* >:D). You progress the story by clicking on "next" or by simply pressing enter. You can skip some parts with F which is really handy in the higher difficulties.
The game offers 3 difficulties. I did play it on the "brutal difficulty designed specially to torture prisoners and for masochists :D" and it was quite enjoyable although there aren't any achievements to unlock.
What I didn't really like is the lack of windowed mode, lack of resolution settings. The steam overlay is a mess, with popups being cut apart and I had trouble making screenshots, which is kinda sad, because I like to take souvenirs.
Summing it up:
Pros: Nice story
Good price
Good BGM
Nice, simple and relaxing gameplay
Trading cards
FUUUUUSION HA!
Several golden puns and character interactions
Decent voice acting (Xanthe's voice reminds me of Estelle from Tales of Vesperia. Good stuff).
Cons:
Probably too easy for hardcore puzzle gamers even on the hardest dificulty.
Short
Lack of achievements
Fullscreen and 1 resolution
Incompatible with steam overlay + had trouble with screenshots
False promise of Weedy showing using The Mod
(personal) Yawnies
Ps. The character gave birth to the MANly style of speech. Which was hellowa confusing to a non native speaker like me (I know... Sucks to be me, man...). But yeah. MANly... :D

Boring and generally a bad design, but it gets points for trying. There are so few real (non-RTS) based strategy games, you could give this one a try. The game is complex and deep, but, by far, the biggest challenge is overcoming the game design. DO NOT PLAY FOR HISTORICAL ACCURANCY. The names, dates, and locations are accurate, but the game play isnt. Ai runs single units around like mice, 30 day turns are used to help AI seem smarter, senarios are made with pre-planned outcomes (no what-ifs). Some of the senerios play out as if it has scripted AI. If the senario wants the AI to get to a town, your army will stop moving. In my current game my army is plotted with a 28 day move up only moves one zone per turn just so the AI can get ahead. IF my army is limited in some way the game should not display my total move as 28 days.
I would have returned this game, but I am over the time limit. I recommend people to play for 30 miuntes and if you have ANY doubts, return it without a second thought
Edit #2: Most importantly, the game is unrealistic and feels broken because of the one month turns. You can have an enemy army on the other side of a river and you decide "I will attack". It might take 2 days to cross the river. Once you end turn you will waste 30 days to start the battle. If the enemy retreats one zone, you are 30 days behind. The Ai will detatch units and run them around your flanks and run across a dozen zone before you can even engage one of their units. No general in history stuck to a one month plan no matter what. This alone makes the game unhistoric. In one of my turns I was determined to use all of my 30 days of my turn and I ran my army around in a circle. This was one of my single greatest turns because I caught so many 1 and 2 unit armies that the AI made.
It is unbeliveable to think that Caeser would say -"Ok troops we are going to march North for 30 days." Sergent says -"North Sir? The scouts say the enemy might be on our west flank." Caeser replies - "Well we will march for 30 days and see what happens after that." THIS WHOLE GAME IS BUILT AROUND SEEING WHAT HAPPENS AFTER 30 DAYS HAVE PAST.
The game does not make it clear what is important and what isnt. And things that are important are not emphasized. The UI is a pain and is not clear. I just count that the UI has about 56 differnent elements and all of them look like boxes or buttons, execpt two. WHY JUST THOSE TWO?  Its like they got toward the end of the design then saw the UI looked ugly without art work, but simultaneously realized they needed two more buttons. My 1st ever Ageod game. I remeber buying the DVD version of it (those were the days!) playing thru the tutorial, a big WTF and then I didnt touch it for 3 years. Then I got somehow back into it, checked the amazing Ageod forums and became a lifelong addict to anything Ageod ever released. This is the best company for lovers of history ever. You will feel the pressure that  generals back then felt. Dont be discourged by the apparently steep learning curve, check the forums (the BEST gaming community out there) and the youtube videos. Theres an excellent tutorial AAR by Narwahl and Loki that teaches everything as well as an incredibly detailed Chalres Cummings youtube series out there. Once you learn one game, youre pretty much ready to tackle any of these company's games. AJE has a somehow simplified supply/OOB structutre that makes it the ideal Ageod to start with. Totally immersive, extremely detailed, this is for real hardcore armchair generals ony. But once you get into Ageod, you will barely find the time to play anything else!

This is one of the more polished of Ageod games and my recommendation for newcomers to this game engine and it's plethora of historical strategy based programs.
Alea Jacta Est.  The Die is Cast. It is challenging with a diabolical AI, that may seem like it cheats, but there is always something to factor in all the complexities. For instance, each leader has their bonuses during certain circumstances which when in play goes unoticed until closer inspection. The gameplay will have you using your judgement often times the main dependent upon victory or defeat relies on attrition and supply points. Outsmarting the AI is based heavily on not only predicting their next move but taking the chance to act upon what you have worked up to and making sure everything is aligned perfectly, even then the elements such as weather and drought can afflict as much damage as the enemy.
I admire the art work of individual units, and there is enough here to fill an encyclopedia with knowledge of the lands and historical accuracy, although there is no ingame database per se. This among all the other  games in its genre captures the mystique best of the era by not divulging the eccentricities of the ancient world, but by displaying the bareboned technologies and warlike culture and not meandering far from that, all held together by the natural episodic musical pieces. There is a Play By Email Multiplayer utility that seems rather ancient, I feel this could be streamlined better, and in some of Ageod's newer games I hear it is.
Once you get the hang of it , it gets very fun. One of the most detailed History Games.

Verdict: This is one of the best strategy games in which you're commanding armies of antiquity.
Pros:
1. Units are quite detailed and seem to be about as effective as their historical counterparts.
2. There is some logistics which prevents you from ahistorical winter fighting - it is really hard to get supplies most of the time, although is possible and might catch your opponent with his pants down.
3. Quite a few nations and different time settings which means a lot of diversity.
4. Many historical characters to command your armies or to fight against.
5. Different events to explore what-ifs, forge alliances or declare wars.
6. Map is actually quite nice and cities are different for each period.
Cons:
1. You're not able to command you men in the field.
2. Graphics are somewhat dated, as is the game's engine in my opinion.
Overall - I do recommend it if you're a history buff, who enjoys a good strategy game.

For the kind of jerk who can't stop playing Clicker Heroes comes a re-skinned clicker/idle game sharing exactly the same mechanics and presentation, but in a 3D FPS universe. If your fetish revolves around sodomizing your mouse, Time Clickers was made for you.
The things that Time Clickers adds or changes from Clicker Heroes are:
+ Since enemies are created from voxels, you can aim and click on specific parts of the enemy. These parts vary in their resistence to your attacks.
+ You receive currency per-block destroyed, so even if you don't kill the boss, you earned money from it.
+ Fewer "heroes" (instead, you level up your team much further).

I don't write a whole lot of reviews, but I felt this game absolutely deserved one more Steam recommendation.
Always Sometimes Monsters is a fine example of an indie game made with heart but moreover an exempliary case of a story rich, content driven game. (Not that the graphics were bad for the retro sort of style. And the music was really good too!) Despite the risk of sounding tacky I'd describe ASM as a deep dive into the wide spectrum of humanity and life. It was funny, sad, clever, delightfully philosophic, beautiful, simple in a complex way - and genuinely thought-provoking at times.
Regardless of the medium, I do enjoy stories and anecdotes that make the gamer/viewer/user reflect some element of their own life, perhaps questioning it or, on the other hand, feeling reassurance over it. Or maybe just cause that, either warm or melancholic, "Yeah, I can relate" feeling.
The freedom of choice contributed to a great atmosphere throughout and I found myself quickly immersed each time I played. Also, unlike in other multiple-choice-type games I decided not to reload and replay each fork on the road and opted to just flow with it instead. It felt right not to see what might've been and instead just experience it uniquely as it happened - kinda like going through life itself.
As someone who dabbles with writing stories as their dear hobby, I must say: hats off to the developers for their vision and unique approach! Video game experiences like this are few and far between! I consider Always Sometimes Monsters a good story, good game, and definately an experience worth recommending!

This is very close to being a game I could get obsessed with. The core gameplay is extremely fun--a really nice mix of action and strategy. It's just not ready to be released, yet. It's just too buggy and the controls are way too sloppy and inconsistent. A few examples. . .
--Bugs--
*The game crashes roughly once every three levels, usually while reloading from checkpoints. Expect to have your progress reset constantly, often during the final fight of a level.
*The thing that prompted me to write this review was a moment where the game put me in a lose state, teleported me through a wall, and immediately checkpointed me. I just had to quit the game, losing all progress. This isn't the first time I've been checkpointed just after being put in a lose state by this game, but it was definitely the most frustrating, right at the end of a long level.
*I've played under three hours and had the game crash on me around four times, and checkpoint me in unwinnable states twice. That's not counting the fact that the game simply does not run on one of my computers.
--Bad Controls--
*The entire game is about avoiding the gunfire from half a dozen guards as you jump around killing them, but the line that tells you where you're going to jump to lies. Things like colliding with an enemy will leave you in a completely unexpected location, almost always getting you killed. Expect a long and frustrating learning period as you learn
*Hitboxes in general are a mystery, which is a bad thing in a game all about precise movement. It's extremely hard to predict where you'll be standing after you kill an enemy, or how tall you'll be standing after a jump, and getting this even a little wrong is instant death. There are fun challenges and frustrating challenges, and trying to guess which if you're going to take a step into a bullet's trajectory or not in order to stab a guard is a frustrating challenge.
*The only way to move in a fight is jumping. This is almost okay, but there are a bunch of moments where jumping simply doesn't work. It's easy to end up in a situation where you need to get up on a ledge, and out of combat you'd be able to just climb up the side effortlessly, but because you're in a fight you have to spend multiple turns hopping around and spamming grappling hooks in the hopes that your momentum will deposit you awkwardly on the lip of the platform you're trying to get on instead of drifting you into a bullet or back where you started from.
*Movement just feels very rough and non-generous in general. Expect a lot of the game to be taken up by guards getting knocked out of your kill range because you jumped at them wrong or just little fiddly things going wrong.
*Stealth is baffling. I still don't understand when guards/civilians can/can't see me, which isn't a good thing since a civilian seeing you is an instant lose condition.
This is so close to being one of my favorite games of the last few months, but all of the good stuff about it just makes all the bad stuff that much more frustrating. If even half of the stuff I posted about here gets addressed I'll change my review to an enthusiastic thumbs up, but if that doesn't happen I can't recommend this game to anyone.

HINT: This is not gunpoint.
No hint from the game dev, it definitely is not.
While it's kinda fun, RONIN lacks a story of any kind really, mangles together a very strange mix of free roaming throughout the stage and turn-based combat the moment your spotted, and tends to throw a ton of enemies at you who can all one shot you, but you have to get within stabbing distance or use one of your skills (which require skill points that you earn) in order to kill them.  Oh, and there are special enemy types, including some regular grunts that will do nothing but call in the lockdown command, a giant samurai who if you land anywhere near him or jump over his personal space in mid-combat, he will, without even using a turn, kill you instantly, and a swat looking grunt that uses a machine gun.
I cannot count the number of times where I have had to desparately bounce around a room because every time I land, my enemies line up another shot on me, and if I dont move out of the line of fire, i'm dead.  However, since I can't get behind cover very often (it's pretty rare) and kill someone without taking fire, I have to just keep bouncing around and either come up with some elaborate plan ahead of time, or hope I get lucky and just get a small openning with which to pick off ONE of probably 6+ enemies.  Also, since combat is turn based, I can't just turn that off temporarily, run somewhere very quickly while they continue to line up a shot (as they would do on their next turn anyway), and then turn the turn based back on.  This has multiple times lead to me being trapped by fire on multiple sides and having to sit there, and forfeit turns, just so I don't die.  Oh, and the skills I mentioned?  Very lacking in variety.  You actually have to spend skill points on empty spots to get to the final skill point of each "tree" (calling it a twig would be more appropriate.  most all of the twigs only have 2 to 3 skills at most, and there are only 5 separate twigs I believe)
Personally, I really enjoyed gunpoint.  it had a story to it that could be both funny and serious, and the gameplay was fun (even if it was admittedly too easy), but RONIN lacks well thoughtout level design and enemy placement, and intsead tends to shoehorn you into one or just two methods of approach.  Pretty much the exact opposite of gunpoint.  I would not recommend this game.

Full review:
Dead Man's Draw is a fantastic card game. Although a lot of it may be luck-based, the AI never appears to have an advantage and, for the most part, the AI plays fair.
The game is really easy to learn. I picked it up in the very first match I played, probably because the concept is simple: Draw cards to fill up the various suites in your hand, but draw too many, and risk losing the currently drawn cards. For example, if I draw three cards from the deck: a sword, an anchor, and a cannon, and then draw another card of the same type (like another cannon), then I lose those three cards and cannot add them to my hand. The goal is to have the highest number of each suite in your hand, combining to form the highest overall score.
Each card ranges from values 2-7. Whatever value is the highest that you currently have in hand will be the one added to your score. You can have others of the same suite, but they wont be counted towards your total score. The optimal hand would consist of a 7 from each suite: anchor, hook, crystal ball (?), cutlass, treasure chest, key, cannon, barnacle, mermaid, and scroll. At the end of the game, the player with the highest score wins.
The gameplay seems simple, yes, but it gets progressively gets increasingly complex the more you play it. Eventually, each suite will have its own ability. The cannon, for example, when drawn from the deck, allows you to discard one of your opponent's cards. If you're smart, you'll usually go for whichever card has the highest value in its suite. Later on, an ability is also added to the cutlass, allowing you to, upon draw, steal the top suite from your opponent for a suite that you currently do not have. Each card will eventually have their own abilities, all of which are very fun to use.
Once you've unlocked all of the card's abilities, you'll get into character traits, which allow you, and you specifically, to make use of a special trait. The first one you'll unlock makes it so the cannon removes an entire suite of cards, instead of the highest number of that suite, from your opponent. This prevents them from having a backup to replace that suite once the higher number is removed.
The AI in the game also puts up a fair fight. They don't seem "too" lucky, but they do know their math, and will make a lot of good decisions. Regardless, I still found the game surprisingly easy, even in the later levels. I only ever lost a couple of times, and those few losses were very close matches too.
Overall, Dead Man's Draw is a must-buy. It is incredibly fun. Although it may appear boring, or simple, it can certainly provide a one-of-a-kind experience.

It's a simple premise of "press your luck" combined with just enough strategy to keep things interesting. Basically, you draw cards for as long as you dare, trying not to "bust out" by drawing two cards of the same suit. Each suit has unique powers that allow you to affect the field. You might steal a card from your opponent, get a card from the discard pile, or get to replay a card you already drew. Equipped traits allow you to further customize your strategy, and there are  number of different gameplay tweaks in the different tournaments. For example, you might need to win while staying under a certain point total. Downsides are a lackluster presentation, lack of game modes, and a probably too high price tag. Still, it's a pretty addicting game that is fun enough to be worth your time.

Dead Man's Draw is hard to explain. It's a card game with pirates, and it's a very casual one. Anyone can play it and anyone will understand it, unlike Magic The Gathering. Just believe me when I say that it's a very fun game and one that I'm still enjoying.
You'll be playing tournaments against other pirates, which start off rather easy, but increase in difficulty after just a few of them. And that's not because the game is becoming harder - it plays out the same way in every tournament you participate in - but the rules do change. Where initially your goal is to get the higest score, there'll be tournaments where you have to get a score of 60 or lower or certain drawn cards will be added to your opponent's score. This keeps things fresh and challenging.
You get XP for every opponent you beat and every tournament you complete. Leveling up allows you to unlock perks and portraits. Perks can be used to make your life a little easier. For example, there's a card that allows you to see the next card on the stack and 'activating' a certain perk might allow you to see 2 more after that. There are many more to be unlocked, but it will require quite a few battles. The limit seems to be level 34, by the way.
I'm not sure how many tournaments there are just yet, but there seems to be tens of them. I think I'm about 10-15% finished now so completing the entire game might take you more than 20 hours if I had to take a guess.
Plenty of content here as you can see. Unfortunately there's not much else to do but to battle opponents and level up. I have the feeling that it's missing something, but I can't quite put my finger on it. Maybe I was hoping to see you get money for tournaments that could then be used to unlock things like portraits (instead of leveling up). It's not even worth mentioning if I look back now, but maybe I'm not the only one.

Mark of the Ninja picked up the spirit of the old Eidos legends - the original Deus Ex, Hitman Trilogy, and Thief Trilogy - then hid it in the shadows of a 2D world while nobody was looking. Yes, Klei made a few references to those within the game, but they also deliver in terms of gameplay.
The gameplay is challenging, open-ended about most rooms of the game, very fluid, and very pleasant over-all. Guard NPCs respond appropriately to most of the absurd situations you will set up for them. Obstacles like traps and lasers will present a challenge for first-time players and yet another way to get things done for more experienced players. Even rats and birds can be of use to a creative ninja. Skillful gameplay, such as stealth and/or pacifism, is rewarded with upgrades which add more possibilities still. Optional objectives and bonus rooms need only be completed once to earn their upgrade point, but they are still acknowledged with the same score bonus if completed on the next play-through. And after you beat the game for the first time, you can enjoy it again in a more challenging mode.
There are just a few spills to this fluid gameplay. Autosaving is automatic and you cannot rewind to a previous save point. Pickpocketing only works with RightMouseButton, but the game gives you bad advice and suggests using the letter E, which always leads to a failed attempt. Using E to open a door before entering focus mode can fail to freeze time, which can mean death. Some of the "upgrades" have their downsides - the upgraded smoke bomb may cost you your stealth bonus, and the upgraded halucinogen dart will cost you your non-lethal bonus - and upgrades cannot be undone. I opted to reset the game after foolishly upgrading my smoke bomb.
A somewhat personal gripe of mine: there are no provisions for completing the game entirely without casualties. Kelly and Karajan both die by the player's sword when their time comes (and get mime'd to death if the player left his sword in his other ninja outfit;) three stalkers bumbled into deathtraps in Tabriz and then blamed me for their own deaths;
adding up to
in what was supposed to be a non-lethal playthrough.
But the many upsides far outweigh the few downsides. I highly enjoyed this game, and strongly recommend it to anyone else who enjoyed the iconic old Eidos masterpieces.

A solid poker game, nice characters, mostly witty dialogue, and features the goddess that is GLaDOS. But the interface is terrible:
- If the resolution is too high and you make the mistake of exiting full screen, you'll be locked into a corner of the screen unable to change it back. Since launch commands don't work with this game, I had to look up the keyboard shortcut for fullscreening a window.
- You can't skip the dialogue, which wouldn't be a problem if it didn't halt the gameplay sometimes.
- No option to change the mouse sensitivity.
- Counter-intuitive menu navigation. After a hand, you have to go through the 'unlockables' tab and then navigate your way back to the main menu from there if you want to exit. There should just be a straight up "main menu" option.
- On a regular basis a character will say "all in" and push all of their chips forward, when what they actually mean is "raise anything [X character / player] has left". The info box below their name will even say "All in" and show all of their money, but will change it a few seconds later. It took a few hands of this occuring for me to figure this out, where a character would go "all in", lose the hand, and yet still somehow be in the game afterward.
I'm very surprised that they'd have the budget to get ahold of Ellen McLain, but the end product would have so many issues. With all these issues, the price should be no higher than £1.99 (I paid £3.99, if it goes down to the former in the future then I'd be happy to reccomend).

This game has a problem. It's too easy. And that's about the only negative thing I can say about it. It's an engaging experience, intellectual challenge, and an all around fun game. I've just completed the main game and am working on PLUS mode currently. I've already gotten the DLC and have all the items and costumes in the game. I'm missing about 5 achievements, but they're pretty easy to get so this game is easily completable, which is good and bad.
This game has just the right amount of pacing. There were few times where I felt like the level was going on forever, however I was never upset by it. The only reason I felt like that was because I was focusing on completion (which required me to backtrack a lot when I missed something) but that's my own personal battle right there, haha.
There is a legitimate concern that bugged me; there are a number of bugs. For instance, I remember jumping off a high building and finding a missing texture. There were a number of times I would die or restart at checkpoint and the game would put me right into a conflict (inescapable btw). This one time I had to run to another checkpoint while the guard was chasing me and respawn just so I could keep my ghost in tact, and after I did so, a door which should have been opened already glitched closed forever. Had to reset the level (UGH). This other time I jumped down a pit and fell straight through the ground into a vent system (which made me miss a scroll). This wasn't so bad because the game's checkpoints are fanominal. Respawning brought me right back to where I jumped from.
If there's one thing I can say though, it's that this game is awesome. It may seem like I'm being negative, but really I'm not. This game is loads of fun and the issues I've experienced are just the result of me screwing around with the game. This is a must play for everyone.

Brawlhalla is a free-to-play fighting game for Steam, Mac, and Playstation 4. Players fight it out in matches where you need to knock off your opponent in arena battles. This can be done by applying damage on your opponents, indicated by the color display around the opponent’s character icon. Damage registers where the indicator changes color from white to red. The closer the damage indicator color is to red, the further your opponents will be knocked back. Matches end when the time runs out. The winner is decided by the opponent who has the most points left.Each legend (Brawlhalla’s name for its characters) has three attack patterns: unarmed, melee, and ranged attacks. Legends start off in-game with unarmed weak and strong attacks and then you switch them up by getting weapons as the stage drops them. Stages even drop a few other weapons like bombs, mines, and a horn that pushes opponents out of the way. Mostly stages drop off weapons instead of items, so you have to rely on your character’s weapons and your skills to win matches.
Currently the game has a total of 34 legends (and counting) that you can choose from. Each legend has four set of stats (Strength, Dexterity, Defense, and Speed) that determine what type of fighter the legend is. However, as you continually use the legends and level them up, you’ll unlock not only other color palettes but also variations of the legend with a different set of stats to add gameplay variety.If you’re playing the game for free, the game cycles its free legends weekly, just like in other F2P style games like League of Legends. This at least gives you enough time to test out heroes before deciding to buy the game to unlock everything.Since the game is free-to-play, you can also purchase other things aesthetic wise by spending real money to purchase “mammoth coins” that open up more visual add-ons for the game.
Even with the addition of Mammoth Coins to the game, you don’t necessarily have to spend money on the game to keep on playing or enjoying it. Of course, if you’re impatient, then you can just unlock all the heroes and the upcoming ones.
Another good thing with Brawlhalla is that the game has a brawl type of game mode where the game presents a random game type per week just like brawl in Hearthstone. It’s fun and a good reason for players to keep on coming back to the game.

I was born and raised on Unreal Tournament. I played probably thousands of hours between the 2003 - 2004, Unreal 3 and the console version. For me, there's never really been a game that quite captured that twitch / skill feel of those days. Titanfall has come pretty close, but was missing that up close and personal battling where the person with the best use of aiming and twitch skills won out. The Unreal series ranks as one of my all time favorite games and definitely my all time favorite shooters.
It might be a little premature, but I'd rank this in my top 5 favorite shooters, ever. I wish Cliff and crew had had a bigger budget to really take the Unreal name and give it that triple AAA feel. Who knows though, maybe it wouldn't be what it is had that happened. As it stands the new "community driven" unreal is stale and stagnant, been in alpha for years and likely will never emerge when people don't get paid to push forward.
Keep in mind, this game takes skill. Perusing forums and reviews I keep seeing comparisons to Overwatch, which I never even thought of, but this is nowhere near anything to do with Overwatch besides maybe being class / character based. The characters are really just gun templates: rocket launcher, energy guns, machine / repeating gun and melee / speed. The characters themselves are serviceable, and somewhat cool, but nothing earth shattering. It all boils down to your skill with the mouse, your timing of shots, your movement, and utilizing your abilities in fights. You'll die, over and over, but not because of a special character, like Bastion sitting in a corner and one shotting you because your pig guy isn't fast enough. You died because of your own choice and skill, or because you flew into a heavily contested point to stop the timer.
You'll probably get frustrated the first 10 games or so as you get used to the mechanics and controls and the game modes. I know I did. The first game I was like "F THIS", but I stuck with it as I do with most games I buy to give it a chance and it brought back that old Unreal feel with modern day mechanics. If you stick with it, and you have a sliver of skill with the mouse, there's currently no game that compares to stealing an objective and darting back to your base with a sliver of health, taking fire from all directions and scoring a point. Slowly plodding to an objective while slow cartoon characters shoot cartoon bullets at you, this isn't. Not to say that that type of game is bad, it's a completely different experience.
Some people have also whined that this should have been "F2P" and hoping it to fail for some unfathomable reason. It's sad what gamers have become in that aspect, almost matching the crybaby / snowflake mentality of the state of the millennial generation now. Personally F2P games to me are pay to win, unpolished garbage. You get nickel and dimed with skins and upgraded weapons and unlocked tiers, it's BS. The only F2P game I've ever stuck around long enough for was Paragon, which even that could have benefited from a proper development with a package price tag. This game is priced at 30 bucks, and if you can't afford that then there are plenty of F2P games where you don't need to spend a dime.
Overall this is one of my favorite games of the year, something that on the surface seems similar, but just is a new fresh feel and take on a stale genre of WW2 military shooters. If you've played intense shooters like Unreal, and even Battlefield where it takes skill to play, you will love this. If you're an overwatch or Counterstrike (slower type shooters) guy this probably won't be your bag. I'd say even if you don't think it is your bag to give it a try, you'd be surprised.
