Always Sometimes Monsters provides a very realistic and rivetting story in which the player is forced to make difficult descisions based on their own morality. As I played through I found myself making choices that I personally believed to be less than admirable, but when faced with awful alternatives it seems as if there is no right or wrong choice. Always Sometimes Monsters does not necessarily set out to make a statement, but under the gritty reality that you are faced to face in this game there are definitely lessons to be learned.

Always Sometimes Monsters is an intriguing game where your decisions impact the narrative. While not an entirely new concept, this game manages to keep things interesting most of the time.
The gameplay in Always Sometimes Monsters is primarily about making choices. In the beginning of the game, you choose your character by deciding who to toast with at a party, and then choose your love interest by going to the balcony and talking with one of the many characters. It makes character selection more interesting than just picking from a menu. Also, you are able to choose from a diverse group of male/female characters and can choose to be either heterosexual or homosexual.
There is an in-game clock of sorts that breaks the day up into 3 parts - morning, afternoon, and night. You can do one job/event per time of day, and some tasks require a certain time of day. After completing the task, that part of the day is automatically over. This is where making choices comes into play. You have to decide what you are going to do for each segment of the day, and the choices you make during those jobs and events affect the way the story unfolds. You have 30 in-game days to reach a particular destination (I won't spoil what that is, since it is a major part of the story).
There are some mini-games as well, but to be honest, they were not too interesting to me. I tried each one once or twice, but I did not have the desire to revisit them. Lastly, there are optional figures to collect that feature characters from various indie games, though I'm not sure if they serve a purpose other than to be collected for fun (they can be sold to the pawn shop for a little extra money, but I preferred to keep them in my collection).
I won't spoil anything, but the actual game starts one year after the party I mentioned previously where you select your character. You are basically trying to get your life back on track. There are several main areas in the game, and each has its own story and set of quests you will need to do in order to make it to the next area. This is unfortunately where the game is hit-or-miss, since it is a story-driven game. Some characters and events are intriguing, while others just simply are not (at least in my opinion). However, keep in mind that I only played through the game once, so my choices may not have led to all of the most interesting events.
Dialogue is good about 70% of the time, but the rest of it is not quite at the same level of quality. It feels like certain parts are trying to be very mature, but they don't always quite hit the mark. It's not terrible by any means, but just something I wanted to point out. There are also some spelling and grammar mistakes that I encountered on more than a few occasions. It's not a deal-breaker, but those kinds of mistakes sometimes took me out of the moment. I understand that this is an indie game and it's not easy to find every little mistake during the development process, though.
The songs are pretty cool for the most part - simple yet catchy electronic music. Be aware that there are some songs that got annoying after a while, but only if I was in a particular area for an extended period of time. If you really love that type of music, you may not find it to be too annoying. I just felt like there was a lack of variety. The sound effects were fine and I have no complaints about them.
Despite its flaws, I do recommend this game. It was made using RPG Maker, and as someone who has used those tools before, I must say that it is impressive what these developers were able to do with it. If you enjoy story-driven games where your choices matter, then Always Sometimes Monsters is worth your time.

You love Grand Strategy Games?
You love historical Settings?
You are willing to read a manual?
You love a challenge?
You are not afraid of your wife?
You know how to handle the "Just one more turn" syndrom?
Graphics and visual presentation is not more important for you than gameplay?
If you can answer all these question with "Yes, Sir, Yes!", you should really consider to buy one of the AGEOD Grand Strategy Games. (The one with the historical setting you are interested in!)
To be honest, I avoided AGEOD games in the past, because I was always too lazy to read another manual besides the one from GG´s War in the East and the long turn processing times from Pride of Nations...
... now I know this was a huge mistake.
The depth of these games (I am talking about all AGEOD Games, not only this one) is awesome, and the rules and mechanics running in the background are incredible deep, so complex that you have to read the manual if you want to master the game.
Moving around your units is easy. To know why your units are out of supply, exhausted, lost half of their manpower is a step to master these games.
In my play time in Alea Jacta Est, I played only 1 Scenario, "The Civil War between Ceasar and Pompeius" and I have to admit, at first it was frustrating, because I played the tutorial first, but reading the manual changed everything and the game became a blast.
Sure, the older AGE games are missing the ability to set up battle tactics (like The Thirty Years War) but I am simply in love with the historical setting and so far, this is the BEST Grand Strategy Game I was able to play for this setting.
What do you get?
Turn based battles? No!
You can´t directly influence the battles, they are automaticly resolved.
The task and challenge is
to pick the right time,
the right place,
the right composition of troops
the right commander in charge
and the right enemy to attack
Some more R´s can be added, but I guess I will cover them later.
Micromanagement?
Compared with games, like Hearts of Iron, or War in the East/West, the micromanagement level is low.
The only real micromanagement I encountered so far, is keeping your supply chain in shape, this requires to move several supply wagons every turn, at least if you really want to be as efficent as possible with your troops.
Building troops, Diplomacy, building province improvements are simple and easy.
Alternate History?
Compared to Paradox Grand Strategy Games = No!
Is this bad = No!
First of all, you can win the Civil War as Pompeius, but many decisions and diplomatic options are only available if you reach a specific turn, not all, but many.
But, it´s still up to you to decide if you use the diplomatic option or how you decide.
Empire building?
No, the games are ALL about WAR Scenarios, not about building an Empire or a Dynasty.

I picked this up on deep discount after hearing Austin Walker talk it up quite a bit recently. This is shocking to me; not only because he likes it (which, still) but because he was also SO bullish about Invisible, Inc.
If Invisible, Inc. is a masterclass in how to make a turn-based stealth combat game really WORK and provide the player with all the information they need to make informed choices (and it is!), this can be considered its antithesis. When in-combat tooltips mention that the projected jump arc -- your ONLY form of in-combat movement, and the only means by which you can avoid instant death to a single bullet -- is "a lie" then you know you're in for a rotten time. The number of deaths to randomly falling short of a projected landing point, stopping dead because you hit someone to knock them out (which usually lets you keep going???) or unexpectedly crossing over an enemy's line of fire are many and infuriating!
The poor signposting and bad readability don't stop there, sadly. Your special abilities, gated by consuming Limit points, are usually OFF-limits, as you'll automatically burn your entire stock upon filling up, getting a free turn that's usually much less useful than a ranged instant kill, but too bad! It's never quite clear how near you need to be to kill enemies -- which is a problem when that is what the gameplay entirely consists of -- you're sometimes able to snatch flying enemies out of the air and sometimes not, sometimes teleport short distances through floors for a killing blow, sometimes not... and the ever-present problem of not knowing where you will be standing when you are DONE killing an enemy often as not leads to your heroine helpfully standing in the line of fire of a shot that would have missed, had you only known.
There are a lot of other problems with polish, like the "humorous" tooltips that "humorously" mention they can't be disabled -- good one dude, glad you prioritized this over working jump arcs -- or the incredibly bad movement both in AND out of combat, the entirely nonfunctional "stealth" elements... just don't get this. Play Mark of the Ninja again, it's still a great game.

The amount of negative reviews surprised me at first, but it's easy to see where they come from. The developer proudly proclaims that Ronin is a ripoff of Gunpoint, which makes people think two incorrect things about this game: a. it's a ripoff of Gunpoint, and b. it's based around stealth. The big thing that proves these assumptions wrong is that in Gunpoint you get bonuses for killing nobody where in Ronin you get bonuses for killing everybody. Ronin is short but addictive, and it's more unique than it gives itself credit for as a turn-based murder-platformer. Definitely worth grabbing on sale due to its size.

I had really high hopes for this game and I still do, but I cannot recommend it in the state it is in right now.

DISCLAIMER: Recommendation is based on gameplay alone and not the plethora of PC port issues.
Birthdays is a fun game, I really enjoyed the actual gameplay but it's terribly obvious that porting this game to PC was an afterthought. The keyboard controls are clunky and unusual with no options to reassign keybinds within the game. Video options are very limited, currently you can choose your resolution or if you wanna play in windowed/fullscreen. The only way to exit the game is either Alt+F4 or hit X in windowed mode, seems like a ridiculous oversight imo. Game plays fine if you run it with a controller, but personally if I'm gonna play a messy port of a PS4 game, I'll just buy it on the PS4 and skip the fluff.
As for the actual gameplay, it can be really fun unlocking new lifeforms and their evolutions. A lot of the progression comes from shaping the land to suit your target lifeforms which can feel pretty hands-off, but there are lots of items to help you push your world in the right direction that can get you a bit more involved. The game does a great job of making it clear what you need to accomplish for certain lifeforms instead of leaving it up to frustrating guess work. This is definitely a great game for winding down after work or just to casually play for half an hour or a couple of hours.
If you like ecosystem games like Niche or Tyto Ecology you'll likely enjoy this game as well. I found it a bit slow for my personal preferences and would prefer more options for micro management, but I believe this game was aimed at a younger audience so it's understandable that they kept it pretty simple. The game also makes a point of teaching you a little bit about each of the lifeforms you unlock as you go, which I really enjoyed and thought it showed the devs' eagerness to teach you about the world you're building.
Judging from the news from late last week it seems like the publisher has heard the feedback from the community echoing more or less the same points I brought up here and it seems like a fix is on the way, but there's currently no timeline. This means that it could be weeks or it could be months if it even comes at all. If you're on the fence about this game, you might be better off waiting until it either goes on sale or gets these fixes to polish it off.
TL;DR: Fun game, especially if this is a genre you enjoy but the PC port is riddled with flaws that scream "This game wasn't meant for this platform". If you don't mind using a controller this can be a fun game, but personally I'd prefer to buy it on the platform it was intended for instead of settling for a rushed PC port. If you're not sold on the game as is, wait for a sale or for some patches to refine the PC experience a bit more.

After hours and hours of playing this card game I need to say it's really well made. While I'm not a huge fan of pirate theme, it's still something I really enjoy playing and I don't think I'll ever get bored of it. For first I'll point out pros of this, because I need to point out few of them:
A) Combination of really easy to learn mechanics combined with amount of strategies you may pull off with cards you have on your hand + traits. Traits is what make this so fun to play and yet allow you to be creative with your plays. Technically after tutorial you learn everything you need, while with each in-game tournament you learn new card combos and gain traits to use.
B) The amount of gameplay which in-game tournaments provide you. Counting all cards when it goes to points ? No problem. You need to reach 50 points first ? Also in. You can't score more than 60 points while beating opponent in points ? In as well. The amount of possible modes to play in is just nice making each tournament pretty much different.
C) Graphics and music are good combination here. For a simple game like this, I would say it fits really well.
D) Still lots of room for improvements and new additions. The amount of cards is good, but not huge enough IMO to add few cards in-game without making it too complicated. There's also a possibility of new traits. In other words - this game has still more potential for improvement.
E) Good AI which actually can not only count well (which is not as obvious in such games) but counter your strategies and eliminate/steal cards which are the main core of your strategy. I'm really happy with this as it makes game challenging.
Although unfortunately I see few problems as well:
A) Lack of multiplayer is outright unacceptable. I would really love to play this game against real players and outright test some traits and card combos against them, especially when this game has the perfect combination of simple mechanics and yet good amount of strategies and combos available to use. Please, do it. It's such a waste otherwise.
B) Price is a bit too high for a card game like this, but I must admit I don't regret spending this money. But still, I would lower the price. Or I won't even bother mentioning this as a con as long as creators will add multiplayer option.
C) While it is luck based (and I don't mind this, it adds additional thrill for example when one lucky pull saves you), but I think game favors AI a bit more than a player. But maybe that's me and I'm a bit biased. But still, you should still win more games than loose if you choose your cards and traits right.
In other words I give this game 8/10 because of small cons and lack of multiplayer. I really recommend this game as it's fun, addicting and challenging, while you don't need to waste time learning complicated mechanics. I would give 9.5/10 with multiplayer, but without it - I can't. Still good buy and certainly not wasted money as long as you enjoy card games ;).

In a nutshell: Populous + Minecraft + SimEarth
I don't think I have ever seen a game that I could compare to the giant of ecology games SimEarth. You take a completely blank world and over time, through the use of terra sculpting and terraforming tools, breed life ranging from the simple plankton to the highly complex humans or tyranosaurus. For a serious challenge, craft a world that can support both dinosaurs and humans without temperature tools. There is a good ingame library that is helpful to know what factors you are looking for in each evolution.
The program is divided between a story mode that guides you through the various ages slowly (And you keep the same world every stage), and a free mode where you can do whatever you wish, incliding importing your story mode world to run full sandbox.
It is worth noting that this is a console port and as of the time of this review, isn't optimized for PC yet. The controls take a bit of getting used to, but outside of that, I got no serious complaints about the game. Just make sure your computer is up to the task before buying. Your not going to be able to run this on an average laptop.

The story starts in any one of the six origins, and in each one you meet Duncan, a member of the fabled Grey Wardens, who serve as the realm's protectors against the Darkspawn; corrupt and grotesque beings that follow the calling of the Archdemon. During each Origin, you do a few key quests that set the story of your character in motion, and thus begins the era of the Fifth Blight.
After your Origin, Duncan invites you to become a Grey Warden, and help fight the Darkspawn and bring peace to the land of Ferelden. After the initial battle, chaos breaks loose, and you, and a few companions journey through Ferelden. Throughout the journey, you face hordes of enemies, including werewolves and demons, and the toughest of quests are taken up by the Warden and his party.
Still one of the best RPGs today, Dragon Age Origins brings you a unique storyline, with a multitude of different choices, all of them shaping the outcome of the game. Immerse yourself in this fantasy epic, and be bewildered by the spectacular level design, the incredible storyline, the fascinating lore of the realm of Thedas, and the unique individuals you encounter along the way.
If you enjoyed the Mass Effect series, then you will definitely enjoy the first game in the Dragon Age series. This is truly another masterpiece by Bioware.

The concept is great, and the backgrounds are beautifully rendered. But that's about all i can say about this game that are good. Everything constantly feels like you're just spamming attacks until something happens. The movement of the characters are strange and floaty; not the good kind of floaty like smash brothers in where you can actively pull off air combos. Most of the moves are just repetitive, and there's no diversity of moveset or characters.
Also, don't get me started on the game's character design. Everything is all lackluster, and every character feels like they took a basic template and repainted them to look different. It's not satisfying to look at a bunch of blobs of highly saturated characters bouncing around a screen. Certain characters even have identical weapons, and have one or two moves to make them different. There's no voice cast for the characters, and everything is awkwardly silent besides the hit sounds and music. If you are to incorporate character designs that you want an audience to remember, maybe set up dialogue for the characters, and create different templates for each character. The animation is well done thought, I must admit. However, it's probably all the work of the engine rather than anything else.
It baffles me that this game has an esports or even a competitive scene. My thumb is tired from just repeatedly pressing attacks with no sense of timing.
Granted, there is in fact a skill level. However, it's not well executed because of the lack of diversity in anything.
It was not a fun experience by any means, but hell, it's simple as ♥♥♥♥. If you're interested in a fighting game with a competitive scene that takes no time to master, this might just be for you.

- Customizable for the game, which give a totally new and more attractive face.

What can i say?
Lawbreakers is a damn enjoyable shooter.
Lawbreakers is actually the first game that i have every played with a mouse and keyboard on my pc, everything that came before was played with controller. Crazy, i know. i obviously sucked my way through the first couple of hours of gametime, but even though i was found at the bottom of the scoreboard pretty much all the time, i was able to learn, adapt and hunger for the next firefight to learn from my opponent again and again and again and again. until top of the scoreboard was mine.
But why did i want to become better like this? because lawbreakers is worth my time and effort.
It is at heart an arena shooter, that i have not seen like this yet. Yes it has classes and characters with their own kit, but those are more in the background. the star here is the movement and the mechanics that come with it. Movement is key. it doesn't matter what character your opponent has, as long as you play the cards that your characters gives you right, you can win against anything, with anyone. Another huge step that was taken away from the classic hero shooter are the modes and maps. no pushing a payload, no string designed maps and no defending a point for 6 minutes. Classic modes and maps, well aside from the 0g zones on them. Emphasize was also moved away from the team based nature of a hero shooter. Classes do not have as much synergy with each other and team pushing is usually not something you see, even though team pushing is a great way to win on some modes.
Another thing i want to praise is the art style and design. i ♥♥♥♥ing love every aspect of it. How the maps, characters and pretty much anything else looks, the light hearted brutality on display is also rather refreshing.
But does the game have issues you ask? yes, of course.
One thing that keeps bugging me most is the lack of regenerating health. ttk is not too high and healing stations are rare. healing packs give almost no health back. being weak is pretty much a death sentence unless a medic, which there off only exists one, shows up. Balance seems to also be an issue for a lot of people. wraith and assassin seem to get a lot of hate. i do not think they are op, a good juggernaut can easily wreck an assassin that comes too close, same thing with wraith. Map design is another issue, soem maps are just plain unusable for a certain mode, which is blitzball. goal and ball spawn are sometimes so close to each other, that killing a fast or tanky carrier is sometimes nigh impossible. Oh and overcharge and that other mode are pretty much the same, i did not know the difference for my entire first day of playtime.
So let's adress the elefant in the room. playerbase. If you don't buy the game due to the players, others won't and♥♥♥♥♥♥will never change. And you can find games very fast, sure you will see players again here and there but i mean... what ever? Please give this game a chance, you can still refund it. I don't want this good game to become another battleborn.
this game is still an outstanding piece of work. only arkham city can match it in terms of overall quality.

This platformer is quickly addicting, thanks to how straightforward it is. Procedurally generated levels (not counting campaign), combined with the various modes and hero types you can unlock keep this game fresh, fun, frustrating and funny all at once. There will be moments where you will die tens or hundreds of times before completing a level, and with that there will undoubtedly be intense frustration.
Reaching the end isn't only incredibly satisfying; it also makes you realize after completing numerous levels that they're meant to be finished quickly. Each generated level has a predetermined path the player should follow that allows them to simultaneously collect everything while practically speed running. If, at any moment, you don't think that's possible and are having a hard time, you can have the AI demonstrate for you how to win the level you're on at the expense of a certain number of crystals. It definitely helps you train your eye to find openings in a sea of death traps, provided that you have the patience and are masochistic enough to endure it all.
As if torturing yourself isn't enough, you can do the same with your friends and that's usually where the comedic value comes in. Bungee mode will either enhance or completely destroy your friendship with others because of the coordination it mandates. If any one player dies, the rest of you get to carry the deadweight and that obviously makes gameplay more difficult, but it can look quite hilarious. You can still play multiplayer without everyone being bound to each other if that's not your style, but I think it's too hard to resist playing that mode once in a while.
Let's not forget level customization. If you ever feel like conjuring up a level of your own, dive into free play. All assets are available to choose from and can be scaled to your taste. As long as you can verify that the AI is able to complete the level, you know you have one that's possible to finish and you can challenge your friends to complete it.
All of the aforementioned and other content makes this game a great buy for casual and hardcore gamers alike. I cannot emphasize the importance of using a controller, though. Sure, this game works fine with a keyboard, but I believe you'll be better off not using that, especially on the more difficult levels.

Possibly the worst NFS game that comes to mind. It's the buggiest, most laughably demented game in the series.
If you're having a bad day and you want to amuse yourself and get a good laugh out of something, here's what you do. You beat the game in about 10-12 hours and spend the rest having fun with the physics engine (or hey, never touch the game again).
So let's analyze the ups and downs with NFS:U.
-Lots of variety with customization, especially with vinyls.
-Graphics may look fantastic on the highest possible settings but depending on your system, the game may run like it's on a toaster.
-Large map with four different regions and lots to explore.
-Many different cars to choose from.
-Great soundtracks.
-So here's one of the two biggest turnoffs of this game:
. Well, what can I say? Some have already pointed this out, but ramming traffic and grinding against a wall will drop your speed by ~80 mph and more often than not, your car will spin out. And this is something that isn't consistent at all. Also, sliding around corners feels incredibly stiff and half the time you wonder if upgrading the handling of your vehicle even did anything. That's when you have to learn how to drift. But even that feels inconsistent. But the best part is, you can watch cruisers or traffic gracefully sail across the air if you adjust your collision just enough to send them flying and bouncing on the ground like their exteriors are made of 6 inch layers of rubber.
-
There's a reason why I said 10-12 hours beforehand. Because the AI racers and cruisers are too easy. The racers have difficulty turning around corners whereas you won't. Yeah, I did say handling and drifting are inconsistent, but really, even if you hit something, you'll still outrun the AI. Also, the cops will sometimes use rubberband AI, and other times they won't and you can very easily evade them.
-Pursuits can be VERY easy to evade. If your Wheelman Level is high enough, the police department will start assigning state/federal units to the chase immediately. However, all chases in free roam begin when a civic unit (the easiest cruisers to deal with in the game) on patrol finds you. Here's the problem: the civic units retreat before dispatch sends backup. The delay can take between 3 to 45 seconds. On another note, in the heat of a pursuit, dispatch will very infrequently send additional units apart from roadblocks. You'll never have 25 cops chasing you at a time unlike the far superior NFS Most Wanted.
-There also seems to be an issue where your pursuit's cooldown meter will occasionally fill up in less than a second, whereas they can take a while to do so even when you're idle in a hiding spot. I'm still not sure what causes this.
-Want to capture an intense moment during a race or police chase or maybe show off your ride? Only if you first get an EA Account, which the game bugs you with every time you launch it. Here's some advice: get DXtory or some other screen capture software, bind a key to take a screenshot, press it, then upload the image on Steam as "Artwork."
-The game is apparently under a constant nuclear attack. That should explain the yellow-orangish filter.
-The story is incredibly forgettable.
-Want to fill your garage with your dreams cars? Better spend most of your playtime grinding. Or just add them to "My Cars" where you can get everything for free, but they will not be stored for career mode.
-Cutscenes/introductions to wanted events are inconsistent with what's actually happening around you (i.e. the beginning intro to an escape/cost-to-state/takeout event can show traffic/crusiers that aren't actually there when the game starts).
-Pursuit breakers are buggy. Sounds may not play, objects may fall through solid objects, and some objects may not move at all.
-No perfect starts at the beginning of races.
-On every event, your speedbreaker starts off empty and you'll have to drive for at least 30 seconds to charge it up completely. Why not just have it available right off the bat?
-Even with so much variety in customization, it's still incomplete. Aftermarket parts have "zone bonuses" or something that don't seem to serve any purpose.
Is it worth the price? No. But is it suitable for brightening your day? Maybe I'm just too easily impressed, but getting into long pursuits and personalizing my own cars has been fun lately. If you're looking for a good NFS game, just play Most Wanted, Carbon, Underground 1/2, or Hot Pursuit.

Pros:
- Lightning fast multiplayer
- Skilled based (you can't expect to get kills or play the objective without getting a grip on arenas/playstyle/loadout)
- Dedicated loadouts (because I just want to jump in and play with a loadout I'm used to and not re-learn a whole character because there are better or faster or quirkier guns I have to choose and upgrade etc.)
- This is half the price of a triple A shooter - €30 without a terribly crap campaign where the majority of the game is cinematic cutscenes to pad out the levels. I'm willing to support games that come out for the community at a reasonable price like this for all the work that's gone into it.
Cons:
- Not enough map/game mode variety (the devs have come out to say that there are new maps, character, and game modes coming out so until then this is pretty much my only con with it)

Sooner or later, when playing Rome Total War, you start getting this uncomfortable feeling that what you're doing on the strategic map is just a stage prop for pixel soldiers to run around in pretty period costumes.
Alea Jacta Est, though very nice to look at, is not about eye candy.
Instead, it gives you a very detailed strategic and operational view of what the opposing sides were dealing with.  When battles or skirmishes take place they are resolved abstractly, though the abstraction gives a pretty detailed depiction of the tactical characteristics that were likely to be in play.
This game is part of a series that includes Birth of Rome (the later phases of Rome's conquest of Italy, including the confrontation with Pyrrhus and the first Punic War), Hannibal (the second Punic War), and the Parthian Wars (Rome's Eastern Front).  These three games aren't on Steam yet, which is unfortunate, because watching the Third Samnite War scenario unfold feels a lot like reading Livy.

It's hard to review this, as it gave me a rush of MANY conflicting emotions. While I personally did not enjoy it to the level most of Steam seems to, I definitely see this game had alot of potential, as well as being an honestly original experience.
"Always Sometimes Monsters" is a strange yet human experience where (after the foreboding intro) your character, an unsuccessful story writer, is invited to their ex's wedding and you go on a quest to make your way there over the course of a month to either try and win them back or be supportive. Along the journey the player can make a multitude of choices all throughout the game which have very distinct impressions on the story, often with an obvious placement of morality as to whether they're considered good choices or bad, which is what half the gameplay is comprised of. The other half of the game being dedicated doing events & oddjobs throughout the game for expenses in order to progress to the next town AND to feed yourself, as you have an actual stamina meter... that is almost redundant because all it really decides is if you die in your sleep or not. I'm serious. I understand why this is the way progression is made, it really gets across the feeling of barely being able to scrape by as economy and almost life itself seems to be against you, and cleverly makes you feel that sometimes you feel to do questionable things such as theft to get by, but I personally feel this negatively impacts the momentum of the story, as there are portions where you might have to grind just to move the story along. There ARE minigames to mix things up should you play them, but there's one that kind of... comes out of nowhere? I lost where the story was going for a second there.
The dialogue itself is fairly well written, characters DO feel human and even minor characters display personality, but alot of the characters just feel like jerks for the sake of being jerks. Or influencing players to do bad things in a few cases. Unfortunately, alot of these characters are major characters, making empathetic or relatable connections very hard to have. Since I have problems caring for the characters, I have a hard time caring for the story. Combined with how dragged out the story feels due to having to spend time managing expenses, and eventually I'm not even playing for the journey, I'm playing for the conclusion. Problem is the game seems to put more emphasis on the journey because, despite there technically being multiple endings, they're all dependant on a copout collection of choices you can make during the end of the game, making the ending also feel slapped on. Another review goes into better detail on this.
As for presentation, there isn't much to say. the 16-bit graphics are detailed. It has no voice acting but I'm alright with that. The main issue I have is with the music. Not that the music is BAD or anything, but the looping for the tracks is HORRIBLE. I really don't think it should start from the very beginning every time, it sounds sloppy.
Again, I didn't like the game too much. Despite the thumbs down however, I WON'T suggest people ACTIVELY avoid it. It is definitely an interesting experience. Just do yourself a favor and get it on a discount or something.

Wasn't going to write a review untill i saw alot of negative ones, so i figured i'd give my two cents. Brought this game on sale as the screenshots showed what seemed to be a well paced action game. And thats exactly what i recieved. I'm just going to do some +/- points to save time.
+Levels are structured well, creating oppertunities to take on all enemies at once in new game and oppertunities to take out some enemies to even the playing field in new game plus.
+Variety of enemies in the game, including people that call in backup, machine gunners and trip mines.
+Games difficulty curve MOSTLY works well, teaching mechanics at the start while slowly adding more enemies to each level, to prepare you for "boss" levels, which lead me onto...
+Boss levels are hard missions designed to make you use all of your skills to overcome a difficult challenge, that wil take many attempts and strategies to complete.
+Skill tree unlocks if you complete the bonus objectives for each mission.
+Fun combat that challenges you to think about your enviroment.
+ Checkpoints work with a load checkpoint system.
- Horrible bug that often occours: when you grapple you go through the wall and get stuck inside with no way out, forcing you to restart.
- Machine gunners made me consider suicide in new game plus.
- Locked 30 fps, but that didn't bother me.
- Need special edition to get a story.
+/- As i said above: difficulty curve MOSTLY works, the WISEGAL and GENERAL missions pump up the difficulty a little bit too much imo, taking me ALOT more attempts to complete, but i suppose some might consider them easy or might enjoy the challenge i suppose.

Idle games are identified primarily by the fact that progress continues even when you are not actively interacting with them.  This typically requires that they be very simplistic, linear, and have a very narrow scope, the same features that allow Donald Trump to keep running for President.
This type of game has certainly enjoyed a resurgence lately.  I say resurgence because idle games have been around for a very long time.  Longer than video games for sure.  Idle games go back about as far as humanity, with discoveries by archaeologists revealing many of the idle games early humans played, such as "Is the tiger still in front of the cave?", and ones that have been played for thousands of years, like "Grow crops in the desert".
The idle games of our ancestors have about as much relevance to our lives as the presidential bids of the aforementioned Donald however, so let us move on to Time Clickers, which in case you have forgotten, is the game I am currently reviewing.
Ahem.  Oddly enough, Time Clickers comes along during a large spike in idle game releases, following such titles as Clicker Heroes, Adventure Capitalist, Wacky Clicky Whatever ♥♥♥♥ It, and FarCry 4.  So what does Time Clickers bring to the table that no one else has?  Seriously, the table is getting kinda crowded.  I tried to eat my cereal this morning and had to keep brushing aside power-ups the whole time.
Time Clickers does, as the name implies, let you spend all of your time clicking enemies, so does every other idle game.  You can also spend your resources to hire and upgrade minions to do the clicking for you, and so does every other idle game.  You can "ascend", and start over while earning a sort of meta-currency to spend on permanent upgrades, and, yeah, so does every other idle game.  Honestly, I'm not having much luck finding any unique features in Time Clickers, so lets just move on, shall we.
The graphics are pretty cool, and are probably the only reason I'm playing it now after getting burned out on other, pretty much identical games.  Time Clickers just looks nice, and the cubes that make up the enemies are animated enough to make it feel like something is happening, so it feels a bit less, um, idly?  Sometimes, if I'm really getting immersed in the game, I like to pretend that the cubes are cylinders, but that's just the creative sort of person I am.
I suppose I recommend Time Clickers, because it can entertain you for a while, and it costs nothing, but it's not the sort of hearty recommendation I would give to a game like Fallout 4, which isn't even out yet.  Idle games just aren't for everyone, but then again neither is Donald Trump, so what the heck.  Time Clickers for President!

Please understand that I really, really wanted to recomend this game, and when I started the review I had indeed clicked that button, but as I wrote more and more I had to change it to no.
I enjoyed this game for a good bit, but not for long enough.  AVWW is almost like several games that I love, it is a little Metroid like, a little Castlevania like, a little Terraria like, and a little (very little) Shining Force EXA like. The controls are a bit awkward at first (do not even bother with attempting to use a controler even though the game is technicaly compatible with one) and there is a very steep learning curve.  Just understanding how to efficiently and properly use the warps located in the game, and to fully understand the map took me several hours of play.  Tutorial boxes do pop up but they are not even close to adequate in their explanations.  Case and point in order to make my life easier when I started the game I felt the need to create my own manual cut together from bits and pieces I could find on their web page.  By the time I was done it was nearly 50 PAGES LONG I KID YOU NOT!  Once you understand the mechanics and how to best do what you need to do you can have fun with it, but it is very rarely satisfying.
You could easily spend hours looking for one particular item to do one particular thing, and that thing almost never feels like a true reward for your efforts.  Hard earned spells need to be replaced near constantly as your world gains levels, and you need a huge (really huge, you have near zero control over this) bit of luck to aquire the spells you want with decent modifiers.  Again as soon as the world levels up your previous spells that you worked so hard to get are one step closer to obsolete, and the process repeats itself.  The other issue I take with the luck factor in the game is that a huge number of the achievments come down to just dumb, blind luck.  I am refering to a set of at least 15 or so goals that are simply "get a legendary this," followed by another "get a legendary that," then "get a legendary one of those."  The only way to get a legendary anything (as far as the enchants the acivement wants goes) is by sheer luck.  the only control you have over this is in leveling up your world via defeating certain "luitenants." I have heard tell that the higher level your word is the better chance you have of getting legenary things, but this like so many other parts of this game, is not clearly explained or stated anywhere so I am not 100% on this and could be mistaken.  Even if that is the case though that only gives you some controll over the legendary part of the requirement and not the item part of the requirement so you could easily just keep getting a "Legendary not what you needed" over and over and over...and over and over...and over.
The last issue I take with AVWW is that it just goes on forever, like litteraly...forever.  Some people may see this as a plus and to them I say "go you, purchase this game ASAP," but I am a person who likes a degree of finality in my games, and this unfortunately doesn't have any.  After several hours of play I found myself asking why am I still playing this? If I beat this continent I am just going to do the same exact thing on the next one, then the next one, then the next one, etc. etc. and none of them change enough to make you feel like you are truly progessing, it feels more like you are stuck in the gaming equivalent of Groundhog Day.
Play this game if you like: Randomly generated maps and dungeons, hack n' slash style gameplay, games that you can put 1000's of hours into.
Don't play this game if you like: Truly finishing a game, being a completionist, power leveling, milestones, a high degree of control over your equipment and spells.

Unfortunately I am forced to recommend against this game. I will make the review short and, if the issues are fixed, will amend my recommendation.
Firstly, I should say that the game can be fun and some of the classes are interesting to play. Graphics wise, everything is nice and the game looks quite good on max settings. The UI is a bit boring I think but that's just my subjective opinion; you might think it looks cool.
My main issue with this game is the matchmaking, or the lack thereof. I find myself being routinely put into games with players who are, quite clearly, far better than me or anyone on my team; people who have already put a considerable amount of time into learning the game and getting very good. The problem this arouses is that landslide-losses are not uncommon, and when they occour they are incredibly frustrating. As far as I can tell, this game doesn't have a visible ranking system - perhaps it has some hidden algorithm to matchmake players, but if it does it doesn't seem to work very well.
What's more, at the end of such games where your team loses 0-8, you might try leaving the lobby and joining another game. However you will probably just be put back into the same lobby three times in a row, which leads me to believe that this game can't have many players... (consider Overwatch - in my entire time playing that game I have been put into the same lobby I just left maybe 10-20 times? In LawBreakers it happens every day).
This issue alone makes LawBreakers an excrutiatingly painful game to play. As someone who just enjoys casually playing, and hasn't the time to invest in improving, I feel the games are usually weighted against my team.
Another issue is that the classes don't seem that balanced. Most games I play, there will be at least 2 people playing Titan (rocket-launcher man) and that also provides great amounts of high blood-pressure and early-onset cardiac arrest.
Perhaps my gripes with this game are founded in my inadequacy. After-all, I don't want to play competitively at all, I don't have the time for it. Just know that if you're buying this game to play casually, it will have no problem pitching you against people who have sunk a lot of time into learning how to be better.
EDIT: For people marking this review as "unhelpful", consider this: any competitive game you can think of has a ranking system; League of legends, Overwatch, CS:GO... In-fact, I'd argue that a good ranking system and a good matchmaker is ESSENTIAL for any game that wants to be competitive. Well, LawBreakers has no such thing. It doesn't even have a "Competitive" game mode, every game is considered "quick match".
An arena shooter that doesn't try to match players against others of equal capability (or, morse for LawBreakers, a game that doesn't have enough players to equally match people), is destined to fail.

Ronin is to games what B-movies are to film - you can tell it exists because other designs inspired its look and feel, but it's an enjoyable enough diversion that the borrowing doesn't offend. Spend any time at all with the game and you'll see its heritage - titles like Gunpoint, Mark of the Ninja and Splinter Cell: Conviction. However, its stealth game heritage has been flavored with doses of Transistor and Hotline Miami, creating something which only looks like  a stealth game.  Stealth kills are available (and necessary at times for three starring levels), but ghosting through a building undetected by all and sundry will not happen - there are going to be several set pieces on each level when you will have to draw your katana and go to work. In combat, if you get hit once, you die, but checkpoints are plentiful and other than the last level, you never need to replay more than your current room.
Killing in Ronin is a turn-based system of taking jumps, knocking enemies down and finding windows in which to finish them off. As you level up, you'll get some extra advantages (decoys, thrown weapons, teleport stuns, etc.), but they never sidestep the core of the experience. At the end of the game, it will still be you, your sword and a bunch of enemy laser sights to avoid. And when everything plays out well, you'll come out feeling just as satisfied as you would after a particularly obnoxious level of Hotline Miami.
There are three kinds of enemies: pistol-packing security guards, armored guards with assault rifles and cybernetic samurai with blades (there are also a few bosses sprinkled in). Each is different - the pistoleros fire single shots while the riflemen put down suppressive fire that is dangerous to leap through (but are consequently slower to shift aim points). Cybernetic samurai take two hits to kill (a stun and then a quick follow up hit).  There are also a few environmental hazards (long falls, laser grids and sensor activated mines) to be navigated - fortunately, all of these can be used against enemies. The enemy A.I. is adequate and has patterns which you will learn to exploit over the game.
To level up, you need to satisfy three criteria on each level - spare the civilians, kill all the guards and prevent the alarm. Sparing civilians is generally a matter of planning (how to dispatch guards without being seen, which should be old hat to any stealth pro). Killing all the guards is just a best practice. The last criteria is the most annoying - during combat, guards will sometimes try to trigger the lockdown, putting you on a clock to stun them (civilians will also trigger the alarm but are much easier to avoid). In large fights (and especially those where there are mutually supporting enemies in different buildings), this can cause a significant amount of tooth gnashing and cursing.
I thought the game controlled reasonably well, except for the grappling hook, which was a bit swingy. The code for walls and windows is a bit off and you will sometimes clip through them, which is sloppy. The soundtrack is first rate, the art design is consistent and the graphics are crisp, so good marks for presentation. The writing, however, is both sparse and weak (even the digital comic offers no real insight into why there is such an all-consuming need for vengeance), but if you go at Ronin with the mindset that it is a diversion and not a meal, you'll be fine.
Length would seem to be about 5-6 hours, I'll let you make your own judgment on what is an acceptable price for that time. There is a new game plus available after finishing the core game for those who want to go at it all again.

AVWW is an interesting game in that it is many types of games at once, which both helps and hurts.  Jumping in and playing the game can be very confusing and it is almost necessary to do research on how to "learn" to play the game.  Once you learn "how" to play the game it only takes a few hours before you realize you are simply repeating the same actions and missions over and over (I will say those first few hours of exploration can be fun, if you like a new challenge).  The look of AVWW seems a bit dated and lackluster and the sound effects become monotonous.  The first 50 or so ACHIEVEMENTS come VERY QUICKLY once you learn what you're doing, but then the other half (all LEGENDARY achievements) are extremely time consuming to get; i.e. lots of grinding.  It's worth owning if you can pick it up very cheap during a sale or through Humble Bundle; Trading Cards help make the cost that much less as you can sell or trade them.  The BEST part of AVWW is the inclusion of an extremely brilliant "transport/warping" system that helps cut down on the time to run back through every area you already cleared (it would be nice if other, better, games would steal this "transport" system).

There are times when I look at Los Santos and think 'why would you even think to build that?' This is, appropriately, a thought that I often have about Los Angeles. In GTA 5's case, the tone is different: baffled wonderment as opposed to baffled, y'know, despair. Rockstar have created one of the most extraordinary game environments you will ever visit. I look at it and I wonder at the vast expense of effort required to render every trash bag in every back alley just so. I marvel at the care evident in San Andreas' gorgeous sunsets, in the way that sunglasses subtly alter the colour balance of the world, in the artfully-chosen selection of licensed music designed to accompany your experience. Everything about Los Santos demonstrates the extraordinary amount of thought and love poured into it by hundreds of developers over many years. The abiding irony of Grand Theft Auto 5 is that everybody who actually lives in Los Santos hates it there.
This is the most beautiful, expansive and generous GTA game and also, by some distance, the nastiest and most nihilistic. Rockstar went through a phase, in Bully, Grand Theft Auto IV and the sadly console-bound Red Dead Redemption, of framing their protagonists as anti-heroes. GTA 4's Niko Bellic did some terrible things, but he had a downtrodden charm that helped you like him as you piloted him through the underworld. He was surrounded by people who were larger-than-life but ultimately, beneath the surface, people. Among those people were some of Rockstar's better female characters—Kate McReary, Mallorie Bardas, The Lost and Damned's Ash Butler.
Grand Theft Auto 5 does away with all of that, deliberately but to its detriment. Its trio of protagonists occupy a city full of vapid, two-dimensional caricatures, and they flirt with that boundary themselves. Michael is a middle-aged former bankrobber, unhappily married and on the edge of a breakdown. Franklin is a young hood, purportedly principled but willing to do almost anything for money. Trevor is a desert-dwelling, meth-dealing psychopath with a homebrew morality that sits uneasily alongside his capacity for violent cruelty and sexual aggression. The campaign explores their relationship through a series of heists and misadventures as they clash with every L.A. stereotype you might imagine—the bored Beverly Hills housewife, the corrupt fed, the bottom-rung fraudster, the smug technology exec, and so on.
Against this backdrop, it's only Michael, Franklin and Trevor that appear to have any kind of internal life. I get the impression that this is deliberate, part of the game's relentless skewering of southern California and indicative of Rockstar's waning interest in romantic anti-heroes. Trevor's introduction, in particular, amounts to a particularly explicit '♥♥♥♥ you' to the characters and themes of Grand Theft Auto IV. GTA 5 is heartless in that way, and as a result I found the narrative difficult to care about. It is ambitious, well-performed, and the production values are extraordinary—but it is also derivative and brutishly adolescent, set in a world where the line between criminality and the rule of law is blurry but where it is always hilarious that somebody might be gay.
It's an R-rated episode of The A-Team where the 'A' stands for '♥♥♥♥♥♥♥'. The campaign's best moments come when your cigar-chomping master strategist, insane former military pilot and talented driver come together, and when you're given the power to choose how to use each of them. These heists are set-piece missions where you pick an approach and perform set-up tasks in the open world before setting out on the job itself. In the best of them, which occur later in the campaign, it really does evoke the satisfaction of having a plan come together. Perhaps you position Trevor on the high-ground with a rocket launcher, Michael on foot with a stealth approach, and Franklin in an armoured ram-raider. With a button press you can flick between the three, dynamically orchestrating a crime caper on your own terms.
It is also in these moments that Rockstar's most ambitious storytelling takes place. Your choice of character, crew, and even certain in-game actions have subtle effects on the dialogue. In an early heist, a crewmember dropped part of the score but, as Franklin, I was able to retrieve it—a side-objective that I'd set for myself but that was subsequently reflected in a later conversation between him and Michael. This is another example of Rockstar's extraordinary attention to detail, and if the rest of the campaign respected your agency in this way it might overcome its weaker moments.
As it is this is a very long game with a lot of filler. There's much driving from A to B, a lot of conversations in cars, a lot of gunfights with hordes of goons who show up just to run into your gunsights over and over. It's far richer in set-piece moments than its predecessor—drug trips, aerial heists, dramatic chases—and many of these look incredible even if they're light on actual interaction. In the best examples, you soak in the atmosphere and happily ignore the fact that you're only really being asked to follow the on-screen instructions. In the worst examples—insta-fail stealth sequences, sniper missions and so on—it's harder to ignore the shackles that are placed on the player in order to preserve the game's cinematic look and feel.
I spent a lot of my time with the campaign frustrated along these lines, bored of the same mission templates that I've been playing through since GTA III and making the most of the scant opportunities to play my own way, like Franklin's refreshingly open assassination missions. Then, inevitably, I'd be doing one of those rote activities—a heavily scripted freeway chase, perhaps—when the magic of that extraordinary world would creep up on me again. It'd hit me: I'm doing 150 km/h along the Pacific Coast Highway at sunset. The rock station is playing 30 Days In The Hole by Humble Pie. It feels incredible, a collision of pop-culture, atmosphere, music and play that is unique to GTA.

I know, shocking isn't it? I actually liked a game that everyone else does. (Although, I could talk about why I don't like Arkham City, but let's think about the positives!)
Batman: Arkham Asylum was a game that everyone expected would be crappy but it turned out to be good... blah blah blah, everyone knows the stories. And if you've seen anyone's review of Arkham Asylum, my opinions are pretty similar, so for once I'll actually condense my thoughts:
PROS:
1- Great voice acting from Kevin Conroy and Mark Hamill, as expected
2- Excellent, intuitive level design and puzzles
3- Well-created world within Arkham Island, that feels very dark and twisted
4- Continues telling a story without beating you over the head, like when Ivy takes over, you see all the plants swarm the island
5- Fantastic stealth and combat gameplay
CONS:
1- Uncreative boss fights
2- Lots of plot holes
3- Sometimes stiff animations (Conversations mainly look very stiff and robot-like)
I played this game years ago, and loved it then, so I'm glad to see that my opinion hasn't changed. I planned on taking a break from Steam to try out some Bayonetta and Lollipop Chainsaw on the console, but the temptation was too strong and I gave in. And I actually went out of my way to find out all 240 Riddler Trophies, which (while a little repetitive) was ultimately fun to find. It makes the replay value just a little bit higher.
Batman: Arkham Asylum gets an 8/10. With all the things it does so flawlessly well, it's very hard to judge it for its shortcomings. I'm definitely coming back in a few more years to play through a third time. I might even go for 100% completion.

Virtually required:
1. Play the game with a controller (I did so with an xBox 360 controller).
2. The desire to play a game that is a mix of the terrain sculpting ability of a city simulator, the "control evolution" (this time, of the world... instead of a single creature) of Spore, with a bit of single player strategy game dynamics (keep watch on temperatures, land types, and moisture levels.  Get this creature to unlock the next in the "tech tree".)
Pros:
1. Simple to learn
2. Once you get used to them, the controls are intuitive.  Further, it has a good "first campaign" to teach you to do so.
3. Overall: Fun (if you generally like games, as described, above)
Cons:
1. A few translation errors still exist in the game.
2. (Related to above) Could use some better wording on some organisms to know whether you need to mutate or evolve them.
3. Some of the Steam achievements will take some considerable time and multiple playthroughs.
Play example (as relates to Cons, 3):
After playing the first campaign to unlock free build mode, I began a huge cube (world) that ended up being a bust without significant rework.  As a result, using what I had learned, I started a second huge world (in order to save time with realistic terrain sculpting).  After 36 total hours activately playing the game (of which 26.5 hours were on the second world), and with active use of the mutate and evolve (NOW, not wait on natural evolution) items, I had seen and "captured" every single organism at least once.
An apparent benefit of capturing every organism is to unlock infinite hp, which will significantly help complete some of the Steam achievements.  (One chain of them is to accumulate 1 billion, then 3 billion, cube years.  Using my huge world on my pc, which will run 270k cube years per minute, the world will need to run... in fast forward... for a bit over 61 hours just to complete the 1 billion one.)  ...  This is why I consider some of the achievements as cons.
Overall:
I have, for years, followed the rule that "for every US Dollar I spend on a game, I need to get one hour of enjoyment from it."  I got it on sale for the $29.99 price, and played 36 hours as of this message.  Money well spent.

Birthdays the Beginning will rope you in with its adorable creature design, but watching your world grow as new lifeforms are born is what will keep you coming back (it's always rewarding to hear the triumphant fanfare when a new lifeform appears). With a multitude of creatures to discover, three different gameplay modes (story, free play and a challenge mode) you'll likely find yourself spending a lot of time with Birthdays the Beginning.
Unfortunately, the PC port isn't without its faults. The game's key bindings are bizarre and cannot be changed, and in my experience the game's controls were more suited towards a controller. Some users are also reporting low framerates, and the lack of a "quit to desktop" button is a puzzling omission. Thankfully, NISA is working on sorting out the latter two issues with a beta branch of the game currently available. My hope is that NISA will also fix the key binding issue to make a kb/m setup that's more practical.
Despite these issues, I still had a lot of fun with the game. Those on the fence might want to wait until NISA fixes up the port, but if you can look past those issues I think it's well worth checking out.

The SP of the game is amazing, with a captivating story line and Side-missions that aren't annoying "find 100 bird feathers on place nobody goes to."
The characters are interesting to play with/as, while the antagonists really make you want to get rid of them.
Compared to previous game, NPCs are now a real threat and challenge, spicing things up.
Except for some small bugs, the SP is a masterpiece.
However, I can't say the same for GTA Online. While it does feature some interesting heists, missions and gameplay, the grindfest it is ruins everything. I can understand, to a certain extent, having a certain micro-transaction system for a "Game" that receive free updates, but Rockstar has done so that getting a good majority of any special content of an update (New buildings, special weaponized vehicles, etc...) Cost around $30,000,000 per updates.
That's 281.25€ of Sharkcards per update. You would think they would add more ways of making money. But to reach just 1,000,000$, here's your solutions:
Farm and Refarm missions rewarding you around 25,000$ for a mission that can take up to 20 minutes to complete. That's up to 800 minutes of gameplay, or ~13 hours.
You'd say "Seems fair, you have to earn it"? But remember, rich people can just buy a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of shark cards (Accurate name seeing how they're sharking us), buy special vehicles that can one-shot anything and transform these 13 hours into an endless loop of pain and frustration.
Grindfest apart, even Blizzard and Valve together manage to make more proper balancing to something than Rockstar can. If you're planning to buy a giant military plane to show off, you're better off buying yourself a golden♥♥♥♥♥♥♥as a small flying bike can fire more rockets in a minute than all of history's rockets artilleries have fired throughout the ages.
The balance choice doesn't make sense. A ♥♥♥♥ing car with 2/3 metal sheets on its side can withstand more direct-hit rockets than an actual tank can.
So in a TL;DR:
SP is good, Online is only good with friends for heist. You're better off wearing an underwear made of sandpaper if you're thinking of enjoying the GTA:O experience

Arkham Asylum in my opinion is probably the best Batman game in terms of capturing the gritty world Batman resides in. After a clever plan plotted by the Joker, Batman is trapped in Arkham Asylum, an institute for the criminally insane. Batman's objective is clear: Find and defeat Joker, put the patients back in their cells, and save Gotham before anything rash happens. This game is a fun time for these reasons:
- It has a nice original story taking place in one of the most "maximum security" prisons for the criminally insane in comics
- Smooth combat system that gets a bit addicting overtime
- Well crafted stealth mechanics
- Great cast from other Batman media
- Tons of collectibles (or "Riddles") that become an obsession to collect!
While playing I have experienced these problems however:
- The last boss in the game was boring, and could have been better in several ways
- Only ONE costume in the entire game (it's just an "armored" version of the default suit)
- Some of the character designs were a little out of the ordinary or just too unrealistic (I know it's based on a comic where not a lot of designs are ordinary)
- Some parts in the game I found were a little stale or just started to become tedious
Should you buy it? Yes you should! Even though there are a few cons, they easily become overlooked by the fun combat, stealth segments, collectibles, storytelling, and more.

I bought this game knowing it was going to be absolute garbage but even with the lowest of expectations it managed to be a disappointment. This is essentially the ridiculously broken beta of a good NFS game and the immense lack of polish makes it near unbearable to play at times. The fact that, once again, it feels like the beta of a GOOD NFS game it just becomes so much more infuriating. This game really could have been like Most Wanted (2005) but instead becomes more like Big Rigs: Over the Road Racing.
List of issues I found:
- As much as touching a wall or a traffic car will slow your speed by at least 100 km/h (60 mph) and make it so that, for the next second or two, you can't turn properly.
- There is a delay (about 5-10 seconds) on using nitrous at the start of a race and once you actually have it it helps more with cornering than acceleration.
- Any bump in the road will make you unable to steer your car and going over large jumps makes your car start bouncing upon landing, steering while bouncing will cause you to spin out.
- Countless graphical errors that, together with washed-out colors, make the game look awful.
- Runs very poorly, my 960 can't run it at high settings with 60 FPS (not that it matters much, higher settings won't make the game look good anyway).
- Several features (cop chases, visual costumization) feel (and most likely are) unfinished.
- The minimap show a far too small area, the line showing the track doesn't necessarily follow the road and swtiches between showing only shortcuts, only the main road, and showing both. The minimap also points to already used pursuit breakers during cop chases and shows to hiding spots that don't actually exist.
- Cops can spawn in normal races but the chase that follows the race is unnecessary as no tasks (cost to state, cop takedown or escape) can be completed in these and instead is it's own seperate event.
- The AI seems to stand for Artificial Incompetence rather than Artificial Intelligence (ha ha ha, I am VERY funny *no sarcasm whatsoever*).
- Both budget and time seems to have been allocated exclusively to the story-progressing cutscenes. Too bad all of the cutscenes are overacted into oblivion and the story they're driving forwards is forgetable, cliché and utterly redundant in an NFS game.
In conclusion I can say that, while I have laughed a lot while playing the game it hasn't been enjoyable. If you want a truly awful game there are much better (worse?) ones out there for a much cheaper price and if all you want is to laugh at something so bad that it's good you most likely are better of watching a movie.

Need for Speed Undercover is, let's say special game. Why? Because we can say two absolutely opposite statements about the game, but most of us would agree with both.
1 - Need for Speed Undercover is one of the worst NFS games ever (one of the, not worst) (in case you didn't see)
2 - Need for Speed Undercover is let's say last member of those GREAT GREAT NFS games.
When you look at the NFS timeline, you might understand both statements and you might even agree on them. Just look at the timeline and that's it.
Now, as always I'm going to put my personal relations with this game, because that's what games are all about. I believe majority of those who read this also read my review on Crysis, because majority of those who read my reviews also read every review of mine because Steam bros :D
I said there, that 10 years ago, in my country basically inflation didn't exist and that Slovakia wasn't ready for Western prices (games, movies, music). It was really rare that somebody went out and bought DVD movie or game or music CD. One of my classmates however wasn't that case. I don't think he was rich, he lived at same place like everybody, his home looked same like everybody but for some reason he had tons of movies, tons of games for consoles and PC, and all was original. I don't remember what was the case and/or what I did, but we end up in supermarket, and he insisted on buying me 4 games for PlayStation 2. I remember that I wanted to get Driver: Parallel Lines and they had it, but wasn't able to check out in the end, so he ended up saying, pick 4 other games and I was like WTF.

To this current day, I still have Carbon on my shelf. Rest was taken or stolen years ago. I know the locations of Underground 2 and Undercover. Most Wanted is missing still. (Same with Tekken 4 and Killzone 1)
Second story is not actually some story, just one memory. I don't have memories in my head, of me playing NFS Undercover except one. When I was born, decades ago, I used to live my first 3 years in one certain room, then I moved. After decade or so, I came back and I used to visit that place frequently up to this date. And so when 9 years ago I got those 4 games from my friend from story above, I only remember one thing out of whole NFS Undercover - sitting on a white blanket, in room where I was "born", chasing Maggie Q on the Gold Coast Highway on my green Porsche 911 GT2. And that's it. And that's the reason why I played this game again in 2017. I wanted to try to relive it.
There was mentions in the beginning that Undercover is one of the worst. And yup, it is.
I know, and I do take into the consideration that it is race game, and 9 years ago it wasn't certainly standard to put stories in some particular genres, and I also do take into the consideration the amount of promo for this game and for the story especially. Thing is, if we look at the story as a movie, it will be like this - Overhead is absolutely disaster.. Script was mediocre, acting was terrible except Maggie Q, but camera was pretty nice. Sometimes. So story-wise NFS Undercover in 2017 is absolutely weak, but in 2008 it was above-average.
Good thing is, that this game runs almost on everything. Graphics are very nice, game looks kinda pretty, city looks cool. Overally visuals are alrighty. Audio was good. I've enjoyed doing revs. Soundtrack was absolutely dope. Freaking dope yess. From Nine Inch Nails to phenomenal Tempest by Pendulum.
Selection of cars is very well-chosen.It has basically everything you need and want. And yes, fully tunned GT-R runs faster than Bugatti :D Tuning of cars is great as it was in games before. Undercover is last to use legendary Autosculpt, which to those who don't remember was very big thing back in the days. So yes.
Game will last you for 6-8 hours. It's hard to say if you will enjoy the game till the finish. Most probably you won't. Even in terms of racing game, Undercover is heavily repetetive, and chances of playing it again anytime soon is really low.
Oh, I almost forgot, physics are totally nasty bad, traffic appears all of a sudden in front of you, and yes, Steam Overlay does not work.
To patch it up, for everybody who played it years ago, grab it and play it again, relive memories. To those, who played it few years ago and did not like it, chances are you still won't like it. To those who never played it, and also never played games before Undercover, don't get it yet, play them first and then go to Undercover. To those who never played Undercover but played games before, get it. In sale for 2,49€ it is MUST COP.

Cloudberry Kingdom is another of those hardcore platformers and a really frustrating one as well. The gameplay is pretty simple and straight foward, you can jump and move left and right. Ocasionally you'll be playing some levels with a mechanic, it can be double jump, using a jetpack, having your body attached to a sphere thing that makes you roll through the level making you calculate precisely where you're going to land, and these are just some of the possible ones that you can experience. The controls are responsive and intuitive, atleast with the 360 controller, I didn't tried playing with the keyboard.
Despite the fact that Cloudberry Kingdom is really enjoying to play and the fact that it provides a great amount of satisfaction when you finally beat a level you were stuck in for quite some minutes, or even hours, I found myself getting really frustraded when I reached around the level 196 in Story Mode. Not that I don't enjoy the game, but I just don't feel like I should invest time playing these levels over and over again until I get the hang of it.
Visually, Cloudberry Kingdom, is nothing to be amazed by but it kinda gets you into the spirit of this little fairy world it takes place. The sound assets are pretty much non existent but the soundtrack is really really good. In the end, I honestly think that if you enjoy titles like Super Meat Boy or VVVVVVV, that provide alot of challenge you'll certainly have a great time with Cloudberry Kingdom. Not only it has a Story Mode that you can beat, but you can also generate random dungeons for you to play and customize your character, which adds alot of replayability. You certainly cannot go wrong with Cloudberry Kingdom if you're a fan of hardcore platformers.

[Warning: This game may cause many players to rage quit and flip tables. You've been warned] Welcome to the world of Cloudberry Kingdom, or what I like to call Death Valley. You play as a hero as he has to go though hundreds of levels of pain and suffering to save the kingdom. You will encounter many hard enemies that will try to stop you. This game is endless, it's randomly generated levels could make your experience fun or hard. It's a good way in killing time when you run out of ideas to do. You could do acrade mode and try to make it past each level. Free play allows a player to choose the skill level, the size of the map, and what hero mode you wanna do. If you call yourself a hardcore gamer this is the game for you! Enjoy this insane but great game.

No self-respecting platformer enthusiast would shirk challenging the behemoth that is Cloudberry Kingdom.  Take on the role of Bob, a retired hero, as you run, duck, jump, double jump, jetpack, fly, bounce, pogo, gravity flip, roll, and rocket your way through story mode, or try your hand at one of the 4 arcade modes that will test your ability to adapt and react to any situation.  Whatever you do, be prepared to die, for once you have begun your journey, there is no mercy to be found.
Plus, one of the outfit color options is "invisible".

Mark of the Ninja was a pleasant surprise that provided me with a great deal of entertainment for only a pittance (around $3). It stars a Ninja imbued with enchanted tattoos that give him special powers but also curse him with increasing madness, whose goal is to complete a mission of assassination and then take his own life before he loses the last remnants of his sanity.
The graphics and music are all appropriately ninja-themed which really helps to draw you into the overall atmosphere of the game. Most characters are fairly well animated for 2d and I was impressed by the level of effort put into the cinematics between levels (they had kind of a Samurai Jack vibe). The game also features helpful sound cues for when enemies are moving around in other rooms and for when you have been seen.
Since this is intended as a stealth game, gameplay consists of you finding your way through each level while avoiding detection and removing any obstacles, human or otherwise. Many of the areas had multiple routes that sometimes took me in completely different directions which I thought was a nice touch and added to overall replay-ability. Of course, it wouldn’t be a ninja game if you didn’t also have an array of ninja tools to deal with pesky enemies and inconvenient light sources. Besides your darts, you also have methods of distraction and extermination, and can customize your loadout at various points denoted by a hanging flag in each level. You will only have a few abilities at the start of the game, but you can unlock more by completing bonus challenges, finding secrets, and completing objectives.
The only gripe I have with Mark of the Ninja is that the controls can be a little quirky at times especially when moving between horizontal and vertical planes with contextual button commands. This wasn’t really a big deal but it did take me until near the end of the game before I finally got used to it. The game is also a bit short, but considering how cheap it is that’s not really a problem.
So, if you’re in the mood for a stealth-action ninja-themed game, try picking this one up. You might end up just as pleasantly surprised as I was!
