Mark of the Ninja is an excellent side scrolling 2D stealth game. Not only does it look gorgeous, with an art style reminiscient of Samurai Jack and Disney movies like Mulan, but its gameplay mechanics are honed to a fine sheen so that you're constantly getting new upgrades, learning how to do new things, or forced to work around new obstacles.
In this game, you play as a ninja who is covered in tatoos that give him special abilities, like enhanced reflexes. This gives the sword wielding assassin an edge over his machine gun wielding enemies, but it comes at a cost. According to legend, the tatoos will eventually drive its host insane, which means they must kill themselves before it's too late.
While the enhanced reflexes are great, that's not the only trick the Ninja has up his sleeve. As you progress, you unlock more abilities you unlock with medals you get for completing levels well (not getting seen, distracting enemies, getting a high score, finding hidden scrolls and completing certain challenges within the level). You get fun distraction tools like flares and firecrackers, which are useful for drawing attention away from you. you can also get attack items, like a spike mine which impales any enemy who walks over it or, my personal favorite, some darts coated in poison that panics enemies, which can cause them to shoot their allies in their fear. These options, coupled with the smart, semi open level design, means you can approach any given situation from several different ways. Do you take out the lights, using the cover of darkness to sneak by? Do you skulk around, eliminating each enemy one by one and hide their bodies in a grate? Or, better yet, do you hang from some perches and string their bodies up to strike fear into the heart of anyone who sees the gruesome display?
So,the gameplay is excellent. The pacing for new abilities and challenges is also really good. Each level adds a new obstacle you must take into account when planning out your approach. The game's challenge is terrific, too. It rewards, careful, methodical play while simultaneously encouraging experimentation thanks to generous checkpoints.
Sadly, the same can't be said for the story. It feels incredibly underwritten, like entire scenes of character and plot development were cut from the final product. It's hard to describe without just playing the game, but let me put it this way: There were several moments that were supposed to have a big impact but didn't because almost none of the characters were well developed. There is a mildly interesting plot twist near the end though, which leads to an intriguing moral choice. But, after I made that choice, the game just... ended. It happened, and that was it.
I guess you can't have everything with smaller games, which is fine. This game is very, very well designed and a lot of fun thanks to its open approach to stealth (pure stealth, too, harkening back to games like Thief the Dark Project, rather than  'action or stealth'). The story is mediocre and underwritten, but that won't matter when you're moving through the shadows and eliminating fools one by one. Highly recommended.

Hi, I'm alex22469, a top 50 brawlhalla player with ~1500 hours. I have played brawlhalla for almost two years, and have reached diamond in every season, as well as top 50 worldwide is seasons 3-6, and top ten in season 5 and early season 6.
As someone who plays this game in a competetive way, it has some issues, which I will adress later. But first, let's look at it from a casual standpoint.
If you are new to fighter games, brawlhalla is an excellent choice to play casually, especially with friends. The community on the subreddit is extremely supportive, as well as many top players making guides on various platforms and streaming constantly to twitch. It is patched every week on wednesday, and balances constantly, making it one of the most balanced fighter games for lower-tier players. Every character can be unlocked for free if you put in the hours, but aditionally you can purchase the DLC to unlock every character. You can also pay for skins for characters, but everything paid is solely cosmetic. All in all, Brawlhalla is extremely friendly to those who are looking for a fun fighter game to play with friends.
Casual Review: 9/10.
Now, this is where the review turns to a competetive standpoint. This is going to look at positives as well as negatives. So, let's start with the positives of playing in high tier. Note: Unless you are intending to play this game non-casually, disregard this next part of the review entirely.
•Ridiculously friendly high tier community.
I cannot say this for lower ranks, but the high tier community is extremely supportive of each other and non-bm. This is mainly because many of us know each other personally, since there are not so many people who play competetively. Aditionally, this makes the community a little better, who like to follow the habits of top players.
•The E-Sports scene is on the rise.
I cannot stress this enough. It seems every few weeks a new top player is sponsored to fly to a LAN event. And speaking of LAN events, the world championship is a 100,000$ prize pool. At the time of writing this review, it is this weekend as a matter of fact. Aditionally, Brawlhalla-endorsed community run online tournaments such as Brawl League also have notable prize pools if you are unable to attend said LAN events. Other community tournaments are run too, with prizes of CCs (community colors, a special code used to give every character you have a special color palette) and metadevs (exclusive skins for certain legends only attainable by developers of the game or these tourneys) as well as cash prizes.
•Most help one another improve.
Even now, as statistically one of the best players in the world, I still learn new things from other top players, including new combos and ways to use game mechanics. Just recently Brawlhalla has undergone a major change, replacing one game mechanic (Mdodge) with Dashing. The top players in the community immediately banded together to test out and discover new ways to use the mechanic in detail. And for those who want to learn more about the game, add me, I can mentor.
Now, let's get to the negatives.
•Balance.
The game has some fundamental issues when it comes to balance, and I wont go into much detail in it right now, but the things being done about it are not being executed well. The forge, the discord the developers created to balance, is not taken seriously by many and because of this it turned into something unfavorable. Brawlhalla is still one of the most balanced fighting games I have ever seen, but the actions being taken to improve it are not so hot.
•Queue problems.
This... is the big one. Since there are so few people playing ranked in higher tier, queues tend to be pretty terrible. If nobody your rank is queueing (which generally nobody is, because they are too scared to lose elo) queue times stretch for a minute or two, which isnt so bad, but when you DO get a match, it is with someone significantly lower elo than you. Meaning, if you lose, that is 9-10 elo's worth of games you just sacrificed. Basically, just play in tournaments.
Competetive Review: 8/10
I hope you found this review helpful. I highly recommend playing it, and I can't see myself quitting anytime soon. With the ps4 release just happening, and Brawlhalla coming out of beta, I hope the community expans in the best way possible. Thanks for reading.

I don't understand all of these negative reviews about "lag issues". I'm guessing that these people either have terrible internet, or, they are playing on the wrong dedicated servers. There are servers dedicated to your region. Play on those and you won't have lag issues. Now, on with the actual review.
Okay, this game is basically a modern version of call of duty from back in the good old days. You get to play as the different classes available and unlock upgrades just by playing the classes. You can then customize the classes in any way that you see fit. Whether it's for more survivability or for some more damage, you can basically have it however you want it to be. You level the classes, which in turn levels your acutal in game level. There are even custom skins and outfits for your weapons and characters that you actually don't have to pay for. Yay! Another great thing is that almost everything is well balanced. I mean, it's obviously not perfect, nothing is. But it is definitely the most balanced out of this style of game that I have seen. The weapons aren't overpowered, the character's perks are just right for each class, everything just seems well thought out. Not saying this game is perfect because it definitely does have some flaws that I am hoping they will eventually fix. First of all, the spawns. Spawn trapping is very common on certain maps, and is even more common on certain game modes. Another negative would have to be the way that some of the maps are layed out. On one map in particular, it is nearly impossible to get out of your spawn because of the way that the spawn is layed out. Now here's the real question; would I recommend this game? Of course I would. After my 7.5 hours of gameplay on this game, I can safely say that it is easily worth 25 even 30 dollars, but only costs 12. And if you can get it on sale, I would highly recommend suggesting a friend pick it up with you or even being the kind hearted individual you are and buy it for them!

Sorry guys, I wanted to like this game.  If I ever learn it, I may even still.  However, the game is not for me.  Overly complicated management systems are fine when they are less obfuscated.  The tutorial teaches you the very basics, and then you are thrown into a set up limited turn scenario where you cannot waste turns figuring things out.  I cannot figure out how the economy works.  Some of that may just be that I am currently playing multiple games and don't want to spend the hours trying to learn it.  There are only a couple lets plays, and they move pretty quickly and either don't explain, or spend 15 minutes explaining the history of a feature in Roman civilization rather than how it functions in game.  I get it, some REALLY love Rome. I enjoy but not on that level.  Basically, I learned the paradox games no problem, but this one remains vague.
To top it off, the game engine is a pig.  You resolve a turn, and the game basically freezes until you get to a battle screen.  Turns take 30 seconds to a minute depending.  I hear that the game this engine is from "Pride of Nations" was much worse.  I really want to try the Civil War 2 game based on the engine, I am just afraid at that price that I won't be able to learn it.  I have limited gaming time these days with kids/wife etc, and don't want to spend a week of gaming time learning a system.
The game looks nice, although I have to play in in a crappy low res because the ffonts are so small I couldn't read it.  The game is all about reading text and figures, and I couldn't.  Not only size, but the particular font didn't blend well with the backgrounds thru my tv.  I play paradox games at 1080 with no problem, so I'm not exactly blind.
I applaud the developers, and I'm sure there is a really nice game here.  For me, as a moderate wargame tactical fan, it is just too much when coupled with the bad UI and long turns that you cant even scroll the map during.  If I ever find the impetus to learn the game and put some time into it, I may change my vote.  Not bad, but not for everyone.  Romanophiles and serious warsim people may enjoy a bit more, or if you have some experience with the engine, which I do not.

Got the game, played it for just under two hours, refunded it.
Maps are too small. Gravity concept is underused (each map features a small bubble in which you'll experience reduced-gravity).
Some characters have no movement skills at all, some of them have too much movement (one class in particular can't double jump, dash, or do anything meanwhile other classes have grappling hooks, jetpacks, teleports, and triple jumps).
Class balance is an issue. Assassin classes tank more damage than tank classes because they heal when they attack.
My own personal quips are that cooldowns are too long; reload times are painful on a select few weapons as well.
Deadzo Deluxe weapon skins are not attractive; dulls the weapon color, removes texturizing on them, adds blue neon lines; Game features a loot-crate system (ala Overwatch style) with weapon, character, and sprays. If you like this kind of stuff, cool.
Characters have little reinforcing their character; The "criminal" variants of characters will say the exact same voicelines that the "police" variant of characters will say when using their ultimate, despite having different lines in situations like having low-health or respawning.
UI is too spaced out and is uninformative. Gun ammo can only be seen by looking at a holographic display on your gun, which is away from where your eyes are paying attention; cooldowns are on the bottom left of your screen, which is also **not where your eyes are looking**. For new players, this makes learning the game annoying.
Maps are too small for my tastes; most of them are diluated into 3 areas: 2 symmetrical "team" bases, an open circular area with a low-gravity field around it. Too many closed areas encourage the shotgun-esque classes to camp in their bases, and the long-range/mobile classes to just swing around the middle low-grav area and hold left-click.
I would suggest avoiding this game and picking up a different FPS; Nexon isn't a very "trustworthy" publisher either to be honest. With FPS ventures such as Counter Strike: Zombies and Combat Arms behind them, they clearly don't know how to manage a competitive shooter for long-term prospects.

I am a fan of historical wargames and obtuse strategic simulations, so I picked this up on sale. Generally speaking it has all of the necessary components for a historical wargame. The battles themselves are quite hands off, the game focuses on the logistics leading up to a battle and then the calculations are made. It seems reasonably well researched, though it's more of a spreadsheet than an immersive experience as a Roman general/politician/powerbroker.
However, what leads me to caution others about the game is the extremely poor optimization. The load times are bad, things get kind of choppy and unresponsive, and it just makes the whole experience a drag. You know this game is going to be a time investment to learn, and that poor optimization is going to drag the whole experience down as it aggregates. In this day and age, the discerning wargamer doesn't mind playing a game that could have been made in 1994, but it is expected to run fast and stable. As such, I cannot reccomend this game, unless you are an absolute fanatic of either Roman History or historical wargames.
I will happily change my review to a reccommend if they improve the optimization. Until then, stay away, especially at retail price.

Total War: Rome II is fine for the plebeian masses, but for the true Romanophile there is Alea Jacta Est.
Not only does it include some of the more popular conflicts such as Caesar's civil war and the slave revolt of Spartacus (DLC), but also has some of lesser known internal struggles like Marius vs. Sulla, and the year of the four emperors (my personal fav).
For those who have never played an AGEOD game before the learning curve may be a little steep, though not nearly as bad as some of the more complicated grand strategy games out there (I'm looking at you HoI3!)
So, if you're a fan of Roman history like I am, and are looking for something with a little more depth than, 'march army here, capture city,' this is the game for you!

Don't check my Steam play time - game just release at Steam Store, while was selling at Matrix Games Store since 2012.
As I have said multiple times: It's incredible - how AGEod engine can simulate Ancient Roman Wars, American Revolution, American Civil War and finally Great War, despite such a large spread in time frame, each game is unique, - I have never had a feeling that I'm buying same game.
AJE is a good start for new AGEod players, since it provides lots of different scenarios differs at scale and time frame - from "Sulla's First Civil War" till "Year of Four Emperors".
Different scenarios and sides provide unique experience in every aspect of  Roman life at picked scenario period.
And that gives you tons of enjoyment playing AJE.
Nicely drawn unit pictures, detailed map and nice music provides incredible experience of the Rome.
If you're interested in Roman Civil Wars or Rome itself(Doesn't matter if it's Republic or Empire)  and/or you enjoyed other AGEod titles, pick Alea Jacta Est.
Especially with this dirty cheap price tag(60% discount).

Guess stealth games just aren't my cup of tea. IMO The art style of Mark of Ninja leaves much to be desired and the cutscenes (they have the guts to call them movies?? LMAF) are laughable at best. The game lacks refinement overall and seems somewhat crudely put together just to provide a barebones sandbox/playground for the particular group of stealth-loving, assassination-happy gamers. (the designers should really take a good look at high quality 2D sidescrollers such as Dragon's Crown, or even Trine, to see what refinement is!)
In other games stealth and assassination is like an exotic spice that can add to the overall flavour of the game, when you successfully pull off a stealth kill, the thrill and excitement is indescribable. But here, all the enemies are no more than boring, silhouetted dummies, devoid of individuality, whose sole purpose of existence is to be snuck upon and slaughtered. (and the assassination animations are quite disappointing too... it's totally not how I'd imagine a ninja master would assassinate a person) And if the opposing force is aware that they are fighting a war against ninjas, (in one of the beginning stages we see they actually managed to capture most of the ninjas, including the Clan Master, in order to wipe out their Clan) they should be sufficiently equipped to detect, fight and eliminate ninjas (do something about the freaking air shafts anyone?) and their personnel should comprise anti-ninja experts or even ninjas too... but NO they are just some random hired security company employees obliviously awaiting to be ambushed by a shady hideous character lurking out there in the shadows, who utilises his ninja sword like an amigo would his machette, MEH. OK so where is the obligatory justification for all this mindless indiscriminating terrorist slaughter? The victims are just average people like you and me living on a payroll. Oh I forget that they are just silhouetted dummies set up on a crude stage for mass stealth kills to satisfy the insatiable needs of excessive stealth-lovers to... stealth kill, (Ahem) what do I even bring up the topics of believability and justification for? Oh, talking about silhouetted dummies, the main character and his marginally-charming female companion also sadly fall into this category. So there goes character design and relatability out the window. No redeeming quality whatsoever.
Also, the controls and handling lack the fluidity that we almost take for granted with almost any sidescroller in this era of gaming. So what the heck? One example is the repeatedly-mentioned grappling hook issue where the main character just attaches himself to whichever hook point he damn well pleases. *facepalm* And the walk and jump... geez I don't even wanna bring them up at all.

Send your people on missions. The main mission? To destroy the Overlord!! You can lower his level before facing him, by killing his Lieutennants around the regional islands, who are amidst an impenetrable slurry of WIND. This game was all I expected it to be, and more ! I read some reviews and knew it was a nervous infiltration ninja game. I also knew the story wasn't so bad and the art pretty cool.
All of this was true, and more. The game was super fun to play, the levels are deep and engaging, it rewards exploration and trying to navigate your ways out of all the danger is always possible, but makes you think a lot.
The best part was that if you think and try to act like a true ninja, it might work, even in your first run. Being cautious is rewarded, but acting and thinking quickly also.
Only flaw might be that killing guards and other ennemies is highly encouraged, storywise it makes perfect sense, you get points for it and hidding the bodies too. You get a no kill bonus at the end of the stage if you successfully kill no one, but it's much more fun and if you kill 10 ennemies properly, you get more points at the end anyway.
So that's the only flaw, not too bad I guess.
You unlock super cool new skins that grants you new powers and really change the flow of your gameplay. For instance, the tatoo skin lets you teleport nightcrawler like, and it's so cool !!! Another one lets you run without making any sounds and gives you more gadgets, but you can't kill anyone anymore, so this is the best way to get those smooth runs you're looking for.
The art is perfect, think samurai jack but better looking. The story really got me hooked, and the ending is simply perfect.
It's a short game, you'll see the end in 10 hours, but to unlock everything might take some more of your time.
In conclusion, Mark of the Ninja is exactly what it sets out to be, a fun, fast paced infiltration game with a great aesthetic, and more !

This is a barely positive recommendation. Although I have enjoyed the game for many hours it's mainly to finish up some achievements. The game starts off as a confusing mess but it becomes enjoyable once you've figured out how to play it.  However, playing it involves a lot of grinding. Grinding for money, grinding for survivors, grinding for buoys and windmills, grinding for trinkets to make survivors happy, etc....
I personally found the game much more enjoyable in the easiest settings. That way I didn't have to worry about babysitting the survivors and their dispositions for missions. Fall damage is significantly reduced and you will fall a lot!  Money is still fairly tight so there's no getting away from grinding to find  missions that drop the rewards you need.
Still, I've often found myself enjoying the game so much that I play for a couple of hours at a time trying to reach the next continent.   However, after fifteen continents and no new gameplay mechanics or biomes, the game has becomes incredibly repetitive -  kill the lieutenants, kill the overlord, find/buy buoys or windmills as needed and move to the next continent.
There's barely any difference in the gameplay when your character is Level 80 versus Level 20.  All the continents start to look the same and the biomes are identical to each other, there's nothing new and little reason to keep playing.....except for those last few achievements.

Once this game/genre gets the attention and people give it a chance, the community will be alive and healthy.

What surprises me the most is how such a horrible game can actually get good reviews from some people. Let's get a few things straight here.
Pros:
- You're a Ninja with a sword
Cons:
- Grappling hook will OFTEN glitch you through walls, floors, and ceilings, breaking the level and forcing a restart
- Entering combat initiates turn based mode, which disables your ability to do ANYTHING but jump (meaning you can't even pull up onto a ledge you're hanging onto. Your only option is to fall off or jump a different direction)
- Turn based combat is very unrefined and bug prone, meaning that often the player character will not do what it is commanded to do and simply stand still instead. Worse yet, half the special skills don't even work after levelling them.
- Game itself and mechanics are very clunky, you're constantly stopped during movement, can't plan jumps while running, and no indication of enemy detection radius
- Very bland progression, no extra weapons or armours, a tiny handful of special skills which you have to complete annoying bonus objectives to be able to unlock (which is pointless, because half of them don't function anyway)
- Bonus objective of not setting off alarm makes absolutely no sense because of how alarms work. If an enemy sees you, a countdown over their head starts ticking from 10 to 0, at which point a lockdown alarm (which also does nothing except fail your secondary objective) is sounded. If you're fighting 5 enemies at once, maybe 2 of them will have alarm countdown timers, and if you kill either of them, the timer is moved to a still living enemy
- Bonus objectives are ALWAYS present and ONLY consist of the following: Spare Civillians + Kill All Enemies + Don't Sound Alarm
- Gameplay itself is incredibly bland. Game starts with a photo of a bunch of people, one of em circled. You go into a level, hack a bunch of terminals by clicking on them (the only gameplay involved is reaching them through an easy maze of rooms), and then exit the level. The next level will be almost identical with some rooms moved around and re-textured, and instead of terminals, you reach and kill the person who's circled. A new person is then circled on the photo and this repeats until endgame.
- Game is generally not fun, a hastle to play, loads you too far back upon death with a loading screen that takes way too long for a game of this type, and to top it all off, it's most certainly not worth the price tag it carries. I got it on sale for 50% off and I'm still gonna try for a refund.
Final thoughts:
This game makes internal mention to another game set in the same style, a brilliant game called Gunpoint, which has a well written story, characters, entertaining and mind-stimulating levels, puzzles and gameplay, and uses similar level design, jump planning, and window breaking mechanics.
Just looking at this game I thought it was a direct copy of  Gunpoint and the in-game text which directly mentions Gunpoint confirms my thoughts that this is a very poorly attempted copy with it's own spin on the theme. I thought it was by the same devs at first and I was going to complain about how it was possible for them to set such a high standard before failing so absolutely miserably, but then I found out it was a different dev and I understood.
TL;DR - Don't waste your time and money on this heaping pile of trash that tries to rip off Gunpoint and Mark of the Ninja, two absolutely brilliant masterpieces that this was inspired by. Go by those instead, you could get BOTH of them for the price I paid for this when this was on sale at the same time as those

Dry, macabre humour is rife throughout this really tight stealth platformer. From the throwing darts tipped with halucinogenic poison, to an optional side quest to be 'smelled by every dog' during an infiltration, there was a bunch of stuff that tickled me. This game is nothing but fun. The sneaking is satisfying, becoming very fluid once you get to grips with your gear and techniques. It is simply beautiful to play, as well as to look at. At no point did I feel the game had cheated me or that I'd been screwed by a glitch, as has happened to me in many older stealth games. You get caught and or killed when you make a mistake or forget to take in your surroundings before you act, simple as that.
One negative that I have is on my first ongoing playthrough, I haven't had the inclination to try the direct combat approach to negating the bad guys and the upgrades for the combat seem a bit redundant as it stands now. BUT I have not finished the story mode, and this very complaint will probably end up adding value to the game as a whole. I am approaching the end and already I'm planning to replay from the start to try out full on combat as well as also trying to beat the game without killing any of the henchmen or dogs. Because ninja.

If you like beautiful 2d platformers, ninja revenge plots, avoiding laser beams, terrifying henchmen so they shoot each other and throwing dead dogs off of rooftops, then this game is for you.

About the only thing that I didn't exactly appreciate was the fact that we're playing a ninja in a modern setting. If it was set during feudal Japan, this game would have been perfect.
That said, I like everything else about this game. It is one of the best stealth games that i've played in a very very long time. From start to end, this game stays 100% true to the stealth genre.
The visuals are impressive. The level designs are good, and missions are fun. Adding on top of that is an amazing soundtrack.
The game's story is also told in a rather unconventional way. Instead of telling you exactly what just happened, the story of this game is told indirectly at times and needs to be interpreted by the players themselves.
The game also rewards you for taking different approaches (as long as you're not detected). Distracting enemies, smart use of gadgets and environments, striking from shadow, sneaking past guards etc. all reward the player with score. Besides, each missions all have multiple paths and multiple ways of approaching them. This adds quite a lot of replay value and encourage players to try different methods.
If you like stealth games, this one is a must own in my opinion.

It's hard for me to properly express how dissapointed I am with Poker Night at the Inventory 2 when comparing it to its predecessor. However, it's not hard for me to point out all of its extremely blatent flaws so I'll cut to the chase.
If you like playing Texas Hold em' or Omaha style poker for fun, move on. If you like playing Texas Hold em' or Omaha style poker at a simulated friendly table, move on. Now, if you like playing Texas Hold em' or Omaha style poker at an unfriendly table AND having the computer always stack the deck in favor of the other players, then this is the poker game for you.
You are forced to play ridiculously conservatively if you want so much as a chance at winning. Have a pair of kings? The computer gets a pair of aces. You have two pair? The computer gets three of a kind. Bluffing might as well not even exist since even if the computer bluffs with a worse hand than yours, they'll still draw what they need to beat you 80% of the time.
On top of feeling more akin to playing a slot machine with two of its reels broken than playing a fair game of poker, this game's dialoge gets grating fast. Most of the longer conversations in the first Poker Night at the Inventory were still about only two thirds as long as some of the drawn out gags in this game. This wouldn't be as bothersome as it is if you could decrease how often characters talk like in the first game, but for seemingly no reason, this and the difficulty option have been removed.
In conclusion, if you want to buy a fun single player poker game that feels fair with entertaining characters, buy Poker Night at the Inventory and skip this sadly inferior sequel.

I am vengeance! I am the night! I am Batman!
Have you ever wanted to be Batman? Then this is the game to play. You play as, who else? Batman! The game starts as you deliver the Joker to Arkham Asylum where his epic plot against Gotham unfolds immediately.
This is a beat'em up game with smooth, hard-hitting, and satisfying combat. Each punch feels solid, every gadget is quick and and responsive. Running, gliding, and swinging around as Batman is so much fun. There are a few mini-games along the way as well that keep things interesting.
The story is engaging and makes you run as fast as you can to the next goal to stop the Joker and all the baddies in between from escaping Arkham Asylum. For the most part the game is pretty linear with maybe one or two side-quests that really don't have an effect on anything, but that being said, there's nothing wrong with being linear.
I honestly don't have much to say negatively about this game. The overall main story takes about 12 hours to complete, and although the combat does lack variation, the game is just the right length that it never becomes too repetitive (not to mention the boss fights certainly shake it up). I suppose maybe the final boss fight could have been more challenging, or maybe more intricate and less of a "punch the big guy" but I didn't really have a problem with it.
If you love Batman or love hack'n'slash type games, or both, then Batman: Arkham Asylum is the game for you.

Lawbreakers is fast, fun, and full of airborne violence.
With the hero-shooter genre on the rise, comparisons are inevitably drawn between the reigning king, Overwatch, and every other arena shooter that comes out with a class system.
Well, this isn’t Overwatch, but it does have its similarities… but they’re only skin deep. Movement, combat, and pacing feel significantly different than Overwatch, and instead remind me of old school FPS games like Unreal Tournament or Tribes with its emphasis on verticality.
The aesthetics, unfortunately, can be described as “generic” with each character becoming a blurry blob in the frantic pace of battle.
I feel like the internet has spoken on this one: low player count and some negative word of mouth may prevent Lawbreakers from being a mainstay, but that would be too bad. There’s a niche in fast, gravity-defying shooters and it is never filled for long.
It’s a shooter in a sea of them, and it does little to differentiate itself besides having tight gunplay and fast gameplay. I recommend it because it’s very solid, and the price is modest and a good value for the time that can be put into it. Lawbreakers deserves a future.

Now, before you yell at me, just hear me out.
If you are new to the series and want to start at the beginning, then this game is fine. If you're also a lore hunter, then sure, get it. However, I have a different story.
I started with Arkham City and played on a console (
). I instantly fell in love with every aspect of the game: mechanics, exploration, combat, stealth, the whole shabang. At the time, I was only slightly aware of its predecessor, Arkham Asylum, and never bothered to buy it. Then Arkham Origins released. I picked it up instantly, and also enjoyed the hell out of it. Wasn't perfect, but a solid game nonetheless. At this point, I realized that I'm missing a link, but once again, I didn't get it. That's because both Arkham Origins and Arkham City were able to fill me in on enough of the story details to warrant a pass. Finally, after migrating to PC, I hear of a new Arkham game coming out: Arkham Knight. Batmobile included. I miss the first time they sold it on Steam, and had to wait until they re-released it. I buy it, and discover it still performs like garbage. Still playable enough for me to enjoy it, though. As an added bonus, I get all the Arkham games for FREE! YAY! Arkham City in glorious 60FPS! I decide to start at the series' roots, Asylum. This is whre I hit a wall. I play through it, and keep getting unimmersed by the fading 90s Batman feel of the time. Compared to Arkham City, Asylum just felt old. The visuals were good, but the combat was less developed, and the exploration and general gameplay was almost unfinished. Playing through Asylum became a chore, trying to finish it so I could get back to Arkham City. I also realized that the story wasn't exciting enough. I already knew what happened from playing Origins and City. Arkham Asylum was still tied to the old 90s Batman, while Arkham City and Origins were able to take a more creative on Batman as a character.
TLDR: Arkham City and Arkham Origins have much better developed core gameplay mechanics, and they fill you in on all the main events that occur in Asylum, making Arkham Asylum a skippable game in the series.

I'll start off by saying that the aesthetic of this game....is an acquired taste. It's typical Cliff B tryhard testosterone; the voice lines are mostly cringe-worthy, the characters are absolutely forgettable and painfully uninspired, the art direction is Unreal-esque and (imo) unoriginal.
Yet I would recommend anyone with an interest in shooters and skill-based team games to buy this immediately. Why?
The gameplay is absolutely SUBLIME. I, a 28-year old man who--it must be said--is mostly "over-the-hill" with this type of game, found myself UNABLE to stop playing yesterday...it was the most sheer, kinetic fun I've had in a game since...well, since a long time. I'm a devoted overwatch player, and while the obvious borrowing from that game (I don't mean the TYPE of game, but actual abilties) was a bit cheapening, I can't deny that the core gameplay of this game is fire. The levels are quite good. Thus far, I haven't seen many players with mics, which is a shame, because I want to play seriously and it's way more fun when people communicate. Also, the classes are unbalanced as of this writing. There are a couple game balance issues that are FIXABLE and if Cliffy B is hip to this, he will get on them quickly. We know he has the chops to make a mechanically good game. This game, with a big community, competitive scene, and some balance and matchmaking problems fixed, could be a truly huge game, I think. The mechanics of the gameplay are really sound and--besides the aforementioned borrowing from overwatch--quite original in how they feel.
For 30$ you have no reason not to get this. I guarantee you some incredible gameplay...if you can stomach the Cliffy B asesthetic.

It's strange the game that I don't like, but I can say that Always Sometimes Monsters is one of those, if you happen to be reading this before you've completed the game and still aren't hooked with it, do yourself a favor and stop playing, I kept going thinking it would get better and it just didn't. The game is LOOOONG and for bad gameplay reasons, since the story is relatively short, issues like movement and dialogue speed make the game feel sluggish, there are some nice story beats every now and then but ultimately they fail to deliver.
The game promises a choice driven experience which is completely false, your decisions are inconsequential until the final moments of the game in which it boils down to the traditional choice structure that you've seen in a million other games.
I have to give credit where its due, the game starts with promise when choosing the main character and the love interest, but it falls short just a couple of hours into the game when it becomes a snorefest of doing chores and getting X amount of money to get Y or doing X thing for Y to get something in return (which usually translates to money or quest items).
The humor wasn't to my liking, some people may be into it but it felt pretty immature and cheessy. I would also have liked an option to get over your love interest, the whole story hinges on the presumption that the player wants to get back the ex, since there is no way to make your character get over him/her, this makes him/her (i.e. your character) feel unidimensional, stupid, and boring.
Also the game developers appear on the game, their inclusion felt like it didn't fit at all and they wanted to give themeselves a semi-important part on the game, appearing on every single city and even on the epilogue, they felt out of place in the game and the wall-breaking wasn't to my taste.
I can see what they (i.e. the developers) were trying to achieve with this but I felt ike they didn't succeed , nevertheless there are some good ideas which could be rescued and I'd like to see them expanded like documenting a journey or dynamic character interaction based on your main character, so I'll be looking forward to the next game they make, but if possible I'd skip their first stab at accomplishing their vision.
I seriously can't recommend this game there are many other things I didn't like but most of the reviews I've read also cover those issues I had with the game (e.g. save scumming, bad endings all around, incoherent story, dumb stamina system, etc.), if you're planning to play a similar game with a great story and even developed on the same engine I'd recommend playing To the Moon, both your time and money would be invested better in that game.

Stylish stealth murder simulator and turn based action rampage. (Stealth is theoretically optional, but not sneaking around picking off straglers from time to time makes combat sections far more difficult.)
-Story-
The story in Ronin is a straightforward revenge mission with not a lot new to say, and I LIKE that the game really OWNS that. They waste no time telling you things you can readily assume, or that you just don't need to know. If you are interested in this game, then you know the tropes already. You can just jump into the action and fill in the blanks yourself.
-Gameplay-
The first few missions are easy enough, and give you a chance to get some starting ninja skills in your arsenal. A ninja must be sneaky and thorough. Allowing someone to notice evidence of your presence without actively threatening them starts them phoning for help, so stray bullets alerting the next room are almost as bad as them hitting you. Eventually you'll start encountering large rooms where enemies guard eachother from all angles, and even from neighboring buildings. Planning and trickery are required to thin their numbers down to manageable levels before you reveal your presence and start turn-based combat. The difficulty ramps up suddenly in a few places, but fortunately the automatic checkpoints are generous.
-Controls-
The game's controls do take a little getting used to, and when you drop into turn based combat you lose some of the flexibility you enjoyed moving around in real time. That can make certain movement tricks difficult or impossible once the bullets start flying. The jump arc indicator does not take the loss of momentum from crashing into enemies into account, and jumping to corners can leave you in unexpected positions. I also experienced a few places where the grappling hook triggered clipping problems, and I ended up on the opposite side of the ceiling from where I wanted to be. Not ideal, but overall manageable.
There is a downside to the game being so light on text: some of the more subtle mechanics are not obvious. They make complete sense in retrospect, but not having them pointed out is a learning curve. For instance, I see some reviewers have complained that the enemy AI is inconsistent about when they can spot you or not, and that seems to be because those people have not noticed or understood the light/darkness mechanic. A ninja in the dark is undetectable, and an enemy in the dark is easy to pick off. Only by standing in the light do the poor guards have any hope of having the alarm raised and their murder avenged. Fits the ninja theme perfectly, but only obvious in hindsight. Perhaps an addition to the "very helpful hints" could be patched in.
-Sound-
The music is a joy. It fits well with the changing level of action, and doesn't get old even after hours of hearing the same loops. I do wish more of the chapter finales had music as sweet as Chapter 2.
-Time/replayability-
Ronin is a bit on the short side, though not upsettingly so, and I don't know if that is a problem. If the game went on much longer, its sparse story and simple mechanics might start to drag. If you want more of a challenge, or just more game, there is always the New Game Plus. There are a few more enemy spawns, and you get to keep your unlocked skills to be a total badass. A second playthrough doesn't start out much different, except that if the alarm is raised at all you fail the mission entirely instead of just that side objective. It's only when you start encountering large numbers of the upgraded machine-gunners that it feels like the difficulty really ramps up.

One of the biggest issues I had was that when in turn-based combat mode, you cannot jump on a ledge.

Furthermore, the only way to gain abilities (and there are some cool ones!) is by basically performing perfectly in levels. This wouldn't be the biggest deal, but it was very difficult to make it through the end part of the game without having some of the abilities that are 'optional' in this way. But once you get 4 or 5 abilities, this game really shines and the fun is through the roof...when it works.

The first thing you'll notice when you start up Haunted House: Cryptic Graves is that the menu screen is a bit laggy; at the very least, that was the case on my snazzy new (not quite "gaming", but ALMOST "gaming") laptop which handles the likes of, say, Bioshock: Infinite and Outlast without any difficulty.  The second thing you'll notice is that if you go into Options to attempt to rectify this, you apparently CANNOT successfully apply any changes to the resolution.  Oooookay...1920 X 1080 it is (I usually settle for 1600 X 900, but let's splash out in this instance).  You can, however, change the Quality level from "Epic" to merely "High", which mostly solved my problems it seems.  Mostly.  Well, praise Beelzebub for small mercies...

So yes, it's been noted by others before me that this game still has quite a number of technical issues, and it's also been noted that some of the voice acting is a bit sub-par.  While our lead (female) protagonist is well-essayed, the first character we actually lay eyes upon is an elderly professor with all the charm of a rotting rodent who has, to be sure, been somewhat...let us be kind, and say "eccentrically" voice-acted.  It's a well-known aspect of the entertainment industry that no screenwriter who wants to work in Hollywood would dare to place a single word in italics, lest a precious actor be offended by being told precisely "how" to deliver their lines.  Well, the actor here could have used some such pointers, let me tell you, as he seems quite determined to place emphasis on PRECISELY the wrong words and leave pauses in PRECISELY the wrong places.  But hey...the first Resident Evil has some of the most shockingly God-awful voice-acting AND scripting in entertainment history and that game is a ♥♥♥♥ing MASTERPIECE, so let's just get past the nit-picking and start following the man in question down the (both literal and proverbial) garden path, shall we?  (At least for as long as he keeps moving, as he has an annoying tendency to turn around and just STARE at us, the old lech.)

Things fortunately pick up the second we actually arrive inside the house.  In addition to the expected grand entry hall complete with stairs and upper landings which we've seen in a million games before - but which, I must confess, sends a small tingle up the centre of my ballsac each and every time (I truly do love this spooky old♥♥♥♥♥♥) - we also have some modernisms one would be more likely to expect in a recent "ghost-hunting" TV show; lots of electronic gadgets and such.  Hmmm...okay...starting to get quite interesting now, and the sins of the first twenty minutes of gameplay/optimisation are starting to be forgotten.  I then spend the next ten minutes either talking to my charismatic host (who seems to be temporarily caught in "broken record" mode) or searching about and trying the many doors now available to me; I only manage to get one open, behind which is what appears to be a decidedly innocuous and tiny bathroom.  What now?  Erm...I'll try and talk to my companion AGAIN; perhaps he has something new to say now?  Lo and behold, he does!  At the end of which we are abruptly transported to...
A children's bedroom.  Another door I can't open.  The only thing I appear to be able to interact with is a trunk, which appears to have a small trap-door beneath it, but alas...how do I MOVE said trunk?  Basically I end up opening the trap-door, WITH the trunk still hovering precariously above it.  I'm getting a tad confused and bemused, to be sure, but at least I now have a key to open the door leading out of this room.
A corridor.  A plethora of predictably unopenable doors.  One eventually opens, and a few notes, keys and a lever-pull later I'm in an alchemy lab of sorts (there's a couple of reasonably spooky scares along the way here, but I'll just bypass those for the moment and stick to the negatives, since they're far more noteworthy on the whole).  I pick up what appears to be the "recipe" to a spell, and a nearby blackboard apparently allows me to craft spells by pressing "C" (good thing they're telling me what buttons to press in-game, 'cause there's certainly no ability to map controls in the Options menu, so we're flying a bit blind here).  To cut a long story short, it isn't long before I'm now STUCK in my new "crafting" menu, so a re-load appears to be in order...but first of all, let's Google this ♥♥♥♥er and see if anyone out there in cyberland can tell me what the controls are in this confounded game, as I also have yet to work out how to access my Inventory...er, presuming I actually HAVE one (I do keep picking stuff up)...
No faqs - I'll skip the video walkthroughs, thanks, I'm sick to death of those - and a wiki page which is EMPTY.  Metacritic it is, then!  Oh look...this isn't a very well-loved game.  I do, however, pick up a hint from a fellow punter's description of his own gameplay experience, and I discover that I should already know how to use my character's psychic "power".  Hmmm...funny that...there's also something about an insta-kill monster just up ahead, but one thing at a time.  Back to the game, and after some trial and error I discover that pressing the TAB button allows me to see everything in a blue-tinged haze with areas of interest duly highlighted.  Now we may be getting somewhere!  Since it wasn't too far back, I regress a save or two and redo the children's room, again working upon the basis of something I have just read.  Ah, look...I activate my newly-discovered power, interact with some crayons on a table, and now when I return to the trunk I CAN pick up and move the dang-blasted thing, in a "hover-y" manner similar to the Amnesia games!  BEHOLD!!  THE POWER OF CRAYOLA!!!  And yes, shortly after that, I did indeed go down some stairs and meet the insta-kill creature alluded to earlier; a creature I was supposed to be able to see with my power, I believe, but alas all I saw was my virtual self die twice and my real self hit the "quit game" button immediately thereafter.
I could mention a number of other problems this product has at this point - the fact that you can see through virtually every wall in the building simply by walking up to it, the fact that you get inexplicably stuck on anything remotely resembling a nook or a cranny - but what it all boils down to is, and it pains me to say this but...THIS GAME HAS AN AWFUL LOT OF POTENTIAL.  They just need to FINISH the ♥♥♥♥ing thing.  The current state it's in is barely forgivable for an "Early Access" game...and according to the Steam Store page, THIS ISN'T EVEN AN EARLY ACCESS GAME!!!
The developers, Dreampainters Software, released a game called Anna about a year-and-a-half ago, and while I ultimately gave that one a thumbs-down, I did concede that the devs showed definite potential, and declared that I was looking forward to their next release realising said potential.  SO WHY DID THEY GO AND ♥♥♥♥ IT ALL UP WITH A GAME WHICH ISN'T EVEN FINISHED?!  Man, I could almost cry.  Instead, I'm going to suck it up like a man, and wait maybe three to six months before checking this game out again, by which time many of the aforementioned problems will hopefully be fixed.  In all fairness to the developers, they do seem to be doing an AWFUL lot of updates of late, but for now I'm regrettably going to have to give this one a big, fat THUMBS-DOWN.  I do look forward, however, to seeing that thumb do a 180 sometime in the next six months or so...stranger things have certainly happened...
Verdict: 4/10 (for now, at least)!

This game is utterly ridiculous. And it's beautiful for that fact. Blood Dragon has not attempted to take itself seriously at all, and has taken enormous licence with its visual style and licence. And it works. Many of the same assets and mechanics are brought over from Far Cry 3, creating an 80s style open world shooter replete with silly but no less entertaining 80s tropes.
Pros:
- Story is deliberately cliched and exaggerated to make itself stand out, and is not too long as to overstay its welcome
- Completely irreverent, with a self-deprecative sense of humour
- Visual style is very unique, reminiscent of 80s action movie design, with great graphical quality
- Mechanics easy to handle, with a brilliantly stupid tutorial
- Voice acting is excellent
Cons:
- Mission variety not great
- Follows the Far Cry 3 formula reasonably closely but with a tighter scope - the main missions and outpost capturing are satisfying enough but aside from that, collectibles and the same kind of side missions as in Far Cry 3 that use the same formula each time are the only diversions. Fortunately, the game does not last so long as to make its wide open world seem *too* empty.
That said, it's brilliant, and as long as you aren't the kind of gamer that doesn't enjoy irreverant, non-serious games, this is easily worth a look.
8/10 can easily recommend

Coming into this, I wasn't sure it would be for me: I'm not really someone who buys the whole 'games that aren't games' genre but I must admit I was pleasantly surprised.  The early access version is a little on the short side with only three stages but already you can see exactly what the designers are setting out to do.  In it you have to cross a zebra crossing as three different people, a child, an adult and an elderly person.  Each sees the world in a completely different way and through playing as them you get to see completely different takes on the zebra crossing.  The game evoked surprisingly different feelings as each character: intimidation, frustration and happiness.  I'm curious to see what other levels they add when the game is brought out of alpha.  My only gripe is that the music was a bit repetitive as around 15 second loops, even on such short levels.
Anyone who's not sure about it should just go for it; it's free, small and doesn't take that long to experience.  You've got nothing to lose and you might just love it like I did.

All right, let's get something clear right off the bat; just because your game symbolizes something...
THAT DOES NOT IMMEDIATELY MAKE IT A GOOD GAME.
sure you can cram in all the motifs and metaphors you like, but that doesn't give you an excuse to skimp out on every other part of the game, especially if the theme you're trying to put across is so mild and so uninspired that it makes the message in this abstract game so blunt that it hurts.
"Oh but it's early access."
"Oh but it's free."
"Oh but don't you see how they switched the order of the ages so that the last one would be of a kid wandering around in his colorful little wonderland, signifying the renewal of our species with every generation and ending it on a happy and unoffensive note."
That's just the problem! A free, early access game? If it's free then why is there any reason to put it on early access, especially since this is obviously supposed to be an artistic game? Yeah I get it you're proud of your one-week project and want to share it with everyone. but the point of an artistic piece of work is that it is
, not the viewer's. Pablo Picasso didn't ask his neighbor if he should do something different with his cubism, so then why do you find it necessary to ask for the player's input on what
should change about
game.
To address the third counter-argument, not taking risks is not something to condone. yes it's very nice, the kid comes last with his vibrant imagination, wandering around in his happy little world, but the "ending" takes absolutely no risk in fear that it might deter anyone of a sensitive nature. And on that note, what purpose is there to add more levels? do you want to add a level about teen angst? puberty? adolescence? retirement? the minimalist method you have right now fits best, despite my not liking the game whatsoever.

The World Is Grim Enough; Let's Just All Get A Crush Crush.
Ordinarily, the main draw of Clicker-type games is seeing numbers turn into exponentially larger numbers, hopefully with some nice animations to distract from the tedium. But Crush Crush has something I didn't expect from such a type of game: fun writing.  Each of the girls has quite a personality, and even if they all share a love of expensive gifts and rapid-fire flirting, it was a joy to interact with each of them.  There are definitely flaws with this game, such as how some of the special events held over the past year have included cosmetics that were unobtainable without a microtransaction.  But overall, I've enjoyed my time with this game, and I look forward to seeing more from Sad Panda Studios in the future.
Also, you can date a bear.  That's just awesome.

Writing this review for a badge, and because I've played for 420 hours.
It's free and the devs have put in more effort than 95% of other idle games, so the price is right and the dialogue and art is charming.

Having followed this game from an early point in its development, I must say, to this day I still find myself talking about, quoting, or otherwise praising Crush Crush. Sure at first glance it has the symptoms of some two-bit clicker game (micro-transactions, long wait times for anything to happen early on, and time sensitive daily rewards) but beyond that, there's a core of great humor, and rewarding entertainment. The game is not at all perfect, but it's leaps and bounds above any other clicker gme out there, and is a game I find myself coming back to time and time again.
If I had to give it some sort of rating: 8/10
P.S. For a bit more skin, the Moist and Uncensored edition exists for those of us that are 18+

This game was recommended to me by PC Gamer magazine. I am an older game who started gaming in the late 80s with an Atari 2600 and spent most of my gaming years in the 90s. I played on the NES, Sega Genesis, and SNES, all the way up until my parents bought me a Nintendo 64. I also played PC games. Then, I quit my gaming for a while and went to college, focusing my attention entirely on my studies. When I returned to see what the world of gaming had to offer, I was largely disappointed. The entire world seemed mostly composed of boring graphic novels and first-person shooters....That is.... until I met this game. It was like fate.
I can now credit Devolver Digital with returning me back to the world of gaming. At first, I thought it was hopeless out there, but now I see that there are different niche genres out there that will even appeal to people like me. With "Always Sometimes Monsters", they hit the nail on the head.
If you grew up with RPG games like Shining Force, Final Fantasy, Phantasy Star and FAFA's Shadowrun for the console, this will most definitely be a treat. You will feel both at home with your past and yet still very much up-to-date in today's modern world. The feeling is surreal and one of utter bliss.
I just hope they either make a sequel or another  similar type of game. I really enjoyed playing this and did not want it to end.

This game is the closest thing to what I've been waiting for (for a long time). A player needs to be fully aware and adept if they are going to get a point, and no noopie is gonna shoot me down, or even land a shot if I don't want them to. You can feel yourself climbing the skill curve as you identify and master different techniques and combos for every char, then tailor them to fit however you'd like to play. Every success feels well earned - high mobility and speed requires you to be very precise with every action - there's not a lot of success in wildly shooting, you need a plan to win.
The only thing that I can see completing my satisfaction would be a more involving social system. I'm not a fan of the new trend of 5v5 QM with a bunch of randos I'll never see again, and no encouragement to communicate during the match. To keep me coming back to a game, I'll need a group that I can get competitive with, and a server I keep coming back to. Lobbies, leagues!

Next, you play as an old geezer! Like the adult you must pass by the two same roads to go next to another old mans while avoiding the cars passing. In the final level...You play as a kid! You get in the level and you notice the big difference on the rest of them! While adult and old man are the boring and simple black and white, the kid is like "MOTHERF*****G COLORS B****!". The level has colours until you say its so. The content is rather simple. In conclusion...A small, yet strong game... Worth my (and yours) 5 minutes!

This game, simply put, is AMAZING.  I don't really like stealth games usually -- I'm a kid of the 80's arcades, and I want ACTION.  But "Mark of the Ninja" gives it to me in all the ways I like it, while also being an absolutely immaculate stealth game.  And you know what?  I've actually ended up getting MOST of the stealth-related achievements at this point, which really says a lot about the game.  I just don't have that kind of patience for the most part.
The game controls like Ninja Gaiden wished it could, with the addition of a grappling hook and said stealth elements.  It really does feel like being a fkn ninja when you play this game, and for anyone of my generation (I am 31) I think I can speak soundly for all of us in saying THAT is a good feeling! :)
Anyway, watch the videos, read the other reviews, etc. etc. if you want to know more about the gameplay.  The game has excellent UI and controller support (how I've been enjoying the game myself) and a fully-featured options menu, so that's really all you need to know there.
ALSO, the DLC content is exceptional as well.  Although at writing I have yet to finish the main game (tho I *am* on the final mission), I finished the main DLC chapter months ago -- and it was also very, very good.  The additional weapons and unlockable content translate over to the main game as well, so I wanted to mention that.  IMO the entire thing is a VERY solid buy.

I always enjoys the immerssion aspect of narrative-driven gaming and I tend to go out of my way to interact and cherish all npc interactions in game. I have 75 biocell and 14 praxis that I haven't activated it.  Believe me, I try my best to maximize the points I gained from hacking every hackable objects.  I don't that reviewers should based the review of the game on microtransactions and dlc practices, but that is just my opinion.

RONIN is what I'd catergorize as a turn-based action strategy game.  A fun, if slightly underexplained mechanic is its combo system.  Learning to manage your combo meter to pull off your coolest moves is part of the fun.  If you want a game that let's you both control the action and makes you think about your next step and strategize I reccomend it.
As for myself I did experience a couple hiccups however.  The first is that when using the grapple gun there are some circumstance where you will end up glitching through walls.  In some places this can even cause you to restart from your last checkpoint, which isn't too bad, as the checkpoints are not too far apart.  The second is that I did not know how to activate the "limit break" ability.  I assumed that there was a "activate limit break key" that I was supposed to use to activate it, but as I played the game I came to understand that limit breaks are done automatically when the combo meter is filled.  If this was explained, I missed it.  If it was not, this could be prevented by simply stating in the brief explanation of the combo meter that when it's filled it will automatically use a limit break to give you an extra turn in combat.
Overall, my experience with RONIN was enjoyable.  The combat is easy enough to pick up but still has a lot of depth.  I'm not sure if it's worth $12 but I'm satisfied with it for picking it up when it was on sale for $8 or so.

This game... Wow. It is going to be hard for me to put in words how much I love this game, but I'll try. I bought this game for $3.99 (Such a low price for such an amazing game!) and was very excited to play it. I load it up, and see the beautifully crafted title screen, which has a close up of the giraffe character (sorry, I am still learning the names) driving their kart. This is a work of art, and should be put in a mueseum. It is up there in the ranks of The Mona Lisa, and Starry Night. This game has a multiplayer function, so you can play online or with a friend locally! This is such an amazing feature. I have grown closer to my family and friends playing this game. Next, is the soundtrack, and oh my goodness, is it wonderful! The songs sound amazing, and never get old! The tracks that are in the game are amazing, and extremely creative. I don't know how you do it, Paul. Next are the characters. There is the giraffe, the elephant, the lioness, the zebra, the rhino, and my personal favortie, the hippo. These characters have a unique playstyle, which makes it fun to play as all of them. The movies you unlock through playing the games offer lore and backstory to these character. Speaking of which, the movies give you an insentive to keep on playing the game. What wacky adventures will these wild animals go on next? That is the question I asked myself as I played, so I raced on, trying to get as much points as I could. I unlocked the dance scene, which costs 5000 points. It showed the giraffe, elephant and hippo dancing in a beautifully crafted room. The way they were dancing was very sexy, (not to mention they were naked!) so shield your child's eyes from that scene. The racing itself controls fluently. I'm a personal fan of the games control scheme. When driving, you don't hold forward, it goes by itself, making this game very realistic. It also stops thumb cramps. The items are very creative, and I have never seen anything like them before! The rocket item you can shoot forward, blasting your opponents out of the way! The bubble shields you from danger, but you can also pop it to surprise your foes! The hammer item lets you hit opponents next to you, making them spin out. My personal favorite, though, is the bannana peel item. It takes the popular gag of slipping on a bannana peel and puts it into a racing game! Truly genius! The AI is very advanced, too. I noticed that the animals were very competitive, and wanted to win first place, like their life depended on it. They even pushed eachother, and even me, sometimes! I guess that is where they get the title 'Wild Animals'. Overall, this game looks, sounds, and controls amazingly. I'd suggest you buy it, if you haven't already.

As a young boy growing up in Greenland, it was a rough beginning to my life. I spent most of my time out of school hunting wolves for dinner with my dad. I didn't have many friends because there was no one in a 75 mile radius of my home. After one season of hunting I had my 8th Birthday. My dad spend half of his life savings on my present. It was this game I had never heard of called Wild Animal Racing. I played it non-stop on my little monitor powered by our sled dogs on a treadmill spinning an electrical generator. I couldn't stop, it was an addiction. The in depth character design and the heartwrenching wins and defeats were all apart of the game I wished to devote my life to. After seeing the 2000+ points being added to my score, I never wanted anything more but to be the best. I spent the next 14 years of my life training and training hard. Every hour I wasn't working to feed my dogs to run the computer, I spent practicing every corner and every secret shortcut there was in this game. I researched it day and night and found a great source for guides and tips, Wild Animal Channel. Doing all this only encouraged me to press on. Then one day I received a letter via my mail pigeon. It read that some important people had been tracking my prgress in the game. They had decided to invite me to McCall, Idaho to compete in the World Racing League Directed by Wild Animal Racing, 3rd Generation (WRLDWAR3 for short). I couldn't stop crying, my dream finally came true. I was going to the big leagues, to play with my heros. Life couldn't get any better. I set off immediately with my dogs and joystick which i used for racing and went straight to idaho. 3 of my dogs drowned on the way there, 6 died from dehydration, but I rode into McCall with 5 dogs left. It was like a whole different world to me, I couldn't beleive my eyes. There were actual people, it was whacky, as we say it in greenland. I was nearly late to the tournement, it was in the basement of a pub off of main street. There was an enourmous turnout and my heart was beating faster than that one time I was almost eaten alive by wolves. This was it, this was my chance to prove myself that I was not just going down in history to be a kid from greenland, no, I was going to be a legend. I sat down in my chair and scoped out the competition. It wasn't much, just a couple of old chubby guys and one empty chair. I was curious as to why this competitor wasn't here yet as the match would start any minute, but I soon found out. The first time I saw Robbie Magistrelli was when he walked on stage, not to mention I didn't even know there was a stage, but the crowd was cheering and whistleing as he waved. He was a tall slim italien man and was wearing all Nike brand, clearly sponsored, and his yellow lensed gaming goggles. The moment I my eyes on him I was filled with rage, but I kept it in. We all sat down and prepared for the race, I was last in the draw and was forced to pick the elephant, which everyone knows is the slowest animal by default, but I told myself it was the racer, not the animal. Robbie was his classic ginger the Giraffe, one of the best picks anyone could ask for. Then we went to choose the map set, World Tour, as it was the only one anyone ever played. The races were close, Robbie was in first by a small amount and I was following close in second, it was a nail biter every race, but the deciding race was the Volcano map. What a intense map that is. At this level of play it was all about the items you get, and wether or not luck was favoring you that day. I got off to a somewhat slow start but it was no biggie, thankfully no one got the bananas the whole round. But as I neared the final curve just a few inches behind Robbie, he sneezed and missed the item box. I saw my oppertunity. I prayed a quick prayer as I picked it up, "Missiles, Missiles please". I grabbed it. Time seemed to stand still, I look to the bottom left of my screen and... It was bubble gum. To this day I never understood the use of it, never understood why it was even in the game! But as I crossed the finish line behind Robbie, as he stood up and the crowd cheered for his victory, I realized something. Life isn't about what you look like, or what possesions you have, it's who you are and what you go thorugh that define you. Realizing it wasn't my fault that I lost the tournament that day changed me, realizing that I was a different and better person because of that experince was arguably the best thing that could ever happen to me. If there is one thing I want everyone to take away from my story, it's that you don't always win, there isn't always a happy ending given to you, but instead, it's what you make of your life that is what it becomes. I'm long time due with a review about Mark of the Ninja, as it's gameplay and way of presentation captivated me from it's first level.
Gameplay-wise the game is an stealth game - but unlike games like Thief series, here you can dispatch your enemies in various ways - if you want to.
You can arm yourself with incredible variety of tools - you can change your skin/cloth, resulting in a different combat style that can alter your health, pool of distraction or offense items, and sometimes introducing unique traits to that combat style.
I mentioned items - you can use sound crackers to throw and distract your enemies, flares to make them dizzy or blind, a good old cardboard box to hide in plain view, or some bombs, plus some extra. In addition, all items have upgrades, for example smoke bomb blocks laser path and vision, but the upgraded one chokes and stuns enemies unlucky enough to be caught inside the cloud.
If you're into more offensive gameplay, you can use darts that will incite terror in your poor victim, who will see enemies in every corner, very likely killing his guard-mates. Or you can use flesh-devouring bugs to make a body disappear or kill someone in a noisy fashion *yikes*, or a spike trap... Besides the straight "kill the poor sod who's targeted" effect offensive weapons are very likely will plant fear in other enemies who see their friends perish, so these simple tools actually have much more strategic usage as it would seem.
Or who need tools? You're a ninja! You can get upgrades that improves your hand-to-hand skills by giving takedown abilities, various ways to catch your enemies off-guard by attacking from above, below, or behind close doors, or you can learn how to float a while after a jump!
The best thing in all of these upgrades that there is no skill tree, no various classes - you unlock whatever you want if you have enough points for them. Said points can be acquired by completing levels with 1-2-3 medals - this require you to get enough points for the three tiers.
And now after mentioning points, back to the gameplay. Getting points is actually really easy, and easy to count on. You can get points for killing an enemy, hiding the body, distracting them in various ways, passing them unnoticed, panicking them, etc, etc. The game is made in a way that it can be completed in a non-lethal fashion (though as story requires you to kill the target, he and his guard in chief are killed in both gameplay styles) and you can still easily get enough point on a level to get all 2 medals.
The game plays wonderfully. Movement is responsive and easy to get used to, the game features a focus mode that's not breaking the game's immersion while let you aim carefully with your tools / re-think your strategy. All the weapons are very easy to use, their indicators are clear, while the whole system absolutely lacks the feel of spoonfeeding. Basically the game features a system that makes really easy to use your gadgets but doesn't really limits you how and when to use them - for good or bad, depending on your choices and the ability of aim that pesky smoke bomb :)
I wanted to point out another feature in the game: New Game Plus. You can keep everything you have from the first gameplay, and the game reasonably makes the game more difficult. Guns will kill in one shot, enemies' cone of sight will be invisible, there won't be visual feedback about how far some noises can be heard, and you too will get a cone of sigh: anything above, below or behind you will be heavily blurred. I was tremendously happy to see such change in the game, because the game's difficulty scales not by the number of the enemies, but making the game technically harder, requiring more attention (Which shouldn't be hard after completing it beforehand)
The game's visual presentation can be seen as plain at a first glance because of the lot of dark areas, but it's really accurate and original. Various styled levels are presented across the game, from the modern city with it's stark edges, catacombs with darkness and decayed, uneven surfaces to the ruins of an old city where most things just want to fall apart, resulting in various traps unique to that few level.   Between the levels the cutscenes use cartoon-like style, which really fits the overall design, and it's really well done - features tell-tale facial expressions while masking parts of the story. Obviously, there's a lot of work in writing the game's story and make the story, design, style, gameplay elements to fit together.
And as a last thing, still part of the graphical feats I'd like to mention one of the game's cutscene (no spoilers) I've found uploaded
and the game's final level as both are gems of the art-like presentation in games - I'm sure I'll remember the closing level of the game in decades, it was so strong and influential, uncovering some things from the story while letting others in darkness. Feel free to look it up, but I won't link it here, being an obvious spoiler.
At the end, if I'd need to rephrase all these things in a sentence of two, it would be pretty hard, as there's so much great things to say about the game, while I haven't found any negatives.
