If you don't want to read to the end, here is the tl;dr:

So, where to begin?
Getting into the game was a bit of a trial.  No full-screen, drop-down settings which didn't seem to work, and no graphics settings to tinker with.  There is also no controller support so it's WASD and mouse all the way. Subtitle text is difficult to read (very cursive) but you might need them because the protagonist's voice is hard to hear.  That's the boring stuff done.
Okay, on with the game then.  The opening grounds are more the setting for a family picnic and not at all ghostly.  Just one slightly curved path past a pile of shiny columns on one side, and what look like Mediterranean arches and Roman statues on the other - a curious setting for a haunted house with 'cryptic graves'.  Never mind. No old trees, no low mists, no overgrown foliage, just plastic-looking grass models that aren't animated.   It's hard not to notice these non-ghostly things because the only other thing to look at is your irritating accomplice: Stan.  He has a maddening habit of stopping dead and pivoting on one heel to face you, say something without moving his lips, then turning his body forward again a moment before his head snaps to follow suit.  And every 3-4 steps he does this same thing, and I was just about ready to punch him when we arrived at the house.  At last!  Finally, I was able to barge past Stan to the doors...
Now, no haunted-house game is complete without a heavy, creaking door slowly opening to reveal a dark interior.  So yeah, you guessed it: no creaking door...  Instead, clicking the doors zaps you back to the opening title screen instead.  Oh!  Has it crashed?  What happened?!   After a delay, the game cuts to you now standing inside the house, robbing you of any chance to hear the doors slam closed behind you (apparently they slammed shut while you were left staring in confusion at the title screen - oh well).   The mouse behaviour has been changed from mouse-look to mouse-click for no good reason whatsoever (a few curse words and bad tempered clicking fixed that) and so I prepared myself for what I hoped was a game that would be ten times better than the opening scene had been....
If you thought Stan was annoying before, he's no better now.  After a few words, he takes to pacing the same route back and forth repeatedly and doing nothing useful whatsoever, so I'm glad he's not on MY pay-cheque.  Oh wait - it's supposed to me playing the game, not Stan, right?  Okay - lots of doors to explore, so I'll make a start.  Maybe Stan will have paced the ground into an escape tunnel by the time I get back.
Now, I was able to recognise the doors easily because, like in any game, they look like doors.  But for any gamers who don't know what doors are, you will be reminded with the word DOOR emblazoned in huge, white letters over them whenever you pass one.  Yet, the game is much less helpful in sharing things you
to know - like, well, how to proceed for starters.  You'll need to know because, whenever you try to open a closed door, a prompt helpfully tells you that "it is not open".  Well, obviously - which is why I'm trying to open it.  After a full trip around upstairs and downstairs without finding a single openable door, I returned to pacing Stan (he didn't seem to know what he was doing either).   I decided to restart at that point because there was simply nothing left to click on except some electrical equipment which non-helpfully pointed out that it was, er, electrical equipment - and yes, unusable.
Confused, I visited old friend Google.  It transpires that what you are
to do is poke pacing-Stan (there is no helpful prompt to inform you of this).  He will then stop pacing to tell you off about your inability to feel anything psychic (unfortunately, you don't get the opportunity to argue: "Well, Stan, the plastic grass and shiny columns outside really didn't help the mood, ya know?").  After that, it's back to trying things again.  Still no doors opening.  As pacing-Stan is the only thing that responds in the game, I finally attempted to poke his eye out with my mouse pointer and yes, I admit that was a little mean of me, but it resulted in him standing VERY close in my personal space and Saying More Things (capitalised for a bit of mood emphasis...).  It seemed that, for artistic effect, someone was pointing a flashlight directly up to his face (Blair Witch style) and his eyes were wide and staring, so I missed what he actually said in that horror moment (oh wait - this isn't one of the game scares...), but I was then teleported into a new area (I guess if I don't know what doors are, it cannot be hoped I could climb stairs...).
I've now visited several bedrooms - and the graphic details are actually really very nice!  The drab curtains, the long-abandoned beds - they look jaded, dusty and forgotten - perfect!  But after admiring this work, it's back to frustration.  The first room I visited (well, teleported to) was a small bedroom with a wardrobe that won't open, an empty bird-cage thing and a child's drawings.  The door out of here is locked (this place sure loves locked doors).  Again, nothing seems to work at first, but it seems you must be VERY precise at clicking a set of crayons.  You're told to hit TAB to see them "through the veil".  Through the veil means a blinding blue and white swirl with strange ghostly noises.  The 'veil' told me nothing about why I was staring at crayons, but I could now drag a trunk around the room, a trunk I could not budge before staring at crayons.  Feel free to send me an explanation that particular connection.   And the game has been pretty much of this nature since.  Nice graphics let down by frustrating and shoddy implementation.
The first scare comes in the form of an entity similar to urban legend's Slender Man (no, not Stan).  It makes a groaning noise then snaps back to invisible (no ghostly fade).  I haven't had any run-ins with it yet.  But what strikes me now is the HUGE missed opportunity of this game to be good.  You can easily see where the atmosphere has been created, a foggy light makes everything a little blurry, the torn wallpaper almost creates the feeling of 'dank' and the bedding looks like it's stayed there unused for 50 years, so that's all nicely done.  It's BEGGING for chilling apparitions!  I'm sure our Thin Dude could be quite frightening if he didn't just jump in as a 2D cut-out and then vanish when you approach it.  Maybe he improves later, but to find out I will have to seriously force myself to continue playing - but I'm not sure I'm up to the task.
I would be cutting the game a little slack if this was an indie by a new developer and it was a couple of quid, but it's an Atari-published title.  The rooms have atmosphere for sure, but it's all let down by frustrating implementation.  I'm not sure whether this will be fixed by any patches.  There has already been (to the developers' credit) patches to fix launch issues, but I think the gameplay problems are likely bigger than any patch.  Sadly, a game I pre-ordered and waited a long time to try, and now I'm disappointed.

First thing you'll notice is that you can't change the settings.  It looks like it's changed but it automatically goes back as soon as you leave the settings page.   This would almost be acceptable if the rest of the game were ok, which it isn't.
On my computer, which runs everything fine, the music pulsates in and out during the opening scene (and other times at random) until you reach the house.  The voice acting is atrocious. The first thing that I really liked about Batman: Arkham Asylum was that Batman kept doing all the things I shouted at him to do in cutscenes. I'm incorrigible in movies; you can't stop me from making jokes about characters and events, pointing out plot holes, and generally riffing on whatever I can. But it seems that the devs took people like me into consideration, because Batman makes essentially no mistakes whatsoever that I could make fun of. Joker's sitting in plain sight and monologueing? "Throw a Batarang at him!" And Batman does. Joker just ducks it.
That's the general thing about Batman: Arkham Asylum. It's like the Die Hard of video games. There's no secret to its success; no magic bullet that makes it great. It's just solidly constructed and well-designed in every way. All of the individual parts have been taken out, inspected, and polished, from the combat to the stealth to the intermixing thereof to the fun story ideas to the voice acting to the...well, actually not the boss fights or cutscene animation, but you can't expect perfection. Overall, it's a very good game, and kept me engaged the whole way through. You (yes, you) should buy it.

As a child you see a fantastical world to be explored, as an adult you struggle against the flow in a dull world, and as an old man your vision gets bad and the world is even dangerous as drivers will just run your decrepid♥♥♥♥♥over if you take too long to cross the street (even if they had already paused).
But symbolism aside, my problem with this game is that the gameplay itself is very frustrating. I suppose you could say "the devs meant it to be frustrating, that's part of their clever symbolism!" Alright.. but it is still frustrating to play!
As the adult trying to get to work the constant stream of people will push you along their little walkway, until you get to the magical invisible wall where they dissapear and you do not, then you navigate a couple more invisible walls until you get to your office. On my first attempt I actually just suicided off the cliff to see what would happen, and apparently "nothing" is the answer as I just stared at a white screen for a while then restarted. And I don't know what the symbolism means for the instant respawn if you so much as graze the side of a stopped car as the old man, but it was a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Then I play as the child, and that's frustrating too! The stairs are arranged in such a way that you can't just run through them, you have to jump, but then all the little flying dragon things can push you off the stairs and you have to restart. I get that it's supposed to be the child's imagination creating some fantastical quest to get to the Candy Realm or whatever, and I know that some people seem to enjoy stairs events in MMOs and what not, but I'm not one of those people. It's just frustrating. And not in any deep symbolic way, but in a "oh f__k this" kind of way.  I'm sorry but as a game that just felt like a horrible first person platforming section, and after a few falls into the lava I couldn't be bothered trying to complete it.
Overall I'd summarize the experience as somewhat interesting and plenty frustrating. But at least the music was pretty good.

I spent about the first three quarters of the game having fun, followed by the remaining quarter of pure tedium. The difficulty ramps up artificially, with various extra capacity of guards expanded without explaining the changes in system through narrative or other means. The trope of "save the character, he's useful, then he dies" is used, as is the stripping away of your abilities for no reason that is gone into. You lose your weapons without that being shown. The plot is beneath me to explain. The guards walk into traps on their own in areas they're guarding and should therefore know about. The guard AI can be broken if a stationary guard (like a sniper) is knocked from their perch. Multiple actions on the controller are assigned to the same buttons, resulting in punching the air when a stealth kill is indicated to trigger via on-screen prompts. The grapple will fire at the locations other than the one aimed at, resulting in being seen by guards or dealing with traps. The slowdown in certain areas of overlapping visual effects (with visual effects switched to lowest settings) is unacceptable, suggesting a lack of testing before release of the game. The visual style is fine for the characters, but the scenery does not convey whether a surface is a wall than can be climbed or a ceiling that can be hung from. Some of the abilities - those around character speed and the amount of noise they make while running - do nothing. The game seems an aweful like an inferior Batman: Arkham Asylum, from the method of kills (like dangling boddies, for instance) to terrifying guards, to halucination sequences, to the pointless, unavoidable walking from the beginning of Arkham Asylum that occurs at least three times in this game (I only remember the one time in Arkham Asylum). One of the many things that can be said for Arkham Asylum here was, as well as proper level design and a working plot (and fun and proper AI), Arkham Asylum didn't have a bit where you dodged endless ♥♥♥♥ing subway trains.
This is a tedius, poorly written, questionably-tested, badly controlling, intentionally unfair mess.
AVOID.

It's a decent game from Tell Tale.  We have the murder-machine Brock Samson from
(highly recommended show to watch), the ever obnoxiously annoying CL4P-TP unit from the
franchise (play the games, they're fun), Ashley Williams from the
franchise (I don't like horror so no opinion), and Sam from the

There are five challenges in total to get through to get the downloadable unlocks, and five felt/chip/card combos to get which have their own set of stories to go with them that don't appear if you only have one or two unlocks on.  The possible challenges are funny, as I don't know if I can actually deploy ninjas, want to take an asprin and call someone in the morning or do the hokey pokey.  Some are challenging as all get out, like "Win with only a high card".
This time around, there is no difficulty setting, which I found disappointing.  The music is amazing, especially the slow piano version of "Still Alive", and the variations on all of the theme tunes, like the opening theme to Borderlands 2 "No Heroes".
The two complaints I really have are these:
1) the game is far too short, and getting the unlocks are too easy for the most part.  I end up deleting all of the saves and starting over, just to keep it interesting.
2) they could have recorded a lot more dialogue, especially for GLaDOS.  Don't get me wrong, the dialogue is really funny, but to be told "Well, that was a clever move that won't come back to bite you in your ample posterior" over and over and over and over and over again gets old fast.  That and their reactions to you going all in.
It took a while for me to get the rules of Omaha, but I finally got it figured out.  Now, if I could only get into a showdown with someone other than Sam...

Cloudberry Kingdom is a game similer to the likes of Super Meat boy however it is strictly horizontal platforming. The game offers a few ways to play.
Arcade: In this mode you select a type of gameplay (Escalation, Time Crisis what have you.) And then you select a cheracter type (Or alternitive gameplay type such as Classic, Double Jump, spaceship ect.) You start out with 15 lives and see how many points you can get. You get points by collecting gems and 25 gems gets you an extra life. Getting a perfect by getting all the gems in a level get's you a multiplier. Every 20 stages the multiplier increses.
Free Play: In this mode you are given a metric crap ton of options such as difficulty and even what obsticles appear and what not. There is loads of replayability since every level is randomized.
Story Mode: You play through a bunch of levels at once. Honestly i havn't gone through this mode an awful lot.
Negitives: Maybe it's my download that sorta crapped out but i see a few glitches. For one the intro where the cheracter is  glitched. It will only show most of the level after a second or two. Moving blocks never show in the intro.
Also the beginning cutscene is......... well you'll find out.
Butt overall a good game.

Other than that the game has very many good points to it that's boosted by the fact that the game comes in at a very reasonable price. The performance is easily great even for lower end hardware. This is not a game that will blow you away with innovation but what it does, it does in a very solid and fun manner. Or how I'd like to call it: NEED FOR SPEED: UNDERDEVELOPED.
No, seriously, this game is objectively a disaster. Horrible handling and physics engine; Horrible optimization; HUGE difficulty spike; brain dead AI; frustrating UI for visual tuning; pointless open world and a completly dumb and forgettable story.
This is the whole package of the game. And the worst part about this? The Steam-version is the unpatched version of the game! If you are thinking: "Well the patched version fixes all of the issues you listed" Then I have to dissapoint you, cause it doesn't fix the issues.
In short, you are an undercover agent who's task is to take down car smuglers / criminals while your partner (I forgot her name, i guess it's Chase Lin or something) "helps" you getting inside the criminal's gangs
or more like: She doesn't do anything gameplaywise. How do you take them down? Well you have to BE a street racer kill hundreds of innocent cops and destroy the city. You don't do anything else "Cop-related" besides the takedown missions, in which case you just have to ram the vehicle untill it's destroyed. You don't have access to back up or anything else and I guarentee you that you will even forget that you are an undercover agent. It would've make more sense if you were a street racer right from the start, getting caught by the police and then being tasked to take down those criminals for you not to land in jail. There are also unnecessary "Plot-Twists", but I'm not going to spoil them.
Like I said, the handling feels completly out of place. The cars feel like they have no weight (You'll quickly notice that if you try to ram your opponnents) and you either turn unnaturaly fast and slam into the wall, or your car won't turn at all.
In addition to the handling the physics of the game make everything worse. Later on in the game, your car is going to constantly jump at crucial curves in which case you will always slam against the wall and loose most of your speed and getting taken over by the opponnents, since they can turn 90° at 250-300 km/h. That's right, the enemy AI (Not cops included) have one of the weirdest rubber band effects you will ever come across. They will mostly be on your tail and drive almost flawelessy with redicilous handling and they will require you to drive perfectly. Using the ideal line most of the time and not even strafing the wall, since you loose around 20 km/h and you can't steer for a second. And you will also be at the mercy of the AI, hoping they crash somewhere so you have some breathing air.
The only type of races you get are:
Sprint
Circuit
Checkpoint
Outrun (1 v 1 Races in the open world, be the first one for a specific time)
and Highway Battles (Thats where you are at the mercy of the AI the most, if you try to dominate the races)
There are also Cop Chases but they are neither fun, not challenging or anything else. It feels completly tagged on and I think it's even possible to complete the story without doing any of those.
It doesn't matter if you have the latest hardware, the game will always have performance issues. I have a ASUS GTX 1060 Strix OC 6GB, 8gb RAM, and an FX 8350 and the game still gets at around 10 fps at specific points and in combination with the incredible speed, the game becomes unplayable at times.
This is one of the biggest issues of the game. At the start, the game becomes super easy and you will outrun your opponnents with ease. Later on, in order to even win a race, you have to dominate it with 10-30 secs faster then the expected time for that. If you don't know what I mean with "dominating", it's basically a time limit you get to complete a race, it's like an extra challenge ontop of winning the race.
Another example: The game has a challenge series similar to Most Wanted etc. where you are given a specific car and task to do in order to complete it. Now imagine you are given a BMW M3 with max speed of 314 km/h and you have to race a Porsche Carrera GT in a Highway battle. You know what happened? I lost multiple times after 20-30 seconds passed since the race started because the opponnent just outran me, eventhough I was at max speed the whole time and didn't crash once. And you can't switch the car, since it is given to you for that "challenge". You just basically have to hope that the opponnent's car is going to crash in order for you to even have a chance to win.
I could go on with the issues, but I won't, since the character limit will prevent that.
If you can look past those flaws and have fun with the game, then it's good for you.
But if you think, that this game is objecively a good game, then you are free to provide counter arguments.
Otherwise:
Don't even bother with this game.

I've had this game recommended to me for months now, and I finally got gifted a copy. Boy, am I glad it was a gift, i would have been♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off otherwise.
As much as I've been told the story and choices/morals in this game are so good, I find it to be pretty damn bad.
The characters for starters are so unlikable it's almost criminal. The player character is such a total ♥♥♥♥-up (even when you are trying your best to be a good person with your choices) that he/she is totally unlikable.
There is a difference between making a character likeable and charismatic AND also flawed. That is good writing and necessary. It also gives you room for a good character arc and growth. But when your main character is instead a flat stereotype of a total screw-up and you are given no incentives to like them, it's impossible to get into the the story or care about them.
The rythm of the game-plot is also slow as molasses and that is also a BAD writing thing. Difference between a slow-paced beginning and a boring one, folks. DOn't make me wade through hours of♥♥♥♥♥♥to get to the good stuff. A story can have a slow start and still grip you, it HAS to. A movie/show/game should get your attention right away (and I'm gonna give you a clear example of a game that gets your total attention in the first 20 seconds: GHOST TRICK).
I also immediately felt like the choices I was making were meaningless and just chores to give me the false illusion of autonomy, thus ruining the immersion further; and the daily tasks/quests are not fun at all.
The music gave me a headache after less than 90 minutes of playing.
In short, if you want a gripping, well-written game with a real moral system and an enjoyable experience, this one is not up to the task.

Early on in the game I save-scummed for money by getting all winning $50 scratch cards and winning constantly at rock-paper-scissors. "Haha!" I told the game, "I am beating your system and successfully keeping my character from ever doing anything monsterous or ending up in too bad a position!"
Then I realized that it was me all along. The person always sometimes being a monster was me as the player gaming the system to give my character a good pool of money she wasn't supposed to have to dip into. So I went "Well then, let me be evil!" and outright used Cheat Engine to give myself thousands of dollars, because if I was going to feel like the game was judging me for my actions I might as well go all out!
I'm recommending the game because it has a well-written story that kept me interested until the end, but let you warn you going in that it can be a slog. The game is full of unpleasant characters and situations that always try to go worse for your character. Even if you try to keep your hands as clean as you possibly be can a good hunk of the game characters will still treat you like dirt (although, to be fair, that is realistic for folks who are trying to turn their lives around after hitting rock bottom). And if you try to keep your funds up the honest way you'll quickly find that the minigames you do for work are dull as ditchwater, in a deliberate commentary on how mindnumbing minimum-wage jobs can be by the developer. Don't play this unless you don't mind a story that treats you like that! But for me personally I found it a fun challenge to try to hunt down (in most cases just having money isn't the answer, my cheatiness mostly just kept me from having to do unpleasant things for food) the "good" choices through any given scenario when they weren't spelled out for you, and I imagine that other people would have an equally fun time seeing just how monstrous they could become!

I spent about the first three quarters of the game having fun, followed by the remaining quarter of pure tedium. The difficulty ramps up artificially, with various extra capacity of guards expanded without explaining the changes in system through narrative or other means. The trope of "save the character, he's useful, then he dies" is used, as is the stripping away of your abilities for no reason that is gone into. You lose your weapons without that being shown. The plot is beneath me to explain. The guards walk into traps on their own in areas they're guarding and should therefore know about. The guard AI can be broken if a stationary guard (like a sniper) is knocked from their perch. Multiple actions on the controller are assigned to the same buttons, resulting in punching the air when a stealth kill is indicated to trigger via on-screen prompts. The grapple will fire at the locations other than the one aimed at, resulting in being seen by guards or dealing with traps. The slowdown in certain areas of overlapping visual effects (with visual effects switched to lowest settings) is unacceptable, suggesting a lack of testing before release of the game. The visual style is fine for the characters, but the scenery does not convey whether a surface is a wall than can be climbed or a ceiling that can be hung from. Some of the abilities - those around character speed and the amount of noise they make while running - do nothing. The game seems an aweful like an inferior Batman: Arkham Asylum, from the method of kills (like dangling boddies, for instance) to terrifying guards, to halucination sequences, to the pointless, unavoidable walking from the beginning of Arkham Asylum that occurs at least three times in this game (I only remember the one time in Arkham Asylum). One of the many things that can be said for Arkham Asylum here was, as well as proper level design and a working plot (and fun and proper AI), Arkham Asylum didn't have a bit where you dodged endless ♥♥♥♥ing subway trains.
This is a tedius, poorly written, questionably-tested, badly controlling, intentionally unfair mess.

Overview: The game has been practically abandoned by the developers, promising completion but never coming close. Bugs, bugs, and more bugs that will never be fixed because of the push for new content to keep people buying. PLEASE DON'T BUY IT! I'M BEGGING YOU!
In Depth: It is straight up sad how this game is. I saw people on youtube play it... they always seemed to have so much fun playing, that it made me want to buy it. When it finally went on sale and I had some extra cash in my wallet, I purchased it. I was immediately dissapointed to find out that 1. there was no single player. 2. the multiplayer was slow and unreliable. The developers only add new content, paying little to no attention to the constant bugs, making the game practically unplayable unless you have an exceptionally strong computer. I've never exactly been a huge fan of the 2D stealth concept. I feel like having your entire enviroment on display cheapens the effect of having to constantly be thikning ahead. You no longer need to take time to methodically scan the enviroment for patrols, traps, objectives, exit points, and I feel that this is what makes stealth games so appealing. A truly good thief/assassin/infiltrator/etc is the one who can make it in and out of an area without every tipping anybody/anything off. It's a mix of strategy, patience, anxiety, freedom, accomplishment and shifting enviroments that I think make a good stealth game truly great.
I'm excited whenever I see or hear about game devs trying new things because that's ultimately how you end up with  enjoyable games like "Mark of the Ninja". An engaging game with a solid premise, fun gameplay and enough replay-ability to keep you coming back for at least a little while. I wouldn't throw it into my top ten, or call it one of the best stealth games ever made, but that doesn't change the fact that it's still a solidly made game for people who want a good mix of platforming and sneakity sneaks.
The basic premise is that you are the champion warrior of one of the last know ninja clans left in the world. The clans refusal to move forward into the modern age, mixed in with disrupting local gang activity, leads their elders to enact the most desperate plan they have in order to ensure the clans survival. You are outfitted with tattoos made from a special ink that is dervied from one the most rare plants on earth. Your clan is the only group that knows of its exsistence, and it's been their fallback, as well as a major source of their power, for hundreds of years. Whoever is marked with the ink gains incredible powers (the ability to stop time, teleport, hightened senses and strength), but it comes at the cost of their sanity. Before they take the ink, they must swear that after the have completed their mission, they will end their own lives. This keeps them from going power mad, and keeps the clan safe from those who wish them harm.
I do really love the concept of a power that hinders as much as it helps. You get something that other people only can dream of possesing, but at the cost of something you know you can't live without. This is one of the strongest parts of the story, and you can tell that the writers think so as well. The inks negative influence on the characters mind becomes increasingly more apparent, and disturbing, as the story progresses. This is, however, one of the only strong parts of the story. The rest of the story itself isn't by any means bad...just a bit shallow. It doesn't really pick up until around the half-way point, and then just sort of falls short at the end. Without spoiling anything, there's a pretty neat little twist right before the finally mission, and it's very cool in regards to the whole "losing your mind" thing, but the end just sort of leaves you without any kind of feeling of accomplishment. Again not bad, just not that great.
The gameplay is what really holds it together, and is probably its strongest point. The stealth isn't exactly keeping you on the edge of your seat and it doesn't really challenge your strategy skills, but there is a lot to be said for the sheer joy of just waiting for a guard to turn, and the absolutely wrecking them with a sword; or, if you're the passive aggressive type (like me) who just likes the sadistic joy that comes from mind♥♥♥♥ing with NPCs, you can always throw a posioned dart at an enemy that causes them to panic and just watching as they point-blank shoot their comrade straight in the face. The platforming and stealth flow together suprisingly well, and it does give off this very neat vibe of puzzle solving, so even if it isn't exactly the rubrics cube of stealth you're still going to feel accomplished.
Overall, "Mark of the Ninja" is a game I would recommend to anybody who enjoys platformers or stories with a psychological edge to them. It has replay value and enough features to make up for its short length, plus plenty of entertainment for people who are just looking for a fun, challenging ♥♥♥♥ around game.

I loved this game!  I have never played a game with a combat system like this one has, but it was fantastic. In two different missions, as a result of using the grappling hook, the player character got stuck in what are normally inaccessible rooms.  Since I couldn't replicate the bug to escape the rooms, I was forced to restart the level both times.
I saw that the default graphics options have anti-aliasing turned off.  I turned it on and, when starting a new mission, the game caused Windows 10 to completely crash, showing the blue screen of death.  This happened consistently for me until I turned anti-aliasing back off. (I have a GeForce GTX 970M, so I'm guessing it's not the GPU.)
As a minor complaint, I am colorblind and there is a heavy use of the color red to show hazards (Lockdown countdown and mine circles, specifically).  I died several times from simply not seeing the text and circles because the red blended into the dark background for me.  Red with a white outline would have greatly improved that for me.
Overall, it's still a fun and challenging game that is highly recommended.  Just be prepared for some bugs.

This game reminds me of old Flash platformers, and I mean that in a good way.
Ronin is a fast-action platformer modded to be a turn-based combat game. This has its pros and cons.
On the one hand, playing this I got a feeling the devs had a good grip on their own gameplay system, enough to keep every new level fresh and more challenging than the previous one. Challenging, and not frustrating, which by itself earns the game a lot of points in terms of design. The game's elements are reactionary, so no two playthroughs are the same, and yet the game always manages to bring out a challenging puzzle-platforming experience. The fact that a lot of what goes on in Ronin isn't pre-scripted says a lot about the robustness of the gameplay.
The robustness of the game itself however is questionable. Playing the newest version as of 10/15/15 on Windows, I've seen the wall-phasing glitch too many times to name and had the game freeze up my computer (though I've yet to replicate this).
Even though I've been gushing about the gameplay, all that comes with a huge caveat. Ronin is basically played in two modes: the first, in which you move freely and can execute stealth techniques on enemies, and the second, combat. Combat is tight and well executed, and the game's movesets lend themselves really well to turn-based battles. The free-roaming, not so much.
This is just my opinion, but playing through the stealth and free movement segments I got a nasty senseof stiffness. The precise jumping controls that make combat so much fun are kept up in non-combat play, and as a result moving around just feels really stiff. I understand that the game is meant to be paused every few seconds, but doing so much as traveling through a ventilation duct feels jerky and unresponsive. If I had to ask the devs to add anything, it would be smoother controls for out of combat gameplay.The hookshot especially is a sore point for me. Usually, when using the hook you'll pull up short and dangle a bit before zooming in to your desired location; this is fine out of combat, but in battles the wonky swing physics become really noticeable. Again, if the devs were to change anything, I'd urge them to tighten up the swinging mechanics.
These complaints aside, Ronin is extremely fun and very challenging. The atmosphere is fantastic, and the Samurai Jack-style art suits the game perfectly.
At the end of the day, it's a fun and challenging platformer that could really benefit from some tightened-up out-of-combat controls and some bugfixes.

This game is great but it's plagued by several problems that prevent it from living up to it's full potential.
NEGATIVES- First of all the UI is just awful and makes world building a very tidious and time consuming task which is horrible considering that the game revolves around this concept. The key bindings are at best tricky and at worst terrible: the game uses WASD for moving, arrow keys for moving the camera (you can use the mouse to do this too, but it does so really slowly), and XFGHJKLI are for menu selections. I (i) is strangely used for both switching between Macro & Micro modes and favoriting items in the item select, which means you'll probably end up with a ton of favorite items, just be careful to not press J and use them by accident. This game really needs to make use of shortcuts in it's UI to make menu navigating easier. Also game saves can't be personalized which means you'll end up with the load menu being cluttered with saves and with no way to delete any of them. The tutorial was a bit of a chore and really held your hand for the first 15-20min of gameplay and the Freeplay mode could use some work as well. Some of the creature models could be improved, as many similar species of animals use the same model just colored differently. I was also disappointed that there were some scientific inaccuracies in the games library entries such as Dimetrodon being the first reptile or Plesiosaurs and Pterosaurs being dinosaurs. I also wish that there was a larger variety of Dinosaur species instead of the six currently present. There are also a few bugs present in the game but that's to be expected from any game on opening week.
POSITIVES- Despite the negatives this game is very addictive and there are so many possibilities for different worlds to create and what lifeforms will be born. Some of the animal models and animations are amazing and help add a little bit of beauty to the world. The game mechanics for birthing and extinction work well. It's a well thought-out mechanic, mostly relying on the worlds temperature, humidity and elevation, but with other factors such as pre-exsisting species thrown in. In order to get the next species on a tree, you end up dropping or raising the temperature to balance the pre-existing organism, and the one you want it to evolve into. This can be a pain sometimes when you want to maintain the current ecosystems but it works very well.
I believe that after a few updates to fix controls and other aspects of gameplay this will become a very very good game.

There is quite a bit of fun to be had here, but the game does suffer from many technical issues.
The first thing I'd like to mention is the controls.  While I feel like I have a good grasp of them now, I would certainly not call them intuitive.  For example, selecting an item from your inventory requires you to press "k", use "f" and "h" to scroll through your items, and then press "j" to use the item.  I believe this was done to allow you to keep moving using wasd while going through your inventory, but I just didn't find it practical.  As others have noted, there are currently no options to rebind keys.
The other main technical issue I had with the game is just a general lack of options.  There are almost no graphical options outside of setting the resolution and full screen or window.  I've noticed many of the reviews for this game mention that they are unable to run the game at a playable framerate, so it's important to know that if the game runs poorly on your machine there's not a lot of options to try to fix it.  I haven't experienced these issues myself, the game runs at 60fps for me most of the time, although it has dropped to 50 for a few seconds a couple of times.  For reference I'm running this using an nvidia gtx 970m, i7-6700hq, and 16gb of RAM.
As far as gameplay, the only real issue I have with the game is a lack of feedback.  This is much more noticable in the tutorial when you're required to try and create certain plants or animals.  I often ran into situations where I met the requirements for the species to be born, but couldn't get it to appear and there wasn't anything available to me to explain why.  The same goes for species going extinct.  I would get warnings that a species was about to go extinct, but no explanation as to why.  It would be much more helpful to have "animal x is about to go extinct due to warm temperature" or something along those lines.
All that said, I have still enjoyed my time with this game.  I found the aesthetic charming enough that I felt it added to the experience.  Shaping the land in a specific way and getting new life forms to appear felt rewarding.  I recommend this game if you have a computer that can power through the poor optimization and you're willing to fight through the controls.  Otherwise, I would recommend holding off for now until they start patching these issues.

This game is an Arcade title synonym of cash well spent.

The platforming of this game is in fact a work of art, not only it's exhilarating to finish a stage and perform multiple jumps in a row dodging fire balls and spikes and moving platforms, but the AI in charge of creating the Infinite Possibilities of the stages is brilliant.
Infinite Stages - AI.
The design and work done on the Level Director AI is amazing. You can customize the types and amount of obstacles in a stage on Free Play, and the AI will pick Specific places to add all the flaming wheels and spikes you want that will Guarantee the level to be both challenging and beatable. Even if you max out the sliders to add every single piece of challenge into a stage and the screen is Filled with things you can't begin to pronounce without getting killed, you can activate a computer AI to display the correct path of the level, and sure enough, it's always there. It's also somehow very visible even at the hardest stages, takes time to nail the correct time to jump and run and stop, but just by starting the stage you can see that there is a way out. Also another thing done very well is that most of the "Correct Paths" on stages are in sync with the time you Start the level, meaning there's almost never a time which you need to stop and Wait too long at starting a level, ensuring quick respawns and retries and a fluid gameplay which you can beat a level, and play the next, over and over and over and again.
Soundtrack.
The soundtrack is definitely one of the best parts of the game, it hypes up the gamer to complete the objectives while adding a fun ambiance to each stage, so that even if you fail you are still enjoying every bit of it, and when you succeed every jump in sync with every beat of the song feels fairly rewarding.
Story Mode.
Story Mode features a very good Game Mode for new players, starts up on new and fairly simple stages introducing new objects and traps along the storyline followed by a very cool animation cutscene in each beginning of Chapter. It gets of course increasingly difficulty but the level design is done incredibly well, in the sense that starting at Chapter One and progressing to Chapter 6 you definitely feel skilled enough to take the challenge and well practiced on the mechanics of the game.
Game Mechanics.
The main features of the game are the ability to customize your character with all the available items and colors for you to have a more personal experience when you play all the stages, and all the Game Modes, while playing Story Mode you are introduced to most, things like "Double Jump" "Jetman" "Wall Level" and many others, to add to even more replay value and different challenges. Also having a very good Local Multiplayer up to 4 gamers to have a blast and face stages. The jumping at first definitely feels a bit "heavy", but being able to hold the jump button to achieve maximum height fixes that with a bit of practice, and works very well on the entire game. Providing precise jumps with precise controls to avoid precise and massive amounts of traps.
Overall, amazing game, fun and hilarious Arcade Title. Well worth for you to play it by yourself, or with friends.
Is the kind of game that if you just want to run a cool fun and quick game to play it for a bit while waiting for a pizza or something, since you already beat the entire Story Mode once you played it for the first time. This is definitely it, right along games like Mario, Sonic, and other Arcade titles that ensure fast and good entertainment.

What can I say.
Positives.
The graphics are absoloutely amazing. Shame you can't tone it down a little more.
Animation is smooth and elegant, as they should be, especially if it's a sneaky ninya game.
The way they've implemented how you can "see" sound, so to speak and the field of view of your enemies is a new and pretty awesome add to a stealth game.
The way light is shown, and the fact there's a difference between being spotted and detected make for some incredible stealth kills.
A majority of the puzzles are riveting, and sometimes even confusing. Which is exactly what a puzzle should be like. In my opinion.
The equipment you can get and buy depending on how well you did in the previous levels are absoloutely superb, especially the box. A different combination of different distraction items, attack items and even your costumes, can make for a gripping and almost irresistible new gameplay every time, creating one of the greatest replay values I've ever seen in any storyline-orientated game. Even then, each costume alone creates a whole new gameplay, sneaky sneaky, terrory-makingy thing, super damage man ninja, and quite a few more. AND EVEN THEN you can decide to try and play the opposite game-style that that costume is trying to help you/make you play (that was clear).
The story is also really confusing yet also mesmerising, as there are many different signs, implying many different things. Unfortunately this doesn't mean you can have multiple story lines depending on how you play the game, or different endings, but it does make you think. Which is awesomeballs.
The art on the main menu is absoloutely delightful.
Negatives.
(I had to spend quite a long time trying to think of these)
First of all, the Mark of Serenity. Absoloutely ruins the game. You can use it in pretty much any puzzle, ruining that. Ruins all the running around and wall-climbing etc that makes the game so fun, and last, but not least, and probably not even last, ruins pretty much the entire game (If you use it, of course).
I found the first play through a tad bit easy, though it did get harder nearer to the end, as it should. However, I would have liked to have seen a bit of a difficulty choice. I am aware of the New Game + at the end, though I would have preferred to see something similar at least, in the main menu.
NITPICKINNNNNNNNNNNNG D=
The main menu could also have a "Load Game", "New Game" type thing going on, but it doesn't. So yeah.
This is not so much as a negative but more of a "What would make the game better" type thing.
Can't think of much so here's one, and I think they would probably do this anyway but. Maybe add more costumes? More equipment and maybe a side story, similar to what they had to "Dosan's Story". Maybe have Azai's story or something like that. Maybe a whole new story line for Dosan, I dunno. It has great replay value nonetheless.
All round, this game is an absoloute blast, definitely worth the £11, and alot of the negatives are nit picks and the Mark of Serenity is something you could easily not have by just having another costume, since it's the only positive on the Final Mark costume. I say costume alot, I should stop.
All in all, I would without a doubt, highly recommend this game to absoloutely anyone who enjoys stealth games. Like pleaseit'samazingafyou'llloveit.

Yes, I'll recommend this game, but with a caveat. If you want to play Texas Hold Em or Omaha, just those card games, then there are better titles to do that. If you want to be entertained while you play, and the winning or losing isn’t really a big deal to you, this game is perfect.
You’ll sit down with Brock, Claptrap, Ash, and Sam in either of the two games above. While you play the characters will converse with each other telling silly stories and generally doing their best to entertain you.  It’s fun.  But god damn you cannot skip ANY of the dialogs, and you can’t do anything until they finish sometimes.  So you are in the middle of your turn and then you’re sitting there, sometimes for a minute or two, while they have their interactions. It really slows down the game play.
If you want to just play cards, they are a distraction.  And when you’re over them talking with each other, they are a bigger distraction.  Combine that with the truth of things (they repeat conversations eventually that you can’t skip) and you come to realize that as a card game it kind of sucks, but as a Telltale character game it works just fine.
It’s fine.  It’s Texas Hold Em with silly characters.  If you like that it’s fun.  It’s not a bad game.  It’s not buggy, the stories and interactions work. It’s just much slower than you’ll probably want your card game to be.

So I replayed this after some years passed, and as an avid NFS-Fan of the older titles, I wrote this review.
The open world, while boring looking, has many alternative paths and offroad-streets.
Good choice of cars (although I wish there were more older japanese vehicles).
Great modification (visual upgrades are on the same level as NFS:Pro Street).
Gameplay is very similar to the likes of NFS:Most Wanted and NFS:Carbon.
Horrible driving physics: Cars feel washy and oversteer at the same time, it's just weird.
Crashing into cops isn't as exciting as in Carbon/Most Wanted.
The in-game camera feels off (it sways weirdly).
Open world looks boring and uninspired.
Generic cutscenes.
Braindead Cop-AI.
The game comes with a lot of settings. World details, car details and so on can be changed. However, the game does not support high resolutions such as 4K. The game has an immense amount of bloom, which can be turned off, but the game just looks ugly without it. I would also recommend turning on Vsync, as menus with sliders can glitch out on fast systems.
Pretty good FPS on a modern system. Slight stutters.
If some of the issues didn't exist (especially the driving-physics problem), it could've been a great game. I can only hope for some mod to fix this game in the future. But until then, I cannot recommend this game to anyone, even if you happen to get it for free.

LawBreakers is by no means a perfect game. It is, however, exactly what I wanted it to be - the successor to Unreal Tournament that is not UT4 stuck in pre-alpha for three years.
This game is NOT Overwatch. It rewards twitch, individual skill as opposed to teamplay. There are no useless characters who only sit in the back and their entire gameplay is to 'Hold Mouse 1 to Heal' for the entire game. There are no 'press Q to win' Ultimate abilities.
I personally find it to be fully worth my 30 euros and I would recommend it to anyone who is willing to put in at least a couple of hours to learn the movement and combat basics. Once you realise those, once you find your favourite class and once you start pwning noobs in pugs, that is when you will realise that this game is what arena shooter fans have been waiting for 10 years, since Unreal 3 was released.
I'd also like to mention that if you still, after five to ten hours, found why your character dies every time it respawns, perhaps you should check out some guides on the forums or YouTube. There might be something to your character's kit that you overlooked (like the Assassin's shotgun being much better than the blades or the fact that you can detonate Titan's rockets in mid-air).

Good Specatating System (Better than steam broadcasting)
Fair ranked matchups (For the most part)

Cons:

Overall this game is good, and pretty fair, I love it and started a clan simply to get better as a team (msg me if you're interested lol). This game has a strong SSB vibe, but at the same time if feels very original.This game is well suitable for new gamers, and gaming veterans, for it has ranked modes, and casual modes. Climbing the ladders is hard to do alone, so you could queue with a partner and do 2v2s.  Like I said there are salty players but its not like theres a competitive game without saltiness. There are in-game purchases, but they do not help you win what-so-ever, similar to tf2, they're cosmetics, but unlike tf2 people don't judge you for not having cosmetics. The cosmetics however are reasonably priced and go on sale often, and the chest system seems pretty fair. Every legend in the game can be bought with gold, something earned for playing games, and completing the tutorials, and if you're not sure who to chose at first, legends go into cycle every week or two. This game offers a large variety of play-styles taking in players of all types.
That's basically all I can say off the top of my head, but if anything I reccomend this game to gamers of all types, especially those that are ssb fans. It might be hard at first but you'll definitely get better if you practice. And I can confirm this game will definitely stick with me for a while.

Let's start by saying this - this game is not an actions rpg, where you fight monsters, gain exp etc. This is game about choices. About... life, really. It's pretty intriguing title, that I've stumbled across by complete accident. This game is definitely different. Special. At the begging, we're choosing are character and his/her love interest - happy times, but the true story begins, when our protagonist are alone in shi*ty apartment, have problems with money and... finds out that his/her ex is going to marry someone. Yeah, that's not good. Since protagonist still love his/her ex, he/she decide to be there on they're wedding day and this decision is a beginning to many different choices.
Is this game boring? Yeah, to be honest, it can be. Works are boring (well, true life I guess). Some parts of the story are too. And for a story with a lot of choices... There aren't that many of those. What's even worse is that the choices seems to be lacking in the moments and situations where they would fit very well and actually be pretty important.
Pros:
+ length (especially if you would like to explore everything, do additional quests, find all collectibles etc.)
+ graphic - most of characters have their own portraits and they're look good
+ individual treatment - if you choose someone of the same gender as your lover, you will receive few comments about this here and there. Same goes for your race and gender
+ plot can be surprising
+ this game is unique, really one of it's kind.
Cons:
- you don't have option to truly shape your character's personality, which would be so much more interesting
- ... this may cause issues with relating to your character - honestly, I couldn't relate to mine at all
- parts of main story and some other quests can get pretty boring
- there's something missing... maybe stats? More impactful choices? I'm not really sure, but when I was playing, I couldn't get rid of feeling, that this game could be so much more interesting and challenging at the same time
- not enough choices. Especially in important or even crucial events
- some choices are just to trivial.

The game is visually beautiful as well as deeply philosophical. When the game begins, your avatar starts talking as if he just became conscious and self-aware. He can only come to the conclusion he must be a god. He will not stop talking about this assumption until the very end of the game. And he talks a lot. An awful lot. The correct word is 'to ramble', I believe.
In the meantime (or after shutting down the voice-over through the game menu), you need to solve a bunch of puzzles. For the most part, these puzzles boil down to one principle: keep certain objects on your screen and/or keep certain objects outside of your screen. So the puzzle-solving for the majority of the puzzles consists of you turning and twisting the game's camera into angles to keep objects inside or outside of the borders of your screen. After a few variations on this principle, you'll find it grows old soon.
The fact that you can't rebind keys at all and the fact that you can't strafe but only rotate the camera doesn't help to solve puzzles where minute camera movements are the key to success.
There are a few puzzles that don't revolve around camera control that are actually a bit of fun to solve, but these come late in the game and they're just too few to make up for the many, many annoying camera-focus puzzles.

Pneuma: Breath of Life is an interesting game that I checked out mainly because one of the secrets in The Turing Test referenced it (likely as a bit of a call-back, as the developers of Pneuma also produced it). It claims to be a puzzle game with puzzles based on perspective and, in all fairness, that is true. However, the puzzles generally fall into two categories: incredibly simple or confusing because it isn't entirely clear what the puzzle even is (or how, exactly, the mechanics work).
As such, trying to compare it to other first-person puzzle games like Portal or The Talos Principle will necessarily be unflattering. But I realized something while listening to the pompous and arrogant narrator/main character Pneuma rattle on, and not just that he was amusing in his arrogance and pettyness (I especially enjoyed it when he boasted his managing to "defeat" a door). I found that, as the story went on, I found Pneuma to be a sympathetic character, and that this game would be better served comparing it to games like Thomas Was Alone and The Stanley Parable: games that are fairly simple to play and win but which have an interesting story to follow. So, if you are looking for a challenging puzzle game, then this probably won't be for you. If you would like to hear a story about a character slowly learning about who they are right after coming into being, then maybe you should give this a try.

A Valley Without Wind is an experimental sort of game by Arcen Games, most well known for their space RTS AI War. A Valley Without Wind is a game that attempts to mix various genres with, heh, mixed results. The game doesn't have an engaging plot by any means, but where it really shines is it's fusion of gameplay mechanics from 2D platformers, turn based strategy games.  Some of these implementations work really well, especially the platforming. It feels really nice and zippy once you get the dash or triple jump skill. The turn based overworld map is a dissapointment, primarily because nothing you do brings any sense of accomplishment. The most interesting thing you can do is unlocking a new biome, but that's generally time consuming and they're not as interesting as one would think. The other big issue with the game is the RPG inspired combat system. Your skills are items you can find in chests and assign to various hotkey, similar to the gem based skills in Path of Exile. Getting a more powerful skill means going to a more difficult area and opening chests until you find one. There are maybe around 15 skills in the game, so there is very little sense of progression. There also isn't any armour and getting new buildings means there are new aesthetic backdrops. Overall the fun in the platforming beat out the clunkiness and lack of depth of some of the other gameplay elements. What's really noticable is the potential the game has. The fusion is bold and daring, and with increased RPG elements, and features such as allowing you to make actual buildings in towns, this game could have been fantastic. All in all if you want a fast, smooth platformer that experiments with some interesting ideas, this game is for you.

I'm going to keep this nice and short ... because that's exactly what the game is: A collection of fantastic puzzles, and a relatively short play-through time. It's a Myst-type game, and done well. The only reason the playtime isn't lengthy is that the storyline doesn't have miles and miles of exploring and walking around like Myst ones do. You simply walk into rooms and buildings (FANTASTICALLY well rendered ones), find the puzzles, solve them, and proceed through the levels. That doesn't really make it 'no-frills'; on the contrary, it makes it solidly interesting the whole way through. Totally worth it.
Only negative I can think of, is the narration. There's an interesting philosophical narative going on, and I enjoyed about 95% of it. There was a puzzle I was trying to work on, and the narrator/character talked through most of it. Most of his blathering is pretty interesting, but THAT one interfered when my mind was trying to work on a puzzle. The story WAS interesting, but as I wouldn't mind playing through the game puzzles again in a few years, I don't think I'd enjoy listening to the story a second time.

I picked this up in the Stealth Game Sale, on the virtue of it looking very similar to Gunpoint. Visuals aside, it's a fairly different game. Importantly: it is not a stealth game! There's a pre-combat positioning phase, where stealth matters, but the core of the game is an quite interesting take on turn-based ninja combat. It turns out to be a lot of fun -- really sells you on the "being a super-fast ninja who's dancing between bullets" concept.

With a lot of good ideas that were, sadly, very poorly realized, Ronin suffers from irritating, unprecise gameplay, a terribly designed checkpoint system, one of the worst final levels I've ever played, and a nagging feeling that the game thinks it's much better than it is.

+ In smaller enemy numbers combat is fun and flows beautifully.
+ The levels are reasonably varied.
+ The game's take on turnbased combat is quite unique and interesting.
- In larger enemy numbers combat becomes an annoying clusterf**k.
- The games seems unsure of its position regarding stealth, simultaneously rewarding and punishing the player for using it.
- The plot is practically non-existant and gives very little context, turning what might have been a powerful finale into an emotional dud.
-The game has an incredibly annoying, incredibly common bug where the player's grappling hook ignores all laws of physics and teleports the player through a wall.
RONIN was, ultimately, a disappointment. The game is very fun and very cool when it works, but it doesn't work often enough for me to give it a recommendation.

Ronin tries too hard to be gunpoint with cool features that just dont work with turn-based combat. Out of combat the controls work well, but once the turn-based function begins you are at the mercy of collision detection and will needlessly grab walls when you would want jump on to them. The level design is somewhat poor and seems as if the enemies had little to no thought on their placement. All in all it is a super cool concpet exectued rather poorly. Play the demo and if you really like it buy it. I can't recomment it until you have a little more freedom in the turn-based mode.

RONIN is a mix of Gunpoint and Mark of the Ninja, and although it lacks the depth and replayability of either of those, it still ends up being a lot of fun. The combat system is, once you get the hang of it, enjoyable to play around with, and the various powerups you can purchase do end up altering your playstyle.
A few issues:
There isn't much variation on offer. Unlike Gunpoint or MotN, there's only a handful of ways to clear a level. You also have to kill everyone (and have no alarms raised) to get a skill point from a level, and pretty much all the levels have mandatory combat sessions, so there's no option to simply stealth through the game, which is a bit of a disappointment. You can, in certain cases, sneak around before the inevitable fight and thin the enemy forces a bit, but this isn't always an option and it doesn't head off the reinforcements that often show up.
Level design also suffers from this - there's often one way in and out of the location, or maybe two, and a clear 1-2-3 path you're expected to follow. This is a shame, because this type of game can and should offer a much larger variety in terms of reaching the objectives, so as to best make use of the stealth mechanics. Instead, it feels a little too linear.
I haven't completed the game, but from what I've seen of the level design and skills on offer, there isn't much replay value. This stems in part from the above problem with variation, but also because there often isn't reason to go back to earlier levels with new skills. The skill points from each level can be unlocked as you play it the first time, and there are no collectibles or points to worry about.
Combat also, especially with larger numbers of enemies, turns into a trial-and-error system, where you figure out the best opening move, then replicate it as you try out the potential avenues of attack after that, going for a new strategy on the last branch each time you die. While it's actually sort of fun to outsmart the enemy soldiers and finally get the strategy that takes them all down, it can get a little frustrating, especially given the occasional variance in jump and bullet predictions.
Ultimately, though, this game (for all its flaws) is a lot of fun. Playing with the combat mechanics, figuring out ways to bypass civilians or sneak up on enemies, replaying a tough section to kill all guards without letting them get an alarm out, all add up to an enjoyable experience, for a few hours at least. While it's not quite worth the asking price, at a decent discount it's a great purchase.

Very disappointing. Save for the better visuals, this one is worse than Invisible War (which got scolded not entirely unfairly). Square lost track of what made Deus Ex great. Sure, there's still sneaking and levels open enough to allow for multiple aproach options, they went the "Rise of the Tomb Raider" route with this one. Meaning more of everything, but less of what matters. Sure, Deus Ex has always been about options and the RPG aspect has always been a great part, but they really lost track with all those augmentations. Too many different places to put points into, not enough focus. Many of the augs seem redundant and could be greatly simplified. Is it to make sure people would buy points for real money? Who knows... Yes, you can buy power in this game using real money. This is just glorified cheating.
The gameplay structure is weak as well. While Deus Ex has always been about you being in some mission location (with a few side quests every now and then), the side quests were meaningful and few, the main story had more focus. Here, the gameplay structure is akin to a budget RPG, not that great main quest and loads and loads and loads of side objectives. Kills the mood.
Speaking of killing the mood and "too much stuff except where it counts", the crafting system. Yes, there's a crafting system so instead of gathering your equipment, you just craft it. Well, you can also put the crafting resources into weapon upgrades, but why? Really, why? Just a tiny bit more damage here, a bit more ammo capacity there, it isn't meaningful. The weapon upgrade system seem to be included just for the sake of adding a few more features to print on the back of the box.
Hacking went the same route too. Previously, hacking encounters were more strategic and while you could improve your chances with either augmentations or items, now you're pretty much forced to use items no matter how high your skill is because they've "enriched" the hacking experience with way more aspects than it needs. Did I mention that those new aspects can ONLY be countered by items, no way to counter them with experience points or pure player skill? Yeah...
Same goes for the Breach mode. All the development time spend here could have been spend much better on more story missions. But no, Square wouldn't be Square if they could concentrate on the important aspects.
All in all, too much of everything benign, not enough of substance. I am rather glad Square ditched Deus Ex because this way, I'll just replay the previous games and remember them for their greatness (yes, including IW) instead of witnessing the horror which is Mankind Divided to unfold further.

At first I was not going to purchase this game but was looking for something new to play and with the return policy as a safety net I decided, "why not?"
-My first problem with this game is it's price. It has a $40.00 price tag for what I consider to be $15.00 to $20.00 content which is a common console marketing strategy that doesn't always work on PC customers. This is a management simulator in that you adjust terrain and that causes the world's temperature to rise or fall. Next you fast forward and see if new creatures spawn. That's about it.
-Technically this game has a lot of flaws. The first and foremost is that it tries to use your on-board graphics instead of your graphics card and v-sync issues cause the frame-rates to drop to nothing. I already have had my rig set up to fix this so my game seems to run smooth enough. There are no graphics options, there is no quit button, there are very few settings at all. This is a PS4 port and is quite obvious. It is pretty hard to play with a mouse and keyboard, so you will need a controller. I am also having an issue where my cube in freemode is incrementally getting hotter and forcing me to fill half my cube with Everests to stabilize my temperatures.
-The tutorial, though is pretty helpful, is very very annoying and found myself skipping through the annoying sound of "Navi" and the soundtrack itself is very repetitive- almost to a fault. You have to complete the tutorial to unlock Freemode (which has a HUGE bug where zooplankton does not spawn unless you redo the tutorial to a certain point, save, then import those settings- OR need millions of phytoplankton and a TON of water.
-I have a problem with the controls in that with using the 1x1 block to raise or lower land, it's REALLY hard to select certain blocks around you and I spend a lot of my points fixing holes and accidental spires. It's also hard to keep from sinking to the bottom of the water, not looking through the earth, and capturing flying creatures.
-Graphics are nice, very family friendly and "cutsie" making for a calm, enjoyable experience.
They released a same day patch as release but it was just a couple aesthetics and no bugfixing etc.
Overall, even without all the technical issues and the lack of the developers even trying to make it an OKAY PC port, I say wait until this goes on sale for 50%+ off and wait until they have fixed a lot of these technical issues.

I would tentatively give this game a thumbs up. In the couple of days since it was released, I have played way too many hours.
First, the many negatives:
- This game has clearly not been fully implemented for PC and keyboard & mouse. The tutorial talks about using the 'left stick' and 'right stick', which makes it even more difficult to understand the controls. The key bindings are at best tricky and at worst terrible: the game uses WASD for moving, arrow keys for moving the camera (the mouse does this too, but very slowly), and XFGHJKLI for menu selections. For some reason, I (i) is used for both favouriting items and switching between macro and micro, which means you end up with a load of favourites, and have to be extra careful not to press J and use them accidentally.
- The menu system is very difficult to navigate. To get to the important Library 'tree', you have to open the menu, then game info, then library, then tree. Then click on it before moving using WASD. From the main menu, to load a freeplay game, you can choose settings from a previous play, but it's difficult to work out what you're deciding on.
- Game saves can't be personalised.
- Graphics settings don't load the next time you load the game (the settings are saved, but you have to re-select them).
- There's no "Close game" so exiting from fullscreen means closing the program from Task Manager.
- Pressing 'esc' on static cut scenes does nothing.
- Some of the animal and flower models need more work. Megatherium just looks like any other bear, and the early avians all might as well be 3D clipart of a duck.
- The tutorial is a chore.
- It's called 'Birthdays the Beginning'...
- The early humans in the game are white, for some reason.
And now the positives:
- The game is addictive. Really addictive. You just want to keep playing to try and get the next creature.
- The game mechanics for 'birthing' and extinction work well. They're really well thought-out, mostly relying on temperature, humidity and elevation, but with other factors (such as co-existing species) thrown in. Amazingly unrealistic, but a great game mechanic! In order to get the next species on a tree, you end up dropping the temperature to balance the pre-existing organism, and the one you want it to evolve into.
- Some of the animal sprites and animations are really brilliant! And the whole landscape is beautiful.
Recommendation to gamers
- Yes, the game is expensive. This sort of game, I would usually play no more than £20 full price (I paid £26.24, full price is currently £34.99). Check out people playing this on YouTube, and if you like the look of it, you'll probably enjoy playing it.
- Don't expect a realistic evolution simulator. Not only is this a game, it's definitely not science. (The idea that evolution was 'aiming for' humans, and that we are the final or best is rather silly. Adaptation and evolution are far more random and unpredictable than this.) But don't let that stop you from playing.
- Don't expect a perfect game.
Recommendations to the developers:
- Go back and completely re-do the controls and tutorial specifically for keyboard and mouse.
- Expand the creatures available. For a game covering the entire history of life on earth, you'd expect it to have a bigger 'Dex' than a handheld Pokémon game.
- Let players have a heat stone AND a cool stone simultaneously. It's a little thing, but so irritating.
- Tone down some of the sound effects. I've got Tetris effect Close Encounters stuck in my head. And that sprint ('increased movement') sound effect is very irritating.

This is a heavily story-focused game.  No combat...which is okay!
You follow a selected protagonist through a series of difficult life choices.  The way Vagabond Dog wrote the story, you really feel invested in the characters and the choices you're making.  That's definitely a positive.  However, as far as the main story goes, I feel that many of your choices don't have too much of an efffect, and sometimes I felt too railroaded.  I don't intend to spoil any story-points, but I felt a little cheated by the ending.
Beyond choice-making, the game has a few minigames to play in order to earn cash.  99 percent of them felt like grinding in an old RPG without any of the fun of a battle system.  As I stated before, no battle system is okay.  However, I would expect the minigames to be somewhat entertaining if they're going to be replacing it completely.
Overall, this game is worth checking out if you enjoy throw-back pixel-graphic games and an interesting story that makes you think.  This game definitely is a standout for being different and interesting.  The entertainment quality simply suffered in a few places.

This is a simple platformer with randomly generated levels. These levels get harder and harder as you go on. While you're in these levels, you can collect gems that allows you to slow down time, be shown where to go, and see a bot do it.
The story mode has you go through these levels with different twists like double jumping, being big or small, and being stuck in a wheel. It also has a pretty cool intro animation.
The Arcade Mode has you go against everyone's score. You can chooses to do it with only double jumps or only being big or having nothing. Score is based on all the gems you get. If you get all the gems in the level, your score multiplier will go up. If you die or don't collect all the gems, this will go down. Currently, I'm addicted to this mode.
Marathon Mode lets you go through a long level after level where you choose the difficulty based on all the monsters in there.
Overall, the idea of improving your skill by upping the difficulty really makes you want to play the game again and again, especially with a high score. If you want a game with tons of replayability, get this!
If I ever meet the creator of this game, I'll give him a greatful handshake, then slap him across the face. :)

The levels get trickier the further you get and you are introduced to new game mechanics along the game. All these things ease you into the game, and by the time you're playing level 160 or so you probably know how to work your way around the levels. No, it doesn't make it any easier, on the contrary, but I salute the developers for not throwing you into the deep right away. It makes the game more accessible for anyone who wants to give it a go. And since the levels are short, it hardly ever becomes frustrating. But if it keeps you interested for that long, that's an entirely different story.
In all honesty though, I still prefer Super Meat Boy because of the better visuals and tighter controls but Cloudberry Kingdom is a fine runner-up. I like you sadistic platformers add this one to your wishlist.
