Who is this Game For?
==================
Batman: Arkham Asylum is packed with fan service as Batman faces off against more than just one big name in the franchise. Sure, you'll encounter The Joker and Harley Quinn, but you're also going to run into the likes of Bane, Killer Croc, Poison Ivy, Scarecrow and Zsasz. A multitude of other villains are referenced in various ways, even though they don't actually appear in person. Either way, for those who are hardcore fans of the franchise, it's a nice touch.
Is it good?
=================
Making your way through the story, three types of game play quickly become apparent: combat, stealth and exploration. In short, pretty much all the fighting is handled with two buttons and timing. Get the timing down, and you'll be whipping out amazing combos with a simple tap-tap-tap. The stealth game play is referred to as "predator mode" by the developers since it is most directly inspired by the classic Batman of the comics. Here, the focus is on creating fear and eliminating enemies when they are vulnerable. Exploration is more or less standard plat forming, but combined with Batman's cool gadgets.
Audio is a strong point for Batman: Arkham Asylum, be it music, sound effects or voice acting. Mark Hamill reprises his role as The Joker, while Kevin Conroy stars as Batman and Arleen Sorkin voices Harley Quinn. It all makes for good visuals, even if things do look a bit plastic at times. PhysX support appears to be PC-only, which means you’ll only find volumetric fog, detailed cloth animation or random destructible items such as paper and tiles here on the PC version.
Does it have any problems?
========================
Where Batman: Arkham Asylum stumbles is in the boss fights. Some, such as the battle against Poison Ivy, are challenging in an old-school, learn the pattern way. Others, such as the (multiple) fights against the Scarecrow, are brilliantly executed. But most are repetitive fights against low level enemies and are more an exercise in button-mashing than any sort of challenge.
Final Thoughts!
====================
In addition to the main game, Batman: Arkham Asylum also features a wealth of unlockable information in the form of characters bios, audio interviews with key inmates, beautifully rendered character trophies and the aforementioned challenge maps. Challenge maps are split into combat and predator style, with the goal of the combat maps being a high score and the goal of the predator maps being elimination of the enemies as quickly as possible. There have been many different Batman games over the years, but none quite so polished as this one. Batman: Arkham Asylum combines the best elements of the classic Batman mythos with the modern-day interpretation of the hero. The end result is a game that outshines its flaws and is quite simply a blast to play.
--------------------------------

Batman: Arkham Asylum is a reboot of the timeless comic-book franchise with thrilling locations, wonderful voice performances and clever, exciting game-play. Taking a darker, grittier look at the Batman Universe, the game leads the character through the Elizabeth Arkham Asylum for the Criminally Insane, in a plot to stop The Joker from using his new batch of Titan to create super-soldiers, battling other well-known villains along the way. It also sets up for an even greater game in that of Batman: Arkham City, yet both are masterpieces.
Mark Hamill as The Joker? Check. Kevin Conroy as Bruce Wayne/Batman? Check. Tara Strong as Harley Quinn? Well... not yet. But this game's line up of recognizable heroes and villains will excite even the most inexperienced Batman fans. While only the better known of the Rogues Gallery appear (such as The Joker, Scarecrow, Bane, etc.), the player can still find numerous amounts of information ripped straight from the franchise's rich and deep lore in the form of secrets hidden around the island.
The game focuses on stealth take-downs, which is essentially Batman picking off inmates/thugs one at a time without being seen. As Batman is the "Dark Knight" etc. this works extremely well and keeps the player on their toes. Also present throughout the story are boss battles which constantly change formula and challenge the player to a whole new level, such as dodging Bane's rampant attacks and dodging Killer Croc's... rampant attacks. Okay, so you may have to use your reflexes in this one but it's better than nothing.
Overall I'd say this game is a flawless visit to the Batman world and should be an inspiration for any other video games adapted from comic books or movies. It's gripping, memorable, challenging but also entertaining.

LawBreakers is by no means a perfect game. It is, however, exactly what I wanted it to be - the successor to Unreal Tournament that is not UT4 stuck in pre-alpha for three years.
This game is NOT Overwatch. It rewards twitch, individual skill as opposed to teamplay. There are no useless characters who only sit in the back and their entire gameplay is to 'Hold Mouse 1 to Heal' for the entire game. There are no 'press Q to win' Ultimate abilities.
I personally find it to be fully worth my 30 euros and I would recommend it to anyone who is willing to put in at least a couple of hours to learn the movement and combat basics. Once you realise those, once you find your favourite class and once you start pwning noobs in pugs, that is when you will realise that this game is what arena shooter fans have been waiting for 10 years, since Unreal 3 was released.
I'd also like to mention that if you still, after five to ten hours, found why your character dies every time it respawns, perhaps you should check out some guides on the forums or YouTube. There might be something to your character's kit that you overlooked (like the Assassin's shotgun being much better than the blades or the fact that you can detonate Titan's rockets in mid-air).

I enjoy this game tremendously. Hands down one of the most fun I've had in an FPS.
Really allows gamers with better mechanics to use their mechanics to win games. This seems like an obvious thing to do, but a lot of class-based shooter games value team class composition/teamwork over skillful mechanics. This is not one of those games. Those things matter, but your individual skill is much more valuable than any team composition.
Additionally, this game allows you to further refine your mechanical aim that translates well to most FPS games. If you are not mechanically gifted, this game is also a great way to improve since the matchmaking will generally put you with players around your skill level unless you are at the top.
Overall, I enjoy this game and feel like it deserves better than it has attained upon release. This game has a lot of potential, but needs to market and advertise to appeal to a broad playerbase.

Pneuma is a short point and click puzzle game with a little bit of walking simulator thrown in (i.e. You have to walk from puzzle to puzzle and there are big, empty rooms that are pretty but are empty apart from the part with the puzzle in it). You play as a character who talks aloud, thinking he is a god and has created the world around him but then begins to realize that there is something else going on.
Pros:
+The puzzles are very good. They have to do mostly with eyes--door switches are shaped like eyes even. They do interesting things with keeping/breaking eye contact, changing perspectives, etc. Mostly looking, but occasionally there are some interactable objects like switches. They're all very clever.
+Pretty locales. Very Roman flavor with lots of marble and columns and such.
+Atmospheric music.
Neutral:
~Minimal handholding. There is an occasional clue in the dialogue over what kind of puzzle you have, but not very often. I thought it was just the right difficulty for me but I can see others getting stuck. Because a lot of puzzles involve looking/not looking at something, there are some puzzles where you don't even see the effect of what you're doing, so it is more difficult, but there are always verbal clues like clicking tiles to let you know something is happening out of frame, Same for more obscure puzzles that require a specific sequence or end result, there's some visual clue to guide you, but you may have to hunt for it. But you can usually puzzle out that 1) there's something happening, then 2) find what's causing it, 3) make the thing happen in the correct way to 4) open a door. I found this kind of puzzling fun, but I list it as neutral because it may not be fore everyone.
Cons:
-Narrator/character was a bit annoying. At the beginning, if you walk faster than the game intends, you get a nonstop stream of dialogue, referring to things you passed a while ago. The first few minutes before the puzzles started were a dialogue dump. It definitely lessens as you go along, with a comment before the puzzle, and one after, so if you can get through the first few minutes without breaking your speakers, you'll be fine.
-Drastic shift in tone. The game starts off humorous, with your character thinking he's the center of the universe with an "Oh, I'm amazing, because I made this amazing place!" Later, he starts questioning what's going on, and instead of following the kind of philosophical tone the game developing, he dives straight into an existential crisis. This wouldn't have been so bad if the game hadn't started out so light and jokey. Emotional whiplash.
-Short playtime. I spent about 2 hours, which was okay to me, but I also got the game for $5, so it felt worth it to me. Absolutely do not pay full price for this or you might feel cheated.
Overall: 7/10. Good puzzles, but short and gets kinda weird at the end.

I obtained this in a bundle for £3.51, so that's the kind of value for money experience I'm basing this review on, rather than it's current list price of £15.99.
TL:DR - Still isn't worth it, just get the Talos Principle instead.
Talos may be 2x the price, but in addition to being 9-11 times the length of Pneuma, has puzzles that are clearly conveyed to the player and are rewarding to solve.
In Pneuma, puzzles are solved by positioning your character to have a line of sight, or lack of line of sight, to certain elements, such as switches.  If you can imagine trying to check if a switch is active, while not deactivating it by looking at it or any other switches in the area that may have to be pressed in a sequence, you can imagine how frustrating this mechanic can be.
Length ~ 100 minutes.
The story is told through a narattor who beleives he is God, and who espouts all kind of philosophical nonsense throughout the entire game.  You'll want to mute the game halfway through so he'll shut up for 15 seconds.
So no, I can't recommend it, even if you can pick it up heavily discounted in a bundle.

Pneuma: Breath of Life is one of the very few first-person adventure games that actually look as good as the screenshots on their store pages. From the beginning to the end it's a visual feast. Along the way a voice accompanies the player and brainstorms about the idea of god and existence in general in a little faster pace than I would have liked. The philosophical tone of this monologue would have interested me a lot more if I was in my early 20s, still, it wasn't unbearable.
The puzzles aren't as bad as other reviewers say, they are just not as interactive as we are accustomed to. There are a few buttons you push in your short journey but almost all of the solutions require adjusting your view the way the developer intended. This method includes a bit of trial & error at the beginning of every puzzle which sometimes becomes frustrating and eventually boring. Then again I can't remember a single adventure game I haven't felt the same at least once so this little issue is part of the whole "1st person narrative experience" package.
The story is wrapped up in about a few hours - unless you get stuck in a puzzle or spend time looking for the secrets - which is not as bad as it sounds because this way you reach the end without losing interest and feeling the story is getting dragged on needlesly. Pneuma's ending was satisfying in my opinion, I liked the sudden change in the narrative although some might find it abrupt.
Pneuma: Breath of Life is recommended to everyone who would like to spend a few hours on a nice looking game without expecting too much.

I can wholeheartedly recommend this game. I honestly have no idea what all the negative reviews are about - could be the game was buggy or something when it was first released, but I personally didn't encounter a single bug during my playthrough. Could also be that some people were expecting a first person shooter, but just like the previous titles of the series Mankind Divided is more like a first person RPG with shooter elements, rather than the other way round. As long as you can wrap your mind round that, you should be good to go.
The story was interesting, perhaps not quite as good as with Deus Ex: Human Revolution, but not bad by any measure. There was a good build-up of suspense throughout the storyline, and the ending came to an exciting climax but still left a nice open end for a sequel. Gameplay-wise all the familiar Deus Ex elements are there, you can sneak your way though the missions or go in guns blazing or try to reason with the characters by talking to them etc. The graphics are alright - not stellar, but definitely good. In all honesty, though, they are quite demaning on your video adapter. If you set the graphics too high, the game might run okay for a while, but then it will eventually crash as the adapter memory runs out. The solution is to reduce the level of detail (or get a card with at least 4GB of memory).
Someone was whining about some single-use microtransactions and how it was a game breaker for him, but listen here, THERE IS NOT A SINGLE MICROTRANSACTION IN THE GAME THAT'S REQUIRED TO COMPLETE OR TO ENJOY THE GAME. Whatever microtransactions there might be, (I don't even know since I didn't need to look into those at all) they are fully optional and superficial.
All in all, Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is a very solid game, definitely recommended for fans of the series and everyone else who might be interested in a good cyberpunk-themed RPG experience. The ONLY negative thing that I can think about the game is that you have to watch all the credits in the end.

There are RPGs that draw you inside their own unique world, there are RPGs that feel boring and colourless... and there are RPGs that could almost provide the perfect roleplaying experience, if only their gameplay wasn't that dreadful.
Dragon Age: Origins belongs into the latter category. Indeed the storyline is far from new and largely inspired by the classic "Humans, Dwarfs-living-in caves, elves-living-in-forests" scenario. The idea of a dark threat lingering in the depths, waiting to eradicate the known world is also nothing new in the RPG world.
Dragon Age: Origins however manages to put a decent emphasis on the roleplay part. The fact that your possible dialogue options merely consist of the standard 3 ones (polite, not interested and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥) does come as a little off, though.
Yet, I do not recommend this game and that is because of the gameplay.
Unfortunately, DA:Os story just isn't good enough to turn it into an "interactive-movie" kind of game. Therefore, the game has to rely on decent gameplay features such as world connection, quality of travel and most importantly battle mechanics. It is these features that take away the fun, in my opinion. The world is not open, but divided into towns and outposts with "level-like" areas connected to them. The battle mechanics rely on you pausing the game and giving 10 different orders before you start the fight and probably fail due to someone not being healed quickly enough.
Even repeatedly pushing an attack button is more fun than this approach Bioware has taken to the game.

Let me preface my review by saying that I enjoy hard games, and I enjoy turn based (and pseudo turn based) games.  Love FTL and Dark Souls, and a ton of different roguelikes.  I also grabbed this game for 50% off during the Stealth sale, so price, genre, and difficulty are not what's turning me off.
Ronin's problem is that it is trying to be a super tight action platformer with a turn based combat system, but the controls are clunky. (aka: the kiss of death for tight action games)  Everything your character can do is controlled by the mouse.  This is mostly fine during the turn based combat bits, but is horrid during the real time platform/stealth bits.  It means that instead of being able to swing in through a window, and tap a button to stab a guy in the back, you instead swing through the window, and have to click on a "stab" button that pops up on screen by the enemy while your character (and the camera) are moving.  This gets especially annoying when you're also using the mouse to aim your next grappling hook. (or when you need to retract your grappling hook by clicking that icon, and quickly follow it up with a stealth kill, requiring another)
Bugs were also plentiful in my short time with the game.  I was able to get my grappling hook to retract me through solid walls/ceilings several times.
One partifuclarly funny instance happened when I was trying to reach the last guard in a room before he sounded the alarm.  Was going to retract up to the ceiling and then pounce on him, but my grappling hook pulled me through to the roof.  Since there was no way to get back into the building from up there, I had  no way to reach the guard before the alarm was set off.
Don't buy this game.  It's not a matter of money; you deserve better.

This review will assume that you have played Deus Ex: Human Revolution, because you would be doing yourself a disservice by playing Mankind Divided first.
In terms of story, this game falls a little short compared to Human Revolution (more on this below). However for all it lacks here, it makes up in all sorts of gameplay improvements.
As with all Deus Ex games, it promises different ways to approach every situation (i.e. combat, stealth, hacking and social interaction) but unlike its predecessor, it no longer punishes the player for going in all guns blazing.
The final product, however, is a prime example of a potentially great game being butchered by the publisher into being "only" good. It's clear that it was originally meant to deliver more in terms of story, but was chopped up (and as of writing this, the sequel is nowhere to be seen) and the microtransactions, while completely unnecessary, just feel bolted on.
The DLC stories, "System Rift", "A Criminal Past", were surprisingly good. While I wouldn't buy them for their original price, do consider them if you can get them in a sale.

If you're looking for an actual review you're wrong. But if your looking for an outstanding lemon bars recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1) 2 cups Flour
2) 1/2 cup Sugar
3) 1/4 teaspoon Salt
4) 2 sticks (1 Cup) Salted Butter, Cut Into Small Cubes
5) Filling
6) 1-1/2 cup Sugar
7) 1/4 cup Flour
8) 4 whole Large Eggs
9) Zest And Juice Of 4 Medium-sized Lemons
10) Powdered Sugar, For Sifting
Directions:
1. For the crust: Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F. Grease a 9-by-13-inch pan with butter.
2. Stir together the flour, sugar, and salt. Add the butter to the bowl and use a pastry cutter to cut it all together until the mixture resembles fine crumbs. Press into the prepared pan and bake until golden around the edges, about 20 minutes.
3. For the filling: Stir together the sugar and flour. Crack in the eggs and whisk to combine. Add the lemon zest and juice and mix until combined. Pour over the crust and bake about 20 minutes.
4. Allow to cool in the fridge for a minimum of 2 hours, then sift powdered sugar over the top before cutting into squares.
(Use an 8 x 10 pan if you'd like the layers to be a little thicker.)﻿

Red Lake - horror shooter with elements of quest.
The protagonist works in a department that is looking for a variety of paranormal places in order to hide them from humanity and prevent someone from using them for their own purposes.
There are rumors of a lake not far from the small village somewhere in Siberia, has changed color and became red. At the same time the behavior of animals around it began to change and strange things started to happen in there.
When the forester, the first who noticed these things stoped communicating, then a agent was sent to investigate. His main task - investigate what happened with the forester and the situation around the lake.
Towards the end of the game, when the main character finds a lake, a large open area for exploration. In order to perform the tasks of the scene, the protagonist will have to survive. During the night, dangerous creatures starts creeping arround the lake, you need to find a place to sleep before the sunset.
This game has real time bullet ballistics and slow motion if you hit critical shots and feature bullet anatomy if the projectile fired is shattered upon impact of up to 3 enemies or more. The game is focused in a post apocalyptic world with unknown entities such as wild dogs which happen to look mutated, ghost-like in appearance dogs in really big caves and unknown sphere's which zap any breathing or moving object causing instant death or suffocation on the spot. The game also has very nice stealth mechanics which allow you to bypass enemies with ease but if you find yourself in a struggle for life, you can simply unload your chamber of 9mm rounds into the enemy causing internal tissue and muscle bleeding and external entry of bullet (wound). The reloading animation is some what hindered depending on your character's state which could be near death (i.e bitten by dogs or fallen off a certain height) or fully healthy (in which case it would be fast and smooth with no hesitation). You often write notes into your noteback after certain horrific events (i.e Sphere zaps multiple ghost-like dogs). You can read the latest events remembering the horror you bypassed by just clicking TAB which is the default binded key. The game also introduces a new mechanic which is masterbation! It helps with stress levels which your character has and can be increased if horrific anomalies are spotted such as a fat ghost flying across your screen.
All in All

First had some graphical/lagging issues but then I forced Steam to open the game with my NVIDIA graphics card instead of the default integrated intel graphics card (and c'mon, really, that's my ♥♥♥♥♥♥ gaming computer's fault for not automatically using the NVIDIA in the first place).
Anyway, once that got sorted, I was able to play the game no problem, with not a single lag.
Bit of a learning curve as this game truly was nearly directly ported from consoles without much adjustment, so get used to using your keyboard completely. It's a bit nice though, you really don't have to bother with the cursor.
The actual game itself: judging by the other reviews, as it is in its current state right now, if you're the impatient kind of person then you won't like the game as-is. It reminds me a bit of Animal Crossing, actually, in how there's only so much you can do at once.
It can get boring. But it's also fun shaping the world to how you want (I love to build worlds and cities!) and witnessing the birth of species. ...But that can also get tedious after a while too, especially with your HP limit. I'd recommend having a balance between letting species grow and shaping the terrain (as I'd imagine what was intended by that in the first place). I do also wish sometimes that there was a faster movement option, especially with bigger maps. (I'm aware that there IS an option, but it's a bit of a pain to have to go in and out of the menu to toggle it when it could just be another button pressed, i.e, SHIFT+WASD to increase speed). Related, a faster time speed (sometimes fast-forward feels slow...!)
I'd love the addition of some caves, both underwater and on land. It'd be cool to have land on the surface and water right under it! Or a big mountain with a little pocket for creatures to chill in :3
Also some issues with it not remembering settings, like fullscreen (I'll set it to fullscreen, exit out the game, go back into it, and it'll be right back to windowed mode). So for now I've accepted it in windowed mode but I hope that'll be fixed.
In the future, it'd be cool if we could somehow adjust the avatar, even if it's just changing color or something. But that's low priority on everything else.
TL;DR: I like the game. I also didn't really go into it with high expectations. I do hope that they pay attention to the feedback and improve it in future patches. As of this review, the full retail price is $40, but it's on sale for $30- which I got it for. However, I feel like it may be more worth $15-20 as it is right now. Hopefully I'll feel like my $30 was worth it someday :)

Anyone who down votes this because it doesn't work are too damn lazy to put any effort to make it work in the first place, so pay no attention to them. Lots of guys on SubSim will help you if you are having problems with your game.
Now, onto the actual review.
This is, without a shadow of doubt, the best submarine simulator on the market. 12 years strong and still going.
In this game, there's single missions you can do, as well as a very good dynamic campaign that will really immerse you as a U-Boat captain. Depending on what time period you start in (I always start in 1939) you usually start with a lesser U-Boat and as you progress and sink more ships, you and your crew get rewards like medals and promotions, which can help you and your crew perform better. You also get points to upgrade your submarine with, everything from your sonar to your coning tower, and even to what submarine type you have.
This game will seem very overwhelming at first, and the tutorials actually do an okay job at helping you get settled in too. There's also a lot of stuff on the internet that can help you out, but from what I've learnt, the only real way to get better is by practicing, trying new things, and being the most ballsy sub commander in the seven seas.
One more thing this game has over other sub sims is it's modifiability. There is an absolute wealth of mods for this game on the internet, from small changes like what uniforms your crew wears to total overhauls, which can make a huge difference. Find what's right for you, and always make sure to keep a backup of your game before you install anything.
Also apparently this game has a multiplayer, but I've never tried it, so I can't speak on that.
Overall, it is definitely worth the small price tag, considering how many endless hours of fun you will have in this.

Cloudberry Kingdom should not be approached like your average platformer. In a way, it's almost like an infinite runner, since in many cases, the best way forward is to just press right and jump at appropriate times. The level-designing algorithm usually manages to create the levels so that the player's momentum is not lost. This plays a major part in making the levels more fun to play.
I've been playing the beta version in the past year for about 7 hours altogether. Do not come here expecting a great story. Do not come here expecting a platformer whose levels will astound you with their creativity. Come here with the expectation of finding a game attempting to do something very different.
Of all the game modes, I find the best ones to be those without additional tweaks to the player character skills, such as jetpack, double-jump, spaceship, pogos and so on. Of particular annoyance are are the game modes in which the skill changes between every level. With the bite-sized levels, usually lasting less than 15 seconds if you clear them as fast as possible without dying, the necessary context-switch becomes jarring.
Cloudberry Kingdom works best in small doses every now and then. You won't be playing it several hours in one go, but is that such a loss? A few gos trying to beat my previous score - and improve my position on the global highscore ranking - are my way of enjoying the game as well as I can.

I've played through this game about 5 times since the 90s and I've always really enjoyed it. The voice acting, humour and original art style were always delightful. The puzzles are mostly logical and it strikes and maintains a good balance of being challenging but not frustrating (there are no puzzles that come to mind that made me mad once I figured out the solution).
The update is mostly excellent, with clearer audio, and remastered music, as well as an old-style/new-style hotkey to toggle between the two (much like the Monkey Island SE games). All the original visuals and audio are still accessible this way. I flipped back a few times to watch certain animations throughout the game. For those familiar with the original, you may notice a few changes in the sound effects - nothing major, but you can get accustomed to the sound of tentacle suckers on the ground and overweight hotel guests falling off beds so it could be marginally jarring for purists in that respect.
The new verb wheel frees up a lot of screen space and, once you get used to it, works well. I slightly prefer the verb coin of Full Throttle/CoMI or the 'click through' style from Sam & Max, and the DotT's new one can get a little busy, but it's really not a detractor from the experience.
My only actual gripe (and it's a minor one) is with the new visuals. The classic LucasArts pixelated style was amazing at the time but this update could be considered *too faithful* in some respects. Things sometimes feel a little too simple - we have higher definition, but we really just get smoother lines with very little in the way of increased detail. This is especially noticeable on the main characters (as opposed to the backgrounds), which feel a little 'traced' at times and almost lose something stylistically from what the limited original artwork implied. This approach is understandable considering the exactness of the graphics toggle feature and the new artwork essentially being an overlay. While it was offputting at the very beginning, this became less of a concern as time went on and I got back into the story.
It's very hard to make a great game bad and, with this update, I can't say that's the case. It's extremely faithful to the original and still thoroughly lovable. There aren't too many games that have such well-written comedy and so few advenures where you seldom feel like you're doing busywork to fill time.
All-in-all, I'd strongly recommend this title as solid nostalgia for veterans or a hilarious new experience for the uninitiated. I'm extremely glad that this title has been brought up to modern standards so all its excellent qualities can be enjoyed by a younger generation (and not be lost to those who would have balked at the original, now 'retro', graphics). It really, really holds up, by any standards.

Day of the Tentacle Remastered brings me back to the days of playing this game at my friend's house in the early 90's so naturally I'm a bit biased. With that being said, this remaster has been done tastefully so newcomers will be able to get into the game while at the same time it's able to satisfy old fans as it doesn't nix anything from the original version. All of the tiny details in the art evoke a sense of wonder and warmth, not to mention it's chock full of easter eggs. The remaster allows for the same excitement one felt yesteryear after initially booting this game up and admiring the graphics to still be there. As an added bonus there is an option to change everything back to the original graphics as well if that's more your speed so this package is truly the best of both worlds.
Day of the Tentacle was so ahead of the times. There is a switching mechanic which allows you to alternate between three different characters who can interact and share items with each other to solve certain puzzles throughout the adventure. The characters are all completely different and equally loveable archetypes of American youth. My favorite character is Hoagie; a heavy-set Heavy rocker kid as he just screams Wayne's World to me.
My only gripe with the game is that a few of the puzzles are a bit illogical and ignore common sense however I urge you to not use a guide as it will taint the experience. Luckily these situations are few and far between and the quirky universe the game is set in allow for one to not mind back tracking a bit more than they should need to. If you want a wonderful game to play on a rainy day which will make you smile like a little kid again do yourself a favor and purchase Day of the Tentacle Remastered. You can feel the love oozing out of every aspect of both the original production and remastering. Mission accomplished Lucas Arts/Double Fine.

This is a new review (15-11-17), I've played a lot more and increased my play time, so I've some important message for those who is considering buying the game. I'll list out the topics on this game
1 - The current problem on the game
2 - The positive side
3 - The gameplay
4 - The VAC system
5 - The community
6 - The negative side
7 - Notes for those who have played the Browser Version of this game
1) This game is schedule based
Ok, don't get me wrong. You still can play the game anytime you want, but don't expect to find a lot of players online at the moment you play. I play at Asia servers, players usually start kicking in around 4pm - 8pm (GMT+8), sometimes players are packing in earlier, sometimes you can't even find a player online. But this don't bother me much, It's prefect on my playing "time-table". I'm sick of saying this to new players in the discussion hub, so imma just throw it on my review
2) Various playstyle
We have 7 Classes in this game, there are some classes that counters another class (you'll find out later once you bought the game) and they have various types of weapon including katana, pistol, heavy machine guns and etc. You can find a playstyle that suits you the most. Each classes have their unique abilities and certain weapons only for them. For example, Shadow class is able to invisible while sprinting, they are the only class who can equip katana.
3) When you play the game....
The maximum players allowed in 1 server are 12. So if there's more than 12 players, you can't join to play the game BUT you can spectate the game. The spectate is on 3rd person mode, so... yeah =c, devs currently cannot add a 1st person spectator cam.
Once you got in, you start with choosing the class you would like to play, you start with 1 loadout on the class, loadout contains the skin, accesories and weapons you selected on the menu. Each class have a maximum of 3 loadouts.
Each class doesn't have a level limit, but the score you earn is limited to 2000 points maximum on each match.
We have 4 gamemodes, they are
Team Deathmatch (TDM)
Capture Point (no nick xD)
Free For All (FFA)
King Of The Hill (KOTH)
Every match ends, we are able to vote for different gamemodes to play, maps can appear the same 2 times, but not for gamemodes, and not the map you are currently playing. If you don't get it, this is what I mean. You play a map called Sunsquare Mall, there will be 2 Maps called Hollow apper during the voting, but the gamemodes are different, and there's no Sunsquare Mall map appear in the voting.
4) Hackers
The gamae doesn't have much hackers, so far I've only seen one, fly hacker and was banned by dev a day after I reported... so yep, hackers aren't that many for now.
The VAC system currently is crap, they are not updated to detect hacks yet. Still need to wait....
5) The community
I guess it's pretty good, I've seen a few trashtalkers that trash talk about this game... idk why he bother to buy it and doesn't refund it.... and a few those who think they are the best, team flaming isn't very frequent. You usually will meet the same player again and again, so... yep.
6) There are no bots support on this game.
Basically means, no single player available for this game. If you're complaining about this, well I've nothing to convince you. But if you really wanted this game and found out there's no bot support, don't get dissapointed, the game is currently growing, hopefully we will have bots added in the game soon =)
7) Browser players, good old times babe
There's no more skill-tree. Each classes are limited to 6 perks, and 2 perks you use for a class. No more hackers infestation like last time, and no more gun renting anymore, each guns you received are premenant now. Shadow class doesn't dominate the game anymore, and Tanks are much more useful now. The maps didn't change much except the Overhead map, and they only added 1 new map called Reinstate.
My last notes
=========
This game is fun btw, I still enjoy playing the game. This game may be a little difficult for beginners, but as long as you practise, you will become better =).
Ballistic Overkill and CSGO is completely different, CSGO is more about tatics, while BO is more on objectives pushing. Therefore you can't use the sensitivity you play on CSGO into this game.
This game needs to be bought, the reason why because this game WAS free to play before, and it's infested with hackers almost every game. So this game better be in purchase mode compare to F2P, and it's quite cheap, not too expensive.
Gameplay   = 9/10
Community = 7/10
Lag / Bugs  = 7/10 (If you play on 200 ping++ server, ggwp for you.)

Buy? Unlikely. AVWW is a action platofrmer/settlement builder that draws similarities from Actraiser, Terraria, and rogue-like games. At first glance, the amount of content and the scope is daunting with a near infinite world (the game is unbeatable), inumerable levels called regions, and countless places to explore. I was originally happy with the immense exploration aspect until the rewards became less and less valuable. Mission success (which can be challenging sometimes, and are creative for a mostly procedurally generated game) earns you more spells, which you'll have more than enough of, and searching buildings or dungeons rewards you enchants, in which you will get too many duplicates of, and crafting ingredients or more missions for guess what? More needless spells. And then gathering currency is a total grind. Arcen deserves alot of credit for a large scope of a game and interesting concepts, but the end result is a major time waste that looks odd and not all that fun in the long run (and it's aLOOOOONG run).

This review will assume that you have played Deus Ex: Human Revolution, because you would be doing yourself a disservice by playing Mankind Divided first.
In terms of story, this game falls a little short compared to Human Revolution (more on this below). However for all it lacks here, it makes up in all sorts of gameplay improvements.
As with all Deus Ex games, it promises different ways to approach every situation (i.e. combat, stealth, hacking and social interaction) but unlike its predecessor, it no longer punishes the player for going in all guns blazing.
The final product, however, is a prime example of a potentially great game being butchered by the publisher into being "only" good. It's clear that it was originally meant to deliver more in terms of story, but was chopped up (and as of writing this, the sequel is nowhere to be seen) and the microtransactions, while completely unnecessary, just feel bolted on.
The DLC stories, "System Rift", "A Criminal Past", were surprisingly good. While I wouldn't buy them for their original price, do consider them if you can get them in a sale.

PROS:
Well designed levels with variations in stealthy or aggressive approach
Simple but surprisingly clever stealth puzzles
Plenty of new mechanics and enemies introduced as you progress
Plenty of different satisfying kills and assasinations
Plenty of unlockable moves, equipment, and costumes
Pleasant, consistent, beautifully stylized art with fluent animation
Good replayabliity in optimizing your score in each level, collecting all the secrets, and beating all the objectives
CONS:
Not the longest game ever to beat if you play straight through, something like 6-8 hours
Story is pretty cliche, general ninja nonsense, honor your clan, commit sepuku, etc.
Slighty awkward control in a couple specific situations, like being next to a door and a dead body at the same time
Framerate seems to be tied to actual game speed; you HAVE to play at high framerate
The main weakness with this game is the actual platforming due to unresponsive control. The control design in the game is actually good; most of the time you won't need to actually do any platforming because once you are on a wall or ledge, you are "attached" and can move and jump fluidly. But jumping over gaps, jumping from the ground to ledges (that you can definitely reach), and other similar things can take many tries. Thankfully, difficult platforming is rarely needed due to a grappling hook and a "blink" ability.
DEFINITELY recommended. Some of the most satisfying fun I've ever had with a 2d game. Action is great, stealth is challenging, completely worth the couple frustrations it has. I didn't pay full price, but it's probably worth it.

This game doesn't feel like a fully fleshed out Deus Ex game to be honest. Unlike the first game there is only one dispointly small Hub area with I think 3 other levels you travel to throughout the game. The guns were my big dissapointment, everyone raves about the upgrade and scrap system but all I can think of is the neat stuff we had from wider variety we had in the last game like the antimaterial sniper or my favorite, the heavy assualt rifle. All the guns feel rather bland and plasticy too, but I suppose your mileage will vary depening on preference.
Most of my playtime felt like it was spent on loading. Loading between the different hub areas, through cut scenes, etc. and the story overall felt pretty meh. That big bald guy you see in the trailer? Yeah, he's a boss battle and pretty much the ONLY real boss battle in the game. Defeating him also promptly ends the game and leaves you scratching your head wondering what the hell is going on. Nothing feels conclusive like the end of Human Revolution, in fact more questions seemed to be raised than answered which leads me to the unfortunate conclusion Ubisoft cut the game ending short on purpose as sequel bait.
I will give it a few props tho in some respects. Jensen gets alot of cool new augments in this game that are much more fun to play with than in the previous game. And the core gameplay is still relatively solid; going in guns blazing or stealthily slipping by are all viable methods. However they still don't overcome my other gripes with the game, or the glaring DLC problems other reviewers have already addressed, and for that I am forced to give this game a thumbs down.

RONIN is a game that seeks to redifine what 'turn-based combat' means. Usually, when you hear the term, you think of JRPG style combat where people stand in place and rush each other to stab them with swords, chipping their mammoth HP before returning to their assigned positions and waiting for their next turn. RONIN is the opposite. It's about quick, mobile, fast-paced combat in which everyone can only take one hit. It's stylish and at its best it's brilliant.
RONIN is also a game about infiltrating buildings, Gunpoint-style. This second game is much worse than the first game, but it would be passable if it didn't use the same controls. Moving around and clicking on icons to perform moves work perfectly during the turn-based sections, but in the real-time infiltration period just turns things into a whack-a-mole. It is not always possible to 'ghost' levels, when it is it's clearly and afterthought, and even then it feels like you missed the main event of the excellent turn-based combat.
Even worse is the lockdown mechanic. If an enemy sees you, and then misses you, they'll call in a lockdown in ten seconds, unless you kill them first, or you enter their line of sight again. A lockdown will make the game slightly harder, and you only get to win a skill point at the end of a level if you fullfill three criteria, one of which is not having a lockdown called. So far so good. Except that enemies are super dumb. They will not take a single step to search you. If they see you, and you drop behind a low wall, they'll call a lockdown. If an enemy across the screen takes a short glimpse of you, they'll call in a lockdown. This means that very often during the game, instead of worrying about dying and killing enemies, I had to worry about trying to get to a small place so that a distant enemy will spot me again and cancel the lockdown. I had to do this every ten turns to stop the lockdown. I soon realized that when I screwed up and let the lockdown happen, I had a lot more fun with the game because I was focusing on dodging and countering attacks.
The game also has a very minimal story. It doesn't tell you who the protagonist is, for instance. Anyone with half a brain can figure it out in a minute; but I'm pretty certain that if this game had been released by an AAA publisher, not only would they tell you repeatedly about that, but they'd treat it as a mindblowing reveal. As it is, the story works flawlessly; just enough to give you a taste of what is happening and let you fill the huge blanks with your own imagination, if you even care to.
It's difficult not to recommend such a great game. But it's also difficult to overlook its flaws. There's even a tip in the loading screen that says it's not a stealth game, so I don't know why it goes through its motions so often if it knows it isn't one. It's like an excellent RTS game that forces you to play a race between each level, using the same controls from the RTS sections, and how you place in the race affects how much resoursces you get. Here's hoping the next game focuses more on the combat and the infiltration is reduced to a sideshow, or even completely eliminated.

chocolate Chip Cookie Dough Brownies
Ingredients:
BROWNIE LAYER:
3/4 cup (1 1/2 sticks) unsalted butter
1 1/2 cups bittersweet chocolate chips
1 cup granulated white sugar
1/2 cup packed light brown sugar
4 large eggs
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
1/2 teaspoon salt
1 cup all-purpose flour
COOKIE DOUGH:
3/4 cup (1 1/2 sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature or almost melted
3/4 cup granulated white sugar
3/4 cup packed light brown sugar
1/4 teaspoon salt
2 tablespoons milk or cream
1 1/2 teaspoons vanilla extract or vanilla bean paste
1 cup all-purpose flour
1 cup miniature chocolate chips
additional miniature chocolate chips, if desired (to garnish the top)
Directions:
Prepare the brownie layer-
1. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F. Spray a 9x9-inch pan with nonstick spray, then line with a strip of parchment paper so that it covers the bottom and comes up two sides of the pan. Spray the parchment with nonstick spray too.
2. In a microwave safe bowl (or in the top of a double boiler or pan set on top of a pan of simmering water), microwave in 30 second bursts to melt butter and chocolate chips together until all is melted and smooth. Whisk in the sugars, then whisk in the eggs, vanilla and salt. Sift flour into the bowl and stir that in too. Scrape the brownie batter into the prepared pan. Bake for 25 to 30 minutes, or until the brownie layer is cooked through (toothpick inserted into the center comes out clean). Place the pan of brownies in the refrigerator to speed up the cooling process (or cool at room temperature and add the cookie dough layer later).
Prepare the cookie dough layer:
3. In a large bowl, use an electric mixer to combine the butter, sugars and salt until soft and creamy (1 to 2 minutes). Mix in the milk and vanilla. Sprinkle in the flour and mix in until combined. Stir in the 1 cup of chocolate chips. Scoop the cookie dough onto the top of the brownies and spread onto the brownie layer. I find that it's easiest to do this if the brownie layer is chilled and firm. Wet your hands or spray them with nonstick spray and pat the cookie dough on top in a even layer. Sprinkle additional chocolate chips on top to create a nicer, visual appearance. For easy, clean cutting, chill the brownies (wrap the brownies with plastic wrap and chill until firm- 1 to 2 hours or up to 2 days).
4. Cut the brownies: Run a knife along the sides of the brownie pan and then use the parchment paper to lift the brownies from the pan and onto a cutting board. Slice the brownies with a sharp knife, wiping the knife with a paper towel between cuts. If you'd like all of your slices of brownies to look clean-cut without edges, use the knife to cut the sides of the brownies off before cutting pieces. Keep brownies slices covered and chilled until ready to serve.

Ronin in an indie turn-based semi-stealth platformer game by Tomasz Wacławek. It admittedly borrows some features from the excellent Gunpoint (I guess the physics, somewhat modified and the jump-system) but otherwise it's combat system that makes it unique - as soon as an enemy notices you, the game changes from real-time roaming into turn based combat - you see where the enemies target, indicated by red lines, and basically you want to not to end your turn on one of those lines, but to knock the enemies up then finish wish a quick stab. Sounds easy, but more than 2-3 enemies can really make hard to pull off this feat.
At the start of the gameplay I was really optimistic about the game, but with time I had less and less enthusiasm. There are really obvious problems with the game and some less noticiable ones, that need time and attention to notice.
Positives:
Negatives: Sadly a lot of thing. A LOT.
I want to mention the feature level bugs - you can make the game almost stay in one place, meaning you can kill 4-5 enemies with sword throws before you even fall as much as one floor - or when you can climb up on a building faster than the elevator even starts :)  Plus the sword throw quite funny - you can call the sword back *towards* you. If you jump and dodge it, it will fly further and can potentially kill someone. And you can repeat this.
One can have quite much fun with cheezing kills with this methods, but at the end the problems will cause the game to be more frustratingly hard, than enjoyable hard.  A last positive aspect - all of the negatives are fixable by the developer, the base features of the game are working well (excluding the clipping), so there's still a possibility that this game can erradicate all the negatives I mentioned.

The Adventures of Jimmy Neutron: Boy Genius is an American computer animated television series created by John A. Davis. It is the first spin-off to the 2001 film Jimmy Neutron: Boy Genius. It originally aired on Nickelodeon for three seasons beginning July 20, 2002, and the final episode aired on November 25, 2006. A second spin-off to the film, Planet Sheen, debuted eight years later.
The pilot, named "Runaway Rocketboy," involves Jimmy testing a rocket ship that he has invented, and later uses it when he inadvertently stumbles upon a Yolkian plot to conquer Earth. The pilot was aired in short mini episodes on Nickelodeon before the film's release, and its plot was used for the film Jimmy Neutron: Boy Genius. The pilot was later included as an extra on the "Confusion Fusion" DVD. It was originally supposed to air as a short on KaBlam!, but the show got cancelled before the episode aired.
The pilot had a few differences from the main series. In it, the clothes were different, Judy's hair was darker, the theme song was longer with a few lines that were cut later, Goddard was voiced by Kim Saxon, in lieu of Frank Welker, Carl Wheezer resembled his father, Sheen Estevez was absent and the title card had a picture in the scene, like all the other Nicktoons at the time. Also, the DNA Productions logo with their original mascot, Helix the purple cat-like creature wearing a lab coat and a bow tie, was shown.
John A. Davis created Jimmy (then named Johnny Quasar) sometime during the 1980s and wrote a script titled Runaway Rocketboy (later the name of the second pilot) which was later abandoned. He later stumbled upon the idea while moving into a new house in the early 1990s. He re-worked it as a short film titled Johnny Quasar and presented it at SIGGRAPH where he met Steve Oedekerk and worked on a television series of the short as well as the movie. Jimmy was still called Johnny Quasar before it was decided to name him Jimmy Neutron.

This is LEGO's first video game adaptation of a film series, and it's definitely not without serious aging. Unless you set up your modern graphics card to very specific settings, the game won't allow you to play in 16:9 HD without freezing up immediately. There are also frame rate issues at certain points mid-game that make you think your computer's a dinosaur.
On the other hand, you have the promising fun of the Star Wars saga combined with the ingenuity and creativity of LEGO. If you want to free Princess Leia as Dex, go ahead. If you want the satisfaction of killing Jar Jar over and over again as Darth Vader, that's your choice! When it comes to thrills and speed however, you may get frustrated with having to run half as fast as you know the character should. No force-boosts there. But the controls all work, the gagetry is fun, and the reimagined scenes from the movies have their fair share of added humor and wit. Just, good luck with your patience.

There is a difference between a
story and a
story.
After a sad story we feel catharsis. We feel like we've explored an idea, like we've walked in another person's shoes. Sure, the story didn't turn out well, but not everything in life does. We can learn from it. Sad stories serve a purpose.
A
story, on the other hand, tells us nothing we don't already know. Life sucks. Work is boring and unfulfilling. Society is cruel and unfair. Damn near nobody cares about us; they're all out to get their own. Connections we make in our lives are all the more precious for being freaking rare, and we have to treasure the few good things we have for the limited time we still have them.
After experiencing a sad story, you feel cleansed. After experiencing a depressing story, you want 1.4 hours of your life back.
Judging by my rating, in which category do you think I place this ridiculous runaround of a game?
I guess someone who's had a much easier life than mine might find a game like this eye-opening. Honestly, though, it's so far removed from reality anyway that it can't even be instructive.

It's an RPG Maker game so you already know it offers the most basic of gameplay in an .exe that hopefully works without having to change some properties. Can't say anything new about that or recommend it to people who are tired with those types of Verge RPG programs from way back. The main draw for this one is its choose-your-own-adventure story system. Unfortunately, that means it had better be written well to be worth $10. Same goes for the $5 soundtrack, which is also too boring and uninspiring to be worth it.
Gamers have a very low bar for what’s considered good writing, it seems. No achievement for shooting that first long-winded bum who kept prattling on about choice? C’mon, we were supposed to not hate that dialogue? The biggest problem with moral dilemma stories written by gamers is that it’s so obvious what the intended choice is. They all think the same. Besides, when you have the choice between “Well, I guess you’re right if you really think about it” and “Get the ♥♥♥♥ out of here, I’m not an awful person ugh,” it’s not hard to figure out which path the writer’s hoping you choose, especially since there’s always a trigger involved. Sex? Kinda sketchy. Drugs? Tools of the devil. Old people? Gotta respect ‘em. Do I steal the game dev’s money or do I leave it alone? I wonder which one results in the Game Over.
“It’s supposed to make you mad/sad so you could think about the other choices you could’ve made/consequences of your actions! That’s what we set out to do. We’re artists.” Ok.
I’m happy to see modern-day RPG Maker stuff, I really am, and I’m impressed that the team was able to make money off of it but they might wanna grab someone from the NaNoWriMo forums who’s desperate to get their grand works out there next time. Who knows, the gimmick might work. “Budding novelist hopeful teams up with indie vidya designer for passion project. Adam Sessler rises from the grave to promote it until it’s written about in Time Magazine. The medium is finally transcending!” It’s not like anyone’s expecting Walden Simulator or A Sport and a Pastime: The Game.
Or, you know, you can just ramble about fate or cry about your ex-girlfriend some more.
12/10 would whine about binary moral decisions again.

This is a tragedy. Why? Because I see an inventive and brilliant puzzle game, that is poorly presented on two fronts:
1) My new computer can run the 2016 Doom, Wolfenstien: The New Order, Metro: Last Light Redux, Dues Ex: Human Revolution, Bioshock Infinite, and so on so forth... smoothly with no problems whatsoever, near or at their graphical max.
So, if Pneuma crashes frequently and refuses to display graphics or lighting correctly (with the correct appearance occationally flashing in like a zoeatrope)... with almost nothing but static environments, well then how could I be blamed for thinking it was a problem with Pneuma, not my computer?
2) The narriation is insipid. I'm sorry. I understand what they were going for and it does not click with me. The main character's  self-praise is not entertaining past the first five minutes, and the hints of self-doubt as you play along are not convincing. At all.
I can also tell the writers were trying to make the dialoge comedic. In my humble opinion, they failed.
The lazy, armchair-philosophy is interesting if you really listen... but I was not really listening... because I was trying to play the game.
------
Otherwise is is actually an excellent puzzle game, based on line-of-sight and movement mechanics. Pretty inventive.
Too bad I won't be playing any more because it looks like dog-poo and keeps crashing. I also find the "god" quite irritating to listen to.
{EDIT} I would probably give this the recomendation if they fixed the crashing and polished the whole thing a bit. I could withstand self-indulgent psedophilosophy if my game would not crash.

10/10: A prime example of a 2d stealth action game and a whole lot of fun. Just enough to challenge without becoming frustrating, and with enough variety in techniques and mechanics to permit a variety of playstyles and approaches without becoming overcomplicated.
Mark of the Ninja is masterful in how it balances stealth with action and problem solving. Whether you're a pacifist who prioritizes lives spared or a brutal assassin, the game rewards either approach amply so long as you remain unnoticed. The incorporation of specialized costumes and a variety of attack and stealth items allow different types of players to focus on terrifying enemies, surviving attacks, and remaining unheard. Personally, I enjoyed throwing Ravenous Insects and Smoke Bombs at my enemies, but regardless of the approach you choose, there are plenty of tactics available for the player to earn enough points by the end of the level.
Storywise, the game is a bit light. Although the subject is heavy, playing heavily on vengeance and growing insanity, the scenes themselves provide a backstory that is more functional than it is deep. Little is known about the player character, save that they were willing to be tattooed using a rare ink that would grant them special powers in order to defeat those who attacked their clan and dojo. The remaining, non-playable characters are even more brief in their relevance, generally showing up only for the occasional serving of exposition. As such, by the end of the game, the meaning and importance of the players actions on the story are truly ambiguous.
However, what the game lacks in narrative it greatly makes up for in technique and visual style. Spatial logic is at a high in this game, demanding the player be aware of light, shadow, sound, and patrol patterns if they seek to traverse the level unnoticed. Even with all of these factors in play, the game rarely becomes frustrating since there are so many ways to deal with the situation. Add to that the near-instantaneous respawn at the most recent checkpoint upon failure, and it becomes very easy to just keep trying until you've overcome the challenge, providing the player with a strong sense of mastery as the game progresses.
All in all, Mark of the Ninja is a deeply satisfying game, to the point of feeling brief. Despite a straightforward narrative, it has a great balance of quality and quantity when it comes to the mechanics and challenges it provides, which makes it a premier example of what stealth action games are all about.

Mark of the Ninja isn't a very long game, but it's the type of game that encourages you to replay levels and challenges to prove your skill at the game. It offers you multiple means of approaching your objectives and for those who like stealth games, presents itself very nicely. It can be fast-paced and action-packed, or slow-and-steady. How your experience plays out depends on your playstyle.
Definitely worth picking up. The ending alone makes it worth it.

I had once heard of a legendary game called Dragon Age: Origins. It never crossed my mind at the time as I was never a fan of buying games on release due to the expensive price. However, now I am no longer naive. I have opened my eyes to this marvelous game. I have played Dragon Age: Origins.
From a story perspective, this game is great. The different openings were exciting and fun and I originally started with a warrior, human noble. The beginning for that is intense, not to spoil anything, but lets just say its quite unexpected and great. The fact that quite a few things in the story are completely connected and effect each other adds to the intrigue of the story. It is immersive, long, large, and awesome. My one critique would have to be
From a gameplay perspective, this game is awesome. I was a big fan of completely controlling the whole fight as in constantly tactical pausing and quaeing up the actions for every single character at every single tick. It really lets you have absolute control of the game. The strategies you can use are great especially with certain combos (shattering) and the boss fights were challenging even on normal difficulty. I got so used to hitting F5(quicksave) and F9(quickload) that sometimes I'd accidentally do it even after I beat an enemy. With the quicksaving and quickloading, it really allows you to formulate a strategy: who goes where, where and how I want to kite an enemy, where I want to lure and enemy, who I want to selectively aggro, etc. Movement was nice and generally not buggy except for some of the DLC. However, one of the mechanics I really and truly hated esepcially at the beginning when I wasn't used to it is the camera. Boy is the camera frustrating but once I got used to it, it wasn't as bad.
Overall, this is one of the best games I've ever played and I realized why everybody loved it.

OK, here we go!
First of all - STORY. Well, it is an excuse for racing. I am not going to go into details of it but in a nuttshell it is just as this-cutscene: "Hey you! This and that happened, you have to race in order to bla bla!" Like all the other games of this type you can not expect it to have some great story. What I am impressed by is the live action cutscenes. Maggie Q and the bunch are actually making an effort here. Don't get me wrong it is not like movie level acting but it is not like those in Most Wanted (the original one) where the acting was so bad that I cringed while watching. The Carbon actors did a good job on that game but here they took it to another level. And, c'mon, who doesn't like to see some of Maggie Q's boobs and legs (bit of Maggie Q bias here).
OK, moving on! Gameplay! Oh, man! I don't know if I should laugh or cry. Here is where I got dissapointed big time. But I am getting ahead of myself. First of all- car list, one word-AWESOME! You get American, European and Japanese cars stacked in these cathegories and each contains the best of the chategory. The list is big, I wont get into all the cars. You can look them up on-line. They handle OK but I can not shake the feeling that the cars have no mass to them. It feels like I'm driving an RC car. The movements are cartoonish and sometimes I get the fieeling that I'm playing Mario Cart. There is none of that speed feeling that I used to get in Underground 2 or in Most wanted.
NPC cars are a whole other story, they are able of quantum leap, turning 90° while going 250 kph and the worst driver in the race suddenly becomes awesome and just wizzes by you when you are just about to win. Police chases play a role in the game but not all that much. These bring their own set of surprises like Police SUVs that take on and subdue a Bugatti Veyron doing 350+ kph on a highway like it was nothing. Sometimes I got the feeling that I was playing a demolition derby rather than racing with them raming me like crazy.
The one thing that made me angry the most were bugs. And there are a lot of them in the sence that it is a marketed product that somebody made money off. Invisible walls that my car ran into, jumping off in the air in the middle of the road from some kind of an invisible ramp and the grand daddy of them all-on the last mission my car fell through the texture and fell into nothingnes. This is where i went crazy. This game is a product like any other that was marketed as a functioning one. It chrashed on me a couple of times  (I have no idea why) but when my carr did the falling down into oblivion that was it for me. I would understand that if the copy of a game was....well... obtained as a leaked product. But I payed money for it and I expect it to work properly. In the end it feels like it is a rush job. I really want to meet the guy/gal who signed off the product as a good one so I can have some words with them about false advertizing. On the plus side the game runs on a toaster so you don't have to worry about your computer being too old and weak. You should always check the system requierments before purchasing but if you bought your machine in the last 5-8 years you should be good. The last but not hte least-car customizing engine is great and specially for the visual part. Performance has the standard kind of bussiness but they really made an effort in order to give you some really good options for making your ride stand out. The world looks good. It feels like your are racing in a big city but I could not help but feel that it is a huge construction site. So many construction cranes!!!! One other thing I noticed (in the start of the game, later is lost track) that you are racing a couple of same racers, wich makes sense. In the previos games I had the feeling that the town I was racing in had like half a milion residents and every school kid and nursing home grandpa, mom and dad, dog, cat were racing.
Soundtrack- As a huge music fan (bigger than gaming) I must say that the track list is good and I discovered ome good bands while playing the game.
Dear reader! I am not a serious gamer. So this review should not influence your decision of buying the product. By all means take a look at other reviews - there are some good ones by more expirienced gamers.
My conclusion: Do I recommend the game......well....I have no idea. As I'm writing this sentence I am trying to figure out if I'll give it a thumbs up or down. There are good features of the game but I feel like they are outweight by the bad ones. If you are someone who is a casual gamer like me you might enjoy the game. But if you are a serious gamer with developed taste in games then I would not recommend it. Personally....I'll keep it installed for some more of the time so i can customize rides. :-D
I think I'm giving it a thumbs down. Sorry EA!

Except a bit slower (than UT), a lot clunkier and the maps are worse… as well as balance and weapon variety.
Recent game balancing (overall HP boost, regenerating health, nerf to skillshot instagibs) is aimed at making the game more casual-friendly to nail that anxious teen's Overwatch vibe even more.
Differing gravity is not a new feature (Facing Worlds map in UT as prime example).
It's not a game seller either, because the novelty of it (if any) fades away in half an hour time.
The only game modes (lo and behold) are two variations of “capture the point” and “deathball”.
Design is kind of COD AW or IW, nothing special there. Another futuristic shooter with exoskeleton body armor.
Characters are generic (lot of females to please SJWs). Few ripoffs from 90s and early 2000s pop culture here and there. Nothing special.
Engine based part of the game runs about fine, menus are bugged for all not US/UK users. Bug is known and not fixed for more than 2 weeks now. (Update: fixed in about 2 more weeks after release)
A mere week from the game launch online is barely alive (
).
Within a month it sunk under 300 players, even during -25% sale.
Why this game this not F2P (when objectively better Unreal Tournament is) is beyond me.

).
Enjoy.

Definitely an improvement over the Shank (the developer's previous game) in terms of gameplay variety and amount of content. And the game definitely succeeds at making you feel like a ninja with its slick stealth mechanics and multiple ways to dispatch and avoid your enemies.
On the whole though the game is just too easy - with infinite lives and generous checkpoints, many times you can just resort to trial and error gameplay rather than precision knowing there's next to no penalty for dying or playing reckless. (unless you're competing for the highest score or trying to unlock new equipment).
This is the same problem that Shank suffered from - the developer seems like it's dumbing down the difficulty in order to appeal to the casual games market.
For $7.00 I can recommend this is a casual diversion, but at $14.99 there are better, longer, and more challenging games out there.

Hi dudes and dudettes my first impression of this game was "Wtf is going on". I was constantly wondering  what the heck was happening around me, people flew across the map, shot at me from all sort of angles, warped away and I found my self in the possession of a talking ball?!
It goes to say that this game is fast paced which I found to me overwhelming in the first hour or so. But once I got the hang of it, daaamn its soo much fun to fly trough the air whilst chasing a foe and bombarding him with bullets. Or to guard a point as a two meter tall mech and just bash those puny humans into bits and pieces.
With that said, I want to give you some brief information. The game runs really well, no issues regarding connectivity, the settings meny is plentiful (as you should expect), there is however loot boxes which you can aquire through real-money purchase or as drops (similar to OW). But who cares they only offer cosmetics. There is an ingame friendslist thats simple, however I find that the chatbox needs improvements sometimes I dont even notice that someone has written. There also needs to be improvements to making the objective markers more visible (sometimes I dont even notice that Im carrying a ball or a battery).
HOWEVER the classes, just wow. They're really well balanced and offer a wide range of playstyles. Healer? Ok. Annoying harrasser? Ok. Big strong gorilla? Ok. This game has it all! Some of the classes takes a bit of practice to understand and get good at but that is to be expected.
There is also a ton of different game modes that has similarities with capture the flag and even som twisted football game (my favorite). The ball talks and it makes me laugh almost every time since the voice is soo similar to
.
I will also adress the "issue" and "similarities" toward Overwatch. There is THREE similarities:
1. Classes
2. Objectives
3. The act of killing foes
I absolutely reccomend this game and I have played it nonstop since it launched. Do you really need the skins though? Noooo, just get the game without skins and play around, its amazing! xx

After completing it long time ago, I came back and finished game once again on "New Game Plus" difficulty and once again, I was reminded how AWESOME this game still is. Though, aside from all the positive points about it, I would like to point out 2 negative points that I found about this game:
1. Rushing forward/head on: While I fully understand that this game was meant to be a "stealth" game, I really wish there was an option to finish the game in a completely different manner. You see, I am the "RUSH FORWARD!!!" type of a player and so, while the stealth gameplay is fine and all, I really wish that you can just CHARGE HEAD ON and kill everything in your path if you so desire to. The sad reality is that you can't just rush forward to kill enemies (especially if there are more than 1 enemy) and the annoying thing is that, even though you wield a sword, it is ONLY used when killing in "stealth mode" but when you attack the enemy head on, you only can "kick" him and have to do that multiple times (which can be very hard at times) until he faints and THEN you get to use your sword to finish him off (#GameLogic). This isn't a huge complain, but I really wish that you can just rush forward and kill everything swiftly/quickly if you wanted to. Oh well......
2. The ending: I didn't like the ending of this game because...... SEMI-SPOILERS..... you are "presumably" given a choice between two different endings, but BOTH ending are BAD endings in my opinion. I wish there was a GOOD ending where the Marked Ninja finds away to CURE himself from the effects of the mark. For example, what the developer could've done is, have the "Good" ending as an alternative/hidden ending and the only way to unlock it is to collect a certain item (for example, CURING HERBS) in ALL LEVELS before you reach the final chapter of the game and then, if you managed to collect all those secret curing herbs, then you are able to unlock a 3rd hidden GOOD ending where the marked Ninja lives on and carries/leads his clan to victory and survival in the modern age they live in.
Anyways, the above doesn't really affect my final score which is a 10/10 FOR SURE! Though, if there are plans for a sequel of this AWESOME game (I really hope there is one in the works), I really hope that the developer takes note of my 2 points above and keep them in mind when making a future sequel for this AWESOME ninja game! :D

When passing judgment on this game I think its important to note what this game is and what Boss Key is trying to do with it. Even if you don't enjoy playing this game it should at least deserve your respect.
I played this game a few times over the beta and got destroyed. I decided I didnt really enjoy it and deleted after a few games. The game really appeals to me and I decided to give it a second go after release. I mean, it only $30!!!!
Lawbreakers has a high skill cap and a high learning curve compared to most other shooters. It doesnt hold your hand getting into it either. Compared to other shooters that try to appeal to everyone, this games target audience are arena shooter fans. Everything happens extremely fast and a lot of times you will die without understanding how.
The more I play Lawbreakers the better I get. The better I get, the more fun I have with it. For the first few hours I did terrible. This game doesnt hide the fact that you are getting wrecked, for me I appeciate that. It drove me to question why I am doing so bad and what I can do to change that. The sharpest swords are forged by fire. After a while I started playing better and honestly have had more fun than any other FPS recently. This game is INTENSE!
It does not worry me that it has a low player count. I think this game will always have a low player count but thats not a bad thing. This is the kind of game that will have a small devoted core playerbase and with support from BOSS KEY will be around for a long time. There are plenty of kinks to work out but this game is also really young.
To summarize, get this game if you want a challanging, fast pace multiplayer FPS. I commend Boss Key for everything they accomplished with Lawbreakers. The game feels like more of a fan service than a big studio trying to make a money grab. In a time when all the other AAA studios are reaming us for our money, Boss Key does it right.

Open engagements with a dozen enemies are an exercise in patience, jumping in circles and waiting for reloads just to be able to pick off one enemy.  Even then, it's sometimes possible to be shot through a solid floor or wall.
I couldn't bring myself to play through even half of the game with these issues.  For me, Ronin is not worth buying at any price.
Overall, I would rate it a very solid 7/10. Good game indeed.

I played this game a few times over the beta and got destroyed. I decided I didnt really enjoy it and deleted after a few games. The game really appeals to me and I decided to give it a second go after release. I mean, it only $30!!!!
Lawbreakers has a high skill cap and a high learning curve compared to most other shooters. It doesnt hold your hand getting into it either. Compared to other shooters that try to appeal to everyone, this games target audience are arena shooter fans. Everything happens extremely fast and a lot of times you will die without understanding how.
The more I play Lawbreakers the better I get. The better I get, the more fun I have with it. For the first few hours I did terrible. This game doesnt hide the fact that you are getting wrecked, for me I appeciate that. It drove me to question why I am doing so bad and what I can do to change that. The sharpest swords are forged by fire. After a while I started playing better and honestly have had more fun than any other FPS recently. This game is INTENSE!
It does not worry me that it has a low player count. I think this game will always have a low player count but thats not a bad thing. This is the kind of game that will have a small devoted core playerbase and with support from BOSS KEY will be around for a long time. There are plenty of kinks to work out but this game is also really young.
To summarize, get this game if you want a challanging, fast pace multiplayer FPS. I commend Boss Key for everything they accomplished with Lawbreakers. The game feels like more of a fan service than a big studio trying to make a money grab. In a time when all the other AAA studios are reaming us for our money, Boss Key does it right.
