Ronin is a turn-based action game about a "vengeful heroine" going on a mission to kill five people who have done something to her. Your father has been killed and his death is somehow linked to five men you can see in a photograph with you and your father. As your father's only child you take it upon yourself
+Great art style which suits the game well
+The skills which you can unlock over the course of the game are really fun to use, for example you can unlock the ability to throw your sword at enemies or hang enemies from the ceiling to kill them stealthily
+Once you've got your head around the turn-based combat mechanics, combat against a small number of enemies can be quite fun. Combat mainly consists of jumping into enemies to knock them over and then stab them but it can be quite challenging when you also have several enemies shooting at you
+Stealth sections of the game are incredibly fun, especially once you've unlocked the hanging enemies skill
+Each mission has three overall objectives (admittedly they're the same across all the levels) which, when all three are completed, grant you a skill point to spend
+Great soundtrack which fits in with the game well
+/-It's locked to 30FPS, personally I'm not bothered by this but I know this is an important issue for a lot of people
+/-While the game does feature a NG+ mode as well as two different endings the game has zero replay value to me, though that may just be because I really didn't enjoy playing it
+/-If you aren't very good at the game then it's incredibly difficult to unlock more than one or two of the skills as completing all three objectives in one go is pretty challenging
-Combat against a large group of enemies in open spaces is incredibly frustrating as it's often very difficult to find an opportunity to single out an enemy and kill them
-Enemy AI detection is awful, it's possible to stand on an enemy without them noticing, it's also possible to stand on a window while someone is looking out of it without them noticing
-Despite feeling like it should be a stealth game, Ronin seems to force open combat on you as much as possible, there's not a single level that be completed without engaging in open combat and very few encounters with enemies can be completed without combat
-The jump arc the game provides you with when you're planning your next move is pretty much always inaccurate which is incredibly frustrating
-The game enters turn-based mode when you enter combat, or at least that's how it's supposed to work. The game often doesn't enter turn-based mode at the right time and it never enters turn-based mode when it's convenient for the player, such as when you can attack an enemy from a rope. Furthermore, the game often leaves turn-based mode too soon, i.e. while there are still enemies left in play
-The backstory of the game is only explained in the Deluxe Edition Digital Comic so if you own the standard edition, like I do, the game effectively has no story
-The game consists of fifteen levels only and can be completed in around four hours, the only reason my playtime is longer than that is because I spent around two hours total stuck on some of the levels
-You can only jump when you're in combat, regular movement isn't allowed, this gets incredibly frustrating when you just need to move a small distance
Verdict:
Ronin has a nice idea behind it but its weak gameplay, poor AI, short length and complete focus on action make it fall short of the mark. If you're looking for the next Gunpoint or Mark of the Ninja, look elsewhere.

I had to let it sink for a week before I sat down to write this review, because I was hoping my recollection of the experience of playing Blood Dragon would change.  It did not.  I went into Black Dragon with the presumption that it was actually a fairly different experience from the mainline Far Cry games.  What sold me was the 80s  silliness, but what I expected was a more streamlined, linear, campaign focused traditional shooter that had a 90s feel the way the whole game was made to look.  Whether this expectation was a fault on my part or not, I do not know - I suppose I am in some capacity to blame for not bothering to read its reviews, but the game's promo material and trailers sure did support that sentiment.  Instead, Blood Dragon is Far Cry 3 reskinned into an 80s action movie parody.  What works of it, mainly the humour and campaign 'story', is fairly entertaining.  What sucks about it is what sucks about Far Cry in general: A mediocre shooter with a boring open world full of checkpoints to clear, stupid side quests, weapon upgrades, enemy patrols, wildlife to kill and collectables scattered around (that make the protagonist break the fourth wall in style with "I hope I don't have to collect any ♥♥♥♥ing flags..").  Ultimately, as much as I enjoyed the setting, and even though the game did deliver on many of its promises, it wasn't what I wanted.  Basically, stay away if you dislike the Ubisoft open world experience (a-la Far Cry).  And in case you want a Far Cry experience, just buy Far Cry 3 - it's overall the better game.

RUNBOW:
~~~~~~~~

Have you heard of this femme fatale named “SATURA?” She dresses in black and looks down at you with her chilling eyes! But you can face her on your own, you debonair player. Naah - I have a better idea . . . let’s call a bunch of friends; at nine against one, I think the odds are slightly in our favour! Or, we can leave the lady alone and see which of us can reach the trophy first! Hmmm, maybe jump in the Arena for bit of a rumble. Whatever tickles your fantasy . . .  It’s RUNBOW time!
RUNBOW is platformer/local and online multi-player game which supports up to nine players in a game session.
Swinging into the main menu (boys and girls, this soundtrack is a cracker), you will be able to select one of five modes of play which includes two single player modes (but you can still have up to nine friends playing with you in these). In the Adventure mode, the goal is to reach a trophy as fast as possible under a specific time to be rewarded with three golden coins. Well, that’s nice and easy but there is a bit of twist in RUNBOW. Every few seconds a different coloured background (a palette of four to eight colours) will pass through (from left to right or from top to bottom, depending on the level) and as you move as fast as possible, you will see platforms appearing or disappearing, depending on their colours and on the colour of the background. So you will be able to jump onto a blue platform that’s on an orange background, but be sure to jump off before the blue background comes by or you will fall down the . . . AAHHHHHH! On top of that, you will have to avoid spikes, defeat strange enemies and clear 140 levels!
In The Bowhemoth, you will have to get out of the beast’s belly and beat the toughest level in the game. This is quite a challenge, to be honest.
For the local and online modes: “Get ready to RUN,” “Step into the ARENA,” and “All hail the KING OF THE HILL” are the three modes of play. Be the first one to reach the shiny silver trophy in the “RUN”. Be the last character standing in the “ARENA” or fight a fierce battle to control a single point in the “KING OF THE HILL.” On the downside, it is difficult to find an online game.
Plenty of challenges, costumes and characters to unlock including seventeen indie special guest characters.
Graphically, RUNBOW looks good and the soundtrack is absolutely marvellous! In terms of the difficulty it increases gradually throughout the adventure, difficulty from start in the Bowhemooth. I think the controls could have been better, especially if you’re trying to do a double jump with a boost (my take on the double jump + attack action), but hopefully you will master it better than I have!
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Good graphics
-	Great gameplay
-	Single player / local and online multiplayer modes
-	140 levels to clear (single player)
-	Plenty of things to unlock including 17 Indie character guests
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Can be frustrating at time (controls)
-	Not many people online
This is a great game to play with your friends, either locally or online, and it also provides a large number of single player levels.
8/10

Runbow is a 9 player party platformer action game which has some cut throat multiplayer battles. Does it race away to victory against its other competitors or gets sweeped across in its own colours, let’s find out:
Runbow tasks you with a very simple job, run and reach the end before any of your friends do while trying not to fall down or get steam rolled in the way. Each game is pretty short too, lasting a minute or two. If you die  One game that instantly came to mind while playing Runbow was Speedrunners. And it’s hard not to compare the two, both of them having similar gameplay and a similar type of target audience.
Runbow has a very interesting mechanic that keeps it different from other games. Every few seconds, a wave of colour sweeps over the screen making various objects and platforms appear and disappear according to their respective colours. This makes for a very fun and refreshing change as you have to be on the lookout for colour pause at the start of screen every time the sweep happens. It is incredibly frustrating when you jump for a platform in reach but the colour changes just in time so that you fall down to your death instead of making a perfect jump.
This mechanic is used everywhere, from the waterfalls to the lasers, with even lasers disappearing in a particular set of colours. Leave its pretty visuals aside and Runbow is a very difficult game. You will die early and quickly if you don’t observe your environment enough. Runbow needs you to stop dead in the tracks and watch how different colours change the obstacles ahead. You also have to watch out and punch and smash your teammates to get them out of the equation. This makes all the difference between winning and watching a skull sarcastically pointing out your mistakes every time you die.
While Runbow is a blast to play with friends, its solo play is very lacking from the get go. There are no bots available for playing solo which is a big dealbreaker. To make up for this, Runbow features a number of game modes including Adventure mode, where a black and white character feels a bit left out of all the fun and colours going on with the characters.
King of the hill and arena mode are reminiscent of Super Smash bros where you try to make other characters fall down from the platforms instead of running to the end. There is a lot of customization available here for the characters too where you can select their colours, hats and a plethora of other things.
All of this still feels lacking when you are playing solo. Without anyone else on the screen, Runbow’s world feels very empty since it’s not designed with that sort of gameplay in mind. The maps are somewhat randomized every time you play so it doesn’t feel as repetitive. Runbow’s pc porting has been decent. The game feels better and easier to play with a controller than with a keyboard. There is an option to change key bindings which is a godsend as it’s default key controls are the weirdest I’ve seen to date in a platformer. There are also a few bugs here and there but nothing gamebreaking.
For a game based on colours, Runbow feels a bit bland when you fire up the game for the first time. There is a drab green background and everything that is an object is made up of black. Slowly though, the game grows on you. When the colour sweep happens the colours truly pop out and give a soothing effect on the eyes.
Some parts like the waterfalls are also very well done and there are fluid animations for everything. The cutscenes are colourful and are done quite nicely. Overall, Runbow stays true to the name and provides a lot of colours in each frame.
The sound design of Runbow is excellent. From the thumping soundtrack to the taunts that your characters make, everything compliments the environment created by the visuals. There were a few audio issues here and there but I hope they will be patched soon enough.
Runbow is made to be played with friends. If you’re expecting decent soloplay then you won’t find it here. There are a lot of game modes available but none of them are built so that you can play it alone. The lack of bots is really frustrating but once your friends arrive on the couch it is a completely different experience. Runbow is like a more methodical and slower version of Speedrunners with a huge emphasis on colours and how they affect your surroundings. If you are looking for a game to play with your friends, you can give Runbow a try.

For anyone that's looking for a serious game in the same vein as the sort you'd find at a table-top RPG session, this game is pretty solid. There's some diverse characters, each with their own preferences, and there's multiple options to achieve the same goal. Character classes cover all the basics, and even within the same class there's a lot of wiggle room for getting a class 'just right'. The like/dislike features are great to help bring characters 'to life' (though, the ones that keep second-guessing me are just downright annoying), and they also tend to jabber between themselves in a manner like real people would.
However, while I do recommend this game, there are definitely others that I tend towards more. While there's a deep narrative and character interactions, I've yet to feel like my decisions have weight, like I'm really a person taking action in the world like I did with Mass Effect. I can choose whether to spare or save people, but it doesn't seem to have a lasting effect that will impact further decisions. The tactical aspects of the game are neat, but the only fights where I feel that I can have a tactical impact are ones where there are NPC fighters along with me, four people just don't have the presence like in other games (like X-Com, things change drastically depending on what sort of classes are readily available or within supporting distance). Being able to pause combat is useful and lends towards developing plans, but the reality is that the controls are somewhat difficult, and I had to mostly figure out how to do things on the fly.
Don't get me wrong, the game is solid. Graphics are good, the combat system does have its good moments more than the bad, and the story is enough that I'm confident that I'll still plod through, but I'm just admitting that it's good while not being really a game I intend to come back to...

Ok, let's forget about the controversial presentation for a second. You know where you fall on that. I want to talk a little about what was accomplished in terms of gameplay.
What Arcen set out to do was create a procedurally generated Metroidvania. What they have arrived at in the 1.207 version of the game, which for the foreseeable future is the final version, is largely successful. The game excels at its sandbox goals, offering ever evolving challenges where success feeds directly back into how powerful your character is and in some situations how dangerous the world becomes.
You can meet your goals through a surprising amount of freedom. Pure exploration, a large amount of fun mission types and fast paced platforming and combat can be pursued at your own pace and discretion. It really is quite an achievement considering everything is procedurally generated, right down to the attributes of the spells you craft with ingredients you discover or win through successful missions.

There are certain elements about games that are needed to be considered good: Appealing visual style, interesting concept, responsive gameplay, and accessibility. This game has all of those features. Unfortunately, there is a much more elusive fifth element that game designers cannot directly program: Fun. I want to love this game so badly, but unfortunately, there is just nothing compelling about it at all. Perhaps future DLC or patches can add some of that in, but for now, this could be the only video game in my library and I still probably wouldn't play it.

This follow-up to
follows the common approach for sequels to tile-based puzzle games of changing the tile shape - as the game's subtitle suggests, instead of squares, puzzles here are based on hexagons. Aside from that, the game imports pretty much all of the mechanics and tile variants from the first game - not necessarily a bad thing, but it means that the game doesn't feel quite as 'fresh' as it might otherwise.
Notably, this sequel presents a significantly tougher level of difficulty, especially when aiming for 'perfect' solutions - this is likely primarily to be the result of each move now having a greater impact (on the six adjacent hexagons, rather than four adjacent squares), so be prepared for that. Conversely, it felt to me that the trial-and-error element may have dropped slightly, though it's still definitely there to some extent and perhaps this feeling is due to my accumulated experience across the two games together. Either way, overall I'd still recommend the game to puzzle game enthusiasts as a lightweight and relaxing, yet challenging, experience.

Ronin is a turn-based action game about a "vengeful heroine" going on a mission to kill five people who have done something to her. Your father has been killed and his death is somehow linked to five men you can see in a photograph with you and your father. As your father's only child you take it upon yourself
+Great art style which suits the game well
+The skills which you can unlock over the course of the game are really fun to use, for example you can unlock the ability to throw your sword at enemies or hang enemies from the ceiling to kill them stealthily
+Once you've got your head around the turn-based combat mechanics, combat against a small number of enemies can be quite fun. Combat mainly consists of jumping into enemies to knock them over and then stab them but it can be quite challenging when you also have several enemies shooting at you
+Stealth sections of the game are incredibly fun, especially once you've unlocked the hanging enemies skill
+Each mission has three overall objectives (admittedly they're the same across all the levels) which, when all three are completed, grant you a skill point to spend
+Great soundtrack which fits in with the game well
+/-It's locked to 30FPS, personally I'm not bothered by this but I know this is an important issue for a lot of people
+/-While the game does feature a NG+ mode as well as two different endings the game has zero replay value to me, though that may just be because I really didn't enjoy playing it
+/-If you aren't very good at the game then it's incredibly difficult to unlock more than one or two of the skills as completing all three objectives in one go is pretty challenging
-Combat against a large group of enemies in open spaces is incredibly frustrating as it's often very difficult to find an opportunity to single out an enemy and kill them
-Enemy AI detection is awful, it's possible to stand on an enemy without them noticing, it's also possible to stand on a window while someone is looking out of it without them noticing
-Despite feeling like it should be a stealth game, Ronin seems to force open combat on you as much as possible, there's not a single level that be completed without engaging in open combat and very few encounters with enemies can be completed without combat
-The jump arc the game provides you with when you're planning your next move is pretty much always inaccurate which is incredibly frustrating
-The game enters turn-based mode when you enter combat, or at least that's how it's supposed to work. The game often doesn't enter turn-based mode at the right time and it never enters turn-based mode when it's convenient for the player, such as when you can attack an enemy from a rope. Furthermore, the game often leaves turn-based mode too soon, i.e. while there are still enemies left in play
-The backstory of the game is only explained in the Deluxe Edition Digital Comic so if you own the standard edition, like I do, the game effectively has no story
-The game consists of fifteen levels only and can be completed in around four hours, the only reason my playtime is longer than that is because I spent around two hours total stuck on some of the levels
-You can only jump when you're in combat, regular movement isn't allowed, this gets incredibly frustrating when you just need to move a small distance
Verdict:
Ronin has a nice idea behind it but its weak gameplay, poor AI, short length and complete focus on action make it fall short of the mark. If you're looking for the next Gunpoint or Mark of the Ninja, look elsewhere.

If you enjoyed Gunpoint and Mark of the Ninja, then Ronin may be up your alley. Having said that, this game makes sure to point out that at it's heart it is NOT a stealth game. One of the recurring objectives is kill all enemies, so a non-lethal approach will not work here.
As for the game itself, the gameplay is very reminiscent of Gunpoint; and while you usually have the ability to pause time at will, if you are spotted time will begin moving forward in one-second increments, making combat turn-based.
(Hint: With the Sword Throw and Sword Recall skill upgrades along with some fancy jumping, there's an awful lot you can do if you remain unseen. This becomes particularly helpful in New Game Plus.)
At time of writing, the game is still buggy - **OH GOD, THE BUGS!** - mainly in the form of clipping issues. Sometimes you'll jump too close to a corner and land at the wrong angle, clipping through the wall to the other side. About half the time, this will result in you needing to return to a checkpoint in order to continue the game now that you're stuck in a wall, or some other place you can't escape from without glitching your way back out again. In earlier levels/difficulty this isn't so bad, but in the more challenging levels it becomes infuriating to progress so far and then have to reset because the game decided to put you into a wall.,, Hopefully this is fixed sooner rather than later.
Treat it like a roguelike, even though it isn't one. You'll die and die again, until eventually you find a better way through a level and manage to overcome it. At first I found this immensely frustrating, but as I started to learn what the character was capable of, it became much more manageable.
The story to this game... is mostly non-existent. Which is disappointing, as the soundtrack is beautiful, the visuals are so very reminiscent of Gunpoint, and the gameplay (when it's not glitching out) is actually pretty fun.
I'm giving this a thumbs-up, but definitely wait until it's on sale before buying RONIN - at least until all the bugs are properly fixed.

I’m going to be honest with you folks. I didn’t like the game at first.
Also still not quite sure why I enjoyed it as much as I did.
Oh and be warned: This game is hard. Or easy. Depends on whether or not you’re familiar with such games and whether or not you make use of your skills.
Anyway let’s get into that stuff now shall we?
The first thing you’ll see is a picture of a little Girl with her Father and five former Associates.
The thing is the young girl, known as the RONIN, has lost her father for unknown reasons and all that’s left of him is this photo. All she knows is that his former Associates are responsible for his death so she’s now taking revenge upon those one at a time.

And that’s pretty much it. It’s you, your blade, your bike and your trusty Helmet versus those guys and a bunch of nameless cannon fodder (Weeeeeeee).
So here’s the deal. I’m pretty sure that you’ve either played or heared about
and therefore notice an incredibly strong resemblance … one could say that the whole game is a
but hold your horses!
While it has been strongly influenced by it
still manages to be rather unique in the way you have to play the game. First things first: This is not a stealth game. Just kill everybody.
In case you’re thinking that I must be kidding … I’m not. Even a hint tells you exactly that.
Your goal is to move from point A to B while murdering every enemy you see and sparing civilians at the same time Most of the time you want to stab the civilians in the face tho but sadly this isn’t part of your agenda. Bummer I know. If you manage to kill every enemy and sparing those civilians without triggering the alarm you can pat yourself on your shoulder because you’ve done a good job. Also you do get a skill point which you will need in order to run amok in a ninja-esque fashion. There’s a Decoy ability for example and, my personal favorite, a Shadow Strike which will basically teleport you to an enemy.
While you’re able to control your character with either the Keyboard or the Control Sticks, depending on your input device, either moving around or jumping from place to place you’re unable to once you’re in combat. But why you must ask? Well little Johnny it’s simple. Sit down and listen. The combat is turn based. This might sound, feel and even look weird at first but after some initial starting problems I can safely say that it’s actually quite charming and fitting.
Before you’re going into your murder frenzy you have to get around. And sadly not on your Motorcycle. In order to locate and murder those former Associates of your beloved Father you have to either move around or, just as in
, you jump from place to place and even through Windows. Hey you’re even wearing a Helmet so don’t be afraid to jump face first into those and your enemies!
There’s also a rather big part of stealth in this game, despite the hint telling you that this isn’t one. So make use of the shadows.
Once you’ve been seen and you’re in open combat you’ll have to make some decisions that will determine whether or not you will stab people in their faces or if you get shot in your face.
In the bottom left corner is your
bar which you’ll have to keep an eye on once you’ve unlocked some Skills. Every action grants you one point and a kill grants you two. It’s pretty straight forward from there.
I have to say that I do like the look of the game and I can see why this certain Art Style was chosen. While I do appreciate that I still have to say that I would have love to seen some variety. Every level and enemy looks the same. This isn’t necessarily a bad thing but it makes things dull rather quickly when you’re feeling like you’re at the same location basically the entire time.
But still like I said I like the way the game looks and it’s fitting.
It’s a shame. It truly is. I want to like the game I really, really do but … it’s mediocre at best.
The reason why I’m still recommending it is simple: It’s okay. It certainly isn’t bad nor fantastic but it’s not garbage. I’d say get it on sale if you’ve enjoyed
or if you like such type of games but it really isn’t worth it’s full price. Which is truly sad. This game could have been so much better.
Here’s to hoping that we will either get a Sequel or just some DLC which could fix a lot of it’s problems.

Pretty good game, but with some hiccups along the way. The game does a great job of telling and interesting story. It is also great how it tackles multiple subjects and can skirt the line of right/wrong with a bunch of decisions. There are multiple paths to take and multiple different things to do to reach your goal. You really get invested in your character and feel like the decisions he makes are what you chose. With all that said there are some problems. Sometimes the game only gives you cut and dry decisions, even though there should be more. Some of the things don't make sense. Like how in one part you have to have the money in a casino to pay a debt beforehand, even though it is reasonable to be able to ask for some time to go get the money or win it. Also, how a casino owner can murder someone in their casino and that is normal. Both of those are both illogical and not possible, only done to force certain things the developers wanted. Also in regards to good or bad endings, I hate how games do this. In order to get a "good" ending, you have to do this long list of irrelevant things that don't actually have an effect on the choice. How would an ex suddenly decide she doesn't like you because you stole money at a part 3 towns ago that she has no idea about. There should be multiple different ways to get a certain conclusion, not one specific set of prechosen things that you didn't know you had to do early on that seemingly didn't matter in the slightest. So i think they dropped the ball bigtime there.
Then there is dealing with money. For some reason you never make money, and it only seems like the game decided to do this to make life more unfair than it actually is. Rigging an election and you get a "city funded credit card" but it only has 200 dollars.....a mayor would pay you 2k or more for that. Also, selling a high level rock star electric guitar and only getting 200 dollars, once again doesn't make sense. Then the idea you need to eat every night and tons, it seems a little much. And suddenly out of the blue you need 5k to attend a wedding and 10k for a debt, when you literally get no money all game. Poor decision making by the game. It is dumb how there are basically 2 endings though, as the game could be much more ambiguous and allow for a multitude of changes. Also could have been more realistic as I said before. Graphics are nice, especially the level of detail, the story so far is pretty cool, gameplay all in all pretty good, you still got the old "stealth or loud" ways with many more options, the levels are somewhat smaller, but thats only an advantage, especially in the city, since you get faster from one objective to the other, overall its a slightly better version of the first one (DE-MD).

I finished my first playthrough at 44 hours in. This game is one of the most pointed social commentaries I've played and fully earns its place in the Deus Ex series. DO NOT BELIEVE THE NEGATIVE REVIEWS. THERE IS A TON OF CONTENT IN THIS GAME.
Now, I believe there may be about 14 hours of idle time where I had to leave my system on and forgot the game was running, but that's it.
This is a must buy and play game and a series that everyone with a brain should play - slowly. Take in the world that's built in this game. Explore everything. It's absolutely amazing.
If you object to the microtransaction model, get Cheat Engine and knock yourself out in singleplayer.
It took a bit of getting used to the controls and how Jensen 'moved', the flow of the game, hacking, etc, but after I had a feel for all of that it was a helluva lot of fun to navigate this game world. The loading screens were incredibly well-done, at least for fast travel.
There are two types of 'big' storylines in role playing games like this. There are the ones where the plot is told in a 'deep' manner, hopping the character along a railroad from mission to mission, and there are the ones that are told in a 'wide' manner, where the game world feels very much alive and vibrant.
This is the latter type of game. In all of the walking around town that I did, the game never once felt 'dead' to me. It was immersive. The detailing of the game world is amazing and surpasses even The Witcher 3 - which is expected, as the square mileage in MK is far less than TW3 - but my point is this:
You can blow through the main story very quickly if your goal is to 'beat' the game.
This game is best played as an exploration game with FPS elements. Be ready to do a lot of reading and a lot of pausing and listening.
Holy cow. What are you waiting for? Is this game on sale? Get it. This is absolutely amazing. You have no excuse not to play this other than apathy!
Let me repeat it one more time - don't rush the storyline. Take your time and explore. There is a LOT of game here. I'm not a completionist and I still spent 30+ hours on the base game alone.

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided (DEMD) will largely be ignored by the gaming community as having failed to live up to the expectations of its predecessors. My recommendation is made with many caveats and criticisms, but DEMD deserves more credit than it receives. Yes, the game's conclusion is not very satisfying and the game could have used additional storytelling. Yes, there are scummy practices such as microtransactions and early DLC. Yet I still recommend this game to fans of the series, gamers into strong narratives, and gamers who are invested in the 0451 genre.
Deus Ex: Mankind Divided deserves more credit than it receives for its accomplishments in the 0451 genre. In an age where mainstream games aim to be increasingly wider with "hundreds of hours" of content, DEMD takes an almost totally opposite design approach and aims for small but deep. This is to be taken in a very literal meaning as the main hub of Prague can be fully walked around in less than thirty minutes. However, nearly every building is unique with many of them occupied with NPCs who have something interesting to say. There are no sidequests asking Adam Jensen to destroy a random secluded nest of monsters or obtaining the diagrams of some antiquated weapon. Instead every side quest is nicely crafted, adding valuable lore to the world while asking very thematically relevant philosophical questions. Every minute of DEMD feels valuable in contrast to juggernaut RPGs that feature "radiant" quests.
Thematically, DEMD is more powerful than Human Revolution. The "aug lives matter" spiel with the marketing was cringy, yet the dynamic of the rich, powerful and privileged trampling over the rights of the poor and discriminated hit hard in the game. While the marketing could have used better phrasing, the intent to connect the political themes to the present reality is overall effective. DEMD is incredibly effective at making the player grow increasingly irritated with authority, as even though you play as a man who is essentially superhero, you are still heavily discriminated against with the rest of the poor and disenfranchised. You face not just mean words from the police and normal citizens, but you face what feels like dozens of security screenings that you know Adam must endure only because he is augmented. When I saw the police actively terrorize augs in the street, I broke my pacifist gameplay with ease.
DEMD nails the gameplay and the narrative, at least until the part where the narrative ends. Technically the narrative is satisfied as it is the logical conclusion of an arc established at the beginning of the game, yet it leaves players with the beginning of an even larger, more important, and frankly more interesting arc. Knowing that the publisher likely cut the game from further development at this point only increases players' frustrations. However, if you can grab this game on a sale I highly recommend giving DEMD a chance.

How many zombie murderfest games are there on Steam now? Probably enough that you don't need to worry about one that came out over 4 years ago. Burn Zombie Burn has exactly one interesting mechanic, and that's that you get a melee attack that sets zombies on fire. Every zombie currently on fire adds one to your score multiplier, and killing a burning zombie can yield better powerups. However, burning zombies move faster, hit harder, and if they burn to death award you no points. So if you want to be grandmaster of zombie murder, you have to balance setting zombies on fire against mowing them down.
Outside of that, you have a standard assortment of guns and chainsaws and bombs. There are some unique zombie types you've seen before like exploding ones and armored ones. You can trigger a special event for each level like the zombies doing the Thriller dance if you get high enough combos with a single weapon. The graphics are ugly cartoony, and the blood spray particle effect wouldn't render for me so I got black boxes every time I hit a zombie. Your character's hair looks like poop. Seriously, play something else.

Who would believe that 2D stealth game can be so fun? Mark of the Ninja does it perfectly in the genre full of action-stealth games. Firstly, the story in the game is presented with average focus. Still, story about traditions, rituals of ninja clans and treasons all that integrate into a main plot and finish nicely.
However, the gameplay is the "King". Stealth is the main element here, and considering the 2D view from the side, its very convenient to inspect every enemy, object around you or just plan your moves. Before starting a level the game lets to choose from many ninja playstyles - "paths", which allows to use the huge variety of ninja gadgets like traps or various distractions. Another interesting detail is that stealth kills require not only a press of the button, but also additional swipe of the analog stick at the same time. Actually sometimes its a problem, as this element at times fails to work and guards around spot you. Also, every stealth kill, hidden body and succesful distraction gives points and combined with nicely designed challenge rooms, creative secondary objectives add so much fun and challenge to this game.
The atmosphere and graphics are dark, as you can expect from stealth game featuring ninjas. Animations of ninja movements are very smooth with nice looking stealth kills. What I really liked is that kills are showed in slow motion, and always looks entertaining.
Sound, music is extraordinary and blends into the game very well. Voice acting is like from a good AAA game.
As of length, it takes more than 10 hours to beat and there are a new game plus, additional dlc level.
Only bigger problem is that the game freezes often, at least on my new video card.

RONIN is a game tha has a great concept but falls flat due to lack of polish and detail, in my opinion. The concept of sneaking around and going into complexes where you use great leaping, critical thinking and flexibility skills to slip or slash your way through complexes to enact revenge is an awesome idea. The game has great and a unique art style and everything has a feeling of adventure with an overtone of revenge to it. The controls are simple but very unique and can lead to moments where you really feel like an urban rogue assassin who intends on getting the job done as efficiently as possible.
HOWEVER, the game is insanely short for the price of 13 dollars (or 20 if you wanted that soundtrack and comic so badly.). It's only a good 4 hours long if you intend to just finish it and, to me, the mechnanics can get iffy quite easily. For example, on a controller, I have great reaction abiity due to being able to just press a face button to chop someone in haf the moment I crash through a window and get an edge in the fight, but using the right thumbstick to jump can easily lead to major mistakes without even meaning it due to the control being very specific on how you release the jump. On the other hand with a mouse and keyboard I can aim my jumps very well, but I have to click on buttons to do actions. Which can easily lead to me being chopped in half if I need to do an action right then. The camera always locking into a specific position every time a fight starts out does not help.
There's no real story either (in the main game anyway) You're just some Ronin who feels wronged by a group of individuals and are determined to kill each one of them. The game never explains why you want to kill them, who you are, and who these people are in general: No names, no backgrounds, nothing.
TLDR: Great concept of a game with good visuals, but there needs to be a story of some kind of this kind of deal and the mechanics need polish and possibly new functions to help make it easier to play the game. Wait for this game to go on a real sale before buying, and even then don't expect hours of gameplay.

The game was fun and I enjoyed playing it. I've gotten a tonne of play out of it and I can see some replayability if I feel like playing it again. Also, visually, the game looks good.
I got a little frustrated at the end when they introduced the
, and when I would occasionally get stuck at a checkpoint that would have me instantly spotted. But this was at the end of the story.
Mechanically, the controls are mostly good. There are instances where he'll jump when you want to change direction on a wall and small curved passages are frustrating; but it never happened often enough to be completely frustrating.
I was playing this on Linux and there were a couple of issues that I had:
In order to fix the key problem: I would need to use the steam overlay to pause the game, go back to the game (which would be in it's pause screen) and exit the game (which would fix it).

It's a poor man's SSB and is a good way to kill time, but you'll mostly be killing other players in this game unless they end up killing you.
Fights are brief and fast-paced and the simplistic controls makes for a limited number of attacks, but I can certainly testify how satisfying it is to send an enemy flying off screen to detonate in a brilliant flash of light.
There's a definite competitive element to it that can induce rage in players. Winning feels good and losing may make you want to go back for more punishment just for another shot at victory, but that's probably already a  given.
Like I said, it's a poor man's SSB. Only things that might cost you real money are the cosmetics, but the graphics don't make them worth it in my opinion.
